definition: A predefined data stream, typically originating from the keyboard or a file, that a program can read data from. It is one of the three standard I/O streams automatically available to most programs, represented by `stdin`.

definition: An instance of a class, representing a real-world entity or concept, that encapsulates data (attributes/properties) and behavior (methods/functions) into a single, self-contained unit. Objects interact with each other by sending messages or invoking methods.

definition: A blueprint or template for creating objects, defining their common structure (attributes/properties) and behavior (methods/functions). A class specifies the properties and actions that all objects of its type will possess.

title: Class (OOP)

definition: A special method in a class that is automatically called when an object of that class is created. Its primary purpose is to initialize the object's state (its fields or properties) and set up any necessary resources.

definition: The bundling of data (attributes) and methods (functions) that operate on the data into a single unit (class), along with restricting direct access to some of an object's components. definition: A mechanism where a new class (subclass or derived class) is created from an existing class (superclass or base class), allowing the new class to reuse, extend, or modify the attributes and behaviors of the existing class. title: Inheritance (OOP)

definition: The ability of an object to take on many forms, enabling objects of different classes to be treated as objects of a common type. title: Polymorphism (OOP)

definition: The process of simplifying complex reality by modeling classes based on the essential properties and behaviors required for a specific context, while hiding unnecessary details from the user. examples: A `Car` object can be driven using a `start()` method without needing to know the intricate internal mechanics of the engine.|An `abstract class Shape` defines an `abstract calculateArea()` method, forcing concrete subclasses like `Circle` and `Rectangle` to implement their specific area calculation.|Interacting with an API by calling its public methods, without needing to understand its internal implementation details.
title: Abstraction (OOP)

definition: A contract that defines a set of methods (and sometimes properties/events) that a class must implement, without providing any implementation details. It specifies what an object can do, enabling polymorphism, enforcing common behavior, and allowing for loose coupling between components.
examples: In Java/C#, `interface IShape { double CalculateArea(); }` where any class implementing `IShape` must define `CalculateArea()`.|The `Comparable` interface in Java, which any class can implement to define a natural ordering for its objects.|A `PaymentGateway` interface specifying methods like `processPayment()` and `refund()`, which different payment providers (e.g., `StripeGateway`, `PayPalGateway`) can implement.
title: Interface (Programming)

definition: A class that cannot be instantiated directly and may contain abstract methods (methods declared without an implementation) along with concrete methods and fields. examples: In Java/C#, `public abstract class Animal { public abstract void MakeSound(); public void Eat() { /* default implementation */ } }`|A `Shape` abstract class with a concrete `getColor()` method and an abstract `calculateArea()` method to be implemented by `Circle` and `Rectangle`.|A `BaseDao` (Data Access Object) abstract class providing common database connection logic, but requiring subclasses to implement specific `save()` or `find()` methods.

definition: A feature that allows a class to have multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists (different number, type, or order of parameters). examples: In Java/C#, `public int Add(int a, int b) { ... }` and `public double Add(double a, double b) { ... }`|In Python, while not explicit overloading, functions can handle different argument types or numbers using default arguments or `*args`/`**kwargs`.|A `print()` function that can accept a string, an integer, or multiple arguments.
title: Method Overloading

definition: A method that belongs to the class itself, rather than to any specific instance (object) of the class. It can be called directly on the class name without creating an object, and it cannot access instance-specific data (non-static fields or methods) because it doesn't operate on a particular object.

title: Static Method

definition: A field (variable) that belongs to the class itself, rather than to any specific instance (object) of the class. There is only one copy of a static field, shared by all instances of the class, and it can be accessed directly using the class name, making it suitable for representing class-wide data.
examples: In Java, `public static int instanceCount;` to track the total number of objects created for that class.|In C#, `public static readonly double PI = 3.14159;` which provides a constant value shared across all instances.|The `Console.Out` field in C# for standard output, accessed via the `Console` class name.

title: Static Field

definition: A programming paradigm that treats computation as the evaluation of mathematical functions and emphasizes immutability, pure functions, and higher-order functions. It seeks to avoid changing state and mutable data, leading to more predictable, testable, and concurrent-friendly code.

title: Functional Programming Paradigm

definition: A function that adheres to two main properties: given the same inputs, it will always return the same output (deterministic), and it produces no observable side effects. examples: A mathematical function: `def add(a, b): return a + b`|Calculating the square of a number: `def square(x): return x * x`|String manipulation functions like `toLowerCase()` that return a new string rather than modifying the original.

definition: The principle that once an object or data structure is created, its internal state cannot be changed. Any operation that appears to modify an immutable object will instead return a new object with the desired changes, leaving the original object untouched. examples: Strings in Java, Python, and C# are immutable; operations like `concat()` or `replace()` return new strings.|Using `const` for primitive variables in JavaScript, or marking objects as frozen.|Tuple data structures in Python, which cannot be modified after creation.

title: Immutability (Programming)

definition: A function that either takes one or more functions as arguments, or returns a function as its result, or both. They are fundamental to functional programming paradigms, enabling powerful abstractions, composition, and code reusability by treating functions as first-class citizens.
examples: The `map(function, iterable)` function in Python, which applies a function to each item of an iterable.|A decorator function that takes another function and returns a new, enhanced function.|JavaScript's `setTimeout(callbackFunction, delay)` where `callbackFunction` is passed as an argument.

definition: A concise way to define an anonymous function (a function without a name) directly at the place where it is used. definition: A programming language concept where functions are treated as first-class citizens, meaning they can be assigned to variables, passed as arguments to other functions, returned from other functions, and stored in data structures, just like any other data type (e.g., numbers or strings). definition: Any observable change to the system's state or behavior that occurs outside the local scope of a function, beyond returning a value. definition: A function that "remembers" its lexical environment (the scope in which it was declared) even after that environment has finished executing. definition: A Trie, also known as a prefix tree, is a tree-like data structure used to store a dynamic set or associative array where keys are typically strings. definition: Average-case complexity analysis determines an algorithm's resource usage (time or space) averaged over all possible inputs, assuming a probabilistic distribution of inputs. It provides a more realistic measure of performance for typical scenarios.

definition: Bubble Sort is a simple sorting algorithm that repeatedly steps through the list, compares adjacent elements, and swaps them if they are in the wrong order. The pass through the list is repeated until no swaps are needed, indicating the list is sorted.

title: Bubble Sort Algorithm

definition: Selection Sort is an in-place comparison sorting algorithm that divides the input list into two parts: a sorted sublist and the remaining unsorted sublist. It repeatedly selects the smallest (or largest) element from the unsorted sublist and moves it to the sorted sublist.

definition: Insertion Sort is a simple sorting algorithm that builds the final sorted array (or list) one item at a time. definition: Merge Sort is an efficient, comparison-based, divide and conquer sorting algorithm. It works by dividing an unsorted list into n sublists, each containing one element, then repeatedly merging sublists to produce new sorted sublists until there is only one sorted list remaining.

title: Merge Sort Algorithm

definition: Quick Sort is an efficient, in-place, comparison-based sorting algorithm that uses a divide and conquer strategy. definition: The Greedy Algorithm paradigm constructs a solution by making the locally optimal choice at each step, hoping that this choice will lead to a globally optimal solution. It typically does not revisit previous choices and makes decisions based on immediate benefit.

definition: The Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) algorithm is an efficient string-searching algorithm that finds occurrences of a 'pattern' string within a 'text' string by pre-processing the pattern to avoid redundant comparisons when a mismatch occurs.

definition: The Euclidean Algorithm is an efficient method for computing the greatest common divisor (GCD) of two integers, based on the principle that the GCD of two numbers also divides their difference, and recursively applies this until one number is zero.

definition: The Sieve of Eratosthenes is an ancient algorithm for finding all prime numbers up to a specified integer by iteratively marking as composite (i.e., not prime) the multiples of each prime, starting with 2.

definition: The Two Pointers technique is an algorithmic approach that uses two pointers (indices) to traverse a data structure, typically an array or list, from different directions or at different speeds to efficiently solve problems involving searching for pairs, subsegments, or partitioning.

definition: The Meet-in-the-Middle algorithm is an optimization technique that divides a problem into two independent subproblems, solves each subproblem, and then combines their results, often reducing the exponential time complexity from O(N^k) to O(N^(k/2)).

definition: A mathematical relation defines a connection or correspondence between elements of two or more sets, typically expressed as a set of ordered pairs where the first element belongs to the first set and the second to the second set.

definition: A branch of mathematical logic and computer science that studies what problems can be solved by algorithms (or effectively by machines) and what problems cannot. definition: The class of decision problems that can be solved by a deterministic Turing machine in polynomial time. Problems in P are generally considered 'tractable' or 'efficiently solvable' in practice.

title: P Complexity Class

definition: The class of decision problems for which a given candidate solution can be verified in polynomial time by a deterministic Turing machine. definition: A property of decision problems that are both in NP and are NP-hard. This means they are among the 'hardest' problems in NP; if any NP-complete problem can be solved in polynomial time, then all problems in NP can be solved in polynomial time (implying P=NP).
examples: The Boolean Satisfiability Problem (SAT) is the canonical NP-complete problem.|The Clique Problem, Vertex Cover, and Hamiltonian Cycle are all NP-complete.|Many combinatorial optimization problems have NP-complete decision versions.

title: NP-Completeness

definition: A property of problems that are at least as hard as any problem in NP. NP-hard problems do not necessarily have to be in NP themselves.
examples: The optimization version of the Traveling Salesperson Problem (finding the actual shortest path).|The Halting Problem is NP-hard (and also undecidable).|Many scheduling and resource allocation problems are NP-hard, indicating no known efficient solution.
title: NP-Hardness

definition: The set of all decision problems that can be solved by a Turing machine using a polynomial amount of space. PSPACE includes P, NP, and co-NP, and generally contains problems harder than NP, implying they may require exponential time but only polynomial memory.

title: PSPACE Complexity Class

definition: The set of all decision problems that can be solved by a deterministic Turing machine using a logarithmic amount of space relative to the input size. This implies that the memory usage is very restricted, allowing only a constant number of pointers into the input.

definition: A mathematical proof technique used to prove that a statement holds for all natural numbers (or more generally, for any well-ordered set). definition: The electronic circuitry within a computer that carries out the instructions of a computer program by performing the basic arithmetic, logical, control, and input/output (I/O) operations specified by the instructions. examples: Green threads in early Java Virtual Machines (JVMs).|Many-to-one mapping model where multiple user threads map to a single kernel thread.

title: User-Level Thread

definition: Threads that are directly supported and managed by the operating system kernel. The kernel performs all thread creation, scheduling, and management, making them more robust as a blocking kernel thread does not block other threads from the same process.
examples: Threads in Windows operating systems (e.g., Pthreads on Linux/Unix systems).|One-to-one mapping model where each user thread maps to a distinct kernel thread.
semantic_tags: Thread Management|Kernel Space|OS Support|Concurrency Model|System Calls
title: Kernel-Level Thread

definition: The ability of different parts of a program or system to execute independently and seemingly simultaneously, often by interleaving their execution over a single processor. It deals with managing multiple tasks that are in progress at the same time, giving the illusion of parallelism.
examples: A web browser tab downloading a file while another tab displays a webpage.|A single CPU switching rapidly between multiple running applications, giving the illusion of simultaneous execution.
title: Concurrency (OS)

definition: The ability to execute multiple tasks or parts of a task at the exact same physical time, typically on multiple CPU cores or processors. It is about actually doing many things at once, requiring hardware support for simultaneous execution.
examples: A multi-core CPU running different processes on different cores simultaneously.|Processing large datasets by distributing computation across multiple machines in a cluster.
title: Parallelism (OS)

definition: A condition where the outcome of multiple threads or processes accessing and modifying shared data depends on the unpredictable relative timing of their execution. It occurs when multiple operations try to affect the same state without proper synchronization, potentially leading to data corruption or unexpected results.
examples: Two threads incrementing a shared counter variable without a lock, potentially leading to a wrong final count.|Multiple users attempting to withdraw from the same bank account simultaneously, resulting in an incorrect balance if not synchronized.
title: Race Condition

definition: A segment of code within a concurrent program that accesses shared resources or data that must not be concurrently accessed by more than one thread or process. Entry to and exit from a critical section must be guarded by synchronization mechanisms to prevent race conditions.
examples: The code block that modifies a shared linked list.|The code that writes to a shared log file.|A `synchronized` block in Java or a `lock` statement in C#.
title: Critical Section

definition: A synchronization primitive that restricts access to a shared resource or critical section to only one thread or process at a time. A thread acquires the lock before entering the critical section and releases it upon exiting, thereby ensuring mutual exclusion.
examples: A `std::mutex` in C++ or `threading.Lock` in Python protecting a shared data structure.|A database record lock preventing multiple transactions from modifying the same record simultaneously.
semantic_tags: Mutual Exclusion|Synchronization Primitive|Critical Section|Shared Resource|Concurrency Control
title: Lock (Synchronization)

definition: A synchronization primitive specifically designed for mutual exclusion, ensuring that only one thread can acquire the lock (or 'own the mutex') at any given time. It is essentially a binary semaphore (value 0 or 1) often used to protect critical sections.
examples: Using `pthread_mutex_t` in C/C++ to protect a global variable.|A `threading.Lock` in Python acting as a mutex for a shared resource.
semantic_tags: Mutual Exclusion|Synchronization Primitive|Binary Semaphore|Critical Section|Thread Safety
title: Mutex (Synchronization)

definition: A synchronization primitive that is a non-negative integer variable used to control access to a common resource by multiple processes or threads. It supports two atomic operations, `wait` (or `P` or `acquire`) and `signal` (or `V` or `release`), to manage a counter that represents available resources.
examples: A counting semaphore initialized to 5 to limit simultaneous access to 5 identical printers.|A binary semaphore (value 0 or 1) used as a mutex to protect a critical section.
title: Semaphore (Synchronization)

definition: A high-level synchronization construct that encapsulates shared data and the procedures that operate on that data, ensuring only one process or thread can be active within the monitor at any given time. It simplifies concurrent programming by automatically handling mutual exclusion and providing condition variables for more complex synchronization.
examples: Java's `synchronized` keyword and `wait()`, `notify()`, `notifyAll()` methods on objects, which together form a monitor-like mechanism.|Concurrent collections like `ConcurrentHashMap` often use internal monitor-like logic for thread safety.
title: Monitor (Synchronization)

definition: A situation in a multi-process or multi-thread system where two or more processes are permanently blocked because each is waiting for the other to release a resource. Deadlocks occur when four conditions are simultaneously met: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait.
examples: Process A holds Resource X and waits for Resource Y, while Process B holds Resource Y and waits for Resource X.|Two trains approaching each other on a single track, both waiting for the other to move.
semantic_tags: Concurrency Issue|Resource Starvation|System Blockage|Synchronization Problem|Circular Wait
title: Deadlock (OS)

definition: A strategy for preventing deadlocks by dynamically analyzing resource-allocation requests to ensure that the system always remains in a 'safe state.' The Banker's Algorithm, a prominent example, checks if granting a resource request would lead to an unsafe state where a deadlock could eventually occur, and only grants the request if the state remains safe.
examples: An operating system evaluating a new memory allocation request to ensure it doesn't lead to a state where future requests cannot be satisfied.|A resource manager using the algorithm to decide whether to grant a printer to a process, checking if all processes can eventually complete.
semantic_tags: Deadlock Prevention|Resource Management|Safe State|Banker's Algorithm|Dynamic Allocation|System Safety
title: Deadlock Avoidance (Banker's Algorithm)

definition: A strategy for handling deadlocks by allowing the system to enter a deadlocked state, then periodically running an algorithm to identify deadlocked processes and resolve the situation. Once detected, the system typically recovers by preempting resources or terminating one or more processes involved in the deadlock.
examples: An operating system periodically constructing a resource-allocation graph to check for cycles, indicating a deadlock.|A database system identifying transactions that are stuck in a deadlock and rolling back one or more of them.
title: Deadlock Detection

definition: The process of determining which process or thread will execute on the CPU next, and for how long, from the set of ready-to-run processes. Its primary goal is to maximize CPU utilization, throughput, and minimize turnaround time, waiting time, and response time.
examples: The Linux scheduler deciding which process gets CPU time after a time slice expires.|Multitasking operating systems using scheduling algorithms to switch between user applications.
semantic_tags: Operating System|Process Management|Resource Allocation|Context Switch|Performance Optimization|Time Sharing
title: CPU Scheduling

definition: A non-preemptive CPU scheduling algorithm where processes are executed strictly in the order they arrive in the ready queue. It is simple to implement but can lead to long waiting times if a long process arrives before several short ones, a phenomenon known as the convoy effect.
examples: A queue at a single-lane toll booth where cars are processed strictly in the order they arrive.|Jobs processed by an old-fashioned batch processing system in the exact order of submission.
title: First-Come, First-Served Scheduling

definition: A CPU scheduling algorithm that selects the process with the smallest estimated execution time to be executed next. It aims to minimize the average waiting time and average turnaround time for a given set of processes but requires accurate prediction of future CPU burst times.
examples: A printer queue prioritizing smaller print jobs to complete them faster.|A custom scheduler in a high-performance computing environment prioritizing short computation tasks.
title: Shortest Job Next Scheduling

definition: A CPU scheduling algorithm where each process is assigned a priority, and the CPU is allocated to the process with the highest priority. It can be preemptive (where a high-priority process can interrupt a low-priority one) or non-preemptive, but it commonly suffers from the potential issue of starvation for low-priority processes.
examples: Operating systems prioritizing interactive processes (e.g., UI updates) over background batch jobs.|An embedded system giving higher priority to safety-critical tasks (e.g., airbag deployment) over diagnostic logging.
title: Priority Scheduling

definition: A CPU scheduling algorithm where each process is assigned a fixed time unit (quantum) in a cyclic queue. Processes are executed in turns, and if a process does not complete within its quantum, it is preempted and added to the end of the queue.
examples: Operating systems scheduling multiple user applications (e.g., web browser, text editor, music player) to share CPU time.|Network routers scheduling packets from different data streams.|Timesharing systems allocating slices of CPU time fairly among active users.
title: Round Robin Scheduling

definition: A set of mechanisms that allow independent processes to communicate and synchronize their actions, share data, or coordinate execution. IPC is crucial for building multi-process applications and operating systems.
examples: A web server process sending data to a separate log analysis process.|A GUI application communicating with a background computation process.|Using pipes to chain commands in a Unix shell (e.g., `ls | grep .txt`).
title: Inter-Process Communication (IPC)

definition: An IPC mechanism where multiple processes can access the same region of physical memory. This allows for very fast data exchange as processes don't need to copy data through the kernel, but requires careful synchronization to prevent race conditions.
examples: A database management system sharing data buffers between different client connection processes.|High-performance computing applications where processes need to rapidly exchange large datasets.|Using POSIX shared memory APIs (`shm_open`, `mmap`) in C/C++ to create a shared buffer.
title: Shared Memory (IPC)

definition: An IPC mechanism where processes communicate by sending and receiving messages. This method simplifies synchronization as messages are typically sent and received atomically, but involves copying data, which can be slower than shared memory.
examples: Using sockets for network communication between client and server processes.|Erlang processes communicating via immutable messages.|Using message queues (e.g., POSIX message queues) to exchange structured data between processes.
title: Message Passing (IPC)

definition: A unidirectional or bidirectional communication channel used for IPC, typically between related processes (e.g., parent-child). Data written to one end of the pipe can be read from the other, acting as a FIFO (First-In, First-Out) buffer.
examples: Chaining commands in a Unix/Linux shell: `ls -l | grep .txt | sort`.|A parent process spawning a child process and using a pipe to send configuration data.|Named pipes (FIFOs) allowing unrelated processes to communicate on the same machine.
title: Pipe (IPC)

definition: An endpoint for communication between processes, often across a network but also locally (Unix domain sockets). Sockets provide a flexible interface for sending and receiving data streams or datagrams, making them fundamental for client-server architectures.
examples: A web browser (client) communicating with a web server over HTTP using TCP sockets.|A chat application sending messages between users across the internet.|Unix domain sockets for high-performance IPC between processes on the same machine without network overhead.
title: Socket (IPC)

definition: A method and data structure that an operating system uses to control how data is stored and retrieved on storage devices. It organizes data into files and directories, providing a logical view to users while managing physical storage allocation.
examples: FAT32, NTFS (Windows), ext4 (Linux), APFS (macOS) are common file systems.|Saving a document to a specific folder on a hard drive.|Listing files in a directory using `ls` or `dir` commands.
title: File System (OS)

definition: A data structure in Unix-like file systems that stores metadata about a file or directory, such as its permissions, owner, timestamps, and pointers to the disk blocks where its data is stored. Each file system object has a unique inode number.
examples: Using `ls -i` command to view the inode number of files in a directory.|A hard link to a file points to the same inode as the original file, while a symbolic link points to a file name.|The `stat()` system call retrieves inode information about a file.
title: Inode

definition: A special type of file in a file system that contains a list of references to other files and directories. It provides a hierarchical structure for organizing files, enabling users and applications to locate data efficiently.
examples: The `C:\Users\username\Documents` folder in Windows.|The `/home/user/projects` directory in Linux.|Creating a new directory with `mkdir` or navigating between directories with `cd`.
title: Directory (OS)

definition: A layer within the operating system kernel that provides a common interface for different file systems. VFS allows applications to access files on various file system types (e.g., ext4, NTFS, network file systems) using the same set of system calls, abstracting away underlying implementation details.
examples: Linux kernel's VFS allows a user to access files on an ext4 partition, an NTFS partition, and an NFS mount using identical `open()`, `read()`, `write()` system calls.|Mounting a USB drive with a FAT32 file system alongside an internal drive with APFS on macOS.|The ability for programs to treat devices like `/dev/null` or `/proc` entries as if they were regular files.
title: Virtual File System (VFS)

definition: Any piece of computer hardware that allows data to be entered into a computer (input) or delivered out of a computer (output). I/O devices are essential for interaction between users and the system, and for data persistence.
examples: Input devices: Keyboard, mouse, microphone, webcam.|Output devices: Monitor, printer, speakers.|Both input/output: Hard drive, network card, touch screen.
title: Input/Output (I/O) Device

definition: A specific type of software that enables an operating system to interact with a particular hardware device. It translates generic I/O requests from the OS into device-specific commands and manages the device's operations, making the hardware accessible to applications.
examples: Printer drivers allowing an OS to send print jobs to a specific printer model.|Graphics card drivers enabling the OS to utilize the GPU for rendering.|USB drivers managing communication with connected USB devices like flash drives or external hard drives.
title: Device Driver

definition: A signal generated by a hardware device to the CPU, indicating that an event has occurred and requires immediate attention. Upon receiving an interrupt, the CPU pauses its current task, saves its state, and executes a specific interrupt handler routine.
examples: A keyboard press generating an interrupt to signal input.|A disk controller generating an interrupt when data transfer is complete.|A network card generating an interrupt when a packet arrives, prompting the OS to process it.
title: Hardware Interrupt

definition: A programmatic way for a computer program to request a service from the operating system kernel. System calls provide an interface between user-level applications and the kernel, allowing access to hardware resources or protected functionalities like file I/O, process creation, or network communication.
examples: `open()`, `read()`, `write()` for file operations in C/C++.|`fork()` or `exec()` for process management in Unix-like systems.|`socket()` for creating a network communication endpoint.
title: System Call

definition: A privileged execution mode of a CPU where the operating system kernel has unrestricted access to all hardware resources and memory. In this mode, the kernel can execute any instruction and directly manage system resources.
examples: The OS kernel executing a device driver to interact with hardware.|Handling hardware interrupts and executing interrupt service routines.|Performing a context switch between processes, manipulating process control blocks.
title: Kernel Mode

definition: A non-privileged execution mode of a CPU where application programs run. In user mode, programs have restricted access to hardware and memory, relying on system calls to request services from the operating system kernel for privileged operations.
examples: A web browser executing JavaScript code.|A text editor processing user input and saving a document.|Any user application running without crashing the entire system due to restricted resource access.
title: User Mode

definition: The process by which a CPU saves the state (context) of one process or thread and restores the state of another process or thread. This allows multiple processes or threads to share a single CPU, enabling multitasking and concurrent execution.
examples: When an operating system switches from one running application to another after a time quantum expires.|Handling an interrupt, where the CPU saves the current process's state before executing the interrupt handler.|A process making a blocking system call, causing the OS to schedule another process.
title: Context Switch

definition: The process of starting up a computer system, from the initial power-on state to the loading and execution of the operating system. It involves a sequence of small, self-executing programs, each loading the next and more complex component, until the full OS kernel is running.
examples: BIOS/UEFI firmware initializing hardware, then loading the boot loader from a disk.|The boot loader (e.g., GRUB) loading the operating system kernel into memory.|The kernel then initializing devices and launching the first user-space process (e.g., `init` or `systemd`).
title: Bootstrapping

definition: A mechanism used by some computer architectures (like x86) to enforce security and fault tolerance by organizing privileges into hierarchical levels or rings. Code running in an inner ring (lower number) has more privileges than code in an outer ring (higher number), typically with the kernel at the innermost ring.
examples: Ring 0: Operating system kernel, device drivers, having direct hardware access.|Ring 3: User applications, which are restricted from direct hardware access.|Attempts by user-mode code (Ring 3) to execute privileged instructions (Ring 0) result in a trap or fault, preventing system instability.
title: Protection Ring

definition: The Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model is a conceptual framework that standardizes the functions of a telecommunication or computing system into seven distinct layers. Each layer performs specific tasks and communicates with the layers directly above and below it, facilitating interoperability and modular design.
examples: Layer 1 (Physical): Ethernet cables, Wi-Fi radio waves, fiber optics for transmitting raw bits.|Layer 4 (Transport): TCP and UDP protocols ensuring reliable or unreliable end-to-end communication for applications.|Layer 7 (Application): HTTP, SMTP, FTP protocols used by user applications like web browsers or email clients.
title: OSI Model

definition: The top-most layer of the OSI model, providing network services directly to end-user applications. It enables users to interact with the network through software applications, handling high-level protocol details.
examples: HTTP for web browsing|FTP for file transfer|SMTP for email
title: Application Layer (OSI)

definition: The sixth layer of the OSI model, responsible for data translation, encryption, compression, and formatting to ensure data is presented in a readable format for the Application Layer. It handles the syntax and semantics of information exchanged between application processes.
examples: ASCII and EBCDIC conversions|JPEG and MPEG data formats|SSL/TLS encryption
title: Presentation Layer (OSI)

definition: The fifth layer of the OSI model, responsible for establishing, managing, and terminating communication sessions between applications. It synchronizes communication and manages dialogue control, allowing for full-duplex, half-duplex, or simplex operations.
examples: NetBIOS for session management|RPC (Remote Procedure Call)|SQL communication sessions
title: Session Layer (OSI)

definition: The fourth layer of the OSI model, providing end-to-end communication services, including segmentation, reassembly, error checking, and flow control. It ensures reliable and ordered delivery of data between processes on source and destination hosts.
examples: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)|UDP (User Datagram Protocol)|Port numbers for process identification
title: Transport Layer (OSI)

definition: The third layer of the OSI model, responsible for logical addressing, routing, and forwarding packets across different networks. It determines the best path for data to travel from the source to the destination host, facilitating internetworking.
examples: IP (Internet Protocol) for logical addressing|Routers forwarding packets based on IP addresses|ICMP for error reporting
title: Network Layer (OSI)

definition: The second layer of the OSI model, responsible for node-to-node data transfer, error detection, and error correction from the physical layer. It manages access to the physical medium using MAC addresses and frames data for transmission.
examples: Ethernet (IEEE 802.3)|Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11)|MAC addresses for hardware identification
semantic_tags: OSI Model|MAC Addressing|Error Detection|Node-to-Node|Framing|Media Access Control
title: Data Link Layer (OSI)

definition: The lowest layer of the OSI model, responsible for the physical transmission of raw data bits over a communication medium. It defines hardware specifications, cabling, connectors, and signaling methods for sending and receiving data.
examples: Ethernet cables (Cat 5e, Cat 6)|Fiber optics for light signals|RJ45 connectors and electrical signals
title: Physical Layer (OSI)

definition: A four-layer conceptual model for network communication that largely replaced the OSI model in practical internet usage. It defines how data should be packetized, addressed, transmitted, routed, and received over a network, forming the foundation of the internet.
examples: Internet communication standards|Web browsing (HTTP over TCP/IP)|Email (SMTP over TCP/IP)
title: TCP/IP Model

definition: The top layer of the TCP/IP model, responsible for providing high-level protocols for specific applications and user processes. It combines the functions of the OSI Application, Presentation, and Session layers, enabling user interaction with network services.
examples: HTTP for web traffic|FTP for file transfers|SMTP for email, DNS for name resolution
semantic_tags: TCP/IP Model|High-Level Protocols|Application Services|User Interaction|Data Exchange
title: Application Layer (TCP/IP)

definition: The second layer of the TCP/IP model, responsible for end-to-end communication between processes on different hosts. It provides segmentation, reassembly, multiplexing, and flow control, using either TCP for reliability or UDP for speed.
examples: TCP for web browsing (reliable connection)|UDP for video streaming (fast, connectionless)|Port numbers to identify applications
title: Transport Layer (TCP/IP)

definition: The third layer of the TCP/IP model, responsible for logical addressing and routing data packets across different networks. It handles the 'internetworking' aspect by using IP addresses to deliver packets to the correct destination network and host.
examples: IPv4 and IPv6 for logical addressing|Routers using IP addresses to forward packets|Packet fragmentation and reassembly
title: Internet Layer (TCP/IP)

definition: The lowest layer of the TCP/IP model, responsible for the physical transmission of data and network access control. It combines the functions of the OSI Data Link and Physical layers, dealing with hardware addresses and medium access control.
examples: Ethernet and Wi-Fi technologies|MAC addresses for hardware identification|Network Interface Cards (NICs)
semantic_tags: TCP/IP Model|Physical Transmission|Data Link|MAC Addressing|Hardware|Network Interface
title: Network Access Layer (TCP/IP)

definition: A 32-bit numerical label assigned to devices connected to a computer network that uses the Internet Protocol for communication. It is typically represented in dot-decimal notation, such as 192.168.1.1, and allows for approximately 4.3 billion unique addresses.
examples: `192.168.1.1` (a common private IP)|`8.8.8.8` (Google's public DNS server)|`10.0.0.1` (another private IP range)
title: IPv4 Addressing

definition: A 128-bit numerical label designed to replace IPv4, providing a vastly larger address space to accommodate the growing number of internet-connected devices. It is typically represented in hexadecimal notation with colons, allowing for approximately 3.4 x 10^38 unique addresses.
examples: `2001:0db8:85a3::8a2e:0370:7334` (abbreviated form)|`fe80::1` (a link-local address)|`::1` (the loopback address, equivalent to 127.0.0.1 in IPv4)
title: IPv6 Addressing

definition: The process of dividing a large IP network into smaller, more efficient subnetworks (subnets). This improves network performance by reducing broadcast traffic, enhances security through network segmentation, and helps manage IP address allocation more effectively within an organization.
examples: Dividing a Class C network (e.g., 192.168.1.0/24) into multiple /27 subnets.|Using a subnet mask like 255.255.255.224 to define smaller network segments.|Allocating specific IP ranges to different departments like Marketing (192.168.1.32/27) and HR (192.168.1.64/27).
title: Subnetting

definition: A 16-bit number used by the Transport Layer protocols (TCP and UDP) to identify specific application processes running on a host. It allows multiple applications to share a single IP address and ensures that data packets are delivered to the correct service or program.
examples: Port 80 for HTTP web traffic|Port 443 for HTTPS secure web traffic|Port 22 for SSH remote access, Port 25 for SMTP email sending
title: Port Number (Networking)

definition: A connection-oriented, reliable, and ordered transport layer protocol that ensures data is delivered accurately and completely between applications. It uses mechanisms like sequencing, acknowledgements, flow control, and congestion control to guarantee delivery.
examples: Web browsing using HTTP/HTTPS|Email communication via SMTP, POP3, IMAP|File Transfer Protocol (FTP) for reliable file exchange
title: Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)

definition: A connectionless and unreliable transport layer protocol that prioritizes speed and low overhead over guaranteed delivery. It sends datagrams without establishing a prior connection or ensuring receipt, making it suitable for applications where occasional data loss is acceptable.
examples: DNS queries for domain name resolution|Video and audio streaming services|Online multiplayer gaming, VoIP (Voice over IP)
title: User Datagram Protocol (UDP)

definition: Hypertext Transfer Protocol, an application-layer protocol for transmitting hypermedia documents, such as HTML. It is the foundation of data communication for the World Wide Web, operating as a stateless request-response protocol between a client and a server.
examples: A web browser requesting a webpage like `www.example.com`|REST APIs using HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE)|Loading images and scripts embedded in a webpage
title: HTTP Protocol

definition: Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure, an extension of HTTP that adds a layer of security through SSL/TLS encryption. It encrypts the communication between a client and server, protecting data from eavesdropping, tampering, and ensuring data integrity and authentication.
examples: Online banking websites and e-commerce sites (`https://bank.com`)|Secure login pages for email or social media|Any website displaying a padlock icon in the browser address bar
title: HTTPS Protocol

definition: A standard network protocol used for transferring computer files between a client and server on a computer network. It operates on a client-server model, utilizing separate control and data connections between the client and the server.
examples: Uploading a website's files to a web server using an FTP client like FileZilla.|Downloading large software updates from a public FTP server.|A developer using `ftp user@host` command-line tool to manage remote files.
title: FTP Protocol

definition: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol is a communication protocol for electronic mail transmission across Internet Protocol (IP) networks. It handles the sending of emails from a client to a server, and between mail servers.
examples: An email client like Outlook sending an email through an outgoing mail server.|Gmail's servers communicating with Yahoo's servers to deliver an email.|A web application using an SMTP library to send transactional emails (e.g., password resets).
title: SMTP Protocol

definition: A hierarchical and decentralized naming system for computers, services, or other resources connected to the Internet or a private network. It translates human-readable domain names (like `google.com`) into numerical IP addresses (like `172.217.160.142`).
examples: Typing `www.example.com` into a browser, and DNS translating it to an IP address to find the server.|Configuring a custom domain name for a web application hosted on a cloud provider.|Using `nslookup` or `dig` commands to query DNS records.
semantic_tags: domain names|IP address resolution|naming system|network service|hostname
title: DNS (Domain Name System)

definition: A method of establishing network connections and sending/receiving data between two processes, potentially on different machines, over a network. It uses network sockets, which are endpoints of a two-way communication link.
examples: Building a simple chat application where clients connect to a server to exchange messages.|Developing a network service that listens on a specific port for incoming client connections.|Using Python's `socket` module to create a TCP server and client.
title: Socket Programming

definition: A distributed application architecture that partitions tasks or workloads between the providers of a resource or service, called servers, and service requesters, called clients. Clients initiate communication, and servers await requests from clients.
examples: A web browser (client) requesting a webpage from a web server.|An email client connecting to an email server to fetch messages.|A gaming console (client) connecting to a game server for online multiplayer.
title: Client-Server Architecture

definition: A decentralized communication model where each participating computer, or "peer," has equivalent capabilities and can function as both a client and a server. Peers directly share resources and services with each other without a central server.
examples: File-sharing networks like BitTorrent, where users directly exchange file segments.|Cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin, where nodes validate transactions and maintain the blockchain collectively.|Some online gaming networks where players connect directly to each other without a dedicated game server.
title: Peer-to-Peer Architecture

definition: A networking device that forwards data packets between computer networks, connecting disparate networks. It inspects the destination IP address of incoming packets and uses routing tables to determine the best path for forwarding them.
examples: Your home Wi-Fi router connecting your local network to the internet.|Enterprise routers directing traffic between different departments' networks within a large company.|Core routers on the internet backbone directing traffic across continents.
title: Router (Networking Device)

definition: A networking device that connects multiple devices (like computers, printers, servers) within a local area network (LAN). It operates at the data link layer (Layer 2) of the OSI model, forwarding data frames only to the specific port connected to the destination MAC address.
examples: Connecting multiple desktop computers in an office to a shared network and the internet.|A server rack where several servers are plugged into a switch for internal communication and external access.|An unmanaged switch used to expand the number of wired network ports in a home.
semantic_tags: network device|LAN|data link layer|MAC address|frame forwarding
title: Switch (Networking Device)

definition: A network security system that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing network traffic based on predetermined security rules. It establishes a barrier between a trusted internal network and untrusted external networks, such as the internet.
examples: A software firewall on your laptop blocking suspicious outbound connections.|An enterprise hardware firewall protecting a company's internal servers from external attacks.|Configuring a firewall to allow only specific ports (e.g., port 80 for HTTP, port 443 for HTTPS) to be accessible from the outside.
semantic_tags: network security|traffic filtering|access control|network protection|cyber security
title: Firewall (Networking Security)

definition: Media Access Control address is a unique identifier assigned to a network interface controller (NIC) for communications at the data link layer of a network segment. It's a hardware address, typically burned into the device's firmware by the manufacturer.
examples: The `00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E` address assigned to your computer's Ethernet port.|A network switch using MAC addresses to learn which device is connected to which port.|Wireless access points using MAC addresses for access control filtering.
semantic_tags: hardware address|data link layer|network interface|unique identifier|Ethernet
title: MAC Address

definition: A communication protocol used for discovering the hardware address (MAC address) associated with a given Internet Protocol (IP) address on a local network segment. It enables IP packets to be encapsulated in data link layer frames for transmission.
examples: A computer needing to send an IP packet to another device on the same LAN, using ARP to find its MAC address.|An operating system's ARP cache storing recently resolved IP-to-MAC mappings to speed up communication.|Using the `arp -a` command to view the ARP cache on a Windows or Linux machine.
semantic_tags: IP to MAC mapping|network protocol|data link layer|local network|address resolution
title: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol)

definition: A network management protocol used on IP networks for automatically assigning IP addresses and other communication parameters to devices connected to the network. It simplifies network administration by eliminating the need for manual IP configuration.
examples: A new device connecting to a Wi-Fi network automatically receiving an IP address, subnet mask, and DNS server information.|A DHCP server managing a pool of available IP addresses and leasing them to client devices.|Releasing and renewing an IP address on a computer using `ipconfig /release` and `ipconfig /renew` commands.
semantic_tags: IP address assignment|network configuration|network protocol|automation|IP management
title: DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol)

definition: A small unit of data sent over a network, formatted according to specific network protocols. Packets contain not only a portion of the actual data but also control information such as source and destination addresses, error detection codes, and sequencing information.
examples: An HTTP request broken down into multiple IP packets sent from your browser to a web server.|Voice data in a VoIP call being transmitted as a continuous stream of small UDP packets.|Analyzing network traffic with a tool like Wireshark to inspect the contents of individual packets.
title: Network Packet

definition: The time delay between a cause and effect in a network system, typically measured as the time it takes for a data packet to travel from its source to its destination. High latency indicates a longer delay, impacting real-time applications.
examples: Experiencing a noticeable delay between clicking a link and a webpage loading, often due to high latency.|A gamer complaining about "lag" in an online game, which is a direct consequence of high network latency.|Using the `ping` command to measure the round-trip time (RTT) to a server.
title: Network Latency

definition: The maximum rate of data transfer across a given path in a network, typically measured in bits per second (bps). It represents the capacity of a communication channel to carry data, not the speed at which data actually travels.
examples: An internet service provider advertising a "100 Mbps" broadband connection, indicating its bandwidth capacity.|Downloading a large file faster on a network with higher available bandwidth.|Streaming 4K video requiring significantly more network bandwidth than standard definition video.

title: Network Bandwidth

definition: The arrangement of the elements (links, nodes, etc.) of a communication network. It describes how devices are physically or logically connected to each other, influencing network performance, reliability, and cost.
examples: A "star topology" where all devices connect to a central hub or switch.|A "mesh topology" where every device is connected to every other device, providing high redundancy.|Designing a new office network by choosing between bus, ring, star, or mesh topologies based on needs.

definition: A server application that acts as an intermediary for requests from clients seeking resources from other servers. It can be used for various purposes like enhancing security, caching web pages, logging traffic, or bypassing geo-restrictions.
examples: A company's proxy server filtering web content and logging employee internet usage.|Using a residential proxy to access region-restricted streaming content.|A web browser configured to route all its traffic through a SOCKS proxy.
title: Proxy Server

definition: A device or software that distributes network traffic efficiently across multiple backend servers to ensure high availability and reliability. It improves resource utilization, maximizes throughput, and prevents any single server from becoming a bottleneck.
examples: Directing incoming web requests to one of several identical web servers in a server farm.|Distributing database query traffic among multiple database replicas to improve response times.|Using NGINX or HAProxy as software load balancers for a microservices application.
title: Load Balancer

definition: A structured data entity in a relational database that organizes data into rows and columns. Each column represents an attribute or field, and each row represents a single record or entry, ensuring data is logically organized and easily retrievable.
examples: A `Users` table with columns like `UserID`, `FirstName`, `LastName`, `Email`.|A `Products` table storing `ProductID`, `Name`, `Price`, and `Description`.|Creating a new table in SQL using `CREATE TABLE Orders (...)`.
title: Database Table

definition: A single, complete entry of related data within a database table, representing a specific instance of the entity the table describes. Each row contains a value for every column defined in the table's schema.
examples: In a `Users` table, a row representing a single user: `(1, 'Alice', 'Smith', 'alice@example.com')`.|A specific product entry in a `Products` table: `(101, 'Laptop', 1200.00, 'Powerful 15-inch laptop')`.|Inserting a new record into a table using `INSERT INTO Customers VALUES (...)`.
title: Database Row (Record)

definition: A fundamental component of a database table, representing a specific attribute or piece of information for each record. All entries in a column typically share the same data type.
examples: In a `Customers` table, 'FirstName', 'LastName', and 'Email' are columns.|A column named `ProductID` in a `Products` table would store unique identifiers for products.
title: Database Column (Field)

definition: A special column or set of columns in a database table that uniquely identifies each record (row) in that table. It must contain unique values for each row and cannot contain NULL values, ensuring data integrity.
examples: `CustomerID` in a `Customers` table.|`ISBN` in a `Books` table.|A combination of `OrderID` and `ProductID` in an `OrderDetails` table could form a composite primary key.
title: Primary Key

definition: A column or set of columns in one database table that refers to the primary key in another table. It establishes and enforces a link between the data in two tables, ensuring referential integrity.
examples: `CustomerID` in an `Orders` table referring to the `CustomerID` primary key in the `Customers` table.|`ProductID` in an `OrderDetails` table referring to the `ProductID` primary key in the `Products` table.
title: Foreign Key

definition: A set of one or more attributes (columns) that, taken together, can uniquely identify a tuple (row) in a relation (table). A primary key is always a super key, but not all super keys are primary keys.
examples: In a `Students` table with `StudentID`, `Name`, `Email`, `Address`: `{StudentID}` is a super key.|`{StudentID, Name}` is also a super key, even if `StudentID` alone is sufficient.|If `Email` is guaranteed unique, `{Email}` is a super key.
title: Super Key

definition: A primary key that consists of two or more attributes (columns) whose values, when combined, uniquely identify each record in a database table. No single attribute in the composite key is sufficient to uniquely identify a record on its own.
examples: In an `OrderDetails` table, `(OrderID, ProductID)` might form a composite primary key.|In a `CourseEnrollment` table, `(StudentID, CourseID)` could be a composite primary key.
title: Composite Key

definition: A standard language for managing and manipulating relational databases. It is used to store, retrieve, manage, and update data, as well as define database schemas.
examples: `SELECT * FROM Customers;` (Retrieving data)|`CREATE TABLE Products (ProductID INT PRIMARY KEY, ProductName VARCHAR(255));` (Defining schema)|`UPDATE Employees SET Salary = 60000 WHERE EmployeeID = 1;` (Updating data)
title: SQL (Structured Query Language)

definition: The most frequently used SQL command, employed to retrieve data from one or more tables in a database. It allows specifying which columns to fetch, from which tables, and under what conditions.
examples: `SELECT FirstName, LastName FROM Employees WHERE DepartmentID = 10;`|`SELECT * FROM Products ORDER BY Price DESC;`|`SELECT COUNT(CustomerID) AS TotalCustomers FROM Customers;`
title: SELECT Statement (SQL)

definition: An SQL Data Manipulation Language (DML) statement used to add new rows (records) of data into a table in a database. It specifies the table name and the values to be inserted into its columns.
examples: `INSERT INTO Customers (FirstName, LastName, Email) VALUES ('John', 'Doe', 'john.doe@example.com');`|`INSERT INTO Products VALUES (101, 'Laptop', 1200.00, 50);` (Assumes column order matches values)
title: INSERT Statement (SQL)

definition: An SQL Data Manipulation Language (DML) statement used to modify existing data within a database table. It specifies the table to update, the new values for columns, and a `WHERE` clause to select which rows to modify.
examples: `UPDATE Employees SET Salary = 65000 WHERE EmployeeID = 101;`|`UPDATE Products SET Price = Price * 1.05, Stock = Stock - 10 WHERE ProductID = 5;`
title: UPDATE Statement (SQL)

definition: An SQL Data Manipulation Language (DML) statement used to remove existing rows (records) from a database table. A `WHERE` clause is typically used to specify which rows to delete; omitting it will delete all rows from the table.
examples: `DELETE FROM Customers WHERE CustomerID = 205;`|`DELETE FROM Orders WHERE OrderDate < '2023-01-01';`|`DELETE FROM TempLogs;` (Deletes all rows in the TempLogs table)
title: DELETE Statement (SQL)

definition: An SQL join operation that returns only the rows from two or more tables where there is a match in the join condition. Rows that do not have a corresponding match in all joined tables are excluded from the result set.
examples: `SELECT Customers.FirstName, Orders.OrderDate FROM Customers INNER JOIN Orders ON Customers.CustomerID = Orders.CustomerID;`|This query retrieves customer names and their order dates, but only for customers who have placed orders.
title: Inner Join (SQL)

definition: An SQL join operation that returns all rows from the left table, and the matching rows from the right table. If there is no match for a row in the left table, NULLs are returned for the columns of the right table.
examples: `SELECT Customers.FirstName, Orders.OrderDate FROM Customers LEFT JOIN Orders ON Customers.CustomerID = Orders.CustomerID;`|This query retrieves all customers and their order dates; customers without orders will still appear, with `NULL` for `OrderDate`.
semantic_tags: SQL|Join|Data Retrieval|Relational Database|All Left Records|Table Relationship
title: Left Join (SQL)

definition: An SQL join operation that returns all rows from the right table, and the matching rows from the left table. If there is no match for a row in the right table, NULLs are returned for the columns of the left table.
examples: `SELECT Products.ProductName, OrderDetails.Quantity FROM Products RIGHT JOIN OrderDetails ON Products.ProductID = OrderDetails.ProductID;`|This query ensures all records from `OrderDetails` are included, linking to product names where a match exists, otherwise showing `NULL` for `ProductName`.
semantic_tags: SQL|Join|Data Retrieval|Relational Database|All Right Records|Table Relationship
title: Right Join (SQL)

definition: An SQL join operation that returns all rows when there is a match in either the left (table1) or the right (table2) table records. If no match exists, NULLs are returned for the columns of the non-matching table.
examples: `SELECT Customers.FirstName, Orders.OrderDate FROM Customers FULL OUTER JOIN Orders ON Customers.CustomerID = Orders.CustomerID;`|This query retrieves all customers (including those without orders) and all orders (including those without a matching customer, if applicable).
title: Full Outer Join (SQL)

definition: A technique used to speed up data retrieval operations on a database table by creating a special lookup structure that can be traversed quickly. It works similar to an index in a book, allowing the database system to find data without scanning the entire table.
examples: Creating an index on the `LastName` column of a `Customers` table to quickly search for customers: `CREATE INDEX idx_lastname ON Customers (LastName);`|A primary key automatically creates a clustered index in many database management systems.
title: Database Indexing

definition: A systematic process of organizing the columns and tables of a relational database to minimize data redundancy and improve data integrity. It involves breaking down large tables into smaller, related tables and defining relationships between them, typically following a series of normal forms.
examples: Splitting a single table with repeated department information for each employee into separate `Employees` and `Departments` tables.|Applying 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF to achieve a well-structured database design.
semantic_tags: Database Design|Data Integrity|Redundancy Reduction|Relational Model|Efficiency|Normal Forms
title: Normalization (Database)

definition: The first and most basic level of database normalization, requiring that each column in a table contains atomic (indivisible) values, and there are no repeating groups of columns. Each row must also be uniquely identifiable through a primary key.
examples: A table where an `Address` column stores '123 Main St, Anytown, CA' is in 1NF.|A table with a `PhoneNumbers` column storing '555-1234, 555-5678' is NOT in 1NF, as the values are not atomic and should be split into separate entries or rows.
semantic_tags: Normalization|Database Design|Atomic Values|Repeating Groups|Data Integrity|Relational Database
title: First Normal Form (1NF)

definition: A database table is in 2NF if it is already in 1NF and all non-key attributes are fully functionally dependent on the primary key. This specifically means no non-key attribute is dependent on only a part of a composite primary key.
examples: Consider an `OrderDetails` table `(OrderID, ProductID, Quantity, ProductName)`. If `(OrderID, ProductID)` is the primary key, `ProductName` depends only on `ProductID` (a part of the key), violating 2NF.|To achieve 2NF, `ProductName` should move to a separate `Products` table `(ProductID, ProductName)`.
semantic_tags: Normalization|Database Design|Functional Dependency|Composite Key|Data Redundancy|Partial Dependency
title: Second Normal Form (2NF)

definition: A database table is in 3NF if it is already in 2NF and all non-key attributes are not transitively dependent on the primary key. This means no non-key attribute is dependent on another non-key attribute.
examples: Consider an `Employees` table `(EmpID, EmpName, DeptID, DeptName)`. If `EmpID` is the primary key, `DeptName` is transitively dependent on `EmpID` (via `DeptID`), violating 3NF.|To achieve 3NF, `DeptName` should move to a separate `Departments` table `(DeptID, DeptName)`.
semantic_tags: Normalization|Database Design|Transitive Dependency|Data Redundancy|Functional Dependency|Data Integrity
title: Third Normal Form (3NF)

definition: The 'A' in ACID properties, Atomicity ensures that a database transaction is treated as a single, indivisible unit of work. Either all of its operations are completed successfully (committed), or none of them are (rolled back), preventing partial updates and ensuring data consistency.
examples: A money transfer between two bank accounts: either money is debited from one and credited to the other, or if any part fails, neither operation occurs.|Updating an order that involves changes in both `OrderHeader` and `OrderDetails` tables: Atomicity guarantees both updates succeed or both fail together.
title: Atomicity (ACID)

definition: Ensures that a transaction brings the database from one valid state to another, maintaining all defined rules, constraints, and triggers. If a transaction violates any constraint, it is rolled back, preventing invalid data from being committed.
examples: A banking transaction transferring funds must ensure the total balance across accounts remains consistent (e.g., sender's balance decreases by amount, receiver's balance increases by amount).|An INSERT operation into a table with a NOT NULL constraint for a column will fail if a NULL value is provided for that column.
title: Consistency (ACID)

definition: Guarantees that concurrent execution of transactions leaves the database in the same state that would have been obtained if the transactions were executed sequentially. This prevents transactions from interfering with each other's intermediate states, ensuring that each transaction appears to run in isolation.
examples: Two users simultaneously trying to withdraw money from the same bank account; isolation ensures one transaction completes before the other can access the updated balance.|A transaction calculating an aggregate sum on a table while another transaction is updating rows will see either the state before all updates or after all updates, but not an inconsistent intermediate state.
title: Isolation (ACID)

definition: Ensures that once a transaction has been committed, it will remain permanent and survive any subsequent system failures, such as power outages or crashes. This is typically achieved by writing transaction data to non-volatile storage and often involves logging and recovery mechanisms.
examples: After a successful credit card payment transaction is committed, even if the payment system immediately crashes, the payment record will persist and the funds will be transferred.|A database server losing power after a COMMIT statement; when the server restarts, the committed changes are still present in the database.
title: Durability (ACID)

definition: A single logical unit of work that accesses and modifies data in a database. It must be executed entirely or not at all (atomicity), adhering to the ACID properties to ensure data integrity and reliability.
examples: Transferring money from Account A to Account B, involving a debit from A and a credit to B, along with a log entry; all these operations must succeed or fail together.|An online retail order submission: checking inventory, deducting items, updating order status, and processing payment are all part of one transaction.
title: Database Transaction

definition: Mechanisms used in database management systems to manage simultaneous operations on shared data, ensuring that multiple transactions can run concurrently without compromising the database's consistency and isolation properties. It prevents phenomena like lost updates, dirty reads, and unrepeatable reads.
examples: Two users attempting to book the last available seat on an airplane at the exact same time; concurrency control ensures only one succeeds.|Using locks (e.g., shared or exclusive) to manage access to data rows or tables.|Implementing multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) where readers don't block writers.
title: Concurrency Control (Database)

definition: A concurrency control mechanism where a database object (like a row, table, or page) is marked as 'in-use' by a transaction, preventing other transactions from accessing or modifying it until the lock is released. Locks can be shared (allowing multiple reads) or exclusive (allowing only one write or read).
examples: A transaction modifying a specific customer record places an exclusive lock on that row, preventing other transactions from reading or writing to it until the update is committed or rolled back.|Multiple transactions reading the same product catalog simultaneously might acquire shared locks, allowing concurrent reads but preventing any writes.
title: Locking (Database)

definition: A situation in concurrency control where two or more transactions are permanently blocked, each waiting for a lock held by another transaction in the cycle. This creates a circular dependency, preventing any of the involved transactions from proceeding.
examples: Transaction A locks resource X, then tries to lock resource Y. Transaction B locks resource Y, then tries to lock resource X; both are now waiting indefinitely.|Two database queries, one updating Table1 then Table2, and the other updating Table2 then Table1, can cause a deadlock if executed concurrently and acquire locks at intermediate steps.
title: Deadlock (Database)

definition: The process of creating a copy of the database's current state, including its schema, data, and transaction logs, to allow for its restoration in case of data loss, corruption, or disaster. Backups are crucial for disaster recovery and business continuity.
examples: Taking a daily full backup of a production database to an off-site storage location.|Performing incremental backups nightly, only copying data that has changed since the last full or incremental backup.|Using a point-in-time recovery strategy with continuous archiving of transaction logs.
title: Database Backup

definition: The process of restoring a database to a consistent and usable state after a failure, typically using a combination of the most recent backup and transaction logs to replay or undo operations. It ensures data durability and integrity, minimizing data loss.
examples: Restoring a database from a full backup and then applying all subsequent transaction log files (roll-forward) to bring it to the point of failure.|Rolling back an incomplete transaction that was active at the time of a system crash.|Using automated recovery mechanisms upon database restart to ensure all committed transactions are reflected and uncommitted ones are undone.
title: Database Recovery

definition: A category of databases that provides a mechanism for storage and retrieval of data modeled in means other than the tabular relations used in relational databases. They are often designed for specific data models, flexible schemas, horizontal scalability, and high performance with large datasets.
examples: MongoDB (Document Database) for storing JSON-like data with flexible schemas.|Cassandra (Column-Family Database) for high-volume write operations and wide column-oriented storage.|Redis (Key-Value Store) for caching and real-time data access.
title: NoSQL Database

definition: A type of NoSQL database that stores data in flexible, semi-structured document formats, typically JSON, BSON, or XML, rather than in fixed rows and columns. They allow for hierarchical data storage and flexible schemas, making them well-suited for rapidly evolving data structures.
examples: MongoDB storing customer profiles where each profile is a document containing varying fields like name, address, orders, and preferences.|Couchbase storing product catalogs where each product document can have different attributes based on the product type without requiring schema migration.
title: Document Database

definition: A type of NoSQL database that stores data in column families, which are groups of related columns treated as a single unit. Unlike relational databases, rows can have different sets of columns, allowing for sparse data and high scalability for wide tables with many attributes.
examples: Apache Cassandra or HBase storing user activity logs where each row (user session) might have different columns (actions, timestamps, page views) depending on the session's events.|Storing sensor data where each sensor (row) reports different metrics (columns) at different times without requiring every row to have every column.
title: Column-Family Database

definition: A type of NoSQL database that uses graph structures with nodes, edges, and properties to represent and store data. They are optimized for highly interconnected data and excel at navigating complex relationships quickly and intuitively.
examples: Neo4j storing social network connections, where users are nodes and friendships are edges, allowing for efficient 'friends of friends' queries.|Storing recommendation engine data, modeling relationships between products, users, and purchases to suggest relevant items based on connections.
title: Graph Database

definition: An alternative set of properties (Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent) for distributed databases, often associated with NoSQL systems. It prioritizes availability and partition tolerance over immediate consistency, allowing data inconsistencies to resolve over time.
examples: A social media feed that might show slightly outdated information for a short period after an update but remains accessible even during network partitions.|An e-commerce site where the inventory count might not be instantly accurate across all replicated nodes but eventually synchronizes to a consistent state.
title: BASE Properties

definition: A transaction that involves multiple participating resources (e.g., databases, message queues) located on different network hosts, requiring coordination to ensure atomicity across all participants. It typically uses protocols like two-phase commit (2PC) to guarantee that all parts of the transaction either commit or abort together.
examples: Transferring money between two different bank accounts hosted on separate database servers, requiring both debit and credit operations to succeed or fail atomically.|An online order system where processing an order involves updating an inventory database, a payment gateway, and a shipping service, all as a single atomic unit.
title: Distributed Transaction

definition: A horizontal partitioning technique for databases where large datasets are divided into smaller, more manageable pieces called 'shards,' which are then distributed across multiple database servers. This improves scalability, performance, and availability by distributing the load and data.
examples: A large e-commerce database sharded by customer ID range, with customers A-M on one server and N-Z on another.|A social media platform sharding user data based on geographical regions to improve latency for local users and distribute storage.
title: Database Sharding

definition: The process of creating and maintaining multiple copies of a database (or parts of it) across different servers to improve data availability, fault tolerance, and read performance. Changes made to the primary database are propagated to its replicas.
examples: A master-slave replication setup where a primary database handles all writes and several secondary databases serve read queries.|Multi-master replication where multiple database instances can accept writes, requiring conflict resolution mechanisms to maintain consistency.
semantic_tags: High Availability|Fault Tolerance|Data Redundancy|Disaster Recovery|Read Scaling|Master-Slave
title: Database Replication

definition: The overall accuracy, completeness, and consistency of data throughout its lifecycle. It ensures that data is valid, reliable, and trustworthy, preventing unauthorized or incorrect modifications.
examples: Enforcing referential integrity with foreign key constraints to ensure a customer cannot be deleted if there are still active orders associated with them.|Using data type constraints (e.g., INT for age) to prevent invalid data entries.|Implementing business rules in the application layer to validate input before storing it in the database.
title: Data Integrity

definition: A comprehensive document that describes the intended purpose, functionalities, and constraints of a software system. It clearly defines what the system should do, serving as a contract between stakeholders and the development team.
examples: A section detailing functional requirements like 'The system shall allow users to register with an email and password.'|A section on non-functional requirements specifying 'The system shall respond to user login requests within 2 seconds 95% of the time.'|Documenting system interfaces, data models, and performance targets within the specification.
semantic_tags: Requirements Engineering|Software Development Lifecycle|Functional Requirements|Non-functional Requirements|Stakeholders|Documentation
title: Software Requirements Specification

definition: A Unified Modeling Language (UML) diagram that visually represents the functional requirements of a system by showing how different actors interact with the system to achieve specific goals (use cases). It helps in understanding the system's scope and its interactions with external entities.
examples: A use case diagram for an online shopping system showing actors like 'Customer' and 'Admin,' and use cases like 'Place Order,' 'View Product,' and 'Manage Inventory.'|An 'Actor' stick figure connected by a line to an 'oval' representing a 'Use Case,' such as 'User logs in,' depicting who performs an action and what that action is.
title: Use Case Diagram (UML)

definition: A Class Diagram is a static structural diagram in UML that describes the structure of a system by showing its classes, their attributes, operations (or methods), and the relationships among objects.
examples: A UML diagram showing `Customer`, `Order`, and `Product` classes in an e-commerce system with associations like 'places' and 'contains'.|Representing a banking system with `Account`, `Customer`, and `Transaction` classes, including inheritance from a base `BankAccount` class.|Visualizing a library system with classes like `Book`, `Member`, and `Librarian`, showing their attributes and methods.
title: Class Diagram (UML)

definition: A Sequence Diagram is a dynamic behavioral diagram in UML that shows the interaction between objects in a time-ordered sequence, depicting the messages passed between them to perform a specific function.
examples: A diagram illustrating the steps of a 'user login' process, showing messages between `UserInterface`, `AuthenticationService`, and `Database`.|Mapping the 'checkout' process in an online store, from adding items to cart, payment processing, and order confirmation.|Showing the flow of an ATM transaction, including user input, bank server communication, and cash dispenser interaction.
title: Sequence Diagram (UML)

definition: An Activity Diagram is a behavioral diagram in UML that illustrates the flow of control or object flow in a system, showing the sequence of activities performed to achieve a goal.
