examples: A Cassandra cluster with a replication factor of 3, meaning every piece of data is stored on three distinct nodes to survive the failure of up to two nodes.|HDFS (Hadoop Distributed File System) storing each data block three times by default to ensure durability and availability.
semantic_tags: data redundancy|fault tolerance|distributed storage|data availability|data durability|consistency
title: Replication Factor

definition: The property of a distributed database system that hides the distribution of data and processing from the user, making it appear as a single, centralized database. It encompasses location, replication, fragmentation, and concurrency transparency.
examples: A user issuing a SQL query `SELECT * FROM Orders` without knowing which server holds specific order data or if the data is fragmented or replicated.|An application connecting to a database endpoint without needing to know the underlying distributed architecture, interacting as if it's a single database instance.
semantic_tags: distributed systems|abstraction|data independence|user experience|complexity hiding|database architecture
title: Transparency (Distributed Database)

definition: A distributed system architecture where each node operates independently, possessing its own CPU, memory, and storage, without sharing any resources with other nodes. Nodes communicate by passing messages over a network.
examples: Massively Parallel Processing (MPP) databases like Teradata, Google Spanner, or Amazon Redshift, where each node manages a subset of the data.|Hadoop clusters, where each DataNode has its own local disk and memory, processing data stored locally.
title: Shared-Nothing Architecture

definition: A database architecture where a client application requests services from a server, which manages database access and processing. The client handles the user interface, while the server handles data storage, retrieval, and business logic.
examples: A desktop application (client) connecting to a local MySQL server (server) to store and retrieve user data.|A web browser (client) making requests to a web server that, in turn, queries a backend PostgreSQL database (server) to display dynamic content.
title: Client-Server Architecture (DB)

definition: A multi-layered client-server architecture where application logic is separated into distinct logical and physical tiers. Common tiers include presentation (user interface), application (business logic), and data (database).
examples: A 3-tier web application where the browser is the presentation tier, a Java Spring Boot application server is the logic tier, and a PostgreSQL database is the data tier.|Enterprise systems using a service-oriented architecture, where various services form the application tier interacting with different data stores.
title: N-Tier Architecture (DB)

definition: A fundamental theorem in distributed systems stating that it is impossible for a distributed data store to simultaneously provide more than two out of three guarantees: Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance. Systems must choose to sacrifice one when a network partition occurs.
examples: A traditional RDBMS often prioritizes Consistency and Availability (CA), becoming unavailable during a network partition (effectively sacrificing Partition Tolerance).|NoSQL databases like Cassandra or DynamoDB often prioritize Availability and Partition tolerance (AP), potentially sacrificing strong consistency during a network partition.|ZooKeeper or etcd prioritize Consistency and Partition tolerance (CP), becoming unavailable to ensure data integrity during a network partition.
title: CAP Theorem

definition: A configurable setting in NoSQL databases that defines the strength of consistency guaranteed for read or write operations, typically ranging from eventual consistency to strong consistency. It allows developers to trade off consistency for availability and performance.
examples: In Cassandra, a write with 'ONE' consistency requires only one replica to acknowledge the write, offering high availability and performance but eventual consistency.|A read operation with 'QUORUM' consistency requires a majority of replicas to respond, providing a stronger, but not necessarily strict, consistency guarantee.|Some systems offer 'LINEARIZABLE' consistency, ensuring that operations appear to execute in a single, global order, but at higher latency costs.
title: Consistency Level (NoSQL)

definition: A decentralized communication protocol where nodes periodically exchange information about their state with a small, random subset of other nodes. This peer-to-peer communication spreads information efficiently and robustly throughout a distributed system.
examples: Apache Cassandra uses a gossip protocol for node discovery, cluster membership management, and metadata propagation, allowing nodes to quickly learn about changes in the cluster topology.|Many distributed key-value stores and peer-to-peer networks utilize gossip for state synchronization and fault detection.
title: Gossip Protocol

definition: A database partitioning technique that divides a large database into smaller, more manageable logical units called 'shards,' which are then distributed across multiple database servers. Each shard is an independent database with its own tables and indexes.
examples: Splitting a global e-commerce database by customer ID range, where customers with IDs 1-1,000,000 are on Shard A, 1,000,001-2,000,000 on Shard B, etc.|Fragmenting a social media user database by geographic region or hash of the user ID to distribute load and improve query performance.
title: Sharding (Database)

definition: A minimum number of nodes that must agree or respond to a request for an operation to be considered successful in a distributed system. Quorum-based protocols are used to ensure consistency and durability in the face of failures.
examples: In a system with N replicas, a read quorum (R) and a write quorum (W) where R + W > N ensures strong consistency by guaranteeing overlap between read and write sets.|DynamoDB's consistency model allows configuring read and write quorums, such as 'LOCAL_QUORUM' for consistency within a data center.
title: Quorum (Distributed Systems)

definition: A replication topology where one node (the leader or primary) is responsible for processing all write operations, and then propagates those changes to multiple other nodes (followers or replicas). Followers typically handle read operations and can take over as leader if the current leader fails.
examples: MySQL primary-replica replication, where the primary handles writes and replicas serve reads and are ready for failover.|PostgreSQL streaming replication and MongoDB replica sets, both using a single primary for writes with multiple secondaries for reads and high availability.
semantic_tags: database replication|fault tolerance|high availability|read scaling|data consistency|primary-replica
title: Leader-Follower Replication

definition: A replication topology where multiple nodes can accept write operations, and changes are asynchronously replicated between all leader nodes. This setup increases write availability and can improve performance for geographically distributed systems, but introduces challenges with conflict resolution.
examples: PostgreSQL Bi-Directional Replication (BDR) allowing writes to multiple nodes and propagating changes.|Some active-active database configurations or distributed systems designed for high write availability across multiple data centers, where conflict resolution mechanisms are crucial.
semantic_tags: database replication|write scaling|high availability|eventual consistency|conflict resolution|distributed systems
title: Multi-Leader Replication

definition: A data structure that can be replicated across multiple servers, allowing concurrent updates to be applied independently and asynchronously without requiring coordination or explicit conflict resolution. All replicas are guaranteed to converge to the same state eventually.
examples: Collaborative text editors (like a simplified Google Docs) where concurrent edits by multiple users converge without explicit merges, using an Operation-based CRDT.|Distributed counters where increments and decrements are applied independently across nodes, such as a G-Counter or PN-Counter, always resulting in the correct total count.
normalized_name: conflict free replicated data type crdt
title: Conflict-free Replicated Data Type (CRDT)

definition: A protocol that allows a group of distributed processes or nodes to agree on a single data value or state, even in the presence of failures. It is fundamental for maintaining consistency and achieving agreement in distributed systems.
examples: Paxos, Raft, and Zab (used by ZooKeeper) are prominent consensus algorithms used for leader election, atomic commits, or maintaining consistent replicated logs in distributed databases.|Used in distributed key-value stores to ensure that all replicas agree on the order of operations, providing strong consistency guarantees.
title: Consensus Algorithm

definition: A family of protocols for solving the consensus problem in an asynchronous network of unreliable processes. It ensures all non-faulty processes agree on a single value, even if some processes fail, making it crucial for fault-tolerant distributed systems.
examples: Google Chubby lock service uses Paxos for strong consistency.|Apache ZooKeeper's Zab protocol is inspired by Paxos concepts.|Ensuring all replicas in a distributed database agree on the order of transactions.
title: Paxos Algorithm

definition: A consensus algorithm designed to be easier to understand than Paxos while providing equivalent fault tolerance and performance. It achieves consensus by electing a leader and replicating log entries from the leader to followers, ensuring all nodes agree on the same sequence of operations.
examples: etcd uses Raft as its core consensus algorithm.|Consul employs Raft for its distributed key-value store.|Kubernetes API server's backend storage relies on etcd, thus leveraging Raft.
title: Raft Algorithm

definition: A database optimized for storing and serving time series data, which are sequences of data points indexed by time. It excels at handling high ingest rates, querying data over specific time ranges, and performing aggregations on temporal data.
examples: InfluxDB is a popular open-source time series database.|Prometheus is often used as a time series database for monitoring systems.|TimescaleDB provides time-series capabilities as an extension to PostgreSQL.
title: Time Series Database

definition: A specialized database designed to store, index, and query unstructured or semi-structured data for full-text search capabilities. It optimizes for fast relevance-based retrieval of documents matching user queries, often employing inverted indexes.
examples: Elasticsearch is widely used for full-text search, logging, and analytics.|Apache Solr provides powerful search capabilities built on Lucene.|Amazon OpenSearch Service offers managed search and analytics.
title: Search Engine Database

definition: A class of relational database management systems that aims to provide the scalability and availability of NoSQL systems while retaining the ACID properties and relational model of traditional SQL databases. They often achieve this through distributed architectures and advanced concurrency control mechanisms.
examples: CockroachDB is a NewSQL database offering global distribution and strong consistency.|TiDB provides a MySQL-compatible interface with horizontal scalability.|Google Spanner is a globally distributed NewSQL database with strong consistency.
title: NewSQL Database

definition: A group of interconnected database servers working together to provide high availability, scalability, and load balancing for a database system. It often involves master-replica configurations, sharding, or distributed storage solutions to handle increased demand and prevent single points of failure.
examples: A PostgreSQL streaming replication cluster with a primary and multiple standby servers.|A MongoDB replica set for high availability and automatic failover.|MySQL NDB Cluster for in-memory, real-time distributed database operations.
title: Database Cluster

definition: A central repository for integrated data from one or more disparate operational sources, designed for reporting and data analysis rather than transaction processing. It stores historical data optimized for complex analytical queries and supports business intelligence activities.
examples: Amazon Redshift is a cloud-based data warehouse service.|Google BigQuery offers a highly scalable, serverless data warehouse.|Snowflake provides a data warehouse-as-a-service platform.
title: Data Warehouse

definition: A subset of a data warehouse, typically focused on a specific business function, department, or subject area. It provides targeted access to relevant data for a particular group of users, often derived from the larger data warehouse for specialized reporting and analysis.
examples: A data mart for the sales department, containing only sales-related data.|A financial reporting data mart for the accounting team.|A marketing analytics data mart for campaign performance tracking.
title: Data Mart

definition: A category of software tools that provide fast, interactive, multi-dimensional analysis of data from a data warehouse or data mart. It supports complex analytical and ad-hoc queries, enabling users to 'slice and dice' data to gain insights into business performance.
examples: Microsoft SQL Server Analysis Services (SSAS) for building OLAP cubes.|Oracle OLAP is a component within the Oracle Database.|Apache Kylin is an open-source distributed analytics engine for OLAP.
title: OLAP (Online Analytical Processing)

definition: A class of systems designed for managing transaction-oriented applications, typically involving a high volume of short, atomic data entry and retrieval operations. It focuses on high transaction throughput, fast query response times, and maintaining data integrity through ACID properties.
examples: E-commerce websites processing customer orders and inventory updates.|Automated Teller Machine (ATM) systems for banking transactions.|Airline reservation systems handling bookings and seat availability.
title: OLTP (Online Transaction Processing)

definition: A common dimensional modeling data architecture characterized by a central 'fact table' surrounded by denormalized 'dimension tables.' It is optimized for querying large datasets and simplifies complex analytical queries by minimizing joins and improving readability.
examples: A sales data warehouse with a central 'Sales Fact' table linked to 'Time', 'Product', and 'Customer' dimension tables.|A web analytics data model where 'Page Views Fact' connects directly to 'User', 'Page', and 'Date' dimensions.|A retail inventory system having an 'Inventory Fact' table linked to 'Store' and 'Item' dimensions.
semantic_tags: Data Warehouse|Dimensional Modeling|Fact Table|Dimension Table|OLAP Schema|Data Architecture
title: Star Schema

definition: An extension of the star schema where dimension tables are normalized into multiple related tables, forming a snowflake-like structure. This design reduces data redundancy but increases the number of joins required for queries, potentially impacting performance compared to a star schema.
examples: A sales data warehouse where a 'Product' dimension table is further normalized into 'Product Category' and 'Supplier' tables.|A 'Customer' dimension normalized into 'Customer Demographics' and 'Address Details' tables.|A 'Time' dimension split into 'Year', 'Quarter', and 'Month' tables.
semantic_tags: Data Warehouse|Dimensional Modeling|Normalization|Fact Table|Dimension Table|OLAP Schema
title: Snowflake Schema

definition: The central table in a star or snowflake schema that contains quantitative, measurable data (metrics) about a business process. It typically stores foreign keys to dimension tables and is designed to be very large, housing the operational measurements.
examples: A 'Sales Fact' table containing quantity sold, unit price, and foreign keys to time, product, and customer dimensions.|A 'Web Traffic Fact' table with page views, session duration, and foreign keys to user, page, and date dimensions.|An 'Inventory Fact' table with stock levels and movement types, linked to item and warehouse dimensions.
title: Fact Table

definition: A companion table in a star or snowflake schema that contains descriptive attributes related to a business process's facts. It provides context for the measures in the fact table and typically contains natural keys and surrogate keys for efficient querying.
examples: A 'Customer Dimension' table with customer name, address, and demographic details.|A 'Product Dimension' table with product name, category, brand, and size.|A 'Time Dimension' table including year, month, day, and holiday indicators.
title: Dimension Table

definition: The lowest level of detail represented in a fact table, defining exactly what a single row in the fact table means. It determines the level of atomicity for the measures and dictates which dimensions are applicable to the facts.
examples: The grain of a 'Sales Fact' table could be 'each line item on a sales order'.|For a 'Web Traffic Fact' table, the grain might be 'each individual page view'.|A 'Daily Sales Fact' table has a coarser grain of 'daily sales total for each product and store'.
semantic_tags: Dimensional Modeling|Fact Table|Level of Detail|Atomicity|Granularity|Data Aggregation
title: Grain (Fact Table)

definition: A dimension table that has the same meaning, content, and structure across multiple fact tables or data marts. It ensures consistency in reporting and analysis across different business areas by allowing accurate drill-across queries and integrated views of data.
examples: A 'Time Dimension' used consistently in sales, inventory, and finance data marts.|A 'Customer Dimension' identical across different product line analyses and customer service reporting.|A 'Product Dimension' used uniformly for sales, returns, and marketing campaign analysis.
semantic_tags: Dimensional Modeling|Data Warehouse|Data Consistency|Data Integration|Shared Dimension|ETL
title: Conformed Dimension

definition: A method for handling changes in dimension attributes by overwriting the old attribute values with the new ones. This approach is simple to implement but results in the loss of historical data for that specific attribute, as only the current value is stored.
examples: If a customer's address changes, the old address is simply replaced with the new one in the 'Customer Dimension' table.|Updating a product's 'category' attribute by overwriting the existing value.|Changing an employee's 'department' in an 'Employee Dimension' table, losing the history of their previous department.
semantic_tags: Dimensional Modeling|Data Warehouse|Data History|Attribute Update|Data Loss|SCD
title: Slowly Changing Dimension (SCD Type 1)

definition: A method for handling changes in dimension attributes by creating a new row in the dimension table for each significant change, preserving the full history of the attribute. This typically involves adding start/end dates and a 'current' flag to track effective periods.
examples: If a customer's address changes, a new row is added for the customer with the new address and a new effective date range, while the old row's end date is updated.|When an employee gets a new title, a new employee record is created in the 'Employee Dimension' with the new title and effective dates.|A product's price change results in a new product dimension record with a new price and validity period.
title: Slowly Changing Dimension (SCD Type 2)

definition: A method for handling changes in dimension attributes by adding new columns to the dimension table to store a limited history of attribute changes, usually just the previous value. This preserves only a short-term or specific historical context without creating new rows.
examples: If a customer's address changes, the 'Customer Dimension' table might have 'Current Address' and 'Previous Address' columns.|An 'Employee Dimension' might include 'Current Department' and 'Former Department' columns.|Storing 'Current Product Color' and 'Previous Product Color' for a dimension that changes infrequently.
semantic_tags: Dimensional Modeling|Data Warehouse|Limited History|Previous Value|Attribute Tracking|SCD
title: Slowly Changing Dimension (SCD Type 3)

definition: A multi-dimensional data structure that aggregates and organizes data from a data warehouse for fast analytical processing. It allows users to view data from different perspectives (dimensions) and quickly perform complex aggregations, facilitating 'slice, dice, and drill-down' operations.
examples: A sales cube with dimensions like 'Time', 'Product', 'Customer', and measures like 'Sales Amount' and 'Quantity'.|A financial cube modeling revenue, costs, and profit across 'Regions', 'Departments', and 'Quarters'.|An inventory cube showing stock levels and movements by 'Warehouse', 'Item', and 'Date'.
title: OLAP Cube

definition: The roll-up operation aggregates data to a higher level of granularity, typically by climbing up a hierarchy or reducing the number of dimensions in a data cube. It summarizes data from a detailed view to a more generalized view.
examples: Aggregating sales data from individual product SKUs to product categories.|Summarizing daily sales figures into monthly or quarterly totals.|Changing a report from showing sales by city to sales by state.
title: Roll-up Operation (OLAP)

definition: The drill-down operation navigates from aggregated, summarized data to more detailed, lower-level data, typically by stepping down a hierarchy or adding more dimensions. It reveals finer data granularity.
examples: Viewing total sales for a country and then breaking it down to sales per state or city.|Analyzing quarterly sales and then examining monthly or daily sales figures.|Expanding a customer segment to view individual customer purchases.
title: Drill-down Operation (OLAP)

definition: The slice operation selects a single dimension from a data cube and fixes it at a specific value, resulting in a two-dimensional sub-cube. It effectively filters the data cube along one dimension.
examples: Filtering a sales data cube to show only data for 'Q1 2023'.|Isolating sales data exclusively for the 'East' sales region.|Creating a view showing product sales for only 'Product Category A'.
title: Slice Operation (OLAP)

definition: The dice operation selects specific values for two or more dimensions from a data cube, creating a smaller, multi-dimensional sub-cube. It is akin to applying multiple slice operations simultaneously to define a specific subset of data.
examples: Filtering a sales cube to show data for 'Q1 2023' AND for the 'East' region.|Analyzing sales of 'Product A' in 'Region B' by 'Salesperson X'.|Retrieving all transactions for 'Customer Type C' in 'Store Location L' during 'Month M'.
title: Dice Operation (OLAP)

definition: The pivot (or rotate) operation reorients the view of a data cube by changing the dimensions displayed on rows, columns, or filters. This allows for different perspectives of the same data, facilitating flexible analysis.
examples: Changing a report from displaying 'Products by Region' to 'Regions by Product'.|Swapping the 'Time' and 'Product' dimensions on a sales analysis dashboard.|Reorganizing a table to show 'Salesperson' as rows and 'Product Category' as columns, instead of vice-versa.
title: Pivot Operation (OLAP)

definition: Multidimensional OLAP (MOLAP) stores data in a proprietary, optimized multidimensional array format, often pre-calculating and aggregating data into a specialized data store called a data cube. It offers very fast query performance but can have scalability limitations for extremely large or sparse datasets.
examples: Using Microsoft SQL Server Analysis Services to build and query pre-aggregated cubes for financial reporting.|Deploying Hyperion Essbase for high-performance budgeting and forecasting applications.|A dedicated OLAP server storing several terabytes of sales data in a dense, indexed cube structure.
title: MOLAP

definition: Relational OLAP (ROLAP) stores data in a standard relational database and performs OLAP operations directly against these relational tables using SQL queries. It leverages the scalability and robustness of relational databases but may incur slower query performance compared to MOLAP for complex aggregations.
examples: Executing complex SQL queries on a star or snowflake schema data warehouse to perform OLAP operations.|Using BI tools like MicroStrategy or Power BI to directly query a relational data warehouse for ad-hoc analysis.|A data analytics platform processing sales data stored in a PostgreSQL database using dynamic SQL for drill-down operations.
title: ROLAP

definition: Hybrid OLAP (HOLAP) combines the strengths of both MOLAP and ROLAP, storing frequently accessed aggregated data in a MOLAP cube for speed, while less frequently accessed detailed data remains in a ROLAP relational database for scalability. This approach optimizes for both performance and data volume.
examples: An OLAP system storing quarterly and annual sales summaries in a MOLAP cube for rapid access, but daily transaction details in a ROLAP database.|Microsoft SQL Server Analysis Services configured to use HOLAP mode, caching summary data in memory while accessing detailed data from SQL tables.|A retail analytics system that pre-aggregates popular product category sales into cubes, while individual transaction logs are kept in a relational data warehouse.
title: HOLAP

definition: Business Intelligence (BI) is a technology-driven process for analyzing data and presenting actionable information to help corporate executives, managers, and other end users make informed business decisions. It encompasses a wide range of tools, applications, and methodologies for collecting, integrating, analyzing, and presenting business information.
examples: Using a dashboard to track real-time sales performance and identify top-selling products.|Generating reports on customer churn rates to inform marketing strategies.|Analyzing historical market trends to forecast future demand and optimize inventory.
title: Business Intelligence (BI)

definition: The Extract process is the initial phase of ETL, where raw data is retrieved or copied from various heterogeneous source systems, such as databases, files, or applications, and prepared for subsequent transformation. The extracted data is often placed in a data staging area.
examples: Copying sales transaction records from an operational PostgreSQL database.|Reading customer contact information from CSV files stored in an S3 bucket.|Fetching product inventory data from a REST API endpoint of an e-commerce platform.
semantic_tags: ETL|Data Source|Data Integration|Data Extraction|Raw Data|Data Acquisition
title: Extract Process (ETL)

definition: The Transform process is the second phase of ETL, where extracted raw data is cleaned, standardized, validated, aggregated, and restructured according to the business rules and requirements of the target system. This critical step ensures data quality and consistency.
examples: Standardizing date formats from 'MM/DD/YY' to 'YYYY-MM-DD' across multiple sources.|Joining customer data from a CRM system with order data from an ERP system.|Calculating new metrics like 'total order value' and aggregating daily sales into monthly summaries.|Filtering out invalid customer records or correcting misspelled city names.
semantic_tags: ETL|Data Cleansing|Data Transformation|Data Quality|Data Integration|Business Rules
title: Transform Process (ETL)

definition: The Load process is the final phase of ETL, where the transformed and validated data is moved from the staging area into the target data warehouse, data mart, or other data repository. This can involve a full load, replacing all existing data, or an incremental load, adding only new or changed data.
examples: Inserting transformed customer and order data into the dimension and fact tables of a data warehouse.|Updating existing product records and inserting new ones in a data mart.|Populating a NoSQL database with pre-processed user activity logs for analytics.
semantic_tags: ETL|Data Warehouse|Data Loading|Data Integration|Target System|Incremental Load
title: Load Process (ETL)

definition: A Data Staging Area is an intermediate storage location, typically a database or file system, used to temporarily hold extracted data during the ETL process before it is transformed and loaded into the target system. It acts as a buffer and workspace for data quality checks and transformations.
examples: A temporary schema in a SQL database where raw extracted data is first ingested.|A set of flat files or directories on a server storing data during various transformation steps.|A cloud storage bucket (e.g., S3, Azure Blob Storage) used for temporary data storage between extract and load phases.
title: Data Staging Area

definition: Data cleansing, also known as data scrubbing, is the process of detecting and correcting (or removing) corrupt, inaccurate, incomplete, or irrelevant records from a dataset. Its primary goal is to improve data quality, consistency, and usability for analysis and decision-making.
examples: Correcting misspelled city names like 'New Yok' to 'New York' within a customer database.|Removing duplicate customer entries based on matching names and addresses.|Filling in missing values for a 'zip code' field using other address components.|Standardizing inconsistent address formats to a unified schema.
title: Data Cleansing

definition: Data profiling is the process of examining the data available from an existing information source and collecting statistics and informative summaries about that data. It helps in understanding the data's structure, content, relationships, and quality before data integration or analysis.
examples: Calculating the minimum, maximum, average, and standard deviation for numeric columns.|Identifying unique values, their frequencies, and the percentage of nulls for categorical columns.|Detecting data type inconsistencies or unexpected patterns within a dataset.|Analyzing the distribution of values in a specific column to understand its range and outliers.
title: Data Profiling

definition: Change Data Capture (CDC) is a set of software design patterns used to identify and track changes made to data in a database, allowing subsequent processes to react to or replicate only the modified data. This approach minimizes data processing load and enables near real-time data synchronization.
examples: Replicating only new or updated customer records from an operational database to a data warehouse.|Using database transaction logs (e.g., binlog in MySQL, WAL in PostgreSQL) to capture changes for streaming analytics.|An event-driven architecture where CDC generates events for every data modification, triggering downstream services.
semantic_tags: Data Synchronization|Data Replication|ETL|Real-time Data|Data Integration|Database Logs
title: Change Data Capture (CDC)

definition: Batch processing is a method of executing a series of programs or tasks on a large volume of data collected over a period, processing them together as a single, non-interactive group. It is efficient for data that does not require immediate processing and can be scheduled during off-peak hours.
examples: Running nightly ETL jobs to update a data warehouse with the previous day's transactions.|Processing all employee payroll transactions once a week or month.|Generating monthly billing statements for all customers at the end of a billing cycle.
title: Batch Processing

definition: Micro-batching is a data processing approach that collects data into very small, time-based batches (e.g., every few seconds or minutes) and processes each batch as a discrete unit. It offers a compromise between traditional batch processing and true stream processing, providing near real-time insights with lower overhead than continuous processing.
examples: Processing data from IoT sensors every 5 minutes to update an operational dashboard.|Using Apache Spark Structured Streaming to ingest and process data in small, recurring intervals.|Updating an analytics report every 30 seconds by processing the latest chunk of web traffic data.
semantic_tags: Data Processing|Near Real-time|Stream Processing|Batch Processing|Latency|Data Pipeline
title: Micro-Batching

definition: Stream processing is a method of continuously processing data as it is generated or received, without storing it first. It enables immediate analysis, transformation, and reaction to incoming data in real-time, making it suitable for scenarios requiring low latency responses.
examples: Analyzing website clickstreams in real-time for personalized content recommendations.|Detecting fraudulent credit card transactions instantly as they occur.|Processing sensor data from autonomous vehicles to make immediate navigational decisions.
semantic_tags: Real-time Data|Continuous Processing|Data Pipelines|Low Latency|Event Processing|Reactive Systems
title: Stream Processing

definition: Data federation is a virtual data integration technique that provides a unified, virtual view of data from multiple disparate, heterogeneous sources without physically moving or duplicating the data. It achieves this by querying the underlying source systems in real-time and consolidating the results.
examples: A virtual database that allows a user to query data residing in both a SQL database and a NoSQL store as if they were a single entity.|A BI tool combining sales data from an ERP system and customer data from a CRM system on the fly for unified reporting.|A data virtualization layer presenting a single interface for diverse data sources like cloud databases, on-premise systems, and flat files.
semantic_tags: Data Integration|Virtualization|Heterogeneous Sources|Real-time Query|Distributed Data|Logical View
title: Data Federation

definition: An approach that creates a unified, real-time, virtual view of data from diverse sources without physically moving or replicating the data. It allows users and applications to access and query data as if it resides in a single location, simplifying data integration and access.
examples: A business intelligence tool querying sales data from a CRM, inventory data from an ERP, and website analytics from a web server, all presented as a single virtual database.|Creating a unified view for customer 360 initiatives, combining customer details from transactional databases, social media feeds, and call center logs without ETL processes.
semantic_tags: Data Integration|Virtual Data Layer|Real-time Access|Data Abstraction|Logical Data Warehouse
title: Data Virtualization

definition: A discipline that enables an organization to define and manage its critical non-transactional data (master data) to achieve a single, consistent, and accurate view across the enterprise. It focuses on creating a single source of truth for key business entities like customers, products, and locations.
examples: A retail company consolidating customer information from online stores, physical stores, and loyalty programs into a single 'golden record' for each customer.|A manufacturing firm standardizing product data (SKUs, descriptions, specs) across design, production, sales, and service departments.
semantic_tags: Master Data|Data Governance|Data Quality|Single Source of Truth|Data Consistency
title: Master Data Management (MDM)

definition: The discipline of managing small, static datasets that classify or categorize other data within an organization, ensuring consistency and accuracy across systems. Examples include country codes, currency types, product categories, or units of measure.
examples: Managing a list of ISO country codes and their corresponding names used consistently across all global applications.|Standardizing a list of product categories (e.g., "Electronics", "Apparel", "Home Goods") for an e-commerce platform.
semantic_tags: Reference Data|Data Classification|Data Standardization|Data Governance|Code Sets
title: Reference Data Management (RDM)

definition: The process of importing, transferring, and loading data from one or more sources into a storage system or processing platform for further analysis or storage. It involves capturing data in various formats and speeds.
examples: Using Apache Kafka to stream real-time sensor data from IoT devices into a data lake.|Employing an ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) tool to load daily sales reports from an operational database into a data warehouse.
title: Data Ingestion

definition: One of the "Vs" of Big Data, referring to the immense amount of data generated, stored, and processed, often exceeding the capacity of traditional databases and data processing techniques. It emphasizes the sheer scale of the dataset.
examples: Terabytes or petabytes of data generated daily by social media platforms like Facebook or Twitter.|Historical sensor readings from thousands of industrial machines collected over several years.
title: Volume (Big Data)

definition: One of the "Vs" of Big Data, describing the speed at which data is generated, collected, and needs to be processed, ranging from batch processing to real-time streaming. It highlights the need for quick data processing and decision-making.
examples: Real-time stock market data updates, requiring immediate analysis for trading decisions.|Clickstream data from e-commerce websites, processed in milliseconds to personalize user experience.
title: Velocity (Big Data)

definition: One of the "Vs" of Big Data, referring to the diverse range of data types and formats, including structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data, that need to be managed and analyzed. It acknowledges the complexity of integrating different data sources.
examples: A healthcare system combining structured patient records, semi-structured medical images (DICOM), and unstructured doctor's notes.|Social media analytics involving text posts, images, videos, and user interaction logs.
semantic_tags: Big Data|Data Types|Structured Data|Unstructured Data|Semi-structured Data|Data Formats
title: Variety (Big Data)

definition: One of the "Vs" of Big Data, concerning the trustworthiness, accuracy, and quality of the data, as data with high volume, velocity, and variety can often be uncertain or imprecise. It emphasizes the importance of data governance and quality checks.
examples: Cleaning sensor data that might contain noise or errors due to device malfunction.|Validating customer contact information collected from various sources to ensure accuracy and remove duplicates.
semantic_tags: Big Data|Data Quality|Data Accuracy|Data Trustworthiness|Data Governance|Data Reliability
title: Veracity (Big Data)

definition: A centralized repository that stores vast amounts of raw data in its native format, including structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data, without a predefined schema. It enables flexible data exploration and analytics, especially for Big Data workloads.
examples: Storing all raw logs from web servers, application events, and IoT devices in Amazon S3 or Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2.|A financial institution archiving years of transaction data, market feeds, and customer communications for compliance and historical analysis.
semantic_tags: Raw Data|Big Data Storage|Unstructured Data|Schema-on-Read|Cloud Storage
title: Data Lake

definition: A new open data management architecture that combines the flexibility and cost-efficiency of data lakes with the data management features and ACID transactions typically found in data warehouses. It aims to provide a single platform for both data warehousing and advanced analytics workloads.
examples: Using Databricks Lakehouse Platform with Delta Lake to store raw data, enable ACID transactions, and perform both BI queries and machine learning on the same data.|Implementing a data platform where data is stored in Parquet or ORC files in an object store, managed by a transactional layer (e.g., Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi), allowing both SQL queries and Spark transformations.
semantic_tags: Data Lake|Data Warehouse|ACID Transactions|Open Formats|Structured Data|Analytics Platform
title: Data Lakehouse

definition: A deteriorated data lake that lacks proper data governance, metadata management, data cataloging, or clear purpose, making it difficult for users to find, understand, and trust the stored data. It becomes a dumping ground rather than a valuable asset.
examples: A data lake containing petabytes of unorganized, untagged files from various departments, with no documentation on their origin, content, or quality.|A scenario where data scientists spend more time trying to locate and understand data in the lake than analyzing it.
semantic_tags: Data Governance|Data Quality|Metadata Management|Data Lake Anti-pattern|Untrustworthy Data
title: Data Swamp

definition: A highly scalable, fault-tolerant distributed file system designed to store very large files across thousands of commodity servers, forming the primary storage layer for Hadoop applications. It's optimized for high-throughput access to large datasets, not low-latency access.
examples: Storing petabytes of web log data across a Hadoop cluster for batch processing with MapReduce or Spark.|Using `hdfs dfs -put localfile /user/hadoop/remote_dir/` to upload a file to HDFS.
semantic_tags: Distributed Storage|Big Data|Hadoop|Fault Tolerance|File System|High Throughput
title: Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS)

definition: Yet Another Resource Negotiator, the resource management layer of Hadoop that separates resource management from data processing, allowing various data processing engines to run on a single Hadoop cluster. It manages resources (CPU, memory) and schedules jobs across the cluster.
examples: Running a Spark job, a MapReduce job, and an Apache Hive query concurrently on the same Hadoop cluster, all managed by YARN.|When a Spark application requests resources, YARN allocates containers on cluster nodes for its executors.
title: YARN (Hadoop)

definition: A fast and general-purpose cluster computing system for large-scale data processing, offering in-memory computation for significantly faster performance than traditional disk-based systems like MapReduce. It supports various workloads including SQL, streaming, machine learning, and graph processing.
examples: Writing a PySpark script to perform ETL operations on data stored in HDFS and then train a machine learning model.|Using Spark Streaming to process real-time events from Kafka and update a dashboard.
semantic_tags: Distributed Computing|Big Data Processing|In-memory Computing|ETL|Machine Learning|Data Analytics
title: Apache Spark

definition: A powerful open-source stream processing framework for unbounded and bounded data streams, offering high-throughput, low-latency, and fault-tolerant processing with support for stateful computations. It excels in real-time analytics and event-driven applications.
examples: Implementing a real-time fraud detection system by processing credit card transactions as they occur.|Building an application to monitor IoT sensor data streams and trigger alerts when thresholds are exceeded.
semantic_tags: Stream Processing|Real-time Analytics|Event Processing|Fault Tolerance|Low Latency|Stateful Processing
title: Apache Flink

definition: A distributed streaming platform that enables publishing, subscribing to, storing, and processing streams of records in a fault-tolerant manner. It's often used for building real-time data pipelines and streaming applications.
examples: Collecting user activity logs from a website and feeding them into Kafka topics for real-time analytics.|Using Kafka as a message broker between microservices for asynchronous communication.
semantic_tags: Distributed Messaging|Stream Processing|Message Queue|Real-time Data|Event Bus|Fault Tolerance
title: Apache Kafka

definition: A data warehouse software project built on top of Hadoop that provides a SQL-like interface (HiveQL) for querying and analyzing large datasets stored in HDFS and other compatible file systems. It translates HiveQL queries into MapReduce, Tez, or Spark jobs.
examples: Running `SELECT * FROM sales_data WHERE region = 'EMEA';` against petabytes of sales data stored in HDFS using Hive.|Creating external tables in Hive that point to Parquet files in a data lake for analytical querying.
title: Apache Hive

definition: A high-level platform for analyzing large datasets that provides Pig Latin, a high-level scripting language, to express data analysis programs. Pig compiles these scripts into MapReduce jobs, abstracting the complexities of writing raw MapReduce code.
examples: Writing a Pig Latin script to filter, join, and aggregate web log data before loading it into a data warehouse.|`A = LOAD 'data.txt' AS (f1:chararray, f2:int); B = FILTER A BY f2 > 10; C = GROUP B BY f1; STORE C INTO 'output';`
semantic_tags: Big Data Analytics|Scripting Language|ETL|Hadoop|MapReduce Abstraction|Data Flow
title: Apache Pig

definition: A centralized service for maintaining configuration information, naming, providing distributed synchronization, and providing group services for large distributed systems. It acts as a consistent and reliable store for shared configuration and state.
examples: Hadoop components (HDFS, YARN) use ZooKeeper for coordination, e.g., electing a NameNode.|Kafka uses ZooKeeper to manage cluster membership, topic configuration, and controller election.
title: Apache ZooKeeper

definition: A massively parallel processing (MPP) SQL query engine for data stored in HDFS and Apache Kudu, designed to provide low-latency, high-concurrency SQL queries on large datasets. It offers interactive analytics on Big Data, directly leveraging existing Hadoop infrastructure.
examples: Running ad-hoc SQL queries on a large dataset in HDFS with sub-second response times, unlike batch-oriented Hive.|Connecting a business intelligence tool directly to Impala for interactive dashboards on petabytes of data.
semantic_tags: SQL Query Engine|MPP|Interactive Analytics|HDFS|Low Latency|Big Data
title: Apache Impala

definition: PrestoDB is an open-source distributed SQL query engine designed for running interactive analytics queries against large datasets. It allows users to query data from multiple disparate sources, such as HDFS, S3, Cassandra, MySQL, and PostgreSQL, using standard ANSI SQL.
examples: An analyst runs a single SQL query in Presto to join customer data from a PostgreSQL database with historical order data stored in S3.|Using Presto to query billions of rows stored in a Hive data warehouse for real-time business intelligence dashboards.
semantic_tags: Distributed SQL|Query Engine|Big Data|Data Lake|Data Federation|Analytics
title: PrestoDB

definition: Apache Airflow is an open-source platform to programmatically author, schedule, and monitor workflows as Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs). It allows for defining complex data pipelines, ensuring tasks run in the correct order with dependencies met, and providing rich visual monitoring.
examples: Scheduling a daily ETL job that extracts data from a transactional database, transforms it using Python scripts, and loads it into a data warehouse.|Defining an Airflow DAG to fetch data from a third-party API every hour, process it, and store it in a staging database.
title: Apache Airflow

definition: Apache NiFi is an open-source software project designed to automate the flow of data between systems. It provides a web-based user interface to create, monitor, and manage data flows, emphasizing ease of use, security, and scalability for data ingestion and processing.
examples: Building a NiFi data flow to ingest real-time log data from various servers, filter out sensitive information, and push the processed logs to a Kafka topic.|Visually designing a flow to pull files from an SFTP server, compress them, split them into smaller chunks, and store them in HDFS.
semantic_tags: Data Flow|ETL|Data Ingestion|Visual Programming|Real-time Data|Data Integration
title: Apache NiFi

definition: Data orchestration refers to the automated coordination, management, and monitoring of data pipelines and workflows across various systems to ensure data is moved, transformed, and processed correctly and efficiently. It involves sequencing tasks, handling dependencies, and managing resources within a data ecosystem.
examples: Using Apache Airflow to define a series of tasks (data extraction, cleaning, transformation, loading) that must run in a specific order daily.|A system that triggers a data validation job only after a new batch of data has been successfully ingested into a staging area and all pre-requisite processing steps are complete.
title: Data Orchestration

definition: A Data Governance Framework is a structured system of rules, processes, and responsibilities that ensures the effective and ethical management of an organization's data assets. Its primary goals are to improve data quality, security, compliance, and usability across the enterprise.
examples: Establishing a framework that defines who owns what data, how it should be accessed, and how long it must be retained to meet regulatory requirements like GDPR.|A company implementing policies for data classification (e.g., public, internal, confidential) and assigning responsibilities for each class of data to specific data stewards.
title: Data Governance Framework

definition: A Data Steward is an individual or group responsible for the quality, integrity, and security of specific data assets within an organization. They act as a liaison between business users and technical teams, ensuring data policies are followed and data assets are understood and trusted.
examples: A 'Customer Data Steward' ensuring that all customer contact information is accurate, up-to-date, and compliant with privacy regulations.|A data steward reviewing data quality reports for the 'Product Inventory' domain and coordinating with engineering teams to fix identified data inconsistencies.
title: Data Steward

definition: A Data Policy is a set of formal rules and guidelines established by an organization to govern how data is collected, stored, used, shared, and protected. These policies ensure data quality, compliance with regulations, and security throughout its lifecycle.
examples: A policy stating that personally identifiable information (PII) must be encrypted both at rest and in transit.|A data retention policy specifying that transactional data must be kept for a minimum of seven years for auditing and regulatory purposes.
title: Data Policy

definition: A Data Catalog is an organized inventory of all data assets within an organization, providing metadata, data lineage, and search capabilities. It helps users discover, understand, and trust available data, promoting effective data utilization and governance.
examples: A tool like Apache Atlas or Informatica EDC listing all tables in a data warehouse, their column descriptions, data owners, and refresh schedules.|An analyst searching a data catalog to find datasets related to 'customer demographics' and understanding their quality scores and usage policies before integration.
semantic_tags: Metadata Management|Data Discovery|Data Inventory|Data Lineage|Data Governance|Data Understanding
title: Data Catalog

definition: A Data Glossary is a centralized repository of business terms and their definitions, ensuring a common understanding of key data concepts across an organization. It promotes consistency, clarity, and accuracy in data usage and reporting by establishing a shared vocabulary.
examples: Defining 'Customer Lifetime Value (CLV)' and its precise calculation method for all business units within a company.|A glossary entry for 'Active User' specifying the criteria (e.g., logged in within the last 30 days) to prevent misinterpretation across different departments.
title: Data Glossary

definition: An Access Control List (ACL) is a list of permissions associated with an object, specifying which users or system processes are granted access to the object and what operations they are allowed to perform. It provides a fine-grained mechanism for controlling access to individual resources.
examples: A file system ACL specifying that `userA` can read and write `file.txt` but `groupB` can only read it.|Database table permissions where `userC` has `SELECT` access on `table_customers` but `userD` has `SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE` privileges.
title: Access Control List (ACL)

definition: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) is an access control model where permissions are associated with roles, and users are assigned to one or more roles. This simplifies access management by centralizing permissions for groups of users based on their job functions.
examples: Defining a 'Data Analyst' role with read-only access to specific production databases and assigning multiple analysts to this role.|A 'Database Administrator' role with full administrative privileges on all databases, assigned only to members of the operations team.
title: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)

definition: Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) is an advanced access control model that grants or denies access based on a combination of attributes associated with the user, the resource, the environment, and the action requested. It offers highly dynamic and context-aware access decisions, allowing for more flexible policies.
examples: A policy stating that 'only employees in the `Finance` department located in `London` can access financial reports during `business hours` from a `corporate IP address`.'|Allowing a user to access a document only if their `security clearance` attribute matches the document's `classification` attribute and they are accessing from a `trusted device`.
title: Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC)

definition: Data Encryption At Rest is the practice of encrypting data while it is stored on persistent storage media, such as hard drives, databases, or cloud storage. This protects data from unauthorized access even if the storage device or database is physically compromised.
examples: Encrypting an entire database's data volume using disk encryption technologies like LUKS or BitLocker.|Storing files in Amazon S3 with server-side encryption enabled (SSE-S3), where S3 encrypts objects before saving them to disk.
title: Data Encryption At Rest

definition: Data Encryption In Transit is the practice of encrypting data as it moves across networks, such as between applications, servers, or client devices. This prevents eavesdropping, tampering, and man-in-the-middle attacks during data transmission.
examples: Using HTTPS (SSL/TLS) to secure communication between a web browser and a server, ensuring user data is protected.|Encrypting data sent over a Virtual Private Network (VPN) tunnel between two corporate offices to secure inter-office communication.
title: Data Encryption In Transit

definition: Data Masking is a technique used to obscure sensitive data by replacing it with realistic, but fictionalized, data. The masked data retains its original format and referential integrity, making it suitable for non-production environments like development, testing, or training without exposing real sensitive information.
examples: Replacing real customer names with made-up names like 'John Doe' or 'Jane Smith' in a test database to protect privacy.|Substituting actual credit card numbers with synthetically generated, valid-looking numbers (e.g., using a Luhn algorithm) for application testing.
semantic_tags: Data Security|Data Anonymization|Data Privacy|Data Protection|Test Data|Obfuscation
title: Data Masking

definition: Data Redaction is the process of permanently removing or blacking out sensitive information from a document or dataset, making it unreadable and irrecoverable. It is typically applied to specific fields or sections to prevent disclosure of confidential data.
examples: Blacking out a social security number on a scanned document image before sharing it publicly.|Automatically replacing the middle digits of a phone number with 'XXX-XXXX' in a report, e.g., changing '(123) 456-7890' to '(123) XXX-XXXX'.
title: Data Redaction

definition: Data Tokenization is a data security technique where sensitive data is replaced with a non-sensitive, unique identifier called a token. The original sensitive data is securely stored in a separate, highly protected token vault, while the token can be safely used in less secure systems.
examples: Replacing a credit card number with a randomly generated token (e.g., 'ABCD123EFGH456') for payment processing, while the actual card number is stored in a PCI-compliant vault.|Tokenizing patient medical record numbers so that non-sensitive systems can refer to patients without having direct access to their true identifiers, enhancing privacy.
semantic_tags: Data Security|Data Privacy|PCI DSS|Token Vault|Data Protection|Cryptography
title: Data Tokenization

definition: Data Auditing is the systematic process of reviewing and examining data access, modification, and usage activities to ensure compliance with policies, identify security breaches, and maintain data integrity. It involves logging all relevant data events and analyzing them for suspicious or unauthorized actions.
examples: Reviewing database logs to identify who accessed a sensitive customer table, when, and from which IP address.|Implementing an audit trail to track every change made to a critical configuration file, including who made the change, at what time, and the previous value.
title: Data Auditing

definition: GDPR Compliance refers to adherence to the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), a comprehensive data privacy and security law enacted by the European Union (EU) and European Economic Area (EEA). It imposes strict rules on how organizations handle and protect the personal data of individuals within these regions.
examples: Implementing mechanisms for users to request access to their personal data held by a company or to request its deletion (Right to be Forgotten).|Obtaining explicit consent from users before collecting and processing their personal data for marketing purposes, clearly stating how the data will be used.
title: GDPR Compliance

definition: CCPA Compliance refers to adherence to the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA), a state statute enacted to enhance privacy rights and consumer protection for residents of California. It grants consumers specific rights regarding their personal information collected by businesses.
examples: Providing a 'Do Not Sell My Personal Information' link on a website for California residents to opt-out of the sale of their data.|Implementing processes for consumers to request disclosure of the categories and specific pieces of personal information a business has collected about them.
title: CCPA Compliance

definition: HIPAA Compliance refers to adhering to the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act in the U.S., which sets national standards for protecting sensitive patient health information (PHI). It ensures the privacy, security, and integrity of medical records and related data, governing who can access and use this information.
examples: Encrypting electronic health records (EHRs) stored in a cloud database to protect patient privacy.|Implementing strict access controls to ensure only authorized healthcare personnel can view specific patient data.|Anonymizing or de-identifying patient data before using it for research purposes to comply with privacy rules.
title: HIPAA Compliance

definition: Homomorphic Encryption is a form of encryption that allows computations to be performed on encrypted data without decrypting it first. The result of this computation, when decrypted, is the same as if the operations were performed on the unencrypted data, enabling privacy-preserving data processing.
examples: A cloud service calculating the average salary of employees from encrypted salary data without ever revealing individual salaries.|Running machine learning model predictions on encrypted user data to protect sensitive information during analysis.|Encrypted voting systems where votes are tallied without revealing individual choices, ensuring voter privacy.
title: Homomorphic Encryption

definition: Database as a Service (DBaaS) is a cloud-based service model that provides users with access to a fully managed database without the need to set up, maintain, or administer the underlying hardware and software. The provider handles operational tasks such as patching, backups, and scaling, allowing users to focus on application development.
examples: Using Amazon RDS (Relational Database Service) to host a PostgreSQL database instance.|Deploying a MongoDB Atlas cluster for a NoSQL application, offloading database management to the cloud provider.|Utilizing Google Cloud Spanner for a globally distributed relational database without managing servers.
title: Database as a Service (DBaaS)

definition: A serverless database is a type of DBaaS where the database automatically scales compute and storage resources up and down based on demand, and users are typically billed only for the resources consumed rather than provisioned capacity. It completely abstracts away server management, providing instant scaling and a pay-per-use model.
examples: Amazon Aurora Serverless, which automatically scales capacity for MySQL and PostgreSQL databases based on application load.|Google Cloud Firestore in native mode, offering pay-per-use and automatic scaling for NoSQL document data.|Azure Cosmos DB with its serverless capacity mode, where you only pay for the operations you perform and the storage you consume.
title: Serverless Database

definition: A Cloud Data Warehouse is a data warehouse solution hosted entirely in the cloud, designed for analytical processing of large volumes of data. It offers elasticity, scalability, and often a pay-as-you-go pricing model, typically separating compute and storage to allow independent scaling.
examples: Using Snowflake for business intelligence and complex analytical queries over vast datasets.|Google BigQuery for analyzing massive datasets with SQL-like queries, benefiting from its serverless architecture.|Amazon Redshift for high-performance analytics, utilizing columnar storage and MPP (Massively Parallel Processing) in the cloud.
title: Cloud Data Warehouse

definition: Graph Analytics is the process of analyzing data represented as a graph (nodes and edges) to discover relationships, patterns, and insights that are difficult to find using traditional relational databases. It focuses on the connections and interdependencies between entities to derive complex insights.
examples: Identifying influential users or communities in a social network using centrality algorithms like PageRank.|Detecting fraudulent transactions by analyzing intricate financial relationships between accounts and entities.|Recommending products or services to users based on their connections and shared preferences with others.
title: Graph Analytics

definition: A Knowledge Graph is a structured representation of knowledge that connects various entities (things, events, concepts) and their relationships in a graph-like structure, often leveraging semantic web technologies. It allows for rich querying, inference, and discovery across diverse and interconnected data sources, providing context to information.
examples: Google's Knowledge Graph, enhancing search results with factual information about entities and their relationships.|Building a company-wide knowledge graph to connect employees, projects, skills, and documents for improved collaboration and information retrieval.|A pharmaceutical knowledge graph linking drugs, diseases, genes, and clinical trials to accelerate drug discovery and research.
title: Knowledge Graph

definition: Event Sourcing is an architectural pattern where the state of an application is not stored directly but derived from a sequence of immutable events representing every change or action that occurred. The complete, ordered log of events is the primary source of truth, allowing reconstruction of any past state.
examples: A banking application storing every transaction (deposit, withdrawal, transfer) as an event, where the account balance is computed by replaying these events.|An e-commerce system where user actions like 'add to cart', 'checkout', and 'ship order' are recorded as events to track the order lifecycle.|Version control systems like Git, where each commit is an event that represents a change to the codebase, and the current state is derived from applying these events.
title: Event Sourcing

definition: Command Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS) is an architectural pattern that separates the operations that modify data (commands) from the operations that read data (queries) into distinct models, and often distinct databases. This separation allows for independent scaling, optimization, and evolution of read and write workloads, enhancing performance and flexibility.
examples: An e-commerce system where order creation/updates (commands) go to a write-optimized transactional database, while product catalog viewing (queries) uses a read-optimized, denormalized data store.|In a banking application, financial transactions (commands) might be processed by a dedicated service, while account balance lookups (queries) are handled by another, potentially using a materialized view or replica.|A social media platform using a graph database for querying friend connections and a relational database for user profile updates.
title: Command Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS)

definition: Data Mesh is a decentralized data architecture approach that treats data as a product, owned and served by domain-oriented teams, using a self-serve data platform. It aims to address scalability, data ownership, and quality issues in large organizations by moving away from a centralized data lake/warehouse model.
examples: A large retail company organizing data by domains like 'Customer,' 'Orders,' and 'Inventory,' with each domain team responsible for providing its own data products to others.|An enterprise where financial data, marketing data, and operational data are managed by separate, autonomous teams, each publishing their data as discoverable, addressable, trustworthy, and interoperable products.|Implementing a federated data governance model across various business units, allowing domain teams to define and enforce their own data policies while adhering to global standards.
title: Data Mesh

definition: Data Fabric is an architectural concept that provides a single, unified, and intelligent layer of data services and capabilities across all data sources and environments, both on-premises and in the cloud. It aims to simplify data access, integration, management, and governance, often leveraging AI and machine learning.
examples: Using a data virtualization tool to provide a unified view across disparate data sources like relational databases, NoSQL stores, and cloud object storage.|Implementing an enterprise-wide metadata management system that automates data discovery, classification, and lineage tracking.|A data catalog combined with automated data integration pipelines to connect data from various systems for analytics, offering self-service data access.
semantic_tags: Data Integration|Data Governance|Metadata Management|Data Virtualization|Unified Data Access
title: Data Fabric

definition: Stream Joins are operations that combine elements from two or more continuous data streams based on a common key and a defined time window. They are crucial for correlating related events flowing through different streams in real-time, enabling richer analysis and reactions.
examples: Joining a stream of user click events with a stream of user profile updates to enrich click data with demographic information within a specific time window.|Correlating a stream of sensor readings with a stream of machine operational status within a 5-minute window to identify performance anomalies.|Combining a stream of financial transactions with a stream of fraud alerts for the same account ID within a 1-second interval to detect suspicious activity.
title: Stream Joins

definition: Windowing Functions in stream processing are mechanisms that group a finite set of records from an unbounded data stream based on time or count to perform aggregate computations. They define logical boundaries for processing continuous data, allowing for calculations over specific intervals.
examples: Calculating the average temperature from a sensor stream every 10 seconds using a tumbling window.|Counting the number of website clicks per user over the last 5 minutes using a sliding window.|Aggregating events for a specific user session, where a session is defined by periods of activity followed by inactivity.
title: Windowing Functions (Stream)

definition: A Tumbling Window is a type of windowing function that divides a data stream into fixed-size, non-overlapping, contiguous time intervals. Each data element belongs to exactly one window, and once a window closes, its aggregates are computed.
examples: Calculating the sum of sales for every 1-hour interval, with each sale falling into one specific hour slot.|Counting the number of unique visitors to a website every 5 minutes, where each 5-minute block is independent.|Aggregating sensor readings into 30-second buckets for average temperature, with no overlap between buckets.
title: Tumbling Window

definition: A Hopping Window is a type of windowing function that divides a data stream into fixed-size, potentially overlapping time intervals, moving forward by a specified 'hop' interval. This allows for more frequent updates of aggregate results than tumbling windows, as new calculations are performed at each hop.
examples: Calculating the average stock price over the last 10 minutes, updated every 1 minute (10-minute window, 1-minute hop).|Counting website clicks in a 30-second window, advancing every 5 seconds to provide near real-time metrics.|Monitoring network traffic: a 60-second window that hops every 10 seconds to detect anomalies more quickly.
title: Hopping Window

definition: A Session Window is a type of windowing function that groups events related to a user or entity session, defined by a period of activity followed by a gap of inactivity (timeout). Windows open when an event occurs and close when no new events arrive within the predefined inactivity duration, resulting in variable-sized windows.
examples: Analyzing user behavior on a website: events are grouped into sessions, where a new session starts after 30 minutes of inactivity.|Grouping all events from a single user's interaction with a mobile app until a 15-minute period of no activity.|Tracking a customer's journey through a purchasing funnel, where the session ends if no interaction occurs for 1 hour.
title: Session Window

definition: Complex Event Processing (CEP) is a technology and methodology that involves processing and analyzing multiple events from various sources in real-time to identify patterns, relationships, and trends, and then reacting to these 'complex events.' It goes beyond simple data aggregation to detect meaningful sequences and derive higher-level insights.
examples: Detecting credit card fraud by analyzing a sequence of small transactions followed by a large transaction in a short period from different geographies.|Monitoring stock markets to identify trading opportunities based on specific patterns of price, volume, and news sentiment changes.|Industrial IoT: Identifying equipment failure precursors by correlating temperature spikes, vibration anomalies, and pressure drops across different sensors.
semantic_tags: Real-time Analytics|Event Streams|Pattern Recognition|Anomaly Detection|Event-Driven Architecture
title: Complex Event Processing (CEP)

definition: Database Change Management (DB SCM) is the practice of systematically managing and tracking changes to database schemas, data, and configurations throughout the development lifecycle, typically integrating with version control systems. It ensures consistency, auditability, and collaboration among teams while minimizing risks associated with database changes.
examples: Using tools like Liquibase or Flyway to script and apply database schema changes (e.g., adding a column) in a controlled, versioned manner.|Storing SQL DDL (Data Definition Language) scripts for table creations and alterations in Git alongside application code.|Automating the deployment of database changes to different environments (development, staging, production) as part of a Continuous Integration/Continuous Delivery (CI/CD) pipeline.
title: Database Change Management (DB SCM)

definition: A Database Migration tool is a software utility designed to manage and apply version-controlled changes to a database schema or data, typically by executing a series of script files in a specific order. These tools help automate the evolution of a database structure across development, testing, and production environments, ensuring consistency and preventing manual errors.
examples: Flyway: `flyway migrate` command to apply pending SQL scripts to a database, tracking executed migrations in a schema history table.|Liquibase: Defining database changes in XML, YAML, JSON, or SQL format and running `liquibase update` to apply them incrementally.|Django Migrations: Python-based migrations that detect model changes and generate SQL to evolve a Django application's database schema.
title: Database Migrations (Tool)

definition: Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT) is a decentralized database managed by multiple participants (nodes) across different locations, where each participant maintains and validates a copy of the ledger independently. It ensures data immutability, transparency, and security through cryptographic hashing and consensus mechanisms, without the need for a central authority.
examples: Blockchain, which is a specific type of DLT used for cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum, where transactions are grouped into blocks.|Supply chain management systems tracking goods provenance and ownership changes across multiple parties on a shared, immutable ledger.|Identity management systems where individuals control their personal data stored on a decentralized ledger, granting access to specific parties as needed.
title: Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT)

definition: A decentralized, distributed, and immutable ledger system that stores data in blocks linked cryptographically. Transactions are validated by a network of nodes, ensuring data integrity and tamper-proof records.
examples: Bitcoin's transaction ledger storing all cryptocurrency transactions.|Ethereum's database managing smart contract states and transaction history.|Hyperledger Fabric for transparently tracking goods in a supply chain.
title: Blockchain Database

definition: The process of updating the data stored in a materialized view to reflect the most recent changes in its underlying base tables. This refresh can be performed either completely (rebuilding the view from scratch) or incrementally (only applying changes).
examples: `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW my_summary_data;` (PostgreSQL complete refresh)|`ALTER MATERIALIZED VIEW sales_agg_mv REFRESH FAST;` (Oracle incremental refresh)|Scheduling a daily batch job to refresh a materialized view used for reporting.
semantic_tags: Data Warehousing|Data Replication|View Update|Performance Optimization|Database Caching|Data Synchronization
title: Materialized View Refresh

definition: The continuous process of observing and collecting data on a database's performance, health, and activity to identify issues, bottlenecks, or potential problems. It involves tracking metrics like CPU usage, memory, disk I/O, query execution times, and connection counts.
examples: Using Prometheus with `mysql_exporter` to track MySQL server metrics.|Monitoring Amazon RDS instances via CloudWatch for CPU utilization, free storage, and connections.|Analyzing slow query logs to detect and troubleshoot underperforming SQL statements.
title: Database Monitoring

definition: The practice of optimizing a database system to improve its speed, efficiency, and resource utilization for faster query execution and higher transaction throughput. This involves adjusting database configurations, optimizing schema designs, and refining query logic.
examples: Adding a B-tree index to a frequently queried column to accelerate `SELECT` operations.|Rewriting a complex SQL query to eliminate unnecessary joins or full table scans.|Adjusting database buffer pool size or increasing server RAM to reduce disk I/O.
title: Database Performance Tuning

definition: A set of policies, tools, and procedures designed to enable the recovery or continuation of vital database operations after a natural disaster, cyberattack, or critical system failure. Its goal is to minimize downtime and data loss (measured by RTO and RPO).
examples: Restoring a database from a daily full backup and applying transaction logs for point-in-time recovery.|Implementing a failover plan to switch to a geographically distant standby database in case of regional outage.|Maintaining offsite backups of critical database files and configuration.
semantic_tags: Data Backup|Data Restoration|Business Continuity|High Availability|RPO/RTO|Data Redundancy
title: Disaster Recovery (DB)

definition: A system design approach ensuring that a database remains operational and accessible for a very high percentage of the time, even in the event of hardware failure, software bugs, or planned maintenance. It focuses on minimizing downtime and ensuring continuous service.
examples: Implementing a primary-standby database cluster with automatic failover mechanism.|Using a multi-node database replication setup like MySQL Group Replication.|Deploying a database across multiple availability zones in a cloud environment to protect against zone failures.
title: High Availability (DB)

definition: A technique where the results of frequently executed database queries are stored in memory or a dedicated cache store to avoid re-executing them against the database. This significantly reduces response times and database load for repetitive requests.
examples: Enabling an in-memory cache like Redis to store the results of expensive analytical reports.|An ORM (Object-Relational Mapper) caching frequently accessed entity data at the application layer.|Using a database's built-in query cache (e.g., historical MySQL Query Cache) to serve identical queries faster.
semantic_tags: Performance Optimization|Database Caching|Response Time|Data Retrieval|In-memory Cache|Database Load Reduction
title: Query Caching

definition: The process of distributing incoming database requests or connections across multiple database servers to prevent any single server from becoming a bottleneck. This improves overall performance, scalability, and availability by evenly spreading the workload.
