examples: Using a database proxy like ProxySQL to distribute read queries among several read replicas.|Employing a cloud load balancer (e.g., AWS ELB) to route application connections to different primary/replica database instances.|Implementing application-level logic to connect to different database shards based on data partitioning.
title: Load Balancing (DB)

definition: A copy of a primary database instance that primarily serves read queries, offloading read traffic from the primary and improving performance and scalability for read-heavy applications. Data is typically asynchronously replicated from the primary to the replica.
examples: Creating an Amazon RDS Read Replica for a MySQL database to handle dashboard queries.|Setting up a PostgreSQL streaming replication instance to serve reporting tools.|An application connecting to a read replica for retrieving product listings, while updates go to the primary.
semantic_tags: Database Replication|Scalability|Performance Optimization|Data Redundancy|Read-heavy Workloads|Asynchronous Replication
title: Read Replica

definition: A W3C standard language for navigating XML documents and selecting nodes or node-sets based on various criteria. It can also be used to compute values (e.g., strings, numbers, booleans) from the content of an XML document.
examples: `//bookstore/book[price > 35]` (Selects all book elements with a price greater than 35, anywhere in the document).|`/catalog/book[1]/title/text()` (Selects the text content of the title of the first book in the catalog).|`count(//author)` (Returns the total number of author elements in the document).
semantic_tags: XML|Data Query|Document Navigation|W3C Standard|Tree Structure|Data Selection
title: XPath Language

definition: A W3C standard functional query language designed for querying and transforming collections of XML data. It allows users to extract relevant information, combine documents, and reshape data into new XML or other formats.
examples: `FOR $b IN doc('books.xml')/bookstore/book WHERE $b/price > 30 RETURN <expensiveBook>{$b/title}</expensiveBook>`|`doc('orders.xml')/orders/order[customer='Alice']` (Selects all orders for 'Alice').|`let $total := sum(doc('products.xml')/items/item/price) return <summary>{$total}</summary>`
semantic_tags: XML|Data Query|Data Transformation|W3C Standard|Functional Programming|Document Database
title: XQuery Language

definition: A declarative graph query language for the Neo4j graph database, designed for expressing queries on property graphs. It allows users to define patterns of nodes and relationships to retrieve, create, and modify graph data.
examples: `MATCH (p:Person)-[:ACTED_IN]->(m:Movie) WHERE p.name = 'Tom Hanks' RETURN m.title`|`CREATE (a:Person {name: 'Alice'})-[:KNOWS]->(b:Person {name: 'Bob'})`|`MATCH (u:User)-[r:LIKES]->(p:Product) DELETE r` (Deletes 'LIKES' relationships).
title: Cypher Query Language

definition: A graph traversal language and API for property graphs, part of Apache TinkerPop. It is a functional, data-flow language that allows users to write highly expressive and imperative queries to navigate and manipulate graph data across various graph databases.
examples: `g.V().has('name', 'Alice').out('knows').values('name')` (Finds people Alice knows).|`g.V(1).addE('friend').to(g.V(2)).property('weight', 0.5)` (Creates a weighted 'friend' edge).|`g.V().hasLabel('person').order().by('age', asc).limit(10)` (Gets the 10 youngest people).
semantic_tags: Graph Database|NoSQL|Graph Traversal|Functional Language|Apache TinkerPop|Data Manipulation
title: Gremlin Query Language

definition: A SQL-like query language for Apache Cassandra, a NoSQL wide-column store database. CQL provides a familiar interface for interacting with Cassandra, allowing users to define, manipulate, and query data in a highly distributed and scalable manner.
examples: `CREATE TABLE users (id UUID PRIMARY KEY, name text, email text);`|`INSERT INTO users (id, name, email) VALUES (uuid(), 'John Doe', 'john.doe@example.com');`|`SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = 'John Doe' ALLOW FILTERING;`
title: Cassandra Query Language (CQL)

definition: A powerful functional query language designed for querying Prometheus time-series data. It allows users to select and aggregate data in real-time, enabling monitoring, alerting, and analysis of metrics collected from various targets.
examples: `http_requests_total{job='api-server', status='200'}` (Selects all successful HTTP requests for an API server).|`rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode='idle'}[5m])` (Calculates the per-second average rate of idle CPU time over 5 minutes).|`sum by (job) (http_requests_total)` (Sums total HTTP requests, grouped by their job label).
title: PromQL (Prometheus Query Language)

definition: An open-source data query and manipulation language for APIs, and a runtime for fulfilling queries with existing data. It allows clients to precisely request the data they need, avoiding over-fetching or under-fetching resources, and enabling powerful API design.
examples: Query: `{ user(id: "1") { name email posts { title } } }` (Fetches user details and their post titles).|Mutation: `mutation { createUser(name: "Alice", email: "alice@example.com") { id name } }` (Creates a new user).|Subscription: `subscription { newComment { id text author { name } } }` (Real-time updates for new comments).
semantic_tags: API Design|Data Query|Data Manipulation|Client-Server Communication|Schema Definition|Data Fetching
title: GraphQL (Query Language)

definition: A formal language comprising a set of instructions used to produce various kinds of output. Programming languages are used in computer programming to implement algorithms and create software.
examples: Python is a high-level, interpreted programming language.|Java is an object-oriented, class-based programming language.|C++ is a compiled, general-purpose programming language.
title: Programming Language

definition: The set of rules that defines the combinations of symbols that are considered to be correctly structured statements or expressions in a particular programming language. It dictates the grammatical structure and form of the code.
examples: In Python, indentation is part of the syntax to define code blocks.|In C++, every statement must end with a semicolon (`;`).|Function declarations must follow a specific parameter list syntax.
title: Syntax

definition: The meaning of constructs in a programming language, defining how valid statements are interpreted and executed by a computer. It concerns what a program actually does when executed, beyond just its grammatical correctness.
examples: The `+` operator has the semantic meaning of addition for numbers and concatenation for strings.|A `for` loop's semantics dictate that a block of code will be repeatedly executed a certain number of times or for each item in a collection.|The semantics of an `if` statement mean that a block of code executes only if a condition is true.
title: Semantics

definition: The study of the practical considerations, implications, and choices made when using a programming language in specific contexts, extending beyond its formal syntax and semantics. It addresses how language features are used effectively and the impact on software development.
examples: Choosing Python for rapid prototyping due to its concise syntax and extensive libraries, despite potential performance limitations.|The pragmatic choice between using recursion or iteration based on readability, performance, and stack limitations.|Using a specific naming convention (e.g., camelCase) for variables to improve code readability.
title: Pragmatics

definition: The sequence of characters in the source code that matches a pattern of a lexical unit (token) and is treated as a single indivisible unit during lexical analysis. It is the actual textual instance of a token recognized by the lexer.
examples: In `int count = 0;`, `int`, `count`, `=`, `0`, and `;` are individual lexemes.|The string `"hello world"` is a single string literal lexeme.|The number `123.45` is a single numeric lexeme.
title: Lexeme

definition: A fundamental unit of meaning in the source code of a program, categorized by its type (e.g., keyword, identifier, operator) and carrying an associated value (its lexeme). It represents a conceptual building block recognized by the lexer and passed to the parser.
examples: The lexeme `if` would be classified as a `KEYWORD_IF` token.|The lexeme `myVariable` would be classified as an `IDENTIFIER` token.|The lexeme `+` would be classified as an `OPERATOR_PLUS` token.
title: Token (Lexical Token)

definition: A user-defined name given to a variable, function, class, or other program entity to uniquely distinguish it within a specific scope. Identifiers must follow the naming rules specified by the programming language.
examples: `userName` is an identifier for a variable storing a user's name.|`calculateArea` is an identifier for a function.|`MyClass` is an identifier for a class definition.
title: Identifier (Programming)

definition: A reserved word in a programming language that has a predefined meaning and purpose, which cannot be used by a programmer as an identifier for variables, functions, or other entities. Keywords are integral to the language's syntax and structure.
examples: `if`, `else`, `while` are keywords for control flow.|`class`, `public`, `static` are keywords used in object-oriented programming.|`return`, `break`, `continue` are keywords for altering program execution.
title: Keyword (Programming)

definition: A special symbol or keyword that performs an operation on one or more operands, producing a result. Operators are used to manipulate data, perform computations, comparisons, or logical evaluations.
examples: `+` (addition), `-` (subtraction), `*` (multiplication), `/` (division) are arithmetic operators.|`=` (assignment), `==` (equality comparison), `>` (greater than) are assignment and comparison operators.|`&&` (logical AND), `||` (logical OR) are logical operators.
title: Operator (Programming)

definition: A fixed value in the source code that represents itself directly without requiring computation. Literals are explicit, hard-coded representations of values of a particular data type.
examples: `123` is an integer literal.|`3.14159` is a floating-point literal.|`"Hello, world!"` is a string literal.|`true` and `false` are boolean literals.
title: Literal (Programming)

definition: A named storage location in memory that holds a value, which can be changed or updated during program execution. Variables are fundamental for storing and manipulating data within a program.
examples: In `int age = 30;`, `age` is a variable that stores the integer value `30`.|In `String name = "Alice";`, `name` is a variable holding a string value.|A variable `counter` might be incremented multiple times in a loop.
title: Variable (Programming)

definition: The process of assigning an initial value to a variable at the time of its declaration or creation. Proper initialization ensures that a variable has a defined state before it is used, preventing potential errors or unexpected behavior.
examples: In C++, `int score = 0;` initializes the variable `score` with `0`.|In Python, `message = "Start"` initializes `message` with a string value.|Failing to initialize `int x;` in C++ leaves `x` with an undefined (garbage) value.
title: Variable Initialization

definition: A named value in a program that, once defined, cannot be changed or reassigned during the program's execution. Constants improve code readability, make programs more maintainable, and prevent unintended modifications of critical values.
examples: In C++, `const float PI = 3.14159;` declares a constant `PI`.|In Java, `final int MAX_USERS = 100;` declares a constant `MAX_USERS`.|Many languages define mathematical values like `Math.PI` as built-in constants.
title: Constant (Programming)

definition: A classification of data which tells the compiler or interpreter how the programmer intends to use the data. It defines the kind of values a variable can hold, the operations that can be performed on it, and its memory representation.
examples: `int` (integer) for whole numbers.|`float` or `double` (floating-point) for decimal numbers.|`string` for sequences of characters.|`boolean` for true/false values.
title: Data Type

definition: A combination of values, variables, operators, and function calls that the programming language interprets and evaluates to produce a single resultant value. Every expression has a value.
examples: `5 + 3` is an expression that evaluates to `8`.|`x * y` is an expression that evaluates to the product of `x` and `y`.|`isEven(number)` is an expression that evaluates to a boolean value.|`"Hello" + name` is a string concatenation expression.
title: Expression (Programming)

definition: A complete instruction in a programming language that performs some action and forms a complete unit of execution. Unlike expressions, statements typically do not evaluate to a value themselves but cause a side effect, such as modifying state or controlling flow.
examples: `x = 10;` is an assignment statement.|`if (condition) { /* ... */ }` is a conditional statement.|`print("Hello");` is a function call statement (often considered a statement depending on language).|`return result;` is a return statement.
title: Statement (Programming)

definition: A group of statements or declarations treated as a single unit, typically enclosed by delimiters such as curly braces `{}` or defined by indentation. Code blocks define scope, control flow, and logical grouping of instructions.
examples: The body of a function or method is a code block.|The statements inside an `if` statement or `for` loop form a code block.|In Python, statements indented after a colon (e.g., `def my_func():`) constitute a code block.
title: Code Block

definition: A type of scope where the visibility and accessibility of a variable are determined by its physical position within the source code at the time it is written, not by where it is called at runtime. Also known as static scope, it is determined by the program's nested structure.
examples: Most modern languages like C++, Java, Python, JavaScript, and Ruby use lexical scoping.|A variable declared in an outer function is accessible to a nested function defined within it.|If you define a variable `x` inside `functionA`, it is only visible within `functionA` and any functions nested inside it, regardless of where `functionA` is called.
title: Lexical Scope

definition: A type of scope where the visibility and accessibility of a variable are determined by the sequence of function calls at runtime, rather than by its physical position in the source code. A variable's scope depends on the call stack at the moment of execution.
examples: Perl (before version 5) and some Lisp dialects historically used dynamic scoping.|If function A calls function B, which then calls function C, a variable declared in A might be visible in C if C doesn't define its own variable with the same name.|Debugging tools often operate in a dynamically scoped manner, letting you inspect variables in the current call stack.
title: Dynamic Scope

definition: The period during program execution when a variable exists in memory and retains its value. It defines when a variable is created (allocated memory) and when it is destroyed (deallocated memory).
examples: Local variables within a function have a lifetime from the function's entry until its exit.|Global variables typically have a lifetime for the entire program execution.|Variables declared within a loop block might be created and destroyed with each iteration in some languages (e.g., C++).
title: Variable Lifetime

definition: Control flow refers to the order in which individual statements, instructions, or function calls of an imperative program are executed or evaluated. It dictates the sequence of operations performed by a program.
examples: Conditional statements like 'if/else' alter execution based on a condition.|Looping constructs such as 'for' and 'while' repeatedly execute a block of code.|Function calls transfer control to a subroutine and return upon completion.
title: Control Flow

definition: In Call by Value, a copy of the actual argument's value is passed to the formal parameter of a function. Any modifications made to the formal parameter inside the function do not affect the original actual argument.
semantic_tags: Argument passing|Function calls|Copy|Local scope|Primitive types|No side effects
title: Parameter Passing (Call by Value)

definition: In Call by Reference, an alias or reference to the actual argument's memory location is passed to the formal parameter. This allows the function to directly access and modify the original argument, with changes being visible outside the function.
examples: C++ uses the '&' operator to declare reference parameters: `void swap(int &a, int &b) { int temp = a; a = b; b = temp; }`|C achieves a similar effect using pointers: `void increment(int *x) { (*x)++; }`|Pascal's `VAR` parameters pass arguments by reference.
title: Parameter Passing (Call by Reference)

definition: In Call by Name, the actual argument expression is textually substituted into the function body and re-evaluated each time the formal parameter is accessed. This 'lazy' evaluation can lead to complex behavior, including unexpected side effects, especially with non-local variables or array indexing.
examples: Algol 60 famously used Call by Name.|Consider `procedure p(x); integer x; begin print(x); i := i+1; print(x); end;` and `p(A[i])`. If `i` changes between the prints, `A[i]` will evaluate to different values.|The 'Jensen's Device' uses Call by Name to implement advanced features like numerical differentiation.
title: Parameter Passing (Call by Name)

definition: In Call by Result, the formal parameter is treated as a local variable initialized without the actual argument's value. Upon function return, the final value of the formal parameter is copied back into the actual argument, overwriting its original value.
examples: Ada's `out` parameters conceptually behave similarly.|If a function `void modify(int x)` is called with `int a = 5; modify(a);`, `x` would be a new local variable, and its final value would be copied back to `a` when `modify` exits.|Ambiguities can arise with aliasing: if `modify(x, x)` were called with two formal parameters and implemented by value-result, the final value of `x` would depend on the order of copy-back.
title: Parameter Passing (Call by Result)

definition: Call by Value-Result combines aspects of Call by Value and Call by Result: the actual argument's value is copied into the formal parameter at function entry, and the final value of the formal parameter is copied back into the actual argument at function exit.
examples: Ada's `in out` parameters typically exhibit Call by Value-Result semantics.|Fortran often implements parameter passing for non-scalar types using a mechanism similar to Call by Value-Result.|If `a` and `b` are aliased (refer to the same memory location), and `func(a, b)` modifies both formal parameters, the final value of the actual argument will depend on the order of the copy-back operations.
normalized_name: parameter passing call by value result
title: Parameter Passing (Call by Value-Result)

definition: Referential transparency is a property of expressions where an expression can be replaced with its computed value without changing the program's behavior. This property is characteristic of pure functions, which always produce the same output for the same input and have no side effects.
examples: The expression `2 + 3` is referentially transparent because it can always be replaced by `5`.|A pure function `square(x)` which returns `x * x` is referentially transparent.|An expression involving a side effect, like `rand()` or `print(x)`, is not referentially transparent as its evaluation might change state or produce different results on subsequent calls.
title: Referential Transparency

definition: Binding time refers to the point in the program's lifecycle when a name is associated with an attribute. This includes associating variable names with types or memory locations, or function names with specific implementations.
examples: In C++, the type of a variable is bound at compile time.|In Python, a variable's type is bound dynamically at runtime when a value is assigned.|The resolution of which method to call for an object can be bound early (static) or late (dynamic).
title: Binding Time (Programming)

definition: Early binding, also known as static binding, occurs when the association between a name and its attribute is resolved at compile time, before the program executes. This method typically results in faster execution and allows for more thorough compile-time error checking.
examples: Function overloading resolution in C++ is usually resolved via early binding.|Accessing a static method in Java, e.g., `Math.max()`, is an example of early binding.|The type of a variable in a statically typed language like C or Java is determined and bound at compile time.
title: Early Binding (Static Binding)

definition: Late binding, also known as dynamic binding, occurs when the association between a name and its attribute is resolved at runtime, during program execution. This provides greater flexibility, enabling polymorphic behavior and dynamic dispatch, but may introduce a performance overhead.
examples: Virtual method calls in C++ and Java are resolved using late binding.|All method calls in dynamically typed languages like Python or JavaScript use late binding.|The `instanceof` operator in Java checks an object's type at runtime, which is related to dynamic binding capabilities.
title: Late Binding (Dynamic Binding)

definition: A primitive data type is a basic data type provided by a programming language that is not composed of other data types and represents fundamental values. These types are typically built-in, have a fixed size, and represent simple data forms like integers, floating-point numbers, or characters.
examples: `int`, `float`, `boolean`, and `char` in C, C++, and Java are primitive types.|Python's `int`, `float`, and `str` are built-in but behave more like objects, although they represent fundamental values.|Primitive types are usually stored directly by value.
title: Primitive Data Type

definition: A composite data type is a data type formed by combining or grouping other data types, including primitive types or other composite types, to represent more complex data structures. They allow for the aggregation of related data into a single, structured unit.
examples: An `Array` stores a collection of elements of the same type.|A `Struct` (or `Record`) groups fields of potentially different types under one name.|Classes and Objects in object-oriented programming are common forms of composite types.
title: Composite Data Type

definition: An array is a composite data structure that stores a fixed-size, sequential collection of elements of the same data type. Elements are typically accessed efficiently via an integer index, representing their position within the array.
examples: `int arr[5];` in C declares an array of 5 integers.|`int[] numbers = new int[10];` in Java creates an array of 10 integers.|`my_list = [10, 20, 30]` in Python is a list, which conceptually functions as a dynamic array.
title: Array (Programming)

definition: A record, often called a `struct` in C-like languages, is a composite data type that groups together a fixed number of fields (or members) under a single name. Each field can have a different data type, allowing for the representation of complex, heterogeneous entities.
title: Record (Struct)

definition: A C-style union type is a special composite data type that allows different data types to be stored in the same memory location. All members of the union share the same memory space, meaning only one member can hold a valid value at any given time.
title: Union Type (C-style)

definition: An enumeration type, or `enum`, is a user-defined data type consisting of a set of named integer constants. It provides a way to assign meaningful, symbolic names to a discrete set of integral values, enhancing code readability and type safety.
examples:
```c
enum Day { SUNDAY, MONDAY, TUESDAY, WEDNESDAY, THURSDAY, FRIDAY, SATURDAY };
enum Color { RED = 1, GREEN, BLUE }; // GREEN gets 2, BLUE gets 3
```|Using `enum Day today = MONDAY;` is more readable than `int today = 1;`.|Many modern languages like C#, Java, and Python (with `Enum` class) have enhanced enumeration features.
title: Enumeration Type (Enum)

definition: A pointer is a variable that stores the memory address of another variable or a memory location. It allows for indirect access to data, enabling direct memory manipulation, dynamic data structures, and efficient parameter passing.
examples: `int *ptr;` in C/C++ declares a pointer to an integer.|`ptr = &myVar;` assigns the address of `myVar` to `ptr`.|Dereferencing `*ptr` accesses the value stored at the memory address pointed to by `ptr`.
title: Pointer (Programming)

definition: A type system is a set of rules that assigns a type property to various constructs of a computer program, such as variables, expressions, and functions, and governs how these types interact. Its primary goal is to help prevent certain kinds of programming errors and ensure program correctness by checking for type consistency.
examples: Languages like C++ and Java have static type systems that check types at compile time.|Languages like Python and JavaScript employ dynamic type systems, performing type checks at runtime.|A type error occurs when an operation is applied to an incompatible type, like adding a string to an integer in a strictly typed context.
semantic_tags: Type checking|Type safety|Error prevention|Program correctness|Language design|Static vs Dynamic
title: Type System

definition: Static typing is a characteristic of a type system where type checking occurs at compile time, meaning the type of a variable or expression is determined and verified before program execution. This approach helps catch type-related errors early and often enables performance optimizations.
examples:
C, C++, Java, Go, and Rust are examples of statically typed languages.|```java
int x = 10;
x = "hello"; // This would cause a compile-time error in Java
```|The compiler can use type information to optimize memory allocation and function calls.
semantic_tags: Compile-time|Type checking|Early error detection|Performance|Explicit types|Type safety
title: Static Typing

definition: Dynamic typing is a characteristic of a type system where type checking occurs at runtime, meaning the type of a variable is determined during program execution and can change. This offers greater flexibility as variable types can be reassigned, but type-related errors are detected later.
examples:
Python, JavaScript, Ruby, and PHP are examples of dynamically typed languages.|```python
x = 5       # x is an integer
x = "hello" # x is now a string; no error, type is implicitly changed
result = x + 10 # This would cause a runtime TypeError
```|Variables are often considered to hold values, not to be of a specific type themselves.
semantic_tags: Runtime|Type checking|Flexibility|Late error detection|Implicit types|Runtime overhead
title: Dynamic Typing

definition: Strong typing refers to a type system where data types are strictly enforced, disallowing implicit conversions between incompatible types that could lead to data loss or unexpected behavior. It prioritizes type safety, often requiring explicit type conversions.
examples: In Python, trying to add an integer to a string (e.g., `1 + '2'`) will raise a TypeError unless one is explicitly converted.|Java requires explicit casting when assigning a floating-point number to an integer type, like `int x = (int)3.14;`.|Rust's type system strictly checks all type interactions at compile time, preventing many potential runtime errors.
title: Strong Typing

definition: Weak typing, or loosely typed, describes a type system that allows implicit type conversions between different data types without explicit casting, which can lead to more flexible but sometimes unpredictable behavior. Values are often coerced to fit the context.
examples: In JavaScript, `1 + '2'` evaluates to the string `'12'` due to implicit type coercion, rather than an error.|PHP allows operations between different types, such as `'5' * 2` resulting in `10`.|C's implicit conversions, like assigning a `float` to an `int` without warning, can result in truncation.
title: Weak Typing

definition: Nominal typing is a type system where type compatibility and equivalence are determined by the explicit declaration or name of a type. Two types are considered compatible only if they are the same type or one is declared as a subtype of the other.
examples: In Java, two classes `Person` and `Employee` with identical members are considered different types unless one explicitly extends the other.|C# uses nominal typing for classes and structs; type identity is based on the declared name.|C++ classes adhere to nominal typing where compatibility is established through inheritance hierarchies or explicit conversion operators.
title: Nominal Typing

definition: Structural typing is a type system where type compatibility and equivalence are determined by the actual structure of the types, specifically their members (properties, methods), rather than by their declared names or explicit relationships. If two types have compatible members, they are considered compatible.
examples: TypeScript interfaces are structurally typed: an object `o` can be assigned to an interface `I` if `o` has all the members specified by `I` with compatible types, regardless of `o`'s declared class.|Go's interfaces are satisfied implicitly by any type that implements the required methods, without explicit declaration.|Haskell's type classes, while not strictly structural typing, allow types to be compatible if they implement certain functions, resembling structural compatibility.
title: Structural Typing

definition: Duck typing is a style of dynamic typing where the suitability of an object for a particular use is determined by the presence of certain methods or properties, rather than by its explicit type or class inheritance. The idiom is 'If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, then it must be a duck.'
examples: In Python, a function expecting an object with a `quack()` method will accept any object that defines `quack()`, regardless of its class.|Ruby methods will accept any object that responds to the messages (methods) they attempt to call.|JavaScript often relies on duck typing for polymorphism, where functions interact with objects based on their available properties and methods.
title: Duck Typing

definition: Type compatibility refers to the rules that determine whether a value of one data type can be used where a value of another data type is expected without causing a type error. This often involves subtyping, implicit conversions, or explicit casting.
examples: In Java, an instance of a subclass `Dog` is compatible with a variable of its superclass `Animal`, allowing `Animal a = new Dog();`.|A `short` integer is generally compatible with an `int` variable in C, allowing `int i = s_val;` without explicit conversion.|In TypeScript, an object literal `{ name: 'Alice', age: 30 }` is compatible with an interface `Person { name: string; }` because it has the required properties.
title: Type Compatibility

definition: Type conversion is the process of changing a value from one data type to another. This can occur either implicitly (type coercion) by the compiler or runtime, or explicitly (type casting) through programmer instruction.
examples: Explicit conversion: `int num = (int)3.14;` in C# casts a `double` to an `int`, truncating the decimal part.|Explicit conversion: `String s = String.valueOf(123);` in Java converts an `int` to a `String`.|Implicit conversion: In JavaScript, `let result = '5' - 2;` converts the string '5' to a number before subtraction, resulting in `3`.
title: Type Conversion

definition: Generics, also known as parametric polymorphism, is a feature that allows code to be written to work with types that are specified as parameters, rather than fixed types. This enables the creation of reusable code components that maintain type safety across different data types.
examples: In Java, `List<String>` specifies a list that can only hold strings, but the `List<T>` class itself is generic, allowing it to work with any type `T`.|C++ templates, such as `template <typename T> T max(T a, T b) { ... }`, define functions or classes that operate on arbitrary types specified at compile time.|Rust's `Vec<T>` allows creating vectors of any type `T`, like `let numbers: Vec<i32> = vec![1, 2, 3];`.
title: Generics (Parametric Polymorphism)

definition: Covariance in type theory means that if `A` is a subtype of `B`, then a generic type `G<A>` is considered a subtype of `G<B>`. This relationship typically applies to 'producer' contexts, such as return types, where values are only read from the generic type.
examples: In C#, `IEnumerable<out T>` is covariant: if `Dog` is a subtype of `Animal`, then `IEnumerable<Dog>` can be assigned to `IEnumerable<Animal>`.|Java's wildcard `? extends T` enables covariance for collections: `List<? extends Animal>` can hold `List<Dog>` or `List<Cat>` objects, but you can only read `Animal`s from it.|Arrays in Java are covariant by design (e.g., `Animal[] a = new Dog[10];`), although this can lead to runtime `ArrayStoreException`.
title: Covariance (Type Theory)

definition: Contravariance in type theory means that if `A` is a subtype of `B`, then a generic type `G<B>` is considered a subtype of `G<A>`. This 'reverse' relationship typically applies to 'consumer' contexts, such as parameter types, where values are only written into the generic type.
examples: In C#, `Action<in T>` is contravariant: if `Animal` is a supertype of `Dog`, then `Action<Animal>` can be assigned to `Action<Dog>` (a handler for `Animal` can also handle `Dog`).|Java's wildcard `? super T` enables contravariance for collections: `List<? super Dog>` can accept `List<Animal>` (you can add `Dog`s to a list that accepts `Animal`s or its supertypes).|A function `f(B)` can be used where a function `f(A)` is expected, if `A` is a subtype of `B`.
title: Contravariance (Type Theory)

definition: Invariance in type theory means that if `A` is a subtype of `B`, then a generic type `G<A>` is neither a subtype nor a supertype of `G<B>`. This is the default behavior for most generic type systems, requiring an exact type match for compatibility.
examples: In Java, `List<Dog>` cannot be assigned to `List<Animal>` (and vice-versa) because `List` is invariant by default.|Rust's generic types are invariant unless explicitly marked otherwise, meaning `Vec<Dog>` is not compatible with `Vec<Animal>`.|C++ templates are generally invariant; `std::vector<Dog>` is a distinct type from `std::vector<Animal>`.
title: Invariance (Type Theory)

definition: An Algebraic Data Type (ADT) is a composite data type built from other types, typically representing either a sum of types (tagged unions/enums) or a product of types (records/structs). ADTs provide a structured way to define complex data structures using fundamental type constructors.
examples: In Haskell, `data Shape = Circle Float | Rectangle Float Float` is an ADT that is a sum type of either a `Circle` or a `Rectangle`.|Kotlin's `sealed class` can be used to define ADTs, such as `sealed class Result { data class Success(val value: Any) : Result() ... }`.|Swift's `enum` with associated values, like `enum Optional<Wrapped> { case none; case some(Wrapped) }`, forms a sum type ADT.
semantic_tags: Composite types|Sum types|Product types|Pattern matching|Functional programming|Type constructors
title: Algebraic Data Type (ADT)

definition: A sum type is an Algebraic Data Type that represents a value which can be one of several different types, but only one at any given time. It is often referred to as a tagged union, discriminated union, or variant type, and typically involves pattern matching for handling its different cases.
examples: Rust's `enum Result<T, E> { Ok(T), Err(E) }` is a sum type where a variable can hold either a successful value `T` or an error `E`.|Swift's `enum Optional<Wrapped> { case none; case some(Wrapped) }` allows a variable to either hold a `Wrapped` value or represent the absence of a value.|Haskell's `data Bool = False | True` is a simple sum type representing two distinct possibilities.
title: Sum Type

definition: A product type is an Algebraic Data Type that represents a value formed by combining values of multiple types into a single structure. It holds all its constituent values simultaneously, similar to a record, struct, or tuple.
examples: In C, a `struct Person { char* name; int age; };` is a product type combining a string and an integer.|Python tuples like `('Alice', 30)` are product types, holding a string and an integer.|Haskell's `data Point = Point { x :: Int, y :: Int }` defines a product type combining two integers.
title: Product Type

definition: An Optional type is a Sum Type that represents the possibility of a value being either present or absent. It explicitly handles the case of 'no value' (often replacing `null` or `nil`), promoting clearer code and preventing null pointer exceptions.
examples: Java's `Optional<String> optionalName = Optional.ofNullable(getName());` can hold a `String` or be `Optional.empty()`.|Rust's `enum Option<T> { Some(T), None }` is used to represent a value that may or may not exist, like `let x: Option<i32> = Some(5);` or `let y: Option<i32> = None;`.|Swift's optionals `String?` allow a variable to either hold a `String` or `nil`, requiring unwrapping to access the underlying value.
title: Optional Type

definition: A Result type is a Sum Type that explicitly represents the outcome of an operation, which can either be a successful value of a specific type or a failure containing an error of another specific type. It encourages robust error handling without relying on exceptions.
examples: Rust's `enum Result<T, E> { Ok(T), Err(E) }` forces callers to explicitly handle both success (`Ok`) and failure (`Err`) cases.|Kotlin's `Result<T>` type can represent either success with a value of type `T` or failure with a `Throwable`.|Haskell's `Either a b` type serves a similar purpose, typically using `Right` for success and `Left` for error.
title: Result Type (Error Handling)

definition: An intersection type is a composite type that combines multiple types, meaning a value of an intersection type must simultaneously possess the properties and members of *all* its constituent types. It specifies that a type belongs to multiple categories at once.
examples: In TypeScript, `type AdminUser = User & Admin;` means that an `AdminUser` must have all the properties of both a `User` and an `Admin` type.|In Scala, `A with B` creates a type that inherits from both trait `A` and trait `B`, requiring the combined capabilities.|Conceptual examples might include an object that is both `Serializable` and `Closable`, adhering to both interfaces simultaneously.
semantic_tags: Type combination|Composite type|Union of members|Multiple inheritance|TypeScript|Type algebra
title: Intersection Type

definition: Procedural programming is a programming paradigm based on the concept of calling procedures (subroutines or functions) that perform computations on data. Programs are typically structured as a sequence of instructions, often organized into modules, operating on shared or passed data.
examples: C programs are typically procedural, with functions like `main()`, `printf()`, and `scanf()` manipulating data.|Pascal, with its emphasis on procedures and functions, is a classic procedural language.|Fortran, designed for scientific computing, structures programs around mathematical procedures operating on arrays and other data structures.
title: Procedural Programming

definition: Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is a programming paradigm based on the concept of 'objects,' which are instances of classes that can contain both data (attributes) and code (methods) that operate on that data. Key principles include encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism.
examples: Java uses classes like `Person` with attributes (`name`, `age`) and methods (`speak()`, `walk()`) to model real-world entities.|C++ allows defining classes and creating objects, supporting inheritance (e.g., `Dog` inheriting from `Animal`) and polymorphism through virtual functions.|Python supports OOP principles, where almost everything is an object, allowing for method invocation and attribute access on instances.
title: Object-Oriented Programming (OOP)

definition: Declarative programming is a programming paradigm where the programmer defines *what* the program should accomplish, without specifying *how* to achieve it. It focuses on expressing the logic of a computation without describing its control flow.
examples: SQL queries, like `SELECT name FROM Users WHERE age > 30;`, declare the desired data without specifying the steps to retrieve it.|HTML describes the structure and content of a web page (what to display), leaving the browser to determine rendering details (how to display).|Haskell, a functional programming language, emphasizes immutable data and pure functions to declaratively express computations.
semantic_tags: What vs how|Abstract control flow|Logic programming|Functional programming|Domain-specific languages|Expression-oriented
title: Declarative Programming

definition: A programming paradigm where multiple computations execute overlapping in time, potentially interacting with each other. It focuses on handling multiple tasks simultaneously to improve throughput and responsiveness by managing access to shared resources.
examples: Multithreading in Java using `Thread` objects.|Go's Goroutines and channels for lightweight concurrency.|Asynchronous I/O operations using `async/await` in C# or Python.
title: Concurrent Programming (Paradigm)

definition: A programming language that typically interprets commands at runtime rather than compiling them into a standalone executable before execution. Scripting languages are often used for automating tasks, web development, and 'glue code', offering rapid development cycles and ease of use.
examples: Python, commonly used for web backend, data science, and scripting.|JavaScript, primarily for client-side web development but also server-side with Node.js.|Shell scripts (e.g., Bash) for system automation.
title: Scripting Language

definition: A system for annotating a document in a way that is syntactically distinguishable from the text, providing instructions for its structure, presentation, or other semantics. Unlike programming languages, it describes content rather than defining computational logic.
examples: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) for structuring web pages.|XML (eXtensible Markup Language) for data description and exchange.|Markdown for simple text formatting.
title: Markup Language

definition: The process of hiding complex implementation details and showing only the essential features of an object or system. It allows programmers to work with high-level concepts and simplify complexity, focusing on 'what' something does rather than 'how' it does it.
examples: An interface defining a contract (e.g., `Drawable`) without specifying implementation.|A function like `sort()` that hides the underlying sorting algorithm.|A class `Car` that exposes methods like `start()` and `stop()` without revealing engine mechanics.
title: Abstraction (Programming)

definition: A distinct, self-contained software component that encapsulates related code, such as functions, classes, and variables, into a single, cohesive unit. Modules promote organization, reusability, and prevent naming collisions by creating a local scope.
examples: A Python `.py` file imported using `import my_module`.|JavaScript modules using `export` to expose specific parts and `import` to use them.|Rust crates, which are collections of modules.
title: Module (Programming)

definition: A collection of related modules or types, often organized hierarchically, that provides a higher level of organization than individual modules. Packages help manage the complexity of large projects, facilitate code distribution, and further prevent naming conflicts.
examples: Java packages like `java.util` containing utility classes.|Python packages, which are directories containing multiple modules and an `__init__.py` file.|Go modules, which define a collection of related packages.
title: Package (Programming)

definition: A declarative region that provides a scope for the identifiers (names of types, functions, variables, etc.) inside it, preventing naming conflicts. It allows the same name to be used for different entities as long as they reside in different namespaces.
examples: The `std::` namespace in C++ for standard library components.|Python modules inherently create their own namespaces.|The `System` namespace in C# containing fundamental classes and base types.
title: Namespace

definition: A function or subroutine associated with an object or class, defining a specific behavior or action that the object can perform. Methods operate on and often modify the data (fields) of an object, contributing to its encapsulated behavior.
examples: A `drive()` method for a `Car` object that changes its speed and location.|The `toString()` method in Java, overridden to provide a string representation of an object.|A `calculateArea()` method in a `Shape` class that returns its area.
title: Method (OOP)

definition: A variable that belongs to a class or an object (an instance of a class), used to store data or state. Fields define the attributes or characteristics of an object, describing its current condition or properties.
examples: A `color` field (e.g., `String color;`) for a `Car` object.|A `name` field (e.g., `private String name;`) for a `Person` object.|An `isActive` boolean field in a `User` class indicating account status.
title: Field (OOP)

definition: A special type of class member that provides a flexible mechanism to read, write, or compute the value of a private field, acting like a public field but implemented with getter and setter methods. It enforces encapsulation by controlling access to data while offering convenient syntax.
examples: C# auto-implemented property: `public string Name { get; set; }`.|Python's `@property` decorator used on a method to make it accessible like an attribute.|Kotlin properties that automatically generate getters and setters by default.
title: Property (OOP)

definition: An object-oriented programming mechanism where a class can inherit properties and behaviors from exactly one parent class. The subclass ('child') extends or specializes the functionality of its single superclass ('parent'), forming a clear 'is-a' relationship in the class hierarchy.
examples: A `Dog` class inheriting from an `Animal` class in Java.|A `Sedan` class inheriting from a `Car` class in C#.|Python classes can specify a single base class in their definition.
title: Single Inheritance

definition: A mechanism for code reuse in object-oriented languages that represents a collection of methods intended to be used by multiple classes without using traditional inheritance. Traits allow for composition of behavior and can mitigate issues like the diamond problem, offering a flexible alternative to abstract classes or interfaces with implementations.
examples: PHP traits (`use MyTrait;`) to add methods to a class.|Scala traits, which are abstract fields and methods that can be mixed into classes.|Rust traits, defining shared behavior that can be implemented for different types.
title: Trait (Programming)

definition: A class or module that provides methods to be included in other classes without the use of inheritance, adding specific functionalities or behaviors. Mixins offer a form of multiple inheritance of behavior, allowing a class to 'mix in' capabilities from various sources.
examples: Ruby modules used as mixins via the `include` keyword, like `Comparable` for comparison methods.|Python classes designed to be inherited alongside other classes to add functionality.|JavaScript class composition patterns that effectively achieve mixin behavior.
title: Mixin (Programming)

definition: A method in a base class that is declared with the intention of being overridden by derived classes, allowing specific implementations to be determined at runtime based on the actual type of the object. This mechanism is crucial for achieving polymorphism and dynamic dispatch in object-oriented programming.
examples: A `virtual` `draw()` method in a `Shape` base class, overridden by `Circle.draw()` and `Square.draw()`.|C++ uses the `virtual` keyword for functions that can be overridden.|C# uses `virtual` in the base class and `override` in derived classes for polymorphic behavior.
title: Virtual Method

definition: The ability to redefine the behavior of standard operators (like `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `=`, etc.) for user-defined types. It allows operators to perform operations relevant to custom classes, making code more intuitive, readable, and consistent with built-in types.
examples: Overloading `+` to concatenate two custom `String` objects.|Overloading `*` to multiply a `Vector` object by a scalar value.|Defining the `__add__` method in Python to enable `+` operation for custom objects.
title: Operator Overloading

definition: A static method that can be called as if it were an instance method on objects of an existing type, without modifying the original type itself. It allows developers to add new functionality to sealed classes, types from external libraries, or interfaces, enhancing readability and maintainability.
examples: C# LINQ methods like `.Where()` or `.Select()` are extension methods on `IEnumerable<T>`.|Kotlin extension functions, which extend the functionality of existing classes.|Adding a custom `ToUpperFirstChar()` method to the built-in `string` type in C#.
semantic_tags: Static Method|Syntactic Sugar|Existing Types|Third-Party Libraries|Fluent API|Retrofitting
title: Extension Method

definition: A control flow statement that executes different blocks of code based on whether a specified boolean condition evaluates to true or false. It allows programs to make decisions and follow distinct paths of execution, providing fundamental branching logic.
examples: `if (temperature > 25) { print('Hot'); } else { print('Cool'); }`|Checking user input validity before processing it.|Branching logic to display different UI elements based on user roles.
title: Conditional Statement (If-Else)

definition: A control flow statement that allows a variable or expression to be tested for equality against a list of predefined constant values (cases). It provides a more concise and often more readable way to handle multiple conditional branches compared to a series of `if-else if` statements for specific equality checks.
examples: `switch (dayOfWeek) { case MONDAY: ... break; case TUESDAY: ... break; default: ... }`|Handling different menu selections in a command-line application.|Processing different states of an enumeration or integer variable.
title: Switch Statement (Control Flow)

definition: The part of a recursive function or algorithm that defines how to reduce the problem towards a base case by calling the function itself with a modified, usually smaller or simpler, version of the input. It is the crucial action that drives the computation closer to its termination condition.
examples: In the factorial function `n * factorial(n-1)`, `factorial(n-1)` is the recursive step.|In `fibonacci(n)` defined as `fibonacci(n-1) + fibonacci(n-2)`, both calls are recursive steps.|Traversing a linked list by calling `traverse(node.next)` on the next node.
title: Recursive Step

definition: A recursive function where the recursive call is the last operation performed in the function, with nothing else remaining to be done after the call returns. This specific structure is crucial because it allows compilers to perform certain optimizations, effectively transforming recursion into iteration.
examples: def factorial(n, acc=1): if n == 0: return acc else: return factorial(n-1, n*acc)|def sum_list(lst, total=0): if not lst: return total else: return sum_list(lst[1:], total + lst[0])
title: Tail Recursion

definition: A compiler optimization technique where a tail call is transformed into a simple jump, preventing the allocation of a new stack frame for the called function. This optimization saves memory by reusing the current stack frame, effectively turning tail recursion into efficient iteration and avoiding stack overflows.
examples: A Scheme compiler transforming a tail-recursive function like `(define (sum-up n acc) (if (= n 0) acc (sum-up (- n 1) (+ acc n))))` into an iterative loop.|Languages like Erlang guarantee TCO, allowing infinite recursion without stack overflow for tail-recursive functions.
title: Tail Call Optimization

definition: The process of repeatedly executing a block of code until a certain condition is met or a sequence of elements has been processed. It is a fundamental control flow construct often implemented using loops like `for` and `while`.
examples: for i in range(5): print(i) # Prints 0, 1, 2, 3, 4|while counter < 10: counter += 1|my_list.forEach(item => console.log(item))
title: Iteration

definition: An unconditional control flow statement that directly transfers program execution to a specified labeled point within the same function or scope. While powerful, its unrestricted use can lead to complex and hard-to-follow 'spaghetti code', hence its omission or discouraged use in many modern languages.
title: Jump Statement (Goto)

definition: A control flow statement that immediately terminates the innermost enclosing loop (`for`, `while`, `do-while`) or `switch` statement. Program execution then continues at the statement immediately following the terminated construct.
examples: for i in range(10): if i == 5: break print(i) # Prints 0, 1, 2, 3, 4|while True: if check_condition(): break else: do_something()
title: Break Statement

definition: A control flow statement that skips the remainder of the current iteration of the innermost enclosing loop (`for`, `while`, `do-while`) and proceeds to the next iteration. It allows a loop to continue its execution without processing the rest of the current block.
examples: for i in range(5): if i == 2: continue print(i) # Prints 0, 1, 3, 4|while processing_data: if item.is_invalid(): continue process_item(item)
title: Continue Statement

definition: A control flow statement that terminates the execution of the current function and returns control to the calling function or program. It can optionally return a value as the result of the function's computation to the caller.
examples: def add(a, b): return a + b|void print_message() { printf("Hello!"); return; }|If (error_condition) { return null; }
title: Return Statement

definition: A structured exception handling construct used to manage potential runtime errors or exceptional situations gracefully. The `try` block encloses code that might throw an exception, and one or more `catch` blocks specify the code to execute if particular types of exceptions occur.
examples: try: value = int('abc') except ValueError: print('Invalid number conversion!')|try { int result = 10 / 0; } catch (ArithmeticException e) { System.err.println("Division by zero!"); }|try { connectToDatabase(); } catch (SQLException e) { logError(e); }
title: Try-Catch Block

definition: An optional part of a `try-catch` (or `try-except`) construct whose code is guaranteed to execute, regardless of whether an exception was thrown, caught, or if the `try` block completed successfully. It is typically used for crucial cleanup operations like closing files or releasing resources.
examples: try: file = open('data.txt', 'r') finally: if file: file.close()|try { connection = openDb(); // ... } catch (Exception e) { // ... } finally { if (connection != null) connection.close(); }
title: Finally Block

definition: The act of explicitly signaling that an exceptional event or error has occurred during program execution by creating an exception object and raising it. This action interrupts the normal flow of control and transfers it to the nearest appropriate exception handler in the call stack.
examples: throw new IllegalArgumentException("Input must be positive.");|raise ValueError("Age cannot be negative.")|if (denominatior == 0) { throw new DivideByZeroException(); }
title: Throwing Exception

definition: An exception that is thrown during program execution but is not handled by any `catch` (or `except`) block within the current call stack. When an uncaught exception occurs, it typically causes the program to terminate abruptly, often displaying a stack trace and an error message.
examples: A Java program crashing with an unhandled `NullPointerException` because no `catch` block was present to manage it.|A Python script exiting due to an unhandled `IndexError` when trying to access an out-of-bounds list element.|A web server process terminating due to an unhandled exception in request processing.
title: Uncaught Exception

definition: A traditional error handling mechanism where a function returns an integer or enumerated value to indicate the success or failure of an operation, and if failure, the specific nature of the error. The caller is then responsible for explicitly checking this code and reacting accordingly.
examples: int result = system_call(); if (result == -1) { printf("Error: %s\n", strerror(errno)); }|HTTP status codes (e.g., 200 OK, 404 Not Found) are a form of error/status codes.|Older C APIs often returned 0 for success and non-zero for various error conditions.
title: Error Code (Error Handling)

definition: A feature that allows for the decomposition of values based on their structure or type, often combined with conditional logic. It provides a concise and expressive way to handle different data shapes, enumerations, or complex nested structures, improving code readability and safety.
title: Pattern Matching (Programming)

definition: A conditional statement placed at the beginning of a function or block that immediately exits or returns if certain preconditions are not met. It is used to simplify complex nested `if-else` logic by handling edge cases early, which improves readability and reduces indentation.
title: Guard Clause

definition: A memory allocation strategy where local variables, function parameters, and return addresses are stored on the program's call stack. This allocation is extremely fast and automatic, with memory being automatically deallocated when the function returns and its stack frame is popped.
examples: int x = 5; // 'x' is typically stack-allocated inside a function|void func(int arg1) { int local_var = 10; } // 'arg1' and 'local_var' are stack-allocated|Return addresses of function calls are stored on the stack.
title: Stack Allocation

definition: A memory allocation strategy where memory is dynamically allocated at runtime from a large pool called the heap, typically for objects whose lifetimes extend beyond the scope of a single function. This memory must be explicitly deallocated by the programmer (e.g., `free`, `delete`) or automatically by a garbage collector.
examples: MyClass obj = new MyClass(); // 'obj' object is heap-allocated in Java/C#|int* arr = (int*)malloc(10 * sizeof(int)); // Array allocated on heap in C|Python lists and dictionaries are typically heap-allocated.
title: Heap Allocation

definition: An automatic memory management process that identifies and reclaims memory occupied by objects that are no longer referenced or reachable by the program. It relieves programmers from manual memory deallocation, significantly reducing common memory errors like leaks and dangling pointers.
examples: The Java Virtual Machine's garbage collector automatically cleans up unused objects.|Python's interpreter uses reference counting and a generational collector for memory management.|JavaScript engines (like V8) employ garbage collection to manage heap memory for objects.
title: Garbage Collection (GC)

definition: A two-phase garbage collection algorithm. In the 'mark' phase, the collector traverses the object graph starting from root references to identify all reachable (live) objects. In the 'sweep' phase, it then iterates through the entire heap, reclaiming memory from all unmarked (unreachable) objects and making it available for future allocations.
examples: Many early JVMs or CLR implementations used variations of Mark-Sweep.|The Go language's garbage collector employs a concurrent tri-color mark-sweep algorithm.|A basic Mark-Sweep collector might experience 'fragmentation' of the heap after repeated sweeps.
title: Mark-Sweep Garbage Collection

definition: A garbage collection algorithm that divides the heap into two or more regions, typically called 'from-space' and 'to-space'. During collection, it copies all live objects from the 'from-space' to the 'to-space', compacting them contiguously, and then the entire 'from-space' is discarded. This method naturally prevents fragmentation.
examples: Used extensively in generational GCs for collecting the 'young generation' (e.g., in HotSpot JVM's Parallel Scavenge collector).|Some functional programming language runtimes, like Scheme, frequently employ copying collectors.|The Cheney's algorithm is a well-known copying garbage collection technique.
title: Copying Garbage Collection

definition: An optimization strategy for garbage collection based on the 'weak generational hypothesis', which states that most objects die young, and old objects are likely to stay alive longer. The heap is divided into different generations (e.g., young, old), with young generations collected more frequently using faster algorithms, while older generations are collected less often using more robust but slower algorithms.
examples: Java's HotSpot JVM uses distinct 'Young' and 'Old' generations for its garbage collection.|The .NET Common Language Runtime (CLR) garbage collector employs a generational approach.|Python's garbage collector, while primarily reference counting, also includes a generational component to collect cyclic references.
title: Generational Garbage Collection

definition: A garbage collection technique where each object maintains a count of references pointing to it. When the reference count drops to zero, the object is considered unreachable and its memory is automatically reclaimed. This method is relatively simple but cannot collect cyclic data structures unless augmented with other techniques.
examples: C++ `std::shared_ptr` uses reference counting.|Python's default garbage collector primarily uses reference counting.|Swift's Automatic Reference Counting (ARC) manages memory for class instances.
semantic_tags: Memory Management|Garbage Collection|Automatic Memory Management|Heap|Cyclic References
title: Reference Counting Garbage Collection

definition: A set of objects that are directly accessible by the running program without traversing other objects. These roots typically include global variables, objects on the call stack, and CPU registers, forming the starting points for tracing garbage collectors to identify all reachable objects.
examples: A global variable holding a reference to an object.|A local variable within an active function on the call stack.|An active CPU register containing a pointer to a heap object.
title: Garbage Collector Root

definition: An error that occurs when a program attempts to access the memory location pointed to by a null pointer. Since a null pointer does not point to a valid object, this operation typically results in a runtime error, such as a segmentation fault or access violation, leading to program termination.
examples: In C: `int* ptr = NULL; *ptr = 10;`|In Java: `MyObject obj = null; obj.callMethod();`|Accessing an element of an uninitialized `Optional` in languages that provide them without first checking for its presence.
title: Null Pointer Dereference

definition: A security vulnerability and program error where a program attempts to write data beyond the allocated boundaries of a fixed-size buffer. This overwrites adjacent memory locations, potentially corrupting data, crashing the program, or enabling arbitrary code execution if exploited.
examples: Using `strcpy` in C with a source string longer than the destination buffer.|Writing past the end of a C-style array declared on the stack.|The `gets()` function in C is notoriously unsafe due to its inability to prevent buffer overflows.
title: Buffer Overflow

definition: A memory corruption vulnerability that occurs when a program attempts to access memory after it has been freed. The freed memory might subsequently be reused for another purpose, leading to unpredictable behavior, data corruption, or even arbitrary code execution if the new data is manipulated.
examples: Freeing memory with `free(ptr)` in C and then later dereferencing `ptr` again, even if `ptr` now points to invalid or reallocated memory.|A pointer becoming 'dangling' after its target object is deallocated.
semantic_tags: Memory Safety|Dangling Pointer|Heap Corruption|Security Vulnerability|C/C++|Memory Error
title: Use-After-Free

definition: A memory corruption vulnerability that occurs when a program attempts to free the same block of dynamically allocated memory twice. This can lead to heap corruption, program crashes, or security vulnerabilities where an attacker could exploit the corrupted heap metadata to gain control.
examples: Calling `free(ptr)` twice on the same pointer `ptr` without reallocating memory between the calls.|A scenario where an error handling path inadvertently calls a deallocation function that has already been executed.
semantic_tags: Memory Safety|Heap Corruption|Security Vulnerability|C/C++|Memory Error|Resource Management
title: Double Free

definition: The property of a programming language or system that ensures memory accesses are always valid and controlled, preventing common errors like buffer overflows, null pointer dereferences, and use-after-free vulnerabilities. Languages with strong memory safety typically employ mechanisms like bounds checking, garbage collection, or ownership systems.
examples: Rust achieves memory safety at compile time using its borrow checker and ownership system.|Java and Python achieve memory safety at runtime through garbage collection and bounds checks.|C and C++ are generally not memory safe by default and require careful programming practices or external tools to ensure safety.
semantic_tags: Programming Language Design|Security|Robustness|Memory Management|Type Safety|Runtime Errors
title: Memory Safety

definition: A compile-time static analysis tool, notably found in Rust, that enforces a set of rules for how references (borrows) to data can be used. It ensures memory safety without a garbage collector by guaranteeing that all borrows are valid and that data is not simultaneously mutable and aliased, preventing data races and common memory errors.
examples: The Rust compiler refusing to compile code where two mutable references to the same data exist simultaneously.|Preventing a `use-after-free` by ensuring a reference does not outlive the data it points to.
title: Borrow Checker

definition: A core concept, particularly central to Rust, where each value in memory has a single 'owner' responsible for its lifetime and deallocation. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is automatically dropped, preventing use-after-free and double-free errors by establishing clear rules for data management.
examples: In Rust, `let s = String::from("hello");` declares `s` as the owner of the string data, which is freed when `s` goes out of scope.|When a value is 'moved' in Rust, ownership is transferred, and the original owner can no longer access the data.|The concept underpins Rust's ability to achieve memory safety without a garbage collector.
title: Ownership (Memory Management)

definition: A programming idiom, primarily in C++, where resource management (like memory, file handles, mutexes, network sockets) is tied to the lifetime of an object. Resources are acquired in the constructor of an object and automatically released in its destructor, ensuring proper cleanup even in the presence of exceptions or early returns.
examples: C++ `std::unique_ptr` managing dynamically allocated memory.|`std::lock_guard` ensuring a mutex is unlocked when the guard object goes out of scope.|`std::fstream` automatically closing a file when the stream object is destroyed.
title: RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization)

definition: Distinct areas within a process's virtual address space, each serving a specific purpose for storing different types of program data and instructions. Common regions include the code (text) segment for executable instructions, the data segment for global/static variables, the heap for dynamic memory allocation, and the stack for local variables and function call information.
examples: Executable machine instructions of `main()` residing in the Code Segment.|A global variable `static int count = 0;` stored in the Data Segment.|Memory allocated by `malloc()` or `new` residing on the Heap.|Local variables of a function and return addresses stored on the Stack.
normalized_name: memory region e g code data heap stack
semantic_tags: Virtual Memory|Process Memory|Operating System|Runtime Environment|Memory Layout|Address Space
title: Memory Region (e.g., Code, Data, Heap, Stack)

definition: A data structure pushed onto the call stack whenever a function or subroutine is invoked, containing all information relevant to that specific function call. This typically includes the function's local variables, arguments passed to it, the return address to the caller, and saved register values.
examples: When `functionA()` calls `functionB(arg)`, an activation record for `functionB` is pushed onto the stack, containing `arg` and `functionB`'s local variables.|During recursion, multiple activation records for the same function are stacked.|The stack pointer (SP) and frame pointer (FP) registers are used to manage activation records.
semantic_tags: Call Stack|Function Call|Local Variables|Return Address|Stack Pointer|Runtime Environment
title: Activation Record (Stack Frame)

definition: The ability of different parts of a program or multiple programs to make progress independently, often by interleaving their execution over time on a single processor or by running truly simultaneously on multiple processors. It deals with managing multiple tasks that *appear* to run at the same time to achieve better responsiveness or throughput.
examples: A web server handling multiple client requests by switching between them.|A graphical user interface remaining responsive while performing a background data load.|An operating system running multiple applications concurrently on a single CPU core.
title: Concurrency (Concept)

definition: The actual simultaneous execution of multiple independent computations or program parts at the exact same instant, typically on multiple processor cores, machines, or hardware threads. It is a specific form of concurrency focused on achieving speedup by performing more work in less time through simultaneous execution.
examples: Performing a large matrix multiplication by distributing segments of the matrix across multiple CPU cores.|Rendering multiple frames of a video game simultaneously on a Graphics Processing Unit (GPU).|Running a parallel `for` loop where each iteration operates independently on a different core.
title: Parallelism (Concept)

definition: An independent execution environment provided by the operating system, encapsulating an entire running program with its own dedicated virtual memory space, resources (e.g., file handles, network connections), and execution state. Processes are isolated from each other by default and communicate only through specific inter-process communication (IPC) mechanisms.
examples: A running web browser application.|A text editor instance.|A command-line shell session.
title: Process (Operating System)

definition: A lightweight unit of execution within a process, sharing the same virtual memory space, open files, and other resources as other threads in that same process. Each thread, however, has its own program counter, stack, and register set, enabling finer-grained concurrency and parallelism within a single program.
examples: A web server process using multiple threads to handle different client requests concurrently.|A word processor application using one thread for GUI updates and another for background spell-checking.|Using `pthread_create` in C or `std::thread` in C++ to launch new threads.
title: Thread (Operating System)

definition: A type of thread managed entirely by the user-level runtime system or library, rather than by the operating system kernel. They are often cheaper to create and context-switch than OS threads, but their scheduling is typically cooperative, and they usually cannot utilize multiple CPU cores simultaneously without explicit runtime support, mapping multiple green threads to fewer OS threads.
examples: Go Goroutines are an example of green threads.|Erlang processes (which are not OS processes) are a form of green thread.|Early versions of Java's threading model used green threads.
title: Green Thread

definition: An even lighter-weight form of concurrency than threads, often user-managed and scheduled entirely cooperatively within a single OS thread. Fibers allow explicit control over scheduling and context switching, enabling very fine-grained and efficient task switching without kernel involvement, making them suitable for high-performance I/O operations.
examples: Microsoft Windows Fibers API for explicit cooperative multitasking.|Boost.Fiber library in C++.|Many async/await implementations abstract underlying state-machine based cooperative concurrency which can be seen as fiber-like.
title: Fiber (Programming)

definition: A condition in concurrent programming where a particular process or thread repeatedly loses the race for a shared resource or CPU time, indefinitely preventing it from making progress. This can happen due to unfair scheduling policies, persistent contention, or biased resource allocation, effectively blocking the starved entity from ever executing.
examples: A low-priority thread continuously being preempted by higher-priority threads and never getting a chance to run.|A thread in a lock-free data structure continuously failing to acquire a compare-and-swap (CAS) operation due to high contention.|A reader thread in a read-write lock continually being denied access because new writer threads keep arriving.
title: Starvation (Concurrency)

definition: A synchronization primitive used in concurrent programming to prevent multiple threads or processes from simultaneously accessing a shared resource or critical section. Only one thread can acquire the mutex (short for mutual exclusion) at a time, ensuring exclusive access and preventing data races and inconsistent states.
examples: Using `pthread_mutex_lock` and `pthread_mutex_unlock` in C to protect a global variable.|`std::mutex` in C++ to guard access to shared data.|The `synchronized` keyword in Java or `lock` statement in C# to protect code blocks accessing shared state.
title: Mutual Exclusion (Mutex)

definition: A synchronization primitive that controls access to a common resource by using a counter. It allows a specified number of threads or processes to acquire access concurrently, blocking others until a resource becomes available.
examples: Limiting concurrent connections to a database to prevent overload.|Controlling access to a fixed-size buffer in a producer-consumer problem.|Java's `java.util.concurrent.Semaphore` class.
title: Semaphore (Programming)

definition: A synchronization primitive that enforces mutual exclusion, ensuring that only one thread or process can access a protected shared resource or critical section at any given time. It prevents race conditions by blocking other attempts to acquire the lock until it is released.
examples: Protecting a shared counter variable in a multi-threaded application.|Using the `synchronized` keyword in Java or `threading.Lock` in Python.|Database row locking to prevent concurrent updates to the same record.
title: Lock (Programming)

definition: A high-level synchronization construct that encapsulates shared data and the procedures that operate on that data, ensuring only one process or thread can be active within the monitor at any given time. It typically combines mutual exclusion with condition variables for inter-process communication and waiting.
examples: Java objects used with the `synchronized` keyword, where each object implicitly acts as a monitor.|C# `Monitor` class methods like `Enter`, `Exit`, `Wait`, `Pulse`.|Hoare or Brinch Hansen monitors as conceptual models in concurrent programming.
title: Monitor (Concurrency)

definition: An operation that appears to occur instantaneously and indivisibly from the perspective of other threads or processes. It either completes entirely and successfully, or has no effect at all, preventing partial updates or race conditions on shared data.
examples: Reading or writing a single machine word on most CPU architectures.|Using `Interlocked.Increment` in C# or `std::atomic<int>::fetch_add` in C++.|Compare-and-swap (CAS) operations for lock-free data structures.
title: Atomic Operation (Concurrency)

definition: A property of a program, function, or data structure that ensures it behaves correctly and produces consistent results when executed concurrently by multiple threads. Thread-safe code prevents data corruption and unexpected behavior through proper synchronization mechanisms.
examples: A stateless function that operates only on its input parameters and local variables is inherently thread-safe.|Java's `ConcurrentHashMap` which is designed to be thread-safe for concurrent access.|Protecting shared mutable state with locks or mutexes to ensure atomicity of operations.
title: Thread Safety

definition: A function that can be safely interrupted during its execution and then called again (re-entered) by another thread or interrupt handler before its previous invocation has completed, without causing data corruption or incorrect behavior. This implies that the function does not rely on non-local static or global variables that might be modified.
examples: Many standard library mathematical functions like `sin()` or `cos()`.|A pure function that only operates on its arguments and local variables stored on the stack.|Recursive functions that avoid modifying global state and manage their state on the call stack.
semantic_tags: Concurrency|Thread Safety|Pure Function|Interrupt Handling|Global State|Side Effects
title: Reentrant Function

definition: A property of an operation such that executing it multiple times produces the same result as executing it once. Subsequent identical calls have no further effect beyond the initial execution, preventing unintended side effects from repetition.
