definition: DHCP is a network management protocol used on Internet Protocol (IP) networks for dynamically assigning IP addresses and other communication parameters to devices connected to the network. It automates the configuration process for new and existing hosts, simplifying network administration.
examples: A new laptop connecting to a Wi-Fi network receives an IP address, subnet mask, default gateway, and DNS server addresses automatically from a DHCP server.|Most home routers include a built-in DHCP server.
title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP)

definition: DHCP Discover is the first message in the DHCP DORA process, broadcast by a client that is searching for a DHCP server on the network. The client sends this message to identify any available DHCP servers that can offer an IP address.
examples: When a newly booted PC without an IP address starts up, it sends a 'DHCP Discover' packet to the broadcast address (255.255.255.255).|A network sniffer would show a 'DHCP Discover' packet originating from an unconfigured client's MAC address.
title: DHCP Discover

definition: A DHCP Offer is a response from a DHCP server to a DHCP Discover message, proposing an available IP address and other configuration parameters to the client. The server also temporarily reserves the offered IP address for the client.
examples: A DHCP server, upon receiving a Discover message, sends a 'DHCP Offer' to the client, proposing IP address 192.168.1.100 along with its subnet mask and default gateway.|Multiple DHCP servers might send an 'Offer' if present on the same network segment.
title: DHCP Offer

definition: A DHCP Request is a message sent by a DHCP client to either formally accept a specific DHCP server's offer (if multiple offers were received) or to renew an existing IP address lease. It's the client's explicit confirmation of the desired IP configuration.
examples: A client, having received an 'Offer', sends a 'DHCP Request' back to the chosen server to confirm acceptance of the proposed IP 192.168.1.100.|A computer whose IP lease is halfway expired will send a 'DHCP Request' to renew it with its current server.
title: DHCP Request

definition: A DHCP ACK (Acknowledgment) is a DHCP server's final message, confirming the IP address lease and all configuration parameters to the client. This message signals the successful completion of the DHCP DORA process, and the client can now use the assigned IP address.
examples: After receiving a 'DHCP Request', the server sends a 'DHCP ACK' to finalize the lease of IP address 192.168.1.100 to the client.|If a client's `ipconfig` or `ifconfig` command shows a valid IP, it means a DHCP ACK was successfully received.
title: DHCP ACK

definition: A DHCP NAK (Negative Acknowledgment) is a DHCP server's message sent to a client if its DHCP Request is invalid or cannot be fulfilled. This might occur if the requested IP address is no longer available, is outside the server's scope, or belongs to a different network.
examples: A client attempts to renew an IP address that the server has already reassigned, prompting the DHCP server to respond with a 'DHCP NAK'.|If a client receives a NAK, it must restart the DHCP DORA process with a new DHCP Discover.
title: DHCP NAK

definition: A DHCP Relay Agent is a network device, typically a router, that forwards DHCP messages between clients and servers located on different IP subnets. It allows a single DHCP server to serve clients across multiple broadcast domains, preventing the need for a DHCP server on every subnet.
examples: A router configured with 'ip helper-address 192.168.10.5' forwards DHCP Discover broadcasts from clients on subnet 192.168.20.0/24 to the DHCP server at 192.168.10.5.|Without a DHCP relay, clients on a remote subnet would not be able to find a DHCP server located on a different subnet.
title: DHCP Relay Agent

definition: ARP is a protocol used by the Internet Protocol (IP) for mapping an IP address to a physical machine address, such as an Ethernet MAC address, on a local area network. ARP is essential for local network communication between devices, allowing them to send data frames to each other.
examples: A host wants to send an IP packet to another host on the same subnet but only knows its IP address; ARP finds the corresponding MAC address.|The `arp -a` command on Windows displays the ARP cache, showing IP-to-MAC mappings.
title: Address Resolution Protocol (ARP)

definition: An ARP Request is a broadcast message sent by a device on a local network to discover the MAC address associated with a specific IP address. The message is sent to all devices on the segment, asking the owner of the target IP to reply with its MAC address.
examples: A computer uses `arp -d` to clear its ARP cache, then pings a local device, triggering an 'ARP Request' for the target's MAC address.|An ARP request packet typically contains the sender's IP and MAC, and the target's IP, with the target MAC address set to all zeros.
title: ARP Request

definition: An ARP Reply is a unicast message sent by a device in response to an ARP Request, providing its own MAC address to the requesting device. This allows the requester to update its ARP cache with the IP-to-MAC mapping and send subsequent IP packets to the correct physical address.
examples: A router receives an 'ARP Request' for its IP address and sends an 'ARP Reply' containing its MAC address back to the requesting host.|Once an 'ARP Reply' is received, the requesting device can encapsulate IP packets into Ethernet frames with the correct destination MAC address.
title: ARP Reply

definition: Proxy ARP is a technique where a router or host responds to ARP requests for IP addresses that are not on its local network segment, effectively acting as a proxy for the actual owner of the IP. It helps devices on a segment reach devices on another segment without needing to know about routing or having a default gateway configured.
examples: A router configured for 'Proxy ARP' intercepts an ARP request for an IP on a different subnet and replies with its own MAC address, then routes the traffic to the actual destination.|It can be used in specific scenarios to simplify IP configuration on hosts or allow communication between subnets without full routing table knowledge on the end device.
title: Proxy ARP

definition: Gratuitous ARP is an ARP request or reply that is not prompted by an ARP request, typically sent by a device to announce its presence and IP-to-MAC mapping on the network. It is used for detecting duplicate IP addresses, updating other devices' ARP caches after an interface comes online, or when an IP address changes.
examples: A server powers on and sends a 'Gratuitous ARP' to inform other devices of its IP and MAC, and to detect if another device is already using its IP address.|Upon a failover in a high-availability cluster, the newly active node sends a 'Gratuitous ARP' for the shared virtual IP address to update switches and hosts.
title: Gratuitous ARP

definition: ICMP is a network layer protocol used for sending error messages and operational information, such as whether a host is reachable or if a service is unavailable. It is fundamental for network diagnostics and reporting problems with IP packet delivery, though it does not carry application data.
examples: The `ping` command uses ICMP Echo Request/Reply messages to test network connectivity.|An 'Destination Host Unreachable' message received when trying to access a website is an ICMP error notification.
title: Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP)

definition: An ICMP Echo Request is an ICMP message sent by a source host to a destination host to test connectivity and measure the round-trip time between them. This message is the primary mechanism utilized by the `ping` utility.
examples: Running `ping 8.8.8.8` sends a series of 'ICMP Echo Request' packets to Google's public DNS server.|Network troubleshooting often starts by sending an 'ICMP Echo Request' to verify basic reachability of a device.
title: ICMP Echo Request

definition: An ICMP Echo Reply is an ICMP message sent by a destination host in response to an ICMP Echo Request, indicating that the destination is reachable and functioning. It completes the round-trip measurement for connectivity tests and is crucial for `ping` to report success.
examples: Upon receiving an 'ICMP Echo Request', a responsive host sends an 'ICMP Echo Reply' back to the source, confirming its presence.|The 'reply from 192.168.1.1: bytes=32 time=5ms TTL=64' output from a `ping` command indicates successful receipt of an 'ICMP Echo Reply'.
title: ICMP Echo Reply

definition: An ICMP Redirect is an ICMP message sent by a router to a host, informing the host that it should use a different router (a more optimal one) for future traffic to a specific destination network. It helps optimize host routing tables by guiding hosts to the most efficient gateway on their segment.
examples: A host attempts to send packets to a remote network via Router A, but Router A realizes Router B is a more direct path for that specific destination and sends an 'ICMP Redirect' to the host, instructing it to use Router B instead.|If a host's traffic repeatedly goes through a suboptimal path, an ICMP Redirect can suggest a better first-hop router.
title: ICMP Redirect

definition: Routing is the process of selecting the optimal path across one or more networks for data packets to travel from their source to their destination. It involves routers making decisions based on routing tables to forward traffic to the next hop.
examples: A router receiving an IP packet and consulting its routing table to determine which interface to send it out of.|Google Maps calculating the best driving route from point A to point B, considering real-time traffic and road conditions.|A corporate network where routers use OSPF to find the most efficient path between different branch offices.
semantic_tags: Path Selection|Next Hop|Network Traffic|Router|IP Routing|Data Transmission
title: Routing (Networking)

definition: Forwarding is the actual process of moving a packet from an incoming interface of a network device (like a router or switch) to an outgoing interface. This decision is based on the information derived from the routing (control plane) process and stored in the forwarding information base (FIB).
examples: A router physically sending an Ethernet frame out of its GigabitEthernet0/1 port after consulting its forwarding table.|A Layer 2 switch looking up a MAC address in its MAC address table to send an incoming frame to the correct destination port.|A packet being processed by an ASIC (Application-Specific Integrated Circuit) on a high-performance router for fast data plane switching.
title: Forwarding (Networking)

definition: A routing table is a data table stored in a router or a networked computer that lists all known network destinations, the associated next-hop addresses, and the outgoing interfaces required to reach those destinations. Routers use this table to make forwarding decisions for incoming packets.
examples: The output of the `show ip route` command on a Cisco router, displaying directly connected networks, static routes, and dynamically learned routes.|The information displayed by `netstat -r` or `route print` on a Windows or Linux operating system, showing local routing entries.|A router having an entry `192.168.2.0/24 via 10.0.0.2, GigabitEthernet0/1` in its table.
semantic_tags: Router Memory|Network Paths|Next Hop|Destination Network|Route Metrics|FIB
title: Routing Table

definition: Static routing is a method of routing where network administrators manually configure and maintain routes in a router's routing table. These routes remain fixed unless manually changed, offering simplicity and security for small, stable networks.
examples: Configuring `ip route 192.168.2.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.0.2` on a router to manually direct traffic for the 192.168.2.0/24 network via next-hop 10.0.0.2.|Setting a default gateway on an end-host or router, which is a form of static route for all unknown destinations.|Using static routes in a stub network where there is only one exit point.
semantic_tags: Manual Configuration|Fixed Routes|Administrator Defined|Network Control|Default Route
title: Static Routing

definition: Dynamic routing is a method that uses routing protocols to automatically discover, maintain, and update routing tables in response to network topology changes. Routers exchange routing information with each other to adapt to network failures or additions.
examples: Routers running OSPF exchanging link-state advertisements to build a common topology database.|EIGRP routers sending hello packets and sharing route updates to find optimal paths and quickly react to link failures.|BGP routers peer with each other to exchange routes between different autonomous systems on the Internet.
title: Dynamic Routing

definition: Distance-vector routing is a class of dynamic routing protocols where each router periodically exchanges its entire routing table with its directly connected neighbors. The best path to a destination is determined by its 'distance' (metric) and the 'vector' (next-hop router) provided by a neighbor.
examples: RIP (Routing Information Protocol) where routers periodically send their full routing table to neighbors, using hop count as the metric.|EIGRP, although advanced, fundamentally operates on a distance-vector principle by relying on neighbors' reported distances.|A router advertising 'I can reach network X with a cost of 5' to its neighbor, and the neighbor adds 1 to that cost if it chooses that path.
title: Distance-Vector Routing

definition: Link-state routing is a class of dynamic routing protocols where each router builds a complete topological map of the entire network. This is achieved by exchanging small 'link-state advertisements' (LSAs) with all other routers within its area, and then running Dijkstra's algorithm to calculate the shortest path to every destination.
examples: OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) routers flooding LSAs throughout an area to build a consistent network topology database.|IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System) also operates as a link-state protocol, suitable for large ISP networks.|A router executing Dijkstra's Shortest Path First (SPF) algorithm on its link-state database to create a routing table.
title: Link-State Routing

definition: RIP is an older, distance-vector routing protocol that uses hop count as its metric to determine the best path to a destination. It is characterized by periodic full routing table updates to neighbors and a maximum hop count of 15, limiting its scalability to smaller networks.
examples: A small office or home network where RIP is configured on routers to learn routes with minimal configuration overhead.|Configuring `router rip` and `network 10.0.0.0` on a Cisco router to enable RIP for the 10.0.0.0/8 network.|A network where routers send their entire routing table every 30 seconds (RIPv1 default) to directly connected peers.
title: Routing Information Protocol (RIP)

definition: RIPv1 is the original, classful version of the Routing Information Protocol. It does not send subnet mask information in its routing updates and therefore does not support Variable Length Subnet Masking (VLSM) or Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR).
examples: A legacy network using only classful IP addressing schemes (e.g., 10.0.0.0/8, 172.16.0.0/16) where RIPv1 could function without subnetting issues.|A router configured with `router rip` without specifying `version 2`, which would default to RIPv1 behavior.|Periodic broadcast updates (255.255.255.255) containing only network addresses and hop counts, without subnet masks.
semantic_tags: Classful Routing|No VLSM|No Subnet Mask|Broadcast Updates|Legacy
title: RIPv1

definition: RIPv2 is an enhanced, classless version of the Routing Information Protocol that overcomes the limitations of RIPv1. It includes subnet mask information in its routing updates, enabling support for Variable Length Subnet Masking (VLSM) and Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR).
examples: A network with various subnetted IP addresses (e.g., 192.168.1.0/24 and 192.168.2.0/27), where RIPv2 can accurately advertise these distinct subnet masks.|Configuring `router rip` followed by `version 2` on a router to enable RIPv2 capabilities and multicast updates.|Routers sending routing updates to the multicast address 224.0.0.9, reducing the load on devices not running RIP.
title: RIPv2

definition: OSPF is a widely used link-state routing protocol that divides a large autonomous system into hierarchical areas for improved scalability and faster convergence. It uses Dijkstra's algorithm to calculate the shortest path to all destinations based on link costs.
examples: A large corporate network with multiple departments or branch offices segmented into OSPF areas (e.g., Area 0 for backbone, Area 1 for a regional office).|Configuring `router ospf 1` and `network 10.0.0.0 0.0.255.255 area 0` on a Cisco router to enable OSPF for a network range.|Routers within an OSPF area flooding Link State Advertisements (LSAs) to build a consistent topological database.
title: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)

definition: OSPFv2 is the version of OSPF specifically designed for routing IPv4 networks. It is the most common implementation of OSPF, supporting VLSM and CIDR, and is defined in RFC 2328.
examples: Most enterprise OSPF deployments today, routing IPv4 addresses across a corporate infrastructure.|Cisco IOS command `router ospf 1` by default configures OSPFv2 for IPv4 routing.|Routers using OSPFv2 exchanging IPv4 routing updates and building an SPF tree based on IPv4 prefixes.
title: OSPFv2

definition: OSPFv3 is the version of OSPF primarily designed to support IPv6 networks, although it was later enhanced to also support IPv4 through address families. It separates the addressing semantics from the routing protocol, making it more flexible.
examples: A network implementing native IPv6, where OSPFv3 is used to route IPv6 prefixes and build the IPv6 forwarding tables.|The command `ipv6 router ospf 1` on a Cisco router to enable OSPFv3 for IPv6 routing.|OSPFv3 using link-local addresses for neighbor discovery and forming adjacencies, while exchanging global IPv6 prefixes.
title: OSPFv3

definition: An OSPF Area is a logical grouping of routers and their connected networks within an OSPF autonomous system. It is used to segment the network, reducing the size of the link-state database, limiting the scope of LSA flooding, and minimizing the frequency of SPF calculations, which improves scalability.
examples: The `Area 0` (backbone area) connecting to `Area 1` (a regular standard area) via an Area Border Router (ABR).|A large data center network designated as OSPF Area 51, providing more efficient routing within the data center itself.|Stub areas or Totally Stubby Areas configured to reduce the number of routes in the routing table for edge routers.
title: OSPF Area

definition: LSAs are data packets used by OSPF routers to share information about their local links and network topology with other routers within the same OSPF area. Different LSA types describe various components of the network, such as router links, network segments, or external routes.
examples: A Type 1 (Router) LSA originated by every router, describing its active interfaces, cost, and neighbors.|A Type 2 (Network) LSA originated by a Designated Router (DR) on a multi-access network, describing all connected routers on that segment.|A Type 3 (Summary) LSA generated by an ABR to advertise routes between different OSPF areas.
semantic_tags: Topology Information|Network Updates|Router Database|Flooding|OSPF Protocol|Link-State Database
title: OSPF Link State Advertisements (LSAs)

definition: The OSPF Designated Router (DR) is a router elected on a multi-access network segment (like Ethernet) to reduce the number of adjacencies and LSA flooding. It serves as a central point for all routers on that segment to exchange link-state information, minimizing overhead.
examples: On an Ethernet LAN with five OSPF routers, one router is elected DR, and all other routers form adjacencies only with the DR and BDR, rather than with each other directly.|A router with the highest OSPF priority or, in case of a tie, the highest router ID, being elected as the DR for a segment.|The DR generating Type 2 (Network) LSAs to represent the multi-access segment and its connected routers.
semantic_tags: Multi-Access Network|LSA Flooding|Adjacency Management|Election Process|OSPF Optimization|Broadcast Network
title: OSPF Designated Router (DR)

definition: The OSPF Backup Designated Router (BDR) is a router elected on a multi-access network segment alongside the DR. Its primary role is to monitor the DR and immediately take over the DR's responsibilities if the DR fails, ensuring high availability and continuous routing operations without re-election.
examples: If the DR on an Ethernet segment becomes unreachable, the BDR automatically transitions to the DR role, and a new BDR is elected.|The router with the second-highest OSPF priority or router ID being elected as the BDR.|Both DR and BDR maintain full adjacencies with all other routers on the segment to ensure rapid failover.
title: OSPF Backup Designated Router (BDR)

definition: EIGRP is an advanced distance-vector routing protocol (originally Cisco proprietary, now open standard) known for its fast convergence and efficiency. It uses the Diffusing Update Algorithm (DUAL) to guarantee loop-free paths and supports unequal-cost load balancing, VLSM, and CIDR.
examples: A network predominantly using Cisco routers leveraging EIGRP for efficient and fast routing convergence across its internal network.|Configuring `router eigrp 1` and `network 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255` on a Cisco router to enable EIGRP for a specific network segment.|Routers forming neighbor adjacencies and exchanging route updates using Reliable Transport Protocol (RTP) to maintain topology tables.
normalized_name: enhanced interior gateway routing protocol eigrp
semantic_tags: Cisco Proprietary|Advanced Distance-Vector|DUAL Algorithm|Fast Convergence|Unequal Cost Load Balancing|RTP
title: Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP)

definition: DUAL (Diffusing Update Algorithm) is the core algorithm used by EIGRP to calculate the shortest, loop-free paths to all destinations. It maintains a topology table that includes both successor (best) routes and feasible successor (backup) routes, allowing for extremely fast convergence in the event of a primary path failure.
examples: When a primary EIGRP path fails, DUAL quickly identifies a pre-calculated feasible successor route from its topology table and immediately switches to it, preventing downtime.|A router using DUAL queries its neighbors if it cannot find a feasible successor for a failed route, ensuring a loop-free path discovery process.|DUAL's use of a 'feasibility condition' to guarantee that backup routes are indeed loop-free before being considered viable.
semantic_tags: Loop-Free Paths|Fast Convergence|Feasible Successor|Successor Route|EIGRP Core|Topology Table
title: EIGRP DUAL Algorithm

definition: BGP is the primary exterior gateway routing protocol (EGP) responsible for exchanging routing and reachability information between different autonomous systems (AS) on the Internet. It is a path-vector protocol, making routing decisions based on network policies, AS path attributes, and rulesets rather than just metrics.
examples: An Internet Service Provider (ISP) using BGP to advertise its customers' IP prefixes to other ISPs on the global Internet.|A large enterprise multihoming with two different ISPs, using BGP to control inbound and outbound traffic paths based on policy.|BGP speakers establishing TCP connections on port 179 to exchange routing updates and build the global routing table.
title: Border Gateway Protocol (BGP)

definition: Border Gateway Protocol version 4 is the current standard exterior gateway protocol used for exchanging routing and reachability information among autonomous systems (AS) on the Internet. It's a path-vector protocol that makes routing decisions based on paths, network policies, and a set of rules.
examples: An ISP using BGP-4 to announce its customer prefixes to other ISPs across the global internet.|Two large enterprises peering directly via BGP-4 to exchange specific routes without traversing an intermediate service provider.
semantic_tags: Routing Protocol|EGP|Internet Routing|Path Vector|Autonomous System|Policy Routing
title: BGP-4

definition: BGP attributes are parameters appended to a BGP route that provide additional information about the route, significantly influencing the BGP best path selection process. They are categorized as well-known mandatory, well-known discretionary, optional transitive, or optional non-transitive.
examples: `AS_PATH`: Lists the AS numbers the route has traversed to reach the destination.|`NEXT_HOP`: Specifies the IP address of the next-hop router to reach the advertised prefix.|`LOCAL_PREF`: A local preference value used to prefer an exit path out of the local AS.
title: BGP Attributes

definition: eBGP refers to BGP sessions established between BGP speakers located in different autonomous systems (AS). It is primarily used for exchanging routing information and establishing reachability between different organizations or ISPs across the internet.
examples: An enterprise router forming an eBGP session with its ISP's router to announce its public IP prefixes.|Two ISPs establishing an eBGP session at an Internet Exchange Point (IXP) to exchange routes and offer peering services.
title: eBGP (External BGP)

definition: iBGP refers to BGP sessions established between BGP speakers within the same autonomous system (AS). Its primary purpose is to ensure consistent routing information within an AS, often used to distribute eBGP-learned routes to all internal BGP routers.
examples: Two routers within an ISP's network forming an iBGP full mesh to propagate routes learned from external peers.|Using iBGP with route reflectors to scale route distribution within a large enterprise AS without requiring a full mesh.
title: iBGP (Internal BGP)

definition: A BGP peer (or neighbor) is a router that has established a BGP session with another router to exchange routing information. This session involves a TCP connection on port 179 and subsequent exchange of BGP messages.
examples: Router A establishing an iBGP peering relationship with Router B using their respective loopback addresses.|An eBGP peer relationship between two routers in different autonomous systems, connecting via their physical interface IPs.
title: BGP Peer

definition: The BGP Router ID is a 32-bit value, typically an IP address, that uniquely identifies a BGP router within an autonomous system. It is used in the BGP best path selection process to break ties and prevent routing loops.
examples: A router's loopback interface IP address (e.g., `10.0.0.1`) explicitly configured as its BGP Router ID.|If not explicitly configured, the highest IP address on any active interface can be chosen as the Router ID when BGP starts.
title: BGP Router ID

definition: The BGP Best Path Selection Algorithm is a deterministic process used by a BGP router to choose the single optimal path from multiple available paths to a destination prefix. It evaluates routes based on a predefined sequence of attributes, such as Weight, LOCAL_PREF, AS_PATH length, Origin code, and MED.
examples: A router receiving two routes to the same destination will prefer the path with a higher configured LOCAL_PREF attribute.|If LOCAL_PREF values are equal, the algorithm might then choose the path with the shortest AS_PATH length.
title: BGP Best Path Selection Algorithm

definition: BGP Communities are optional, transitive attributes that provide a way to group destinations and apply a common policy to them, independent of their AS. They are used for simplified route tagging and policy application across networks.
examples: `no-export` community: Prevents a route from being advertised to eBGP peers, keeping it within the local AS.|`internet` community: Advertises the route to all BGP peers.|Custom communities (e.g., `65000:100`) to tag routes for specific customer types or routing policies.
title: BGP Communities

definition: A BGP Route Reflector is a mechanism used to scale iBGP deployments by reducing the need for a full mesh of iBGP sessions within an AS. It allows a BGP router to advertise iBGP-learned routes to other iBGP peers, effectively breaking the standard iBGP split-horizon rule.
examples: In a large AS with 50 iBGP routers, Route Reflectors can reduce the number of required iBGP sessions from 1225 to a more manageable number.|A router configured with the command `neighbor 10.0.0.2 route-reflector-client` on a Cisco device to act as a Route Reflector.
title: BGP Route Reflector

definition: A BGP Confederation is an advanced iBGP scaling technique that divides a large autonomous system (AS) into multiple sub-autonomous systems, appearing as a single AS to the outside world. This reduces the number of iBGP sessions required by using eBGP-like peering between sub-ASes and iBGP within them.
examples: A large ISP using a confederation to manage its extensive internal network by breaking it into smaller, more manageable administrative domains.|Configuring `bgp confederation identifier <main_AS>` and `bgp confederation peers <sub_AS_numbers>` on a router.
title: BGP Confederation

definition: Multicast routing is a method of sending network traffic from a single source to multiple selected destinations simultaneously, forming a 'one-to-many' communication. It efficiently delivers data to groups of receivers that have explicitly joined a multicast group, avoiding unnecessary replication and flooding.
examples: Live video streaming services transmitting a single stream to multiple subscribed viewers (e.g., IPTV).|Online gaming servers sending game state updates to all active players in a session.|Financial market data distribution to interested trading terminals.
title: Multicast Routing

definition: Anycast addressing is a network addressing and routing method where data is routed to the 'nearest' or 'best' available service endpoint among a group of potential receivers identified by the same IP address. It is often used for redundancy, load distribution, and improved latency.
examples: Multiple DNS root servers around the world sharing the same IP address (e.g., `192.0.2.1`), directing users to the geographically closest server.|Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) using anycast to direct users to the closest server copy of requested content.
title: Anycast Addressing

definition: Unicast addressing is a one-to-one communication method where a packet is sent from a single source to a single specific destination device on a network. It is the most common and fundamental form of data transmission used in IP networks.
examples: A web browser requesting a page from a specific web server using its IP address.|Two computers exchanging files directly using FTP or SMB.|Your smartphone connecting to a single Wi-Fi access point for internet access.
title: Unicast Addressing

definition: Broadcast addressing is a one-to-all communication method where a packet is sent from a single source to all devices on a specific network segment or subnet. Devices typically listen for their own address and the broadcast address to receive relevant messages.
examples: An ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) request to discover the MAC address for a given IP address on the local network.|DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) discovery messages from a client looking for a DHCP server on the network.|Legacy LAN games sending presence announcements to all machines on the subnet.
title: Broadcast Addressing

definition: IP fragmentation is the process of breaking down an IP packet into smaller pieces (fragments) when its size exceeds the Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) of a network link it needs to traverse. This allows the packet to pass through links with smaller MTUs, with reassembly occurring at the destination.
examples: A large UDP packet (e.g., 2000 bytes) needing to cross an Ethernet link with a 1500-byte MTU, causing it to be fragmented.|A `ping` command with a large payload (e.g., `ping -s 2000 host`) on a network path having a smaller MTU, forcing fragmentation if the DF bit is not set.
title: IP Fragmentation

definition: Time To Live (TTL) is an 8-bit field in the IP header that specifies the maximum number of hops an IP packet can traverse before being discarded by a router. It prevents packets from looping indefinitely on a network, consuming resources and causing congestion.
examples: A `traceroute` command uses incrementally increasing TTL values to map the network path to a destination.|A packet starting with TTL=64 will have this value decremented by 1 at each router it crosses; if it reaches 0 before the destination, it is dropped.|DNS records also have a TTL value, indicating how long a DNS resolver should cache that record.
title: Time To Live (TTL)

definition: Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD) is a process that determines the largest Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) that can be used on the entire network path between two IP hosts without causing IP fragmentation. It typically works by sending packets with the 'Don't Fragment' (DF) bit set and reacting to 'Fragmentation Needed' ICMP messages.
examples: A TCP connection establishing its segment size after PMTUD has determined the path's effective MTU, preventing fragmentation.|A host sending a large packet with the DF bit set, receiving an ICMP Type 3, Code 4 message indicating the next-hop MTU, and then adjusting its sending size.
title: Path MTU Discovery

definition: The TCP Segment Header is a control block prepended to application data, containing essential information for reliable, ordered, and error-checked delivery of data over an IP network. Key fields include Source and Destination Ports, Sequence and Acknowledgement Numbers, Window Size, and Checksum.
examples: Source Port `80` (HTTP) and Destination Port `49152` (a client ephemeral port) indicating communication to a web server.|A Sequence Number of `12345` for the first byte of data in a segment, ensuring ordered delivery.|Flags like `SYN` for connection establishment, `ACK` for acknowledgment, and `FIN` for connection termination.
title: TCP Segment Header

definition: The UDP Segment Header is a minimal control block prepended to application data, providing connectionless, unreliable, and unordered datagram service over an IP network. It contains only Source and Destination Ports, Length, and an optional Checksum, offering efficiency over reliability.
examples: Source Port `53` (DNS client) and Destination Port `53` (DNS server) for a DNS query.|A UDP packet with a length field of `100` bytes, indicating the total size of the UDP header and its data.|The checksum field can be zero if checksumming is not utilized, common in environments with inherent link-layer error detection.
title: UDP Segment Header

definition: The TCP Checksum is a 16-bit field in the TCP header used for error detection, verifying the integrity of the TCP header, TCP data, and a pseudo-header derived from the IP header. It helps ensure that no bits have been accidentally altered during transmission across the network.
examples: If a single bit flip occurs in the TCP segment during transmission, the receiver's calculated checksum will not match the one in the header, indicating corruption and triggering retransmission.|The pseudo-header includes source and destination IP addresses, the protocol number, and TCP length, extending the checksum's coverage beyond just the TCP segment itself.
title: TCP Checksum

definition: The UDP checksum is an optional (but commonly used) 16-bit field in the UDP header used for error detection, allowing the receiver to determine if any bits in the UDP datagram (header and data) have been flipped during transmission.
examples: A DNS client sending a query to a DNS server, where a corrupted checksum would cause the server to drop the datagram.|An NTP client synchronizing its clock with a time server, relying on the checksum to ensure integrity of time packets.|Real-time voice over IP (VoIP) traffic, where minor packet loss is acceptable but corrupted packets should be discarded.
title: UDP Checksum

definition: The TCP three-way handshake is a fundamental process used to establish a reliable, full-duplex TCP connection between a client and a server, involving the exchange of three segments: SYN, SYN-ACK, and ACK.
examples: A web browser initiating a connection to a web server (client sends SYN, server responds SYN-ACK, client sends ACK).|An SSH client connecting to an SSH server to establish a secure shell session.|An FTP client setting up a control connection with an FTP server.
title: TCP Three-Way Handshake

definition: TCP connection establishment is the overall process of initiating and setting up a logical end-to-end communication path between two hosts, primarily achieved through the three-way handshake, before any application data can be reliably exchanged.
examples: When a user clicks a link in a web browser, a TCP connection is established to the web server.|An email client establishing a connection to an SMTP server to send an email.|A database client setting up a connection to a database server to query data.
title: TCP Connection Establishment

definition: TCP connection termination is the process of gracefully closing an existing TCP connection, typically involving a four-way handshake (FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK) to ensure both sides have finished sending data and acknowledged receipt before tearing down the connection.
examples: Closing a web browser tab or navigating away from a secure site (HTTPS).|Exiting an SSH session, which closes the underlying TCP connection.|An FTP client sending a QUIT command to terminate a file transfer session.
title: TCP Connection Termination

definition: TCP flow control is a mechanism designed to prevent a fast sender from overwhelming a slower receiver by dynamically adjusting the sender's data transmission rate based on the receiver's available buffer space, advertised via the receive window.
examples: A server sending a large file to a client, where the client's slower processing or disk write speed dictates the transfer rate.|A video streaming service adjusting its send rate to match the viewer's device processing capabilities and available memory.|A client with limited buffer space informing the server to pause or slow down data transmission.
semantic_tags: TCP|Flow Control|Receiver Buffer|Sliding Window|Window Size|Buffer Management
title: TCP Flow Control

definition: TCP congestion control is a set of algorithms that aim to prevent network collapse by adapting the sender's transmission rate to the current network conditions, primarily by detecting and reacting to signs of congestion like packet loss or increased round-trip times.
examples: An internet router experiencing high traffic dropping packets, prompting TCP senders to reduce their window size.|Streaming video quality dynamically adjusting based on network load to prevent buffering.|Large-scale cloud data transfers efficiently utilizing shared network infrastructure without causing bottlenecks.
title: TCP Congestion Control

definition: Slow Start is a TCP congestion control algorithm phase where the congestion window (cwnd) begins at a small value and increases exponentially with each received acknowledgment, quickly probing for available network bandwidth until a congestion event occurs or a slow start threshold (ssthresh) is reached.
examples: The initial phase of any new TCP connection, where the sender rapidly increases its transmission rate.|After a TCP retransmission timeout, the congestion window is reset, and slow start recommences.|A large file download starting, with the download speed quickly accelerating until it hits a network limit.
title: Slow Start

definition: Congestion Avoidance is a TCP congestion control phase that follows Slow Start, where the congestion window (cwnd) increases linearly (additively) for each Round Trip Time (RTT), allowing a more conservative probe for additional bandwidth after the slow start threshold (ssthresh) has been met.
examples: A long-running data transfer (e.g., a large software update) maintaining a steady but slowly increasing throughput after initial connection.|When a TCP connection has found most of the available bandwidth and is carefully probing for more capacity.|Network traffic that adapts to subtle changes in network conditions without drastic fluctuations in transmission rate.
title: Congestion Avoidance (TCP)

definition: Fast Retransmit is a TCP congestion control enhancement that allows the sender to retransmit a lost segment without waiting for a retransmission timeout, by inferring packet loss from the receipt of three duplicate ACKs for the same unacknowledged segment.
examples: A client receiving segments 1, 2, 4, 5 and sending duplicate ACKs for segment 2 (missing 3), triggering the server to retransmit segment 3 quickly.|In a high-bandwidth, low-latency network, recovering from a single lost packet with minimal delay.|Gaming applications relying on quick recovery from minor packet loss to maintain a smooth experience.
title: Fast Retransmit

definition: Fast Recovery is a TCP congestion control algorithm used in conjunction with Fast Retransmit, which, upon detecting packet loss via duplicate ACKs, reduces the congestion window by half and enters a phase of additive increase, avoiding the drastic reset of slow start while data continues to be sent.
examples: A TCP connection experiencing occasional packet drops on a busy Wi-Fi network, where Fast Recovery helps maintain high throughput.|When a server quickly adapts to transient network congestion without completely pausing data transmission.|Enabling a continuous flow of data even with minor network disturbances, common in wide-area networks.
title: Fast Recovery

definition: TCP retransmission is the mechanism by which TCP ensures reliable data delivery by re-sending unacknowledged data segments, either after a retransmission timeout (RTO) or upon receiving multiple duplicate acknowledgments (Fast Retransmit), to recover from packet loss.
examples: Sending a large file over a lossy Wi-Fi connection, where lost segments are automatically retransmitted by TCP.|A network router drops a TCP segment due to congestion, and the sender retransmits it after a timeout.|Streaming video over a cellular network experiencing intermittent signal loss, with TCP ensuring missing frames are resent.
title: TCP Retransmission

definition: TCP BBR (Bottleneck Bandwidth and RTT) is a congestion control algorithm developed by Google that optimizes network throughput and minimizes latency by actively estimating the bottleneck bandwidth and round-trip time of the network path, rather than solely reacting to packet loss.
examples: Google's services like YouTube and Google Cloud using BBR to deliver content more efficiently to users globally.|Data centers employing BBR to maximize data transfer rates across their internal networks.|Any application sensitive to both throughput and latency, such as high-frequency trading platforms, benefiting from BBR.
title: TCP BBR

definition: Multipath TCP (MPTCP) is an extension to TCP that enables a single TCP connection to simultaneously utilize multiple distinct network paths (e.g., Wi-Fi and cellular data), aggregating bandwidth, enhancing resilience, and improving performance.
examples: A smartphone downloading a large file using both its Wi-Fi and 4G/5G cellular connections concurrently.|Data centers using MPTCP to distribute traffic across redundant network links for improved fault tolerance and higher throughput.|Vehicular communication systems maintaining seamless connectivity by switching or combining multiple wireless interfaces.
title: Multipath TCP (MPTCP)

definition: Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) is a transport layer protocol that provides reliable, message-oriented data transfer with features such as multihoming, support for multiple independent data streams within a single association, and resilience against network failures.
examples: Signaling traffic in VoIP networks, such as SS7 over IP, where reliability and multi-streaming are crucial.|The Diameter protocol, used for authentication, authorization, and accounting (AAA) in mobile networks.|Applications requiring ordered delivery of messages but allowing head-of-line blocking only within independent streams.
title: Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP)

definition: A network socket is an endpoint of a bidirectional inter-process communication (IPC) flow across a computer network, defined by an IP address, a port number, and the protocol (e.g., TCP or UDP), enabling applications to send and receive data.
examples: A web server opening a listening socket on port 80 (HTTP) to accept incoming client connections.|A client application creating a socket to connect to a remote server's IP address and port.|Using Python's `socket` module to build network applications, like a simple chat client or server.
title: Socket (Networking)

definition: Multiplexing at the transport layer is the process of gathering data from multiple different application processes on a host and encapsulating it into segments, allowing these applications to share a single network connection using distinct port numbers.
examples: A single web server simultaneously handling HTTP requests from numerous clients, all via port 80.|Multiple applications (e.g., web browser, email client, chat app) on a computer sending data over the same physical network interface.|An operating system directing packets from various applications to be sent out over a single Ethernet cable.
title: Multiplexing (Transport Layer)

definition: Demultiplexing at the transport layer is the process of delivering incoming data segments from the network to the correct destination application process on a host, using the port numbers within the segment header to identify the target application.
examples: An operating system receiving an incoming IP packet and using the TCP/UDP port number to deliver it to the correct running application (e.g., web browser tab, game client).|A server receiving data and routing it to the specific service (e.g., HTTP server on port 80, SSH server on port 22).|An email client receiving new messages, with the OS using the destination port to direct the data to the email application.
semantic_tags: Transport Layer|Port Numbers|Destination Application|Data Delivery|Routing|Packet Processing
title: Demultiplexing (Transport Layer)

definition: Reliable data transfer (RDT) is a service model that guarantees the delivery of data without errors, loss, or duplication, and in the correct order, despite underlying unreliable network conditions, typically achieved through mechanisms like acknowledgments, retransmissions, and sequencing.
examples: TCP provides reliable data transfer for applications like web browsing (HTTP), email (SMTP), and file transfer (FTP).|A file synchronization service ensuring that all file changes are replicated accurately between devices.|A secure messaging application guaranteeing that messages are delivered exactly once and in the correct sequence.
title: Reliable Data Transfer

definition: Go-Back-N (GBN) is a sliding window protocol for reliable data transfer where the sender maintains a window of unacknowledged packets and, upon detecting a lost packet (e.g., via timeout), retransmits that lost packet along with all subsequent packets that were already sent.
examples: A simple data link layer protocol on a noisy channel where retransmitting a block of data is less complex than tracking individual losses.|Older satellite communication systems where the high latency makes selective retransmission less efficient.|A theoretical example of a reliable transport protocol in an educational setting to illustrate basic sliding window concepts.
title: Go-Back-N Protocol

definition: Selective Repeat (SR) is a sliding window protocol for reliable data transfer where the sender only retransmits specific packets that are detected as lost or corrupted, and the receiver accepts and buffers out-of-order packets, sending individual acknowledgments for correctly received segments.
examples: Modern wireless communication protocols, where packet loss is frequent and selective retransmission improves efficiency significantly.|High-speed data networks where retransmitting entire windows would severely reduce throughput.|TCP's SACK (Selective Acknowledgment) option, which allows TCP to behave more like Selective Repeat.
title: Selective Repeat Protocol

definition: A basic Automatic Repeat Request (ARQ) protocol where the sender transmits a single data frame and then waits for an acknowledgment (ACK) from the receiver before sending the next frame. This simple mechanism ensures reliable data transfer but is highly inefficient for links with high latency or low bandwidth.
examples: A sender transmitting one packet and waiting for its ACK, even if other packets are ready.|Theoretical explanation of reliable data transfer in educational settings.|A very slow, highly error-prone communication link where simplicity outweighs throughput.
title: Stop-and-Wait Protocol

definition: An Automatic Repeat Request (ARQ) protocol that allows a sender to transmit multiple data frames (a 'window' of data) without waiting for an acknowledgment for each one, thereby improving throughput. It uses a sequence numbering scheme and a window size to manage outstanding frames and ensures reliable, in-order delivery.
examples: TCP's use of a sliding window for reliable data transfer and flow/congestion control.|Go-Back-N protocol, where the sender retransmits all unacknowledged frames starting from the lost one.|Selective Repeat protocol, where only specific lost or corrupted frames are retransmitted.
title: Sliding Window Protocol

definition: In networking, the window size refers to the maximum amount of unacknowledged data that a sender is permitted to transmit before receiving an acknowledgment from the receiver. It is a critical parameter for flow control, preventing a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver, and also plays a role in congestion control.
examples: TCP's receive window, which the receiver advertises to control the rate of incoming data.|TCP's congestion window, dynamically adjusted by the sender based on network congestion.|A window size of 1 in the Sliding Window Protocol effectively reverts it to Stop-and-Wait.
title: Window Size (Networking)

definition: The total time it takes for a data packet to travel from a source to a destination and for an acknowledgment packet to be sent back to the source. RTT is a fundamental measure of network latency, impacting the perceived responsiveness of network applications.
examples: Pinging a server (e.g., `ping google.com`) and observing the `time=` value in milliseconds.|The delay experienced when clicking a link on a webpage until the new page begins to load.|VoIP calls experiencing noticeable lag due to high RTT between participants.
title: Round Trip Time (RTT)

definition: A measure of the maximum amount of data that can be in transit on a network link at any given time, calculated by multiplying the link's bandwidth by its Round Trip Time (RTT). It represents the 'volume' of the network pipe, indicating how much data can fill the path without being acknowledged.
examples: A 100 Mbps link with a 100ms RTT has a BDP of 100 Mbps * 0.1s = 10 Megabits (or 1.25 Megabytes).|Determining the optimal TCP window size to fully utilize a high-bandwidth, high-latency satellite link.|Calculating the buffer size needed for network devices to prevent packet loss on long-distance, fast connections.
title: Bandwidth-Delay Product

definition: A severe degradation of network performance that occurs when network congestion becomes so extreme that effective network throughput drops drastically, often approaching zero. It is characterized by excessive packet retransmissions, increased queueing delays, and routers dropping most incoming packets.
examples: The state of the early internet before the widespread adoption of TCP congestion control algorithms.|A network segment experiencing a denial-of-service (DoS) attack that overwhelms routers and links.|During peak traffic, a router's buffers becoming consistently full, leading to dropped packets and retransmissions that further exacerbate the problem.
title: Congestion Collapse

definition: A mechanism that allows network routers to signal impending congestion to end hosts by marking packets, rather than dropping them. This proactive notification enables ECN-aware senders to reduce their transmission rate before actual packet loss occurs, thus improving network efficiency and reducing retransmissions.
examples: A router seeing its queue build up might set the ECN bits in the IP header of incoming packets instead of dropping them.|A TCP sender receiving an ECN-marked packet interprets it as a signal of congestion and reduces its congestion window, similar to a packet loss event.|Enabling ECN in Linux kernel parameters for better TCP performance in congested networks.
title: Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN)

definition: An active queue management algorithm used in network routers to prevent congestion collapse by proactively dropping packets or marking them for Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) before queues become full. RED randomly drops packets based on a calculated average queue length and configured thresholds, aiming to signal congestion to senders early.
examples: A router's interface buffer configured with RED, starting to drop packets with a low probability when 50% full, and increasing that probability as it nears 100% capacity.|Network devices implementing RED to provide a smoother degradation of service under load rather than sudden drops.|Cisco routers using RED to manage buffer utilization and improve overall network responsiveness.
semantic_tags: Congestion Control|Active Queue Management|Packet Dropping|QoS|Router|Buffer Management
title: Random Early Detection (RED)

definition: An enhancement to the Random Early Detection (RED) algorithm that provides differentiated congestion management based on traffic type or priority. WRED applies different RED parameters, such as minimum and maximum thresholds and drop probabilities, to different classes of traffic (e.g., distinguished by IP precedence or DSCP values), allowing higher-priority traffic to experience less packet loss during congestion.
examples: A network router configured to assign lower WRED drop probabilities to Voice over IP (VoIP) traffic than to best-effort web browsing traffic.|Using WRED to protect critical business applications from congestion while allowing less critical traffic to be dropped first.|Implementing QoS policies in a network where video streaming packets are less likely to be dropped than file downloads during periods of high network load.
semantic_tags: Congestion Control|QoS|Differentiated Services|Active Queue Management|Router|Traffic Management
title: Weighted Random Early Detection (WRED)

definition: A set of rules and procedures that define how applications communicate and exchange data over a network. Operating at the highest layer of the TCP/IP or OSI model, these protocols provide high-level services directly to end-user applications, abstracting the underlying network complexities.
examples: HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) for web browsing and data exchange.|FTP (File Transfer Protocol) for transferring files between computers.|SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) for sending and receiving email.|DNS (Domain Name System) for translating domain names to IP addresses.
semantic_tags: OSI Model|TCP/IP Model|End-User Services|Network Services|Protocol Stack|Client-Server
title: Application Layer Protocol

definition: A distributed network architecture where individual participants, known as peers, act as both clients and servers to other peers, directly sharing resources and processing power without relying on a central server. This model promotes decentralization, scalability, and resilience.
examples: BitTorrent, a protocol for file sharing where users download and upload parts of files directly from/to other users.|Some Voice over IP (VoIP) applications like early Skype versions used P2P for direct calls.|Cryptocurrency networks like Bitcoin and Ethereum, where nodes directly validate and relay transactions.
title: Peer-to-Peer (P2P) Model

definition: A hierarchical and distributed naming system for computers, services, or any resource connected to the Internet or a private network. DNS translates human-readable domain names (e.g., `www.example.com`) into machine-readable numerical IP addresses (e.g., `192.0.2.1`), making internet navigation user-friendly.
examples: Translating `www.google.com` into its corresponding IPv4 or IPv6 address.|The lookup service that allows your web browser to find the server hosting a website.|Email servers using DNS to find the mail exchange (MX) records for a domain to deliver email.
semantic_tags: Naming Service|IP Address|Domain Name|Internet Foundation|Name Resolution|Distributed System
title: Domain Name System (DNS)

definition: The multi-step process by which a DNS client (resolver) queries various DNS servers to translate a human-readable domain name into its corresponding IP address. This typically involves an iterative or recursive series of queries starting from a root server, proceeding through Top-Level Domain (TLD) servers, and finally reaching authoritative name servers.
examples: When you type a website URL into a browser, your computer performs DNS resolution to find the server's IP address before initiating a connection.|Using command-line tools like `nslookup` or `dig` to trace the path of a DNS query.|A local DNS resolver caching results to speed up subsequent queries for popular domain names.
title: DNS Resolution

definition: Different categories of information stored in DNS zone files, each defining a specific type of resource or mapping associated with a domain name. These records are fundamental to how DNS functions, directing traffic and providing various services.
examples: `A` record: Maps a domain name to an IPv4 address (e.g., `example.com` to `192.0.2.1`).|`AAAA` record: Maps a domain name to an IPv6 address (e.g., `example.com` to `2001:0db8::1`).|`CNAME` record: Creates an alias from one domain name to another (e.g., `www.example.com` to `example.com`).|`MX` record: Specifies the mail server responsible for accepting email messages on behalf of a domain.
title: DNS Record Types

definition: The absolute top-level servers in the DNS hierarchy, forming the starting point for all DNS resolution queries that cannot be answered from cache. There are 13 logical root server names, managed by various organizations, which primarily direct requests to the appropriate Top-Level Domain (TLD) servers.
examples: When a DNS resolver doesn't know how to find `example.com`, it first asks a root server for the address of the `.com` TLD server.|The 'A.ROOT-SERVERS.NET' server, one of the 13 root server instances, responding with a list of `.com` TLD servers.|A DNS recursive resolver's initial query always targets a root server if it has no cached information about a domain.
semantic_tags: DNS Hierarchy|Internet Foundation|TLD|Name Resolution|Critical Infrastructure|Global DNS
title: DNS Root Servers

definition: Servers in the DNS hierarchy responsible for managing all the domain names under a specific top-level domain, such as `.com`, `.org`, `.net`, or country-code TLDs like `.uk`. They don't store individual host records but respond to queries by pointing to the authoritative name servers for the specific second-level domain (e.g., `google.com`).
examples: A TLD server for `.com` would respond to a query for `google.com` by providing the IP addresses of Google's authoritative name servers.|The `.org` TLD server listing the authoritative name servers for a non-profit organization's website.|The `.io` TLD server directing queries to the name servers of various tech startups using that domain.
