semantic_tags: DNS Hierarchy|Domain Name|TLD|Name Resolution|Authoritative Server|DNS Zone
title: DNS Top-Level Domain (TLD) Servers

definition: DNS servers that hold the definitive, original DNS records for a specific domain and are the ultimate source of truth for its DNS information. When a DNS resolver needs an IP address for a domain, it eventually queries the authoritative name servers for that domain to get the final answer.
examples: The name servers (e.g., `ns1.google.com`) that Google configures to host the `google.com` DNS records.|When you register a new domain name, you typically point it to your web host's or DNS provider's authoritative name servers.|A query for `www.example.com` will ultimately be answered directly by `example.com`'s authoritative name server.
semantic_tags: DNS|Domain Management|Name Resolution|Zone File|Truth Source|DNS Hosting
title: DNS Authoritative Name Servers

definition: DNS servers that handle a client's DNS query by performing all the necessary steps to find the IP address, including querying root, TLD, and authoritative servers on behalf of the client. They then return the final answer to the client and typically cache results to speed up future identical queries.
examples: Your Internet Service Provider's (ISP) DNS server, which your computer automatically uses for DNS lookups.|Public DNS services like Google Public DNS (`8.8.8.8`) or Cloudflare DNS (`1.1.1.1`) acting as recursive resolvers.|A local network router often functions as a DNS recursive resolver for devices on the local network.
title: DNS Recursive Resolvers

definition: A protocol for performing remote Domain Name System (DNS) resolution via the HTTPS protocol, encrypting DNS traffic between the client and the DoH resolver. By encapsulating DNS queries within encrypted HTTPS traffic, DoH enhances user privacy, prevents eavesdropping, and mitigates DNS manipulation.
examples: Configuring a web browser (e.g., Firefox, Chrome) to use a DoH service like Cloudflare (1.1.1.1) or Google Public DNS (8.8.8.8).|Using a DoH-enabled proxy or client application to secure DNS queries over an untrusted network.|Organizations deploying DoH to prevent internal DNS queries from being intercepted or modified by external threats.
title: DNS over HTTPS (DoH)

definition: A protocol for encrypting DNS queries and responses using the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol, typically over a dedicated port (853). Similar to DoH, DoT aims to enhance user privacy and prevent DNS spoofing by establishing an encrypted connection between the DNS client and the DoT server, thereby protecting DNS traffic from eavesdropping and tampering.
examples: Android P and newer versions supporting DoT for system-wide private DNS resolution.|Configuring a network router or firewall to forward DNS queries to a DoT server (e.g., `dns.google` on port 853).|Using a command-line utility or daemon that supports DoT to secure DNS lookups on a Linux system.
title: DNS over TLS (DoT)

definition: HTTP is an application-layer protocol for transmitting hypermedia documents, such as HTML, forming the foundation of data communication for the World Wide Web. It operates as a stateless, request-response protocol between a client and a server, typically over TCP.
examples: A web browser requesting an HTML page from a server.|A client fetching an image or a JavaScript file from a website.|Submitting data via an HTML form to a web server.
title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP)

definition: HTTPS is an extension of HTTP that encrypts communication between a web browser and a website server using SSL/TLS protocols. It ensures data confidentiality, integrity, and server authentication, protecting sensitive information exchanged over the internet.
examples: Accessing online banking websites (e.g., `https://bank.com`).|Secure login pages where usernames and passwords are submitted.|E-commerce checkout processes to protect payment information.
title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS)

definition: HTTP methods, also known as HTTP verbs, are standardized actions used to indicate the desired operation to be performed on the target resource identified by a given URL. They define the semantics of a request, enabling clients to interact with web resources.
examples: `GET /products` (retrieve all products from the server).|`POST /products` with a JSON body (create a new product on the server).|`PUT /products/123` with a JSON body (update product with ID 123).|`DELETE /products/123` (remove product with ID 123 from the server).
normalized_name: http methods get post put delete
title: HTTP Methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE)

definition: HTTP Status Codes are three-digit numbers returned by a server in response to an HTTP client's request, indicating whether a particular HTTP request has been successfully completed, and if not, why. They are grouped into five classes: Informational (1xx), Success (2xx), Redirection (3xx), Client Error (4xx), and Server Error (5xx).
examples: `200 OK` (Request successfully processed).|`404 Not Found` (Resource does not exist).|`500 Internal Server Error` (Server encountered an unexpected condition).|`301 Moved Permanently` (Resource has been permanently moved to a new URL).
title: HTTP Status Codes

definition: HTTP/2 is a major revision of the HTTP network protocol designed to improve web performance by addressing limitations of HTTP/1.1. Key features include multiplexing multiple requests over a single TCP connection, header compression, and server push, making web applications faster and more robust.
examples: Modern web browsers loading complex websites that utilize HTTP/2 for faster page rendering.|Serving multiple CSS, JavaScript, and image files concurrently over one connection.|A server proactively sending resources to a client that it anticipates the client will need.
title: HTTP/2 Protocol

definition: HTTP/3 is the third major version of the HTTP protocol, built atop QUIC rather than TCP, aiming to further enhance web performance and reliability, especially on unreliable networks. It addresses head-of-line blocking at the transport layer, a common issue in HTTP/2 due to TCP.
examples: Google services and Cloudflare-enabled websites leveraging QUIC for faster load times.|Mobile users on patchy network connections experiencing more stable and quicker web interactions.|Applications benefiting from reduced latency and improved stream multiplexing.
title: HTTP/3 Protocol

definition: QUIC (Quick UDP Internet Connections) is a general-purpose transport layer network protocol developed by Google, designed to provide security equivalent to TLS/SSL, reduce connection and transport latency, and avoid head-of-line blocking. It runs over UDP, offering stream multiplexing and improved congestion control.
examples: Serving as the underlying transport for HTTP/3, replacing TCP and TLS.|Used by Google Chrome to connect to Google services, improving browsing speed.|Applications requiring faster connection setup and reliable stream delivery over UDP.
title: QUIC Protocol

definition: The WebSockets protocol provides full-duplex communication channels over a single TCP connection, enabling real-time, bidirectional data exchange between a client and a server. Unlike HTTP's request-response model, WebSockets maintain a persistent connection, allowing either party to send data at any time.
examples: Real-time chat applications, where messages are instantly sent and received.|Live sports tickers or stock market updates that push data to clients.|Multiplayer online gaming or collaborative editing tools requiring immediate interaction.
title: WebSockets Protocol

definition: FTP is a standard network protocol used for transferring computer files between a client and server on a computer network. It uses separate control and data connections between the client and the server, typically operating over TCP.
examples: Uploading website files from a local machine to a web hosting server.|Downloading software, documents, or media files from an archive site.|Sharing large files with others by placing them on an FTP server.
title: File Transfer Protocol (FTP)

definition: SMTP is an application-layer protocol used for sending and distributing email messages between mail servers. It defines the mechanism for transmitting email messages from a sender to a recipient's mail server, and from a client to an outgoing mail server.
examples: Sending an email from an email client (e.g., Outlook, Gmail) to a recipient.|Mail servers exchanging messages between different email domains (e.g., Gmail to Yahoo Mail).|Automated systems sending notification emails.
title: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP)

definition: POP3 is an application-layer protocol used by email clients to retrieve email from a remote mail server. It typically downloads all new messages to the local device and, by default, deletes them from the server, making it suitable for single-device access.
examples: Configuring an email client to download new messages to a desktop computer.|Accessing email primarily from one device where local storage is preferred.|Older email setups where server space was limited and messages were archived locally.
title: Post Office Protocol version 3 (POP3)

definition: IMAP is an application-layer protocol that allows an email client to access and manage email messages directly on a remote mail server. Unlike POP3, IMAP keeps messages on the server, enabling synchronization across multiple devices and persistent server-side storage of emails.
examples: Accessing your email inbox from multiple devices (phone, laptop, tablet) with synchronized status.|Gmail, Outlook.com, and most modern email services using IMAP for client access.|Organizing emails into folders directly on the server.
title: Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP)

definition: SSH is a cryptographic network protocol for operating network services securely over an unsecured network. It provides a secure channel over an unsecured network by using strong encryption to authenticate the communicating parties and encrypt data.
examples: Remotely logging into a Linux server to execute commands via a terminal.|Securely transferring files between computers using SCP or SFTP.|Creating a secure tunnel for other network services, such as port forwarding.
title: Secure Shell (SSH)

definition: Telnet is an older network protocol used to provide a bidirectional interactive text-oriented communication facility using a virtual terminal connection over TCP. It transmits data, including login credentials, in plain text, making it insecure for sensitive information and largely superseded by SSH.
examples: Connecting to a legacy network device's command-line interface.|Basic testing of open ports on a server (e.g., `telnet example.com 80`).|Interacting with text-based services that don't require encryption.
title: Telnet

definition: NTP is a networking protocol for clock synchronization between computer systems over packet-switched, variable-latency data networks. It ensures accurate and synchronized timekeeping across devices, which is critical for logging, distributed systems, security, and many network operations.
examples: Servers synchronizing their internal clocks with a global NTP server for accurate timestamps.|Network devices (routers, switches) maintaining consistent time for event logs.|Ensuring correct timestamping for file modifications and distributed database transactions.
title: Network Time Protocol (NTP)

definition: SNMP is an application-layer protocol used to manage and monitor network devices, collect data, and modify device configuration across an IP network. It is a widely used protocol in network management systems to oversee network performance and diagnose problems.
examples: Monitoring the CPU usage and memory utilization of routers and switches.|Tracking the amount of data transferred through network interfaces.|Collecting information about printer toner levels or server temperatures.
title: Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)

definition: An SNMP Agent is a software component that runs on a network device (e.g., router, switch, server, printer) and collects management information about the device's state, performance, and configuration. It responds to requests from an SNMP Manager, providing access to the device's Management Information Base (MIB).
examples: A daemon running on a Linux server that reports its current CPU load and free memory.|Firmware on a network switch that provides statistics on port traffic and errors.|Software on a networked printer that reports toner levels and paper jams.
title: SNMP Agent

definition: An SNMP Manager is a software application that typically runs on a network management station and communicates with SNMP Agents to query device information, receive event notifications (traps), and configure devices. It provides a centralized interface for network administrators to oversee and control network infrastructure.
examples: Network monitoring systems like Nagios, Zabbix, or PRTG that poll SNMP agents.|A command-line tool (e.g., `snmpwalk`) used by an administrator to retrieve device data.|A graphical dashboard displaying the health and performance of multiple network devices.
title: SNMP Manager

definition: An SNMP Trap is an unsolicited notification message sent by an SNMP Agent to an SNMP Manager to report an asynchronous event or alert, such as a critical error, a change in device status, or a threshold violation. Traps allow for immediate notification of significant events without the manager needing to poll continuously.
examples: A server sending a trap when its hard disk space falls below a critical threshold.|A router sending a trap when a network interface goes down or comes back up.|A UPS sending a trap to alert about a power failure or battery issue.
title: SNMP Trap

definition: A MIB is a hierarchical database structure that formally describes all the network objects that an SNMP Agent can manage on a device. It defines the specific data points, their types, and relationships, which an SNMP Manager can query or modify using unique Object Identifiers (OIDs).
examples: The `sysUpTime` object, which indicates how long a device has been operating.|The `ifInOctets` object, which represents the total number of input octets on a network interface.|The `hrStorageUsed` object, detailing the amount of used storage on a host system.
title: Management Information Base (MIB)

definition: A signaling protocol used for initiating, maintaining, modifying, and terminating real-time multimedia communication sessions, such as voice and video calls over Internet Protocol (IP) networks. It operates at the application layer and is independent of the underlying transport layer.
examples: Making a VoIP call using a SIP phone or software client.|Setting up a video conference between multiple participants.|Sending instant messages in a SIP-enabled communication platform.
title: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)

definition: A network protocol for delivering audio and video over IP networks, specifically designed for real-time applications like streaming media and video conferencing. It provides mechanisms for sequencing, timestamping, and payload type identification to handle out-of-order delivery and data loss.
examples: Streaming live video content on platforms like YouTube Live.|Voice communication in VoIP applications and online gaming.|Transmitting sensor data that requires timely delivery.
title: Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP)

definition: A companion protocol to RTP that provides out-of-band control information for RTP streams, enabling quality of service (QoS) monitoring and synchronization between different media streams. It periodically sends control packets to all participants in a session to report reception quality and participant information.
examples: Monitoring the latency, jitter, and packet loss rates in a VoIP call.|Synchronizing audio and video tracks in a live streaming application.|Adjusting encoding rates based on network feedback for improved quality.
normalized_name: real time transport control protocol rtcp
title: Real-time Transport Control Protocol (RTCP)

definition: A lightweight, publish-subscribe network protocol designed for low-bandwidth, high-latency, or unreliable networks, making it ideal for Internet of Things (IoT) devices. It uses a broker-based architecture to facilitate efficient message exchange between numerous clients.
examples: Smart home devices communicating sensor data to a central hub.|Industrial IoT sensors sending telemetry data to a cloud platform.|Real-time updates for vehicle tracking or asset management systems.
title: Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT)

definition: A specialized web transfer protocol for use with constrained nodes and networks in the Internet of Things (IoT). Designed to be similar to HTTP but optimized for resource-constrained devices, it often runs over User Datagram Protocol (UDP) for efficiency.
examples: A battery-powered sensor device reporting temperature readings to a gateway.|Controlling a smart light bulb or other actuator in a low-power wireless network.|Resource discovery and interaction among IoT devices without a full HTTP stack.
title: Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP)

definition: A proprietary protocol developed by Microsoft that provides a user with a graphical interface to connect to another computer over a network connection. It enables users to view and interact with the remote computer's desktop as if they were physically present.
examples: Remotely accessing a work computer from home to use installed applications.|IT support technicians troubleshooting a client's machine from a different location.|Administering a server without physical access, using its graphical interface.
title: Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP)

definition: A distributed file system protocol that allows a user on a client computer to access files over a network as if they were stored locally. It enables transparent file sharing and remote access primarily between Unix-like operating systems and other platforms.
examples: Sharing home directories across multiple Linux servers for consistent user environments.|Accessing a central data repository from various workstations in a research lab.|Mounting a remote storage volume from a network-attached storage (NAS) device.
semantic_tags: Distributed File System|File Sharing|Unix|Client-Server|Remote Access|Data Storage
title: Network File System (NFS)

definition: A network file sharing protocol primarily used by Microsoft Windows to provide shared access to files, printers, serial ports, and other communications between nodes on a network. It is also known as Common Internet File System (CIFS).
examples: Accessing shared folders and files on a Windows server from a client PC.|Printing to a network printer connected to a Windows print server.|Mapping network drives on a Windows client to a remote file share.
title: Server Message Block (SMB)

definition: An open, vendor-neutral, industry-standard application protocol for accessing and maintaining distributed directory information services. It is commonly used for storing and retrieving user, group, and device information, often for authentication and authorization purposes.
examples: Centralized user authentication for logging into multiple enterprise systems (e.g., Active Directory).|Providing a corporate address book or contact directory for employees.|Retrieving configuration information for network devices or applications.
title: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP)

definition: A network authentication protocol that works on the basis of 'tickets' to allow nodes communicating over a non-secure network to prove their identity to one another in a secure manner. It provides strong authentication for client/server applications by using secret-key cryptography, preventing eavesdropping and replay attacks.
examples: Logging into an Active Directory domain, where users are authenticated by a Kerberos KDC.|Accessing network services like shared files (SMB) or databases in an enterprise environment.|Implementing Single Sign-On (SSO) for users accessing multiple corporate applications.
title: Kerberos Authentication

definition: The security principle that prevents unauthorized disclosure of information, ensuring that data is accessible only to those authorized to have access. It is a cornerstone of information security, often achieved through encryption, access controls, and data segregation.
examples: Encrypting sensitive data stored on a hard drive or transmitted over a network.|Implementing strong access control lists (ACLs) on files and folders.|Redacting personal identifiable information (PII) from public documents.
title: Confidentiality (Security)

definition: The security principle that ensures data has not been altered or destroyed in an unauthorized or accidental manner, guaranteeing that information is accurate, complete, and trustworthy. It is often maintained using hashing, digital signatures, and version control.
examples: Using checksums or cryptographic hashes to verify the integrity of downloaded files.|Employing digital signatures to ensure the authenticity and non-tampering of software updates.|Implementing database constraints and transaction logs to prevent unauthorized data modification.
title: Integrity (Security)

definition: The security principle that ensures authorized users can reliably access and use systems and data when needed, focusing on preventing denial-of-service and ensuring reliable operation of IT infrastructure. It involves measures like redundancy, backup, and disaster recovery.
examples: Implementing redundant servers and network links to prevent single points of failure.|Regularly backing up data and having a robust disaster recovery plan.|Deploying anti-DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) solutions to protect web services.
title: Availability (Security)

definition: A security service that provides undeniable proof of an action's origin and integrity, preventing a sender from falsely denying having sent a message or a receiver from falsely denying having received it. It is typically achieved through digital signatures and trusted third-party services.
examples: Digitally signing an electronic contract to prove the signer's identity and intent.|Transaction records in a blockchain where each entry is cryptographically linked and immutable.|A certified email delivery service that provides proof of sending and receipt.
semantic_tags: Accountability|Proof of Origin|Proof of Receipt|Digital Signatures|Legal Evidence|Trust
title: Non-repudiation

definition: The process of transforming readable information (plaintext) into an unreadable secret code (ciphertext) to conceal its content and prevent unauthorized access. It is a fundamental method for achieving data confidentiality and is reversible only with the correct key.
examples: Encrypting an email before sending it to protect its contents from interception.|Securing web traffic using SSL/TLS (HTTPS) to prevent eavesdropping.|Enabling full disk encryption on a laptop to protect data if the device is lost or stolen.
title: Encryption

definition: The process of converting encrypted information (ciphertext) back into its original readable form (plaintext) using a specific cryptographic key and algorithm. It is the inverse operation of encryption, allowing authorized parties to access the concealed data.
examples: Opening an encrypted file by providing the correct password or key.|A web browser decrypting the data received over an HTTPS connection.|Recovering data from an encrypted backup using the associated decryption key.
title: Decryption

definition: A cryptographic system where the same secret key is used for both encryption and decryption of data. Both the sender and receiver must possess this shared key, making secure key distribution a critical challenge.
examples: Using Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) to encrypt a local file with a password.|Data encryption in Wi-Fi Protected Access 2 (WPA2) and WPA3 protocols.|Virtual Private Network (VPN) tunnels often use symmetric keys for bulk data encryption.
title: Symmetric-key Cryptography

definition: A cryptographic system that uses a pair of mathematically linked keys: a public key for encryption (or verification) and a private key for decryption (or signing). The public key can be freely distributed, while the private key must be kept secret by its owner.
examples: RSA algorithm used for secure key exchange or digital signatures.|Encrypting data to a recipient's public key, which only they can decrypt with their private key.|Establishing secure communication channels using Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) and SSL/TLS.
title: Asymmetric-key Cryptography

definition: A symmetric-key encryption standard adopted by the U.S. government and widely used globally, replacing DES. It is a block cipher that supports key sizes of 128, 192, and 256 bits, offering strong security and efficient performance for various applications.
examples: Securing data in Wi-Fi Protected Access II (WPA2) and WPA3 protocols.|Encrypting hard drives and solid-state drives using full disk encryption software.|Protecting sensitive data in cloud storage services and secure communication protocols.
title: Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)

definition: An older symmetric-key block cipher standard that was widely used but is now considered insecure for most applications due to its relatively small 56-bit key size. It is vulnerable to brute-force attacks and has been officially deprecated, superseded by AES.
examples: Historical applications in financial services and government (mostly deprecated).|Used in some legacy systems where strong encryption is not a primary concern or for compatibility.|Triple DES (3DES), a more secure variant that applies DES three times, is still in use but also being phased out.
title: Data Encryption Standard (DES)

definition: A symmetric-key block cipher that applies the DES algorithm three times to each data block for enhanced security, using either two or three distinct DES keys. It addresses the security vulnerabilities of the original DES by increasing the effective key length.
examples: Encrypting financial transactions in older banking systems.|Used in some payment card industry (PCI) applications.|IPSec VPNs could historically use 3DES for data encryption.
title: Triple DES (3DES)

definition: An asymmetric (public-key) encryption algorithm widely used for secure data transmission and digital signatures, based on the computational difficulty of factoring large prime numbers. It uses a pair of keys: a public key for encryption and a private key for decryption.
examples: TLS/SSL handshakes for key exchange and server authentication.|Digitally signing software updates or emails.|Encrypting small amounts of data, like symmetric keys.
title: RSA Cryptosystem

definition: A public-key cryptosystem that uses the algebraic structure of elliptic curves over finite fields to create more efficient and secure cryptographic keys compared to RSA for the same level of security. It provides strong security with shorter key lengths.
examples: Used in TLS 1.2 and 1.3 for key exchange (ECDHE).|Digital signatures (ECDSA) in cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin.|Securing communication in mobile devices and low-power environments.
title: Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC)

definition: A cryptographic hash function belonging to the SHA-2 (Secure Hash Algorithm 2) family that takes an input (message) and produces a fixed-size 256-bit (32-byte) hash value, also known as a message digest. It is designed to be a one-way function, making it computationally infeasible to reverse or find collisions.
examples: Verifying data integrity of downloaded files.|Hashing passwords before storing them in a database.|Used extensively in blockchain technology for transaction linking.
title: SHA-256 Hashing Algorithm

definition: A widely used cryptographic hash function that produces a 128-bit (16-byte) hash value. While once popular for verifying data integrity, it is now considered cryptographically broken due to significant vulnerabilities, including the ease of finding collisions, and should not be used for security-critical applications.
examples: Historically used for verifying file integrity (e.g., checksums).|Was used in some digital certificate signatures (now replaced).|Detecting accidental data corruption, but not malicious tampering.
title: MD5 Hashing Algorithm (deprecated)

definition: A trusted entity in a Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) responsible for issuing, managing, revoking, and renewing digital certificates. CAs bind public keys to specific identities, ensuring trust in digital communications.
examples: VeriSign (now DigiCert) issuing SSL/TLS certificates.|Let's Encrypt providing free, automated certificates.|An enterprise's internal CA for intranet services.
title: Certificate Authority (CA)

definition: An electronic document used to prove the ownership of a public key, issued by a Certificate Authority (CA). It includes the public key, information about the owner, the issuer's digital signature, and validity dates, providing authentication and facilitating secure communication.
examples: An SSL/TLS certificate securing a website (e.g., for `https://example.com`).|An email signing certificate for S/MIME.|A code signing certificate used by software developers.
title: Digital Certificate

definition: A list maintained and published by a Certificate Authority (CA) that contains the serial numbers of digital certificates that have been revoked before their scheduled expiration date. Browsers and applications can check CRLs to determine if a certificate they are presented with is still valid.
examples: A web browser checking a CRL before trusting a website's certificate.|An email client consulting a CRL to verify the sender's signing certificate.|A system administrator adding a compromised certificate to the CRL.
title: Certificate Revocation List (CRL)

definition: An internet protocol used for obtaining the revocation status of an X.509 digital certificate in real-time. Instead of downloading an entire CRL, OCSP allows a client to send a request to an OCSP responder for the status of a specific certificate, receiving a 'good', 'revoked', or 'unknown' response.
examples: A web browser querying an OCSP responder to check a server's certificate status during a TLS handshake.|Applications using OCSP stapling to include the OCSP response directly in the TLS handshake.|A server refusing a client certificate based on an OCSP check.
title: Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP)

definition: A cryptographic protocol designed to provide communication security over a computer network, widely used for encrypting communications between web applications and servers. TLS establishes a secure channel by authenticating parties, encrypting data, and ensuring data integrity between two communicating applications.
examples: Securing HTTPS connections to websites.|Encrypting email communication via SMTPS or IMAPS.|Securing VPN connections (e.g., OpenVPN uses TLS).
title: Transport Layer Security (TLS)

definition: A multi-step process that initiates a TLS connection, allowing the client and server to establish cryptographic parameters, authenticate each other (optional for client), and agree on a session key before any application data is exchanged. It involves messages like ClientHello, ServerHello, Certificate, ServerKeyExchange, ClientKeyExchange, and Finished.
examples: When a web browser connects to an HTTPS website for the first time in a session.|A client authenticating a server using its digital certificate.|Negotiating a symmetric encryption algorithm and key for secure data transfer.
title: TLS Handshake

definition: A cryptographic protocol that preceded TLS, designed to provide secure communication over a computer network. While its original versions are now deprecated due to known security vulnerabilities, the term "SSL" is still commonly used informally to refer to TLS, especially in the context of web security certificates.
examples: Older web servers and clients might have supported SSLv3 (now highly discouraged).|The `https` protocol was initially secured by SSL.|The "SSL certificate" is a common misnomer for a TLS certificate.
title: Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) (deprecated)

definition: A suite of protocols that provides cryptographic security services at the Internet Layer (Layer 3) of the TCP/IP model. IPSec ensures data confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity for IP packets, commonly used to create Virtual Private Networks (VPNs).
examples: Building a secure VPN tunnel between two corporate networks.|Securing communication between a client and a server within an internal network.|Protecting data transmission between routers.
title: IP Security (IPSec)

definition: An IPSec mode where the entire original IP packet (header and payload) is encrypted and authenticated, then encapsulated within a new IP packet with a new header. This mode is typically used for connecting networks (e.g., site-to-site VPNs) or connecting remote users to a private network, as it hides the internal network topology.
examples: A router establishing a VPN connection to another router to secure traffic between two branch offices.|A remote access VPN where a client connects to a corporate network.|Encrypting all traffic from a virtual machine to an external network.
title: IPSec Tunnel Mode

definition: An IPSec mode where only the payload of the original IP packet is encrypted and/or authenticated, while the original IP header remains intact. This mode is typically used for end-to-end communication between two hosts, offering security for the application data without hiding the source and destination IP addresses.
examples: Securing communication directly between a web server and a database server.|Protecting an individual TCP connection between two hosts on the same network segment.|When a host-to-host VPN is established using IPSec.
title: IPSec Transport Mode

definition: An IPSec protocol that provides confidentiality (encryption), data origin authentication, data integrity, and anti-replay services for IP packets. ESP encapsulates the data to be protected, adding an ESP header and trailer, and can be used in both transport and tunnel modes.
examples: Encrypting the payload of an IP packet in IPSec Transport Mode.|Protecting the entire inner IP packet in IPSec Tunnel Mode.|Providing both encryption and authentication for VPN traffic.
title: Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP)

definition: An IPSec protocol that provides data origin authentication, data integrity, and anti-replay services for IP packets, but does NOT provide confidentiality (encryption). AH authenticates the entire IP packet, including the mutable parts of the IP header that ESP does not protect.
examples: Ensuring the integrity of network management traffic without needing encryption.|Authenticating the sender and guaranteeing that an IP packet hasn't been tampered with.|Used in scenarios where confidentiality is not required, but integrity is paramount.
title: Authentication Header (AH)

definition: A protocol used in conjunction with IPSec to set up a Security Association (SA) between two peers. IKE handles the negotiation of cryptographic algorithms, exchange of keys (e.g., using Diffie-Hellman), and authentication of the peers, establishing a secure channel for subsequent IPSec communication.
examples: Initiating an IPSec VPN tunnel by securely exchanging symmetric keys.|Authenticating the two endpoints of an IPSec connection using pre-shared keys or digital certificates.|Negotiating parameters like encryption algorithms (e.g., AES, 3DES) and hashing algorithms (e.g., SHA-256).
title: Internet Key Exchange (IKE) Protocol

definition: A technology that creates a secure, encrypted connection over a less secure network, such as the internet. VPNs allow users to send and receive data as if their computing devices were directly connected to the private network, enhancing privacy and security.
examples: An employee securely accessing corporate resources from home.|Using a commercial VPN service to anonymize browsing activity.|Connecting two geographically separate office networks securely.
title: Virtual Private Network (VPN)

definition: A type of Virtual Private Network (VPN) that establishes a secure, encrypted connection between two or more fixed networks, such as two branch offices of an organization. Unlike remote access VPNs, individual clients do not connect directly, but rather entire networks communicate securely through VPN gateways (e.g., routers or firewalls).
examples: Connecting a company's main headquarters network to its branch office network.|Securely linking a corporate data center with a cloud provider's private network.|Enabling secure data exchange between two business partners' internal networks.
title: Site-to-Site VPN

definition: A type of Virtual Private Network (VPN) that allows individual users to securely connect to a private network, such as a company's internal network, from a remote location over a public internet connection. It typically involves client software on the user's device that establishes an encrypted tunnel.
examples: An employee working from home using a VPN client to access shared files and applications on their company's internal server.|A student connecting to their university's network via VPN to access licensed academic databases from off-campus.|A traveler securely accessing their home network's resources, like a NAS drive, from a hotel Wi-Fi connection.
semantic_tags: VPN|Remote Work|Network Security|Encrypted Tunnel|Client Software|Secure Access
title: Remote Access VPN

definition: A network security system that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing network traffic based on predefined security rules. It acts as a barrier between a trusted internal network and untrusted external networks, such as the internet, preventing unauthorized access.
examples: A hardware firewall appliance protecting an entire corporate network by filtering all traffic entering and leaving.|A software firewall, like Windows Defender Firewall, running on a personal computer to control application network access.|A cloud-based firewall service safeguarding virtual machines and applications in a public cloud environment.
semantic_tags: Network Security|Traffic Control|Security Rules|Access Control|Network Protection|Barrier
title: Firewall (Networking)

definition: A firewall that monitors the state of active network connections, enabling it to make decisions based on the context of traffic flow rather than just individual packets. It remembers outgoing requests and automatically permits corresponding incoming responses, significantly enhancing security and efficiency.
examples: A corporate firewall allowing an incoming HTTP response only if an internal user explicitly initiated the outgoing HTTP request.|Most modern enterprise-grade firewalls, which track TCP sessions to permit legitimate return traffic.|A firewall allowing return UDP traffic for a DNS query only after an internal client has sent the initial query.
title: Stateful Firewall

definition: A firewall that inspects each network packet individually, without considering the context of previous packets or the overall connection state. It applies rules based solely on information contained within the packet header, making it simpler but less secure than stateful firewalls.
examples: A simple router's Access Control List (ACL) configured to block all traffic from a specific IP address, regardless of whether it's part of an established session.|An early generation hardware firewall that might permit all incoming traffic on port 80 if a rule exists, even if no internal request initiated it.|A basic packet filter that denies any packet with a destination port of 23 (Telnet) without checking its connection state.
semantic_tags: Packet Filtering|No Session State|Simplicity|ACLs|Basic Security|Header Inspection
title: Stateless Firewall

definition: A basic type of firewall that operates at the network (Layer 3) and transport (Layer 4) layers of the OSI model. It inspects individual packets and applies rules to permit or deny them based on criteria such as source/destination IP addresses, port numbers, and protocols.
examples: A router configured with an Access Control List (ACL) to block all incoming traffic on TCP port 23 (Telnet).|A firewall rule blocking all traffic originating from a specific public IP subnet.|A filter allowing only UDP traffic on port 53 (DNS) to a specific internal DNS server.
semantic_tags: OSI Layer 3/4|IP Address|Port Number|Protocol|Basic Firewall|Access Control List
title: Packet Filtering Firewall

definition: A firewall that operates at the application layer (Layer 7) of the OSI model, providing deep packet inspection and understanding specific application protocols to enforce more granular security policies. It acts as a proxy, terminating and re-establishing connections, offering enhanced security for application-specific traffic.
examples: An ALG inspecting FTP traffic to ensure only authorized FTP commands (e.g., GET but not PUT) are executed.|A firewall module that understands SIP (Voice over IP) traffic to properly manage call setup and teardown across NAT.|A proxy server acting as an ALG for HTTP/HTTPS, inspecting web traffic for malicious content before forwarding it to internal clients.
semantic_tags: OSI Layer 7|Deep Packet Inspection|Proxy|Application Protocol|Granular Control|Protocol Awareness
title: Application Layer Gateway (Firewall)

definition: A firewall that extends traditional firewall capabilities by integrating advanced features like deep packet inspection, intrusion prevention systems (IPS), application awareness, and identity awareness. NGFWs provide more comprehensive network security and visibility beyond basic port and protocol inspection.
examples: A Palo Alto Networks firewall blocking specific applications (e.g., torrenting) while allowing web browsing, regardless of port.|A FortiGate firewall integrating antivirus, anti-spam, and IPS functionalities to offer unified threat management (UTM).|A Cisco Firepower NGFW enforcing policies based on specific user identities rather than just IP addresses.
semantic_tags: Advanced Firewall|IPS|Application Control|Identity Awareness|Deep Packet Inspection|Unified Threat Management
title: Next-Generation Firewall (NGFW)

definition: A set of instructions or criteria configured within a firewall that dictate how network traffic should be handled. These rules specify whether to permit, deny, or block packets based on various attributes like source/destination IP, port, protocol, application, and user identity.
examples: A rule: `ALLOW TCP port 80 (HTTP) from ANY to ANY` to permit web traffic.|A rule: `DENY ALL traffic from IP address 192.168.1.100` to block a specific malicious host.|A rule: `ALLOW established TCP connections from internal network to external network` for legitimate outbound communication.
title: Firewall Rules

definition: A security technology that monitors network or system activities for malicious activity or policy violations and alerts administrators when potential threats are detected. An IDS is a passive listening device that does not actively prevent the detected intrusion.
examples: A Snort sensor deployed on a network segment detecting a signature of a known malware attack and logging an alert for security analysts.|A HIDS monitoring system logs on a server for suspicious login attempts or unauthorized file access.|An IDS flagging unusually high outbound traffic as a potential data exfiltration attempt.
title: Intrusion Detection System (IDS)

definition: A network security device that actively monitors network or system activities for malicious activity and immediately blocks or prevents detected threats in real-time. Unlike an IDS, an IPS operates as an inline device, taking direct action on traffic to stop intrusions.
examples: A Cisco Firepower IPS blocking a detected SQL injection attempt before it reaches the web server.|An IPS dropping packets that match a known denial-of-service attack signature.|A network IPS quarantining a host that is attempting to spread malware based on observed suspicious behavior.
semantic_tags: Threat Prevention|Active Blocking|Real-time Security|Inline Device|Network Security|Mitigation
title: Intrusion Prevention System (IPS)

definition: An Intrusion Detection System that runs on individual host computers or servers, monitoring system files, log files, processes, and network connections specific to that host for suspicious activities or policy violations. HIDS provides granular visibility into individual endpoint behavior.
examples: OSSEC HIDS monitoring file integrity on a critical web server, alerting if unauthorized changes are detected in configuration files.|An endpoint detection and response (EDR) agent on a workstation detecting suspicious process behavior, such as a browser launching PowerShell.|A HIDS analyzing Windows event logs for patterns indicative of a brute-force attack against a local user account.
semantic_tags: Endpoint Security|System Monitoring|File Integrity|Local Logs|Host-specific|Process Monitoring
title: Host-based IDS (HIDS)

definition: An Intrusion Detection System that monitors network traffic across an entire network segment by analyzing packet headers and payloads for signatures of known attacks or anomalous behavior. NIDS typically operates on a promiscuous interface, passively observing traffic without interfering.
examples: A Snort NIDS deployed at the network perimeter to detect incoming attacks from the internet.|A Suricata sensor analyzing traffic on a core switch's span port for malicious patterns like port scans or botnet C2 communications.|A NIDS alerting on a flood of malformed packets targeting a web server, indicating a potential denial-of-service attempt.
title: Network-based IDS (NIDS)

definition: A cyberattack where multiple compromised computer systems, often forming a 'botnet,' are orchestrated to flood a target server, service, or network with a massive volume of illegitimate traffic. This overwhelms the target's resources, making it unavailable to legitimate users.
examples: A popular e-commerce website being taken offline for hours due to millions of requests originating from thousands of compromised machines worldwide.|A gaming server experiencing severe latency and disconnections as a result of a UDP flood from a botnet targeting its IP address.|An attacker using a botnet to launch a volumetric attack against an organization's DNS servers, preventing legitimate users from resolving domain names.
normalized_name: distributed denial of service ddos attack
title: Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) Attack

definition: A type of cyberattack where an attacker secretly intercepts and relays messages between two parties who believe they are communicating directly with each other. This allows the attacker to eavesdrop on, or alter, the communication without the knowledge of the legitimate parties.
examples: An attacker setting up a rogue Wi-Fi hotspot to intercept traffic from unsuspecting users browsing the internet.|ARP spoofing used to redirect local network traffic through an attacker's machine, allowing them to capture and modify data.|HTTPS stripping, where an attacker downgrades a secure HTTPS connection to an insecure HTTP connection to view unencrypted traffic.
normalized_name: man in the middle mitm attack
title: Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) Attack

definition: The process of intercepting and logging network traffic as it passes over a digital network, often performed using specialized software or hardware tools. This technique allows for the capture and analysis of data packets, revealing information exchanged between devices.
examples: Using Wireshark to capture and analyze network traffic on a local network for troubleshooting connectivity issues.|An attacker using tcpdump to capture credentials transmitted over an unencrypted connection.|A network administrator performing packet sniffing to identify abnormal network behavior or potential malware activity.
title: Packet Sniffing

definition: An attack technique used to identify open ports and services running on a target network host. By sending connection requests to a range of ports, attackers can discover potential vulnerabilities that could be exploited to gain unauthorized access.
examples: Using Nmap to scan a server's IP address and discover open ports like 22 (SSH), 80 (HTTP), and 443 (HTTPS).|An attacker sending SYN packets to a range of ports on a target machine to see which ones respond with SYN-ACK, indicating an open port.|A penetration tester performing a UDP scan to identify open UDP services like DNS (port 53) or SNMP (port 161).
title: Port Scanning

definition: Short for 'malicious software,' malware is any software intentionally designed to cause disruption to a computer, server, client, or network, leak private information, gain unauthorized access, or otherwise exploit, compromise, or incapacitate computer systems.
examples: A computer virus infecting executable files and spreading to other systems when those files are run.|Ransomware encrypting a user's files and demanding payment for their decryption.|A worm replicating itself across a network without user interaction, consuming bandwidth and resources.|A Trojan horse disguised as legitimate software that secretly installs a backdoor for remote access.
title: Malware

definition: A type of social engineering attack where attackers attempt to trick individuals into divulging sensitive information (e.g., usernames, passwords, credit card details) or performing malicious actions (e.g., clicking dangerous links) by impersonating a trustworthy entity in electronic communication.
examples: An email seemingly from a bank asking for login credentials due to a 'security breach' and directing the user to a fake login page.|A text message (smishing) from a supposed shipping company asking for payment to redeliver a package via a malicious link.|Spear phishing: a highly targeted email attack tailored to a specific individual or organization, often referencing internal projects or colleagues.
title: Phishing

definition: The creation of Internet Protocol (IP) packets with a falsified source IP address, used to masquerade as another computer system. This technique is often employed to hide the attacker's identity, bypass security measures, or launch denial-of-service attacks by making traceback difficult.
examples: An attacker sending packets with a trusted internal IP address to bypass a firewall's access control list that only allows traffic from specific internal hosts.|Using a spoofed IP address in a DDoS attack to flood a target, making it harder to identify the true origin of the attack.|An attacker manipulating network routing by sending packets with a fake source IP, causing confusion and potential traffic misdirection.
title: IP Spoofing

definition: The act of changing a network interface controller's (NIC) factory-assigned Media Access Control (MAC) address. This is often done to bypass MAC-based access controls, impersonate another device on a local network, or hide one's true identity to evade tracking.
examples: An attacker changing their laptop's MAC address to one that is whitelisted on a Wi-Fi network with MAC filtering, gaining unauthorized access.|A user spoofing their MAC address to receive a new IP address from a DHCP server, potentially bypassing IP address restrictions.|A cybercriminal altering their device's MAC address to avoid being identified or tracked by network monitoring systems.
semantic_tags: Identity Concealment|Deception|MAC Address|NIC|Access Control Bypass|Local Network
title: MAC Spoofing

definition: A malicious attack where an attacker sends forged ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) messages over a local area network. This links the attacker's MAC address with the IP address of another legitimate host or router, thereby intercepting or modifying network traffic intended for the legitimate device.
examples: An attacker sending fake ARP replies to a victim, claiming to be the default gateway, to intercept all internet traffic (Man-in-the-Middle attack).|Using tools like `arpspoof` or `ettercap` to perform a man-in-the-middle attack by redirecting traffic through the attacker's machine.
title: ARP Spoofing

definition: An attack where an attacker intercepts or corrupts DNS queries and responses to redirect users to malicious websites instead of legitimate ones. This is typically achieved by associating a legitimate domain name with the attacker's IP address.
examples: An attacker modifying the `/etc/hosts` file on a victim's machine to redirect `google.com` to a local IP address controlled by the attacker.|A rogue DNS server providing incorrect IP addresses for popular websites, leading users to phishing sites.|Performing a cache poisoning attack on a recursive DNS server to inject forged DNS records.
title: DNS Spoofing

definition: An attack where a malicious actor takes control of a user's authenticated session with a web server or application. This usually occurs after the user has logged in, by stealing or predicting a valid session ID or token.
examples: An attacker stealing a user's session cookie to gain unauthorized access to their online banking account without needing a password.|Using a tool like `Burp Suite` to capture and replay a valid session cookie to bypass authentication.|A Cross-site Scripting (XSS) attack used to steal a user's session cookie, allowing the attacker to impersonate the user.
title: Session Hijacking

definition: A wireless computer network that links two or more devices using wireless communication to form a local area network (LAN). WLANs typically operate within a limited area such as a home, school, or office building, enabling devices to connect without physical cables.
examples: A home Wi-Fi network allowing laptops, smartphones, and smart TVs to connect to the internet wirelessly.|An office network providing wireless internet access to employees' devices throughout the building.|A public Wi-Fi hotspot in a coffee shop enabling customers to access the internet.
title: Wireless Local Area Network (WLAN)

definition: A family of technical specifications for implementing wireless local area network (WLAN) computer communication, primarily in the 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, and 6 GHz frequency bands. These standards are commonly known as Wi-Fi and define the protocols for wireless connectivity.
examples: IEEE 802.11a, operating in the 5 GHz band, offering speeds up to 54 Mbps.|IEEE 802.11g, operating in the 2.4 GHz band, also offering speeds up to 54 Mbps.|IEEE 802.11n (Wi-Fi 4), introducing MIMO and supporting both 2.4/5 GHz bands for speeds up to 600 Mbps.|IEEE 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6), focused on high efficiency and performance in crowded environments, using OFDMA.
title: IEEE 802.11 Standards

definition: A popular wireless technology that allows devices such as computers, mobile devices, and other equipment to connect to the Internet or communicate with one another wirelessly within a particular area. It is based on the IEEE 802.11 standards for wireless local area networking.
examples: Connecting a laptop to a home router's Wi-Fi network to access the internet.|Using public Wi-Fi at a coffee shop or airport to stay connected.|A smartphone creating a personal Wi-Fi hotspot to share its cellular data connection with other devices.
title: Wi-Fi

definition: A series of security protocols designed to protect wireless networks from unauthorized access and data interception by providing authentication and encryption for data transmitted over Wi-Fi. Each iteration offers enhanced security features over its predecessors.
examples: **WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy):** An older, easily crackable protocol, largely obsolete due to significant security flaws.|**WPA (Wi-Fi Protected Access):** An improvement over WEP, using TKIP (Temporal Key Integrity Protocol) for stronger encryption.|**WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access II):** The widely adopted standard, using AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) encryption and CCMP for robust security.|**WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access III):** The latest standard, offering enhanced features like Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE) for stronger password-based authentication and individualized data encryption.
normalized_name: wireless security protocols wep wpa wpa2 wpa3
title: Wireless Security Protocols (WEP, WPA, WPA2, WPA3)

definition: The act of clandestinely listening to or intercepting private communications transmitted over wireless networks, often to gain unauthorized access to sensitive information. This can involve passively capturing data packets or actively decrypting them.
examples: Using a Wi-Fi analyzer tool to capture unencrypted network traffic from nearby devices on an insecure network.|An attacker intercepting data packets from an unsecured public Wi-Fi network to steal login credentials.|Listening to cordless phone conversations using specialized radio scanning equipment.
title: Wireless Eavesdropping

definition: A type of malicious attack where an attacker sets up a fraudulent Wi-Fi access point that mimics a legitimate one (e.g., using the same SSID). The goal is to trick users into connecting to it, allowing the attacker to intercept their traffic, steal credentials, or inject malware.
examples: An attacker setting up a Wi-Fi network named 'Free_Public_Wifi' in a cafe, indistinguishable from the legitimate network, to capture user data.|Creating a fake corporate Wi-Fi network with the same name as the real one to capture employee login credentials for network access.|Using a portable device to broadcast an SSID identical to a trusted network, prompting users to connect and reveal sensitive information.
title: Evil Twin Attack

definition: An unauthorized wireless access point that has been installed on a secure network without explicit permission or knowledge of the network administrator. It creates a significant security vulnerability by potentially allowing unauthorized access to the network or facilitating man-in-the-middle attacks.
examples: An employee plugging in a personal Wi-Fi router to the corporate network without permission, bypassing security policies.|An attacker setting up an access point near a target network (e.g., in a parking lot) to lure unsuspecting users into connecting.|A compromised device within a network secretly acting as an access point, opening a back door for external access.
title: Rogue Access Point

definition: A type of denial-of-service (DoS) attack specifically targeting wireless networks, where an attacker sends forged deauthentication frames to one or more clients connected to a Wi-Fi access point. This forces the clients to disconnect from the network, often as a precursor to other attacks like an Evil Twin attack or Wi-Fi password cracking.
examples: An attacker sending deauthentication frames to all clients connected to a public Wi-Fi network, disrupting their internet access.|Using tools from the `aircrack-ng` suite (e.g., `aireplay-ng`) to specifically target and disconnect a client from a Wi-Fi network.|Forcing a client to disconnect and then reconnect to capture the WPA/WPA2 handshake for offline password cracking.

definition: A Protocol Data Unit (PDU) is a single unit of information exchanged between peer entities of a computer network, consisting of control information (headers and trailers) and user data. It represents the data unit at a specific layer of the OSI or TCP/IP model.

definition: Decapsulation is the reverse process of encapsulation, where a protocol layer removes its specific header (and potentially trailer) from a received Protocol Data Unit (PDU). title: Network Slicing (5G)

definition: Massive MIMO (Multiple-Input Multiple-Output) is a 5G antenna technology that employs a very large number of antennas (tens to hundreds) at the base station to serve multiple user devices simultaneously within the same frequency and time resources. This significantly boosts spectral efficiency, capacity, and coverage through advanced beamforming.
examples: A 5G base station equipped with 64 or 128 antenna elements creating multiple highly focused beams to individual users.|Improved coverage and reduced interference in dense urban environments or large venues due to precise beamforming.|Increased aggregate throughput for many users accessing the network concurrently on the same cell.
title: Massive MIMO (5G)

definition: Millimeter Wave (mmWave) communication in 5G refers to the utilization of radio frequencies in the 24 GHz to 100 GHz range. This spectrum enables extremely high bandwidth and data rates, crucial for enhanced mobile broadband, but is characterized by shorter range and susceptibility to physical obstructions.
examples: Fixed Wireless Access (FWA) deployments using mmWave to deliver fiber-like internet speeds to homes in urban areas.|High-density venue deployments (e.g., stadiums, concert halls) using mmWave for ultra-fast mobile connectivity where line-of-sight is prevalent.|Short-range, high-throughput wireless backhaul links between base stations and fiber points.
title: Millimeter Wave (mmWave) Communication (5G)

definition: URLLC is one of the three primary 5G service categories, focusing on providing extremely high reliability (e.g., 99.999%) and very low end-to-end latency (e.g., <1ms) for mission-critical applications. It addresses use cases where even tiny delays or failures can have severe consequences.
examples: Remote surgery or tactile internet applications requiring instantaneous feedback.|Vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication for autonomous driving and traffic safety.|Industrial automation and control in smart factories, where machines need to communicate with minimal delay.
normalized_name: ultra reliable low latency communication urllc 5g
title: Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication (URLLC) (5G)

definition: eMBB is one of the three primary 5G service categories, designed to deliver significantly higher data rates, increased network capacity, and improved coverage compared to 4G technologies. Its main objective is to provide a superior mobile internet experience for consumers and enterprises.
examples: Seamless 4K/8K video streaming and ultra-high-definition content consumption on mobile devices.|Rapid download of large files, such as downloading a full-length movie in seconds.|Immersive Augmented Reality (AR) and Virtual Reality (VR) applications requiring high bandwidth and low-ish latency.
title: Enhanced Mobile Broadband (eMBB) (5G)

definition: mMTC is one of the three primary 5G service categories, focused on enabling connectivity for an extremely large number of low-cost, low-power devices over a wide geographical area. These devices typically transmit small amounts of data infrequently, making power efficiency and scalability paramount.
examples: Smart city applications connecting millions of environmental sensors, smart parking meters, and streetlights.|Smart agriculture systems with soil moisture sensors, weather stations, and livestock trackers across vast farms.|Large-scale utility metering for electricity, gas, and water, where devices send readings periodically.
title: Massive Machine Type Communications (mMTC) (5G)

definition: Open RAN is an industry movement towards open, disaggregated, and virtualized radio access network (RAN) architectures. It advocates for open interfaces between RAN components (e.g., radio unit, distributed unit, centralized unit) to foster multi-vendor interoperability, innovation, and competition.
examples: A mobile operator deploying an Open RAN solution where a radio unit from Vendor A connects to a distributed unit from Vendor B via an O-RAN compliant fronthaul interface.|A software-defined centralized unit (CU) from one vendor managing radio resources from multiple remote radio units (RUs) from different vendors.|Using open-source software for RAN Intelligent Controller (RIC) to manage and optimize network performance.
normalized_name: open radio access network open ran
title: Open Radio Access Network (Open RAN)

definition: Virtual RAN (vRAN) is a Radio Access Network (RAN) architecture that centralizes and virtualizes baseband processing functions, moving them from proprietary hardware appliances to software running on commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) servers. This allows for greater flexibility, scalability, and resource pooling compared to traditional RANs.
examples: Running the baseband unit (BBU) software as virtual machines or containers on x86 servers in a data center.|Dynamically allocating computing resources to baseband processing based on real-time traffic demands.|Consolidating multiple BBUs from different cell sites into a shared pool of virtualized resources.
title: Virtual RAN (vRAN)

definition: Cloud RAN (CRAN) is an advanced architectural evolution of vRAN that centralizes baseband processing units (BBUs) into cloud-based data centers, connecting them to remote radio units (RRUs) via high-bandwidth fronthaul links. This centralization enables advanced coordination, dynamic resource allocation, and reduced operational costs.
examples: Multiple RRUs deployed across a city neighborhood connecting via fiber optic cables to a centralized BBU pool hosted in a regional data center.|Implementing advanced interference coordination and cooperative multipoint (CoMP) processing for improved network performance across cell sites.|Dynamically scaling baseband processing capacity up or down by spinning up or down virtualized BBU instances in the cloud.
title: Cloud RAN (CRAN)

definition: The Network Exposure Function (NEF) is a key functional element within the 5G Core Network's Service-Based Architecture (SBA). Its primary role is to securely expose the capabilities and events of the 5G network to authorized third-party applications and services, enabling new business models and innovative use cases.
examples: An application requesting specific Quality of Service (QoS) parameters or bandwidth guarantees for a user's session via the NEF.|A smart city platform subscribing through the NEF to receive real-time notifications about device location changes or network congestion in a specific area.|An enterprise application utilizing the NEF to authenticate and authorize IoT devices connecting to the 5G network.
title: Network Exposure Function (NEF)

definition: A key component in the 5G Core Network architecture that acts as a central repository for network function (NF) profiles and discovery services. It enables other NFs to discover and interact with each other without hardcoded configurations, facilitating a flexible and scalable network.
examples: An AMF querying the NRF to find an available SMF for a new PDU session.|An SMF registering its capabilities and available services with the NRF upon startup or changes in its status.
title: Network Repository Function (NRF)

definition: The central control plane function in the 5G Core Network responsible for connection and mobility management, including User Equipment (UE) registration, authentication, authorization, and tracking. It handles non-access stratum (NAS) signaling between the UE and the core network.
examples: A smartphone registering with the 5G network, with the AMF handling the initial attachment procedure and security negotiations.|A UE moving between different gNodeBs (5G base stations), where the AMF manages the mobility state and handover procedures.
normalized_name: access and mobility management function amf
title: Access and Mobility Management Function (AMF)

definition: A 5G Core Network control plane function responsible for managing Protocol Data Unit (PDU) sessions, which are the logical connections carrying user data. This includes IP address allocation, session establishment, modification, and release, interacting with the UPF for user plane routing.
examples: Setting up an internet browsing session for a user on a 5G device, where the SMF assigns an IP address and configures routing rules in the UPF.|Modifying Quality of Service (QoS) parameters for a video streaming session based on network conditions or user subscription, orchestrated by the SMF.
semantic_tags: 5G Core|PDU Session|IP Address Management|Control Plane|QoS|User Plane Management
title: Session Management Function (SMF)

definition: The 5G Core Network function responsible for handling all user plane traffic, including packet routing, forwarding, inspection, and application of QoS rules. It serves as the data anchor for PDU sessions and interconnects with the data network.
examples: Routing actual data packets between a 5G smartphone and the internet, based on instructions from the SMF.|Applying deep packet inspection (DPI) and traffic steering policies to user data streams as dictated by the policy control function (PCF).
semantic_tags: 5G Core|User Plane|Data Forwarding|Packet Routing|QoS Enforcement|Traffic Management
title: User Plane Function (UPF)

definition: A central 5G Core Network function that stores and manages user subscription data, authentication credentials, and access authorization policies. It provides a unified interface for other network functions (like AMF, SMF, AUSF) to access this critical subscriber information.
examples: Authenticating a user attempting to connect to the 5G network, where the AUSF queries the UDM for the subscriber's credentials.|Retrieving a user's service profile (e.g., allowed data rates, subscribed services) from the UDM to apply appropriate policies via the PCF.
title: Unified Data Management (UDM)

definition: A 5G Core Network function dedicated to performing authentication of User Equipment (UE) and network functions, ensuring that only authorized entities can access network services. It collaborates with the UDM to retrieve authentication credentials.
examples: A UE attempting to attach to the 5G network undergoing mutual authentication with the AUSF to verify its identity and establish a secure connection.|Verifying the identity of a network function before it can provide or consume services, ensuring network integrity.
title: Authentication Server Function (AUSF)

definition: A 5G Core Network function that provides policy rules to control network behavior, including Quality of Service (QoS), traffic routing, and charging parameters. These policies are based on subscriber profiles, network conditions, and operator-defined business rules.
examples: Instructing the SMF and UPF to apply a specific QoS policy (e.g., higher bandwidth, lower latency) for a user's video streaming application.|Enforcing parental control policies for specific users by applying traffic filtering rules or limiting access to certain content categories.
title: Policy Control Function (PCF)

definition: A 5G Core Network function responsible for collecting charging-related events from other network functions and generating charging data records (CDRs) for billing purposes. It supports both online (real-time) and offline charging models.
examples: Collecting real-time data usage information from the UPF to enable online credit control for a prepaid user during an active session.|Generating detailed CDRs at the end of a session or usage period for post-paid billing based on service consumption.
title: Charging Function (CHF)

definition: A 5G Core Network function designed to collect network data from various sources, perform analytics using AI/ML, and provide insights, predictions, and recommendations to other network functions. This enables optimized network operation, resource management, and automated decision-making.
examples: Predicting network congestion in a specific geographical area to allow the AMF to proactively offload traffic or adjust mobility parameters.|Analyzing user behavior patterns and service demands to optimize resource allocation for specific services, improving user experience and network efficiency.
title: Network Data Analytics Function (NWDAF)

definition: A technology that enables 4G (LTE) and 5G New Radio (NR) to operate simultaneously within the same frequency band by dynamically allocating spectrum resources between the two technologies based on real-time demand. DSS facilitates a smoother and faster transition to 5G coverage using existing spectrum assets.
examples: A mobile network operator deploying initial 5G coverage on existing 4G LTE frequency bands without needing to refarm spectrum immediately.|A cell tower dynamically shifting spectrum usage from 4G to 5G during peak 5G usage times, maximizing spectrum efficiency.
semantic_tags: 5G NR|4G LTE|Spectrum Sharing|Radio Access Network|Wireless Communication|Network Modernization
title: Dynamic Spectrum Sharing (DSS)

definition: Communication networks that utilize airborne or space-borne platforms, such as satellites, high-altitude platform stations (HAPS), or drones, to provide connectivity. NTNs are crucial for extending coverage to remote or underserved areas, supporting IoT, and enhancing network resilience.
examples: Starlink satellites providing high-speed internet access to rural and remote regions globally.|Drones acting as temporary mobile base stations to restore communication in disaster-stricken areas where terrestrial infrastructure is damaged.
title: Non-Terrestrial Networks (NTN)

definition: A set of IEEE 802.1 standards that extend standard Ethernet to provide deterministic data delivery with guaranteed bandwidth, ultra-low latency, and high reliability. TSN is critical for real-time applications in industrial automation, automotive, and professional audio/video.
examples: Controlling robotic arms on a factory floor with guaranteed message delivery times to ensure precise synchronization and safety.|In-vehicle networking for autonomous driving systems where sensor data and control commands must be transmitted with ultra-reliable low latency.
title: Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN)

definition: An IETF-defined architecture that provides bounded latency, low packet loss, and high reliability over Layer 2 and Layer 3 networks, enabling time-sensitive applications to operate predictably over IP networks. DetNet often leverages TSN capabilities at Layer 2 to achieve end-to-end determinism.
examples: Ensuring critical control messages in smart grids arrive within strict time limits to maintain grid stability and prevent blackouts.|Transmitting high-fidelity professional audio/video streams over an IP network with guaranteed quality and synchronization for live production.
title: Deterministic Networking (DetNet)

definition: A communication method that uses principles of quantum mechanics to establish a shared, secret cryptographic key between two parties. QKD's unique property is that any attempt by an eavesdropper to intercept the key is physically detectable, thereby guaranteeing the key's security.
examples: Two banks establishing a secure key for confidential financial transactions using quantum entanglement over a dedicated fiber optic link.|A government agency setting up an ultra-secure communication channel where any potential eavesdropping attempt on the key exchange is immediately detected.
title: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD)

definition: Cryptographic algorithms designed to be secure against attacks by quantum computers, which are capable of breaking many current public-key cryptosystems like RSA and ECC. PQC aims to future-proof digital communications and data security against the advent of large-scale quantum computing.
examples: Implementing a new digital signature algorithm (e.g., Dilithium) that is resistant to Shor's algorithm, used for software updates or identity verification.|Upgrading TLS/SSL protocols to use quantum-safe key exchange methods to protect web traffic from future quantum attacks.
title: Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC)

definition: An architectural approach to managing Wide Area Networks (WANs) that leverages software-defined networking (SDN) principles to abstract the underlying network hardware. It enables centralized control, intelligent traffic routing, and simplified management over multiple connection types, improving performance and reducing costs.
examples: A global enterprise automatically routing mission-critical application traffic over a high-priority MPLS link and less critical traffic over a lower-cost internet broadband connection.|Deploying new branch office network policies from a central controller without requiring manual configuration at each physical site.
normalized_name: software defined wide area network sd wan
title: Software-Defined Wide Area Network (SD-WAN)

definition: A cloud-native security model that converges wide area networking (WAN) and a comprehensive set of security functions into a single, cloud-delivered service. SASE provides secure, optimized access for users and devices regardless of their location, embodying Zero Trust principles.
examples: A remote employee accessing company resources securely through a SASE platform that integrates firewall, VPN, secure web gateway, and data loss prevention services.|Applying consistent security policies across all users and devices, whether in the office or remote, via a single cloud-based service, simplifying management and enhancing protection.
title: Secure Access Service Edge (SASE)

definition: A security framework that operates on the principle 'never trust, always verify,' requiring strict identity verification and device posture assessment for every user and device attempting to access network resources. Access is granted based on the least privilege needed, irrespective of the user's location.
examples: An employee attempting to access an internal application needing to re-authenticate and have their device posture (e.g., up-to-date antivirus) checked, even if already connected to the corporate VPN.|Granting access to specific applications rather than entire network segments, ensuring users only access what they explicitly need.
title: Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA)

definition: A unified security platform that automatically collects and correlates security data from multiple sources, including endpoints, networks, cloud environments, and email. XDR provides broader visibility, enhanced threat detection capabilities, and faster, more efficient incident response across an organization's entire attack surface.
examples: An XDR system detecting a suspicious email attachment, tracking its execution on an endpoint, and then automatically isolating the affected device and user account.|Correlating network intrusion alerts with unusual user login patterns and cloud access attempts to identify and respond to sophisticated, multi-stage attacks.
title: Extended Detection and Response (XDR)

definition: A security solution that integrates disparate security tools, automates security tasks, and orchestrates incident response workflows. SOAR platforms enable security operations teams to manage and respond to threats more efficiently by standardizing processes and reducing manual effort.
examples: A SOAR playbook automatically blocking a malicious IP address detected by an intrusion detection system (IDS) and isolating affected endpoints based on predefined rules.|Automating the collection of forensic data, correlating alerts from multiple systems, and creating a detailed ticket in a help desk system upon a security incident.
normalized_name: security orchestration automation and response soar
