definition: A mathematical ring is a set R equipped with two binary operations, usually called addition (+) and multiplication (*), such that R is an abelian group under addition, multiplication is associative, and multiplication distributes over addition. Unlike a field, multiplication does not necessarily have inverses for all non-zero elements, nor is it necessarily commutative.
examples: The set of integers Z with standard addition and multiplication (Z, +, *) forms a commutative ring with unity.|The set of polynomials with real coefficients (R[x], +, *) forms a commutative ring.|The set of n x n matrices with matrix addition and multiplication forms a non-commutative ring.
title: Mathematical Ring

definition: A mathematical field is a commutative ring where every non-zero element has a multiplicative inverse. It is an algebraic structure where addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division (except by zero) are well-defined and behave as expected.
examples: The set of real numbers R with standard addition and multiplication (R, +, *) is a field.|The set of rational numbers Q (Q, +, *) and complex numbers C (C, +, *) are also fields.|Finite fields (Galois fields) like GF(p) for a prime p, are crucial in cryptography and coding theory.
title: Mathematical Field

definition: An algebraic homomorphism is a structure-preserving map between two algebraic structures of the same type (e.g., groups, rings, or vector spaces). It means that applying the map and then the operation is equivalent to applying the operation and then the map.
examples: For groups (G,*) and (H,.), a map f: G -> H is a homomorphism if f(a*b) = f(a).f(b) for all a,b in G.|The determinant function for matrices is a homomorphism from the multiplicative group of invertible matrices to the multiplicative group of non-zero real numbers.|The exponential function f(x) = e^x is a group homomorphism from (R, +) to (R^+, *) because e^(x+y) = e^x * e^y.
title: Algebraic Homomorphism

definition: An algebraic isomorphism is a bijective (one-to-one and onto) homomorphism between two algebraic structures of the same type. If an isomorphism exists, the two structures are considered 'algebraically identical' or structurally equivalent, differing only in the names of their elements.
examples: The group of integers under addition (Z, +) is isomorphic to the group of even integers under addition (2Z, +) via the map f(x) = 2x.|Any two vector spaces of the same finite dimension over the same field are isomorphic.|In object-oriented programming, two data structures could be considered isomorphic if they store data in an equivalent way, allowing perfect conversion between them without loss of information.
title: Algebraic Isomorphism

definition: The four fundamental axioms that define a mathematical group (G, *): 1) Closure: For all a, b in G, a * b is in G. 2) Associativity: For all a, b, c in G, (a * b) * c = a * (b * c). 3) Identity Element: There exists an element e in G such that for every a in G, a * e = e * a = a. 4) Inverse Element: For every a in G, there exists an element a⁻¹ in G such that a * a⁻¹ = a⁻¹ * a = e.
examples: The integers under addition (Z, +) satisfy closure (a+b is an integer), associativity, identity (0), and inverse (-a).|The set of non-zero real numbers under multiplication (R*, *) satisfies closure, associativity, identity (1), and inverse (1/a).|When designing an abstract data type like a 'set with concatenation', ensuring these axioms hold can guarantee predictable behavior.
title: Group Axioms

definition: The axioms defining a mathematical ring (R, +, *): 1) (R, +) is an abelian group. 2) Multiplication is associative: (a * b) * c = a * (b * c). 3) Multiplication distributes over addition: a * (b + c) = (a * b) + (a * c) and (a + b) * c = (a * c) + (b * c).
examples: The set of integers (Z, +, *) satisfies all ring axioms, forming a commutative ring with unity.|The set of 2x2 matrices with matrix addition and multiplication forms a non-commutative ring (multiplication is not commutative).|Polynomial rings are fundamental in algebra, satisfying these axioms for polynomial addition and multiplication.
title: Ring Axioms

definition: The axioms defining a mathematical field (F, +, *): 1) (F, +, *) is a commutative ring. 2) The multiplicative identity (1) is not equal to the additive identity (0). 3) Every non-zero element 'a' in F has a multiplicative inverse a⁻¹ such that a * a⁻¹ = 1. These axioms ensure all standard arithmetic operations are well-defined.
examples: The real numbers (R, +, *) satisfy all field axioms, including commutative multiplication and multiplicative inverses for all non-zero numbers.|The rational numbers (Q, +, *) form a field, as does the set of complex numbers (C, +, *).|Finite fields (Galois Fields) are abstract structures crucial for error-correcting codes and cryptography due to their well-behaved arithmetic.

definition: A scalar is a quantity that is completely described by a single numerical value, representing only magnitude. It has no associated direction in space.

definition: A vector is a quantity that has both magnitude and direction. It is typically represented as an arrow in geometric contexts or as an ordered list of numbers (components) in algebraic contexts.
examples: Velocity (e.g., 60 mph North).|Force (e.g., 10 Newtons downwards).|Displacement (e.g., 5 meters East).|A 3D position vector in computer graphics, [x, y, z].
title: Vector

definition: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers, symbols, or expressions, arranged in rows and columns. It is a fundamental data structure in linear algebra used to represent data or linear transformations.
examples: Image pixel data: A 2x2 matrix `[[R, G], [B, A]]` representing color channels.|A transformation matrix for 2D rotation: `[[cos(theta), -sin(theta)], [sin(theta), cos(theta)]]`.|A spreadsheet representing sales data where rows are products and columns are months.
title: Matrix

definition: Vector addition is the operation of combining two or more vectors to produce a single resultant vector. This is done by adding their corresponding components.
examples: Adding two displacement vectors: If `v1 = [2, 3]` and `v2 = [1, -5]`, then `v1 + v2 = [2+1, 3-5] = [3, -2]`.|Combining forces acting on an object, where each force is a vector.|In a Python list: `[a+x for a,x in zip([1,2],[3,4])]` results in `[4,6]`.
title: Vector Addition

definition: Scalar multiplication of a vector involves multiplying each component of the vector by a single scalar value. This operation scales the magnitude of the vector while preserving its direction (or reversing it if the scalar is negative).
examples: Scaling a vector: If `v = [2, 3]` and scalar `k = 5`, then `k * v = [5*2, 5*3] = [10, 15]`.|Changing the magnitude of a force vector without altering its direction.|Multiplying `np.array([1, 2, 3])` by `2` in NumPy results in `[2, 4, 6]`.
title: Scalar Multiplication (Vector)

definition: The dot product, also known as the scalar product, is an algebraic operation that takes two equal-length sequences of numbers (usually coordinate vectors) and returns a single number. Geometrically, it is the product of the Euclidean magnitudes of the two vectors and the cosine of the angle between them, indicating how much one vector goes in the direction of the other.
examples: Calculating work in physics: Work = Force ⋅ Displacement.|Finding similarity between two document vectors in natural language processing.|For `v1 = [1, 2, 3]` and `v2 = [4, -5, 6]`, the dot product is `(1*4) + (2*-5) + (3*6) = 4 - 10 + 18 = 12`.
title: Dot Product (Scalar Product)

definition: The cross product, also known as the vector product, is a binary operation on two vectors in three-dimensional space that results in a vector perpendicular to both input vectors. Its magnitude is equal to the area of the parallelogram that the vectors span, and its direction follows the right-hand rule.
examples: Calculating torque in physics, where torque is the cross product of the force vector and the position vector.|Finding a normal vector to a plane defined by two vectors.|For `v1 = [1, 0, 0]` (x-axis) and `v2 = [0, 1, 0]` (y-axis), their cross product is `[0, 0, 1]` (z-axis).
title: Cross Product (Vector Product)

definition: Matrix addition is the operation of adding two matrices of the same dimensions by adding their corresponding elements. The result is a new matrix with the same dimensions.
examples: Adding two 2x2 matrices: `[[1, 2], [3, 4]] + [[5, 6], [7, 8]] = [[1+5, 2+6], [3+7, 4+8]] = [[6, 8], [10, 12]]`.|Combining two datasets represented as matrices, such as daily sales figures from two different stores.|In image processing, blending two images by adding their pixel intensity matrices.
title: Matrix Addition

definition: Matrix subtraction is the operation of subtracting one matrix from another of the same dimensions. This is performed by subtracting their corresponding elements to produce a new matrix with identical dimensions.
examples: Subtracting two 2x2 matrices: `[[5, 6], [7, 8]] - [[1, 2], [3, 4]] = [[5-1, 6-2], [7-3, 8-4]] = [[4, 4], [4, 4]]`.|Calculating the difference between two sets of measurements collected at different times.|Determining the change in pixel values between two frames in a video sequence.
title: Matrix Subtraction

definition: Matrix multiplication is a binary operation that produces a matrix from two matrices. For two matrices A (m x n) and B (n x p), their product C (m x p) is calculated by taking the dot product of each row of A with each column of B.
examples: Applying multiple linear transformations (e.g., rotation then scaling) to a point, represented by multiplying their respective transformation matrices.|In neural networks, the computation of a layer's output involves multiplying input vectors by a weight matrix.|If `A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]` and `B = [[5, 6], [7, 8]]`, then `C[0,0] = (1*5) + (2*7) = 19` and `C[0,1] = (1*6) + (2*8) = 22`.
title: Matrix Multiplication

definition: An identity matrix, denoted as 'I', is a square matrix where all the elements on the main diagonal are ones, and all other elements are zeros. It serves as the multiplicative identity in matrix algebra, meaning that multiplying any matrix by an identity matrix leaves the original matrix unchanged (A * I = I * A = A).
examples: A 3x3 identity matrix: `[[1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1]]`.|In computer graphics, applying an identity transformation means no change in position, rotation, or scale.|In NumPy, `np.identity(3)` creates a 3x3 identity matrix.
title: Identity Matrix

definition: A zero matrix, or null matrix, is a matrix where every element is zero. It acts as the additive identity in matrix algebra, meaning that adding a zero matrix to any other matrix of the same dimensions leaves the original matrix unchanged.
examples: A 2x3 zero matrix: `[[0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]]`.|Initializing a matrix of weights in a neural network to zeros before training.|In NumPy, `np.zeros((2, 3))` creates a 2x3 zero matrix.
title: Zero Matrix (Null Matrix)

definition: The transpose of a matrix is a new matrix formed by swapping the rows and columns of the original matrix. If the original matrix A has dimensions m x n, its transpose Aᵀ will have dimensions n x m.
examples: If `A = [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]]`, then `Aᵀ = [[1, 3, 5], [2, 4, 6]]`.|Converting a row vector to a column vector or vice-versa.|In data analysis, transposing a table to view data from a different perspective (e.g., columns become rows for different features).
title: Transpose of a Matrix

definition: The determinant is a scalar value that can be computed from the elements of a square matrix. It provides crucial information about the matrix, such as whether it is invertible (non-zero determinant) and how it scales geometric transformations (area or volume scaling factor).
examples: For a 2x2 matrix `[[a, b], [c, d]]`, the determinant is `ad - bc`.|If `det(A) = 0`, the matrix A is singular, meaning it does not have an inverse and represents a transformation that collapses dimensions.|Used in Cramer's Rule to solve systems of linear equations.

title: Determinant of a Matrix

definition: For a square matrix A, its inverse, denoted A⁻¹, is another square matrix such that when multiplied by A, it yields the identity matrix (A * A⁻¹ = A⁻¹ * A = I). A matrix is invertible only if its determinant is non-zero.
examples: Solving a system of linear equations `Ax = b` by multiplying both sides by A⁻¹ to get `x = A⁻¹b`.|If `A = [[2, 1], [5, 3]]`, then `A⁻¹ = [[3, -1], [-5, 2]]`.|Used in cryptography for encoding and decoding messages using matrix transformations.
title: Inverse of a Matrix

definition: A singular matrix is a square matrix whose determinant is equal to zero. This implies that the matrix does not have an inverse, and the linear transformation it represents collapses at least one dimension, meaning it maps multiple non-zero vectors to the zero vector.
examples: A 2x2 matrix `[[1, 2], [2, 4]]` has a determinant of `(1*4) - (2*2) = 0`, making it singular.|Matrices representing projections onto a lower-dimensional subspace are typically singular.|If a system of linear equations `Ax = b` has a singular matrix A, it either has no solution or infinitely many solutions.
title: Singular Matrix

definition: A non-singular matrix, also known as an invertible matrix, is a square matrix whose determinant is non-zero. Consequently, a non-singular matrix always possesses a unique inverse, and the linear transformation it represents preserves dimensionality.
examples: A 2x2 matrix `[[1, 2], [3, 4]]` has a determinant of `(1*4) - (2*3) = -2`, making it non-singular.|Rotation matrices are non-singular as they represent invertible transformations that preserve space.|A system of linear equations `Ax = b` with a non-singular matrix A always has a unique solution.
title: Non-singular Matrix

definition: A system of linear equations is a collection of one or more linear equations involving the same set of variables. These systems are used to model problems where several quantities are linearly related.
examples: A simple system: `2x + 3y = 7` and `x - y = 1`.|Modeling resource allocation problems, such as distributing raw materials to production lines.|Circuit analysis, where Kirchhoff's laws result in systems of linear equations for currents and voltages.
title: System of Linear Equations

definition: A consistent system of linear equations is one that has at least one solution. This means the lines or planes represented by the equations intersect at one point (unique solution) or overlap (infinitely many solutions).
examples: Unique solution: `x + y = 2`, `x - y = 0` (solution: `x=1, y=1`).|Infinitely many solutions: `x + y = 2`, `2x + 2y = 4` (the equations represent the same line).|In geometric terms, intersecting lines or identical lines/planes.
title: Consistent System

definition: An inconsistent system of linear equations is one that has no solution. Geometrically, this occurs when the lines or planes represented by the equations are parallel and distinct, meaning they never intersect.
examples: A simple example: `x + y = 2`, `x + y = 3` (these conditions cannot both be true simultaneously).|Two parallel lines in 2D space that never meet.|A system where applying Gaussian elimination leads to a contradictory row like `[0 0 | 1]`.
title: Inconsistent System

definition: Gauss-Jordan elimination is an algorithm used to solve systems of linear equations or to find the inverse of a matrix. It works by performing a sequence of elementary row operations (swapping rows, multiplying a row by a non-zero scalar, adding a multiple of one row to another) to transform an augmented matrix into reduced row echelon form.
examples: Solving `2x + y = 7`, `x - 3y = -7` by transforming the augmented matrix `[[2, 1 | 7], [1, -3 | -7]]`.|Finding the inverse of a matrix A by augmenting it with the identity matrix `[A | I]` and transforming it to `[I | A⁻¹]`.|Used in computer science for linear programming and solving various computational problems.

title: Gauss-Jordan Elimination

definition: Row Echelon Form (REF) is a specific structure for a matrix obtained through Gaussian elimination, where: 1) All non-zero rows are above any rows of all zeros. 2) The leading entry (pivot) of each non-zero row is 1. 3) Each leading entry is to the right of the leading entry in the row above it.
examples: Example of a matrix in REF: `[[1, 2, 3], [0, 1, 4], [0, 0, 0]]`.|An intermediate step when solving systems of linear equations using Gaussian elimination.|The process of reducing a matrix to REF helps determine the rank of the matrix and analyze the consistency of a linear system.
title: Row Echelon Form

definition: A matrix is in reduced row echelon form (RREF) if it satisfies four conditions: (1) all zero rows are at the bottom, (2) the leading entry (pivot) of each non-zero row is 1, (3) each pivot is to the right of the pivot in the row above it, and (4) each pivot is the only non-zero entry in its column. RREF is unique for any given matrix and is used to solve systems of linear equations and find matrix inverses.
examples: The identity matrix `[[1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1]]` is in RREF.|A matrix like `[[1, 0, 2, 0], [0, 1, 3, 0], [0, 0, 0, 1]]` is in RREF.|Using `numpy.linalg.matrix_rank` on a matrix after converting it to RREF (though not directly available, the concept underpins many linear algebra solvers).

title: Reduced Row Echelon Form

definition: The rank of a matrix is the maximum number of linearly independent row vectors or column vectors in the matrix. It is also equal to the dimension of the column space (image) or row space of the matrix, and the number of pivot positions in its row echelon form.
examples: A 3x3 identity matrix has rank 3.|The matrix `[[1, 2], [2, 4]]` has rank 1, as the second row is a scalar multiple of the first.|In data science, the rank of a data matrix indicates the number of independent features or components.
title: Rank of a Matrix

definition: The null space (or kernel) of a matrix A is the set of all vectors x such that Ax = 0, where 0 is the zero vector. It represents all input vectors that are mapped to the zero vector by the linear transformation associated with A, forming a subspace of the domain.
examples: For `A = [[1, 1], [2, 2]]`, the null space is `span{[-1, 1]}` since `A * [-1, 1]^T = [0, 0]^T`.|Solving `Ax = 0` to find a basis for the null space.|In control theory, the null space of a system's matrix can represent unobservable or uncontrollable states.
title: Null Space (Kernel)

definition: The column space (or image) of a matrix A is the set of all possible linear combinations of the column vectors of A. It represents the range of the linear transformation associated with A, forming a subspace of the codomain.
examples: For `A = [[1, 0], [0, 1]]`, the column space is `R^2`.|For `A = [[1, 2], [2, 4]]`, the column space is `span{[1, 2]}`.|In data analysis, the column space of a feature matrix spans the space of possible outputs or feature combinations.
title: Column Space (Image)

definition: The row space of a matrix A is the set of all possible linear combinations of the row vectors of A. It is a subspace of the domain of the linear transformation associated with A, and its dimension is equal to the rank of the matrix.
examples: For `A = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]`, the row space is `span{[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]}`.|The row space is orthogonal to the null space of the matrix.|In principal component analysis (PCA), the principal components often form a basis for the row space of the data matrix after centering.
title: Row Space

definition: A vector space is a set V of objects called vectors, equipped with two operations: vector addition and scalar multiplication, which satisfy ten axioms (e.g., commutativity, associativity, existence of zero vector and additive inverse, distributive properties). These axioms ensure that vectors can be manipulated in a consistent and intuitive way.
examples: The set of all n-tuples of real numbers, `R^n`, with standard vector addition and scalar multiplication.|The set of all `m x n` matrices.|The set of all continuous real-valued functions on an interval `[a,b]`.
title: Vector Space

definition: A subspace of a vector space V is a subset H of V that is itself a vector space under the operations of vector addition and scalar multiplication defined on V. For H to be a subspace, it must satisfy three conditions: (1) the zero vector of V is in H, (2) H is closed under vector addition, and (3) H is closed under scalar multiplication.
examples: Any line or plane passing through the origin in `R^3` is a subspace of `R^3`.|The null space and column space of a matrix are subspaces.|The set of all polynomials of degree less than or equal to n, `P_n`, is a subspace of the vector space of all polynomials.
title: Subspace (Linear Algebra)

definition: A linear combination of a set of vectors `v_1, v_2, ..., v_k` is an expression of the form `c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + ... + c_kv_k`, where `c_1, c_2, ..., c_k` are scalars. This concept is fundamental to understanding vector spaces and how vectors can be constructed from others.
examples: Given vectors `v1=[1,0]` and `v2=[0,1]`, `2v1 + 3v2 = [2,3]` is a linear combination.|The output of a neural network layer is often a linear combination of its inputs (before activation).|In physics, the resultant force can be a linear combination of component forces.
title: Linear Combination

definition: The span of a set of vectors `v_1, v_2, ..., v_k`, denoted as `span{v_1, ..., v_k}`, is the set of all possible linear combinations of those vectors. It forms the smallest subspace containing all the vectors in the set.
examples: `span{[1,0], [0,1]}` in `R^2` is `R^2` itself.|`span{[1,2]}` in `R^2` is the line `y=2x` through the origin.|In feature engineering, a new feature might be within the span of existing features, indicating linear dependence and potential redundancy.
title: Span of Vectors

definition: A basis for a vector space V is a set of linearly independent vectors that span V. Any vector in V can be uniquely expressed as a linear combination of the basis vectors, and the number of vectors in any basis for V is constant (which defines the dimension of V).
examples: The standard basis for `R^n` consists of `n` unit vectors along each axis.|For `P_2` (polynomials of degree up to 2), a basis is `{1, x, x^2}`.|In PCA, the principal components form a basis for the transformed feature space.
title: Basis (Vector Space)

definition: The dimension of a vector space V, denoted `dim(V)`, is the number of vectors in any basis for V. If a vector space cannot be spanned by a finite number of vectors, it is said to be infinite-dimensional.
examples: The dimension of `R^3` is 3, as its standard basis has 3 vectors.|The dimension of the null space of a matrix is called the nullity.|The dimension of the column space (image) of a matrix is equal to its rank.
title: Dimension (Vector Space)

definition: An orthonormal basis for an inner product space is a basis whose vectors are mutually orthogonal (their inner product is zero) and each have a unit length (their norm is one). Such bases simplify calculations involving projections and coordinates.
examples: The standard basis vectors `e_1=[1,0]` and `e_2=[0,1]` in `R^2` form an orthonormal basis.|Fourier series utilize an orthonormal basis of sine and cosine functions.|In machine learning, orthogonal transformations (like PCA) often aim to find an orthonormal basis for data representation.
title: Orthonormal Basis

definition: The Gram-Schmidt process is an algorithm for orthonormalizing a set of linearly independent vectors in an inner product space. It systematically constructs an orthogonal basis from the given set, and then normalizes each vector to unit length to produce an orthonormal basis.
examples: Given `v1=[1,1,0]`, `v2=[1,0,1]`, `v3=[0,1,1]`, apply Gram-Schmidt to find an orthonormal basis for `R^3`.|Used in numerical algorithms for orthogonal decomposition, such as QR factorization.|In signal processing, it can be employed to construct orthogonal filter banks.
title: Gram-Schmidt Process

definition: A linear transformation (or linear map) is a function between two vector spaces that preserves the operations of vector addition and scalar multiplication. Specifically, for any vectors u, v and scalar c, it satisfies `T(u+v) = T(u) + T(v)` (additivity) and `T(cu) = cT(u)` (homogeneity).
examples: Rotation, scaling, and reflection operations in `R^n` are linear transformations.|Matrix multiplication `T(x) = Ax` is a linear transformation.|Differentiation and integration operators in calculus are linear transformations on function spaces.
title: Linear Transformation

definition: Every linear transformation `T: V -> W` between finite-dimensional vector spaces can be represented by a unique matrix with respect to chosen bases for V and W. This matrix, when multiplied by the coordinate vector of an input in V, yields the coordinate vector of its image in W.
examples: A 90-degree counter-clockwise rotation in `R^2` is represented by the matrix `[[0, -1], [1, 0]]`.|A scaling transformation `T(x,y) = (2x, 3y)` is represented by `[[2, 0], [0, 3]]`.|In computer graphics, 3D transformations (rotation, scaling, shear) are represented by matrices for efficient computation.
title: Matrix Representation of Linear Transformation

definition: The eigenspace of a matrix A corresponding to an eigenvalue `λ` is the set of all eigenvectors associated with `λ`, along with the zero vector. It forms a subspace of the vector space and represents the set of all vectors that are only scaled (by `λ`) when the linear transformation A is applied.
examples: For an identity matrix `I`, the eigenspace for `λ=1` is the entire `R^n`, as all non-zero vectors are eigenvectors.|To find an eigenspace, one solves the homogeneous system `(A - λI)x = 0`, which is the null space of `(A - λI)`.|In PCA, principal components for a specific variance (eigenvalue) define an eigenspace representing directions of significant data variation.
title: Eigenspace

definition: The characteristic equation of a square matrix A is given by `det(A - λI) = 0`, where `λ` is a scalar variable and `I` is the identity matrix of the same dimension as A. The roots of this polynomial equation are the eigenvalues of the matrix A.
examples: For `A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]]`, the characteristic equation is `(2-λ)^2 - 1 = 0`.|Solving `det(A - λI) = 0` is the initial step in finding the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix.|Used in stability analysis of dynamical systems and to solve systems of linear differential equations.
title: Characteristic Equation

definition: A square matrix A is diagonalizable if it is similar to a diagonal matrix D, meaning there exists an invertible matrix P such that `A = PDP⁻¹`. This is possible if and only if A has a complete set of linearly independent eigenvectors, which form the columns of P, and the diagonal entries of D are the corresponding eigenvalues.
examples: If `A` has distinct eigenvalues, it is diagonalizable; e.g., `A = [[2, 1], [0, 3]]` can be diagonalized into `D = [[2, 0], [0, 3]]`.|Diagonalization simplifies calculating powers of matrices: `A^k = PD^kP⁻¹`.|It is crucial in solving systems of differential equations and in principal component analysis for simplifying computations.
title: Diagonalization of a Matrix

definition: A square matrix A is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose, i.e., `A = Aᵀ`. This means that the element in the i-th row and j-th column is equal to the element in the j-th row and i-th column (`a_ij = a_ji`).
examples: The matrix `[[1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 5], [3, 5, 6]]` is a symmetric matrix.|Covariance matrices in statistics, which describe relationships between variables, are always symmetric.|Adjacency matrices of undirected graphs are symmetric, representing connections between nodes.
title: Symmetric Matrix

definition: A square matrix A is skew-symmetric (or anti-symmetric) if it is equal to the negative of its transpose, i.e., `A = -Aᵀ`. This implies that `a_ij = -a_ji` for all i and j, and consequently, the diagonal elements must all be zero.
examples: The matrix `[[0, -2, 3], [2, 0, -1], [-3, 1, 0]]` is a skew-symmetric matrix.|The cross product operator in 3D vector algebra can be represented by a skew-symmetric matrix.|In mechanics, the angular velocity tensor is represented by a skew-symmetric matrix.
title: Skew-Symmetric Matrix

definition: A square matrix A is orthogonal if its columns and rows are orthogonal unit vectors (orthonormal vectors). Equivalently, its transpose is equal to its inverse, i.e., AᵀA = AAᵀ = I, where I is the identity matrix.
examples: A rotation matrix used in computer graphics to rotate objects without scaling or shearing.|A reflection matrix that reflects points across a line or plane.
title: Orthogonal Matrix

definition: A complex square matrix U is unitary if its conjugate transpose (Hermitian transpose) is equal to its inverse, i.e., UᴴU = UUᴴ = I, where I is the identity matrix. It is the complex analogue of an orthogonal matrix, preserving the inner product.
examples: Quantum gate matrices like the Hadamard gate or Pauli-X gate in quantum computing.|The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) matrix, which is unitary (up to a scaling factor).
title: Unitary Matrix

definition: A complex square matrix A is Hermitian if it is equal to its own conjugate transpose (Hermitian transpose), i.e., A = Aᴴ. All eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix are real numbers.
examples: Covariance matrices used in quantum mechanics to describe observables.|The Hamiltonian operator in quantum mechanics, which represents the total energy of a system.
title: Hermitian Matrix

definition: A symmetric (or Hermitian for complex) matrix M is positive definite if for every non-zero column vector x, the quadratic form xᵀMx > 0. This implies all its eigenvalues are strictly positive.
examples: The Hessian matrix of a multivariate function at a local minimum.|Covariance matrices of a set of linearly independent random variables.
title: Positive Definite Matrix

definition: A symmetric (or Hermitian for complex) matrix M is positive semidefinite if for every non-zero column vector x, the quadratic form xᵀMx ≥ 0. This means all its eigenvalues are non-negative (greater than or equal to zero).
examples: A Gram matrix formed from any set of vectors.|Covariance matrices in statistics, which are always positive semidefinite.
title: Positive Semidefinite Matrix

definition: A linear transformation P from a vector space to itself such that applying the transformation twice yields the same result as applying it once, i.e., P² = P. It maps vectors onto a subspace.
examples: Projecting a 3D vector onto the XY-plane by setting its z-component to zero.|The projection operator P = vvᵀ for a unit vector v, which projects any vector onto the direction of v.
title: Linear Projection

definition: A linear projection P that maps a vector onto a subspace such that the difference between the original vector and its projection is orthogonal to the subspace. If P is a matrix, it satisfies P = Pᵀ and P² = P.
examples: Finding the closest point in a given subspace to a particular vector.|Projecting a vector onto the column space of a matrix to solve a least squares problem.
title: Orthogonal Projection

definition: A statistical method used to find the best-fitting line or curve for a set of data points by minimizing the sum of the squares of the residuals (the differences between observed and predicted values). It is widely used to estimate parameters in linear models.
examples: Linear regression to model the relationship between two variables, like predicting house prices based on size.|Curve fitting to experimental data in science and engineering.
title: Least Squares Method

definition: A matrix factorization that decomposes a square matrix A into the product of a lower triangular matrix L and an upper triangular matrix U, i.e., A = LU. This decomposition is highly efficient for solving systems of linear equations, calculating determinants, and inverting matrices.
examples: Solving a system of linear equations Ax=b by first solving Ly=b for y, then Ux=y for x.|Calculating the determinant of a large matrix, as det(A) = det(L)det(U).
title: LU Decomposition

definition: A matrix factorization that decomposes a matrix A into the product of an orthogonal matrix Q and an upper triangular matrix R, i.e., A = QR. It is commonly used for solving linear least squares problems and for eigenvalue computations.
examples: Solving overdetermined systems of linear equations in a numerically stable way for least squares.|The QR algorithm, an iterative method for finding the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix.
title: QR Decomposition

definition: A matrix factorization that decomposes a symmetric, positive-definite matrix A into the product of a lower triangular matrix L and its conjugate transpose Lᴴ (or transpose Lᵀ for real matrices), i.e., A = LLᴴ. It is an efficient method often used in numerical analysis.
examples: Efficiently solving linear systems Ax=b where A is symmetric and positive definite.|Simulating correlated random variables in Monte Carlo methods or financial modeling.

title: Cholesky Decomposition

definition: A factorization of a square matrix A into the product A = PΛP⁻¹, where P is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of A and Λ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the corresponding eigenvalues. It reveals the fundamental directions and scaling factors of the linear transformation represented by A.
examples: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) for dimensionality reduction, where eigenvectors represent principal components.|Analyzing the stability of dynamical systems by examining the eigenvalues of the system matrix.
title: Eigen Decomposition

definition: A matrix norm defined as the square root of the sum of the absolute squares of its elements, i.e., ||A||_F = √(Σᵢⱼ |aᵢⱼ|²). It is analogous to the Euclidean (L2) norm for vectors and is often used to measure the 'size' of a matrix.
examples: Measuring the distance between two matrices, for instance, in matrix completion algorithms.|Used as a regularization term in some machine learning models to prevent overfitting.
