title: Twofish

definition: Blowfish is a symmetric-key block cipher designed by Bruce Schneier in 1993, notable for its speed and security, especially as an alternative to the then-prevalent DES. It operates on 64-bit blocks of data and supports variable-length keys, ranging from 32 bits to 448 bits, making it highly configurable.
examples: Used in the `bcrypt` password hashing function to securely store user passwords.|Integrated into various disk encryption tools and file archivers for data protection.|Included in many cryptographic libraries and secure shell (SSH) implementations as an available cipher.
semantic_tags: Block cipher|Symmetric encryption|Bruce Schneier|Password hashing|64-bit block|Encryption algorithm
title: Blowfish

definition: Serpent is a symmetric-key block cipher that was one of the five finalists in the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) competition, designed by Ross Anderson, Eli Biham, and Lars Knudsen. Known for its conservative security design and high security margin, it encrypts 128-bit data blocks and supports key sizes of 128, 192, and 256 bits.
examples: Though not selected for AES, Serpent is considered cryptographically very strong and is used as an option in various security software.|Implemented in several cryptographic libraries, such as OpenSSL (though less commonly used than AES).|Evaluated for high-security applications where extreme resistance to cryptanalysis is prioritized.

title: Serpent

definition: The ElGamal Cryptosystem is an asymmetric-key encryption and digital signature scheme based on the computational Diffie-Hellman problem and the difficulty of the discrete logarithm problem. It allows secure communication over an insecure channel but typically results in ciphertext that is twice the size of the plaintext.
examples: Used in GNU Privacy Guard (GnuPG) as an option for encrypting emails and files.|Forms the basis for some digital signature algorithms, providing authenticity and non-repudiation.|Implemented in certain secure communication protocols where discrete logarithm-based cryptography is preferred.
semantic_tags: Public-key cryptography|Asymmetric encryption|Digital signature|Diffie-Hellman|Number theory|Discrete logarithm
title: ElGamal Cryptosystem

definition: A Cryptographic Hash Function is a mathematical algorithm that takes an input of arbitrary size (message) and returns a fixed-size bit string, called a hash value or message digest. It possesses properties like collision resistance, pre-image resistance, and second pre-image resistance, making it computationally infeasible to reverse or find two different inputs that produce the same hash, thereby ensuring data integrity and authenticity.
examples: SHA-256 is used extensively in blockchain technologies like Bitcoin to secure transactions and blocks.|File integrity checks use hash functions (e.g., `sha256sum` in Linux) to verify that a downloaded file has not been altered.|Password storage often uses hash functions (combined with salts) to store password digests instead of plain text.
title: Cryptographic Hash Function

definition: MD5 (Message-Digest Algorithm 5) is a widely-used cryptographic hash function that produces a 128-bit (16-byte) hash value. While historically popular for verifying data integrity, it is now considered cryptographically broken due to known and exploitable collision vulnerabilities, making it unsuitable for security-critical applications like digital signatures or SSL certificates.
examples: Used for generating checksums to verify the integrity of files after download, e.g., using the `md5sum` command.|Previously used for password hashing in some systems, but this practice is now strongly discouraged due to collision attacks.|Demonstrated collision attacks showed two different executables could have the same MD5 hash.
semantic_tags: Hash function|Deprecated|Collision vulnerability|Integrity check|128-bit hash|Cryptographically broken
title: MD5

definition: SHA-1 (Secure Hash Algorithm 1) is a cryptographic hash function that produces a 160-bit (20-byte) hash value, designed by the NSA and standardized by NIST. Like MD5, SHA-1 has known theoretical and practical collision vulnerabilities, leading to its deprecation for most security-critical applications where collision resistance is paramount.
examples: Formerly used in Git for version control to uniquely identify commits and objects (now moving to SHA-256).|Deprecated for use in SSL/TLS certificates by major web browsers and certificate authorities.|Used in various digital signature schemes, but its use is now phased out due to collision risks.
title: SHA-1

definition: SHA-3 (Secure Hash Algorithm 3) is the latest member of the Secure Hash Algorithm family, standardized by NIST in 2015, based on the Keccak algorithm. It provides the same output sizes as SHA-2 (224, 256, 384, 512 bits) but uses a different internal sponge construction, offering a distinct and potentially more secure alternative to SHA-2, particularly as a defense against future cryptanalytic breaks.
examples: Used in modern cryptographic protocols and applications requiring strong collision resistance.|Ethereum blockchain uses a variant of Keccak-256 (SHA-3 predecessor) for addresses and block hashing.|Implemented in various software libraries and hardware for cryptographic operations, often alongside SHA-2.
title: SHA-3

definition: HMAC is a specific type of Message Authentication Code (MAC) constructed using a cryptographic hash function and a secret cryptographic key. It is used to simultaneously verify both the data integrity and the authenticity of a message, protecting against both accidental alteration and malicious tampering, provided the key is known only to the sender and intended receiver.
examples: Used in TLS/SSL protocols to ensure the integrity and authenticity of communication between a client and server.|Integral to IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) for providing connectionless integrity and data origin authentication.|Generates one-time passwords in multi-factor authentication systems like TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password).
normalized_name: hmac hash based message authentication code
title: HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code)

definition: The Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA) is a Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS) for digital signatures, based on the mathematical properties of discrete logarithms. It allows for the authentication of the sender's identity and the integrity of a message, providing non-repudiation, but unlike RSA, it is used exclusively for signing and cannot be used for encryption.
examples: Used in government applications and various digital certificate standards to verify the authenticity of documents and software.|Implemented in cryptographic libraries like OpenSSL for generating and verifying digital signatures.|Provides digital signatures for certain types of secure email and file transfer protocols.
title: Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA)

definition: Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) is a variant of the Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA) that employs elliptic curve cryptography (ECC) instead of traditional finite field cryptography. ECDSA offers comparable or higher levels of security with significantly smaller key sizes compared to DSA or RSA, leading to increased efficiency in computation, storage, and bandwidth.
examples: Used extensively in cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum for signing transactions.|Implemented in TLS/SSL certificates (e.g., ECDSA certificates) for secure web communication.|Forms the basis for hardware security tokens and two-factor authentication methods such as FIDO U2F.
normalized_name: elliptic curve digital signature algorithm ecdsa
semantic_tags: Digital signature|Elliptic curve cryptography|ECC|DSA|Public-key cryptography|Smaller keys
title: Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA)

definition: RSA Digital Signatures are a digital signature scheme based on the RSA cryptosystem, leveraging the computational difficulty of factoring large numbers. A sender signs a message using their private key, and anyone with the corresponding public key can verify the signature, thus providing authenticity, integrity, and non-repudiation for the message.
examples: Widely used in X.509 digital certificates to establish the authenticity of websites in SSL/TLS handshakes.|Employed for code signing, allowing users to verify the origin and integrity of software.|Used in secure email protocols like PGP/GnuPG and S/MIME to digitally sign messages.
title: RSA Digital Signatures

definition: Key Management encompasses the comprehensive set of practices and technologies related to the entire lifecycle of cryptographic keys, from their generation and secure exchange to storage, use, revocation, and ultimate destruction. Proper key management is a critical foundation for the security and trustworthiness of any cryptographic system and the data it protects.
examples: Using Hardware Security Modules (HSMs) to securely generate, store, and manage master encryption keys.|Implementing a robust Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) to manage digital certificates and their associated keys.|Establishing secure key ceremonies and policies for handling sensitive keys in data centers.
title: Key Management

definition: Key generation is the process of creating cryptographic keys, which are essential for encryption, decryption, digital signatures, and other security functions. These keys must be sufficiently random, complex, and long enough to resist cryptanalytic attacks.
examples: Generating an RSA key pair (public and private keys) for secure communication using `openssl genrsa`.|Deriving a symmetric AES session key from a Diffie-Hellman key exchange.|Creating a strong password-based encryption key using a key derivation function like PBKDF2.
title: Key Generation

definition: Key distribution refers to the secure process of sharing cryptographic keys between communicating parties so they can establish secure channels. It is a fundamental challenge in cryptography, requiring methods to ensure confidentiality and authenticity of the shared keys.
examples: Using the Diffie-Hellman key exchange algorithm for two parties to agree on a shared secret key over an insecure channel.|A Certificate Authority (CA) distributing its public key to be trusted by web browsers.|Physical delivery of encryption keys on a secure hardware token to remote sites.
title: Key Distribution

definition: Key revocation is the process of invalidating a cryptographic key before its scheduled expiration date. This action is necessary when a key is compromised, lost, no longer needed, or if the associated entity's credentials change, preventing its further use for cryptographic operations.
examples: A Certificate Authority (CA) publishing a Certificate Revocation List (CRL) for compromised X.509 certificates.|An administrator revoking a user's PGP key due to suspicion of compromise or the user leaving the organization.|A server refusing connections from clients presenting an SSL/TLS certificate marked as revoked via OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol).
title: Key Revocation

definition: Key escrow is a practice where a cryptographic key is stored by a trusted third party, often for recovery purposes or to grant access to encrypted data under specific circumstances. While it can aid in data recovery and legal access, it introduces potential security and privacy risks.
examples: An enterprise system storing copies of employees' private keys with an escrow agent to ensure access to company data if an employee leaves or loses their key.|A government agency mandating that encryption keys be escrowed to allow lawful access to encrypted communications or data.|Using a secure multi-party computation scheme to distribute key shares among several escrow agents.
semantic_tags: Key Management|Data Recovery|Privacy Concerns|Third Party|Surveillance|Cryptographic Policy
title: Key Escrow

definition: An X.509 certificate is a digital certificate standard that uses Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) to bind an identity (such as a person, organization, or device) to a public key. It is digitally signed by a trusted Certificate Authority (CA) to verify the authenticity of the public key's owner.
examples: SSL/TLS certificates used by web browsers for HTTPS connections to verify website identity and encrypt communication.|Code signing certificates used to verify the integrity and origin of software.|S/MIME certificates used for secure email communication, providing encryption and digital signatures.
title: X.509 Certificate

definition: A Hardware Security Module (HSM) is a physical computing device that safeguards and manages digital keys, performs cryptographic operations, and provides strong authentication. It is designed to be tamper-resistant and often certified to national or international standards like FIPS 140-2.
examples: An HSM used in a data center to protect root Certificate Authority (CA) private keys and perform certificate signing operations.|Bank ATMs using HSMs to protect cryptographic keys for transaction processing and customer PIN verification.|Cloud providers offering virtual HSM services to protect customers' encryption keys.
title: Hardware Security Module (HSM)

definition: Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) is a deprecated cryptographic protocol that provided secure communication over a computer network, widely used for internet security. It has been superseded by Transport Layer Security (TLS), which offers enhanced security features, though the term 'SSL' is still colloquially used.
examples: A web browser connecting to a website via HTTPS, which originally stood for HTTP over SSL but now uses TLS.|Email clients using 'SSL' to secure connections to mail servers (e.g., SMTPS, POP3S, IMAPS), although they actually employ TLS.|Early versions of VPNs or secure remote access solutions that implemented the SSL protocol.
title: Secure Sockets Layer (SSL)

definition: IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) is a suite of protocols used to secure Internet Protocol (IP) communications by authenticating and encrypting each IP packet in a data stream. It operates at the network layer, providing confidentiality, integrity, and authentication services.
examples: Establishing a Virtual Private Network (VPN) connection between two corporate networks using IPsec tunnels.|Securing communication between a client device and a corporate server over an untrusted network.|Using IPsec to encrypt data traveling between cloud instances in a private network.
title: IPsec

definition: Pretty Good Privacy (PGP) is an encryption program that provides cryptographic privacy and authentication for data communication. It is widely used for signing, encrypting, and decrypting texts, emails, files, and whole disk partitions, employing a 'Web of Trust' model.
examples: Encrypting an email message before sending it to ensure confidentiality and integrity between sender and recipient.|Digitally signing a software release to allow users to verify its authenticity and ensure it hasn't been tampered with.|Encrypting a file on a local disk to protect sensitive information.

title: Pretty Good Privacy (PGP)

definition: Gnu Privacy Guard (GPG or GnuPG) is a free and open-source implementation of the OpenPGP standard, providing cryptographic services for data and communication. It allows users to encrypt and sign data and communications, featuring flexible key management and integration with various applications.
examples: Using the `gpg` command-line tool to encrypt a file with a recipient's public key: `gpg -e -r recipient_id file.txt`.|Verifying the digital signature of a downloaded software package using `gpg --verify signature.asc package.tar.gz`.|Integrating with email clients like Thunderbird (via Enigmail) to encrypt and sign emails.

definition: Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS), also known as forward secrecy, is a property of a key agreement protocol that ensures compromise of long-term secret keys does not compromise past session keys. Each session key is ephemeral and generated independently, preventing decryption of previously recorded traffic.
examples: TLS 1.2 and 1.3 handshakes using ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (DHE or ECDHE) key exchange, ensuring that a server's long-term private key compromise doesn't expose past communications.|Encrypted messaging apps like Signal employing DHE for every new chat session.|SSH connections configured to use KEX (Key Exchange) algorithms that generate ephemeral session keys.
title: Perfect Forward Secrecy

definition: A Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZKP) is a method by which one party (the prover) can prove to another party (the verifier) that they know a certain piece of information, without revealing any details about that information itself. It ensures the verifier learns nothing beyond the fact that the prover possesses the knowledge.
examples: Proving you are over 18 without revealing your exact birthdate or age.|Authenticating to a server by proving you know a password without sending the password itself.|Blockchain applications like Zcash using ZKPs (specifically zk-SNARKs) to allow private transactions where transaction details remain confidential but verifiable.
title: Zero-Knowledge Proof

definition: Quantum Cryptography is a field of cryptography that leverages the principles of quantum mechanics to perform cryptographic tasks, primarily secure key distribution. Its most prominent application, Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), allows for information-theoretically secure key exchange, where eavesdropping is physically detectable.
examples: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) systems using photons to transmit cryptographic keys, relying on principles like the no-cloning theorem to detect eavesdroppers.|Developing quantum-resistant cryptographic algorithms, even though strictly, this refers to 'Post-Quantum Cryptography' rather than quantum cryptography itself.|Experimental networks demonstrating secure communication links using QKD protocols like BB84.
title: Quantum Cryptography

definition: Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC), also known as quantum-resistant cryptography, refers to cryptographic algorithms designed to be secure against attacks from large-scale quantum computers. These algorithms are based on hard mathematical problems that are believed to remain intractable even for quantum computers, unlike current widely used public-key schemes.
examples: NIST's standardization efforts to select new PQC algorithms, such as lattice-based cryptography (e.g., CRYSTALS-Kyber for key exchange, CRYSTALS-Dilithium for signatures).|Implementing hash-based signatures like XMSS or SPHINCS+ for long-term secure digital signatures.|Research into code-based cryptography (e.g., Classic McEliece) for encryption.

title: Post-Quantum Cryptography

definition: ChaCha20-Poly1305 is a modern authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD) algorithm. It combines the ChaCha20 stream cipher for confidentiality with the Poly1305 message authentication code for integrity and authenticity, offering high performance and strong security, especially on software platforms.
examples: Used as a cipher suite in TLS 1.3 for secure web communication.|Implemented in various VPN protocols, such as WireGuard, for encrypting network traffic.|Integrated into OpenSSH for securing remote shell connections.
semantic_tags: Stream Cipher|Authenticated Encryption|AEAD|Message Authentication Code|Modern Cryptography|TLS
title: Chacha20-Poly1305

definition: Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) is an authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD) mode of operation for block ciphers, typically AES. It provides both confidentiality (encryption) and authenticity (integrity protection) for data, making it highly secure and widely adopted for network protocols.
examples: Used extensively in TLS 1.2 and 1.3 cipher suites for securing HTTPS connections.|Implemented in IPsec to provide encrypted and authenticated network communication.|Securing data at rest in cloud storage systems where both confidentiality and integrity are paramount.
title: Galois/Counter Mode (GCM)

definition: Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) is a mode of operation for block ciphers where each block of plaintext is XORed with the previous ciphertext block before being encrypted. This chaining mechanism makes the ciphertext dependent on all preceding plaintext blocks, enhancing security compared to ECB, and requires an Initialization Vector (IV).
examples: Encrypting a file using AES in CBC mode with a randomly generated IV.|Used in older versions of SSL/TLS and various disk encryption schemes.|Applying padding to the last block of data to fit the block size before CBC encryption.
title: Cipher Block Chaining (CBC)

definition: Counter Mode (CTR) is a block cipher mode of operation that effectively turns a block cipher into a stream cipher. It encrypts a sequential counter value, which is then XORed with the plaintext to produce ciphertext, allowing for parallel encryption/decryption and direct access to any block.
examples: Encrypting data streams where parallel processing is advantageous, such as in high-performance network devices.|Used in modern protocols and applications due to its efficiency and the fact that errors in one ciphertext block do not propagate to others.|Combining with an HMAC to achieve authenticated encryption, similar to GCM's approach.
title: Counter Mode (CTR)

definition: Electronic Codebook (ECB) is the simplest mode of operation for block ciphers, where each block of plaintext is encrypted independently using the same cryptographic key. This mode is generally insecure for data larger than one block because identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks, revealing patterns and making it unsuitable for most applications.
examples: Encrypting a very small, single block of data where no repetitive patterns are expected.|Historically used in some early cryptographic applications before more secure modes were widely adopted.|Demonstrating the weakness of block cipher modes by showing how an image encrypted with ECB reveals the original image's outline.
semantic_tags: Block Cipher Mode|Encryption|Cryptographic Weakness|Pattern Leakage|Symmetric Cryptography|Confidentiality
title: Electronic Codebook (ECB)

definition: Output Feedback Mode (OFB) is a block cipher mode of operation that turns a block cipher into a synchronous stream cipher. It generates a keystream by repeatedly encrypting an Initialization Vector (IV), and this keystream is then XORed with the plaintext to produce ciphertext. OFB's keystream generation is independent of the plaintext or ciphertext, making it susceptible to certain types of attacks if the IV is reused.
examples: Encrypting streaming data where errors in transmission should not propagate.|Used in some older secure communication systems that required a stream cipher for efficient data processing.|Applications where pre-computation of the keystream is advantageous before the plaintext is available.
title: Output Feedback Mode (OFB)

definition: A block cipher mode of operation that makes a block cipher behave like a self-synchronizing stream cipher, encrypting data in smaller units than the block size. It uses the previous ciphertext block as input to the encryption algorithm to produce a keystream, which is then XORed with the plaintext.
examples: Encrypting data streams where errors propagate for a limited number of blocks.|Legacy systems using older block ciphers like DES might have implemented CFB mode for certain applications.
title: Cipher Feedback Mode (CFB)

definition: A cryptographic hash function that takes a secret (like a master key or password) and other parameters (like a salt) to deterministically generate one or more cryptographically strong secret keys. KDFs are designed to make brute-force attacks on the input secret more computationally expensive.
examples: Generating encryption keys from a user's password for file encryption.|Deriving session keys from a shared secret in key exchange protocols (e.g., HKDF).|Used in modern secure protocols to create multiple sub-keys from a single master key.
title: Key Derivation Function (KDF)

definition: Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2, a specific type of KDF designed to make brute-force attacks against passwords more difficult by repeatedly applying a pseudorandom function (like HMAC). It takes a password, a salt, and an iteration count as inputs to produce a derived key.
examples: Used in WPA2 for deriving the Pairwise Master Key (PMK) from a passphrase.|Many password managers use PBKDF2 to derive encryption keys from master passwords.|Securely storing user passwords in web applications before the advent of more memory-hard functions.
title: PBKDF2

definition: A password hashing function designed by Niels Provos and David Mazières, based on the Blowfish cipher. It incorporates a salt and an adaptive iteration count (cost factor) to make brute-force attacks computationally intensive and slow, even with specialized hardware.
examples: Storing user passwords securely in web application databases using libraries like `bcrypt.hashpw()`.|Authentication systems requiring strong password protection against dictionary and brute-force attacks.|Used in various programming languages and frameworks for password security.
title: Bcrypt

definition: A password-based key derivation function explicitly designed to be memory-hard, making it resistant to brute-force attacks even with custom hardware (ASICs/GPUs). It requires a significant amount of memory and CPU time, making it expensive for attackers to parallelize and perform large-scale attacks.
examples: Secure storage of cryptocurrencies where proof-of-work is memory-intensive (e.g., Litecoin).|Password hashing in applications where strong resistance to hardware-accelerated attacks is critical.|Used in some encrypted file systems and disk encryption tools.
title: Scrypt

definition: The winner of the Password Hashing Competition (PHC), Argon2 is a highly tunable password hashing function that can be configured to be memory-hard, CPU-hard, or both. It offers strong resistance against both brute-force and side-channel attacks through parameters like memory cost, time cost, and parallelism.
examples: The recommended standard for password hashing in new applications and systems due to its configurability and security.|Used in various authentication frameworks for secure password storage.|Implementing secure user registration and login processes.
title: Argon2

definition: A random, unique value added to a password or other data before hashing, designed to prevent precomputed rainbow table attacks and ensure that identical passwords yield different hash values. Each user typically has a distinct salt, which is stored alongside the hash.
examples: When a user registers, a unique salt is generated, combined with their password, and the result is hashed.|Using `PBKDF2(password, salt, iterations)` where the salt ensures uniqueness of the hash output for the same password.|Preventing attackers from using pre-computed hash tables (rainbow tables) to crack multiple passwords simultaneously.
title: Salt (Cryptography)

definition: A fixed-size input to a cryptographic primitive that is typically required to be random or pseudorandom and unique for each encryption operation under the same key. Its purpose is to ensure that identical plaintexts produce different ciphertexts, preventing patterns from emerging and enhancing security.
examples: Used in block cipher modes like CBC, CTR, and GCM to randomize the encryption process.|Encrypting multiple files with the same key, each using a unique IV to avoid replay attacks.|Included in the encrypted message or communicated separately to the recipient for decryption.
title: Initialization Vector (IV)

definition: A "number used once," a random or pseudorandom value that is used only once within a specific scope, often to prevent replay attacks or to provide uniqueness. Nonces are critical in cryptographic protocols and modes of operation to ensure freshness and prevent misuse of cryptographic primitives.
examples: An Initialization Vector (IV) is a type of nonce, specifically one used in encryption.|Used in authentication protocols like Kerberos to prevent replay attacks by ensuring a message is fresh.|The counter value in Counter Mode (CTR) of a block cipher.
title: Nonce (Cryptography)

definition: A hardware device or process that generates random numbers based on physical, unpredictable phenomena, such as thermal noise, atmospheric static, or radioactive decay. TRNGs are considered cryptographically strong because their output is truly non-deterministic and cannot be replicated.

definition: An algorithm that generates a sequence of numbers that approximates the properties of random numbers but are deterministically produced from an initial value called a "seed." definition: A source of true randomness, typically from unpredictable physical phenomena or external events, used to seed cryptographic random number generators. The quality and unpredictability of an entropy source are crucial for the security of cryptographic keys and random values.
examples: Thermal noise from electronic circuits or atmospheric static.|User input events like mouse movements and keyboard timings on a computer.|Hardware-based randomness gathered from device-specific unpredictable characteristics.

definition: The ability of a cryptographic system to easily adapt to changes in cryptographic algorithms, key lengths, or protocols without requiring a complete redesign or significant disruption. This allows systems to evolve as new vulnerabilities are discovered or new, stronger algorithms become available, ensuring long-term security.

definition: A type of firewall that operates at the application layer (Layer 7) of the OSI model, inspecting and filtering traffic based on the content of specific applications or services. definition: A security technique that divides data centers and cloud environments into distinct, isolated security segments down to the workload level, enabling granular security policies to be applied between each segment. definition: A security measure that transforms untrusted input into a safe format before displaying it, preventing the browser from misinterpreting user-supplied data as executable code or markup. definition: The process of securely handling and maintaining the state of a user's interaction with a web application over multiple requests. It involves identifying authenticated users, controlling their access to resources, and ensuring session integrity and confidentiality.

definition: An open standard for authorization that allows a user to grant a third-party application limited access to their resources on another service without sharing their credentials. It allows a user to authenticate once at an identity provider (IdP) and gain access to multiple service providers (SPs) without re-authenticating.

definition: An identity layer built on top of the OAuth 2.0 framework, providing a simple identity verification layer that allows clients to verify the identity of the end-user based on authentication performed by an Authorization Server. definition: An access control model where the owner of a resource or a designated administrator can grant or revoke access permissions to other users or groups at their discretion. definition: An access control model where the operating system or a central authority enforces access policies based on security labels assigned to both subjects (users/processes) and objects (files/resources). Access decisions are not at the discretion of the owner, but rather based on predefined security classifications and clearances, often used in high-security environments.

definition: A software defect that occurs when a program attempts to write more data into a fixed-size buffer than it can hold, overwriting adjacent memory locations. This can lead to program crashes, data corruption, or the execution of arbitrary malicious code.
examples: A C program using `strcpy` without bounds checking, writing beyond the allocated buffer for a user input string.|An attacker providing an overly long username to a login prompt, overwriting the return address on the stack to execute their own code.|Heap-based buffer overflows corrupting data structures in memory.

definition: A flaw that occurs when the output of a concurrent program depends on the sequence or timing of uncontrollable events, such as the interleaving of threads or processes. In a security context, this can allow an attacker to exploit a window of vulnerability to gain unauthorized access or manipulate system state.

definition: A malicious technique where an attacker overlays a transparent or opaque layer over a legitimate webpage, tricking a user into clicking on hidden elements of the underlying page. definition: The Shared Responsibility Model is a framework that delineates the security responsibilities between a cloud service provider (CSP) and its customers. definition: A brute force attack is a trial-and-error method used by attackers to guess credentials, cryptographic keys, or encrypted data by systematically trying every possible combination of characters. These attacks are typically automated and can be very time-consuming but effective against weak or short passwords.
examples: A tool like Hydra attempts to log into an SSH server by systematically trying every password from 'aaaaaa' to 'zzzzzz' and beyond.|An attacker uses a GPU-accelerated cracking tool to test billions of permutations per second against a hashed password file.|A script iterates through all possible 6-digit PINs (000000 to 999999) to unlock a protected archive.
title: Brute Force Attack (Passwords)

definition: A dictionary attack is a type of brute force attack that attempts to guess a password by trying a pre-compiled list of common words, phrases, and previously compromised passwords. This method exploits the human tendency to choose easily memorable and weak passwords.
examples: An attacker uses a tool like John the Ripper with a dictionary file containing words like 'password', '123456', 'qwerty', and common names to crack hashed passwords.|A script tries all entries from the RockYou.txt password list (a famous compilation of leaked passwords) against a login form.|An attacker targets a Wi-Fi network's WPA/WPA2 passphrase using a dictionary of common network passwords found online.
title: Dictionary Attack (Passwords)

definition: A rainbow table attack is an attack technique used to crack hashed passwords more efficiently than a traditional brute-force attack by employing precomputed tables of hashes for a large number of potential passwords. It sacrifices storage space for computation time, enabling rapid reversal of hashes to their original plaintext passwords without having to recompute each hash individually.
examples: An attacker obtains an NTLM password hash from a Windows system and uses a pre-generated rainbow table to quickly find the original plaintext password.|A penetration tester uses a large rainbow table to crack password hashes obtained from a compromised Linux `/etc/shadow` file.|A tool queries a database of precomputed hashes to match a given hash and retrieve the original password, bypassing the need for a full brute-force search.
title: Rainbow Table Attack (Passwords)

definition: A Threat Intelligence Platform (TIP) is a software solution that aggregates, processes, and disseminates threat intelligence from various internal and external sources, helping organizations manage, analyze, and act upon relevant security information. TIPs enhance an organization's ability to detect, prevent, and respond to cyber threats more effectively by providing actionable context.
examples: A TIP integrates feeds from industry groups, government agencies, and open-source intelligence to provide a consolidated view of active malware campaigns and IP blacklists.|A security analyst uses a TIP to research a suspicious IP address, checking if it's associated with known botnets, phishing operations, or command-and-control servers.|The platform automatically correlates internal security event data with external threat indicators to identify potential breaches and prioritize remediation efforts.
title: Threat Intelligence Platform (TIP)

definition: An Incident Response Plan (IRP) is a documented set of procedures and guidelines an organization follows to prepare for, detect, contain, eradicate, recover from, and analyze cybersecurity incidents. Its primary purpose is to minimize damage, reduce recovery time, and prevent future occurrences through systematic and coordinated action.
examples: A company's incident response plan details specific steps for a ransomware attack, including system isolation, stakeholder notification, and data restoration protocols.|The plan specifies roles and responsibilities for the incident response team during a data breach, including legal, public relations, and technical leads.|A documented procedure outlines how to handle a denial-of-service attack, from identifying the source to deploying mitigation techniques and engaging ISPs.
semantic_tags: Incident Management|Cybersecurity|Crisis Management|Security Policy|Disaster Recovery|Business Continuity
title: Incident Response Plan

definition: Incident identification is the initial phase of incident response, involving the detection of anomalous or malicious activity and determining whether it constitutes a security incident requiring a formal response. This phase often relies on security monitoring tools, alert systems, and user reports to flag potential threats.
examples: A Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) system generates an alert for multiple failed login attempts from an unusual geographical location, prompting an investigation.|An employee reports receiving a suspicious phishing email asking for their credentials, triggering a security team review.|Antivirus software detects and flags a known piece of malware on a workstation, initiating a formal incident response process.
title: Incident Identification

definition: Incident containment is the phase of incident response focused on limiting the scope and impact of a security incident to prevent further damage, unauthorized access, or spread of the attack. This often involves isolating affected systems, networks, or accounts.
examples: Upon detecting a malware infection, a network administrator immediately disconnects the compromised workstation from the corporate network.|During a denial-of-service (DoS) attack, a security team implements rate limiting and diverts traffic through a scrubbing center to protect core services.|Database access is temporarily revoked for a compromised user account to prevent further data exfiltration until the root cause is addressed.
title: Incident Containment

definition: Incident eradication is the phase of incident response focused on removing the root cause of the incident and any remnants of the attack from affected systems and networks. This includes cleaning malware, patching exploited vulnerabilities, removing unauthorized accounts, and strengthening security controls to prevent re-infection.
examples: After a malware infection, the security team performs a full scan of all systems, removes the malware, and patches the exploited vulnerability that allowed initial access.|Following a successful phishing attack, all compromised credentials are reset, and multifactor authentication is enforced for affected users.|Backdoors and persistent access mechanisms installed by an attacker are identified and removed from compromised servers, along with any unauthorized configuration changes.
title: Incident Eradication

definition: Incident recovery is the phase of incident response focused on restoring affected systems and services to normal operation, verifying their integrity, and closely monitoring them for signs of re-infection or residual compromise. This often involves restoring from clean backups, implementing stronger security measures, and extensive testing.
examples: After a ransomware attack, encrypted data is restored from clean, verified backups, and all systems are brought back online in a controlled and phased manner.|Following a website defacement, the original website content is deployed, and all links, functionalities, and security configurations are verified.|Services are gradually brought back online after a Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attack, with continuous monitoring for unusual traffic patterns and performance issues.
semantic_tags: Incident Response|Restoration|Business Continuity|Disaster Recovery|System Hardening|Service Restoration
title: Incident Recovery

definition: Post-incident analysis, also known as 'lessons learned,' is the final phase of incident response, involving a detailed review of the entire incident to understand what happened, why it happened, and how to prevent similar incidents in the future. This phase is crucial for continuous improvement of security posture and incident response capabilities.
examples: An incident response team conducts a 'lessons learned' meeting to discuss the timeline of a breach, identifying shortcomings in detection, containment, and recovery procedures.|A comprehensive report is generated detailing the root cause of an outage, recommended system improvements, and updated security policies and procedures.|The team reviews the effectiveness of the containment strategies used during an attack and proposes new automated isolation mechanisms or improved threat intelligence integration.
semantic_tags: Incident Response|Lessons Learned|Root Cause Analysis|Continuous Improvement|Security Audit|Review
title: Post-Incident Analysis

definition: Digital forensics is the scientific process of identifying, preserving, collecting, analyzing, and presenting digital evidence in a legally admissible manner to investigate cybercrimes, security incidents, or policy violations. It involves specialized techniques and tools to extract meaningful information from digital devices and systems.
examples: A forensic investigator recovers deleted files and artifacts from a suspect's hard drive to prove unauthorized data access or intellectual property theft.|Analysis of network traffic logs, firewall logs, and intrusion detection system alerts helps reconstruct the timeline of an attack and identify the attacker's methods.|An expert examines email headers and content, along with server logs, to trace the origin and propagation of a sophisticated phishing campaign.
title: Digital Forensics

definition: Disk forensics is a specialized branch of digital forensics focused on the acquisition, preservation, and analysis of data stored on computer hard drives, solid-state drives, and other storage media. Its goal is to uncover hidden, deleted, or otherwise unobservable information relevant to an investigation without altering the original evidence.
examples: A forensic analyst creates a bit-for-bit image of a suspect's hard drive using a write-blocker to analyze its contents without altering the original evidence.|Deleted partitions and files are recovered from a seized laptop's SSD using specialized forensic software to find incriminating documents.|The Master File Table (MFT) on an NTFS volume is analyzed to reconstruct file system activity, file access times, and determine user actions.
semantic_tags: Forensics|Data Recovery|Digital Evidence|Storage Media|File Systems|Evidence Preservation
title: Disk Forensics

definition: Mobile device forensics is a specialized branch of digital forensics dedicated to the extraction, preservation, and analysis of data from mobile devices like smartphones and tablets. It addresses unique technical challenges posed by device encryption, diverse operating systems (iOS, Android), and proprietary hardware.
examples: A forensic tool extracts call logs, SMS messages, chat histories, and GPS location data from a suspect's iPhone using a physical acquisition method.|Data from a locked Android phone, including application data and browser history, is acquired using advanced techniques like JTAG or chip-off.|WhatsApp chat histories, contact lists, and multimedia files are recovered from a mobile device as evidence in a legal case or corporate investigation.
title: Mobile Device Forensics

definition: Cloud forensics is a specialized branch of digital forensics concerned with the investigation of incidents and the acquisition of digital evidence within cloud computing environments. It addresses unique challenges related to data locality, multi-tenancy, elasticity, legal jurisdiction, and the ephemeral nature of cloud resources.
examples: An investigator collects audit logs, virtual machine snapshots, and network flow data from an AWS EC2 instance involved in a security breach.|Data from a compromised Microsoft 365 tenant, including email archives, SharePoint files, and user activity logs, is acquired for an investigation.|A forensic analysis is performed on container logs, Kubernetes audit trails, and serverless function execution logs in a cloud-native application environment to trace an attacker's actions.
title: Cloud Forensics

definition: The Chain of Custody in forensics refers to a documented, unbroken chronological record of the possession, handling, transfer, analysis, and disposition of physical or electronic evidence. Maintaining a strict chain of custody is crucial to ensure the integrity, authenticity, and legal admissibility of evidence in legal proceedings.
examples: A detailed form is filled out every time a piece of evidence (e.g., a hard drive) is transferred between forensic analysts, detailing who handled it, when, and for what purpose.|Digital hashes (like MD5 or SHA256) are computed for forensic images upon creation and verification to prove that no data has been altered during transport or storage.|A secure evidence locker is used to store physical evidence, with access logs maintained for all entries and retrievals, timestamped and signed by personnel.
title: Chain of Custody (Forensics)

definition: Forensic imaging is the process of creating an exact, bit-for-bit duplicate of a digital storage medium (like a hard drive, USB drive, or memory card) in a forensically sound manner. This ensures that the original evidence remains unaltered while analysis and investigation are performed on the duplicate copy.
examples: An investigator uses a hardware write-blocker and tools like `dd` or FTK Imager to create a raw `.dd` image of a suspect's laptop hard drive.|A memory dump (RAM capture) is performed on a running system to preserve volatile data before powering it off, capturing active processes and network connections.|A full disk image of a server is created and cryptographically hashed to ensure its integrity before any forensic analysis begins on the copy.
semantic_tags: Forensics|Evidence Preservation|Data Acquisition|Bit-for-Bit Copy|Write Blocker|Digital Evidence
title: Forensic Imaging

definition: Log analysis is the process of systematically reviewing and interpreting computer-generated records (logs) of events that occur within an operating system, application, or network device. It is a critical activity for security monitoring, incident detection, troubleshooting, performance analysis, and forensic investigations.
examples: A security analyst sifts through firewall logs to identify unusual outbound connections to suspicious IP addresses or unexpected open ports.|A SIEM system aggregates logs from multiple servers to detect a pattern of failed logins followed by a successful login from a new IP, indicating a potential compromise.|Web server access logs are analyzed to determine the source, target, and method of a brute-force attack against a web application or to track user behavior.
title: Log Analysis

definition: Indicators of Attack (IoAs) are forensic artifacts or patterns of behavior that reveal an ongoing malicious attempt to compromise a system or network, focusing on the attacker's tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) rather than just known bad files or IPs. Unlike Indicators of Compromise (IoCs) which are reactive, IoAs are proactive signals that indicate an attack is in progress, allowing for early detection and intervention. They are typically behavioral and context-rich, providing insights into the attacker's objectives and methods.
examples: A process injecting code into another legitimate process (e.g., svchost.exe).|Multiple failed login attempts followed by successful administrative access from a new, unusual IP address.|An uncommon or unsigned executable attempting to modify critical system registry keys or install a root certificate.
semantic_tags: Threat detection|Behavioral analysis|Cyber defense|Proactive security|TTPs|Incident response
title: Indicators of Attack (IoA)

definition: Adversary emulation is a cybersecurity testing methodology that simulates the actions of a specific, known threat actor or group by replicating their tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs). This approach aims to provide a realistic assessment of an organization's security posture and its ability to detect, prevent, and respond to sophisticated real-world attacks. It goes beyond generic vulnerability scanning or penetration testing by focusing on how a specific adversary would operate.
examples: A red team performing an operation that mimics the TTPs of an Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) group like APT28.|Using open-source intelligence to reconstruct and simulate a known ransomware gang's specific lateral movement and data exfiltration techniques.|Testing an organization's defenses against a recreated supply chain attack vector previously used by a state-sponsored actor.
semantic_tags: Threat simulation|Red teaming|Cybersecurity testing|TTPs|Attack simulation|Threat intelligence
title: Adversary Emulation

definition: An incident playbook is a documented, step-by-step guide outlining predefined procedures and actions to be taken by an organization in response to specific types of cybersecurity incidents. It standardizes the incident response process, ensuring consistent and efficient handling of security events by providing clear roles, responsibilities, communication protocols, and technical steps. Playbooks help minimize damage, reduce recovery time, and improve overall incident management maturity.
examples: A 'Phishing Email Response Playbook' detailing steps from user reporting to email analysis, containment, and user notification.|A 'Data Breach Playbook' guiding legal, PR, IT, and security teams through data exfiltration detection, forensics, regulatory reporting, and public disclosure.|A 'DDoS Attack Playbook' describing traffic monitoring, mitigation techniques, ISP coordination, and communication strategies during a denial-of-service event.
semantic_tags: Incident response|Security operations|Procedural guide|Documentation|Crisis management|Cybersecurity framework
title: Incident Playbook

definition: Digital forensics readiness refers to the proactive measures taken by an organization to ensure that digital evidence can be efficiently and effectively collected, preserved, analyzed, and presented in a legally admissible manner, should a cybersecurity incident occur. It involves planning, establishing policies, configuring systems, and training personnel to facilitate potential future forensic investigations. By being ready, organizations can accelerate incident response and improve the chances of successful prosecution or recovery.
examples: Implementing comprehensive logging policies across all critical systems and applications to capture security events and user activities.|Establishing clear data retention policies and mechanisms for imaging hard drives or virtual machines in a forensically sound manner.|Developing an incident response plan that includes procedures for evidence collection, chain of custody documentation, and secure storage.
title: Digital Forensics Readiness

definition: Spyware is a type of malicious software designed to secretly gather information about a person or organization and relay it to an unauthorized third party, without the user's knowledge or consent. It typically monitors user activities, collects personal data, and can install additional harmful software. The collected information can include browsing history, personal files, credentials, and keystrokes.
examples: A commercial spyware program like Pegasus, used to monitor mobile phone activities including calls, messages, and location.|An information stealer that surreptitiously collects banking credentials and credit card numbers from a compromised computer.|Adware that tracks user browsing habits to deliver targeted advertisements, often considered a form of spyware due to data collection.
title: Spyware

definition: Adware is software that automatically displays or downloads unwanted advertisements, often in the form of pop-ups, banners, or redirecting browser traffic to specific websites. While some adware may be benign, many forms are considered malicious as they can track user browsing habits, slow down system performance, and sometimes act as a conduit for installing other malware. It typically arrives bundled with legitimate software or via drive-by downloads.
examples: Web browser pop-up windows appearing frequently, even when not actively browsing for new content.|Unwanted toolbars installed in a web browser that redirect searches or display extra ads on legitimate websites.|Software that constantly changes the browser's homepage or default search engine without user permission.
title: Adware

definition: A botnet is a network of compromised computer systems, often referred to as 'bots' or 'zombies,' that are controlled by a single attacker or 'bot-herder' without the knowledge of their owners. These compromised devices, which can include PCs, servers, and IoT devices, are typically used to perform coordinated malicious tasks on a large scale, such as launching Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks, sending spam, or distributing malware. The bot-herder uses a command-and-control (C2) server to direct the botnet.
examples: The Mirai botnet, which primarily compromised insecure IoT devices (e.g., CCTV cameras, routers) to launch massive DDoS attacks.|The Emotet botnet, initially a banking Trojan, evolved into a modular botnet used for distributing other malware like ransomware.|A network of compromised computers used to send millions of spam emails daily, bypassing individual email provider defenses.
title: Botnet

definition: A keylogger is a type of surveillance technology used to record every keystroke made on a specific computer or mobile device. These can be implemented as hardware devices, software programs, or even within web browsers, operating covertly to capture sensitive information like usernames, passwords, credit card numbers, and other personal data. Keyloggers are often used by attackers to steal credentials or spy on users.
examples: A malicious software program installed on a victim's computer that captures all typed characters and periodically sends them to an attacker.|A small physical USB device inserted between a keyboard and computer, intercepting and storing keystrokes for later retrieval.|A JavaScript snippet embedded in a phishing website that captures credentials as they are typed into a fake login form before submission.
title: Keylogger

definition: A backdoor is a covert method of bypassing normal authentication or encryption to gain unauthorized, remote access to a computer system, application, or network. It is often created intentionally by developers for maintenance purposes but can also be inserted maliciously by attackers or malware to maintain persistent access. Backdoors allow attackers to control or access a system without being detected by standard security protocols.
examples: A hardcoded username and password combination left in a device's firmware that grants administrative access, known only to the developer or attacker.|A Remote Access Trojan (RAT) that installs a hidden service allowing an attacker to connect and control the infected machine from anywhere.|A web shell uploaded to a compromised web server, providing a command-line interface via a web browser to execute commands on the server.
title: Backdoor

definition: Fileless malware is a sophisticated type of malicious software that operates entirely in computer memory, without writing any files to disk, making it extremely difficult to detect by traditional signature-based antivirus solutions. Instead, it leverages legitimate system tools, built-in operating system processes, and memory-resident techniques to execute its payload and persist across reboots. This technique significantly reduces the attack's footprint and improves stealth.
examples: A PowerShell script executed directly from memory via a malicious command, performing actions like injecting code into legitimate processes.|Malware utilizing Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) to execute commands, establish persistence, and move laterally across a network.|Reflective DLL injection where a malicious DLL is loaded directly into a legitimate process's memory space without being stored on disk.
semantic_tags: Malware|Memory-resident|Stealth|Advanced Persistent Threat|Evasion|Living off the Land
title: Fileless Malware

definition: An exploit kit is a software package designed to automate the process of exploiting known vulnerabilities in client-side software, typically web browsers and their plugins (like Adobe Flash, Java, or Acrobat Reader). Attackers use exploit kits by driving traffic to malicious web pages hosting the kit, which then probes the visitor's system for vulnerable software. If a vulnerability is found, the kit delivers a payload, often malware, to compromise the system without user interaction.
examples: The Angler Exploit Kit, known for its sophistication in evading detection and delivering various malware payloads, including ransomware.|The RIG Exploit Kit, a popular choice among cybercriminals for exploiting vulnerabilities in web browsers and delivering information stealers or cryptominers.|A malicious website redirecting users to a landing page where an exploit kit attempts to compromise their browser based on its version and installed plugins.
title: Exploit Kit

definition: A zero-day exploit is a cyberattack that takes advantage of a software vulnerability that is unknown to the software vendor or public, meaning there is no existing patch or workaround available. The term 'zero-day' refers to the fact that the vendor has had zero days to fix the vulnerability once it's discovered and exploited. These exploits are highly prized by attackers due to their effectiveness and difficulty of detection, often used in targeted attacks by sophisticated adversaries.
examples: The Stuxnet worm, which famously exploited multiple zero-day vulnerabilities in Windows and Siemens industrial control systems.|A newly discovered flaw in a popular web browser that allows remote code execution, being actively exploited by attackers before the browser vendor can release a security update.|A vulnerability in a mobile operating system that allows an attacker to gain root access to a device, for which the operating system developer has no immediate fix.
title: Zero-Day Exploit

definition: A Denial of Service (DoS) attack is a cyberattack designed to make a machine or network resource unavailable to its intended users by temporarily or indefinitely disrupting services of a host connected to the Internet. DoS attacks typically overwhelm the target with a flood of traffic or requests, or by exploiting a vulnerability that causes the system to crash. The goal is to deny legitimate users access to information or services.
examples: A 'SYN flood' attack, where an attacker sends a high volume of SYN requests to a server but never completes the handshake, exhausting the server's connection resources.|A 'ping of death' attack, sending oversized or malformed ICMP packets to a target system, causing it to crash or freeze.|Exploiting a software bug that causes an application to consume excessive resources and become unresponsive, leading to service disruption.
title: Denial of Service (DoS)

definition: A Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack is a more powerful and complex form of DoS attack that uses multiple compromised computer systems as sources of attack traffic. These 'botnet' devices simultaneously target a single victim, overwhelming the target's network, server, or application with a massive flood of legitimate-looking requests or malicious data. DDoS attacks are harder to mitigate due to their distributed nature and high volume, making it difficult to distinguish malicious traffic from legitimate user requests.
examples: The Mirai botnet launching a massive DDoS attack against DNS provider Dyn, disrupting access to numerous major websites.|An application-layer DDoS attack targeting a web server with a flood of HTTP GET requests for complex database queries, exhausting its processing power.|A large-scale volumetric attack where millions of compromised IoT devices send enormous amounts of junk data to saturate a target's network bandwidth.
title: Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS)

definition: Social engineering is a manipulation technique that exploits human psychology and trust to trick individuals into divulging confidential information or performing actions that benefit an attacker. It relies on psychological tactics rather than technical hacking, leveraging deception, persuasion, and impersonation to bypass security measures. Common motives include gaining unauthorized access, stealing data, or financial fraud.
examples: An attacker impersonating an IT support technician on the phone to convince an employee to provide their login credentials.|Sending a fake email disguised as a trusted entity (e.g., bank, service provider) that tricks a user into clicking a malicious link or downloading an infected attachment.|An attacker creating a sense of urgency or fear (e.g., 'your account will be locked') to pressure a victim into making a hasty decision.
title: Social Engineering

definition: Spear phishing is a highly targeted form of phishing attack where an attacker sends a fraudulent email or electronic message to a specific individual, organization, or business, often appearing to be from a trusted sender. Unlike generic phishing, spear phishing messages are meticulously crafted using specific information about the target, gleaned from public or stolen sources, to make the communication seem legitimate and increase the likelihood of success. The goal is typically to steal sensitive data, deploy malware, or gain unauthorized access.
examples: An email sent to a specific employee, referencing an internal project they are working on, from a spoofed email address that appears to be their manager, asking them to review a malicious 'project document'.|An attacker sending a personalized LinkedIn message to a company's HR manager, posing as a recruiter with an attached 'resume' containing malware.|A fraudulent email to a company's finance department, appearing to be from the CEO, requesting an urgent wire transfer to an unfamiliar account.
title: Spear Phishing

definition: Whaling is a highly specific type of spear phishing attack that targets high-profile individuals within an organization, such as senior executives, CEOs, or high-level managers. The attackers often pose as a superior or another trusted authority to trick the victim into performing critical actions like authorizing large financial transfers, revealing sensitive company information, or granting access to critical systems. Due to the victim's position, the potential impact of a successful whaling attack can be severe.
examples: An email sent to a CFO, seemingly from the CEO, requesting an urgent and large wire transfer to a specific vendor account outside of normal procedures.|A fraudulent message targeting a vice president, appearing to be from the company's legal counsel, asking for confidential merger and acquisition documents.|An attacker impersonating a board member to trick an executive assistant into providing login details for the CEO's calendar or email account.
semantic_tags: Phishing|Social engineering|Executive target|Fraud|Business Email Compromise|Targeted attack
title: Whaling (Phishing)

definition: Vishing, a portmanteau of 'voice' and 'phishing,' is a form of social engineering attack that uses voice communication, typically over the phone, to trick individuals into revealing personal information or performing actions. Attackers often impersonate trusted entities like banks, government agencies, or tech support to gain the victim's trust and manipulate them. The goal is usually to steal credentials, financial data, or induce monetary transfers.
examples: A phone call from someone claiming to be from your bank's fraud department, asking for your account number and PIN to 'verify a suspicious transaction'.|A scammer calling and impersonating an IRS agent, threatening legal action if immediate payment is not made via gift cards or wire transfer.|An attacker calling an employee, posing as a helpdesk technician, to guide them through installing 'security software' that is actually malware or gives the attacker remote access.
title: Vishing

definition: Smishing, a portmanteau of 'SMS' and 'phishing,' is a social engineering attack that uses text messages (SMS) to trick victims into clicking malicious links, downloading malware, or divulging sensitive personal information. Attackers typically send messages that appear to be from legitimate sources like banks, delivery services, or government agencies, often creating a sense of urgency or offering an enticing reward to prompt immediate action. The goal is usually to steal credentials, financial information, or install malicious software.
examples: A text message appearing to be from a bank, asking you to click a link to 'verify your account details' due to suspicious activity.|A message from a 'delivery company' stating there's an issue with your package and asking you to click a link to 'reschedule delivery' or 'pay a fee'.|A text message offering a fake prize or discount, prompting the recipient to click a link to claim it, leading to a phishing site or malware download.
semantic_tags: Phishing|Social engineering|SMS scam|Mobile fraud|Deception|Text message security
title: Smishing

definition: Baiting is a social engineering technique where an attacker offers something enticing, a 'bait,' to lure a victim into compromising their security or disclosing information. The bait often appeals to curiosity or greed and typically involves physical media infected with malware or a deceptive online offer. Once the victim takes the bait, their system may be compromised, or their credentials stolen.
examples: Leaving a USB flash drive labeled 'Confidential HR Data' or 'Employee Salaries' in a public place within a corporate office, hoping an employee will pick it up and insert it into their computer, thus infecting it with malware.|Offering free music or movie downloads through a malicious website that requires users to install a 'media player' which is actually spyware or adware.|Setting up a fake public Wi-Fi hotspot named 'Free Airport WiFi' to capture user credentials when they attempt to connect and log in to various services.
title: Baiting (Social Engineering)

definition: Pretexting is a form of social engineering where an attacker creates a fabricated scenario or false identity (a 'pretext') to manipulate a victim into divulging sensitive information or performing an action beneficial to the attacker. The attacker uses this deception to build trust and bypass security protocols.
examples: An attacker calls an employee pretending to be from IT support, claiming a 'security issue' requires their login credentials.|A scammer impersonates a bank official, asking a customer to 'verify' their account details due to 'suspicious activity'.|An attacker emails a human resources department pretending to be a senior executive, requesting a list of employee salaries.
title: Pretexting

definition: Tailgating, also known as piggybacking, is a physical security breach where an unauthorized individual gains access to a restricted area by closely following an authorized person through a controlled entry point, often without the authorized person's explicit consent or knowledge.
examples: An attacker follows an employee through a card-access door into a secure office area, pretending to be a colleague.|An unauthorized person slips into a server room behind a delivery person who has just used their key card.|An individual blends in with a group of employees entering a building to bypass the reception desk.
title: Tailgating

definition: Shoulder surfing is the act of obtaining sensitive information by visually observing a victim's private actions, such as their screen, keyboard, or physical documents, often from an advantageous position in public or semi-public spaces.
examples: Looking over someone's shoulder to see their PIN as they enter it at an ATM.|Observing a user type their password or credit card details on a laptop in a coffee shop or airport lounge.|An attacker watching a user's phone screen to glimpse a one-time password (OTP) or confidential message.
title: Shoulder Surfing

definition: A watering hole attack is a type of cyberattack where an attacker identifies and infects a website frequently visited by a specific target group, such as employees of a particular company or members of an industry, with the goal of compromising members of that group when they visit the site.
examples: Compromising a popular industry-specific forum website to inject malware that infects visitors' computers.|An attacker infects a local restaurant's website, knowing that employees of a target company frequently check its menu or hours.|Injecting an exploit kit into a compromised news site popular among journalists to target specific reporting agencies.
title: Watering Hole Attack

definition: A Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attack is a form of cyberattack where an attacker secretly intercepts, relays, and potentially alters communication between two parties who believe they are communicating directly. The attacker positions themselves in the communication path, gaining full control over the information exchanged.
examples: An attacker sets up a rogue Wi-Fi hotspot to intercept traffic between unsuspecting users and legitimate websites.|Using ARP spoofing on a local network to redirect traffic through the attacker's machine, allowing them to capture or modify data.|An attacker intercepts an SSL/TLS handshake to present a fake certificate, then decrypts and re-encrypts traffic before forwarding it.
normalized_name: man in the middle attack mitm
title: Man-in-the-Middle Attack (MITM)

definition: A Man-in-the-Browser (MITB) attack is a type of Man-in-the-Middle attack specifically targeting a web browser, typically through a Trojan horse or malicious browser extension. The malware infects the browser, allowing the attacker to intercept, modify, or insert data directly within the victim's browser session before it is sent to the web server or displayed to the user.
examples: Malware injecting malicious scripts into an online banking page to alter transaction details (e.g., recipient account number) before they are sent to the bank.|A rogue browser extension stealing login credentials or session tokens as a user interacts with a website.|A Trojan modifying the content of a secure web page to trick a user into revealing additional personal information.
normalized_name: man in the browser attack mitb
title: Man-in-the-Browser Attack (MITB)

definition: A supply chain attack is a cyberattack that targets less secure elements in an organization's supply chain to gain unauthorized access to the main target. This typically involves tampering with legitimate software, hardware, or third-party services before they reach the end user, introducing vulnerabilities or backdoors.
examples: Injecting malicious code into a widely used software library that many companies incorporate into their products, like in the SolarWinds attack.|Compromising a hardware manufacturer to embed backdoors or surveillance mechanisms into their devices before shipment.|An attacker compromising a software update server to distribute malware disguised as a legitimate update to many users.
semantic_tags: Software Security|Third-Party Risk|Vendor Compromise|Trust Exploitation|Systemic Risk
title: Supply Chain Attack

definition: An insider threat is a security risk that originates from within the targeted organization, typically from current or former employees, contractors, or business partners who have legitimate access to systems, data, or physical premises. These threats can be malicious (intentional harm) or unintentional (negligence or error).
examples: A disgruntled employee intentionally leaking confidential company data to a competitor or the public.|An employee accidentally clicking on a phishing link, thereby compromising the company network from the inside.|An IT administrator abusing their elevated privileges to access and misuse sensitive customer records for personal gain.
