definition: An Operating System (OS) is system software that manages computer hardware and software resources, providing common services for computer programs. It acts as an intermediary between the user of a computer and the computer hardware, abstracting complexities and managing concurrent operations.
examples: Microsoft Windows (e.g., Windows 11)|Linux distributions (e.g., Ubuntu)|macOS (e.g., Sonoma)
title: Operating System Definition

definition: The primary goals of an operating system are convenience, efficiency, and the ability to evolve. It aims to make the computer system convenient to use, utilize computer hardware efficiently, and be constructed in a modular fashion to permit new features and improvements.
examples: Providing a graphical user interface (GUI) for ease of use.|Optimizing CPU scheduling to maximize throughput.|Allowing device drivers to be updated without reinstalling the entire OS.
title: Operating System Goals

definition: Operating system services are functions provided by the OS to assist users and programs, making the system easier to use and develop applications for. These services include program execution, I/O operations, file system manipulation, communications, and error detection.
examples: Loading and executing a user application (e.g., double-clicking an icon).|Reading data from a file or writing to a printer.|Creating, deleting, or renaming files and directories.|Using pipes or sockets for inter-process communication.
semantic_tags: System Calls|Process Management|File Management|I/O Management|Resource Allocation
title: Operating System Services

definition: A monolithic kernel is an operating system architecture where the entire operating system, including device drivers, file systems, and the kernel itself, runs in a single address space in kernel mode. This design offers high performance due to direct function calls between components but can be complex to maintain and less robust as a crash in one component can bring down the entire system.
examples: Linux Kernel|Traditional UNIX kernels|MS-DOS
title: Monolithic Kernel

definition: A microkernel is an operating system architecture that provides only the minimal necessary services in kernel mode, such as inter-process communication (IPC), memory management, and low-level scheduling. Most other OS services, like device drivers and file systems, run as user-space processes (servers), improving modularity, security, and reliability at the potential cost of performance due to increased IPC overhead.
examples: GNU Hurd|Mach (kernel for macOS, though macOS is hybrid)|MINIX 3
title: Microkernel

definition: A hybrid kernel is an operating system architecture that combines aspects of both monolithic and microkernels. It aims to achieve the performance of a monolithic kernel while retaining some of the modularity and reliability benefits of a microkernel, typically by keeping some services (like device drivers or file systems) in kernel space for speed but allowing others to be loaded or run in user space.
examples: Microsoft Windows NT kernel (and its descendants, e.g., Windows 11)|macOS (XNU kernel)|DragonFly BSD
title: Hybrid Kernel

definition: A layered operating system structures the OS into a hierarchy of layers, with each layer built upon the services of the layers below it. This modular approach simplifies development, debugging, and verification, as each layer only interacts with the adjacent layers, but can suffer from performance overhead due to multiple function calls across layers.
examples: THE Multiprogramming System (early example)|UNIX systems (conceptual layering for certain components, less strict than THE)|Network protocol stacks (e.g., TCP/IP model)
title: Layered Operating System

definition: An exokernel is an operating system architecture that aims to provide minimal hardware abstractions to user-level applications, allowing them to manage their own resources more directly. Instead of providing high-level abstractions, an exokernel securely multiplexes hardware resources, giving applications more control over physical resources and potentially greater performance and flexibility.
examples: MIT Exokernel|Nemesis OS
title: Exokernel

definition: A Virtual Machine Monitor (VMM), also known as a hypervisor, is a software layer that creates and runs virtual machines (VMs). It manages and isolates multiple guest operating systems, allowing them to share the underlying physical hardware resources without interfering with each other.
examples: VMware ESXi (Type-1 hypervisor)|Oracle VirtualBox (Type-2 hypervisor)|Microsoft Hyper-V (Type-1 hypervisor)
title: Virtual Machine Monitor (VMM)

definition: A batch operating system processes jobs in batches, without direct user interaction during execution. Users submit jobs (programs, data, and control commands) to an operator, who groups similar jobs together and executes them sequentially, optimizing for CPU utilization rather than response time.
examples: Early mainframe systems (e.g., IBM OS/360 for batch processing)|Payroll processing systems that run overnight.|Scientific simulations executed as a series of pre-defined tasks.
title: Batch Operating System

definition: A time-sharing operating system allows multiple users to share a single computer system simultaneously, and also allows a single user to run multiple programs concurrently. It achieves this by rapidly switching the CPU between different jobs, giving each a small slice of time, creating the illusion of parallel execution and providing interactive computing.
examples: UNIX systems (e.g., Solaris, AIX)|Modern desktop operating systems (e.g., Windows, macOS, Linux)|Cloud computing environments where multiple users share server resources.
title: Time-Sharing Operating System

definition: A Real-Time Operating System (RTOS) is an operating system intended to serve real-time applications that process data as it comes in, without buffering delays. RTOS are designed to guarantee a certain capability within a specified deadline, crucial for systems where timing constraints are critical to correct operation, often categorized as hard (strict deadlines) or soft (tolerable delays) real-time.
examples: Operating systems for automotive control systems (e.g., QNX, VxWorks).|Medical imaging devices (e.g., MRI machines).|Industrial control systems and robotics.
title: Real-Time Operating System

definition: A distributed operating system manages a collection of independent computers that appear to the users as a single coherent system. It handles resource management, process synchronization, and communication across multiple machines, abstracting the underlying network complexities and facilitating transparent resource sharing.
examples: Google's Cluster Management Systems (e.g., Borg, Kubernetes)|Amoeba (research OS)|Chorus OS (research OS)
title: Distributed Operating System

definition: A network operating system (NOS) runs on servers and provides capabilities to manage data, users, groups, security, applications, and other networking functions. Unlike a distributed OS, a NOS typically treats each machine as distinct, where users are aware of the network structure and explicitly access remote resources.
examples: Windows Server (e.g., Windows Server 2019)|Novell NetWare (historical)|UNIX/Linux-based servers configured for network services (e.g., file servers, print servers).
title: Network Operating System

definition: An embedded operating system is a specialized OS designed to run on embedded computer systems, which are typically dedicated to specific functions within larger mechanical or electrical systems. These OS are often resource-constrained, real-time capable, and optimized for compactness, efficiency, and reliability for their specific task.
examples: Operating systems in smart appliances (e.g., refrigerators, washing machines).|Firmware in routers or network switches.|Automotive infotainment systems (e.g., Android Automotive OS).
title: Embedded Operating System

definition: A mobile operating system is an OS specifically designed to power mobile devices such as smartphones, tablets, and wearables. It emphasizes touch-based user interfaces, power management, connectivity options (cellular, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth), and features like app stores and location services.
examples: Android by Google|iOS by Apple|watchOS for Apple Watch
title: Mobile Operating System

definition: Multi-programming is the technique of keeping multiple jobs (programs) in memory at the same time and executing them concurrently by rapidly switching the CPU among them. When one job needs to wait for an I/O operation, the OS switches the CPU to another job, thereby maximizing CPU utilization and throughput.
examples: A user editing a document while a web browser downloads files in the background.|Running a compiler on one program while another program's output is being printed.|Modern operating systems actively managing several user applications and background services.
title: Multi-programming

definition: Multi-tasking is the logical extension of multi-programming, where multiple processes are executing concurrently on a single CPU by rapidly switching between them. This creates the illusion that all tasks are running simultaneously, providing interactivity for users and efficient resource utilization.
examples: Running a web browser, a music player, and a text editor simultaneously on a desktop PC.|Switching between different apps on a smartphone.|The operating system managing background updates while a user works on a foreground application.
title: Multi-tasking

definition: Multi-threading is a programming concept where a single process can have multiple execution paths (threads) that run concurrently. Threads within the same process share the same memory space and resources, making them lightweight to create and switch between, improving application responsiveness and parallelism within a single program.
examples: A web browser using one thread to render the UI and another to download data.|A word processor using a separate thread for spell-checking in the background.|Database servers using multiple threads to handle concurrent client requests.
title: Multi-threading

definition: Dual-mode operation is a hardware-supported mechanism that allows an operating system to protect itself and other system components from misbehaving user programs. It typically involves at least two modes: user mode, for user applications with restricted privileges, and kernel mode (or supervisor mode), for the OS kernel with full hardware access and unrestricted privileges.
examples: A user program attempting to directly access hardware registers triggers a trap to the kernel.|Executing a system call (e.g., `fork()`, `open()`) to transition from user mode to kernel mode.|The operating system kernel performing privileged I/O operations.
title: Dual-mode Operation

definition: Protection rings are a hierarchical privilege level system used by hardware to protect system resources and prevent unauthorized access by software. The rings determine which operations a program is allowed to perform, with lower ring numbers typically indicating higher privileges.
examples: Ring 0 represents the most privileged level, typically where the operating system kernel runs.|Ring 3 represents the least privileged level, where user applications operate.|In x86 architecture, accessing certain hardware registers is restricted to Ring 0.
title: Protection Rings

definition: Privileged instructions are CPU instructions that can only be executed by the operating system kernel or other highly privileged software when operating in a privileged mode (e.g., kernel mode). Their execution in user mode would result in a protection fault.
examples: Modifying page tables to change memory mappings.|Disabling or enabling interrupts to control hardware responsiveness.|Directly accessing I/O ports to communicate with peripheral devices.
title: Privileged Instructions

definition: Non-privileged instructions are CPU instructions that can be executed by any program, including user-level applications, without requiring special permissions or operating in a privileged mode.
examples: Arithmetic operations like addition, subtraction, or multiplication.|Data movement instructions for moving values between registers or memory locations.|Conditional jump instructions that alter program flow based on certain conditions.
title: Non-privileged Instructions

definition: The system boot process is the sequence of operations performed by a computer from the moment it is powered on until the operating system is fully loaded and ready for user interaction.
examples: The Power-on Self-Test (POST) checking hardware components.|Loading the bootloader from a storage device.|The bootloader then loading the operating system kernel into memory.
title: System Boot Process

definition: BIOS is legacy firmware stored on a motherboard's non-volatile memory, responsible for performing basic hardware initialization during the boot process and providing basic runtime services for the operating system.
examples: Initializing hardware components like the keyboard, mouse, and disk drives at startup.|Loading the Master Boot Record (MBR) from the primary boot device.|Providing basic I/O routines for disk access or screen display before the OS loads.
title: BIOS (Basic Input/Output System)

definition: UEFI is a modern firmware interface that replaces BIOS, offering advanced features like secure boot, support for larger disk partitions (GPT), network capabilities, and a more flexible pre-boot environment.
examples: Implementing Secure Boot to prevent unauthorized operating systems or malware from loading during startup.|Booting from GPT (GUID Partition Table) disk partitions, which overcomes MBR's size limitations.|Providing a graphical user interface (GUI) within the firmware setup utility.
title: UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface)

definition: Firmware is a specific class of computer software that provides low-level control for a device's specific hardware, often embedded directly into hardware components or non-volatile memory.
examples: BIOS or UEFI on a computer motherboard that manages the boot process.|The microcode that controls a CPU's internal operations.|Software embedded in a hard drive or SSD controller that manages data storage and retrieval.
title: Firmware

definition: An init system is the first process started by the kernel (Process ID 1) in a Unix-like operating system, responsible for initializing the rest of the operating system services and managing them throughout the system's runtime.
examples: System V init, a traditional init system found in older Unix and Linux distributions.|systemd, the modern and widely adopted init system in contemporary Linux distributions.|launchd, the init system used in macOS.
title: Init System

definition: systemd is a modern, backward-compatible init system and service manager for Linux operating systems, designed to aggressively parallelize services, start them on demand, and manage their dependencies.
examples: Using `systemctl start apache2.service` to launch the Apache web server.|Configuring units (`.service`, `.target` files) to define how services and system states are managed.|Automatically restarting a failed database service.
title: systemd (Linux Init System)

definition: A service manager is a component of an operating system responsible for starting, stopping, and managing system services (often called daemons) and other background processes.
examples: systemd on Linux, which manages system services like network interfaces and web servers.|Windows Service Control Manager, which handles services like DHCP Client or Print Spooler.|launchd on macOS, which manages daemons and agents for the system and users.
title: Service Manager

definition: A process is an instance of a computer program that is being executed, comprising the program code, its current activity (program counter, registers), and its associated resources such as memory, open files, and I/O devices.
examples: When a user double-clicks on an application icon (e.g., a web browser), a new process is created.|Executing a shell command like `ls` creates a process to list directory contents.|The operating system kernel itself runs as one or more processes or threads.
title: Process Definition

definition: Process state refers to the current condition or phase a process is in during its lifecycle, as perceived by the operating system's scheduler.
examples: A process actively executing instructions on the CPU is in the 'Running' state.|A process waiting for an I/O operation to complete is in the 'Waiting' (or Blocked) state.|A process ready to be assigned to the CPU but currently not executing is in the 'Ready' state.
title: Process State

definition: Process creation is the act of bringing a new process into existence, typically initiated by an existing process (the parent) or by the operating system itself.
examples: A user running an application, which causes the shell process to create a new child process.|A web server spawning multiple child processes to handle concurrent client requests.|The `fork()` system call creating a new process that is a duplicate of the calling process.
title: Process Creation

definition: Process termination is the act of ending a process's execution and releasing all its allocated resources, such as memory and open files, back to the operating system.
examples: A program completing its intended task and naturally exiting.|A user manually closing an application window, triggering its termination.|The operating system forcefully terminating a process due to an error or a `kill` command.
title: Process Termination

definition: A zombie process is a process that has completed its execution but still has an entry in the process table because its parent process has not yet read its exit status.
examples: A child process exits using `exit()` before its parent process has called `wait()` or `waitpid()` to collect its status.|Running `ps aux | grep Z` in Linux to find processes with 'Z' in the STAT column.
title: Zombie Process

definition: An orphan process is a process whose parent process has terminated without waiting for its child processes to finish their execution.
examples: A long-running background process started from a shell, where the shell itself is closed before the background process completes.|In Unix-like systems, orphan processes are typically adopted by the `init` process (PID 1) which becomes their new parent and handles their `wait()` calls.
title: Orphan Process

definition: The `fork()` system call creates a new process (the child process) by duplicating the calling process (the parent process), with both processes continuing execution from the point of the `fork()` call, but with distinct memory spaces.
examples: In C, `pid_t pid = fork();` where `pid` will be 0 in the child and the child's PID in the parent.|Web servers often use `fork()` to create new child processes to handle concurrent client requests.|A shell program uses `fork()` to create a new process for each command it executes.
title: Fork System Call

definition: The `exec()` system call (or family of calls like `execve`, `execl`) replaces the current process's memory space and program with a new program specified by its arguments, without creating a new process ID.
examples: After a `fork()` call, the child process typically calls `exec()` to load and run a different program.|The C standard library function `system()` often uses `fork()` followed by `exec()` to execute a shell command.|A shell program uses `exec()` to run the actual command after `fork()`.

title: Exec System Call

definition: The `wait()` system call causes the calling parent process to pause its execution until one of its child processes terminates, allowing the parent to retrieve the child's exit status and prevent it from becoming a zombie.
examples: In C, `wait(&status)` or `waitpid(pid, &status, 0)` are used by a parent process to synchronize with its children.|A shell program uses `wait()` to wait for a foreground command to complete before displaying a new prompt.|Ensuring proper cleanup of child processes to avoid zombie processes.
title: Wait System Call

definition: The `exit()` system call is used to explicitly terminate the calling process, releasing its allocated resources back to the operating system and returning an exit status code to its parent process.
examples: In C, `exit(0)` is used to indicate successful program termination.|Returning from the `main` function in a C program implicitly calls `exit()`.|A program might call `exit(1)` to signal an error during its execution.
title: Exit System Call

definition: A thread is the smallest unit of processing that can be scheduled by an operating system, representing a single sequence of execution within a process. Threads within the same process share the same memory space, code, and resources but have their own program counter, stack, and register set. This allows for concurrent execution paths within a single application.
examples: A web server handling multiple client requests concurrently, each by a separate thread.|A word processor using one thread for user input, another for spell-checking, and another for saving the document.
title: Thread Definition

definition: User-level threads (ULTs) are managed entirely by the user-level thread library without kernel involvement. The kernel is unaware of the existence of ULTs and sees only the process as a single thread of control. This makes thread creation and management fast, but if one ULT blocks, the entire process blocks.
examples: POSIX Pthreads library on Linux when configured for user-level threading (though often implemented as kernel-level).|Early versions of Java threads before native thread support.|Green threads in some older or specialized virtual machines.
semantic_tags: thread library|context switching|kernel unaware|process blocking|user space
title: User-Level Threads

definition: Kernel-level threads (KLTs) are managed and scheduled directly by the operating system kernel. The kernel maintains context information for each thread and handles thread creation, scheduling, and synchronization. This allows multiple threads within the same process to run concurrently on different CPUs and ensures that if one thread blocks, other threads in the same process can continue executing.
examples: Windows threads (Win32 API).|Linux threads (NPTL - Native POSIX Thread Library).|Solaris LWP (Lightweight Processes).
semantic_tags: kernel management|OS scheduler|parallel execution|independent threads|system calls
title: Kernel-Level Threads

definition: The Many-to-One model maps many user-level threads to a single kernel-level thread. Thread management is handled by the user-level thread library. While efficient for thread creation and context switching within the application, a major drawback is that if one user-level thread performs a blocking system call, the entire process, including all other user threads, will block.
examples: Early implementations of Green threads in Java.|GNU Portable Threads.
semantic_tags: user threads|single kernel thread|blocking issue|thread library|efficiency
title: Many-to-One Thread Model

definition: The One-to-One model maps each user-level thread directly to a kernel-level thread. This provides more concurrency as it allows multiple threads to run in parallel on multiprocessor systems and prevents one thread from blocking the entire process with a blocking system call. However, this model has more overhead in terms of creating and managing threads compared to user-level models.
examples: Windows threads.|Linux NPTL (Native POSIX Thread Library).|Modern Java Virtual Machines typically use this model.
title: One-to-One Thread Model

definition: The Many-to-Many model multiplexes many user-level threads onto a smaller or equal number of kernel-level threads. This model aims to combine the benefits of both User-Level and Kernel-Level threads, allowing for efficient creation of user threads while enabling true concurrency and avoiding the blocking problem. The operating system dynamically adjusts the number of kernel threads based on application needs.
examples: Solaris Green Threads (older implementations used a variation of this).|Some modern thread pool implementations might conceptually operate similarly.
title: Many-to-Many Thread Model

definition: Thread creation is the process of generating a new independent path of execution within an existing process. This involves allocating a new thread ID, program counter, register set, and a stack, and then making the new thread ready for scheduling by the operating system. Threads can be created explicitly by an application or implicitly by a runtime system.
examples: `pthread_create()` in C/C++ using the Pthreads library.|`new Thread().start()` in Java.|`CreateThread()` in the Windows API.
title: Thread Creation

definition: Thread termination is the process by which a thread completes its execution and is removed from the system. A thread can terminate either implicitly by returning from its starting function or explicitly by calling a termination routine. Upon termination, resources allocated specifically to the thread, such as its stack, are reclaimed by the system.
examples: A thread function returning `NULL` in C/C++.|`pthread_exit()` in C/C++ Pthreads.|`thread.join()` (waiting for termination) or allowing a Java `run()` method to complete.
title: Thread Termination

definition: Thread synchronization refers to the coordination of multiple threads to ensure proper execution ordering and consistent access to shared resources. It is essential to prevent data corruption and race conditions that can arise when threads concurrently modify shared data or depend on specific execution sequences. Mechanisms like locks, semaphores, and condition variables are used for this purpose.
examples: Using a mutex to protect a shared counter variable, ensuring atomic increments.|A producer-consumer problem where a semaphore coordinates access to a shared buffer.|Using condition variables to signal when a resource becomes available for other threads.
title: Thread Synchronization

definition: Mutual exclusion is a synchronization property that ensures that only one thread or process can access a shared resource or critical section at any given time. This mechanism prevents race conditions and data inconsistency by serializing access to protected data structures or code segments. It is a fundamental requirement for correct concurrent programming.
examples: Using a mutex lock to protect a linked list, allowing only one thread to add or remove nodes at a time.|A single writer lock on a database, preventing other writers or readers during a critical update.
semantic_tags: critical section|atomic access|race condition prevention|shared resource|concurrent programming
title: Mutual Exclusion (Synchronization)

definition: A semaphore is a signaling mechanism used for thread synchronization that maintains an integer value. It provides two atomic operations: `wait` (also known as `P` or `down`), which decrements the semaphore value and blocks if it's zero; and `signal` (also known as `V` or `up`), which increments the value and potentially unblocks a waiting thread. Semaphores can be counting (for resource management) or binary (acting as a mutex).
examples: A counting semaphore initialized to 5 to control access to 5 identical printers.|A binary semaphore (mutex) protecting a critical section.|Coordinating producer-consumer threads using `empty` and `full` semaphores for a shared buffer.
title: Semaphores

definition: A mutex (short for mutual exclusion) lock is a synchronization primitive that grants exclusive access to a shared resource to only one thread at a time. A thread acquires the lock before entering a critical section and releases it upon exiting, ensuring that no other thread can access the protected resource concurrently. If another thread tries to acquire an already locked mutex, it will block until the lock is released.
examples: `pthread_mutex_lock()` and `pthread_mutex_unlock()` in C/C++.|`synchronized` keyword in Java or `ReentrantLock`.|Protecting a shared counter in a multithreaded application.
title: Mutex Lock

definition: Deadlock is a situation in a multiprocessing system where two or more competing actions are perpetually waiting for each other to finish, such that none ever complete. It typically occurs when multiple threads or processes each hold resources and request resources held by others, forming a circular chain of dependencies.
examples: Two trains approaching a single track intersection from opposite directions, each waiting for the other to move.|Two threads, T1 and T2, where T1 holds Lock A and waits for Lock B, while T2 holds Lock B and waits for Lock A.
semantic_tags: resource contention|circular wait|indefinite blocking|system freeze|concurrency issue
title: Deadlock Definition

definition: Mutual exclusion, as a condition for deadlock, states that at least one resource must be held in a non-sharable mode; that is, only one process at a time can use the resource. If another process requests that resource, the requesting process must be delayed until the resource has been released. This condition is inherent for resources that cannot be simultaneously shared.
examples: A printer, which can only be used by one process at a time.|A shared write lock on a file, allowing only one writer at a time.
semantic_tags: non-sharable resource|exclusive access|critical resource|single user|deadlock prerequisite
title: Mutual Exclusion (Deadlock Condition)

definition: Hold and Wait, as a condition for deadlock, states that a process must be holding at least one resource and simultaneously waiting to acquire additional resources that are currently being held by other processes. This creates a scenario where processes are reluctant to release resources they already possess while waiting for others.
examples: A process holds a scanner and is waiting for a printer, which is held by another process.|A thread holds `Lock A` and is attempting to acquire `Lock B`.
title: Hold and Wait (Deadlock Condition)

definition: No Preemption, as a condition for deadlock, states that resources cannot be forcibly taken away from a process that is holding them. A resource can only be released voluntarily by the process that is holding it, after that process has completed its task with that resource. This means that once a resource is allocated, it remains with the process until explicitly released.
examples: A CPU cannot arbitrarily take a memory block away from a process that has allocated it.|A thread holding a mutex lock cannot have the lock forcibly removed by another thread.
title: No Preemption (Deadlock Condition)

definition: Circular Wait, as a condition for deadlock, states that a set of processes {P0, P1, ..., Pn} must exist such that P0 is waiting for a resource held by P1, P1 is waiting for a resource held by P2, ..., Pn-1 is waiting for a resource held by Pn, and Pn is waiting for a resource held by P0. This forms a closed chain of resource dependencies.
examples: Process A waits for resource X held by B, Process B waits for resource Y held by C, and Process C waits for resource Z held by A.|Two threads each acquire one of two mutexes and then attempt to acquire the other, creating a cycle.
semantic_tags: resource dependency|closed chain|graph cycle|waiting cycle|deadlock prerequisite
title: Circular Wait (Deadlock Condition)

definition: Starvation is a problem in concurrent systems where a process or thread is perpetually denied access to a resource or CPU time, even though the resource periodically becomes available. This often happens due to unfair scheduling policies or biased resource allocation, where other processes are always chosen over the "starving" one. Unlike deadlock, the system is not necessarily stuck, but one or more specific entities never make progress.
examples: A low-priority thread continuously being preempted by high-priority threads, never getting CPU time.|A dining philosophers solution where some philosophers always pick up the right fork before the left, and if unlucky, never get both.|A reader-writer lock that heavily favors writers, causing readers to wait indefinitely.
semantic_tags: indefinite postponement|unfair scheduling|resource denial|liveness problem|priority inversion
title: Starvation (Synchronization)

definition: Pipes are a form of inter-process communication (IPC) that allow unidirectional data flow between two related processes, typically a parent and child process. Data written to one end of the pipe is buffered by the operating system and can be read from the other end. They are a simple and effective mechanism for processes to exchange small amounts of data.
examples: `ls | grep "foo"` in a Unix-like shell, where the output of `ls` is piped as input to `grep`.|Using `pipe()` system call in C to create a communication channel between a parent and child process.
title: Pipes (IPC)

definition: Named pipes, also known as FIFOs (First-In, First-Out), are a type of inter-process communication (IPC) mechanism that allow two or more unrelated processes to communicate by reading and writing to a special file on the filesystem. Unlike regular pipes, named pipes have a directory entry, persist until explicitly deleted, and enable communication between processes that do not share a common ancestor.
examples: Creating a FIFO using `mkfifo` command in Unix/Linux (`mkfifo my_fifo`) and then having one process write to it while another reads from it.|A client-server application where clients write requests to a well-known FIFO and servers read from it.
title: Named Pipes (FIFOs)

definition: A list of messages stored within the kernel, allowing processes to send and receive data asynchronously. Each message has a type, and processes can selectively read messages based on type, facilitating structured communication between unrelated processes.
examples: A server process placing task requests into a message queue for multiple worker processes to retrieve and process.|In a real-time system, sensor data is placed into a queue, and an analysis process consumes it asynchronously.|Using `mq_send()` and `mq_receive()` functions in POSIX message queues to exchange data.
title: Message Queues (IPC)

definition: An endpoint for sending and receiving data across a network or between processes on the same machine. Sockets enable bidirectional communication, supporting various protocols like TCP and UDP, and are fundamental for network programming.
examples: A web browser communicating with a web server over TCP/IP using a network socket.|Two distinct applications on the same computer exchanging data using Unix domain sockets.|Using `socket()`, `bind()`, `listen()`, `accept()`, `send()`, `recv()` system calls for network communication.
title: Sockets (IPC)

definition: A limited form of inter-process communication used to notify a process of an event. Signals are asynchronous notifications sent to a process, interrupting its normal flow of execution to handle specific events like termination requests or errors.
examples: Pressing Ctrl+C in a terminal sends a SIGINT signal to the foreground process to request termination.|A process receiving a SIGSEGV signal due to an illegal memory access, causing it to crash.|Using the `kill()` system call to send a signal from one process to another.

title: Signals (IPC)

definition: A unblockable and uncatchable signal that forcefully terminates a process immediately. It is considered the most severe signal because the target process cannot ignore it or perform any cleanup actions before exiting.
examples: Using `kill -9 PID` in Linux to forcibly terminate a runaway or unresponsive process.|The operating system sending SIGKILL to processes during system shutdown if they fail to respond to SIGTERM.|A debugger forcibly stopping a process that is unresponsive or stuck in an infinite loop.
title: SIGKILL Signal

definition: A standard signal used to request a process to terminate gracefully. Unlike SIGKILL, SIGTERM can be caught, ignored, or handled by a process, allowing it to perform cleanup tasks like saving data or closing files before exiting.
examples: Using `kill PID` (which defaults to SIGTERM) to politely ask a running application to shut down.|A web server receiving SIGTERM and gracefully shutting down all active connections before exiting.|A shell sending SIGTERM to background processes when a user logs out, allowing them to clean up.
title: SIGTERM Signal

definition: A collection of one or more related processes, typically created by the same job, that can be managed together by the operating system. All processes in a group share a common process group ID (PGID) and can receive signals as a unit.
examples: A shell pipeline like `cat file | grep pattern | less` forms a process group, where all processes can be signaled together (e.g., Ctrl+C).|A single user command launched from a terminal often creates a process group for itself and all its child processes.|A graphical application and all its helper processes running in a single process group for easier management.
title: Process Group

definition: The process that creates a new session, typically a shell or login process. The session leader serves as the anchor for a collection of process groups, and its termination often triggers the termination of all associated processes in the session (orphaning them).
examples: The login shell (e.g., bash, zsh) is the session leader for all processes initiated from that terminal session.|An SSH daemon process creating a new session for a remote user upon successful login.|A graphical desktop environment's display manager acting as a session leader for the user's graphical session.
title: Session Leader

definition: The activity of the operating system to manage and allocate the CPU time among competing processes. It determines which process runs when, for how long, and in what order, aiming to optimize system performance metrics like throughput, response time, and fairness.
examples: A web server managing requests from multiple clients by scheduling various worker processes.|A multi-tasking operating system allowing a user to browse the web, listen to music, and compile code concurrently.|Real-time operating systems prioritizing critical tasks for industrial control applications.
title: Process Scheduling

definition: The operating system component responsible for selecting which ready process should be executed by the CPU next. It implements various scheduling algorithms to efficiently manage CPU resources, deciding when to switch processes and which one to run.
examples: The Linux Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) deciding which runnable task gets the CPU slice.|A scheduler in an embedded system prioritizing interrupts over background tasks.|The core logic within the kernel that manages the run queue of processes.
semantic_tags: CPU Management|Operating System Kernel|Scheduling Algorithm|Context Switch|Process Management|Resource Allocation
title: Scheduler (OS Component)

definition: Also known as the job scheduler, it selects processes from the job pool and loads them into memory for execution. It controls the degree of multiprogramming by deciding which new jobs are admitted into the system, aiming to achieve a good mix of I/O-bound and CPU-bound processes.
examples: In batch processing systems, the long-term scheduler picks jobs from a queue to be processed overnight.|When a user submits a large compilation task, the long-term scheduler might decide to admit it into the system's ready queue.|Modern interactive operating systems typically have less emphasis on a distinct long-term scheduler.
title: Long-Term Scheduler

definition: Responsible for selecting one of the processes that are in the ready queue to be executed by the CPU next. It executes very frequently (milliseconds), making fine-grained decisions about which process gets the CPU next, aiming for rapid context switching and low latency.
examples: When a time slice expires, the short-term scheduler picks the next process from the run queue.|After an I/O operation completes and a waiting process becomes ready, the short-term scheduler decides if it should preempt the current process.|Implementing Round Robin or Priority scheduling to choose the next task to run on the CPU.

title: Short-Term Scheduler (CPU Scheduler)

definition: Primarily responsible for swapping processes out of memory and onto disk (and vice-versa) to reduce the degree of multiprogramming or free up memory. It improves system performance by temporarily removing processes from active contention for the CPU when memory is scarce.
examples: When physical memory is low, the medium-term scheduler swaps out an inactive process to disk to free up RAM.|A user opens many applications, and the OS swaps out background tabs of a web browser to make room for the active application.|Swapping a process back into memory when it transitions from a blocked state to ready and there's available RAM.
semantic_tags: Swapper|Memory Management|Degree of Multiprogramming|Virtual Memory|Paging|Disk I/O
title: Medium-Term Scheduler (Swapper)

definition: The module that gives control of the CPU to the process selected by the short-term scheduler. Its functions include context switching, switching to user mode, and jumping to the proper location in the user program to restart execution.
examples: After the scheduler selects process A, the dispatcher saves the state of the current process and loads the state of process A onto the CPU registers.|Restoring the program counter (PC) and stack pointer (SP) to resume a process from where it last left off.|Handling the transition from kernel mode to user mode for the newly scheduled process.
semantic_tags: Context Switch|CPU Control|Kernel Mode|User Mode|Program Counter|Scheduler Component|Dispatch Latency
title: Dispatcher (OS Component)

definition: A scheduling approach where, once a process starts executing, it continues to run until it voluntarily yields the CPU, blocks for an I/O operation, or terminates. The currently running process cannot be interrupted by the scheduler for another higher-priority or time-sliced process.
examples: First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) scheduling in its pure form.|Shortest Job Next (SJN) when executed without preemption.|Early batch systems where jobs would run to completion without interruption.
title: Non-Preemptive Scheduling

definition: A non-preemptive scheduling algorithm that selects the process with the smallest estimated execution time (CPU burst) to run next. It minimizes the average waiting time for a given set of processes, but requires accurate prediction of future CPU burst times.
examples: A set of print jobs where the smallest job is printed first to clear the queue quickly.|Calculating the average waiting time for processes P1(10ms), P2(2ms), P3(5ms) using SJN would execute P2, P3, then P1.|While theoretically optimal for average waiting time, it's impractical in interactive systems due to unknown burst times.
title: Shortest Job Next (SJN) Scheduling

definition: A preemptive version of Shortest Job Next (SJN), where the scheduler always selects the process with the shortest remaining execution time. If a new process arrives with a shorter remaining time than the currently executing process, the current process is preempted.
examples: In a multitasking system, if a short, new interactive task arrives while a long batch job is running, SRTF would preempt the batch job.|Calculating the average turnaround time for processes using a Gantt chart where preemption occurs based on remaining time.|Often used in real-time systems where responsiveness to short, critical tasks is vital.
