semantic_tags: CPU Scheduling|Preemptive|Optimal|Average Waiting Time|Remaining Time|Context Switch|Starvation
title: Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) Scheduling

definition: A preemptive scheduling algorithm designed for time-sharing systems, where each process is given a small unit of CPU time, called a time quantum or time slice, in a cyclic order. Once the quantum expires, the process is preempted and added to the end of the ready queue.
examples: A typical desktop operating system using RR to give users the illusion of multiple applications running simultaneously.|Scheduling multiple users on a mainframe system, ensuring each user gets a fair share of CPU time.|When a CPU burst for a process is 10ms and quantum is 4ms, the process runs for 4ms, then another 4ms, then 2ms, with context switches in between.
semantic_tags: CPU Scheduling|Preemptive|Time Sharing|Time Quantum|Fairness|Context Switch|Ready Queue
title: Round Robin (RR) Scheduling

definition: A scheduling approach that partitions the ready queue into several separate queues, each with its own scheduling algorithm. Processes are permanently assigned to a specific queue based on characteristics like process type (e.g., foreground, background, real-time).
examples: A system with a 'System Processes' queue (high priority, e.g., FCFS), an 'Interactive Processes' queue (medium priority, e.g., RR), and a 'Batch Processes' queue (low priority, e.g., FCFS).|Real-time operating systems often use multi-level queues for critical tasks versus general-purpose tasks.|A desktop OS prioritizing GUI applications over background command-line tools by placing them in different queues.
semantic_tags: CPU Scheduling|Priority Queues|Static Assignment|Starvation|FCFS|Round Robin|Process Classification
title: Multi-level Queue Scheduling

definition: A more flexible version of multi-level queue scheduling that allows processes to move between queues based on their behavior or age. It typically uses multiple queues with different time quanta and priority levels, promoting I/O-bound and interactive processes while demoting CPU-bound ones.
examples: A new process starts in a high-priority queue with a small time quantum; if it doesn't finish, it moves to a lower-priority queue with a larger quantum.|The Linux Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) implicitly achieves similar goals by dynamically adjusting priorities and time slices.|Processes that frequently block for I/O might be kept in higher-priority queues to improve responsiveness.
title: Multi-level Feedback Queue Scheduling

definition: A scheduling metric that measures the percentage of time the CPU is busy executing processes. High CPU utilization indicates that the CPU is being effectively used, but it must be balanced with other metrics like response time to avoid system sluggishness.
examples: A server running at 95% CPU utilization suggests it's processing many tasks efficiently.|If the CPU is idle for 30% of the time, then its utilization is 70%.|Monitoring tools reporting CPU usage show this metric, helping administrators gauge system load and performance.
title: CPU Utilization (Scheduling Metric)

definition: The total number of processes or tasks completed per unit of time by the CPU scheduler. It measures the rate at which the system successfully finishes work.
examples: A web server processing 1000 requests per second.|A batch system completing 5 jobs per hour.|A CPU scheduler finishing 25 processes in 10 seconds.
title: Throughput (Scheduling Metric)

definition: The total time elapsed from the submission of a process until its completion. This includes time spent waiting in the ready queue, executing on the CPU, and performing I/O operations.
examples: A user submitting a print job at 10:00 AM, and it finishes printing at 10:05 AM, resulting in a 5-minute turnaround time.|A program starting at t=0 and finishing at t=100 units has a turnaround time of 100 units.
title: Turnaround Time (Scheduling Metric)

definition: The total amount of time a process spends waiting in the ready queue for the CPU to become available. This metric excludes time spent executing or performing I/O.
examples: A process arrives at t=0, but only starts executing at t=5, so its initial waiting time is 5 units.|If a process is preempted and returns to the ready queue, any subsequent wait before resuming execution adds to its total waiting time.
title: Waiting Time (Scheduling Metric)

definition: The time interval from when a request is submitted until the first response is produced. It is a critical metric for interactive systems, indicating the perceived responsiveness to a user.
examples: Clicking an application icon and seeing the window appear after 0.5 seconds indicates a 0.5-second response time.|Typing a command in a terminal and seeing the first output or prompt return.
title: Response Time (Scheduling Metric)

definition: A scheduling technique where a process or thread, once assigned to a specific CPU core, is preferentially scheduled on that same core in subsequent executions. This strategy leverages CPU cache locality to improve performance by reducing cache misses.
examples: A multi-threaded application where a thread frequently accesses data already present in its previously used core's L1 cache.|The Linux Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) attempts to keep threads on the same core for cache benefits.
title: Affinity Scheduling

definition: The process of distributing workload evenly across multiple processing units (CPUs, cores, or machines) to maximize resource utilization, minimize response times, and prevent any single unit from becoming a bottleneck.
examples: A web server distributing incoming client requests across an array of backend server instances.|An operating system scheduler migrating threads between CPU cores to ensure no single core is overloaded while others are idle.
title: Load Balancing (Scheduling)

definition: A collection of pre-instantiated, idle threads that are available to execute a queue of incoming tasks. This design avoids the overhead of creating and destroying threads for each new task, thereby improving performance and resource management.
examples: A web server using a thread pool to handle concurrent client connections without creating a new thread for every request.|Java's `ExecutorService` creating a pool of worker threads to process tasks.|Database connection pools reusing established connections.
title: Thread Pools

definition: A dynamic load-balancing technique where an idle processor (the 'stealer') actively seeks and 'steals' tasks from the task queue of an overburdened processor (the 'victim'). This helps to efficiently distribute work in parallel computing environments.
examples: Cilk/Cilk++ runtime systems employ work-stealing for efficient parallel task execution.|The Go runtime scheduler uses work-stealing for balancing goroutines across OS threads.
title: Work-stealing (Scheduling)

definition: An architecture where two or more identical processors are connected to a single shared main memory and controlled by a single operating system. All processors can execute any task and share resources symmetrically.
examples: A typical modern desktop computer with a multi-core CPU (e.g., a quad-core Intel i7 or AMD Ryzen processor).|Servers with multiple physical CPU sockets, each containing multiple cores, operating under one OS instance.
title: Symmetric Multi-Processing (SMP)

definition: A technology that enables a single physical CPU core to execute multiple independent threads concurrently by duplicating architectural state (e.g., registers) while sharing most of the core's execution resources. This makes a single physical core appear as multiple logical processors to the operating system.
examples: An Intel i7 processor with 4 physical cores reporting 8 logical processors to the operating system due to hyperthreading.|Observing 'logical processors' in system monitoring tools that exceed the count of physical cores.
title: Hyperthreading (Simultaneous Multi-threading)

definition: From an OS perspective, CPU caching involves the operating system's efforts to utilize and manage CPU caches (L1, L2, L3) effectively by strategically placing data and instructions in memory. While hardware physically manages the cache, the OS's memory management, scheduling, and process layout decisions significantly impact cache performance by influencing cache hit rates.
examples: The OS arranging related data structures in contiguous memory regions to improve spatial locality and cache hits.|Affinity scheduling policies that try to keep processes on the same core to benefit from data already present in that core's cache.
title: CPU Caching (OS Perspective)

definition: A mechanism that ensures data consistency across all processor caches and main memory in a multi-processor system. It defines a set of rules and states for cache lines to guarantee that all processors have a unified and up-to-date view of shared memory.
examples: The MESI protocol, widely used in modern CPU architectures, is a common cache coherence protocol.|When multiple CPU cores in an SMP system try to read and write the same shared variable, the protocol ensures they always access the most current value.
title: Cache Coherence Protocol

definition: A widely adopted write-invalidate cache coherence protocol that defines four states for each cache line: Modified (M), Exclusive (E), Shared (S), and Invalid (I). These states dictate how a cache line can be read, written, or shared among multiple processor caches to maintain data consistency in a multi-processor system.
examples: When CPU A writes to a cache line in the 'Shared' state, it transitions to 'Modified', and all other CPU caches with a copy of that line transition to 'Invalid'.|If CPU B wants to read a cache line that CPU A holds in the 'Modified' state, CPU A must write the data back to main memory and transition its own copy to 'Shared' before CPU B can get its copy in 'Shared' state.
title: MESI Protocol

definition: The process of mapping logical addresses, generated by the CPU, to corresponding physical addresses in main memory. This binding can occur at compile time, load time, or execution time, with execution-time binding offering the most flexibility for dynamic memory management.
examples: A C program compiled to an executable where logical addresses are relative offsets, which are then translated to physical RAM addresses by the OS's memory management unit (MMU) at runtime.|Relocatable code where a linker leaves symbols to be resolved and mapped to specific physical memory locations at load time or runtime.
title: Address Binding

definition: A hardware register, also known as a base register, that stores the starting physical address of a process's assigned memory partition. Every logical address generated by the CPU is added to the value in the relocation register to produce the actual physical address, providing memory protection and address translation.
examples: If a process generates a logical address 100 and the relocation register holds 5000, the physical address accessed is 5100.|Used in simple contiguous memory allocation schemes to protect processes from accessing each other's memory space.
title: Relocation Register

definition: A hardware register that specifies the size or the maximum valid logical address range for a process. Any logical address generated by the CPU must be less than the value in the limit register; otherwise, a memory access violation (trap) is generated, enforcing memory protection boundaries.
examples: If a process is allocated a memory segment of 1000 bytes and the limit register holds 1000, a logical address of 1001 or greater would trigger an error.|Used in conjunction with a relocation register to define the precise and protected boundaries of a process's address space.
title: Limit Register

definition: A memory management scheme where each process is allocated a single, unbroken block of main memory. While simple to implement, this approach can suffer from external fragmentation, where available memory is scattered in small, unusable chunks.
examples: Early operating systems like MS-DOS frequently used contiguous memory allocation for programs.|A simple embedded system might reserve a fixed, contiguous chunk of RAM for a specific application at boot time.
title: Contiguous Memory Allocation

definition: A dynamic memory allocation algorithm that allocates the first available memory block (hole) from the beginning of the free list that is large enough to satisfy a process's request. It is simple and relatively fast but can lead to internal and external fragmentation.
examples: Given free memory holes of sizes: 5KB, 20KB, 15KB. A request for 10KB would be allocated from the 20KB hole, as it is the first large enough.|Often used in systems where allocation speed is prioritized over optimal space utilization.
title: First-Fit Memory Allocation

definition: A dynamic memory allocation algorithm that searches the entire list of free memory blocks (holes) and allocates the smallest hole that is large enough to satisfy a process's request. This strategy aims to minimize the amount of wasted space (external fragmentation) left after allocation.
examples: Given free memory holes of sizes: 5KB, 20KB, 12KB. A request for 10KB would be allocated from the 12KB hole, leaving a 2KB fragment.|While it minimizes external fragmentation, it can lead to many very small, unusable holes.
title: Best-Fit Memory Allocation

definition: A dynamic memory allocation algorithm that searches the entire list of free memory blocks (holes) and allocates the largest available hole to satisfy a process's request. The goal is to leave a remaining large enough hole that might be useful for future, potentially larger, requests.
examples: Given free memory holes of sizes: 5KB, 20KB, 12KB. A request for 10KB would be allocated from the 20KB hole, leaving a 10KB fragment.|This strategy often performs poorly in terms of fragmentation, leading to quick exhaustion of large blocks.
title: Worst-Fit Memory Allocation

definition: A memory allocation scheme where a process's logical address space is mapped to physical memory that is not necessarily contiguous, allowing a process to be spread across different, non-adjacent physical memory blocks. This approach efficiently utilizes physical memory by avoiding external fragmentation and allowing larger logical address spaces than available contiguous physical memory.
examples: Paging systems, where a process's virtual pages can be scattered throughout physical memory.|Segmentation, where logical segments are loaded into non-contiguous physical memory regions.|Paged segmentation, combining aspects of both paging and segmentation for memory allocation.
title: Non-Contiguous Memory Allocation

definition: A paging technique used to manage very large logical address spaces by breaking the page table itself into smaller, more manageable page tables, typically forming a multi-level structure (e.g., two-level paging). This reduces the memory required for the page table by only allocating parts of the inner page tables that are actively in use.
examples: A 32-bit system with 4KB pages might use a two-level page table: an outer page table points to inner page tables, which then point to physical frames.|Modern 64-bit systems often use three-level or four-level hierarchical page tables (e.g., in x86-64 architecture) to manage their vast virtual address spaces.
semantic_tags: Paging|Page Table|Memory Management|Virtual Memory|Address Translation|Multi-level Paging
title: Hierarchical Paging

definition: A page table structure designed for address spaces larger than 32 bits, particularly sparse ones, where a hash function maps virtual page numbers to entries in a hash table. This method significantly reduces the memory overhead compared to traditional linear page tables by only storing entries for active virtual pages.
examples: Used in 64-bit systems where the virtual address space is extremely large but sparsely populated, avoiding the allocation of a full linear page table that would consume excessive physical memory.|A page lookup involves hashing the virtual page number to find a potential entry in the table, then comparing the full virtual page number stored in the entry to resolve collisions.
title: Hashed Page Table

definition: A page table structure that maintains a single entry for each physical memory frame, rather than an entry for each virtual page for each process. Each entry stores the virtual page number and process ID that currently occupies that physical frame.
examples: Some PowerPC and MIPS architectures have historically utilized inverted page tables to reduce the memory footprint of page tables.|When a CPU generates a virtual address, the system must search the inverted page table to find the matching virtual page number and process ID, which can be slower than direct page table lookups.
title: Inverted Page Table

definition: Physical memory pages that are mapped into the address spaces of multiple distinct processes, allowing them to access the same code or data. This technique reduces overall memory usage and facilitates efficient inter-process communication.
examples: Sharing standard library code (e.g., `libc.so`) among multiple processes, where each process's page table points to the same physical pages containing the library code.|Shared memory segments used for Inter-Process Communication (IPC), allowing processes to directly read and write to a common memory region.|The text (code) segment of multiple running instances of the same program (e.g., multiple instances of a text editor) can be shared read-only.
semantic_tags: Paging|Memory Management|Inter-Process Communication (IPC)|Code Sharing|Data Sharing|Virtual Memory
title: Shared Pages

definition: A resource management optimization technique where resources (e.g., memory pages) are initially shared between processes until one of them attempts to modify the resource. At that point, a private copy of the modified resource is created for the modifying process, while others continue to share the original.
examples: The `fork()` system call often uses COW: the child process initially shares all of the parent's memory pages. If either process attempts to write to a shared page, a private copy of that page is made for the writing process.|Virtual machine snapshots or container cloning often employ COW for disk images, sharing base images and only storing changes in new blocks.
title: Copy-on-Write (COW)

definition: A memory management scheme that divides a process's logical address space into logically meaningful, variable-sized units called segments. Each segment corresponds to a specific program component, such as code, data, or stack, offering modularity and enhanced protection.
examples: A program's memory might be divided into distinct segments for its executable code, its global variables (data segment), and its call stack (stack segment).|In early Intel x86 architectures, memory was explicitly managed using segments, requiring segment registers to access different parts of memory.
title: Segmentation

definition: A table used in segmentation to map logical segment addresses to physical memory addresses, containing an entry for each segment owned by a process. Each entry typically specifies the segment's base address in physical memory and its limit (size), along with protection information.
examples: When a CPU generates a logical address (segment_number, offset), the segment_number is used as an index into the segment table to retrieve the segment's physical base address.|If a program has a code segment, data segment, and stack segment, its segment table would contain three entries, one for each.
title: Segment Table

definition: An individual entry within a Segment Table, which describes a single memory segment. It typically includes the physical base address where the segment begins, its length or limit (size), and protection bits indicating allowed access types (e.g., read, write, execute).
examples: An STE for a program's code segment might contain a base address of 0x10000, a limit of 0x5000 bytes, and protection flags allowing read and execute access but denying write access.|Accessing an address beyond the limit specified in the STE for a given segment would trigger a segmentation fault.
title: Segment Table Entry (STE)

definition: The frequency or percentage of memory accesses that result in a page fault, indicating how often a requested virtual page is not found in physical memory and must be retrieved from secondary storage. A high page fault rate can significantly degrade system performance due to increased disk I/O.
examples: If a process makes 1000 memory accesses and 10 of them cause a page fault, the page fault rate is 1% (10/1000).|Monitoring the page fault rate can help diagnose thrashing, where a system spends more time swapping pages than executing useful work.
title: Page Fault Rate

definition: The average time taken to access a memory location, calculated by considering the probabilities and access times of different memory levels, such as main memory and secondary storage in a paged virtual memory system. It quantifies the performance impact of page faults.
examples: For a system with a 98% page hit ratio (20ns access time) and a 2% page fault rate (10ms fault penalty), EAT = (0.98 * 20ns) + (0.02 * 10,000,000ns).|EAT can also be calculated for cache-memory hierarchies, incorporating cache hit rates and main memory access times.
title: Effective Access Time (EAT)

definition: A memory management model that attempts to keep in physical memory the set of pages that a process is actively using, defined as the set of pages referenced by a process during a specific time window (the working-set window). The goal is to prevent thrashing by ensuring processes have enough memory for their current needs.
examples: If a process frequently accesses pages A, B, and C within a 10-millisecond window, these pages constitute its working set and should ideally reside in RAM.|Operating systems might estimate the working set by tracking page reference bits over time and periodically resetting them, thereby identifying currently active pages.
semantic_tags: Virtual Memory|Thrashing|Locality of Reference|Page Replacement|Memory Management|Performance
title: Working Set Model

definition: A theoretical page replacement algorithm that replaces the page that will not be used for the longest period of time in the future. Although impossible to implement in practice because it requires future knowledge, it serves as a benchmark to evaluate the efficiency of other page replacement algorithms.
examples: Given a page reference string (e.g., 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5) and a limited number of frames, OPT would replace page 4 with 5 at a certain point because 4 is not referenced again for a longer duration than other resident pages.|Used in simulations to establish the minimum possible page fault rate for a given reference string.
title: Optimal Page Replacement (OPT)

definition: A page replacement algorithm that evicts the page that has been in physical memory for the longest time, treating pages like a simple queue. It is easy to implement but often suffers from poor performance because it ignores the actual usage frequency or recency of pages.
examples: If pages A, B, C were loaded into memory in that order, and a new page D needs space, page A would be replaced first, regardless of whether it's frequently used.|Can suffer from Belady's Anomaly, where increasing the number of available frames can sometimes lead to more page faults.
normalized_name: first in first out fifo page replacement
title: First-In, First-Out (FIFO) Page Replacement

definition: A page replacement algorithm that replaces the page that has not been accessed for the longest period of time, based on the principle of locality that pages used recently are likely to be used again soon. LRU generally performs well but is complex to implement efficiently, often requiring hardware support.
examples: If pages A, B, C are in memory and C was the most recently used, then B, then A, and a new page D needs space, page A would be replaced.|Implementing true LRU typically requires tracking the exact time of last use for each page, often approximated by algorithms like Clock or Second Chance.
normalized_name: least recently used lru page replacement
title: Least Recently Used (LRU) Page Replacement

definition: A practical approximation of LRU that uses a reference bit for each page frame, arranged in a circular list. When a page needs replacement, the algorithm scans the list, clearing reference bits until it finds a page with a cleared bit, which it then replaces.
examples: Imagine a clock hand sweeping through page frames; if a page's reference bit is 0, it's replaced. If the bit is 1, it's cleared, and the hand moves to the next page, giving the page a 'second chance'.|Often implemented by hardware that sets a reference bit when a page is accessed.
semantic_tags: Page Replacement|Paging|Virtual Memory|LRU Approximation|Algorithm|Reference Bit|Second Chance
title: Clock Page Replacement Algorithm

definition: An improvement over FIFO that gives a page a 'second chance' before being replaced; if the page at the head of the FIFO queue has its reference bit set, the bit is cleared, and the page is moved to the tail of the queue, effectively postponing its replacement. This is conceptually identical to the Clock algorithm.
examples: When page A is selected for replacement (as the oldest page), if its reference bit is 1, it's given another chance (bit cleared, moved to end of queue), and the next oldest page B is then considered.|A page that is actively being used (reference bit 1) gets to stay in memory longer than a page that hasn't been used (reference bit 0).
title: Second Chance Page Replacement

definition: A counter-intuitive phenomenon observed in some page replacement algorithms (most notably FIFO) where increasing the number of available physical memory frames can, under certain specific page reference strings, lead to an increase in the number of page faults. This indicates that more memory doesn't always guarantee better performance.
examples: With the page reference string 3, 2, 1, 0, 3, 2, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0, 4, the FIFO algorithm might incur more page faults when allocated 4 frames than when allocated 3 frames.|The anomaly does not occur with stack-based algorithms like LRU or OPT.
title: Belady's Anomaly

definition: The process by which the operating system decides how many physical memory frames to allocate to each running process and how to distribute those frames among the processes. This decision impacts overall system performance and the potential for thrashing.
examples: Equal allocation: Each process is allocated an equal number of frames, regardless of its size or priority.|Proportional allocation: Frames are allocated to processes based on their size (e.g., larger processes get more frames).|Establishing minimum and maximum frame counts per process to prevent a single process from monopolizing memory or suffering excessive page faults.
title: Frame Allocation

definition: A page replacement policy where any page in physical memory can be selected for replacement, regardless of which process currently owns it. The replacement decision is made based on the system-wide set of resident pages, aiming to optimize overall system throughput.
examples: When a process incurs a page fault, the OS might choose to replace a page belonging to a different process that hasn't been used recently, if that page is deemed the best candidate.|Commonly used in modern operating systems as it can lead to higher overall CPU utilization, though it might reduce the predictability of individual process performance.
title: Global Page Replacement

definition: A page replacement strategy where each process is allocated a fixed or variable number of memory frames, and it can only replace pages within its own allocated set of frames. This prevents a process from stealing frames from other processes and potentially impacting their performance unfairly.
examples: A process with a fixed working set size is limited to replacing pages only from that set.|In a multi-programmed system, if process A causes a page fault, it can only evict one of its own pages to load the new one.
title: Local Page Replacement

definition: A technique that maps a file directly into a process's virtual address space, allowing the file's content to be accessed as if it were an in-memory array. This bypasses traditional read/write system calls, enabling faster I/O and shared memory functionality.
examples: Using the `mmap()` system call in Unix-like systems to map a large data file for direct memory access.|Loading shared libraries (DLLs on Windows, SO files on Linux) into a process's address space for execution.|Implementing inter-process communication (IPC) by having multiple processes map the same file region.
semantic_tags: Virtual Memory|File I/O|Memory Management|System Calls|Inter-Process Communication|Performance
title: Memory-Mapped Files

definition: A page replacement strategy where the operating system attempts to predict which pages a process will need next and loads them into memory before they are explicitly referenced. This proactive approach aims to reduce the number of page faults and improve application performance.
examples: Loading an entire executable's text segment into memory when a program starts, rather than faulting on each page.|Bringing in a cluster of pages (e.g., adjacent pages) around a page that just caused a fault, anticipating sequential access.|Detecting sequential file access patterns and prefetching subsequent file blocks into the page cache.
title: Prepaging

definition: A security feature that marks certain memory regions (like the stack or heap) as non-executable, preventing code from being run from these data segments. This mitigates various types of exploits, such as buffer overflows, that attempt to inject and execute malicious code.
examples: The NX (No eXecute) bit on modern CPUs (e.g., x86-64) that disallows execution from data pages.|Data Execution Prevention (DEP) in Microsoft Windows, which utilizes the NX bit functionality.|W^X (Write XOR Execute) policy used in some operating systems, ensuring a page cannot be both writable and executable simultaneously.
normalized_name: executable space protection nx bit dep
title: Executable Space Protection (NX bit, DEP)

definition: Mechanisms designed to detect and prevent stack overflows, which occur when a program writes beyond the allocated bounds of the call stack. These protections help guard against program crashes and security vulnerabilities that can arise from stack-based buffer overflows.
examples: Stack canary values (sentinels) placed on the stack before function return addresses, checked for corruption before returning.|Compiler-generated code that adds checks for stack pointer bounds at function entry and exit.|Operating system enforced stack limits, which trigger a protection fault if a program attempts to access memory beyond its allocated stack region.
title: Stack Overflow Protection

definition: Techniques used to detect and mitigate heap overflows, which happen when a program writes beyond the boundary of a dynamically allocated buffer on the heap. These protections are crucial for preventing data corruption, crashes, and security exploits targeting heap-allocated memory.
examples: Heap metadata integrity checks performed by the memory allocator to detect corruption of allocation headers.|Boundary tags or cookies placed around heap allocations to verify that writes do not extend beyond the intended buffer.|Address Sanitizer (ASan) in compilers, which instruments code to detect various memory errors, including heap overflows, at runtime.
title: Heap Overflow Protection

definition: A memory allocation algorithm that divides memory into blocks whose sizes are powers of two. When a request for memory is made, the smallest available block large enough to satisfy the request is found; if it's too large, it's recursively split into two 'buddies' until an appropriately sized block is formed.
examples: The Linux kernel's physical page allocator uses a buddy system to manage free physical pages of memory.|A simple memory manager in an embedded system dividing a 1MB memory region into smaller power-of-two blocks.|A request for 10KB of memory from a 32KB block would split it into two 16KB buddies, then one 16KB buddy into two 8KB buddies, allocating one 8KB and leaving other buddies for future use.
title: Buddy System Memory Allocation

definition: A hardware-assisted memory safety feature, exemplified by ARM Memory Tagging Extension (MTE), that assigns a small, cryptographically strong tag to both memory allocations and corresponding pointers. It detects memory errors like spatial (buffer overflows) and temporal (use-after-free) violations by comparing pointer tags with memory tags upon access.
examples: An ARM processor with MTE detecting a use-after-free vulnerability when a program attempts to access memory whose tag no longer matches the pointer's tag.|Using MTE in development to catch buffer overflows in C/C++ applications that write beyond allocated array bounds.|Runtime enforcement of memory safety in security-critical applications without significant performance overhead by leveraging hardware.
title: Memory Tagging (ARM MTE)

definition: A file is a named collection of related information, typically stored on non-volatile storage, that an operating system treats as a single logical unit. It serves as the basic unit for persistent data storage and retrieval.
examples: A text document (`.txt`) containing plain characters.|A JPEG image (`.jpg`) storing visual data.|An executable program (`.exe` or binary) that the OS can load and run.
title: File Definition

definition: Metadata associated with a file that describes its characteristics and properties, stored separately from the file's actual data content. These attributes are used by the operating system and applications to manage and access files.
examples: File name, type (e.g., directory, regular file), and size.|Access permissions (read, write, execute) for owner, group, and others.|Creation date, last modification date, and last access date.
title: File Attributes

definition: The set of system calls and functionalities provided by the operating system for processes to interact with files. These operations allow applications to create, delete, manipulate, and access the content of files.
examples: `open()` and `close()` to establish or terminate access to a file.|`read()` and `write()` to transfer data between a file and memory.|`delete()` or `remove()` to permanently erase a file from storage.
title: File Operations

definition: Categories of files distinguished by their structure, content, and intended use, which helps the operating system and applications determine how to interpret and interact with them. File types can be identified by extensions, magic numbers, or internal metadata.
examples: Regular files: ordinary files containing user data (text, images, programs).|Directories: special files that organize other files and directories.|Symbolic links (symlinks): pointers to other files or directories.
title: File Types

definition: A special type of file that serves as a container or index, organizing the file system hierarchy by mapping human-readable names to the locations of other files and subdirectories. Directories are crucial for navigating and structuring persistent storage.
examples: The root directory (`/` on Unix-like systems, `C:\` on Windows) which is the starting point of the file system.|A user's 'Documents' folder, containing various personal files and subfolders.|A 'bin' directory, containing executable programs.
title: Directory Definition

definition: The set of system calls and functions provided by the operating system for managing directories. These operations allow users and programs to create, delete, rename, list the contents of, and navigate through the hierarchical file system structure.
examples: `mkdir()` to create a new directory.|`rmdir()` to remove an empty directory.|`chdir()` to change the current working directory.
title: Directory Operations

definition: A hierarchical directory structure where all files and directories are organized in a tree-like fashion, starting from a single root directory. In this model, every file and subdirectory (except the root) has exactly one parent directory, ensuring a clear and intuitive organization.
examples: The file system organization in Unix/Linux operating systems, where everything branches from the '/' root.|The directory structure in Windows, starting from drive letters (e.g., C:\) which can be thought of as roots of separate trees.|A typical user's home directory containing 'Documents', 'Downloads', and 'Pictures' subdirectories.
title: Tree-Structured Directory

definition: A directory structure that extends the tree-structured model by allowing files or subdirectories to have multiple parent directories through the use of links (e.g., hard links or symbolic links), forming a directed acyclic graph. This enables sharing of files and directories without creating cycles.
examples: A hard link in Unix-like systems, where a single file can appear in multiple directories with different names.|A symbolic link (symlink) pointing to a file or directory located in a different part of the file system, allowing easy access from multiple locations.|Sharing a common `utils` directory across several project directories using symlinks.
title: Acyclic-Graph Directory

definition: The overall organization and layout of data on secondary storage, defining how files and directories are stored, managed, and accessed. This includes the logical structure visible to users and applications, as well as the physical layout of metadata and data blocks on the disk.
examples: The structure of an Ext4 file system on Linux, encompassing its superblock, inode table, and data blocks.|The organization of an NTFS file system on Windows, including the Master File Table (MFT) and data clusters.|The logical and physical arrangement of data within a flash memory-based file system (e.g., F2FS).
title: File System Structure

definition: A critical sector or block on a storage device (e.g., disk partition) that contains bootstrap code and information necessary to load an operating system. It is the first block of a partitioned volume and is read by the system's firmware during the boot process.
examples: The Volume Boot Record (VBR) on an NTFS partition in Windows, which contains code to load the operating system loader.|The first sector of a USB drive formatted with a bootable file system, containing instructions for the BIOS/UEFI.|A legacy Master Boot Record (MBR) on an entire disk, which holds the partition table and a small boot loader.
normalized_name: boot control block volume boot record
title: Boot Control Block (Volume Boot Record)

definition: A data structure found at a fixed and well-known location on a file system volume (e.g., a disk partition) that contains essential metadata about the entire file system. It describes the file system's overall properties, such as its type, size, block counts, and pointers to free block and inode lists.
examples: The superblock in an Ext4 file system (Linux), which stores critical information like the total number of blocks, number of free blocks, inode count, and pointers to inode tables.|The primary metadata block for the entire file system on a given partition.|A copy of the superblock stored at various locations on the disk to provide redundancy against corruption.
semantic_tags: File System|Metadata|Volume Management|Disk Structure|File System State|Recovery
title: Volume Control Block (Superblock)

definition: A data structure maintained by the operating system that stores all metadata about a specific file or directory, excluding its actual name and data content. It contains crucial information such as file type, permissions, owner, timestamps, and pointers to the disk blocks where the file's data is physically stored.
examples: An inode in Unix-like file systems (e.g., Ext4, XFS) uniquely identifies a file and holds its attributes and direct/indirect block addresses.|When a program opens a file, the OS retrieves its corresponding inode to access metadata and locate data blocks.|The `stat()` system call retrieves information directly from a file's inode.
title: File Control Block (Inode)

definition: Contiguous allocation stores each file as a single contiguous block of disk addresses, meaning all its data blocks are physically adjacent on the disk. This method offers excellent read performance for sequential access but suffers from external fragmentation and difficulty in file growth.
examples: Early file systems like MS-DOS used contiguous allocation for simplicity.|A raw disk image file is often stored contiguously to allow direct access to its contents.|Storing small, fixed-size log files where fast sequential writes are critical.
title: Contiguous Allocation (File)

definition: Linked allocation stores a file as a linked list of disk blocks, where each block contains a pointer to the next block in the file. This method eliminates external fragmentation and allows dynamic file growth but suffers from poor random access performance and potential reliability issues if a pointer is corrupted.
examples: Early versions of MS-DOS FAT file systems used variations of linked allocation.|A file whose blocks are scattered across the disk but logically connected via pointers.|Storing very large files where frequent appending might be needed without pre-allocating contiguous space.
title: Linked Allocation (File)

definition: Indexed allocation stores all pointers to a file's data blocks in a single, dedicated index block (or multiple blocks for large files). This method provides direct access to any block, supports dynamic file growth, and avoids external fragmentation, making it the most common allocation scheme for modern file systems.
examples: UNIX/Linux inodes use an indexed allocation scheme, often with multi-level indexing for large files.|NTFS file systems also utilize a form of indexed allocation within their Master File Table (MFT).|Accessing an arbitrary byte within a large video file is efficient due to direct block lookup via an index.
title: Indexed Allocation (File)

definition: Block size refers to the fixed-size unit of data that a file system reads from or writes to the disk. Choosing an appropriate block size impacts disk space utilization (internal fragmentation), I/O performance, and the maximum file system size.
examples: Common block sizes include 512 bytes, 1 KB, 2 KB, 4 KB, 8 KB, or 16 KB.|A 4KB block size is standard for many modern file systems like ext4 and NTFS.|If a 1KB file is stored in a 4KB block, 3KB of space is wasted due to internal fragmentation.
title: Block Size (File System)

definition: Disk space allocation is the process by which an operating system determines where on a storage device a file's data blocks are physically stored. The primary goal is to efficiently utilize available disk space while providing acceptable file access performance.
examples: Contiguous, Linked, and Indexed allocation are common strategies for disk space allocation.|When a user saves a new document, the OS's file system allocation algorithm finds free blocks for it.|The 'defrag' utility attempts to improve allocation by rearranging blocks to be more contiguous.
title: Disk Space Allocation

definition: Free space management is the operating system's mechanism for keeping track of which disk blocks are available for allocation to new files or for extending existing ones. Effective free space management is crucial for preventing data loss and ensuring efficient disk utilization.
examples: Bitmaps (Bit Vectors) are commonly used to represent free blocks, where each bit corresponds to a disk block.|Linked lists of free blocks can also be maintained, though less common for large disks.|When a file is deleted, its blocks are marked as free using the chosen free space management technique.
title: Free Space Management

definition: A bit vector, also known as a bitmap, is a simple and efficient data structure used for free space management where each bit in the vector corresponds to a disk block. A bit value of '0' typically indicates a free block, and '1' indicates an allocated block, or vice-versa.
examples: A disk with 1 million blocks would require a bit vector of 1 million bits (125 KB).|When a file needs 10 blocks, the OS scans the bit vector for 10 consecutive or scattered '0' bits.|Upon file deletion, the corresponding bits in the vector are reset to '0'.
title: Bit Vector (Free Space)

definition: A linked list method for free space management maintains a list of all free disk blocks, where each free block contains a pointer to the next free block. While simple, traversing the list to find a suitable block can be slow, especially on large disks with scattered free space.
examples: Early file systems might have used a linked list approach for smaller storage devices.|If block 100 is free and points to block 250, and block 250 points to block 50, these form part of the free list.|Finding 5 contiguous free blocks using a linked list requires linear traversal and comparison.
semantic_tags: Free Space Management|Linked List|Disk Allocation|Data Structure|Performance
title: Linked List (Free Space)

definition: FCFS (First-Come, First-Served) disk scheduling processes disk I/O requests in the order they arrive in the queue. It is fair to all requests and simple to implement but often results in inefficient disk arm movement, leading to poor average seek time and throughput.
examples: Requests for cylinders 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67 would be serviced in exactly that order.|A simple printer queue or basic network packet processing might use FCFS.|If requests are 5, 90, 10 (current head at 50), FCFS will move from 50 to 5, then to 90, then to 10.
title: FCFS Disk Scheduling

definition: SSTF (Shortest Seek Time First) disk scheduling services the request that is closest to the current head position. This algorithm minimizes the total seek time and improves throughput but can lead to starvation for requests far from the current head, as the head might repeatedly service closer requests.
examples: With requests at 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67 and head at 50, SSTF would move to 65, then 67, then 37, etc.|Similar to a cashier serving the customer with the shortest queue first.|If the head is at 50 and requests are at 40, 60, 100, 20, SSTF might repeatedly serve 40 and 60 while 20 and 100 starve.
title: SSTF Disk Scheduling

definition: SCAN disk scheduling, also known as the elevator algorithm, moves the disk arm in one direction, servicing all requests in its path, until it reaches the end of the disk. It then reverses direction and services requests while moving back, effectively preventing starvation compared to SSTF.
examples: If the head is at 50 and moving towards higher cylinders, with requests at 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67, it would serve 65, 67, 98, 122, 124, 183, then reverse to 37, 14.|An elevator in a building goes up, services floors, reaches the top, then comes down servicing floors.|Better for heavily loaded systems where requests span the entire disk range.
title: SCAN Disk Scheduling (Elevator)

definition: C-SCAN (Circular SCAN) disk scheduling is a variation of SCAN where the disk arm moves in only one direction (e.g., inwards), servicing requests, and upon reaching the end, it immediately jumps back to the beginning of the disk without servicing any requests on the return trip. This provides more uniform wait times by reducing the variance in seek times.
examples: If the head is at 50, moving towards higher cylinders, with requests at 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67, it would serve 65, 67, 98, 122, 124, 183, then jump back to cylinder 0, and then start servicing from 14, 37 on its next pass towards higher cylinders.|Similar to a conveyor belt that moves items in one direction and then quickly resets.|Often used in modern hard disk drives due to its predictability and reduced variance.
title: C-SCAN Disk Scheduling

definition: LOOK disk scheduling is a refinement of the SCAN algorithm where the disk arm only moves as far as the last request in the current direction before reversing. Instead of going all the way to the end of the disk, it 'looks' for pending requests and only travels to the outermost pending request, reducing unnecessary arm movement.
examples: If the head is at 50, moving right, with requests at 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67, and the highest request is 183, it serves up to 183 (65, 67, 98, 122, 124, 183) and immediately reverses, without going to the absolute end.|A more optimized elevator that only goes to the highest floor with passengers, not necessarily the top floor.|Offers better performance than SCAN by reducing total seek time.
title: LOOK Disk Scheduling

definition: Rotational latency is the time it takes for the desired sector of a disk track to rotate under the read/write head after the head has been positioned over the correct track. It is a significant component of disk access time and is inversely proportional to the disk's rotational speed (RPM).
examples: For a 7200 RPM disk, a full rotation takes about 8.33 milliseconds; average rotational latency is half of that, around 4.17 ms.|If data is needed from a sector that has just passed the head, the disk must complete almost a full rotation.|SSD drives virtually eliminate rotational latency, as they have no spinning platters.
semantic_tags: Disk I/O|Disk Access Time|Hard Drive|Performance|Rotational Speed
title: Rotational Latency

definition: Seek time is the time it takes for the read/write head of a hard disk drive to move from its current position to the track containing the desired data. It is the dominant factor in disk access time for hard drives and heavily influenced by disk scheduling algorithms.
examples: Moving the head from cylinder 50 to cylinder 100 involves a certain seek time.|Average seek times for HDDs typically range from 3 to 15 milliseconds.|Solid-state drives (SSDs) have near-zero seek time as there are no mechanical moving parts.
semantic_tags: Disk I/O|Disk Access Time|Hard Drive|Performance|Disk Scheduling|Mechanical Delay
title: Seek Time

definition: Transfer time is the actual time required to move data between the disk's surface and the disk controller, once the read/write head is positioned over the correct sector. It depends on the amount of data being transferred and the disk's data transfer rate.
examples: If a disk has a transfer rate of 100 MB/s, transferring a 10 MB file would take approximately 0.1 seconds (10 MB / 100 MB/s).|Reading a large contiguous block of data primarily consists of transfer time, after the initial seek and rotational latency.|USB 3.0 external drives have higher transfer rates than older USB 2.0 drives.
title: Transfer Time

definition: Disk formatting is the process of preparing a data storage device for initial use, which typically involves two main parts: low-level formatting (creating tracks, sectors, and control structures) and high-level formatting (creating a file system structure and sometimes a boot sector).
examples: Using the `format C:` command in Windows or `mkfs` in Linux to prepare a partition for a new file system.|When you buy a new hard drive, it usually needs to be partitioned and high-level formatted before use.|Quick format only rebuilds the file system structure, while full format also scans for bad blocks.
semantic_tags: File System|Disk Management|Storage Initialization|Low-Level Formatting|High-Level Formatting|Partitioning
title: Disk Formatting

definition: Bad blocks are sectors on a hard disk drive that are permanently damaged and can no longer reliably store data. Modern disk drives typically manage bad blocks by remapping them to spare sectors, preventing data loss, though an increasing number of bad blocks can indicate imminent drive failure.
examples: During disk formatting or using utilities like `chkdsk` (Windows) or `fsck` (Linux), bad blocks can be identified.|If a file tries to write data to a bad block, the OS or firmware might remap it to a good, spare block.|SMART (Self-Monitoring, Analysis and Reporting Technology) can detect and report on bad blocks.

title: Bad Blocks

definition: RAID is a data storage virtualization technology that combines multiple physical disk drives into a single logical unit to improve performance, provide data redundancy, or both. Different RAID levels offer varying trade-offs between cost, reliability, and performance.
examples: Setting up a RAID 1 array for a critical database server to mirror data across two drives for redundancy.|A home server using RAID 0 for maximum speed when editing large video files, accepting data loss risk.|Large enterprise storage arrays extensively use various RAID levels (e.g., RAID 5, RAID 6, RAID 10) for high availability.

definition: RAID Level 5 stripes data across multiple disk drives and distributes parity information among all drives in the array. This setup provides fault tolerance against a single drive failure and offers good read performance, making it a popular choice for many servers.
examples: A three-disk RAID 5 array where data blocks A1, A2, A3 are striped across drives 1, 2, 3 respectively, and parity block P(A) is on drive 1.|If one drive fails in a RAID 5 array, the data can be reconstructed using the remaining data blocks and parity information.|Commonly used in network-attached storage (NAS) devices and database servers requiring a balance of performance and redundancy.

title: RAID Level 5 (Striping with Distributed Parity)

definition: File system journaling is a technique used by file systems to ensure data consistency and quick recovery after a system crash or power failure by first writing metadata changes to a special log (journal) before committing them to the main file system structures.
examples: EXT3/EXT4 file systems use journaling to protect against metadata corruption.|NTFS utilizes a journal to ensure transactional consistency for file operations.|During boot, an OS can replay the journal to restore the file system to a consistent state.

definition: A Log-Structured File System (LFS) treats the disk as a continuous log, writing all changes (data and metadata) sequentially to the end of the log to optimize for write performance, especially for small, random writes.
examples: The original LFS developed at Berkeley for the Sprite operating system.|Write-ahead logging in databases shares conceptual similarities with LFS.|Flash-friendly file systems often employ log-structured principles to reduce write amplification.

definition: SMB (Server Message Block), historically known as CIFS (Common Internet File System), is a network file sharing protocol that allows client applications to read, write, and manage files on remote servers, as well as perform inter-process communication.

definition: HDFS is a distributed file system designed to run on commodity hardware, providing high-throughput access to application data and excellent fault tolerance, making it suitable for very large datasets and big data applications like Apache Hadoop.

definition: An inode (index node) is a data structure in Unix-like file systems that stores all metadata about a file or directory, such as ownership, permissions, timestamps, and pointers to the disk blocks containing the actual data, but not its name or directory path.

title: Inode (File System)

examples: Creating a symbolic link: `ln -s /path/to/original /path/to/link`.|The `/usr/bin/python` symlink often points to a specific Python interpreter like `/usr/bin/python3`.|A desktop shortcut on Windows is analogous to a symbolic link.

definition: Unix permissions define access rights for files and directories using read (r), write (w), and execute (x) attributes, applicable to three distinct categories: the file owner, the group owner, and all other users.
examples: `chmod 755 script.sh` sets read/write/execute for owner, read/execute for group/others.|The `ls -l` command displays file permissions like `drwxr-xr-x`.|A file with `rw-r--r--` permissions allows the owner to read and write, but others only to read.

definition: The Set-UID (Set User ID) bit is a special permission bit on executable files in Unix-like systems; when set, it causes the program to run with the privileges of the file's owner, rather than the privileges of the user executing it.
examples: The `passwd` command, owned by root and Set-UID, allows regular users to change their password by running with root privileges.|`chmod u+s executable_file` sets the Set-UID bit.|A program with Set-UID bit set will show 's' in the owner's execute permission: `-rwsr-xr-x`.

examples: `chmod g+s executable_file` sets the Set-GID bit for an executable.|A shared project directory with Set-GID bit set ensures all new files belong to the project's group.|A program with Set-GID bit set will show 's' in the group's execute permission: `-rwxr-sr-x`.

definition: The Sticky Bit is a special permission primarily used on directories in Unix-like systems; when set, it ensures that only the owner of a file (or the directory's owner, or root) can delete or rename files within that directory, even if other users have write permissions to the directory.
examples: The `/tmp` directory often has the sticky bit set (`drwxrwxrwt`) to prevent users from deleting others' temporary files.|`chmod +t shared_directory` sets the sticky bit.|A directory with the sticky bit will show 't' in the 'others' execute permission: `drwxrwxrwt`.

examples: A keyboard and mouse for user input.|A printer for outputting documents.|A network interface card (NIC) for network communication.|Hard disk drives and SSDs for persistent storage.
title: I/O Hardware

definition: A device controller is an electronic circuit board or chip that acts as an interface between the CPU and an I/O device, managing the device's specific operations, buffering data, and translating commands between the generic CPU interface and the device's specific protocols.
examples: A USB controller managing communication with USB devices.|A SATA controller facilitating data transfer with hard drives or SSDs.|The GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) acting as a display controller for monitors.
title: Device Controller

definition: An I/O port is a specific memory address or register accessible by the CPU, used for sending commands to and receiving status or data from an I/O device controller, forming a communication channel between the CPU and the device.
examples: The legacy parallel port (LPT1) often used I/O addresses starting at 0x378.|Memory-mapped I/O (MMIO) where device registers appear as memory locations.|Reading the status register of a serial port controller to check if data is available.
title: I/O Port

definition: Programmed I/O (PIO) is a method of I/O where the CPU directly controls all aspects of an I/O operation by repeatedly checking the status of an I/O device through its controller registers (polling) and moving data to or from the device one word or byte at a time.
examples: Early serial port communication often relied on the CPU polling the port's status register.|Simple device drivers for basic microcontrollers might use PIO for sensor readings.|The CPU sending individual bytes to a printer's data register and then polling its busy status.
title: Programmed I/O (PIO)

definition: A hardware component that enables I/O devices to transfer data directly to and from main memory without requiring constant CPU intervention. This mechanism significantly offloads the CPU and improves system performance for data-intensive operations.
examples: A disk controller uses DMA to transfer data blocks from the hard drive directly into a memory buffer.|A network interface card (NIC) uses DMA to move incoming network packets into system RAM.|Graphics processing units (GPUs) often use DMA for texture and buffer transfers to/from system memory.
title: DMA Controller

definition: A special software routine, part of the operating system kernel, that is executed by the CPU in response to an interrupt signal. Its purpose is to process the event that caused the interrupt, such as I/O completion or a timer expiration, and then return control.
examples: A disk I/O completion interrupt triggers a handler to mark the I/O request as finished and potentially wake up a waiting process.|Pressing a key on the keyboard generates an interrupt that invokes a keyboard interrupt handler to read the key code.|A timer interrupt handler is regularly invoked to update the system clock or perform context switching.
title: Interrupt Handler

definition: A table in memory, maintained by the operating system, that stores the starting addresses of interrupt handlers. When an interrupt occurs, the CPU uses the unique interrupt number as an index into this vector to locate and execute the corresponding handler.
examples: The OS maintains a vector table where entry '0x20' might point to the timer interrupt handler.|A system call, often implemented as a software interrupt, uses an entry in the interrupt vector to jump to the kernel's system call dispatcher.|Hardware exceptions like a page fault or division by zero use specific interrupt vector entries to invoke their respective error handlers.
title: Interrupt Vector

definition: A method of I/O where the CPU repeatedly checks the status of an I/O device to determine if it is ready for data transfer or if an operation has completed. This approach consumes significant CPU cycles as the CPU constantly busy-waits for device readiness.
examples: A simple embedded system continuously checking a sensor's data-ready flag in a loop.|An early serial port communication setup where the CPU checks the 'transmit buffer empty' flag before sending the next byte.|Many very basic hardware interfaces (e.g., specific GPIO pins) might use polling if interrupt capabilities are not available or too complex.
title: Polling (I/O)

definition: The technique of storing copies of frequently accessed I/O data in a smaller, faster storage area (cache), typically located in main memory, to reduce access latency and improve overall system performance. When data is requested, the system first checks the cache.
examples: A disk cache in RAM stores recently read or frequently accessed disk blocks to avoid slower disk I/O.|Web browsers cache recently visited web pages and images locally to speed up subsequent visits.|CPU cache (L1, L2, L3) storing instructions and data to reduce access time to main memory.
title: Caching (I/O)

definition: Software modules that facilitate communication between the operating system and specific hardware devices. They translate abstract OS requests into device-specific commands and handle device responses, abstracting away hardware complexities.
examples: A graphics card driver allows the OS to use the GPU for rendering without needing to understand the GPU's specific instruction set.|A network adapter driver enables the OS to send and receive network packets via the NIC.|A printer driver allows applications to print documents using a standard interface, regardless of the printer model.
semantic_tags: Hardware Abstraction|Software Interface|Kernel Module|I/O Control|Device Specific|System Calls
title: Device Drivers

definition: I/O devices that store and transfer data in fixed-size blocks, allowing for random access to any block. They are typically used for persistent storage where data is organized into filesystems.
examples: Hard disk drives (HDDs) and Solid-state drives (SSDs) are primary block devices for storing operating systems and user data.|USB flash drives act as block devices, allowing files to be stored and accessed in blocks.|CD-ROMs and DVDs, though read-only, are accessed as block devices.
title: Block Devices

definition: I/O devices that transfer data one character (byte) at a time, often without buffering, and are typically accessed sequentially. They are generally used for stream-oriented input/output.
examples: Keyboards and mice are character devices that send individual keystrokes or pointer movements.|Serial ports (e.g., `/dev/ttyS0` in Linux) operate as character devices for byte-stream communication.|Printers are often viewed as character devices, receiving a stream of data to be printed.
title: Character Devices

definition: Hardware components that facilitate a computer's connection to a network, enabling the sending and receiving of data packets. The operating system interacts with these devices through specific device drivers.
examples: An Ethernet card (NIC) connects a computer to a local area network (LAN) via a cable.|A Wi-Fi adapter allows wireless communication with a network router.|A Bluetooth module enables short-range wireless connections for data transfer and peripheral communication.
title: Network Devices (I/O)

definition: Mechanisms implemented by the operating system and hardware to prevent user-mode programs from directly accessing I/O devices. This ensures system stability, integrity, and security by routing all I/O requests through the trusted kernel via system calls.
examples: If a user program tries to execute a privileged I/O instruction (e.g., writing directly to a disk controller register), the hardware will trap to the OS kernel.|The OS provides system calls like `read()` and `write()` as the only legitimate way for user processes to perform I/O.|Memory protection mechanisms prevent user processes from accessing kernel data structures related to I/O devices.
title: I/O Protection

definition: An I/O operation that initiates a data transfer and immediately returns control to the calling process, allowing it to continue execution while the I/O operation proceeds in the background. The process is notified later, typically via a callback or event, when the I/O completes.
examples: Using `aio_read()` or `io_submit()` in POSIX to read a file without blocking the calling thread.|Node.js applications heavily rely on asynchronous I/O for network requests and file operations.|Modern GUI applications often use asynchronous I/O to keep the user interface responsive during long-running data operations.
title: Asynchronous I/O

definition: An I/O operation where the calling process is suspended and must wait until the data transfer is fully completed before it can resume execution. The program flow is halted at the point of the I/O call.
examples: A standard `read()` system call on a file descriptor that blocks until all requested data is available or an error occurs.|Using `fwrite()` in C to write data to a file, which typically blocks until the data is written to the kernel buffer (and potentially to disk).|Most simple command-line programs use synchronous I/O when reading user input or writing output to the console.
title: Synchronous I/O

definition: A characteristic of an I/O operation where the calling process is paused and enters a waiting state until the I/O request has finished. This means the process cannot perform any other computations or tasks while waiting for the I/O to complete.
examples: A call to `read()` on a network socket will block until data is received.|The `accept()` system call blocks a server process until a new client connection is established.|When a program attempts to read from an empty pipe, the `read()` call will block until data is written to the pipe.
title: Blocking I/O

definition: A characteristic of an I/O operation where a process requesting I/O receives an immediate return, even if the data transfer is not yet complete. If the operation cannot finish right away, it returns an error code (e.g., `EAGAIN` or `EWOULDBLOCK`) rather than suspending the process.
examples: Setting a file descriptor to non-blocking mode with `fcntl(fd, F_SETFL, O_NONBLOCK)` allows `read()` to return immediately if no data is available.|Using `select()`, `poll()`, or `epoll()` to monitor multiple non-blocking I/O descriptors for readiness before attempting `read()` or `write()`.|Network server applications often use non-blocking sockets to handle many client connections concurrently within a single thread.
title: Non-blocking I/O

definition: A technique designed to reduce CPU overhead and memory bandwidth consumption by transferring data between an I/O device and user-space memory without redundant copying into intermediate kernel buffers. Data moves directly from source to destination.
examples: The `sendfile()` system call in Linux directly transfers data between two file descriptors (e.g., from a file to a network socket) without copying to user space.|Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) is a form of zero-copy networking where data moves directly between application memory on different hosts.|Some high-performance network stacks use zero-copy mechanisms to deliver incoming packets directly into application buffers.
title: Zero-Copy I/O

definition: A method where applications access storage devices directly, bypassing the operating system's buffer cache in RAM. This is typically used by applications that manage their own caching, require strict control over data consistency, or perform large sequential I/O operations.
examples: Database systems often use `O_DIRECT` flag with `open()` in Linux to perform direct I/O, managing their own page cache for performance and data integrity.|Virtual machine hypervisors might use direct I/O for virtual disk images to avoid double-caching and improve I/O predictability.|Benchmarking tools for storage performance often use direct I/O to measure raw device throughput without OS caching interference.
title: Direct I/O

definition: A modern, highly efficient asynchronous I/O interface introduced in the Linux kernel, designed to allow user-space applications to submit and complete multiple I/O requests with minimal overhead. It supports a wide range of I/O operations, including both buffered and direct I/O.
examples: High-performance web servers leverage `io_uring` to handle thousands of concurrent client connections with reduced latency and higher throughput.|Database systems can use `io_uring` for faster and more efficient disk I/O, optimizing transaction processing.|The `liburing` library provides a user-friendly wrapper for interacting with the `io_uring` kernel interface in C/C++ applications.
normalized_name: io uring linux asynchronous i o
title: io_uring (Linux Asynchronous I/O)

definition: Software libraries that provide a programming interface for applications to perform I/O operations, typically wrapping underlying operating system system calls. These libraries often offer higher-level abstractions, buffering, and convenience functions to simplify I/O programming.
examples: The C standard library's `stdio.h` functions (e.g., `fopen()`, `fread()`, `fwrite()`) provide buffered file I/O operations.|Python's built-in `open()` function and file object methods abstract low-level file system calls.|Java's `java.io` and `java.nio` packages offer comprehensive classes for stream, file, and network I/O.
title: User-Space I/O Libraries

definition: A technology that allows a computer to directly access memory in another computer's main memory without involving the operating system or CPU of the remote machine. This bypasses the typical network stack, significantly reducing latency and CPU overhead for data transfers.
examples: High-Performance Computing (HPC) clusters use RDMA over InfiniBand or RoCE to achieve extremely fast inter-node communication for parallel computations.|Storage Area Networks (SANs) leverage RDMA to enable servers to access remote storage directly from their memory, bypassing local CPU I/O processing.|Data centers use RDMA for fast data transfer between servers, critical for applications like distributed databases and caching systems.
title: RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access)

definition: A conceptual model used in operating systems to represent and enforce protection and access rights. It visualizes subjects (like users or processes) as rows and objects (like files, devices, or memory segments) as columns, with each cell defining the specific access rights (e.g., read, write, execute) a subject has to an object.
examples: A simplified access matrix could show 'User A' having 'read' access to 'File X' but 'read/write' access to 'File Y', and 'execute' access to 'Program Z'.|In a multi-user system, the access matrix conceptually dictates which processes can interact with specific hardware devices like a printer or network card.|This model is fundamental to understanding how permission systems (like ACLs or capabilities) are designed and implemented in real operating systems.
title: Access Matrix

definition: An Access List (often called an Access Control List or ACL) is a list associated with an object (e.g., file, printer) that explicitly specifies which subjects (users or processes) have what type of access (e.g., read, write, execute) to that object. It is a common model for implementing discretionary access control, mediating access requests by checking entries in the list.
examples: A file's Access Control List on a Linux system (e.g., using `setfacl`) defining permissions for specific users or groups beyond standard Unix permissions.|NTFS permissions on a Windows file server specifying who can read, write, or modify specific folders and files.|A firewall rule specifying which IP addresses or networks can access a certain port or service on a server.
title: Access List

definition: Revocation of Access Rights is the process of withdrawing or canceling previously granted permissions or privileges for a subject to access an object. This mechanism is crucial for maintaining security policies dynamically and for responding to changes in user roles, system states, or security incidents.
examples: Disabling a user account when an employee leaves the company, immediately removing all their associated operating system access rights and privileges.|Changing file permissions (e.g., using `chmod o-rwx sensitive.txt` on Linux) to explicitly deny all access to a sensitive document for 'other' users.|Revoking a cryptographic certificate that was previously used for authentication or authorization, rendering it invalid for future access attempts.
title: Revocation of Access Rights

definition: A Security Mechanism is a tool, technique, or component, often implemented within an operating system, designed to enforce a security policy, protect system resources, or prevent unauthorized access and malicious activity. These mechanisms are the fundamental building blocks used to achieve overall system security goals.
examples: User authentication via passwords or biometric data to verify identity.|File system permissions (like ACLs or Unix modes) to control access to files and directories.|Memory protection units (MMU) that prevent processes from accessing memory outside their allocated segments.|Encryption algorithms used for data at rest or in transit.
title: Security Mechanism

definition: Authentication, in an operating system context, is the process by which the OS verifies the claimed identity of a user or system entity attempting to access its resources. It answers the question 'who are you?' by checking credentials against a stored record.
examples: Logging into a computer with a username and password combination.|Using biometric data, such as a fingerprint or facial scan, to unlock an operating system session.|Employing two-factor authentication (2FA) where a password is combined with a temporary code from a mobile application to gain access.
title: Authentication (OS Context)

definition: Authorization, in an operating system context, is the process by which the OS determines what specific actions an already authenticated user or process is permitted to perform on system resources. It answers the question 'what are you allowed to do?' based on predefined policies and granted privileges.
examples: A user account being able to read a specific file but not modify or delete it, based on file system permissions.|An administrator account having the privilege to install new software or change system-wide settings, while a standard user account does not.|A network service being granted permission to bind to a specific port number on the operating system.
title: Authorization (OS Context)

definition: Capability-Based Security is an access control model where a subject possesses unforgeable tokens, called capabilities, which directly grant specific rights to perform operations on an object. Unlike Access Control Lists (ACLs) that associate permissions with objects, capabilities are held by subjects and presented to objects to prove authorization.
examples: In a microkernel operating system like seL4, capabilities are fundamental for controlling inter-process communication and access to hardware resources.|The 'object-capability' model in some programming languages or distributed systems, where possessing a reference to an object implicitly grants the right to invoke its methods.|Certain web browser security models that grant specific, limited capabilities to web content (e.g., access to a specific local file only after user interaction).
title: Capability-Based Security

definition: Separation of Privilege is a security principle stating that a single entity should not be granted all the necessary permissions to complete a sensitive operation; instead, multiple distinct entities or conditions must be met to perform the action. This reduces the impact of a single point of failure or compromise, as an attacker would need to compromise multiple components to achieve their goal.
examples: Requiring both an administrator's password and a confirmation from a separate security officer to change critical system security settings.|The `sudo` mechanism on Unix-like systems, which allows a non-root user to execute commands with root privileges only after re-authenticating and for specific, configured commands.|Multi-factor authentication (MFA), where different authentication factors (e.g., password and a hardware token) must both be present to log in.
