title: Precomputed Radiance Transfer (PRT)

definition: Image-Based Lighting (IBL) is a rendering technique that illuminates a scene or object using a high-dynamic-range image, typically an environment map (like a cubemap), as the light source. This captures and applies complex real-world or virtual lighting conditions, providing realistic diffuse and specular reflections.
examples: Lighting a 3D model placed in a virtual studio using an HDR panorama of a real-world location.|Using a cubemap of a sky and city to provide both ambient light and realistic reflections on metallic objects in a game.|Applying pre-filtered environment maps for diffuse and specular contributions in physically based rendering workflows.
title: Image-Based Lighting (IBL)

definition: An environment map is a texture that stores an image of the distant surroundings of a point in space, capturing light and visual information from all directions. It is commonly used for representing distant scenery (skyboxes), providing lighting for Image-Based Lighting (IBL), and generating reflections.
examples: A cubemap representing the sky, clouds, and distant buildings around a scene for background and reflections.|A panoramic HDR image used as an input for Image-Based Lighting.|A spherical map texture capturing the lighting from a virtual world for reflections on a glossy surface.
title: Environment Map

definition: A reflection map is a specialized environment map specifically designed to simulate reflections on surfaces, often generated from the perspective of an object or region within the scene. It stores the visual information that would be reflected by a mirror-like surface.
examples: A cubemap generated from the center of a shiny car model to show reflections of the surrounding garage.|A planar reflection texture used to simulate a mirror on a wall or a puddle on the ground.|Real-time reflection probes in game engines that capture local reflections for nearby objects.
title: Reflection Map

definition: A refraction map is a technique or texture used to simulate the bending and distortion of light as it passes through transparent objects, based on principles like Snell's Law. It often involves distorting the background image or rendering what is 'behind' the object from a different perspective.
examples: Simulating the wavy distortion seen when looking through a pane of thick glass or rippling water.|Applying a refraction shader to an ice material to bend light passing through it.|Creating the visual effect of a lens or magnifying glass.
title: Refraction Map

definition: The Specular Glossiness workflow is a Physically Based Rendering (PBR) approach where material properties are defined by a base color (albedo), a separate specular color that dictates the tint and intensity of reflections, and a glossiness (or smoothness) map controlling the sharpness of those reflections. This workflow explicitly separates diffuse and specular colors.
examples: In Substance Painter, an artist defines the base color, then sets a specific specular color for metallic parts, and adjusts glossiness.|Using a set of textures for Albedo, Specular Color, and Glossiness in a game engine like CryEngine or older Unity PBR.|A material where a gold object has a yellow specular tint, while a plastic object has a colorless specular tint.
title: Specular Glossiness Workflow (PBR)

definition: The Metallic Roughness workflow is a Physically Based Rendering (PBR) approach where material properties are defined by a base color (albedo), a metallic value (typically 0 for dielectrics, 1 for metals), and a roughness map. This workflow infers specular properties based on whether the material is defined as metallic or non-metallic, adhering to energy conservation.
examples: In Unity or Unreal Engine, artists use an Albedo map, a Metallic map, and a Roughness map to define materials.|Setting a material's 'metallic' value to 1.0 for polished chrome and a low 'roughness' for a sharp reflection.|A material where the metallic value switches from 0 to 1, causing the base color to become the specular color for metals.
title: Metallic Roughness Workflow (PBR)

definition: Energy Conservation is a fundamental principle in Physically Based Rendering (PBR) that dictates a surface cannot reflect more light than it receives. This means that as the amount of light reflected specularly increases (e.g., a shinier surface), the amount of light reflected diffusely must decrease proportionally, and vice-versa, ensuring realistic light interaction.
examples: A highly reflective mirror surface reflects almost all incident light specularly, leaving virtually no light for diffuse reflection.|As a material's roughness increases, its specular highlight spreads out, and more light energy becomes available for diffuse scattering.|PBR shaders enforce this principle to prevent materials from appearing 'supernaturally' bright or creating light out of nowhere.
title: Energy Conservation (PBR)

definition: Describes rendering techniques or material properties that aim to simulate the behavior of light and matter in a way that is consistent with real-world physics, even if not perfectly accurate, to produce visually convincing and believable results. It prioritizes realistic light interaction over artistic freedom that might violate physical laws.
examples: Physically Based Rendering (PBR) materials are designed to be physically plausible, reacting predictably to different lighting conditions.|Shadows that accurately soften with distance from the caster and respect light source size are physically plausible.|A shader adhering to energy conservation and Fresnel effects is considered physically plausible.
title: Physically Plausible

definition: Anisotropy is a material property where the reflection or scattering of light varies depending on the direction of incidence or the viewing angle, causing specular highlights to appear stretched or directional. This effect typically arises from microscopic surface structures like parallel grooves or fibers.
examples: The stretched, linear highlight seen on brushed metal surfaces like aluminum or stainless steel.|The distinct directional shine on hair or fur that follows the strand direction.|The unique sheen observed on satin or corduroy fabrics where highlights appear along the weave.
title: Anisotropy (material property)

definition: A clear coat is an additional, typically thin and transparent, highly reflective layer applied on top of a base material, often used to simulate varnishes, car paint, or lacquered surfaces. It introduces an extra specular reflection that overlays the base material's appearance.
examples: Car paint shaders often feature a clear coat layer to achieve their characteristic glossy, reflective finish.|Simulating a polished wooden table with a reflective top layer over the wood grain.|Adding a clear protective film effect over a metallic surface in a material editor.
title: Clear Coat (material layer)

definition: Sheen is a material property or layer that simulates a soft, subtle 'fuzz' or highlight effect typically observed on rough, fibrous surfaces like velvet or certain fabrics, especially visible at glancing angles. It represents scattered light from microscopic fibers on the surface.
examples: Rendering velvet upholstery where a soft glow appears along the edges and folds of the fabric.|Simulating the subtle, diffuse highlight on brushed cotton or felt materials.|Fabric shaders in PBR often include a sheen component to enhance realism for cloth.
title: Sheen (material layer)

definition: The Microfacet Normal Distribution Function (NDF) is a core component of microfacet BRDFs, describing the statistical distribution of microscopic surface normals (microfacets) relative to the macroscopic surface normal. It dictates how many microfacets are aligned in a given direction, thereby determining the shape and spread of specular reflections based on roughness.
examples: The Beckmann, GGX, and Trowbridge-Reitz (TR) NDFs are common choices used in physically based rendering.|A sharp specular highlight (low roughness) implies an NDF where microfacets are tightly clustered around the macroscopic normal.|A broader, softer specular highlight (high roughness) results from an NDF with a wider spread of microfacet orientations.
title: Microfacet Normal Distribution Function (NDF)

definition: A texture map is a 2D image or data array applied to the surface of a 3D model to add visual detail, color, or material properties without increasing geometric complexity. These maps are indexed using texture coordinates to determine where on the model the image data should be placed.
examples: An 'albedo' or 'diffuse' map providing the base color of a character's skin.|A 'normal map' simulating fine surface details like bumps and grooves without extra polygons.|A 'roughness map' controlling the specularity and blurriness of reflections across a surface.
title: Texture Map

definition: UV mapping is the process of projecting a 3D model's surface geometry onto a 2D plane, typically referred to as UV space, to create a set of coordinates (U and V) for each vertex. These UV coordinates define how a 2D texture map should be precisely applied or 'wrapped' onto the 3D surface.
examples: Unwrapping a 3D character model into a flat, organized 2D layout in a software like Blender for texture painting.|Adjusting UVs on a 3D object to prevent texture stretching or visible seams.|Creating unique UV layouts for different parts of a complex asset to optimize texture resolution.
title: UV Mapping

definition: Texture coordinate generation refers to the various methods and algorithms used to compute or assign 2D coordinates (UVs) to the vertices or fragments of a 3D model, dictating how a texture image is sampled and mapped onto its surface. This can be automatic, procedural, or manual.
examples: Using 'planar projection' to generate UVs for a wall by projecting them from a single direction.|Employing 'automatic UV unwrapping' algorithms in 3D software to create a seam-cut flat map of a complex object.|Writing a shader that procedurally generates spherical texture coordinates for a sphere primitive.
title: Texture Coordinate Generation

definition: The process of determining the final color of a pixel on a rendered surface when the texture's resolution doesn't directly match the screen space, involving interpolation or selection of texels. It prevents aliasing artifacts and improves visual quality when textures are magnified or minified.
examples: Magnifying a low-resolution texture on a large object, requiring interpolation to avoid blockiness.|Minifying a high-resolution texture on a distant object, requiring averaging to prevent shimmering.|Implementing in a shader: `texture2D(sampler, uv)` implicitly uses configured filtering.
title: Texture Filtering

definition: A basic texture filtering method that selects the color of the single texel whose center is closest to the sampled texture coordinate. It results in a blocky, pixelated appearance when textures are magnified and can cause aliasing artifacts during minification.
examples: Retro video games (e.g., original Doom) often used this for pixel art aesthetics.|Magnifying a texture in an image editor with 'nearest neighbor' resampling.|Setting `GL_TEXTURE_MIN_FILTER` or `GL_TEXTURE_MAG_FILTER` to `GL_NEAREST` in OpenGL.
title: Nearest Neighbor Filtering

definition: A texture filtering method that interpolates the colors of the four texels closest to the sampled texture coordinate. It provides a smoother appearance than nearest neighbor filtering, reducing blockiness during magnification, but can still produce blurriness and aliasing artifacts during minification.
examples: Early 3D games using smoother textures compared to pixelated ones.|Setting `GL_TEXTURE_MAG_FILTER` to `GL_LINEAR` in OpenGL.|Used for basic smoothing in image resizing algorithms.
title: Bilinear Filtering

definition: An advanced texture filtering method that combines bilinear filtering across two adjacent mipmap levels, then linearly interpolates between the resulting two colors. It significantly reduces aliasing and shimmering artifacts that occur when textures are minified, especially at varying distances.
examples: Modern 3D games use this as a default for improved distant texture quality.|Setting `GL_TEXTURE_MIN_FILTER` to `GL_LINEAR_MIPMAP_LINEAR` in OpenGL.|Rendering a large ground plane texture that recedes into the distance without noticeable shimmering.
title: Trilinear Filtering

definition: The most advanced common texture filtering technique, which samples textures non-uniformly based on the angle and distance of the surface relative to the camera. It effectively reduces blurring and aliasing artifacts on surfaces viewed at oblique angles, providing much sharper texture detail compared to trilinear filtering.
examples: Viewing a long, flat road texture in a racing game at a shallow angle, where it remains sharp.|Configuring 'Anisotropic Filtering 16x' in a game's graphics settings.|Used in high-fidelity rendering engines for realistic texture clarity.
title: Anisotropic Filtering

definition: A technique where a series of pre-calculated, progressively smaller versions (mipmaps) of a texture are stored alongside the original. During rendering, the appropriate mipmap level is selected based on the projected size of the texture on screen, reducing aliasing and improving rendering performance for distant objects.
examples: A texture's mipmap chain containing a 1024x1024, 512x512, 256x256, down to 1x1 version.|OpenGL's `glGenerateMipmap()` function to create mip levels.|Visible artifacts like shimmering and flickering on distant textures without mipmapping.
title: Mipmapping

definition: A single, larger image file that contains multiple smaller sub-images or textures packed together. Each sub-image within the atlas is typically identified by a specific region (UV coordinates), allowing a single texture bind to render multiple different sprites or texture elements.
examples: A sprite sheet containing all animation frames for a character in a 2D game.|Packing many UI icons into one large texture to minimize draw calls.|Using a tool like TexturePacker to generate an atlas and its corresponding coordinate data.
title: Texture Atlas

definition: The process of creating and utilizing texture atlases, involving packing multiple smaller textures into a single larger texture and then referencing sub-regions of this larger texture for rendering. It's primarily used to reduce the number of texture state changes and draw calls, improving rendering performance.
examples: A game engine's asset pipeline automatically combining individual sprite textures into atlases.|Manually arranging character clothing textures onto a single sheet for a character model.|Rendering a complex UI with many distinct elements using a single atlas for all icons.
title: Texture Atlasing

definition: A type of texture resource that consists of an ordered collection of 2D textures, all having the same format and dimensions, treated as a single texture object. They allow shaders to sample from different layers (individual textures) using an additional array index, often reducing binding overhead compared to individual textures.
examples: Storing multiple terrain layers (grass, dirt, rock) as slices in a single texture array to be sampled based on a heightmap.|Storing different variations of a model's texture (e.g., damaged, pristine) in an array.|OpenGL's `GL_TEXTURE_2D_ARRAY` target for defining and using a texture array.
title: Texture Arrays

definition: A modern graphics API feature that allows shaders to directly access an arbitrary number of textures by their GPU memory addresses (handles) without explicit binding to texture units. This significantly reduces CPU overhead by eliminating the need for frequent texture state changes, especially in scenes with many unique textures.
examples: A renderer processing a scene with thousands of unique meshes, each using different texture sets, without performance bottlenecks from binding.|Using `GL_ARB_bindless_texture` extension in OpenGL or descriptor sets in Vulkan/DirectX 12.|Implementing a deferred renderer where g-buffer textures are accessed via handles.
title: Bindless Textures

definition: A texture that stores directional information (normals) in its color channels (typically RGB for X, Y, Z components) for each texel, rather than direct color data. When applied during rendering, it modifies the surface normal used for lighting calculations, creating the illusion of detailed surface relief without requiring additional geometry.
examples: Making a flat wall surface appear to have bricks or rivets without adding actual brick geometry.|Creating fine wrinkles on a character's face.|Generating a normal map from a high-polygon model to apply to a low-polygon model (baking).
title: Normal Map

definition: An older technique that uses a grayscale texture to store height field data, which is then used to perturb surface normals during lighting calculations. Similar to normal mapping, it creates an illusion of surface detail and relief without changing geometry, though typically less convincing than normal maps.
examples: Adding subtle texture to an otherwise smooth surface, like the grain of wood.|Creating the appearance of small bumps or indentations on a surface.|A simple shader perturbing normals based on a grayscale height value from the map.
title: Bump Map

definition: A grayscale texture that directly modifies the geometry of a surface by offsetting its vertices along their normals, based on the pixel's intensity. Unlike normal or bump maps, which only affect lighting, displacement maps physically alter the mesh, allowing for true silhouette changes and more realistic relief.
examples: Creating rugged mountain terrain from a flat plane using a heightmap as a displacement map.|Adding detailed scales to a dragon's skin, which are visible in silhouette.|Requiring tessellation shaders or similar techniques to add sufficient geometry.
title: Displacement Map

definition: A grayscale 2D texture where the intensity of each pixel represents the height or altitude at a corresponding point in a 3D space. It is commonly used to generate terrain, create displacement maps, or define surface features for bump mapping.
examples: A grayscale image used to procedurally generate a mountain range or island landscape.|Creating a terrain mesh by offsetting vertices of a grid based on pixel values.|Storing data for a displacement map or a bump map.
title: Height Map

definition: A grayscale texture used in Physically Based Rendering (PBR) that defines the micro-surface roughness of a material, where brighter values indicate rougher surfaces and darker values indicate smoother, more reflective surfaces. It influences how light scatters and reflects from the material.
examples: A rough metal appearing dull and diffuse, while a smooth metal is highly reflective and shiny.|Creating a material with both polished and worn areas by varying roughness across its surface.|Used in conjunction with a metallic map to define a material's appearance.
title: Roughness Map

definition: A grayscale texture used in Physically Based Rendering (PBR) that specifies how 'metallic' a material is at each point, where white (1.0) indicates a pure metal and black (0.0) indicates a dielectric (non-metal). It governs the material's albedo and specular reflection properties.
examples: Defining areas of rust on a metallic object by setting their metallic value to 0.0.|Creating a material that transitions from painted wood (dielectric) to a metal trim.|Often paired with an albedo map and roughness map for PBR materials.
title: Metallic Map

definition: A grayscale texture that pre-calculates and stores how much ambient light each point on a surface receives, based on surrounding geometry. Darker areas indicate regions less exposed to ambient light (e.g., crevices, corners), enhancing perceived depth and contact shadows without complex real-time global illumination.
examples: Adding subtle shadows in the creases of a character's clothing.|Darkening the areas where a wall meets the floor in a room.|Baking ambient occlusion from a high-poly model to a low-poly model.
title: Ambient Occlusion Map

definition: A general term for a texture that provides information about environmental occlusion, most commonly referring to an Ambient Occlusion Map. It stores grayscale values representing how much ambient light is blocked at different points on a surface due to nearby geometry.
examples: Synonymous with Ambient Occlusion Map in most practical contexts.|Used by shaders to darken crevices and contact points, improving realism.|A texture baked from a 3D model to simulate light blocking.
title: Occlusion Map (texture)

definition: A texture that provides the base color of a material without any lighting information, representing the diffuse color of a surface when lit by a flat, white, orthogonal light. In Physically Based Rendering (PBR), it specifically represents the diffuse color for dielectric materials or the 'F0' color for metallic materials.
examples: The pure color texture of a wooden plank without any shadows or highlights baked in.|The base color for a character's skin or clothing.|The `baseColorMap` in glTF materials or `_MainTex` in Unity for PBR setups.
title: Albedo Map

definition: A secondary texture, typically with fine, repeating patterns (e.g., noise, fine cracks, fabric weave), blended over a main albedo or normal map at a smaller scale. It is used to add high-frequency visual detail to surfaces when the camera is close, preventing textures from looking blurry or stretched.
examples: Adding subtle fabric weave to a character's clothing texture that becomes visible up close.|Overlaying a fine noise pattern on a large terrain texture to break up repetition.|A shader blending a detail normal map and a detail albedo map based on camera distance.
title: Detail Map

definition: A collection of six square textures representing the reflections or surroundings of an object from a central point, mapped to the faces of a cube. It is primarily used for environment mapping, skyboxes, and capturing reflections or lighting information.
examples: A skybox in a 3D game, rendering the distant environment around the player.|Simulating reflections on a metallic car body by sampling the cube map.|Capturing the surrounding light for Image-Based Lighting (IBL) calculations.
title: Cube Map

definition: A texture that stores information about the distant surroundings of an object, typically used to simulate reflections on shiny surfaces or to create skyboxes. It can be implemented using cube maps, sphere maps, or paraboloid maps.
examples: A panoramic image wrapped around a scene to provide ambient lighting (Image-Based Lighting).|A cube map applied to a reflective sphere to show its surroundings.|A sphere map used in older graphics for faked reflections.
title: Environment Map (texture)

definition: A technique where a texture is projected onto 3D geometry from a specific viewpoint, similar to how a slide projector works. This allows for dynamic and view-dependent texture mapping effects without altering UV coordinates.
examples: Projecting a flashlight beam's texture onto a wall in a dark scene.|Using a shadow map to project shadows from a light source's perspective.|Displaying a movie or image onto a complex, irregular 3D model in real-time.
title: Projective Texturing

definition: A small texture or image projected onto a larger surface, often used to add details like bullet holes, blood splatters, or signs without altering the base geometry or creating new complex UV maps. Decals typically blend with the underlying surface.
examples: Applying a bullet hole texture to a wall after it's been shot.|Projecting road lines, cracks, or dirt onto a ground texture.|Adding a painted logo or warning sign onto a vehicle model.
title: Decal (graphics)

definition: Methods used to reduce the memory footprint and bandwidth requirements of texture data, often sacrificing some image quality. Compressed textures can sometimes be sampled directly by graphics hardware, improving performance and reducing loading times.
examples: Using DXT/BCn formats (e.g., DXT1, DXT5) for GPU-friendly compression in desktop games.|Employing PVRTC (PowerVR Texture Compression) for textures on mobile platforms like iOS.|ETC2 compression used for Android game assets to save memory.
title: Texture Compression

definition: A texture generated algorithmically rather than being loaded from an image file. These textures are defined by mathematical functions and parameters, allowing for infinite detail, low memory usage, and easy variation.
examples: Generating realistic cloud patterns or marble textures using Perlin noise.|Creating intricate rock formations or terrain details with fractal algorithms.|Using mathematical functions to simulate wood grain or brick patterns.
title: Procedural Texture

definition: A small program executed on the GPU, designed to determine how vertices or pixels are processed and rendered. Shaders provide immense flexibility in controlling lighting, coloring, and various visual effects within the rendering pipeline.
examples: A vertex shader transforming an object's position from model space to clip space.|A fragment (pixel) shader calculating the final color of each pixel based on light and material properties.|A geometry shader generating new primitives from existing ones.
title: Shader (general concept)

definition: A complete set of compiled and linked shaders (e.g., a vertex shader and a fragment shader) that together perform a specific rendering task. This program is uploaded to the GPU and controls the entire rendering process for a given object or effect.
examples: A basic shader program for rendering unlit, solid-colored triangles.|A Physically Based Rendering (PBR) shader program that calculates realistic lighting and reflections.|A shader program specifically for rendering a full-screen post-processing effect like a Gaussian blur.
title: Shader Program

definition: A collection of properties that define how a surface interacts with light and how it appears visually, often including colors, textures, shininess, transparency, and the shader program used to render it. Materials describe the visual attributes of an object's surface.
examples: A simple 'plastic' material with a diffuse color of red and a low specular highlight.|A 'metallic' material with a high reflection texture and a complex Physically Based Rendering (PBR) shader.|A 'glass' material with transparency, a refractive index, and a shader that simulates refraction.
title: Material (graphics)

definition: A type of shader, particularly common in game engines like Unity, that abstracts away some of the complexities of lighting calculations. Developers define properties like albedo, normal, and emissive maps, and the engine automatically generates the underlying vertex and fragment shaders for various lighting models.
examples: Writing a Unity surface shader to quickly define the base color, normal map, and metallic properties of a character's skin.|Using a surface shader to implement a standard PBR material without manually writing complex lighting equations.|Defining a custom surface shader to add a unique glitter effect to an object while still integrating with the engine's lighting.
title: Surface Shader

definition: A shader applied to the entire rendered scene *after* all 3D objects have been drawn, typically operating on the final rendered image as a 2D texture. These shaders are used to apply full-screen visual effects that modify the overall look of the scene.
examples: A bloom shader to enhance bright areas and simulate lens glow, making lights appear more intense.|A grayscale or sepia tone shader to change the overall color palette for artistic effect.|A blur shader to create depth of field, motion blur, or other visual distortions.
title: Post-processing Shader

definition: A rigid-body transformation that moves every point of an object by the same distance in a given direction, effectively shifting its position in space without changing its orientation or size. It is represented by a 4x4 transformation matrix.
examples: Moving a character model forward by (0, 0, 5) units in a game world.|Shifting the camera's position to view a different part of the scene.|Applying an offset to a UI element's coordinates on the screen.
title: Translation (geometry)

definition: A rigid-body transformation that turns an object around a fixed point or axis, changing its orientation without altering its position or size. It is typically represented by a 4x4 transformation matrix or quaternions.
examples: Rotating a car model around its Y-axis to simulate a turn.|Orienting a camera to look at a specific target point in the scene.|Spinning a character's arm around its shoulder joint during an animation.
title: Rotation (geometry)

definition: A non-rigid-body transformation that changes the size of an object along one or more axes, effectively stretching or shrinking it. It is represented by a 4x4 transformation matrix where diagonal elements control the scaling factors.
examples: Making a character model appear larger or smaller in the game world.|Stretching a UI button to fit new content horizontally.|Applying non-uniform scaling to squash or stretch an object for a cartoon-like effect.
title: Scaling (geometry)

definition: A transformation that distorts an object by shifting its points in a specific direction proportional to their distance from a fixed line or plane, causing it to 'slant' or 'skew.' It is often represented as part of a general 4x4 affine transformation matrix.
examples: Applying a shear transformation to text to make it appear italicized.|Simulating the deformation of a material under a shearing force.|Creating a perspective effect where parallel lines appear to converge non-uniformly.
title: Shear (geometry)

definition: A 4x4 transformation matrix that converts an object's vertices from its local object space into the global world space. It typically combines the object's unique translation, rotation, and scaling transformations.
examples: Positioning, orienting, and sizing a character model within the game world.|Placing multiple instances of a tree model at different locations, rotations, and scales.|Transforming a car model from its local origin (0,0,0) to its desired spot and orientation on the track.
title: Model Matrix

definition: A 4x4 transformation matrix that transforms vertices from world space into camera (or view) space. It effectively positions and orients the camera (or viewer) within the world, typically by inverting the camera's own world transformation.
examples: Moving the camera to a specific position and pointing it towards a target in the scene.|Implementing a first-person or third-person camera system.|Using a 'lookAt' function to set the camera's orientation based on an eye position, target, and up vector.
title: View Matrix

definition: A 4x4 transformation matrix that defines how 3D objects are projected onto a 2D viewport, typically using either a perspective projection (simulating real-world optics) or an orthographic projection (for engineering or 2D views). It also sets the boundaries of the viewing frustum.
examples: Creating a realistic perspective view where distant objects appear smaller.|Setting up an orthographic projection for a 2D platformer game or UI elements where depth doesn't affect size.|Adjusting the field of view (FOV) or aspect ratio for a camera to control what's visible.
title: Projection Matrix

definition: A single 4x4 transformation matrix obtained by multiplying the Projection, View, and Model matrices in order (Projection * View * Model). It efficiently transforms a vertex from its local object space directly to clip space, ready for rasterization.
examples: Sending a single MVP matrix as a uniform to a vertex shader to perform all necessary transformations in one step.|Calculating the final screen-space position of a 3D point for UI overlay.|Optimizing matrix calculations by pre-multiplying matrices on the CPU before sending them to the GPU.
title: Model-View-Projection (MVP) Matrix

definition: A system where objects are organized in a parent-child relationship, and the transformation of a parent object (e.g., translation, rotation, scaling) is inherited by all its child objects. This allows for the construction and manipulation of complex articulated models and scene graphs.
examples: A human character model where the forearm is a child of the upper arm, which is a child of the torso, allowing for realistic joint movements.|A solar system model where planets orbit the sun, and moons orbit planets, with each transformation being relative to its parent.|Attaching a weapon to a character's hand, so it moves and rotates with the hand's animation.
title: Transformation Hierarchies

definition: A tree-like data structure that organizes and manages the logical and spatial representation of a 3D scene's objects, lights, cameras, and their transformations. It simplifies scene management and rendering by allowing transformations to be inherited by child nodes.
examples: Blender's Outliner panel, which shows a hierarchical list of objects in a scene.|An Ogre3D `SceneManager` using `SceneNode` objects to arrange entities.|The Unity Hierarchy window, where parent-child relationships define spatial inheritance.
title: Scene Graph

definition: A conceptual object in 3D graphics that defines the viewpoint from which a scene is rendered, encompassing its position, orientation, and perspective properties. It determines what portion of the 3D world is visible and how it's projected onto a 2D image plane.
examples: A `PerspectiveCamera` object in Three.js used to set up the viewing angle for a web scene.|The `gluPerspective` function call in older OpenGL used to define the projection.|The player's viewpoint in a first-person shooter game, which moves and rotates with the character.
title: Camera (graphics)

definition: A pyramid-like region in 3D space, truncated by a near plane and a far plane, that defines the volume visible to a camera. Only objects or parts of objects within this frustum are considered for rendering, an optimization technique known as frustum culling.
examples: The visible area in a 3D game engine's editor viewport, often outlined by wireframes.|The boundaries defined by `glFrustum` or `glm::perspective` in OpenGL, which specify the clipping volume.|An optimization where objects outside the frustum are not sent to the rendering pipeline, saving computational resources.
title: View Frustum

definition: The front clipping plane of the view frustum, defining the closest boundary beyond which objects become visible to the camera. It helps prevent objects very close to the camera from being rendered incorrectly or infinitely large due to perspective projection issues.
examples: The `near` parameter in a `glFrustum` or `glm::perspective` function call.|Setting a minimum distance for rendered objects in a game to avoid Z-fighting or clipping artifacts close to the player.|An object partially obscured because it's too close to the camera and intersects the near plane.
title: Near Plane

definition: The back clipping plane of the view frustum, defining the farthest boundary beyond which objects are no longer visible to the camera. It helps manage rendering depth precision and can be used to limit the draw distance of a scene.
examples: The `far` parameter in a `glFrustum` or `glm::perspective` function call.|Setting a maximum draw distance in a video game to improve performance or create atmospheric effects like fog.|Distant mountains or objects disappearing as they cross the far plane.
title: Far Plane

definition: The angular extent of a scene visible to the camera, typically measured in degrees, determining how much of the 3D world appears on the screen. A wider FOV encompasses more of the scene but can introduce more distortion, while a narrower FOV provides a zoomed-in, less distorted view.
examples: Adjusting the FOV setting in a first-person shooter game to match personal preference or reduce motion sickness.|The `fovy` parameter in `gluPerspective`, which controls the vertical field of view.|The difference in perspective between a wide-angle camera lens (high FOV) and a telephoto lens (low FOV).
title: Field of View (FOV)

definition: The proportional relationship between the width and height of an image, screen, or viewport, typically expressed as `width:height` or as a decimal ratio. In graphics, it is crucial for correct perspective projection and preventing image distortion.
examples: A common aspect ratio for modern widescreen monitors is 16:9 (1.777...).|Older televisions often used a 4:3 aspect ratio (1.333...).|The ratio of `width / height` is often passed to projection matrix functions like `glm::perspective`.
title: Aspect Ratio (graphics)

definition: A rectangular region on the rendering target, such as a window or a texture, where the 3D scene is actually drawn. It defines the mapping from Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) to screen coordinates, specifying the final size and position of the rendered image.
examples: A `glViewport(x, y, width, height)` call in OpenGL, defining the rendering area within a window.|Displaying a minimap in a game by rendering a separate camera view to a smaller viewport.|Rendering to only a portion of a larger texture when using Framebuffer Objects (FBOs).
title: Viewport (graphics)

semantic_tags: HCI|natural interaction|computer vision|motion tracking|non-verbal communication|spatial interaction
title: Gesture Recognition (graphics)

definition: Force feedback, a form of haptic technology, provides physical sensations to the user by applying forces, vibrations, or motions through an input device. It enhances immersion and realism by simulating physical interactions and environmental cues.
examples: A game controller rumbling to simulate an in-game explosion or collision.|A smartphone vibrating to indicate a notification or haptic click.|A surgical robot providing resistance to a surgeon's hand, simulating the feel of tissue.
title: Force Feedback (HCI)

definition: In visualization, a data type defines the kind of values a dataset or a specific variable can hold, dictating the appropriate visual encodings and analytical operations. Understanding data types is crucial for effective and accurate graphical representation.
examples: A numerical 'integer' data type representing quantities like counts or ranks.|A 'string' data type for labels or categories, such as names of countries.|A 'date' data type for temporal information, enabling time-series visualizations.
semantic_tags: Data classification|data modeling|variable type|information theory|data structure|statistics
title: Data Type (visualization)

definition: Categorical data, also known as qualitative data, consists of values that can be divided into distinct groups or categories, without any inherent numerical meaning or order. It is used to classify observations based on specific attributes.
examples: Types of fruit: 'apple', 'banana', 'orange'.|Gender: 'male', 'female', 'non-binary'.|Car colors: 'red', 'blue', 'green', 'black'.
title: Categorical Data

definition: Quantitative data represents measurable quantities, expressed numerically, and can be subjected to mathematical operations. This type of data is essential for visualizations that show magnitude, trends, and relationships between numerical variables.
examples: Temperature readings: 25.5°C, 30°C, 18.2°C.|Population counts: 1,000,000, 50,000.|Height measurements: 1.75m, 1.62m.
title: Quantitative Data

definition: Ordinal data is a type of categorical data where categories have a meaningful order or rank, but the intervals between ranks are not necessarily equal or measurable. While there's a sequence, the 'distance' between categories cannot be quantified.
examples: Education levels: 'High School', 'Bachelor's', 'Master's', 'PhD'.|Customer satisfaction ratings: 'Very Poor', 'Poor', 'Neutral', 'Good', 'Excellent'.|Military ranks: 'Private', 'Corporal', 'Sergeant'.
title: Ordinal Data

definition: Nominal data is a type of categorical data where categories have no inherent order, rank, or numerical value, serving only to label or classify observations. It is the most basic form of qualitative data.
examples: Hair colors: 'blonde', 'brown', 'black', 'red'.|Countries of origin: 'USA', 'Canada', 'Mexico'.|Types of animals: 'dog', 'cat', 'bird', 'fish'.
title: Nominal Data

definition: Visual encoding is the process of systematically mapping data attributes to visual properties or variables (such as position, color, size, shape, or orientation) to create a visual representation. The choice of encoding directly impacts how effectively information is conveyed and perceived by the viewer.
examples: Mapping the 'population' of cities to the 'height' of bars in a bar chart.|Encoding different 'product categories' with distinct 'hues' (colors) in a pie chart.|Representing 'temperature' values with a color gradient from blue (cold) to red (hot) on a map.
title: Visual Encoding

definition: Perceptual guidelines in visualization are principles derived from studies of human perception and cognition that inform the design of effective and understandable visual representations. They help designers create visualizations that are easy to interpret, minimize cognitive load, and prevent misinterpretation of data.
examples: Using a consistent color palette to represent the same variable across multiple charts.|Arranging data points along a common baseline to facilitate accurate comparison of lengths.|Avoiding the use of too many distinct colors or pie slices, as the human eye struggles to differentiate them.
title: Perceptual Guidelines (visualization)

definition: Color perception refers to the physiological and psychological process by which the human visual system interprets different wavelengths of light as distinct colors. In graphics and visualization, understanding color perception is crucial for effective visual communication, avoiding issues like color blindness, and leveraging color to convey meaning.
examples: Distinguishing between red and green based on different light wavelengths.|Perceiving differences in saturation (intensity) or lightness (brightness) of a color.|Recognizing that certain color combinations can be problematic for individuals with color vision deficiencies.
title: Color Perception

definition: Pre-attentive attributes are visual properties that are processed rapidly and unconsciously by the human visual system, allowing certain features to 'pop out' from a display without conscious effort or focused attention. Leveraging these attributes helps viewers quickly identify important information in a visualization.
examples: Instantly noticing a single red circle among many blue circles.|Quickly identifying the longest line segment in a group of lines.|Spotting a unique shape (e.g., a square) among an array of circles.
semantic_tags: Visual processing|rapid perception|pop-out effect|cognitive load|visual search|attention
title: Pre-attentive Attributes

definition: A visual mark or symbol used to represent data values or attributes, often by varying its shape, color, size, or orientation. Glyphs can encode multiple data dimensions within a single visual element.
examples: Arrows indicating wind direction and speed on a weather map|Chernoff faces where facial features represent different data dimensions|Star plots where each spoke's length corresponds to a variable
title: Glyph (visualization)

definition: A system of pictograms or ideograms used for visual communication of quantitative information in a standardized, easily understandable way, often representing a unit of data. Developed by Otto Neurath, it emphasizes clarity and universality.
examples: A series of human figures, where each figure represents 1 million people|Traffic signs using standardized symbols|Infographic showing product sales with product icons
title: Isotype (visualization)

definition: Any unnecessary or non-essential visual elements in a chart or graph that do not convey data information, distracting from the data itself and potentially hindering interpretation. It includes excessive ornamentation, redundant labels, or misleading 3D effects.
examples: Decorative borders around a bar chart|Excessive grid lines that obscure bars|3D pie charts where depth distorts slice perception
title: Chart Junk

definition: A concept introduced by Edward Tufte, it measures the proportion of ink used to display actual data information compared to the total ink used in a graphic. A high data-ink ratio means more ink is dedicated to data and less to non-data or redundant elements.
examples: A simple scatter plot with only points and axes (high ratio)|A bar chart with thick, decorative borders and excessive gridlines (low ratio)|Removing redundant labels from a line chart
title: Data-Ink Ratio

definition: A set of guidelines for effective visual display of quantitative information, advocated by Edward Tufte, emphasizing clarity, precision, efficiency, and truthfulness in data representation. Key principles include maximizing the data-ink ratio, avoiding chart junk, and using small multiples.
examples: Designing a graph to have a high data-ink ratio|Using small multiples to compare different categories instead of one complex chart|Ensuring the visual representation of numbers is directly proportional to the numerical quantities
title: Tufte Principles

definition: A measure introduced by Edward Tufte to quantify the degree to which a graphic misrepresents the underlying data, calculated as the ratio of the size of the effect shown in the graphic to the size of the effect in the data. A lie factor greater than 1.05 or less than 0.95 suggests significant misrepresentation.
examples: A bar chart where the height of a bar is twice as large but represents only a 1.5 times increase in data|An area chart where visual areas are not proportional to values|A map distorting geographic sizes relative to underlying data
title: Lie Factor

definition: A graphic primitive or dimension (such as position, size, shape, color, orientation, texture) that can be manipulated to encode data attributes in a visualization. Jacques Bertin formalized these as fundamental components of graphical semiology.
examples: Using different colors to represent different categories (nominal data)|Varying the size of points to represent quantitative values (ordinal/quantitative data)|Using horizontal position to encode time
title: Visual Variable

definition: The process of assigning data attributes (e.g., categorical values, numerical quantities) to visual variables (e.g., color, size, position, shape) to create a graphical representation. Effective mapping ensures that the visual properties accurately reflect the data relationships.
examples: Mapping 'temperature' (quantitative) to 'color intensity' (visual variable) on a heatmap|Mapping 'product category' (categorical) to 'shape' (visual variable) in a scatter plot|Mapping 'time' to the x-axis position in a line chart
title: Mapping (data to visual)

definition: Techniques and methods used to visually represent and communicate the inherent imprecision, variability, or doubt associated with data, models, or predictions. It helps users understand the reliability and limits of information.
examples: Error bars on a bar chart showing confidence intervals|Probabilistic contours on a weather map indicating hurricane paths|Faded colors or transparency to show lower confidence in geospatial data
title: Uncertainty Visualization

definition: The dynamic capability within a visualization that allows users to manipulate, explore, and gain deeper insights from data by directly engaging with the visual representation. It includes actions like filtering, zooming, panning, and linking views.
examples: Clicking on a bar in a bar chart to filter a connected scatter plot|Dragging a slider to change a time range on a line graph|Hovering over a data point to reveal a tooltip with detailed information
title: Interaction (visualization)

definition: The process of iteratively investigating a dataset through interactive visualizations to discover patterns, anomalies, relationships, and insights without a predefined hypothesis. It leverages human perception and cognition to navigate complex data spaces.
examples: Using a linked brushing technique to select subsets of data across multiple views|Interactively filtering a large dataset to find correlations|Dynamically adjusting parameters in a scatter plot matrix to identify clusters
title: Exploration (visualization)

definition: A visualization strategy that aims to provide detailed information about a specific area of interest (focus) while simultaneously preserving the broader surrounding information (context) at a lower level of detail. This helps users maintain orientation without losing sight of the bigger picture.
examples: A fisheye lens distortion on a graph or map, magnifying a central area while compressing the periphery|A magic lens tool that magnifies content under the cursor|Hierarchical edge bundles where the focus area expands
title: Focus+Context

definition: A visualization technique where two separate views are presented: one showing a comprehensive overview of the entire dataset or display, and another showing a magnified or detailed portion of the overview. These views are often linked, with the overview indicating the location of the detailed view.
examples: A minimap in a geographic information system showing the entire map with a rectangle indicating the current zoomed-in area|A large text document with a scrollbar thumbnail showing the current reading position|A network graph with an interactive subgraph that highlights the corresponding overview section
title: Overview+Detail

definition: A technique, championed by Edward Tufte, that displays multiple small, simplified versions of the same graphic or chart, each representing a different subset of the data (e.g., by time, category, or region). This allows for easy comparison of patterns and trends across different dimensions.
examples: A grid of line charts, each showing sales trends for a different product category|Multiple bar charts, each representing quarterly profits for a different region|A series of maps showing population density changes over decades
title: Small Multiples

definition: A visual display of the most important information needed to achieve one or more objectives, consolidated and arranged on a single screen so the information can be monitored at a glance. Dashboards typically integrate multiple linked visualizations and performance indicators.
examples: A business intelligence dashboard showing key performance indicators (KPIs) like sales, customer acquisition, and website traffic|A server monitoring dashboard displaying CPU usage, memory, and network activity|A healthcare dashboard tracking patient vitals
title: Dashboard (visualization)

definition: Visual representations of information, data, or knowledge designed to present complex information quickly and clearly. They often combine text, images, and various charts to tell a story or explain a topic in an engaging and easily digestible format.
examples: A visual timeline illustrating historical events|A poster explaining how to recycle different materials using icons and diagrams|A chart summarizing statistics about a social issue with relevant imagery
title: Infographics

definition: The practice of combining data, visuals, and narrative to communicate insights and persuade an audience. It involves crafting a compelling sequence of information that highlights key findings and their implications, making complex data accessible and memorable.
examples: A presentation using a series of linked charts and explanations to demonstrate the impact of a marketing campaign|A news article using interactive visualizations to walk readers through the rise of a particular trend|A report guiding stakeholders through critical business metrics with commentary
title: Data Storytelling

definition: A chart that presents categorical data with rectangular bars, where the length or height of each bar is proportional to the values they represent. Bars can be plotted vertically or horizontally and are used for comparing quantities across discrete categories.
examples: A bar chart showing sales figures for different product categories|A chart displaying the number of students in various academic departments|Comparing monthly website visitors over a year
title: Bar Chart

definition: A chart that displays information as a series of data points called 'markers' connected by straight line segments. It is primarily used to visualize trends in data over a continuous period or sequence, especially for time-series data.
examples: A line chart showing stock prices over several months|A chart illustrating temperature fluctuations throughout a day|Tracking population growth over decades
title: Line Chart

definition: A graphical representation of data where individual values contained in a matrix are represented as colors. It is often used to show the magnitude of a phenomenon as color in two dimensions, enabling easy perception of density, clusters, or gradients.
examples: A genomic heatmap showing gene expression levels across different samples|A website heatmap showing user click density|A correlation matrix where color intensity represents the strength of correlation between variables
title: Heatmap (visualization)

definition: A visualization used to display hierarchical data as a set of nested rectangles. Each rectangle's area is proportional to a quantitative value, and they are tiled to fill the entire space.
examples: Visualizing file system disk usage where larger rectangles represent larger folders.|Displaying stock market performance by sector, with rectangle size showing market capitalization.|Illustrating budget allocation across departments and sub-departments.
title: Treemap

definition: A radial visualization for hierarchical data, where concentric rings represent levels of the hierarchy. Each arc within a ring is proportional to a quantitative value, similar to a treemap in a radial layout.
examples: Showing the breakdown of a website's audience by country, region, and city.|Visualizing the organizational structure of a company with department sizes.|Exploring a product catalog's categories and subcategories by sales volume.
semantic_tags: Hierarchical data|Radial layout|Concentric rings|Proportional representation|Categorical data
title: Sunburst Chart

definition: A circular statistical graphic divided into slices to illustrate numerical proportion. Each slice represents a category's share of the whole, with the arc length and area proportional to the quantity it represents.
examples: Displaying market share of different companies in an industry.|Illustrating the percentage breakdown of a household budget.|Showing survey responses for multiple-choice questions as proportions.
title: Pie Chart

definition: A line chart with the area between the line and the axis filled with color or shading. It is typically used to show the magnitude of change over time for one or more categories, emphasizing cumulative totals.
examples: Tracking website traffic over months, with the area showing total page views.|Visualizing population growth trends over decades.|Representing sales volume of a product over a fiscal year.
title: Area Chart

definition: An extension of the scatterplot where data points are replaced with bubbles. It allows for the visualization of three or four dimensions of data, with two dimensions represented by the x and y axes, a third by the bubble size, and an optional fourth by color.
examples: Comparing GDP (x-axis) and life expectancy (y-axis) of countries, with population size as bubble size.|Analyzing product sales (x-axis), profit margin (y-axis), and unit volume (bubble size).|Visualizing research and development spending vs. patent applications, with company revenue as bubble size.
title: Bubble Chart

definition: A method of plotting numeric data, similar to a box plot, but showing the probability density of the data at different values. The 'violin' shape is wider where the data distribution is denser, providing a richer view of the data's shape and spread.
examples: Comparing the distribution of test scores between different classes.|Analyzing the spread of salaries across various job roles.|Visualizing the distribution of drug efficacy results for different treatment groups.
semantic_tags: Distribution|Quantitative data|Probability density|Kernel density estimate|Data comparison|Statistical plots
title: Violin Plot

definition: A visual representation of relationships between entities, known as nodes or vertices, which are connected by links or edges. It is used to display and analyze complex systems of interconnected items.
examples: Mapping social connections between users on a platform.|Visualizing the structure of a computer network.|Illustrating citation patterns between academic papers.
title: Network Graph

definition: A category of algorithms for drawing network graphs, which simulates physical forces (e.g., repulsive forces between nodes, attractive forces along edges) to position nodes in a way that minimizes edge crossings and clusters related nodes. The goal is to achieve an aesthetically pleasing and interpretable layout.
examples: Visualizing clusters within a social network, where friends naturally group together.|Mapping complex protein-protein interaction networks in biology.|Laying out a software dependency graph to show module relationships.
semantic_tags: Network layout|Graph visualization|Physical simulation|Node positioning|Relational data|Clustering
title: Force-directed Graph

definition: A circular visualization that displays the inter-relationships or flow between a set of entities. Nodes are arranged in a circle, and arcs (chords) connect them, with the width of the arc typically indicating the magnitude or strength of the relationship.
examples: Showing trade relationships between multiple countries.|Visualizing migration patterns between different regions.|Illustrating transitions between different music genres within a playlist.
title: Chord Diagram

definition: A visualization technique used to plot high-dimensional data, where each dimension is represented by a vertical axis. Data points are shown as a series of connected line segments (polylines) across these axes, revealing patterns, clusters, and correlations between dimensions.
examples: Comparing multiple car attributes (MPG, HP, weight, acceleration) across various models.|Analyzing multi-criteria decision-making scenarios with many variables.|Exploring relationships in climate sensor data (temperature, humidity, pressure, light).
semantic_tags: High-dimensional data|Multivariate analysis|Pattern detection|Data comparison|Axis mapping|Polylines
title: Parallel Coordinates

definition: A type of stacked area chart that displaces the baseline to the center, creating a flowing, organic shape. It is particularly effective for visualizing the changing magnitude of multiple categories over time, emphasizing cumulative totals and individual contributions.
examples: Illustrating the popularity of different music genres over several decades.|Showing the evolution of search engine query terms over time.|Visualizing website traffic breakdown by content type across months.
semantic_tags: Time-series|Categorical data|Magnitude over time|Stacked area|Flow visualization|Trend analysis
title: Streamgraph

definition: A visual representation of an area of the Earth's surface, typically two-dimensional, displaying geographical features, boundaries, and often used as a foundational layer for spatial data visualization.
examples: A world map showing continents and oceans.|A city street map for navigation.|A topological map indicating elevation and terrain.
title: Geographic Map

definition: A type of thematic map in which geographic areas, such as countries or states, are shaded or colored in proportion to a statistical variable. It effectively visualizes how a variable varies across a region.
examples: Showing population density across different counties.|Illustrating electoral results by state, with color intensity representing vote percentage.|Mapping average income levels across various neighborhoods.
semantic_tags: Spatial data|Statistical variable|Area shading|Thematic mapping|Geographic data|Quantitative data
title: Choropleth Map

definition: A thematic map where the size of a geographic region is distorted, often dramatically, to be proportional to a specific statistical variable, rather than its actual land area. This emphasizes the magnitude of the variable over true geographical size.
examples: A map of the United States where states are resized according to their population.|Visualizing global GDP by country, with larger countries representing higher GDP.|Showing the number of electoral votes by state, with states scaled accordingly.
semantic_tags: Spatial data|Geographic distortion|Proportional representation|Thematic mapping|Quantitative data|Area scaling
title: Cartogram

definition: A thematic map that visualizes the movement or flow of phenomena (e.g., people, goods, information) between geographic locations. It typically uses lines or arrows whose thickness, color, or other visual properties indicate the quantity or direction of the flow.
examples: Illustrating migration patterns between countries.|Mapping global trade routes and the volume of goods exchanged.|Visualizing traffic volume on a road network.
title: Flow Map

definition: A grid of scatterplots, where each plot displays the relationship between a pair of variables from a multivariate dataset. It allows for quick visual inspection of pairwise relationships, correlations, and potential outliers across many variables simultaneously.
examples: Analyzing the relationships between car features like horsepower, weight, MPG, and acceleration.|Exploring correlations in financial data, such as stock prices, trading volume, and volatility.|Investigating multiple chemical properties in a scientific experiment.
semantic_tags: Multivariate data|Pairwise relationships|Quantitative data|Correlation|Pattern detection|Data exploration
title: Scatterplot Matrix (SPLOM)

definition: A method of displaying multivariate data in the form of a two-dimensional chart of three or more quantitative variables represented on axes starting from the same point. Data points are plotted on each axis and connected to form a polygon, ideal for comparing multiple items across several metrics.
examples: Comparing the performance of different athletes across various skill metrics (speed, strength, agility).|Assessing product features like battery life, camera quality, and processing power for smartphones.|Evaluating a person's skills across different competencies in a professional review.
title: Radar Chart

definition: A type of financial chart used to describe price movements of a security, derivative, or currency over time. Each 'candlestick' typically displays the open, high, low, and close prices for a specific time period.
examples: Analyzing stock price fluctuations over daily or hourly intervals.|Tracking cryptocurrency market trends.|Visualizing currency exchange rate movements in forex trading.
title: Candlestick Chart

definition: A visual representation of text data, where the size and often color of each word indicate its frequency or importance within a given text body. More frequent or significant words appear larger.
examples: Summarizing the main themes of customer feedback by showing common keywords.|Analyzing the most frequent words in a speech or document.|Displaying trending topics from social media posts.
semantic_tags: Text data|Frequency analysis|Qualitative data|Data summarization|Text visualization|Tag cloud
title: Word Cloud

definition: A fundamental graph visualization method where entities (nodes) are represented as points or shapes, and relationships (links or edges) are represented as lines connecting them. It is widely used to illustrate network structures and connections.
examples: Visualizing a company's organizational chart with employees as nodes and reporting lines as links.|Mapping the navigation structure of a website.|Representing chemical compounds with atoms as nodes and bonds as links.
title: Node-link Diagram

definition: A graphical representation of hierarchical data, showing relationships between nodes as a tree structure with a root, branches, and leaves.
examples: A computer file system showing directories and files.|An organizational chart depicting management hierarchy.|A phylogenetic tree illustrating evolutionary relationships.
title: Tree Diagram

definition: A specific type of tree diagram used to illustrate the arrangement of clusters produced by hierarchical clustering, showing the sequence of mergers or divisions.
examples: A tree representing the results of agglomerative clustering on a dataset.|A phylogenetic tree in biology showing the evolutionary divergence of species.|Visualizing the output of taxonomic classification algorithms.
title: Dendrogram

definition: A visualization method that organizes events or data points chronologically within a calendar grid structure, typically showing days, weeks, or months.
examples: Google Calendar displaying daily or weekly appointments.|Project management software showing tasks scheduled over a month.|A website's event section organized by date in a grid.
title: Calendar View

definition: A graphical representation that displays events, periods, or tasks in chronological order along a linear axis, often showing durations and relationships.
examples: A Gantt chart for project planning.|An infographic showing key historical events in sequence.|A user interface displaying a sequence of media playback events.
title: Timeline Visualization

definition: A type of flow diagram that visualizes the magnitude of flows between different nodes in a system, where the width of the arrows is proportional to the quantity of the flow.
examples: Illustrating energy flow from generation to consumption in a system.|Showing the movement of money in financial transactions.|Visualizing user navigation paths through a website.
title: Sankey Diagram

definition: The process of generating a 3D surface within a volumetric dataset where all points on the surface have a constant, specified scalar value (isovalue).
examples: Generating a 3D model of a specific organ from a medical CT scan at a certain tissue density.|Visualizing a specific temperature contour in a weather simulation.|Extracting the interface between two materials in a computational fluid dynamics simulation.
title: Isosurface Extraction

definition: Data that represents information within a 3D space, typically sampled on a regular grid (voxel grid) where each point (voxel) stores one or more scalar values.
examples: Medical imaging data from CT or MRI scans.|Outputs from scientific simulations like fluid dynamics or weather models (e.g., temperature, pressure).|Seismic data representing subsurface geological structures.
title: Volume Data

definition: A portmanteau of 'volume' and 'pixel,' representing a data point on a regular grid in 3D space, carrying one or more scalar values like density, color, or opacity. It is the fundamental building block of volume data.
examples: A single cubic element within a medical CT scan representing tissue density.|A data point in a 3D temperature field of a simulated environment.|The basic unit of data for representing the world in games like Minecraft (though often refers to block, concept is similar).
title: Voxel (volume rendering)

definition: A mapping that assigns visual properties (such as color and opacity) to scalar values within a volumetric dataset, allowing different materials or structures to be distinguished during rendering.
examples: Mapping Hounsfield units from a CT scan to specific colors and opacities to differentiate bone, soft tissue, and air.|A gradient editor in visualization software used to assign colors based on data magnitude.|Defining how a specific range of simulation data (e.g., pressure) appears visually.
title: Transfer Function

definition: A surface embedded in a 3D volume that connects all points having an equal, constant scalar value (an isovalue) within a given scalar field.
examples: A 3D representation of a specific tissue boundary in a medical image.|A surface showing constant pressure in a fluid dynamics simulation.|In 2D, this is analogous to a contour line on a topographic map indicating constant elevation.
title: Isosurface (general concept)

definition: A classic algorithm used for isosurface extraction from a discrete volumetric dataset, which traverses the volume cell by cell and generates small triangles to approximate the isosurface within each cell.
examples: Generating a polygonal mesh model of an organ from MRI data.|Extracting a specific density surface from scientific simulation outputs.|Used in some game engines to create deformable 'liquid' or 'goo' surfaces.
title: Marching Cubes Algorithm

definition: A set of techniques that directly visualize volumetric data without first converting it into geometric primitives (like polygons), typically by assigning color and opacity to voxels and projecting them onto a 2D image plane.
examples: Volume Ray Casting used for high-quality medical imaging.|Splatting for faster, approximate rendering of large datasets.|Texture-based Volume Rendering leveraging GPU capabilities for real-time interaction.
title: Direct Volume Rendering

definition: A direct volume rendering technique where rays are cast from the viewer's eye through each pixel of the image plane into the volume, sampling data along the ray and accumulating color and opacity to determine the final pixel color.
examples: Producing high-fidelity visualizations of human anatomy from CT/MRI scans.|Rendering volumetric effects like clouds or smoke in physically-based simulations.|Used in medical diagnostic software for interactive 3D views.
semantic_tags: Direct Volume Rendering|Ray Tracing|Sampling|Opacity Accumulation|Rendering Algorithm
title: Volume Ray Casting (volume rendering)

definition: A direct volume rendering technique that projects each voxel in the volume onto the 2D image plane, distributing its contribution (color and opacity) across several pixels using a filter kernel (a 'splat').
examples: Early real-time volume rendering systems prioritizing interactivity over perfect image quality.|Quickly generating an overview visualization of a large scientific dataset.|Used where the computational cost of ray casting is prohibitive.
title: Splatting (volume rendering)

definition: A direct volume rendering technique that leverages 3D texture mapping capabilities of graphics hardware to store volumetric data, rendering slices (2D textures) of the volume and blending them to approximate the final image.
examples: Interactive 3D visualization of medical scans in real-time using modern GPUs.|Rendering volumetric effects like smoke or fog in video games efficiently.|Visualizing fluid simulation data where slices are rendered and combined.
title: Texture-based Volume Rendering

definition: A direct volume rendering technique where for each ray cast through the volume, only the voxel with the maximum scalar intensity (e.g., density) along that ray is projected onto the 2D image plane.
examples: Visualizing blood vessels in Magnetic Resonance Angiography (MRA) or CT Angiography (CTA) scans.|Highlighting highly dense or contrasted structures in medical images, such as calcifications.|Quickly identifying regions of peak activity or concentration in scientific data.
title: Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP)

definition: A direct volume rendering technique where for each ray cast through the volume, only the voxel with the minimum scalar intensity (e.g., density) along that ray is projected onto the 2D image plane.
examples: Highlighting air-filled structures like airways or intestines in CT scans.|Visualizing low-density regions or cavities within a volume.|Analyzing areas of minimal concentration in scientific datasets.
title: Minimum Intensity Projection (MinIP)

definition: The process of combining the color and opacity contributions of sampled voxels along a ray to produce a final pixel color, typically using the 'over' operator (front-to-back or back-to-front accumulation).
examples: The core blending operation performed in Volume Ray Casting to accumulate visual properties.|Combining multiple semi-transparent layers in image editing software.|Rendering transparent particles or effects in a 3D scene where contributions must be ordered.
title: Alpha Compositing (volume rendering)

definition: A technique used in volume rendering to improve image quality and reduce artifacts by analytically integrating the transfer function and material properties *between* adjacent sampling points along a ray, rather than just at the sampling points themselves.
examples: Enhancing the visual fidelity of thin structures or boundaries in medical visualizations.|Achieving smoother gradients and reducing banding artifacts in rendered volumetric clouds.|Improving the accuracy of opacity and color accumulation in volume ray casting.
title: Pre-integration (volume rendering)

definition: An artifact in volume rendering, particularly noticeable in texture-based or slicing methods, where gaps or visible seams appear between slices or layers of the volume, often due to inadequate blending, precision issues, or incorrect sorting.
examples: Visible 'bands' or 'steps' when rotating a volume rendered with 2D texture slices.|Shimmering or flickering artifacts in real-time volumetric effects.|Incorrect alpha blending causing hard edges instead of smooth transitions between layers.
title: Volume Tearing

definition: A conceptual plane used in volume rendering to selectively remove or 'clip' portions of a 3D dataset, revealing internal structures or providing cross-sectional views. It allows for interactive exploration of volumetric data by defining a boundary beyond which data is not rendered.
examples: Slicing through a medical CT scan to visualize a specific organ's internal structure.|Cutting away the exterior of a cloud simulation to observe wind patterns inside.|Using a clipping plane in a 3D architectural model viewer to show interior room layouts.
semantic_tags: Volume Rendering|3D Graphics|Visualization|Medical Imaging|Data Exploration|Cutting Plane
title: Clipping Plane (volume rendering)

definition: The graphical representation of data where each point in space is associated with a vector (having both magnitude and direction). This visualization helps understand flows, forces, or orientations across a domain.
examples: Using arrows or streamlines to depict wind patterns on a weather map.|Visualizing magnetic fields around a magnet using field lines.|Displaying fluid dynamics simulations with glyphs indicating velocity and direction.
title: Vector Field Visualization

definition: The graphical representation of data where each point in space is associated with a single scalar value (a magnitude without direction). This is often achieved through color mapping, isolines, or isosurfaces.
examples: A heatmap showing temperature distribution across a surface.|Contour lines on a topographic map indicating elevation.|Isosurfaces in a medical scan to delineate regions of constant tissue density.
title: Scalar Field Visualization

definition: The graphical representation of data where each point in space is associated with a tensor, which describes multi-directional properties or relationships. This complex visualization often uses glyphs (e.g., ellipsoids) to represent the tensor's anisotropic characteristics.
examples: Visualizing diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) in the brain to show fiber tract orientations using ellipsoids.|Representing stress and strain distributions in engineering simulations.|Displaying anisotropic material properties in materials science.
title: Tensor Field Visualization

definition: An algorithm applied to an image to modify its pixels' values, typically to enhance certain features, remove noise, or alter its appearance. Filters operate on local neighborhoods of pixels to produce a new output image.
examples: Applying a blur filter to soften edges in a photo.|Using a sharpen filter to make details more prominent.|A median filter to remove salt-and-pepper noise.
title: Image Filter

definition: A mathematical operation fundamental to many image filters, where a small matrix (kernel) is slid over an image, performing element-wise multiplication and summation with the underlying pixels to calculate a new pixel value. It effectively applies a weighted average or difference to a pixel's neighborhood.
examples: Applying a 3x3 sharpening kernel to an image.|Calculating a Gaussian blur by convolving with a Gaussian kernel.|Edge detection using Sobel or Laplacian operators.
title: Convolution (image processing)

definition: An unbiased global illumination rendering technique that simultaneously traces light paths from light sources and camera paths from the camera, connecting their endpoints to form complete light paths. definition: A path tracing technique that uses a Markov Chain Monte Carlo method to explore the space of light paths by making small, correlated mutations to existing paths. This allows the algorithm to efficiently discover and sample complex, high-contributing light paths that might be rare and difficult to find with standard Monte Carlo sampling.

definition: A two-pass global illumination algorithm where the first pass emits photons from light sources and stores their bounces in a 3D data structure (the photon map), and the second pass uses ray tracing from the camera to gather illumination from this map. It is efficient for rendering caustics and diffuse interreflection but is a biased technique.

definition: A global illumination technique that models light energy transfer between surfaces by dividing surfaces into small patches and calculating form factors to determine how much energy each patch radiates to others. It is primarily suitable for scenes with predominantly diffuse reflection and calculates the complete diffuse lighting solution independently of the camera position.

definition: An acceleration technique for global illumination (especially for Monte Carlo methods like path tracing) that caches computed irradiance values at various points in a scene and interpolates between them for nearby points.
