definition: Symmetrical elements tend to be perceived as unified and belonging together, creating a sense of balance, harmony, and order. This principle contributes to the aesthetic appeal and perceived stability of an interface.
examples: A web page layout with a central column and equal margins on both sides.|Icons that are perfectly mirrored on either side of a central axis.|Navigation menus where items are balanced visually around a central point.
title: Symmetry (Gestalt)

definition: Elements that move in the same direction, at the same speed, or respond to the same input are perceived as being more related than those that are stationary or move in different ways. This principle is particularly relevant in animated interfaces and dynamic elements.
examples: A group of items fading in or out together simultaneously.|Multiple windows minimizing to the same corner of the screen.|Icons in a carousel moving in unison when the user swipes.
title: Common Fate (Gestalt)

definition: A set of general principles for user interface design that serve as guidelines for evaluating the usability of a system. These heuristics are widely used in heuristic evaluations to identify common usability problems.
examples: Visibility of system status: A loading spinner indicating that content is being fetched.|Match between system and the real world: Using a shopping cart icon for e-commerce checkouts.|Help and documentation: Providing a comprehensive FAQ section or context-sensitive help tips.
title: Jakob Nielsen's 10 Usability Heuristics

definition: A usability inspection method where evaluators 'walk through' a series of tasks from a user's perspective, focusing on the cognitive processes and potential problems users might encounter at each step. It aims to identify obstacles to learning and task completion, especially for first-time users.
examples: Evaluating the steps a user takes to register for a new account, checking if required information is clear and obvious.|Analyzing the process of booking a flight online, considering how a new user would discover and use filters or select dates.|Assessing the ease of changing a setting in a software application by mentally simulating the user's thought process and actions.
semantic_tags: Usability Testing|Evaluation Method|Cognitive Psychology|Task Analysis|UX Research
title: Cognitive Walkthrough

definition: A theoretical framework that views cognition not solely as an individual's mental process but as a phenomenon distributed across individuals, tools, artifacts, and the environment. It emphasizes how people use external resources to think and solve problems collectively.
examples: A pilot and co-pilot working together in a cockpit, where instruments, checklists, and their communication form a distributed cognitive system.|A team of designers collaborating on a shared digital whiteboard, externalizing and manipulating ideas collectively.|An individual using a calculator, notebook, and their own memory to solve a complex math problem.
title: Distributed Cognition

definition: A philosophical and cross-disciplinary framework that analyzes human activity as a mediated interaction between a subject, an object (goal), and a community, using tools and rules within a division of labor. In HCI, it helps understand how users interact with systems within their broader work and social contexts.
examples: Analyzing a doctor's use of an Electronic Health Record (EHR) system, considering their goal (patient care), tools (EHR), rules (hospital policies), community (staff), and division of labor.|Studying how students use a learning management system (LMS) for collaborative projects, mapping the activity system of learning, tools, and social dynamics.|Designing a shared design tool for architects, considering the various roles, communication needs, and common goals within an architectural firm.
semantic_tags: HCI Theory|Contextual Design|Socio-Technical Systems|Work Systems|Cultural Psychology
title: Activity Theory (HCI)

definition: An approach to interface design that aims to support human decision-making and problem-solving in complex, dynamic systems by representing the underlying constraints and invariant properties of the work domain. It focuses on providing information about the system's 'ecology' rather than just its components.
examples: Control room displays for power plants that show aggregated energy flow and thermodynamic principles, not just individual sensor readings.|Aviation cockpits displaying flight envelope limits and energy state rather than just raw airspeed and altitude data.|Process control systems that visualize the relationships and dependencies between different chemical reactions or physical processes.
semantic_tags: System Design|Complex Systems|Decision Support|Cognitive Engineering|Safety Critical
title: Ecological Interface Design

definition: The perception of elements in the environment within a volume of time and space, the comprehension of their meaning, and the projection of their status in the near future. In HCI, it refers to a user's understanding of the current state of a system, its context, and how their actions will affect it.
examples: A pilot maintaining situational awareness of aircraft position, weather, air traffic, and system status to make informed decisions.|A user of a complex application understanding which mode they are in, what actions are available, and the implications of their next click.|A driver using a navigation system that clearly shows their current location, traffic conditions, and upcoming turns.
semantic_tags: Cognitive Psychology|Decision Making|Complex Systems|User State|System Status
title: Situational Awareness (HCI)

definition: An external device, tool, or representation that supports, extends, or mediates cognitive processes. These artifacts are designed to offload mental effort, structure thinking, or facilitate communication, thereby enhancing human cognitive capabilities.
examples: A calculator for performing arithmetic operations, reducing the mental load of complex calculations.|A to-do list application used to externalize memory and organize tasks.|A graphical user interface (GUI) itself, which organizes information visually and provides affordances for interaction.
title: Cognitive Artifact

definition: The scientific discipline concerned with the understanding of interactions among humans and other elements of a system, and the profession that applies theory, principles, data, and methods to design in order to optimize human well-being and overall system performance. It focuses on designing systems that fit human capabilities and limitations.
examples: Designing an aircraft cockpit layout to minimize pilot error and optimize control accessibility.|Developing medical equipment interfaces that are intuitive and reduce cognitive load for healthcare professionals.|Optimizing the design of control panels in a factory to prevent fatigue and improve operator efficiency and safety.
title: Human Factors (Discipline)

definition: The applied science of designing and arranging workplaces, products, and systems so that they fit the people who use them. It primarily focuses on physical fit, comfort, safety, and efficiency to reduce physical strain and improve productivity.
examples: Designing an adjustable office chair that supports proper posture for different body types.|Placing frequently used controls within easy reach in a car's dashboard.|Creating a keyboard and mouse that reduce the risk of repetitive strain injuries.
title: Ergonomics

definition: The scientific study of the measurements and proportions of the human body. In design, anthropometric data is used to ensure that products, systems, and environments are appropriately sized and shaped for the target user population.
examples: Using average hand measurements to design the grip of a power tool.|Sizing computer monitors and desks based on typical sitting and standing heights.|Designing public seating dimensions (seat height, depth, width) to accommodate a wide range of body sizes.
title: Anthropometry

definition: A sub-discipline of ergonomics concerned with mental processes such as perception, memory, reasoning, and motor response as they affect interactions among humans and other elements of a system. It focuses on designing systems that minimize cognitive load, reduce errors, and support effective decision-making.
examples: Designing a complex software interface with clear labels, consistent navigation, and minimal steps to reduce mental effort.|Optimizing warning systems in an industrial control room to ensure critical information is perceived and understood quickly.|Structuring information on a dashboard to facilitate rapid interpretation and reduce memory burden for users.
semantic_tags: Mental Workload|Decision Support|Cognitive Psychology|Human Error|Information Design
title: Cognitive Ergonomics

definition: An approach to design that intentionally considers and aims to evoke specific human emotions (e.g., joy, trust, excitement) in users through products and interfaces. It recognizes that design impacts not just usability but also how users feel and connect with a product.
examples: An app using playful animations and celebratory sounds to acknowledge user achievements.|Websites employing warm colors, inviting imagery, and friendly language to create a sense of welcome and trust.|Digital onboarding processes designed to reduce anxiety and build confidence through clear, supportive messaging.
semantic_tags: UX Design|Affective Computing|User Experience|Emotions|Psychology of Design
title: Emotional Design

definition: The lowest and most fundamental level of emotional design, focusing on immediate, pre-cognitive reactions to a product's appearance, feel, and sound. It's about raw aesthetic appeal, perceived quality, and instinctual attraction or repulsion.
examples: The sleek, minimalist aesthetic and high-quality materials of premium smartphones, evoking a sense of luxury.|The deep, satisfying thud of a car door closing, suggesting robustness and quality.|A brightly colored, toy-like interface designed for children, immediately appealing to their sense of playfulness.
title: Visceral Design

definition: Behavioral Design is an approach that applies insights from psychology and behavioral economics to deliberately influence user actions and choices within a system. It aims to make desired behaviors easier or more appealing, and undesirable behaviors harder, often leveraging cognitive biases and motivational principles.
examples: A fitness app using gamification and streaks to encourage users to exercise daily.|E-commerce websites using 'people also bought' recommendations to nudge users towards additional purchases.|Default settings in software that guide users towards a specific, often beneficial, course of action (e.g., opting into security updates).
title: Behavioral Design

definition: Reflective Design focuses on creating experiences that evoke reflection, self-identity, and personal meaning for the user, going beyond immediate usability and pleasure. It addresses the higher-level cognitive, emotional, and social aspects of human-computer interaction, aiming for long-term satisfaction and a deeper connection.
examples: A journaling application designed to prompt users to contemplate their emotions and personal growth over time.|A smart home device that learns user habits and suggests environmentally friendly routines, fostering a sense of responsibility.|An interactive museum exhibit that encourages visitors to consider their societal role and personal values.
title: Reflective Design

definition: Hedonic Quality in User Experience refers to the non-instrumental attributes of a product that evoke pleasure, enjoyment, stimulation, and the fulfillment of psychological needs. It encompasses aspects like aesthetics, novelty, identity, and the overall experiential delight that goes beyond mere functionality.
examples: The delightful animations and satisfying sound effects in a mobile game.|The premium feel, sleek aesthetics, and unique branding of a high-end smartphone.|The sense of accomplishment and social connection derived from sharing a perfectly edited photo on a social media platform.
title: Hedonic Quality (UX)

definition: Pragmatic Quality in User Experience relates to the instrumental attributes of a product that enable users to achieve their goals efficiently and effectively. It focuses on how useful, usable, functional, and reliable a system is, allowing users to complete tasks with ease and without errors.
examples: A clearly structured navigation menu that allows users to quickly locate desired information.|Software that provides precise, actionable error messages guiding users to resolve issues.|A task management application that simplifies complex project organization through an intuitive interface and efficient workflows.
title: Pragmatic Quality (UX)

definition: The Flow State is a mental condition where a person is fully immersed, focused, and absorbed in an activity, characterized by feelings of energized focus, complete involvement, and enjoyment in the process. In HCI, designs often aim to facilitate this state to create highly engaging and satisfying user experiences.
examples: A programmer deeply engrossed in coding, losing all sense of time and external distractions.|A gamer who is completely absorbed in a video game, facing challenges that perfectly match their skill level.|A user seamlessly navigating and creating within a well-designed creative application, feeling productive and unhindered by the interface.
title: Flow State (Psychology)

definition: Decision Fatigue is a psychological phenomenon where making a large number of decisions over time leads to a deterioration in the quality of subsequent decisions. This can result in increased impulsivity, procrastination, or a tendency to avoid making any further choices, due to depleted mental energy.
examples: An e-commerce website offering too many customization options (e.g., colors, sizes, materials), causing users to abandon their shopping cart.|A complex software application presenting users with countless configuration choices during the initial setup, leading to frustration and disengagement.|A user choosing the default option in an app simply because they are mentally exhausted from making numerous choices elsewhere.
semantic_tags: Cognitive load|Decision making|Choice overload|Mental exhaustion|User interface design|Psychology
title: Decision Fatigue

definition: A Cognitive Bias is a systematic pattern of deviation from rationality in judgment, often arising from mental shortcuts (heuristics) that the brain uses to process information quickly. These biases can influence perception, memory, and decision-making, leading to illogical or irrational conclusions.
examples: Believing a product is of higher quality simply because it has a higher price (price-quality bias).|Overestimating the number of people who share your opinions or beliefs (false consensus effect).|A user preferring an older, familiar software interface over a new, more efficient one due to the status quo bias.
title: Cognitive Bias

definition: Anchoring Bias is a cognitive bias where an individual relies too heavily on the first piece of information offered (the 'anchor') when making decisions. Subsequent judgments are then adjusted around this anchor, often insufficiently, even if the initial information is arbitrary or irrelevant.
examples: An e-commerce site displaying a 'Was $99, Now $49' price, where the original higher price serves as an anchor to make the current price seem more attractive.|An initial estimate for a software development task influencing all subsequent timeline adjustments, despite new information emerging.|A user's perception of a product's quality being heavily influenced by the first review they read, before considering others.
title: Anchoring Bias

definition: Confirmation Bias is a cognitive bias where individuals tend to search for, interpret, favor, and recall information in a way that confirms or supports their existing beliefs or hypotheses. This can lead to selective exposure to information and a reluctance to consider contradictory evidence.
examples: A user actively seeking out and only reading positive reviews for a product they have already decided to purchase.|A social media algorithm showing a user more content that aligns with their previously expressed political views.|A designer selectively highlighting user feedback that supports their initial design ideas, while downplaying or ignoring critical feedback.
title: Confirmation Bias

definition: The Availability Heuristic is a mental shortcut where people estimate the likelihood or frequency of an event based on how easily examples or instances come to mind. Events that are more vivid, recent, or emotionally salient are often perceived as more common or probable, even if they are not.
examples: A user thinking a software bug is widespread because they encountered it personally a few times, despite it being a rare occurrence for the overall user base.|Prominent news coverage of a data breach causing users to overestimate the general risk of online banking, despite its overall high security.|Recalling numerous examples of successful startups from media stories, leading to an overestimation of one's own chances of launching a successful business.
title: Availability Heuristic

definition: The Framing Effect is a cognitive bias where people react to a particular choice in different ways depending on how it is presented or 'framed,' even if the underlying options are objectively identical. This often involves presenting information in terms of potential gains or losses.
examples: Presenting a subscription cost as '$10 a month' versus '$120 a year', with the monthly frame often perceived as less costly.|Describing a medical treatment as having a '90% success rate' versus a '10% failure rate,' influencing patient willingness to undergo it.|A warning message phrased as 'Clicking 'No' will delete your unsaved work' (loss frame) versus 'Click 'Yes' to save your work' (gain frame).
title: Framing Effect

definition: The Endowment Effect is a cognitive bias where individuals place a higher value on items they own compared to identical items they do not own. This perceived added value often means they demand more to sell an item than they would be willing to pay to acquire it.
examples: Users being reluctant to switch from an existing, customized software setup they have invested time in, even if a new system is objectively superior.|A freemium model that 'gives' users a premium feature for a trial period, making them more likely to subscribe to avoid the 'loss' of that feature.|People overestimating the resale value of their used car due to personal attachment and the effort they put into maintaining it.
title: Endowment Effect

definition: The Mere-Exposure Effect is a psychological phenomenon where people tend to develop a preference for things merely because they are familiar with them. The more often an individual is exposed to a stimulus, the more positively they tend to feel towards it, even without conscious recognition.
examples: Users often prefer familiar interface layouts and icon designs, even if novel designs are objectively more efficient or modern.|Repeated exposure to a brand logo or advertising slogan can increase brand recognition and positive sentiment over time.|A new feature being slowly introduced or subtly rolled out to users, allowing them to become accustomed to it gradually, leading to greater acceptance.
title: Mere-Exposure Effect

definition: Loss Aversion is a cognitive bias where the psychological impact of losing something is felt more intensely than the pleasure of gaining an equivalent item. This means people are generally more motivated to avoid losses than they are to acquire equivalent gains.
examples: A subscription service offering a free trial period, knowing that users will feel a stronger sense of loss if they cancel than the initial joy of gaining the service.|Displaying a progress bar for completing a user profile, emphasizing the 'loss' of benefits or features if the profile remains incomplete.|Users becoming more upset by a minor reduction in their internet data cap than pleased by an equivalent increase in speed.
title: Loss Aversion

definition: System 1 Thinking refers to fast, automatic, intuitive, and emotional processing that operates subconsciously and requires little mental effort. It quickly generates impressions, feelings, and inclinations, which are often the source of our explicit beliefs and deliberate choices.
examples: Instantly recognizing a familiar face or object without conscious thought.|Reacting instinctively to a sudden loud noise or an unexpected visual stimulus.|Understanding simple, well-designed icons or traffic signs without needing to consciously analyze them.
title: System 1 Thinking

definition: System 2 Thinking refers to slow, effortful, deliberate, and logical reasoning that involves complex calculations, conscious reflection, and sustained attention. It monitors and can override the impulses and associations generated by System 1, allowing for more rational and controlled decision-making.
examples: Carefully solving a complex mathematical equation or a logical puzzle.|Diligently comparing detailed product specifications and reviews before making a significant purchase.|Debugging a complex piece of software by systematically tracing its execution path and analyzing variables.
title: System 2 Thinking

definition: Tesler's Law, also known as the Law of Conservation of Complexity, states that for any system, there is an inherent amount of complexity that cannot be reduced. This complexity must be managed, either by the user or by the designer, meaning that if designers simplify the user's experience, they must absorb that complexity in the system's backend or design.
examples: A simple, user-friendly email client (low complexity for the user) requires significant underlying complexity in its development to manage protocols, server interactions, and data synchronization.|A smart home system that simplifies user interaction to a single voice command requires sophisticated programming and integration logic behind the scenes.|Refactoring a complex codebase to make it easier for other developers to integrate with shifts the inherent complexity from future users (developers) to the refactoring team.
normalized_name: tesler s law law of conservation of complexity
title: Tesler's Law (Law of Conservation of Complexity)

definition: In UX, the Pareto Principle, or 80/20 Rule, suggests that roughly 80% of a system's effects or outcomes come from 20% of its causes or features. This often means that a small percentage of features satisfy the majority of user needs, or that a small percentage of users account for the majority of usage.
examples: Identifying that 20% of an application's features are used by 80% of its users, informing product development priorities.|Addressing the top 20% of most critical usability issues often resolves 80% of user complaints or frustrations.|Focusing UX research efforts on the core 20% of tasks that users perform most frequently to achieve the greatest impact.
title: Pareto Principle (80/20 Rule) in UX

definition: The Aesthetic-Usability Effect is a phenomenon where users often perceive aesthetically pleasing designs as more usable, even if they are not objectively more efficient or effective. Visual appeal can create a positive first impression, foster goodwill, and make users more forgiving of minor usability issues.
examples: Users being more forgiving of minor navigation glitches in a beautifully designed mobile application.|A website with clean typography, appealing visuals, and harmonious colors being judged as more professional and easier to navigate.|A visually appealing operating system leading users to perceive its performance as smoother or faster, despite similar technical specifications to a less attractive one.
title: Aesthetic-Usability Effect

definition: The Serial Position Effect is a cognitive bias that describes the tendency of a person to recall the first items (primacy effect) and the last items (recency effect) in a list more accurately than the items in the middle. This effect is crucial for designing interfaces where item recall or selection is important.
examples: Placing the most critical or frequently used navigation links at the beginning or end of a menu to improve discoverability and recall.|Users remembering the first and last steps of a multi-step onboarding wizard more clearly than the intermediate steps.|Items positioned at the beginning and end of a dropdown list or search results being clicked more often than those buried in the middle.
title: Serial Position Effect

definition: The Goal-Gradient Effect describes the psychological phenomenon where individuals increase their effort and accelerate their pace as they get closer to achieving a goal. In HCI, this principle is often used to motivate users to complete tasks by showing their progress.
examples: A progress bar filling up as a user completes steps in an online checkout process.|Loyalty programs that offer bigger rewards or faster accumulation of points as a customer nears a higher status or redemption threshold.|A software installation wizard showing 90% completion, encouraging the user not to quit.
title: Goal-Gradient Effect

definition: The Von Restorff Effect, also known as the isolation effect, states that an item that stands out from a group of similar items is more likely to be remembered. This principle suggests that distinctiveness aids memory recall.
examples: Highlighting a crucial call-to-action button in a unique color or larger font compared to other elements on a webpage.|A single error message displayed in red within a form field, drawing immediate attention.|Using a distinct icon for an important feature among a set of similar-looking icons.
title: Von Restorff Effect

definition: The Zeigarnik Effect describes the tendency to remember uncompleted or interrupted tasks better than completed ones. This cognitive bias suggests that our minds keep 'open' tasks in short-term memory until they are resolved.
examples: A multi-step onboarding process that shows incomplete steps, motivating users to finish.|An e-commerce site reminding users about items left in their abandoned shopping cart.|A 'save for later' feature in an application that makes it easy for users to return to partially completed work.
title: Zeigarnik Effect

definition: In design, Occam's Razor is the principle that among competing designs or explanations, the simplest one is usually the best. It advocates for parsimony and removing unnecessary complexity to achieve clarity and efficiency.
examples: Simplifying a user interface by removing redundant buttons or extraneous visual elements.|Choosing a single, clear navigation path over multiple confusing options for a user task.|A minimalist design approach that focuses on core functionality, reducing cognitive load for users.
title: Occam's Razor (in Design)

definition: User-Centered Design (UCD) is an iterative design philosophy and process that places the user and their needs at the center of every stage of the design and development lifecycle. It involves extensive user research, usability testing, and continuous feedback to create highly usable and accessible products.
examples: Conducting interviews and creating personas to understand target users' goals and pain points.|Developing wireframes and prototypes, then testing them with actual users to gather feedback.|Incorporating user feedback from usability tests to refine product features and interactions.
title: User-Centered Design (UCD)

definition: Iterative design is a cyclic process of prototyping, testing, analyzing, and refining a design or product based on continuous feedback and evaluation. This approach allows designers to learn from user interactions and gradually improve the design.
examples: Creating multiple versions of a wireframe, testing each with users, and making improvements based on observations.|Conducting A/B tests on different UI elements to determine which performs better before full implementation.|Releasing software updates frequently based on user feedback and analytics data to incrementally enhance the product.
title: Iterative Design

definition: Design Thinking is a human-centered, iterative approach to problem-solving and innovation that emphasizes understanding user needs, challenging assumptions, and redefining problems to identify alternative strategies and solutions. It typically involves phases such as Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype, and Test.
examples: Teams conducting empathy mapping workshops to deeply understand user perspectives before defining a problem.|Brainstorming a wide range of creative solutions (Ideate) for a defined user challenge.|Building low-fidelity prototypes quickly to test assumptions and gather user feedback (Prototype & Test).
title: Design Thinking

definition: The Double Diamond Design Process is a visual framework, often used within Design Thinking, that illustrates a structured approach to solving design challenges. It consists of four distinct phases—Discover, Define, Develop, and Deliver—which alternate between divergent (exploring) and convergent (focusing) thinking.
examples: During 'Discover,' conducting extensive user research and market analysis to understand a problem space broadly.|In 'Define,' synthesizing research findings to articulate a clear, actionable problem statement or design brief.|During 'Develop,' ideating multiple potential solutions and creating prototypes, then selecting the best ones in 'Deliver' for testing and implementation.
title: Double Diamond Design Process

definition: Agile UX is the integration of user experience (UX) design activities and principles into Agile software development methodologies. It emphasizes continuous collaboration between UX designers and development teams, iterative design, rapid prototyping, and ongoing user feedback within short development cycles.
examples: A UX designer participating daily in a Scrum team's stand-ups and sprint planning sessions.|Integrating user research and usability testing into each sprint, rather than as separate, upfront phases.|Creating low-fidelity prototypes or sketches for immediate developer feedback and rapid iteration within a sprint.
semantic_tags: Agile Development|UX Integration|Iterative Design|Collaboration|Rapid Development|User Feedback
title: Agile UX

definition: Lean UX is a design methodology focused on validated learning, rapid experimentation, and minimizing waste, inspired by Lean Startup principles. It prioritizes building a Minimum Viable Product (MVP) and iterating based on continuous user feedback and empirical data rather than extensive upfront documentation.
examples: Formulating a hypothesis about a user need, then quickly building a simple prototype to test it.|Using A/B testing on different UI elements to validate design choices with real user behavior data.|Releasing an MVP with core features to gather early user feedback and inform subsequent development cycles.
semantic_tags: Lean Startup|Validated Learning|MVP|Rapid Experimentation|Continuous Improvement|User Feedback
title: Lean UX

definition: A Design Sprint is a five-day (or shorter) structured process for answering critical business questions through design, prototyping, and testing ideas with target users. It's a 'greatest hits' of business strategy, innovation, behavior science, and design thinking, packaged into a battle-tested process.
examples: A team dedicating a week to brainstorm, prototype, and test a new feature for an existing product.|Running a 3-day sprint to explore potential solutions for a complex user onboarding problem.|Using a Design Sprint to validate a new product concept with real users before committing significant resources to full development.
title: Design Sprint

definition: Requirements Elicitation in HCI is the process of gathering and discovering information from users and stakeholders to understand their needs, goals, tasks, and constraints for a new or existing system or product. It involves various research methods to uncover explicit and implicit requirements.
examples: Conducting user interviews to understand current workflows and pain points.|Distributing surveys to a large user base to gather quantitative data on feature preferences.|Performing contextual inquiry by observing users in their natural environment to identify unstated needs.
semantic_tags: User Research|Requirements Engineering|Data Gathering|Stakeholder Engagement|Needs Analysis|Discovery
title: Requirements Elicitation (HCI)

definition: Requirements Specification in HCI is the process of formally documenting the agreed-upon user needs, functional, and non-functional requirements for a system or product in a clear, unambiguous, and testable manner. This documentation serves as a blueprint for design and development.
examples: Writing detailed user stories that describe functionality from an end-user perspective (e.g., 'As a customer, I want to be able to track my order so I can know its delivery status').|Creating use cases that outline interaction sequences between users and the system.|Developing a functional specification document that details how the system should behave under various conditions.
title: Requirements Specification (HCI)

definition: Stakeholder Analysis in HCI is the systematic process of identifying all individuals, groups, or organizations who have an interest in or can be affected by a project, and then understanding their influence, interests, needs, and potential impact. This helps in managing expectations and gaining buy-in.
examples: Creating a power/interest grid to categorize stakeholders (e.g., end-users, product managers, developers, executives) and prioritize engagement.|Interviewing representatives from different departments (e.g., marketing, sales, customer support) to gather diverse perspectives on product requirements.|Identifying conflicting stakeholder interests early in a project to mitigate potential issues during design and development.
title: Stakeholder Analysis (HCI)

definition: Contextual Inquiry is a user research method that involves observing users in their natural work environment while they perform tasks, combined with an interview process where the researcher engages with the user about their work. This method aims to uncover deep insights into user behavior, motivations, and pain points.
examples: Observing a nurse using a new electronic health record system in a hospital setting while asking clarifying questions about their workflow.|Visiting a customer's home to watch them set up and interact with a smart home device, prompting them to explain their actions.|Shadowing an office worker to understand how they use a specific software application throughout their day.
title: Contextual Inquiry

definition: Task Analysis is the systematic study of how users perform their tasks, aiming to understand the goals, steps, actions, and cognitive processes involved. It decomposes a task into smaller sub-tasks and actions to identify complexities, potential errors, and opportunities for design improvement.
examples: Creating a Hierarchical Task Analysis (HTA) to break down the goal of 'booking a flight online' into sub-goals and specific actions.|Mapping out the exact steps a user takes to register for an account, including decisions and potential error points.|Analyzing the sequence of interactions required to complete a complex data entry form, identifying areas of cognitive load.
title: Task Analysis

definition: In HCI, a scenario is a narrative description of a user performing a task within a specific context, outlining their goals, motivations, and the steps they take when interacting with a system. Scenarios help designers visualize user experiences and communicate design ideas effectively.
examples: "Alice, a busy professional, wants to quickly check her email on her phone while commuting on a crowded train, using only one hand."|A story detailing how a student uses a library's online catalog to find and reserve a specific book for their research project.|A narrative describing a user attempting to troubleshoot a common problem with a smart home device, highlighting potential frustrations.
title: Scenario (HCI)

definition: The Jobs-to-be-Done (JTBD) framework is a user-centered approach that focuses on understanding what a customer is trying to achieve—their fundamental 'job'—when they purchase and use a product or service, rather than just their demographics or product features. It emphasizes the underlying goals and circumstances that drive customer behavior.
examples: A user 'hires' a social media app not just to share photos, but for the 'job' of staying connected with friends or being entertained.|People buy a drill because they need the 'job' of making a hole, not because they specifically want a drill.|Customers use a food delivery service for the 'job' of eating conveniently without cooking, rather than just to order food.
title: Jobs-to-be-Done Framework

definition: A Design Brief is a concise foundational document that outlines the project goals, scope, target audience, key requirements, constraints, and deliverables for a design project. It serves as a shared understanding between the client and the design team, guiding the design process and ensuring alignment.
examples: A document stating the objective to redesign a company's e-commerce website to improve conversion rates by 15%, targeting young adults aged 18-35.|A brief for a mobile app project specifying the core problem to solve, the primary user personas, and a list of mandatory features.|An outline detailing the brand guidelines, technical limitations, and timeline for creating a new digital advertising campaign.
title: Design Brief

definition: A Design Specification in HCI is a detailed document that translates user requirements and design principles into concrete design decisions for a system or product. It outlines the user interface elements, interaction flows, visual style, content, and often technical considerations necessary for implementation.
examples: Detailed wireframes and mockups illustrating every screen, its layout, and interactive elements.|Flowcharts and user journey maps detailing interaction sequences and potential decision points.|A comprehensive style guide that defines typography, color palettes, iconography, and spacing for consistent branding.
title: Design Specification (HCI)

definition: A comprehensive set of reusable components, guidelines, and principles that help design and develop consistent digital products efficiently. It acts as a single source of truth for an organization's design, ensuring coherence and scalability.
examples: Google's Material Design, providing components like buttons, cards, and typography with usage guidelines.|Apple's Human Interface Guidelines, offering principles and patterns for iOS app development.|Atlassian Design System (Forge), used across products like Jira and Confluence.
title: Design System (UI/UX)

definition: The overarching set of visual and interaction principles, patterns, and aesthetics that define the look, feel, and behavior of a product or brand across all its touchpoints. It communicates the brand's unique identity through cohesive design elements.
examples: Apple's minimalist, intuitive, and elegant design language across its hardware and software.|IBM's Carbon Design System embodying its brand's design language through clear, functional, and consistent interfaces.|The consistent use of flat design and vibrant colors by companies like Spotify.
title: Design Language (UI/UX)

definition: A methodology for creating design systems that breaks down user interfaces into their fundamental building blocks and then assembles them into larger, more complex structures. It categorizes UI elements into atoms, molecules, organisms, templates, and pages.
examples: Defining a basic button as an 'atom'.|Combining an input field and a button to form a search bar 'molecule'.|Assembling a header with a logo, navigation, and a search bar to create an 'organism'.
title: Atomic Design Methodology

definition: Research focused on understanding the underlying reasons, opinions, and motivations behind user behavior, often exploring 'why' and 'how.' It typically involves small, non-representative samples and yields non-numerical data.
examples: Conducting user interviews to understand pain points in a workflow.|Observing users during a usability test to gather insights on their experience.|Analyzing open-ended survey responses to explore user sentiments.
title: Qualitative Research (HCI)

definition: Research focused on collecting and analyzing numerical data to identify patterns, test hypotheses, and generalize findings to a larger population. It aims to quantify user behavior, attitudes, or preferences.
examples: Running A/B tests to compare conversion rates between two website designs.|Analyzing survey data to determine average user satisfaction scores (e.g., NPS).|Measuring task completion times and error rates in a usability study with many participants.
title: Quantitative Research (HCI)

definition: A one-on-one conversation between a researcher and a user, designed to gather in-depth information about the user's experiences, needs, motivations, and perceptions related to a product or task. It is a primary method for qualitative data collection, seeking detailed personal insights.
examples: Asking a user, 'Can you describe your typical process for booking a flight online?'|Probing a user with, 'What challenges do you face when trying to manage your schedule with existing tools?'|Conducting a remote interview with a potential customer to understand their current needs.
title: User Interview (Qualitative Research)

definition: A qualitative research method where a small group of participants (typically 6-10) discusses a specific topic, product, or service under the guidance of a moderator. It aims to gather diverse perspectives, observe group dynamics, and explore collective attitudes.
examples: A moderator leading a discussion among potential customers about their reactions to new product concepts for a mobile app.|Gathering a group of elderly users to discuss their experiences with smart home devices.|Observing how a group of students interacts and shares opinions on an educational platform.
title: Focus Group

definition: An in-depth qualitative research method that involves observing and interacting with users in their natural environments over an extended period. The goal is to understand user behaviors, cultures, and contexts without imposing artificial constraints, uncovering unspoken needs and practices.
examples: A researcher spending weeks observing how doctors and nurses use electronic health records in a hospital setting.|Living with a family for several days to understand their technology usage patterns and daily routines at home.|Shadowing construction workers on a job site to understand their interactions with specialized equipment.
title: Ethnographic Study

definition: A research method where researchers observe and interact with users in their natural environments or contexts of use, rather than in a controlled lab setting. It aims to understand how users interact with products or perform tasks in real-world conditions, providing authentic insights.
examples: Observing commuters using a public transport app while riding a bus or train during peak hours.|Watching how employees use a new software tool in their actual office workspace during a typical workday.|Conducting contextual inquiries by visiting users' homes to see how they use smart home devices.
title: Field Study (HCI)

definition: A qualitative research method where participants document their activities, thoughts, and feelings related to a specific topic or product over a period of time. Users typically record entries in a diary (physical or digital) at predefined intervals or trigger points, capturing in-the-moment experiences.
examples: Asking users to record every instance they feel frustrated or delighted while using a new app for a week.|Participants documenting their daily routine of healthy eating habits and associated technology usage for a month.|Users taking photos or videos of their environment whenever they encounter a specific design element.
title: Diary Study

definition: A quantitative research method used to collect data from a large number of participants through a standardized set of questions. Surveys can gather information about user demographics, attitudes, preferences, and behaviors, allowing for statistical analysis and generalization.
examples: A post-purchase survey asking customers to rate their satisfaction with an e-commerce experience on a 5-point scale.|A website pop-up survey asking users about features they'd like to see added or improved.|An email survey distributed to a large user base to gauge overall product satisfaction (e.g., Net Promoter Score).
title: Surveys (User Research)

definition: A data collection instrument consisting of a series of questions designed to gather information from respondents, often used within surveys but can also be part of other research methods. Questionnaires can include various question types (e.g., multiple choice, open-ended, rating scales) to capture diverse data.
examples: The System Usability Scale (SUS) questionnaire, a 10-item scale for measuring perceived usability.|A pre-test questionnaire given to usability participants to gather demographic information and prior experience.|A short feedback questionnaire embedded within a software application after a feature interaction.
title: Questionnaires (User Research)

definition: A quantitative research method where two or more versions (A, B, and potentially more 'n' versions) of a webpage, app feature, or email are shown to different segments of users simultaneously. The goal is to determine which version performs better against a specific, predefined metric.
examples: Testing two different call-to-action button colors on a landing page to see which leads to a higher click-through rate.|Comparing three variations of a headline for an email campaign to optimize open rates.|Running an experiment with two different onboarding flows for a mobile app to measure conversion to feature usage.
title: A/B/n Testing

definition: A qualitative and sometimes quantitative research method conducted in a controlled environment (a 'lab') where users are observed performing specific tasks with a product. The goal is to identify usability problems, gather direct feedback, and measure performance metrics under consistent conditions.
examples: Bringing users into a dedicated observation room with a one-way mirror to watch them navigate a prototype e-commerce website.|Asking participants to complete a specific task on a new mobile app while researchers take notes and record screen interactions.|Measuring the time it takes for users to complete a registration process in a controlled lab setting.
title: Usability Testing (Lab-based)

definition: Usability testing conducted with participants who are not physically present with the moderator or researcher, typically using screen-sharing software, specialized platforms, or recording tools. It allows for broader participant reach, reduces logistical overhead, and often captures users in their natural environments.
examples: Using video conferencing software like Zoom to share screens and observe a user interacting with a website from their home office.|Employing a platform like UserTesting.com where participants record their sessions and verbal commentary on a given task.|Distributing a test link to users who then complete tasks on their own device, with their interactions automatically recorded.
title: Remote Usability Testing

definition: Usability testing where a trained moderator guides participants through tasks, asks probing questions, and interacts with them in real-time. This allows for clarification, follow-up questions, and deeper insights into user behavior and thoughts, adapting the session as needed.
examples: A researcher in a lab (or remotely via video call) asking a user, 'What were you thinking when you clicked that particular button?' immediately after an action.|Providing gentle assistance or clarifying instructions if a user gets stuck on a task during a live session.|Conducting a remote moderated test where the moderator asks about the user's expectations versus their actual experience with a feature.
title: Moderated Usability Testing

definition: Usability testing where participants complete tasks independently without direct interaction from a moderator, typically using specialized software that records their screen, audio, and sometimes webcam. It is often used for quick feedback from a larger number of users, focusing on task completion and efficiency.
examples: A platform automatically recording a user's screen and voice as they attempt to sign up for a new online service from their home.|A tool tracking clicks, paths, and task completion rates across hundreds of users without any human intervention during the test.|Sending out a link to a prototype where users complete a set of tasks and provide written feedback at the end.
title: Unmoderated Usability Testing

definition: A qualitative data collection technique used during usability testing where participants are asked to continuously verbalize their thoughts, feelings, and actions as they interact with a product or system. This provides valuable insight into their cognitive processes, assumptions, and decision-making.
examples: A user saying aloud, 'Okay, I'm looking for the 'Add to Cart' button... I see it here, but it's grayed out, I wonder why it's not active?' while navigating an e-commerce site.|A participant narrating, 'I thought clicking this icon would open the menu, but it seems to be taking me to a different page instead,' during a mobile app test.|Asking a user to verbalize their steps as they try to accomplish a task like 'find and reset your password'.
title: Think-Aloud Protocol

definition: A specific type of Think-Aloud Protocol where participants verbalize their thoughts, feelings, and actions *while* they are performing tasks. This captures insights in real-time, minimizing recall bias and providing immediate context for observed behaviors.
examples: During a usability test, a participant continuously narrating their thought process as they navigate a new software interface, saying, 'I'm trying to find the settings icon; usually, it's in the top right, but I don't see it here.'|A user describing their steps and expectations aloud as they attempt to fill out an online form.|Asking a user to comment in real-time on any confusion or unexpected behavior they encounter while using a prototype.
title: Concurrent Think-Aloud

definition: A specific type of Think-Aloud Protocol where participants describe their thoughts, feelings, and actions *after* completing a task or an entire session, often aided by video recordings of their interaction. This helps mitigate the potential impact of thinking aloud on performance during the task.
examples: A researcher playing back a video recording of a participant's interaction with an app, pausing at key moments and asking, 'What were you thinking here?' or 'Why did you click there?'|After a user completes a complex task, the researcher reviews the recorded session with them, prompting them to recall their mental state and decisions.|Showing a user a heatmap of their clicks on a webpage after they've finished browsing, then asking them to explain their intentions behind certain interactions.
title: Retrospective Think-Aloud

definition: Eyetracking is a research method that measures eye movements, gaze direction, and pupil dilation to understand a user's visual attention and cognitive processes when interacting with an interface or physical environment. It provides objective data on what users are looking at, for how long, and in what sequence, revealing insights into usability, discoverability, and information processing.
examples: Analyzing a heat map of users' gaze patterns on a webpage to identify overlooked elements or areas of high attention.|Using a gaze plot to observe the reading path of participants interacting with a complex data visualization.|Measuring pupil dilation as an indicator of cognitive load when users perform a difficult task on a mobile app.

title: Eyetracking (HCI Research)

definition: Physiological measurement in HCI involves the use of sensors to capture objective data about a user's bodily responses (e.g., heart rate, skin conductance, brain activity) during interaction. These measurements provide insights into a user's emotional state, cognitive load, stress levels, and engagement, complementing subjective self-report data.
examples: Using an EEG headset to measure brain activity patterns indicative of user engagement or frustration with a VR experience.|Monitoring changes in heart rate variability during a complex task to assess cognitive load and stress.|Collecting galvanic skin response data to detect moments of heightened emotional arousal when a user encounters errors in software.

title: Physiological Measurement (HCI)

definition: Electroencephalography (EEG) in HCI is a technique that measures electrical activity in the brain through electrodes placed on the scalp to infer cognitive states such as attention, engagement, mental workload, and frustration. It offers direct, real-time insights into neural processes during user interaction, providing objective data on user experience.
examples: Detecting alpha wave suppression as an indicator of increased mental effort while a user navigates a new software interface.|Monitoring frontal asymmetry to gauge emotional valence (e.g., positive vs. negative affect) during gameplay.|Using event-related potentials (ERPs) to study cognitive responses to specific stimuli, like an unexpected error message.
title: Electroencephalography (EEG) in HCI

definition: Galvanic Skin Response (GSR), also known as electrodermal activity (EDA), measures changes in the electrical conductivity of the skin, primarily due to sweat gland activity, which correlates with sympathetic nervous system arousal. In HCI, GSR is used to detect and quantify emotional arousal, stress, or engagement in response to interactive experiences.
examples: Observing a spike in GSR readings when a user encounters a critical error message in a banking app, indicating stress.|Using continuous GSR measurement to identify moments of high emotional impact during a virtual reality horror game.|Comparing average GSR levels between two interface designs to assess which elicits more user engagement or anxiety during a task.

title: Galvanic Skin Response (GSR) in HCI

definition: Heart Rate Variability (HRV) is the physiological phenomenon of the variation in the time interval between consecutive heartbeats, reflecting the activity of the autonomic nervous system. In HCI, HRV is measured to infer a user's cognitive load, mental stress, emotional state, and attention levels during interaction with technology.
examples: Analyzing a decrease in HRV during a particularly challenging task in a control system, indicating increased mental workload.|Comparing HRV patterns before and after an interface redesign to assess its impact on user stress.|Using real-time HRV feedback in biofeedback training applications to help users manage stress during complex interactions.

title: Heart Rate Variability (HRV) in HCI

definition: The System Usability Scale (SUS) is a widely used, ten-item questionnaire providing a quick and reliable measure of perceived usability of a system. Users rate their agreement with statements on a 5-point Likert scale, and the scores are aggregated to produce a single score from 0 to 100, representing overall usability.
examples: After participants complete a usability test, they are asked to fill out the SUS questionnaire to quantify their perception of the system's ease of use.|Comparing the SUS scores of a new software version against a previous one to track improvements in perceived usability.|Using SUS as a benchmark to assess whether a product meets a target usability standard (e.g., a SUS score of 68 is considered average).

title: System Usability Scale (SUS)

definition: The Net Promoter Score (NPS) is a widely used metric that measures customer loyalty and satisfaction by asking a single question: 'How likely are you to recommend [product/service/company] to a friend or colleague?' Respondents are categorized as Promoters (9-10), Passives (7-8), or Detractors (0-6), and the score is calculated as % Promoters minus % Detractors.
examples: Including an NPS question at the end of a user onboarding flow to gauge initial satisfaction and likelihood to recommend.|Periodically surveying existing users with NPS to track overall customer loyalty and identify trends over time.|Using NPS to compare user sentiment between different product features or versions following release.
semantic_tags: Customer Loyalty|Satisfaction Metric|Survey|User Experience|Quantitative Data|Product Management
title: Net Promoter Score (NPS)

definition: The Customer Satisfaction Score (CSAT) is a direct measure of how satisfied a customer is with a product, service, or interaction. It is typically captured by asking a simple question like 'How satisfied are you with [product/service]?' with responses on a scale (e.g., 1-5 or satisfied/dissatisfied), and often reported as a percentage of satisfied customers.
examples: Asking users for a CSAT rating immediately after they complete a customer support interaction to assess service quality.|Placing a CSAT question at the end of a critical user flow, such as completing an online purchase, to measure satisfaction with that specific experience.|Using CSAT to compare user satisfaction with specific features within an application after an update.
title: Customer Satisfaction Score (CSAT)

definition: The Customer Effort Score (CES) measures how much effort a customer had to exert to complete a task or resolve an issue with a product or service. Typically, users are asked to rate their agreement with a statement like 'The company made it easy for me to handle my issue' on a Likert scale, aiming to identify friction points and improve user experience by reducing effort.
examples: After a user submits a bug report, asking them to rate the effort required for the submission process.|Using CES to evaluate the ease of completing a self-service task on a website, such as updating account information.|Comparing CES scores for different checkout flows to determine which one requires less effort for users to complete a purchase.
title: Customer Effort Score (CES)

definition: A user persona is a semi-fictional, archetypal representation of an ideal or target user, based on user research and data. It embodies a specific user group's demographics, behaviors, motivations, goals, and pain points, helping designers and developers empathize with users and make user-centered design decisions.
examples: Creating 'Sarah, the Busy Professional,' who needs quick, efficient mobile tools due to her demanding schedule and frequent travel.|Developing a persona for 'David, the Tech-Savvy Gamer,' highlighting his desire for high performance, customization, and community features.|Using a set of personas during a brainstorming session to ensure proposed features address the diverse needs of different user segments.

title: User Persona

definition: An empathy map is a collaborative visualization tool that helps teams understand user needs by externalizing knowledge about a user's 'Says, Thinks, Feels, and Does.' It focuses on creating a shared understanding of a user's worldview, fostering empathy, and revealing insights into their pain points and motivations.
examples: A design team fills out an empathy map for a persona, noting what the user 'says' about a product, what they 'think' privately, how they 'feel' emotionally, and what actions they 'do'.|During a workshop, different team members contribute to an empathy map based on interview transcripts and observations to synthesize qualitative data.|Using an empathy map to identify unmet needs or frustrations (pain points) that can be addressed by a new feature or design.
semantic_tags: User Research|Empathy|Design Thinking|Qualitative Data|User Understanding|Collaboration Tool
title: Empathy Map

definition: A journey map (or customer journey map) visually illustrates the step-by-step experience of a user as they interact with a product, service, or brand over time to achieve a goal. It details the user's actions, thoughts, feelings, pain points, and opportunities at each stage, providing a holistic view of the user experience from their perspective.
examples: Mapping a user's journey from discovering an online store, through browsing, adding to cart, checkout, and post-purchase support.|Creating a journey map to understand the experience of a patient interacting with a healthcare system, from initial symptom to recovery.|Using a journey map to identify critical touchpoints and pain points in a mobile app's onboarding process, revealing opportunities for improvement.
title: Journey Map

definition: A service blueprint is an operational tool that visualizes the entire service process, detailing the touchpoints, user actions, and the visible and invisible organizational processes, people, and systems involved. It maps out frontstage (customer-facing) and backstage (internal) activities, highlighting dependencies and potential failure points to improve service delivery.
examples: Blueprinting the process of ordering food delivery, showing customer actions (frontstage) and restaurant preparation, driver dispatch, and payment processing (backstage).|Creating a service blueprint for a library's book borrowing system, illustrating both the user's journey and the staff's internal workflows, technology, and support systems.|Using a service blueprint to identify bottlenecks and areas for improvement in a complex customer support system that spans multiple departments and digital tools.
semantic_tags: Service Design|System Design|User Experience|Process Mapping|Operational Design|Touchpoints
title: Service Blueprint

definition: A user flow diagram is a visual representation of the path a user takes to complete a specific task or achieve a goal within a product or system. It illustrates the sequence of steps, decisions, and interactions from the user's entry point to their final action, helping designers understand and optimize user navigation and experience.
examples: Diagramming the user flow for creating a new account, showing steps like 'Enter Email', 'Set Password', 'Verify Email', and 'Complete Profile'.|Creating a user flow to visualize the purchasing process on an e-commerce website, from product selection to payment confirmation.|Using a user flow to identify redundant steps or potential points of confusion in a mobile app's core functionality.
title: User Flow (Diagram)

definition: Qualitative data analysis in HCI involves interpreting non-numerical data, such as interview transcripts, field notes, or open-ended survey responses, to identify patterns, themes, and insights into user behaviors, motivations, and experiences. It focuses on understanding the 'why' and 'how' behind phenomena, often using methods like thematic analysis or content analysis.
examples: Reviewing interview recordings and transcribing them to identify common pain points expressed by users during a usability study.|Coding open-ended survey responses to categorize user feedback into distinct categories like 'feature request' or 'usability issue'.|Analyzing observational notes from a field study to uncover recurring behaviors or contextual factors influencing technology use.
title: Data Analysis (Qualitative)

definition: Thematic analysis is a qualitative research method used to identify, analyze, and report patterns (themes) within qualitative data, such as interview transcripts, focus group discussions, or open-ended survey responses. It involves systematically coding the data, grouping codes into broader themes, and interpreting their meaning in relation to the research question.
examples: Analyzing transcripts from user interviews to identify recurring themes related to user satisfaction, frustration, and feature desires.|Applying thematic analysis to field study notes to uncover patterns in how users interact with a new device in their natural environment.|Coding user diary study entries to reveal overarching themes about their daily technology usage habits and emotional responses.
title: Thematic Analysis

definition: Qualitative content analysis is a research method used to systematically interpret the meaning from text or other media data, such as user reviews, forum posts, or website content. It involves coding and categorizing explicit and implicit content to identify patterns, themes, and underlying meanings, often used to understand user opinions, perceptions, or communication styles.
examples: Analyzing thousands of user reviews for a mobile app to identify common complaints, praises, and feature requests.|Systematically reviewing forum discussions about a new product to understand public sentiment and recurring issues.|Coding the content of error messages in software to evaluate their clarity, helpfulness, and tone.
title: Content Analysis (Qualitative)

definition: An affinity diagram is a business tool used to organize and synthesize large amounts of qualitative data, particularly ideas and insights generated during brainstorming or user research. It involves writing individual pieces of data on separate cards and then grouping related ideas together based on their natural relationships or 'affinity,' to identify overarching themes and patterns.
examples: After a brainstorming session, team members write down all ideas on sticky notes and then collaboratively group similar ideas to form categories for new features.|Organizing raw user research findings from interviews and observations into logical groups to identify key user pain points and needs.|Using an affinity diagram to synthesize a wide range of user feedback into actionable design recommendations by clustering related comments.
semantic_tags: Qualitative Data|Brainstorming|User Research|Data Synthesis|Information Organization|Collaboration Tool
title: Affinity Diagram

definition: Card sorting is a user research technique where participants organize topics written on cards into groups that make sense to them, and then often label these groups. This method helps reveal users' mental models of information, guiding the design of intuitive information architectures, navigation structures, and menu systems.
examples: Asking users to sort cards labeled with website content pages (e.g., 'About Us', 'Contact', 'Product Catalog', 'Support') into logical categories for a new website navigation.|Using an open card sort to discover natural groupings for features within a complex software application.|Conducting a closed card sort where users categorize items into predefined categories to validate an existing information architecture.
semantic_tags: Information Architecture|User Research|Mental Models|Navigation Design|Usability Testing|Categorization
title: Card Sorting

definition: Tree testing (also known as reverse card sorting or 'card-based classification') is a usability technique for evaluating the findability of topics within an existing or proposed hierarchical information architecture, independent of navigational aids or visual design. Participants are given tasks and must navigate a text-only 'tree' structure to find the correct location, revealing how well users can find information.
examples: Participants are asked to 'find where to change your password' within a text-based tree representing a website's navigation, to test its clarity.|Comparing the success rates and directness scores of two different information architectures for a mobile app by having users complete tasks on each tree.|Using tree testing early in the design process to validate an information architecture before investing in visual design and development.
title: Tree Testing

definition: A UX research method that measures the efficiency of user navigation by tracking where users click first on a page or interface to complete a given task. It helps identify if users can quickly find what they are looking for and assess the clarity of information architecture.
examples: Asking users to find the 'Contact Us' page on a website and observing their initial click.|Presenting a product page and asking users to locate the 'Add to Cart' button.|Monitoring where participants click first when prompted to find their account settings.
title: First Click Testing

definition: A systematic UX research process of evaluating direct and indirect competitors' products or services to identify their strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats, informing design decisions and strategic positioning for a new or existing product.
examples: Comparing the onboarding flow of three rival social media applications.|Analyzing the feature set, usability, and pricing of leading project management software.|Assessing user reviews and satisfaction levels for competing e-commerce platforms.
title: Competitive Analysis (UX Research)

definition: The process of measuring a product's performance, user experience, or specific metrics against a set of predetermined standards, industry averages, competitors, or its own past performance over time. It helps track progress and identify areas for improvement.
examples: Tracking the average task completion time for a specific feature across monthly releases to ensure improvements.|Comparing a website's conversion rate to industry benchmarks for similar e-commerce sites.|Measuring user satisfaction (e.g., using NPS) against a key competitor's product.
title: Benchmarking (UX)

definition: A qualitative UX research method used to gauge users' emotional responses, perceptions, and aesthetic impressions of a product, interface, or specific design elements. Participants typically choose descriptive adjectives from a list to express their feelings.
examples: Asking users to select five adjectives from a list (e.g., 'modern', 'trustworthy', 'confusing') that describe a new app's visual design.|Presenting different logo options and asking which evokes qualities like 'friendly' or 'professional'.|Evaluating users' emotional reactions to a website's color scheme and typography using a preference matrix.
title: Desirability Testing

definition: A UX research method where participants are shown two or more design alternatives (e.g., layouts, images, copy) and asked to choose their preferred option, often with an explanation. It is typically used for evaluating visual elements or calls to action.
examples: Showing users two versions of a product page layout and asking which they prefer for ease of use.|Asking participants to select their favorite icon design from a set of options for a new feature.|Determining which call-to-action button color or text is more appealing and effective for the target audience.
semantic_tags: UX Research|A/B Testing|Design Evaluation|User Choice|Visual Design|Quantitative Research
title: Preference Testing

definition: A research method where participants are prompted at multiple, often random, times throughout their daily lives to report on their current experiences, thoughts, and feelings. This method captures user experiences in real-world contexts, providing rich, ecologically valid data.
examples: A smartphone app periodically sending notifications to users, asking them to rate their current mood and activity while using a specific product.|Participants receiving SMS prompts to describe their interaction and satisfaction level with a wearable device at different points during the day.|Researchers collecting data on users' frustration levels while interacting with a new software feature in their natural work environment via scheduled prompts.
semantic_tags: UX Research|In-situ Research|Contextual Inquiry|Longitudinal Study|Ecological Validity|Diary Study
title: Experience Sampling Method (ESM)

definition: A research design in UX where data is collected from the same participants over an extended period, allowing researchers to observe changes, trends, and long-term effects on user behavior, satisfaction, and product adoption. It provides insights into how user experience evolves over time.
examples: Tracking a group of users' adoption and continued use of a new operating system over a year.|Observing changes in user satisfaction and task efficiency with a software product across multiple major updates.|Monitoring the learning curve and sustained engagement with a complex professional application over several months.
semantic_tags: UX Research|Long-term Study|User Behavior|Trends|Time-series Data|Product Adoption
title: Longitudinal Study (UX Research)

definition: A qualitative research method used to collect specific, concrete observations of human behavior that have a significant impact (either positive or negative) on the outcome of an event or interaction. Researchers ask participants to recall and describe specific instances that were particularly successful, frustrating, or memorable.
examples: Interviewing users about a particularly frustrating moment they encountered when trying to accomplish a task with a website.|Asking customer support agents to recall specific instances where a software bug caused a major problem or a delightful resolution for a user.|Having users describe a 'critical incident' of a delightful interaction they had with a mobile app that exceeded their expectations.
semantic_tags: UX Research|Qualitative Research|User Feedback|Pain Points|Delight Moments|User Stories
title: Critical Incident Technique (CIT)

definition: A survey administered to participants immediately after they complete a usability test, interview, or other research session. It gathers their feedback, overall satisfaction levels, perceived ease of use, and general impressions of the product or experience.
examples: Administering the System Usability Scale (SUS) questionnaire after a usability test session.|A short survey asking participants about their perceived ease of use and satisfaction with a new feature they just tested.|Questions about whether a participant would recommend the product to a friend after trying it out.
title: Post-Study Questionnaire

definition: A survey administered to potential or recruited participants before a usability test, interview, or research session. Its primary purpose is to gather demographic information, relevant experience, or screen for specific criteria to ensure the participant pool is appropriate for the study.
examples: A questionnaire used to screen potential participants for specific experience with competitor products or certain technologies.|Collecting demographic data (age, occupation, tech-savviness) to ensure a diverse and representative participant group.|Asking about participants' familiarity with particular software or tasks to understand their baseline knowledge before a study.
title: Pre-Study Questionnaire

definition: A fundamental style or conceptual model that defines how users interact with a computer system, guiding the design of interfaces and shaping the overall user experience. It encompasses the metaphors, methods, and principles governing human-computer communication.
examples: The 'Direct Manipulation' paradigm, where users interact with visual representations of objects (e.g., dragging files).|The 'Conversational' paradigm, used in chatbots and voice assistants.|The 'Ubiquitous Computing' paradigm, integrating technology seamlessly into the environment (e.g., smart home devices).
semantic_tags: HCI Theory|Design Models|User Experience|Interaction Design|Interface Types|Conceptual Model
title: Interaction Paradigm

definition: An interaction paradigm where users directly interact with visual representations of objects and actions on a screen, rather than through abstract commands. It provides immediate visual feedback, a strong sense of control, and a feeling of 'direct engagement' with the system.
examples: Dragging and dropping a file from one folder to another on a desktop operating system.|Resizing a window by clicking and dragging its border with a mouse.|Using a slider control to adjust volume or brightness in a media player application.
title: Direct Manipulation

definition: A common Graphical User Interface (GUI) paradigm characterized by the use of distinct, resizable 'Windows' for applications, symbolic 'Icons' to represent files or functions, organized 'Menus' for commands, and a 'Pointer' controlled by a mouse or trackpad for navigation and selection. It is a cornerstone of modern desktop computing.
examples: The traditional desktop environment of operating systems like Microsoft Windows or macOS.|Most modern web browsers, featuring multiple tabs (windows), navigation icons, dropdown menus, and a mouse pointer.|Classic paint programs where tools are represented by icons, functions are accessed via menus, and canvases appear in windows.
normalized_name: wimp interface windows icons menus pointers
title: WIMP Interface (Windows, Icons, Menus, Pointers)

definition: A type of user interface that allows users to interact with electronic devices through graphical icons and visual indicators, such as buttons, menus, and windows, rather than relying on text-based commands. GUIs are designed to be intuitive and user-friendly.
examples: The operating system interface of a smartphone (e.g., iOS, Android) with its apps and widgets.|A web-based application like an online banking portal with its visual layout, forms, and clickable elements.|Desktop applications such as word processors or image editors, which present tools and documents visually.
title: Graphical User Interface (GUI)

definition: An interaction paradigm designed to make human-computer interaction intuitive and seamless by leveraging natural human behaviors and senses, such as touch, gesture, voice, and gaze. NUIs often aim to make the interface itself 'invisible' by mimicking real-world interactions.
examples: Using voice commands with a smart speaker like Amazon Alexa or Google Assistant.|Interacting with a smartphone or tablet using multi-touch gestures like pinch-to-zoom or swiping.|Controlling a video game with body movements detected by a sensor, such as the Xbox Kinect.
title: Natural User Interface (NUI)

definition: An interaction paradigm where users interact with digital information through physical objects, giving digital data a physical representation. TUIs blend the physical and digital worlds, allowing for manipulation of digital content by interacting with tangible artifacts.
examples: Interacting with a digital map by physically moving blocks or tokens on a smart table, where each block controls a different aspect of the map.|Using physical dials and sliders on a mixing console to control digital audio parameters in real-time.|Children's educational toys that use physical blocks or shapes to control on-screen characters or puzzles by placing them on a smart surface.
