semantic_tags: Interaction Paradigm|Physical Computing|Embodied Interaction|Real-world Objects|Augmented Reality|Digital-Physical
title: Tangible User Interface (TUI)

definition: An interaction paradigm where users primarily interact with a system using spoken language, enabling hands-free and often eyes-free operation. VUIs rely on speech recognition and natural language processing to understand and respond to user commands and queries.
examples: Asking a smart assistant like Siri or Google Assistant to set a timer or play a specific song.|Interacting with an automated phone banking system by speaking commands and account numbers.|Dictating text into a word processor or email client using speech recognition software.
title: Voice User Interface (VUI)

definition: An interaction paradigm where users control a system through physical movements of their body, hands, or fingers, often detected by sensors, cameras, or touchscreens. It allows for more natural and direct ways of interacting with digital content without traditional input devices.
examples: Swiping left or right on a smartphone screen to navigate through photos in a gallery.|Waving a hand in the air to change slides in a presentation using a motion sensor (e.g., Leap Motion).|Using specific hand shapes or body movements to cast spells in a virtual reality game environment.
semantic_tags: Interaction Paradigm|Natural User Interface|Motion Sensing|Touchless Interaction|VR/AR|Multi-Touch
title: Gesture-Based Interaction

definition: A specific type of gesture-based interaction where a touch-sensitive surface can detect and respond to multiple points of contact simultaneously. This allows for complex gestures involving more than one finger or hand, enabling intuitive manipulation of digital content.
examples: Pinching two fingers together or spreading them apart on a smartphone or tablet to zoom in or out on an image or map.|Rotating an object on a screen using two fingers, simulating physical rotation.|Scrolling through a document or webpage with a two-finger swipe on a laptop trackpad.
semantic_tags: Gesture-Based Interaction|Touchscreen|Natural User Interface|Direct Manipulation|Mobile UX|Tablets
title: Multi-Touch Interaction

definition: A technology that superimposes digital information and virtual objects onto a user's view of the real world, typically through a device like a smartphone, tablet, or smart glasses. AR enhances the user's perception of reality by layering computer-generated content over live footage or direct sight.
examples: Using a smartphone app to see how a piece of furniture would look in a user's living room before purchasing it.|Playing a game like Pokémon Go, where digital creatures appear to exist in real-world locations through a phone's camera.|Surgeons using AR glasses to overlay patient data, such as vital signs or 3D anatomical models, onto their view during an operation.
semantic_tags: HCI Technology|Mixed Reality|Virtual Reality|Immersive Experience|Digital Overlay|Spatial Computing
title: Augmented Reality (AR)

definition: An immersive, simulated environment that can be similar to or completely different from the real world, typically experienced through a head-mounted display. VR systems track user movements and provide real-time visual and auditory feedback, aiming to create a sense of presence within the virtual space.
examples: Playing Beat Saber on an Oculus Quest 2|Conducting a virtual architectural walkthrough of a building design|Training surgeons using a VR simulation for complex procedures
title: Virtual Reality (VR)

definition: A paradigm where digital information is integrated with and interacts with the physical world, allowing users to perceive and manipulate digital content within a three-dimensional space. It encompasses technologies like augmented reality, mixed reality, and virtual reality, focusing on understanding and utilizing spatial relationships for interaction.
examples: An AR app overlaying furniture models onto a real room through a phone camera|Workers using mixed reality headsets to view interactive digital instructions on physical machinery|Using hand gestures to manipulate 3D models floating in a physical space
semantic_tags: Augmented Reality|Mixed Reality|3D Interaction|Context-aware computing|Environment understanding|Ubiquitous computing
title: Spatial Computing

definition: The use of touch to communicate information to users, typically through vibrations, force, or tactile sensations. It enhances user experience by providing physical confirmation or cues during interaction with digital interfaces or virtual environments.
examples: A phone vibrating to signal an incoming call or message|A game controller rumbling when a character takes damage or an explosion occurs|A force feedback steering wheel resisting turns in a racing simulator
semantic_tags: Tactile feedback|Touch interaction|User experience|Sensory feedback|Vibration|Force feedback
title: Haptic Feedback

definition: The use of non-speech audio to convey information, indicate status, or provide cues to a user in an interactive system. Sonification specifically refers to the mapping of data to sound to communicate trends or patterns.
examples: A 'click' sound playing when a virtual button is pressed|A rising pitch sound indicating an increase in a stock market graph's value|An alarm sound alerting a user to a system error
semantic_tags: Sound design|Non-speech audio|User interface|Sensory feedback|Acoustic cues|Audio display
title: Auditory Feedback (Sonification)

definition: Information communicated to a user through visual means on a display or interface, indicating the status of a system, the result of an action, or providing guidance. It is crucial for user understanding and interaction within a graphical user interface.
examples: A progress bar showing the completion status of a file download|A button changing color when a mouse cursor hovers over it|An error message appearing on screen after an invalid input
semantic_tags: Graphical user interface|User interface|Display|Visual cues|Information display|Status indicators
title: Visual Feedback

definition: A hardware peripheral that allows a user to send data, commands, or signals to a computer or information processing system. It translates user actions into a format that the system can understand and process.
examples: Keyboard for typing text|Mouse for navigating and clicking on a screen|Microphone for capturing voice commands
title: Input Device

definition: A flat, rectangular surface on a laptop or standalone accessory that detects the position and movement of a user's finger, translating it into cursor movement and input commands on a screen. It typically supports multi-touch gestures for various interactions.
examples: The integrated trackpad on a laptop for cursor control|An external USB touchpad used with a desktop computer|A specialized touchpad on a smart keyboard for gesture navigation
semantic_tags: Pointing device|Laptop component|Gesture control|Capacitive sensing|Multi-touch|Cursor control
title: Touchpad

definition: An input and output device that allows users to interact directly with what is displayed by touching the screen with a finger or stylus. It combines the functionality of a display screen with a pointing device, enabling direct manipulation of on-screen elements.
examples: A smartphone display used for navigating apps and typing|An interactive kiosk screen for ordering food or checking in|A tablet device screen for drawing or taking notes
title: Touchscreen

definition: A pointing device consisting of a ball held within a socket, containing sensors that detect the ball's rotation about two axes. The user rolls the ball with a finger or palm to move the cursor on a screen, while the device itself remains stationary.
examples: A desktop trackball mouse used for precise graphic design work|Integrated trackballs on older CAD workstations|Classic arcade games featuring a large trackball for control
semantic_tags: Pointing device|Ergonomics|Roller ball|Stationary input|Cursor control|Precision input
title: Trackball

definition: An input device consisting of a stick that pivots on a base and reports its angle or direction to the computer. It is primarily used for controlling objects or characters in video games, flight simulators, or for precise control in professional applications.
examples: A flight stick controller for airplane simulation games|An arcade game joystick for character movement|Industrial joysticks used to operate heavy machinery
semantic_tags: Gaming input|Directional control|Analog input|Game controller|Ergonomics|Control stick
title: Joystick

definition: An input device used to interact with a video game, typically containing an array of buttons, joysticks, and directional pads. It provides a specialized interface designed for gaming actions, often incorporating haptic feedback.
examples: An Xbox Wireless Controller for playing console games|A PlayStation DualSense controller featuring adaptive triggers and haptic feedback|Nintendo Switch Joy-Cons used for motion-controlled gaming
title: Game Controller

definition: An input device that converts sound waves into electrical signals, allowing a computer to capture audio for recording, communication, or voice command processing. It serves as a primary interface for voice-based interaction.
examples: A headset microphone for online calls and gaming|The built-in microphone on a smartphone for voice notes or virtual assistants|A studio microphone for professional audio recording
semantic_tags: Audio input|Voice recognition|Speech processing|Sound capture|Transducer|Voice interface
title: Microphone (Input Device)

definition: An input device that captures still images or video footage, converting optical images into digital data for a computer to process. It is used for visual communication, object recognition, environmental sensing, and augmented reality applications.
examples: A webcam used for video conferencing|A smartphone camera for taking photos and scanning QR codes|A security camera providing visual input for surveillance systems
semantic_tags: Video input|Image capture|Computer vision|Visual sensing|Optical input|Perception
title: Camera (Input Device)

definition: A specialized input device that measures the distance to objects in its field of view, generating a 3D depth map of the environment. It is crucial for applications requiring spatial understanding, such as gesture recognition, augmented reality, and robotics.
examples: The Microsoft Kinect sensor used for full-body motion tracking in games|The TrueDepth camera system in iPhones for Face ID and AR applications|LiDAR sensors in autonomous vehicles for mapping their surroundings
semantic_tags: 3D sensing|Spatial mapping|Computer vision|Gesture recognition|Augmented reality|Environmental understanding
title: Depth Sensor

definition: An input device that measures eye movements and gaze direction, allowing a computer system to determine where a user is looking on a screen or in a physical environment. It enables gaze-based interaction, user experience analysis, and accessibility features.
examples: A research-grade eye tracker used to study user attention on websites|Integrated eye tracking in VR headsets for foveated rendering and interaction|Assistive technology that allows users to control a cursor or type using only their gaze
semantic_tags: Gaze input|Eye movement|User interface|Accessibility|Attention tracking|Biometric input
title: Eye Tracker (Input Device)

definition: A small, body-worn input device that collects physiological or environmental data from the user or their surroundings. These sensors enable continuous monitoring and provide input for health tracking, activity recognition, and context-aware systems.
examples: A fitness tracker collecting heart rate, step count, and sleep data|A smartwatch with a gyroscope and accelerometer for activity recognition and gesture input|Smart clothing with embedded sensors for monitoring posture or muscle activity
title: Wearable Sensor

definition: A system that directly translates brain activity into commands for an external device, without relying on peripheral nerves and muscles. BCIs enable communication and control for individuals with severe motor disabilities and are also explored for augmenting human capabilities.
examples: A user with paralysis controlling a robotic arm through thought alone|Typing on a virtual keyboard by focusing on specific letters, detected by EEG signals|Neurofeedback systems where users learn to modulate their brainwaves for relaxation or focus
title: Brain-Computer Interface (BCI)

definition: A hardware peripheral that presents processed information or data from a computer to a user in a human-readable form. It translates digital signals into perceivable forms like visual, auditory, or tactile output.
examples: A monitor displaying images and text|A printer producing hard copies of documents|Speakers playing audio
title: Output Device

definition: An output device that visually presents information, images, and video generated by a computer to the user. It is the primary visual interface for most interactive systems, crucial for displaying graphical user interfaces and content.
examples: An LCD monitor connected to a desktop computer|The OLED screen of a smartphone|A projection screen displaying content from a projector
title: Display Screen

definition: An output device that converts electrical audio signals into sound waves, allowing a computer to produce audible output such as speech, music, or system sounds. Speakers are essential for auditory feedback and multimedia consumption.
examples: Desktop computer speakers for playing music|Headphones used for private audio listening|The built-in speaker on a smartphone for calls and media playback
title: Speaker (Output Device)

definition: A small electric motor designed to provide tactile feedback (haptics) by vibrating, often found in mobile devices, game controllers, and wearables to alert users or enhance immersion. These motors translate electrical signals into physical vibrations that users can feel.
examples: A smartphone vibrating for an incoming call or notification.|A game controller vibrating to simulate an in-game explosion or impact.|A smartwatch providing a silent alarm or directional cues through haptic pulses.
title: Vibration Motor (Haptic Output)

definition: A component that translates an electrical signal into a physical motion or force, specifically referring to devices like vibration motors, solenoids, or piezoelectric transducers that produce tactile sensations for haptic feedback in HCI. These enable an interface to physically 'touch' the user.
examples: A linear resonant actuator (LRA) in a phone creating a sharp click sensation for virtual buttons.|An eccentric rotating mass (ERM) motor generating sustained vibrations in a joystick.|A voice coil motor in advanced haptic devices providing precise texture or force feedback.
title: Actuator (Haptic Output)

definition: A peripheral device that produces a hard copy of electronic data, typically text or images, onto physical media such as paper, transparencies, or other materials. It serves as a primary means of translating digital information into a tangible physical form.
examples: An inkjet printer producing color photographs or documents.|A laser printer printing high-volume black-and-white text pages for office use.|A 3D printer creating a physical prototype from a digital model.
title: Printer (Output Device)

definition: A conceptual model that maps familiar real-world objects, actions, or situations onto the virtual world of a user interface. This approach makes complex digital tasks more intuitive and easier to learn by leveraging users' existing knowledge and mental models.
examples: The 'desktop metaphor' for operating systems, treating digital files as papers.|The 'shopping cart' metaphor used in e-commerce websites for collecting items for purchase.|The 'folder' icon used for organizing digital files, resembling a physical file folder.
title: Interaction Metaphor

definition: A specific interaction metaphor that represents a computer's interface as a virtual desk, where files are like papers, folders are like file cabinets, and applications are like tools. This model allows users to intuitively manage digital information by interacting with graphical representations that mimic their physical counterparts.
examples: The graphical user interface (GUI) of Windows, macOS, or Linux, featuring icons, windows, and a pointer.|Dragging and dropping files between folder icons on a computer screen.|Minimizing windows to a taskbar or dock as if clearing items from a physical desk.
title: Desktop Metaphor

definition: A design principle where UI elements are intentionally made to resemble their real-world counterparts in appearance and texture, often including shadows, reflections, and material details. This approach provides familiarity and aims to ease the transition for users learning new digital interfaces.
examples: A calculator app with buttons that look like physical calculator buttons, complete with bevels and shadows.|An early iOS notes app featuring a lined paper background and a torn-edge effect.|The original iBooks app interface designed to look like a wooden bookshelf.
title: Skeuomorphism

definition: A minimalist UI design style characterized by the absence of three-dimensional effects like shadows, gradients, and textures, favoring clean lines, sharp edges, solid colors, and simple iconography. Its primary goal is to create a sleek, uncluttered, and highly readable user interface.
examples: The 'Metro' interface introduced in Windows 8/10.|Many modern website designs that emphasize simplicity and directness.|Early iterations of Google's Material Design before the introduction of more pronounced shadows and depth.
title: Flat Design

definition: A comprehensive design language developed by Google that combines principles of good design with innovation and technology, using a metaphor of 'digital paper' and 'ink' with depth, shadows, and motion. It aims to create realistic, responsive, and intuitive user experiences across platforms.
examples: The user interface of Google's Android operating system and its core applications like Gmail or Google Maps.|Web applications built with Angular Material, adhering to Google's design guidelines.|Many third-party mobile applications that adopt Material Design components and aesthetics.
title: Material Design

definition: A design language developed by Microsoft emphasizing five key components: Light, Depth, Motion, Material, and Scale, aimed at creating intuitive, accessible, and beautiful experiences. It provides guidelines and components for designing user interfaces that adapt across a wide range of devices and input methods.
examples: The user interface of Microsoft Windows 10/11, including elements like Mica and Acrylic materials.|Microsoft Office applications (e.g., Word, Excel) that incorporate Fluent Design principles.|The Xbox dashboard and other Microsoft applications that deliver cohesive experiences across devices.
title: Fluent Design System

definition: A reusable solution to a common usability problem in user interface design, representing a proven way of structuring interactive elements to achieve specific user goals efficiently and predictably. These patterns provide consistent and familiar interaction experiences.
examples: The 'Master-detail view' pattern for displaying a list of items and their corresponding details (e.g., email inbox).|The 'pagination' pattern for handling large sets of data by breaking them into navigable pages.|The 'wizard' pattern for guiding users step-by-step through multi-stage processes like setup or configuration.
title: Interaction Pattern

definition: The process by which users move through an interface, discover content, and understand their current location within a system. Effective navigation design is crucial for usability, allowing users to efficiently find information and accomplish tasks.
examples: Using a main menu bar or hamburger menu on a website to browse different sections.|Tapping a tab bar at the bottom of a mobile app to switch between primary views (e.g., Home, Search, Profile).|Following 'back' and 'forward' arrows in a web browser to revisit pages or move ahead.
title: Navigation (Interaction)

definition: An interaction allowing users to actively look for specific information or content within a system by inputting keywords, queries, or criteria, typically yielding a list of relevant results. It is a fundamental method for users to find what they need when direct navigation is insufficient.
examples: Typing a query into a search bar on an e-commerce website to find specific products.|Using a search icon in a mobile app to locate a particular contact or setting.|Filtering results in a large database or library catalog by author or title keywords.
title: Search (Interaction)

definition: The process of structuring and styling input fields, labels, buttons, and other controls to collect information from users efficiently, accurately, and with minimal cognitive load. Good form design ensures clarity, ease of use, and reduces user errors.
examples: A registration form for a new online account, requesting username, email, and password.|An online checkout form requiring shipping address, payment details, and order confirmation.|A survey form collecting user feedback on a product or service.
semantic_tags: UI Design|Data Entry|Usability|User Experience|Input Fields|Information Collection
title: Form Design

definition: The process of inputting information into a computer system, typically via a user interface, requiring users to type, select, or otherwise provide data. It is a critical interaction step in most applications, impacting efficiency and accuracy of data within a system.
examples: Typing an email address and password into a login field.|Selecting options from a dropdown menu or radio buttons on a web form.|Scanning a barcode into an inventory management system using a physical scanner.
title: Data Entry (HCI)

definition: Design strategies implemented to anticipate and mitigate potential user errors before they occur, by guiding users, providing constraints, or clearly communicating expected inputs. The goal is to design systems that make it difficult or impossible for users to make mistakes.
examples: Disabling a 'Submit' button until all required fields in a form are filled correctly.|Providing real-time input validation, such as immediately showing a warning if a password doesn't meet complexity requirements.|Offering default values for common selections or auto-filling known information to reduce typing errors.
title: Error Prevention (HCI)

definition: Mechanisms and designs that help users understand and fix mistakes they have made, allowing them to easily return to a valid state and complete their task without frustration. Effective error recovery transforms errors from roadblocks into learning opportunities.
examples: Clear, specific error messages explaining what went wrong and how to fix it, rather than generic codes.|Providing an 'Undo' option after an unintended action, such as accidentally deleting text.|Allowing users to edit invalid input directly in a form field instead of forcing them to restart.
title: Error Recovery (HCI)

definition: A common interaction pattern that allows users to reverse (undo) or reapply (redo) one or more previous actions, providing a safety net for mistakes and encouraging exploration without fear of permanent errors. This feature significantly enhances user control and forgiveness in an interface.
examples: Pressing Ctrl+Z (or Cmd+Z) in a text editor to revert the last typing action.|Using the 'Undo' button in a graphic design software to remove a recent change, like applying a filter.|Reapplying a previously undone action with Ctrl+Y (or Cmd+Y) to restore it.
title: Undo/Redo Functionality

definition: A modal window or message that appears to ask the user to verify their intention before executing a potentially destructive, irreversible, or significant action. It acts as a final safeguard to prevent unintended consequences from user input.
examples: A dialog asking 'Are you sure you want to delete this file?' before moving it to the trash.|A prompt 'Save changes before closing?' when exiting an application with unsaved work.|A warning message before sending a large email campaign or publishing content to a live site.
title: Confirmation Dialog

definition: A visual cue that informs users about the ongoing status of a system operation, especially for tasks that take more than a few moments, reassuring them that the system is working and often estimating completion time. It manages user expectations and reduces perceived waiting time.
examples: A spinning loader icon (spinner) indicating that data is being fetched or processed.|A progress bar showing the percentage complete during a large file download or software installation.|A 'please wait' message or animated dots while an application is starting up or performing a complex calculation.
title: Progress Indicator

definition: A direct manipulation interaction technique where users select an object by 'dragging' it (moving it while holding down a mouse button or finger) and then 'dropping' it (releasing the button/finger) at a new location or onto another object to perform an action. This provides a natural and intuitive way to interact with graphical interfaces.
examples: Moving a file from one folder to another on a desktop by dragging its icon.|Reordering items in a list or within a kanban board by dragging them to a new position.|Attaching a file to an email by dragging it from a file explorer window into the email composition window.
semantic_tags: Direct Manipulation|User Input|Interaction Technique|UI Element|Efficiency|Spatial Interaction
title: Drag and Drop

definition: A menu that appears upon user interaction, typically a right-click or long-press, on a specific UI element, offering actions relevant to that element's current state or context. It provides quick access to frequently used or contextual commands without navigating through main menus.
examples: Right-clicking a file on a desktop to show 'Open,' 'Cut,' 'Copy,' 'Delete' options.|Long-pressing an app icon on a smartphone to reveal quick actions like 'Uninstall' or specific app functionalities.|Right-clicking on text in a word processor to access 'Copy,' 'Paste,' 'Spell Check' options.
title: Context Menu

definition: The visual appearance of a UI element when a user's mouse cursor is positioned over it but not clicked. This state provides immediate feedback to the user, indicating that the element is interactive and can be engaged.
examples: A button changing its background color when the mouse pointer is moved over it.|A hyperlink underlining or changing color when hovered upon.|An icon subtly growing in size or showing a tooltip when the cursor rests on it.
semantic_tags: User Feedback|Mouse Interaction|Visual Cue|UI State|Interaction Design|HCI
title: Hover State

definition: The visual appearance of a UI element when it is selected and ready to receive user input, typically via keyboard or assistive technologies. This state is crucial for accessibility, allowing users to understand which element is currently active.
examples: A text input field displaying a blinking cursor and a colored border when clicked or tabbed into.|A button showing an outline or a different background when selected via keyboard navigation.|A dropdown menu highlighting its currently selected option when it has focus.
title: Focus State

definition: A combination of keystrokes that, when pressed simultaneously, trigger a specific command or action within an application, offering a faster alternative to using a mouse or navigating menus. They enhance efficiency and productivity for experienced users.
examples: Ctrl+C (or Cmd+C on macOS) to copy selected content.|Ctrl+S (or Cmd+S on macOS) to save the current document.|Alt+Tab (or Cmd+Tab on macOS) to switch between open applications.
title: Keyboard Shortcut

definition: An interactive control element that, when activated by a user (e.g., clicked or tapped), triggers an immediate action or event within the application. Buttons are fundamental for initiating processes, confirming choices, or navigating.
examples: A 'Submit' button on a web form to send data.|An 'OK' or 'Cancel' button in a dialog box.|A 'Play' button in a media player to start content playback.
title: Button (UI Component)

definition: An interactive input area that allows users to type and edit single or multiple lines of alphanumeric characters. It is commonly used for collecting user information, search queries, or content creation.
examples: A 'Username' or 'Email' input field on a login form.|A 'Search' box on a website.|A 'Comment' box allowing multiple lines of text entry.
semantic_tags: Input Control|Text Entry|Form Element|User Interface|Data Collection|HCI
title: Text Field (UI Component)

definition: A compact list of options that becomes visible only when activated by the user, typically by clicking a button or an input field. It allows users to select a single item from a predefined set without occupying much screen space initially.
examples: A 'Country' selector in a registration form.|A font selection menu in a word processor.|A 'Sort By' option on an e-commerce website.
title: Dropdown Menu (UI Component)

definition: A graphical control element that allows a user to select only one option from a mutually exclusive set of choices. When one radio button in a group is selected, any previously selected button in that same group automatically becomes deselected.
examples: Selecting 'Male', 'Female', or 'Other' for gender in a profile.|Choosing a shipping method like 'Standard', 'Express', or 'Overnight'.|Answering a multiple-choice question where only one answer is correct.
semantic_tags: Single Selection|Mutually Exclusive|Form Element|Option Group|User Interface|HCI
title: Radio Button (UI Component)

definition: A graphical control element that allows a user to make a binary choice, typically 'yes' or 'no', 'on' or 'off'. Unlike radio buttons, users can select multiple checkboxes independently within a group, or none at all.
examples: Agreeing to 'Terms and Conditions' by checking a box.|Selecting multiple preferences like 'Receive email notifications' or 'Remember me'.|Filtering items by category where multiple categories can be chosen.
semantic_tags: Binary Choice|Multiple Selection|Form Element|Boolean State|User Interface|HCI
title: Checkbox (UI Component)

definition: A UI control that allows users to switch between two distinct states, typically 'on' and 'off', with immediate effect. It visually represents the current state and allows for quick state changes, often with an animated transition.
examples: Turning 'Wi-Fi' on or off in a phone's settings.|Enabling or disabling 'Dark Mode' in an application.|A switch for 'Push Notifications' preferences.
title: Toggle Switch (UI Component)

definition: A graphical control element that allows a user to select a value or a range of values by moving a 'thumb' or 'handle' along a track. It is ideal for continuous or approximate adjustments rather than precise numerical input.
examples: Adjusting the 'Volume' level of audio.|Selecting a 'Brightness' level for a screen.|Filtering products by a 'Price Range' on an e-commerce site.
title: Slider (UI Component)

definition: A UI control that enables users to incrementally increase or decrease a numerical value using two dedicated buttons, typically '+' and '-'. It is well-suited for adjusting quantities where exact integer values are needed.
examples: Adjusting the 'Quantity' of an item in a shopping cart.|Setting the 'Number of Guests' for a reservation.|Modifying the 'Font Size' in a text editor.
title: Stepper (UI Component)

definition: A graphical indicator that visually represents the progress of an operation, task, or download that takes a discernible amount of time. It provides users with feedback about the ongoing process and an estimate of completion.
examples: Showing the percentage completion of a file download.|Indicating the installation progress of software.|A bar filling up during a video buffering process.
title: Progress Bar (UI Component)

definition: A visual animation or icon indicating that content is being retrieved, processed, or an action is underway and the system is busy. Loaders reassure users that the application has not frozen and is actively working.
examples: A spinning circle animation while a page is loading.|A pulsating icon indicating data submission.|A skeleton screen showing placeholder content while actual content is fetched.
title: Loader (UI Component)

definition: An interactive graphical control that allows users to select a specific date, often by interacting with a calendar view. It simplifies date input and reduces errors compared to manual text entry.
examples: Selecting a 'Date of Birth' in a registration form.|Choosing a 'Check-in' and 'Check-out' date for hotel booking.|Picking a 'Due Date' for a task in a project management tool.
title: Date Picker (UI Component)

definition: An interactive graphical control that enables users to select a specific time, often through dropdowns for hours and minutes, or a clock-like interface. It standardizes time input and minimizes formatting issues.
examples: Setting an 'Appointment Time' for a meeting.|Specifying an 'Alarm Time' on a mobile device.|Choosing 'Departure Time' for a flight booking.
title: Time Picker (UI Component)

definition: A UI component that displays a list of header titles, where clicking a title expands its associated content panel while collapsing any other open panels. It is used to present multiple sections of content in a compact way, allowing users to focus on one section at a time.
examples: An 'FAQ' section where questions expand to reveal answers.|A product details page with 'Specifications,' 'Reviews,' and 'Related Items' sections.|A form with multiple collapsible steps, each revealing further input fields.
title: Accordion (UI Component)

definition: A UI component that displays a set of content, such as images or cards, one at a time within a limited space, allowing users to cycle through them horizontally or vertically. It is often used for showcasing featured content or galleries.
examples: A homepage banner displaying rotating promotional images or headlines.|A product page showcasing multiple images of an item.|A series of testimonials or featured articles sliding into view.
title: Carousel (UI Component)

definition: A UI component that organizes content into distinct, overlapping sections, accessible by clicking on corresponding 'tabs'. Only one tab's content is visible at a time, providing a clear way to switch between related information or functionalities without navigating away from the current page.
examples: A profile page with 'Overview', 'Settings', and 'Activity' tabs.|A product details page with 'Description', 'Reviews', and 'Q&A' tabs.|An application's preferences window with 'General', 'Privacy', and 'Notifications' tabs.
title: Tabbed Navigation (UI Component)

definition: A secondary navigation aid that shows the user's current location within a hierarchical structure, typically in a website or application. It displays a trail of links, allowing users to easily navigate back to previous parent pages.
examples: Homepage > Products > Electronics > Laptops.|Departments > Clothing > Men's > Shirts.|A file explorer showing the path: C:\Users\Documents\Projects\Report.docx.
title: Breadcrumbs (UI Component)

definition: A UI component that divides content into discrete pages, allowing users to navigate through large datasets or lists sequentially without loading everything at once. It typically includes page numbers, 'next' and 'previous' buttons, and sometimes 'first' and 'last' links.
examples: Google search results showing '1 2 3 ... Next' at the bottom.|An e-commerce product listing page displaying items across multiple pages.|Blog archives where posts are split into chronological pages.
semantic_tags: Navigation|Content Management|Large Datasets|User Interface|Scrolling Alternative|Data Display
title: Pagination (UI Component)

definition: An input field UI component designed to allow users to type in keywords or phrases to find specific content within a website, application, or dataset. It often includes an accompanying search icon or button to initiate the search.
examples: The search box at the top of an Amazon e-commerce website.|The Google search input field on its homepage.|A search bar within a document editor to find specific text.
title: Search Bar (UI Component)

definition: A UI component used to inform users about events, updates, or messages that require their attention, often appearing as a small banner, alert, or icon indicator. Notifications can be persistent or temporary and are crucial for providing timely feedback without interrupting the user's primary task.
examples: A push notification from a mobile app informing about a new message.|A system tray icon on a desktop OS showing unread emails.|A bell icon in a social media app indicating new activity.
title: Notification (UI Component)

definition: A small, non-interactive, and non-intrusive UI component that provides brief, transient feedback or messages to the user, typically appearing temporarily at the bottom or top of the screen and fading away automatically after a few seconds. It informs without requiring explicit dismissal.
examples: 'Item added to cart' message appearing briefly after clicking an add button.|'Changes saved successfully' message after saving a document.|'No internet connection' message briefly displayed in a mobile app.
title: Toast Message (UI Component)

definition: A UI component that appears as an overlay on top of the main content, demanding user interaction before they can return to the underlying application. It is used to capture user focus for critical information, confirmations, or input, effectively blocking interaction with the rest of the page.
examples: A 'Save Changes?' prompt when closing an unsaved document.|A login form appearing over a darkened page background.|A confirmation dialog asking 'Are you sure you want to delete this item?'.
title: Modal Dialog (UI Component)

definition: A small, ephemeral UI component that displays supplementary information or a brief description of an element when a user hovers over it with a mouse cursor or focuses on it using keyboard navigation. Tooltips are designed to provide context or clarify function without permanently occupying screen space.
examples: Hovering over an icon button in an editor to see its function, e.g., 'Save'.|A small box appearing with the full text of a truncated label.|Explaining a cryptic field label with additional details.
title: Tooltip (UI Component)

definition: A UI component that displays additional content, controls, or contextual information in a floating panel that appears adjacent to a triggering element, typically dismissed by clicking outside of it or pressing the escape key. Unlike tooltips, popovers can contain rich, interactive content and are more persistent.
examples: Clicking a user's avatar to reveal a mini-profile card with options.|A date picker widget appearing next to an input field.|A share button that opens a small panel with social media sharing options.
semantic_tags: Contextual Content|Interaction Panel|Floating UI|User Input|Information Display|Rich Content
title: Popover (UI Component)

definition: A persistent UI component typically located on the left or right side of a screen, containing a list of links or menu items that allow users to navigate between different sections or features of an application or website. It provides always-visible access to primary navigation paths.
examples: The navigation menu in Google Drive showing 'My Drive', 'Shared with me', 'Recent'.|The main navigation in a content management system dashboard.|The left-hand menu in desktop applications like Slack or VS Code.
title: Sidebar Navigation

definition: A common UI component, represented by three horizontal lines stacked vertically, that functions as a toggle for expanding and collapsing a navigation menu, especially prevalent in mobile and responsive web designs to save screen space. When clicked, it reveals a full navigation list, often in a sidebar or full-screen overlay.
examples: The menu icon on most mobile websites to reveal navigation links.|Apps like Facebook or Twitter using it to show main navigation.|Responsive designs on smaller screens often collapse main navigation into a hamburger.
title: Hamburger Menu

definition: A prominent, circular UI button that typically 'floats' above the rest of the UI, usually anchored to the bottom-right of the screen, representing the primary or most common action users can take on a given screen. It provides quick access to a key function and often has a distinct visual style.
examples: The '+' button in Gmail to compose a new email.|The 'record' button in a voice recorder app.|The 'Add New' button in many mobile task management apps.
title: Floating Action Button (FAB)

definition: A self-contained UI component, typically rectangular with rounded corners, that serves as a flexible container for related information and actions, often representing a single topic or entity. Cards are highly versatile for displaying diverse content in a digestible and organized manner, especially in grid layouts.
examples: Product listings on an e-commerce site, each in its own card.|News articles or blog post previews displayed as individual cards.|Contact cards in a directory showing a person's photo, name, and role.
title: Card (UI Component)

definition: A small graphical representation, often a user's profile picture or an initialed placeholder, used to visually identify a user within an application or system. Avatars contribute to personalization, recognition, and social presence in collaborative or community-focused interfaces.
examples: A user's profile picture displayed next to their comments on a forum.|The circular image representing a contact in a messaging app.|Default letter-based avatars when a user hasn't uploaded a photo.
title: Avatar (UI Component)

definition: A small, often circular or oval-shaped UI component typically used to display a small amount of dynamic information, such as counts, status indicators, or labels, associated with another UI element. Badges draw attention to important updates or quantities without cluttering the main interface.
examples: The red circle with a number indicating unread messages on an app icon or a notification bell.|A 'New' label on a product card to highlight recently added items.|A count of items in a shopping cart icon.
semantic_tags: Status Indicator|Counter|Notification|Attention Grabber|Contextual Information|UI Element Annotation
title: Badge (UI Component)

definition: A UI component that allows users to provide qualitative feedback or express their subjective opinion on an item, service, or content, typically using a visual scale like stars or thumbs up/down. It helps aggregate user sentiment and inform other users' decisions.
examples: A 5-star rating system for products on an e-commerce website.|Thumbs up/down buttons for videos on YouTube.|A numerical rating out of 10 for movies on a review site.
title: Rating System (UI Component)

definition: A UI component enabling users to assign keywords or descriptive labels (tags) to content, facilitating categorization, search, and organization of information. Tags improve content discoverability and allow for flexible, user-generated classification beyond hierarchical structures.
examples: Adding tags like 'web development', 'JavaScript', 'frontend' to a blog post.|Categorizing photos with tags like 'vacation', 'beach', 'family'.|Email clients allowing users to apply custom labels to messages.
title: Tagging System (UI Component)

definition: A UI component that provides an area for users to post textual feedback, discussions, or reactions related to specific content, such as articles, products, or videos. It fosters community engagement, allows for user-generated content, and often includes features like replies, moderation, and upvoting.
examples: The section below a blog post where readers can leave comments.|User reviews and discussions for a product on an online store.|The comments thread on a YouTube video.
title: Comment Section (UI Component)

definition: A prominent UI element, typically a button or a clear link, designed to prompt an immediate response or encourage users to take a specific, desired action. CTAs are crucial for guiding users through a conversion funnel or towards primary goals within an interface.
examples: A 'Sign Up Now' button on a landing page.|A 'Add to Cart' button on a product detail page.|A 'Download Free Ebook' link.
title: Call to Action (CTA)

definition: The UI design of a screen or component when it contains no content, data, or items, providing helpful information, instructions, or a clear call to action to guide the user on how to populate it. Well-designed empty states prevent confusion and encourage user engagement from the start.
examples: A 'No tasks yet! Click here to add your first task' message in a new to-do list app.|A blank inbox with a 'Your inbox is empty. Start a new conversation!' prompt.|A search results page showing 'No results found. Try a different query.'
title: Empty State (UI)

definition: The UI design displayed to users while content, data, or a process is being actively retrieved or computed in the background, signaling that the system is working and preventing user frustration. Common forms include spinners, progress bars, or skeleton screens.
examples: A spinning wheel or 'Loading...' text appearing while a page fetches data.|A progress bar indicating the upload status of a file.|Skeleton screens showing greyed-out shapes where content will eventually appear.
title: Loading State (UI)

definition: The UI design presented to users when an unexpected problem or failure occurs, providing clear and actionable feedback about what went wrong and how to potentially resolve it. Effective error states include concise explanations, specific error codes, and suggested next steps.
examples: A '404 Page Not Found' message with a link back to the homepage.|An invalid form field highlighted in red with a message like 'Please enter a valid email address.'|A network error message 'Could not connect to the server. Please check your internet connection.'
semantic_tags: Error Handling|User Feedback|Problem Resolution|UX Design|System Status|Troubleshooting
title: Error State (UI)

definition: A user interface screen displayed after a user successfully completes a significant action, such as submitting a form or making a purchase. It provides feedback that the action was successful, often summarizes its details, and may offer next steps.
examples: A 'Thank You for Your Order' page after an online purchase with order number and delivery estimate.|A 'Your message has been sent!' page after submitting a contact form.|A registration success page summarizing new account details.
title: Confirmation Page (UI)

definition: The guided sequence of steps and interactions designed to introduce new users to a product or service. Its goal is to help users understand key features, complete initial setup, and achieve their first successful experience, fostering product adoption.
examples: A 'Welcome to our app!' wizard guiding users through initial account setup and permissions.|A series of sequential tooltips highlighting core functionalities upon first login.|An interactive tutorial explaining how to create your first project in a new software.
title: Onboarding Flow (UX)

definition: A step-by-step guided tour within a product that demonstrates how to use its features or accomplish a specific task. Walkthroughs are often interactive, requiring user participation to advance, and focus on practical application.
examples: An interactive tutorial showing users how to create their first document in a word processing application.|A guided process within a mobile app for setting up privacy settings step-by-step.|A simulated task completion guide for using a new analytics dashboard feature.
title: Walkthrough (Product)

definition: A guided overview, typically visual and sequential, that highlights and briefly explains key features or areas of a product or a specific feature set. Unlike a walkthrough, it is often less interactive and serves more as an informational presentation.
examples: A series of overlaid pop-ups pointing out and labeling new features in an updated application version.|A slideshow demonstrating the capabilities of a new camera mode within a smartphone app.|A short introductory video showcasing a product's main benefits and interface elements.
title: Tour (Product Feature)

definition: A display setting that inverts the default color scheme, typically using a dark background with light text and UI elements. It is designed to reduce eye strain in low-light environments, conserve battery life on OLED screens, and offer a different aesthetic preference.
examples: An operating system's global setting to switch its interface to a dark theme.|A website offering a toggle to switch its content background to black with white text.|A mobile application with an optional dark interface chosen by the user.
title: Dark Mode (UI)

definition: The conventional or default display setting characterized by a light background with dark text and UI elements. It provides strong contrast and readability in well-lit environments and is the most common visual presentation for digital interfaces.
examples: The standard appearance of most websites and applications when no theme is specified.|A document editor with a white page background and black text.|An operating system's default visual theme before any customization.
title: Light Mode (UI)

definition: A web design approach that enables a website or application to automatically adapt its layout and content to fit various screen sizes and orientations, from desktops to mobile devices. It utilizes fluid grids, flexible images, and CSS media queries to create a single, adaptable codebase.
examples: A news website that reflows its articles from multiple columns to a single column on a smartphone.|An e-commerce site where product grids adjust from four columns on a desktop to two or one column on tablets and phones.|An image gallery that automatically scales and rearranges images based on the browser window size.
title: Responsive Design

definition: A design approach where multiple distinct layouts are created for different screen sizes or device types, and the appropriate layout is served based on the detected environment. It typically involves fixed breakpoints where the layout changes entirely rather than fluidly adjusting.
examples: A website that loads a completely different, simplified layout and navigation for mobile browsers compared to desktop.|An application with specific, custom-built UIs for phone, tablet, and desktop versions.|A 'm.example.com' sub-domain serving a separate mobile-optimized site.
title: Adaptive Design

definition: A design philosophy that prioritizes designing for mobile devices first, then progressively enhancing the experience for larger screens. This approach ensures that core functionality and content are optimized for the most constrained environment, simplifying the design process and often improving performance.
examples: Designing a web application's layout and core features specifically for a small smartphone screen before considering tablet or desktop layouts.|Developing an app focusing on touch interactions and minimal navigation before adding desktop mouse/keyboard support.|Starting wireframing with the smallest screen size and gradually adding complexity for larger viewports.
title: Mobile-First Design

definition: A quality attribute that assesses how easy user interfaces are to use, encompassing factors such as learnability, efficiency, memorability, error prevention, and user satisfaction. High usability means users can interact with a system effectively, efficiently, and with satisfaction.
examples: A well-designed ATM that clearly guides users through transaction steps, minimizing errors.|A software application with intuitive icons, consistent navigation, and clear feedback.|An online form where fields are logically ordered and error messages are helpful.
semantic_tags: UX|user interface|ease of use|quality attribute|HCI|human factors
title: Usability (Definition)

definition: A usability attribute that describes how easy it is for new or infrequent users to accomplish basic tasks the first time they encounter a design. It is often measured by the time taken to learn the system or the error rate for novice users.
examples: A new email client where users can immediately send and receive messages without needing to consult a manual.|A self-checkout machine that requires no prior training for basic operations.|An onboarding process that quickly teaches a user how to perform a key action within an application.
semantic_tags: Usability|new user|first impression|ease of learning|cognitive load|user training
title: Learnability

definition: A usability attribute describing how quickly expert users can accomplish tasks once they have learned the system. It is typically measured by the time it takes to complete tasks after initial learning, focusing on speed and productivity for proficient users.
examples: A keyboard shortcut system that allows power users to navigate and edit documents quickly without relying on a mouse.|A data entry interface optimized for rapid input by experienced operators.|A graphic design software that enables designers to perform complex operations with minimal clicks.
title: Efficiency (Usability)

definition: A usability attribute that describes how easy it is for users to re-establish proficiency with a system after a period of not using it. It focuses on how quickly users can recall how to perform tasks and remember the system's structure.
examples: An infrequently used application whose navigation and functions remain intuitive and easily recalled even after months.|An online banking interface whose layout and labels are easily remembered, even for users who only log in once a month.|A photo editor where saved settings or frequently used tools are easily found upon returning to the app.
title: Memorability (Usability)

definition: A usability metric that quantifies the number and severity of mistakes users make while interacting with a system, as well as their ability to recover from these errors. It includes both slips (unintentional actions) and mistakes (incorrect mental models).
examples: Tracking the number of failed login attempts or incorrect password entries.|Counting instances where users select the wrong menu item or click on a non-interactive element.|Measuring how often users need to use an 'undo' function or correct input errors.
semantic_tags: Usability metric|user error|error rate|task success|problem identification|data collection
title: Errors (Usability Metric)

definition: A usability metric that measures users' subjective feelings and attitudes towards a system, including their perceived pleasantness, comfort, and general liking of the interface. It often captures emotional and affective aspects of the user experience.
examples: Collecting user ratings on a Likert scale after a task completion (e.g., 'How satisfied are you with this process?').|Conducting surveys asking about enjoyment, frustration, or ease of use (e.g., System Usability Scale - SUS).|Analyzing unsolicited positive or negative user comments and feedback.
title: Satisfaction (Usability Metric)

definition: A dimension of usability that refers to whether a system provides the functionality and features users need to accomplish their goals. It answers the fundamental question: 'Does this system do what I need it to do to be useful?'
examples: A project management tool that includes essential features like task assignment, deadline tracking, and file sharing for a team.|A photo editor that provides the necessary cropping, color correction, and filter tools required by amateur photographers.|An online shopping website that allows users to search, filter, and purchase products effectively.
title: Utility (Usability)

definition: A usability attribute that refers to the accuracy and completeness with which users achieve specific goals using a system. It is often measured by the rate of successful task completion and the quality of the outcomes produced.
examples: The percentage of users successfully completing an online purchase from start to finish.|The accuracy of data entered into a form, measuring how many fields contain correct information.|Whether a user can correctly configure a new device according to instructions provided by the interface.
semantic_tags: Usability|task completion|goal achievement|accuracy|quality of outcome|success rate
title: Effectiveness (Usability)

definition: The overall experience a user has when interacting with a product, service, or system, encompassing their emotions, attitudes, perceptions, and responses before, during, and after use. UX extends beyond usability to include aspects like aesthetics, branding, value, and emotional connection.
examples: The holistic feeling of delight and ease when using a beautifully designed and intuitive mobile app.|The frustration of navigating a confusing website compounded by slow loading times and irrelevant content.|The sense of accomplishment and satisfaction after successfully using a complex professional tool that streamlines a workflow.
title: User Experience (UX) (Definition)

definition: A specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound (SMART) objective related to improving or maintaining the ease of use and effectiveness of a system for its target users. These goals guide design and evaluation efforts.
examples: "Reduce the time it takes for new users to complete their first successful file upload by 20% within 3 months."|"Achieve a user satisfaction score of at least 4.5 out of 5 on the System Usability Scale (SUS) questionnaire for experienced users."|"Decrease the error rate for critical data entry tasks by 15% in the next release."
title: Usability Goal

definition: A quantitative or qualitative measure used to evaluate a system's usability, typically focusing on aspects like learnability, efficiency, errors, memorability, and user satisfaction. Metrics provide empirical data to assess and compare user performance and experience.
examples: Task completion rate (e.g., 90% of users successfully submitted the form).|Time on task (e.g., average 30 seconds to find product information).|Error rate (e.g., 2 errors per task), System Usability Scale (SUS) score, or subjective satisfaction ratings.
title: Usability Metric

definition: The proportion of users who successfully complete a defined task without significant errors or external assistance, serving as a primary measure of a system's effectiveness.
examples: 90% of users successfully registered for an account during user testing.|Only 75% of users managed to find the correct help article within the given time, indicating a lower success rate for that specific task.
title: Success Rate (Usability Metric)

definition: The amount of time a user takes to complete a specific task, typically measured from the start of the task until its successful completion, reflecting the efficiency of a system.
examples: The average time to complete a purchase on the e-commerce site was 2 minutes and 15 seconds.|Median time for new users to locate and change their profile picture was 45 seconds.
title: Time on Task (Usability Metric)

definition: The frequency or proportion of errors made by users while attempting to complete a task, often categorized by type (e.g., critical, non-critical), indicating how error-prone a system is.
examples: During the checkout process, users averaged 0.5 critical errors per task.|15% of users clicked the wrong navigation button before finding the correct one, contributing to the overall error rate.
title: Error Rate (Usability Metric)

definition: A user's personal assessment of their experience with a system or product, typically gathered through questionnaires, surveys, or rating scales after task completion or overall usage.
examples: Users rated the system 4.5 out of 5 for ease of use on a post-task questionnaire.|A System Usability Scale (SUS) score of 80 indicated a high level of user satisfaction with the application.
title: Subjective Satisfaction Score

definition: A quantitative measure reflecting how disoriented or lost a user feels while navigating through a system, particularly in information architectures, often calculated based on the number of unique pages visited versus total pages visited to complete a task.
examples: A user navigating an e-commerce site visited 15 pages but only 5 were relevant to finding their product, indicating high lostness for that task.|A lostness score of 0.6 suggests users are moderately disoriented when searching for specific content on the website.
title: Lostness (Usability Metric)

definition: A user's subjective impression or belief about how easy and pleasant a system is to use, often formed before or during interaction, which significantly influences their overall satisfaction and adoption.
examples: Users commented that the new app 'looks intuitive' and 'easy to figure out' even before using it, reflecting high perceived usability.|A visually appealing and uncluttered interface often leads to higher perceived usability, even if actual performance metrics are not superior.
title: Perceived Usability

definition: Usability characteristics of a system measured objectively through empirical data, such as task success rate, time on task, and error rate, gathered during user testing with real users performing specific tasks.
examples: During formal user testing, users completed 90% of tasks, taking an average of 60 seconds each, demonstrating high observed usability for effectiveness and efficiency.|A discrepancy between high perceived usability and low observed usability (e.g., many errors during tasks) indicates a problem with the actual user experience.
semantic_tags: Empirical data|Objective measurement|User testing|Performance metrics|Actual use|Behavioral data
title: Observed Usability

definition: A usability inspection method where HCI experts evaluate a user interface against established usability principles, heuristics, or guidelines to identify potential usability problems without direct user involvement.
examples: A heuristic evaluation conducted by two UX experts found 15 critical usability issues in a new software prototype.|An expert review identified that the 'back' button in an application violated Nielsen's heuristic of 'user control and freedom' because it didn't behave predictably.
semantic_tags: Usability inspection|Heuristic evaluation|Expert analysis|Design review|Cost-effective|Evaluation method
title: Expert Review (Usability)

definition: A usability inspection technique where evaluators simulate the steps a user would take to accomplish a specific task, often focusing on the user's cognitive processes and potential difficulties at each step, such as a cognitive walkthrough.
examples: In a cognitive walkthrough for an online banking feature, evaluators stepped through 'transfer money,' asking 'will the user know what to do at this step?' and 'will the user understand the system's feedback?'.|A design team conducted a task-based walkthrough to identify where a user might get stuck or confused in a complex software installation process.
semantic_tags: Usability inspection|Cognitive walkthrough|Task simulation|Expert review|User task flow|Mental model
title: Walkthrough Method

definition: A computational model used to estimate human performance with a user interface, typically based on theoretical principles and empirical data, without requiring actual user testing, enabling early design evaluation.
examples: Using a predictive model like KLM to estimate the time an expert user will take to complete a specific data entry task based on the number of keystrokes and mouse movements.|A designer uses a predictive model to compare the efficiency of two different menu designs, selecting the one that theoretically requires less time for frequent tasks.
semantic_tags: Human performance|Theoretical model|Efficiency prediction|Design evaluation|Analytical method|Cognitive modeling
title: Predictive Model (HCI)

definition: A family of predictive human performance models used to estimate the time an expert user will take to complete a task by breaking it down into specific Goals (what the user wants to achieve), elementary Operators (actions), Methods (sequences of operators), and Selection Rules for choosing between methods.
examples: Analyzing the task 'save a document' with GOMS involves defining the Goal (save document), Methods (e.g., Ctrl+S, File->Save), Operators (keystrokes, mouse clicks, mental preps), and Selection Rules (e.g., if shortcut known, use Ctrl+S; else, use menu).|A GOMS model can predict that using a keyboard shortcut will be faster than navigating through a menu for a frequent task.
normalized_name: goms model goals operators methods selection rules
semantic_tags: Predictive model|Human performance|Task analysis|Expert users|Cognitive modeling|Efficiency
title: GOMS Model (Goals, Operators, Methods, Selection Rules)

definition: A simplified GOMS model that predicts task completion time for expert users by summing the execution times of atomic operations like keystrokes, mouse clicks, pointing, and mental preparation, often used for fine-grained interface analysis.
examples: Calculating the time to open a file using KLM involves summing the time for a mouse click, two short keystrokes (for filename), and a mental preparation operator.|Comparing two interface designs for a data entry screen using KLM showed that Design A was 1.5 seconds faster due to fewer mouse movements and keystrokes.
title: KLM (Keystroke-Level Model)

definition: A method used to describe the actions users perform to achieve a goal by breaking down tasks into sub-tasks and operations, organized hierarchically, and often accompanied by plans that specify the order or conditions for executing sub-tasks.
examples: Analyzing the task 'make coffee' using HTA involves breaking it down into sub-tasks like 'grind beans,' 'boil water,' 'add coffee,' with plans specifying their sequence and conditions (e.g., 'only grind beans if they are whole').|An HTA for using an ATM would detail tasks like 'insert card', 'enter PIN', 'select transaction', each with sub-tasks and conditions.
semantic_tags: Task analysis|Task decomposition|User goals|System design|Requirements engineering|Cognitive psychology
title: Hierarchical Task Analysis (HTA)

definition: A variation of the cognitive walkthrough where a diverse team consisting of usability experts, developers, and actual users collaboratively steps through a series of tasks, identifying usability issues from multiple perspectives.
examples: A team comprising a UX designer, a software engineer, and two potential end-users together walked through the process of setting up a new smart home device, identifying issues from both technical and user viewpoints.|During a pluralistic walkthrough, a developer explained system logic, while a user highlighted where the interface diverged from their expectations.
semantic_tags: Usability inspection|Cognitive walkthrough|Multidisciplinary team|Collaborative evaluation|User involvement|Expert review
title: Pluralistic Walkthrough

definition: An assessment of the impact or criticality of a usability problem, typically categorized by factors such as frequency, impact on task completion, and persistence, to prioritize design fixes.
examples: A 'critical' severity rating was assigned to an issue that completely prevented users from completing a primary task, requiring immediate attention.|A 'minor' severity was given to a confusing label that caused slight hesitation but did not stop task progression, indicating a lower priority fix.
semantic_tags: Usability evaluation|Issue prioritization|Impact assessment|Heuristic evaluation|Bug severity|Problem classification
title: Severity Rating (Usability Issue)

definition: A framework of 14 generic usability heuristics or 'dimensions' for analyzing the design of information artifacts (notations) like programming languages, visual representations, or user interfaces, focusing on how well they support cognitive tasks.
examples: Analyzing a programming language's syntax for 'visibility' (how easily components can be seen) or 'diffuseness' (how many symbols are needed to express a simple idea).|Evaluating a visual dashboard for its 'closeness of mapping' to the underlying data or its 'hard mental operations' required to interpret complex graphs.
semantic_tags: Notation design|Cognitive psychology|Usability heuristics|Information representation|Mental effort|System analysis
title: Cognitive Dimensions of Notations

definition: The design of products and environments to be usable by all people, to the greatest extent possible, without the need for adaptation or specialized design, aiming to maximize inclusivity from the outset.
examples: A building entrance with both stairs and a ramp, allowing access for individuals with mobility impairments, parents with strollers, and delivery personnel.|Web interfaces designed to be operable via keyboard navigation alone, benefiting both sighted and visually impaired users without requiring a separate 'accessibility mode'.
title: Universal Design

definition: A design methodology that considers the full range of human diversity with respect to ability, language, culture, gender, and other forms of human difference, aiming to create products usable by as many people as possible, often by designing for specific excluded groups.
examples: Designing a mobile app that offers adjustable text sizes and high-contrast modes for users with visual impairments, or translating content into multiple languages.|Developing a gaming controller that can be customized for users with different physical abilities, ensuring a wider audience can participate.
title: Inclusive Design

definition: A set of internationally recognized guidelines for making web content more accessible to people with disabilities, published by the Web Accessibility Initiative (WAI) of the W3C, structured around four core principles.
examples: Ensuring all images on a webpage have descriptive `alt` text for screen readers, fulfilling WCAG Success Criterion 1.1.1 (Non-text Content).|Providing full keyboard navigation for all interactive elements of a website, complying with WCAG Success Criterion 2.1.1 (Keyboard).
title: WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines)

definition: The four fundamental principles of web accessibility defined by WCAG: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, and Robust, which serve as the foundation for all specific accessibility guidelines and criteria.
examples: **P**erceivable: Providing text alternatives for non-text content (e.g., image alt text) so it can be 'perceived' by assistive technologies.|**O**perable: Making all functionality available from a keyboard, ensuring it is 'operable' without a mouse.|**U**nderstandable: Ensuring predictable navigation and consistent identification, making the content 'understandable' to users.|**R**obust: Maximizing compatibility with current and future user agents, including assistive technologies, so the content remains 'robust'.
title: POUR Principles (WCAG)

definition: Information and user interface components must be presentable to users in ways they can perceive. This means content cannot be invisible to all their senses, addressing visual, auditory, and cognitive aspects.
examples: Providing alternative text for images so screen readers can describe them.|Offering captions for videos to convey spoken content and important sounds.|Ensuring sufficient color contrast between text and background for readability.
title: Perceivable (WCAG Principle)

definition: User interface components and navigation must be operable, meaning users must be able to interact with the interface regardless of the tools or methods they use. This includes keyboard access, adequate time limits, and avoidance of seizure-inducing content.
examples: All website functionality is accessible and usable via keyboard alone.|Users are given sufficient time to complete tasks without premature timeouts.|Avoiding flashing content that could trigger seizures in susceptible individuals.
title: Operable (WCAG Principle)

definition: Information and the operation of the user interface must be understandable. This principle ensures that users can comprehend both the content itself and how to effectively use the interface to achieve their goals.
examples: Using clear, simple language and consistent navigation patterns.|Providing clear instructions and error messages for form inputs.|Predictable behavior of interactive components across a website or application.
title: Understandable (WCAG Principle)

definition: Content must be robust enough that it can be interpreted reliably by a wide variety of user agents, including assistive technologies, and across different platforms and versions. This ensures compatibility and future-proof accessibility.
examples: Using valid HTML and ARIA attributes to properly convey element semantics.|Ensuring custom UI components are built to be compatible with different assistive technologies.|Testing web applications across various browsers and device types.
title: Robust (WCAG Principle)

definition: ARIA is a set of attributes that define ways to make web content and web applications more accessible to people with disabilities, especially for dynamic content and advanced user interface controls developed with JavaScript. It helps convey semantics to assistive technologies that are not otherwise available in standard HTML.
examples: Adding `role="button"` and `aria-label="Add to cart"` to a custom button element.|Using `aria-expanded="true"` on a menu toggle button to indicate its state.|Implementing `aria-labelledby` to associate a complex form field with its label and description.
title: ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications)

definition: Screen reader is a software application that interprets and reads aloud the text and image content displayed on a screen, allowing users who are blind or have low vision to interact with digital interfaces. It converts visual information into an auditory format.
examples: JAWS (Job Access With Speech) for Windows.|NVDA (NonVisual Desktop Access) for Windows.|VoiceOver integrated into macOS and iOS devices.
title: Screen Reader

definition: Alternative text, or alt text, is a brief, descriptive text associated with non-text content, such as images, to provide a textual alternative for users who cannot see the image. It is crucial for screen readers, search engine optimization, and when images fail to load.
examples: ``|For a purely decorative image, `alt=""` (an empty alt attribute).|A complex chart described in the surrounding text, with `alt="Chart of quarterly sales growth"` indicating its purpose.
title: Alternative Text (Alt Text)

definition: Captions are textual representations of the audio content in video, including spoken dialogue and descriptions of non-speech sounds (like music or sound effects), synchronized with the video. They are primarily for users who are deaf or hard of hearing, or for noisy environments.
examples: Closed captions (CC) that can be turned on or off by the viewer, typically seen on TV or streaming services.|Transcribing dialogue like 'Hello, everyone!' and sound effects like '[Dramatic music]' in a video.|Live captions provided during a virtual meeting or broadcast.
title: Captions (Accessibility)

definition: A transcript is a full textual record of spoken content, often from audio or video, that may also include descriptions of important visual information or non-speech sounds. Unlike captions, transcripts do not need to be synchronized with the media, providing a complete, navigable text version.
examples: A downloadable text document of an entire podcast episode.|A webpage containing all dialogue and visual descriptions from a webinar, suitable for screen readers.|Written minutes of a meeting that includes all spoken contributions and key actions.
title: Transcripts (Accessibility)

definition: Sign language interpretation is the process of translating spoken language into a visual sign language (e.g., American Sign Language, British Sign Language) or vice-versa, facilitating communication between hearing and deaf or hard of hearing individuals. It provides crucial access to auditory information in real-time.
examples: A sign language interpreter appearing in a picture-in-picture window during a live news broadcast.|An interpreter present at a conference to convey presentations to deaf attendees.|Using a video remote interpreting (VRI) service for a medical appointment.
title: Sign Language Interpretation

definition: Keyboard navigation is the ability to interact with and operate all functionality of a digital interface using only a keyboard, without requiring a mouse or other pointing device. This is essential for users with motor impairments, certain cognitive disabilities, or who use screen readers.
examples: Using the Tab key to move sequentially through interactive elements like links, buttons, and form fields.|Activating a button or link by pressing Enter or Spacebar.|Navigating through menu items using arrow keys and selecting with Enter.
title: Keyboard Navigation (Accessibility)

definition: Focus management involves the programmatic control and clear visual indication of which interactive element on a user interface currently receives keyboard input. Effective focus management ensures that keyboard-only users can easily understand their position and interact with content logically.
examples: A distinct visual outline appearing around a button when it receives keyboard focus.|Ensuring that when a modal dialog opens, keyboard focus is moved inside the dialog and trapped there.|Programmatically returning keyboard focus to the element that triggered a modal after it closes.
title: Focus Management (Accessibility)

definition: Color contrast refers to the difference in luminance or perceived brightness between foreground (text, icons, UI components) and background colors, which significantly impacts readability for users with low vision or color blindness. WCAG provides specific guidelines for minimum contrast ratios.
examples: Black text on a pure white background provides very high contrast.|Light gray text on a white background typically has insufficient contrast.|Using a color contrast checker tool to verify that a design meets WCAG 2.1 AA or AAA standards.
title: Color Contrast (Accessibility)

definition: Large print is the presentation of text content with increased font size and often adjusted line spacing to improve readability for individuals with low vision. It is a common accessibility accommodation in both digital and physical formats.
