examples: A script on `https://example.com` cannot directly make an AJAX request to `https://api.thirdparty.com` unless `api.thirdparty.com` explicitly allows it via CORS headers.|A document loaded from `http://mybank.com` cannot read the content of an `<iframe>` embedding `http://malicious.com`.|A JavaScript script hosted on `www.mysite.com` cannot interact with cookies set by `subdomain.mysite.com` due to differing origins.
title: Same-Origin Policy (SOP)

definition: SCSS (Sassy CSS) is the main syntax of Sass, a powerful CSS preprocessor that extends standard CSS with features like variables, nesting, mixins, and functions. It compiles down to standard CSS, making stylesheets more maintainable, organized, and reusable.
examples: Using `$primary-color: #336699;` to define a color variable for consistent theming across a website.|Nesting CSS rules like `nav { ul { li { a { color: $primary-color; } } } }` to reflect HTML structure and avoid repetitive selectors.|Creating a `@mixin button-styles($bg-color)` to encapsulate reusable button styling logic and include it in multiple selectors.
title: SCSS (Sass) Preprocessor

definition: Introduced in iOS 13, the Scene Delegate manages the lifecycle of a single instance (or 'scene') of your app's UI, including states like active, inactive, and background. This allows apps to support multiple windows or instances on iPadOS and macOS Catalyst, each with its own UI and lifecycle.
examples: Implementing `scene(_:willConnectTo:options:)` to set up the initial view controller and window for a new scene instance.|Handling `sceneDidBecomeActive(_:)` to prepare the UI for user interaction when a scene enters the foreground.|Using `sceneDidEnterBackground(_:)` to save data or release resources when a scene moves to the background.
title: Scene Delegate (iOS)

definition: A system's ability to handle an increasing amount of work or demand by adding resources (horizontal scaling) or upgrading existing resources (vertical scaling) without compromising performance, functionality, or user experience. It's a key consideration in designing robust and high-traffic applications.
examples: Adding more web servers to a load-balanced cluster to handle increased user traffic for a popular e-commerce site (horizontal scaling).|Upgrading a database server with more RAM and faster CPUs to improve query performance under heavier loads (vertical scaling).|Designing a microservices architecture that allows individual services to be scaled independently based on their specific demands.
title: Scalability (System Design)

definition: HTTP response headers sent by a web server to a client browser to enhance security by protecting against common web vulnerabilities. These headers instruct the browser on how to behave when rendering content or handling data from the server, mitigating risks like XSS, clickjacking, and insecure data transmission.
examples: `Content-Security-Policy` (CSP) to restrict sources of content (scripts, styles, images) a browser is allowed to load.|`Strict-Transport-Security` (HSTS) to enforce HTTPS-only connections, preventing downgrade attacks.|`X-Frame-Options` to prevent clickjacking by disallowing pages from being embedded in iframes on other domains.|`X-Content-Type-Options` to prevent MIME-sniffing, ensuring the browser treats content as declared by the `Content-Type` header.
title: Security Headers (HTTP)

definition: A suite of tools for automating web browsers, primarily used for functional and regression testing of web applications by simulating user interactions directly in a browser. It supports various programming languages and browsers, enabling comprehensive end-to-end test automation.
examples: Writing a Python script using Selenium WebDriver to open a browser, navigate to a website, fill out a login form, click a button, and verify a successful login message.|Automating the process of adding items to a shopping cart, proceeding to checkout, and validating the order confirmation.|Performing cross-browser compatibility testing by running the same test suite on Chrome, Firefox, and Edge.
title: Selenium UI Testing

definition: A set of APIs in mobile operating systems (like Android or iOS) that allows applications to access and utilize data from various hardware sensors embedded in the device. These sensors include accelerometers, gyroscopes, magnetometers, ambient light sensors, and GPS receivers, providing rich context about the device's environment and motion.
examples: An Android app using the `SensorManager` to get accelerometer data for step counting or detecting device orientation changes.|An iOS app accessing `CLLocationManager` for GPS coordinates to display a user's current location on a map or provide turn-by-turn navigation.|A game using gyroscope data to control in-game movement by tilting the device.
title: Sensors API (Mobile)

definition: The process of setting up a server with the necessary hardware, software, networking, and configurations to make it ready for its intended purpose. This often involves installing an operating system, configuring network settings, deploying required software, and setting up security parameters, frequently automated using tools like Ansible or Chef.
examples: Using Ansible to automate the installation of an Nginx web server, Node.js runtime, and a PostgreSQL database on a new Ubuntu virtual machine.|Manually installing an operating system, configuring network settings, and deploying an application on a physical server in a data center.|Scripting the creation of cloud instances (e.g., AWS EC2) and applying a predefined configuration template to ensure consistency.
title: Server Provisioning

definition: A web rendering technique where the server processes and generates the initial HTML for a web page, sending a fully formed page to the browser. This allows content to be displayed faster, improves SEO, and provides a better initial user experience before client-side JavaScript takes over for interactivity (hydration).
examples: A Next.js application fetching data on the server for each request and sending a pre-rendered HTML page to the client, improving initial load times for dynamic content.|Traditional PHP or ASP.NET applications dynamically generating entire HTML pages on the server based on user requests.|A blog website using SSR to ensure search engine crawlers can easily index all content without needing to execute JavaScript.
title: Server-Side Rendering (SSR)

definition: A W3C standard for one-way, client-initiated, persistent connections over HTTP, allowing a server to push data updates to a browser client automatically whenever new data is available. Unlike WebSockets, SSE is optimized for server-to-client data streaming, providing a simpler alternative for unidirectional data flow.
examples: A stock ticker application displaying real-time price updates pushed from a server to client browsers.|A notification system pushing new notifications to users as they arrive, without the client continuously polling.|A dashboard displaying live analytics data, where the server streams updates as they occur.
title: Server-Sent Events (SSE)

definition: A cloud computing execution model where the cloud provider dynamically manages the server infrastructure, allowing developers to deploy and run code (functions) in response to events without provisioning or managing servers. AWS Lambda is a prominent 'Function-as-a-Service' (FaaS) offering that epitomizes this model.
examples: An AWS Lambda function triggered by an S3 event to resize uploaded images whenever a new image file is added to a bucket.|An Azure Function invoked by an HTTP request to process API calls for a mobile application backend.|A Google Cloud Function executing code when a new message arrives in a Pub/Sub topic to process data streams.
title: Serverless Functions (AWS Lambda)

definition: A type of web worker that runs in the background of a web page, separate from the main browser thread. Service Workers act as a programmable network proxy between the browser and the network, enabling features like offline experiences, push notifications, and advanced asset caching for Progressive Web Apps (PWAs).
examples: A Progressive Web App (PWA) using a Service Worker to cache all website assets, allowing users to browse content even when offline.|Receiving push notifications from a web application even when the browser tab is closed.|Intercepting network requests to serve cached responses for improved performance and reliability.
title: Service Workers

definition: An Android application component that can perform long-running operations in the background without a user interface. Services are typically used for tasks that don't require direct user interaction, such as playing music, downloading files, or fetching data from a network, even when the app is not actively in the foreground.
examples: A music player app using a foreground service to continue playing audio when the user navigates away from the app or locks the screen.|A background service periodically syncing data with a remote server, independent of the UI's lifecycle.|A file download manager using a service to handle large file downloads, providing progress notifications even if the app is closed.
title: Services (Android)

definition: The process by which a server maintains stateful information about a user's interaction over multiple stateless HTTP requests, essentially creating a 'session' for a continuous user experience. This typically involves issuing a unique session ID (often stored in a cookie) to identify subsequent requests from the same user.
examples: After a user logs in, the server creates a session, stores their user ID and permissions, and sends a session cookie to the browser.|For subsequent requests, the server uses the session cookie to retrieve the user's session data from its storage and verify their authentication and authorization status.|Managing a user's shopping cart contents across multiple page views on an e-commerce site without requiring them to log in for each page.
title: Session Management (Backend)

definition: A web standard that allows developers to encapsulate a subtree of DOM elements and styles within a component, isolating them from the main document's DOM and CSS. This encapsulation prevents style conflicts and enables the creation of robust, reusable web components.
examples: A custom `<my-button>` web component defining its internal structure and styling within a Shadow DOM, ensuring its styles don't leak out and global styles don't inadvertently affect it.|Browser-native elements like `<video>` or `<input type="range">` internally use Shadow DOM to encapsulate their complex structure and default styling.|Creating a widget that can be embedded on any website without worrying about its CSS conflicting with the host page's styles.
title: Shadow DOM

definition: Sockets are endpoints for communication between two programs on a network, allowing data to be sent and received over a network connection. They are fundamental to network programming, enabling applications to interact across different machines.
examples: A web browser uses sockets to establish a connection with a web server to retrieve web pages.|Real-time chat applications employ sockets for continuous, two-way communication between users.|Game servers use sockets to send game state updates and receive player input from clients.
title: Sockets (Networking)

definition: An SPA is a web application that loads a single HTML page and dynamically updates content as the user interacts with it, rather than reloading entire new pages from the server. This approach provides a smoother, app-like user experience by fetching data and updating only necessary parts of the DOM.
examples: Gmail loads once and updates email content and navigation without full page refreshes.|Social media feeds like Facebook or Twitter update content as you scroll without new page loads.|Applications built with frameworks like React, Angular, or Vue.js are commonly SPAs.
title: SPA (Single Page Application)

definition: HTTP methods (or verbs) define the type of action a client wants to perform on a resource identified by a URL. Common methods include GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, and OPTIONS, each indicating a distinct semantic intent for interacting with web resources.
examples: `GET /products/123`: Retrieve information about the product with ID 123.|`POST /users`: Create a new user by sending data in the request body.|`DELETE /orders/456`: Remove the order with ID 456 from the server.
title: Specific HTTP Methods

definition: The SQL DELETE statement is used to remove one or more existing rows from a table in a relational database. It often includes a `WHERE` clause to specify which rows should be deleted; without this clause, all rows in the table will be removed.
examples: `DELETE FROM Customers WHERE CustomerID = 5;` (Removes a specific customer record)|`DELETE FROM Orders WHERE OrderDate < '2023-01-01';` (Removes all orders placed before a certain date)|`DELETE FROM TempLogs;` (Removes all records from the TempLogs table)
title: SQL DELETE Statement

definition: The SQL INSERT statement is used to add new rows of data into a table in a relational database. It specifies the table name, the columns to insert into (optional), and the corresponding values for those columns.
examples: `INSERT INTO Products (ProductName, Price) VALUES ('Widget A', 29.99);` (Adds a new product with specified name and price)|`INSERT INTO Users VALUES (1, 'john_doe', 'john@example.com', 'password123');` (Adds a new user, assuming values match column order)|`INSERT INTO ArchivedOrders SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE OrderStatus = 'Completed';` (Copies completed orders into an archive table)
title: SQL INSERT Statement

definition: The SQL SELECT statement is the most common and fundamental SQL command, used to retrieve data from one or more tables in a relational database. It allows specifying columns, filtering rows with `WHERE` clauses, grouping data, and ordering results, providing powerful data querying capabilities.
examples: `SELECT ProductName, Price FROM Products WHERE Category = 'Electronics';` (Retrieves specific columns for products in a category)|`SELECT * FROM Users ORDER BY LastName DESC;` (Retrieves all columns for users, sorted by last name descending)|`SELECT COUNT(OrderID) FROM Orders WHERE OrderDate >= '2024-01-01';` (Counts orders placed since the start of 2024)
title: SQL SELECT Statement

definition: The SQL UPDATE statement is used to modify existing data in one or more rows of a table in a relational database. It requires specifying the table, the columns to update, their new values using the `SET` clause, and a `WHERE` clause to filter which rows are affected.
examples: `UPDATE Employees SET Salary = 75000 WHERE EmployeeID = 101;` (Updates the salary of a specific employee)|`UPDATE Products SET Price = Price * 1.05 WHERE Category = 'Books';` (Increases the price of all books by 5%)|`UPDATE Users SET Status = 'Inactive' WHERE LastLogin < '2023-01-01';` (Deactivates users who haven't logged in recently)
title: SQL UPDATE Statement

definition: SQLite is a self-contained, serverless, zero-configuration, transactional SQL database engine commonly used for local storage in mobile, desktop, and embedded applications. It embeds directly into the end program and stores its entire database in a single disk file, making it lightweight and easy to use.
examples: Storing user preferences, cached data, or offline content within an Android or iOS application.|Web browsers like Google Chrome and Mozilla Firefox use SQLite for managing history, bookmarks, and cookies.|Many IoT devices and embedded systems leverage SQLite for local data persistence due to its small footprint.
title: SQLite (Mobile Database)

definition: The Spring Framework is a comprehensive open-source application framework for Java, providing extensive infrastructure support for developing robust, scalable enterprise-level applications. It promotes best practices like dependency injection and aspect-oriented programming, making development easier and more efficient.
examples: Building RESTful web services and APIs using Spring Boot and Spring Web MVC for a backend application.|Developing enterprise-grade microservices for cloud-native deployments with Spring Cloud.|Integrating with various data sources and performing database operations using Spring Data JPA.
title: Spring Framework (Java)

definition: Static Site Generation (SSG) is a web development approach where HTML pages are pre-built at compile or build time, rather than being generated on-demand by a server for each request. This results in incredibly fast, secure, and easily scalable websites because they serve pre-rendered static files directly from a CDN.
examples: Using Next.js, Gatsby, or Jekyll to generate a blog, portfolio, or documentation website.|Pre-rendering e-commerce product pages that display information updated infrequently.|Deploying a marketing site or landing page where content is mostly static and requires high performance.
title: Static Site Generation (SSG)

definition: Storyboards are a visual tool in Xcode for designing and laying out the user interface (UI) of an iOS application, showing screens (View Controllers) and the transitions (Segues) between them. They provide an intuitive, drag-and-drop way to visualize the flow and structure of an app's UI.
examples: Dragging and dropping UI elements like buttons, labels, and image views onto a View Controller to design a screen.|Defining a 'show' segue to visually represent navigation from a login screen to a main dashboard.|Creating an entire app's navigation flow, including tab bars and navigation controllers, all within a single file.
title: Storyboards (iOS)

definition: Stubbing in testing involves replacing a real component or object with a simplified substitute (a 'stub') that provides predefined answers to method calls during a test. This isolates the code under test from its external dependencies, ensuring consistent and repeatable test results without relying on actual external systems.
examples: Stubbing an external API call to return a specific JSON response rather than making a network request.|Replacing a database connection with a stub that returns a fixed set of data for a unit test.|Using a mocking framework (e.g., Mockito in Java, Sinon.js in JavaScript) to create stubs for service interfaces.
title: Stubbing (Testing)

definition: Subscription models in mobile applications allow users to access premium content, features, or services for a recurring fee, typically on a monthly or annual basis. This monetization strategy provides predictable revenue for developers and ongoing value and access for users.
examples: A meditation app offering premium guided meditations and sleep stories for a monthly subscription.|A news app providing ad-free reading, exclusive articles, and offline access to subscribers.|An in-app purchase for unlocking all levels or removing ads via a recurring subscription.
title: Subscription Models (Mobile)

definition: Swift is a powerful and intuitive open-source programming language developed by Apple for building apps across Apple's platforms (iOS, macOS, watchOS, tvOS) and beyond. It is designed for safety, performance, and modern software design patterns, making it popular for mobile and backend development.
examples: Developing native iOS applications for iPhones and iPads, such as social media apps or games.|Creating macOS desktop applications with a rich user interface.|Building server-side applications and APIs using frameworks like Vapor or Kitura for backend services.
title: Swift (Programming Language)

definition: Swift Package Manager (SPM) is a dependency management tool integrated into the Swift build system, used for automating the distribution of Swift code. It simplifies the process of declaring, fetching, building, and linking dependencies for Swift projects on Apple platforms and Linux, ensuring consistent project setups.
examples: Adding a third-party networking library like Alamofire to an iOS project by listing it in a `Package.swift` file.|Managing dependencies for a server-side Swift application built with the Vapor framework.|Creating reusable modules of Swift code that can be easily shared across multiple projects or published for public use.
semantic_tags: Swift|Dependency Management|Build System|Package Manager|iOS Development|Open Source
title: Swift Package Manager (SPM)

definition: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is a core protocol of the Internet Protocol Suite, providing reliable, ordered, and error-checked delivery of a stream of bytes between applications running on hosts. It establishes a connection before data transmission, ensuring data integrity, flow control, and retransmission of lost packets.
examples: Web browsers use TCP to establish connections with web servers (HTTP/HTTPS) for reliable transmission of web pages.|Email clients use TCP for sending and receiving emails via protocols like SMTP, POP3, and IMAP.|File Transfer Protocol (FTP) relies on TCP for reliable and ordered transfer of files between systems.
title: TCP Protocol

definition: Test coverage is a metric used in software testing to describe the degree to which the source code of a program is executed when a particular test suite runs. It indicates how much of the code has been tested, measured by statements, branches, functions, or lines, providing insight into the thoroughness of testing.
examples: A test suite achieving 80% line coverage means 80% of the executable lines in the codebase are run by tests.|Using tools like JaCoCo (Java), Istanbul (JavaScript), or Xcode's built-in coverage reports to generate coverage metrics.|Setting a target, such as 75% branch coverage, as a quality gate for pull requests in a CI/CD pipeline.
title: Test Coverage

definition: Terraform is an open-source Infrastructure as Code (IaC) tool that allows users to define and provision datacenter infrastructure using a declarative configuration language. It enables managing various cloud and on-premise resources consistently, reproducibly, and automatically across different providers.
examples: Provisioning virtual machines, networks, and databases on AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud using declarative HCL files.|Deploying and managing Kubernetes clusters and their configurations across different cloud providers.|Managing DNS records, load balancers, and content delivery networks (CDNs) as code rather than manual operations.
title: Terraform (Infrastructure as Code)

definition: Software testing is the process of evaluating a system or its components to determine whether it satisfies specified requirements and to identify defects. It encompasses various levels: Unit tests verify individual components, Integration tests check interactions between units, and End-to-End (E2E) tests simulate full user scenarios through the entire system.
examples: Unit test: Testing a single function that calculates a shopping cart's total price.|Integration test: Verifying if a user registration module successfully interacts with the database and an email sending service.|E2E test: Simulating a user logging into a web application, adding items to a cart, and completing a purchase, including UI interactions.
semantic_tags: Software Testing|Quality Assurance|Unit Testing|Integration Testing|End-to-End Testing|Quality Control
title: Testing (Unit, Integration, E2E)

definition: Time complexity analysis, commonly expressed using Big O notation, is a mathematical way to describe how the runtime or space requirements of an algorithm grow as the input size increases. It provides an upper bound on the growth rate, helping evaluate an algorithm's efficiency, scalability, and performance characteristics.
examples: An algorithm that iterates through an array once to find an item has O(n) (linear) time complexity.|Binary search has O(log n) (logarithmic) time complexity, making it very efficient for large, sorted datasets.|An algorithm with nested loops iterating over the same dataset typically results in O(n^2) (quadratic) time complexity.
title: Time Complexity Analysis (Big O)

definition: Digital certificates that bind an organization's identity to a cryptographic key pair, enabling encrypted communication and verifying server authenticity over the internet. They are crucial for establishing secure HTTPS connections and building trust.
examples: A website like example.com purchasing an SSL certificate from a Certificate Authority (CA) like Let's Encrypt or DigiCert.|A web browser displaying a padlock icon and 'HTTPS' in the address bar, indicating that the site's certificate has been validated.|Mobile apps using certificate pinning to ensure they only connect to servers with a specific, pre-approved certificate.
title: TLS/SSL Certificates

definition: A cryptographic protocol that establishes a secure communication session between a client and a server using TLS/SSL certificates, negotiating encryption algorithms and exchanging session keys. It ensures data confidentiality and integrity before application data transmission begins.
examples: When a web browser connects to an HTTPS website, the browser and server perform a handshake to agree on encryption methods and verify identities.|An API client establishing a secure connection to a REST API endpoint, during which cryptographic parameters are negotiated.|Observing network traffic in developer tools, showing the 'Client Hello', 'Server Hello', certificate exchange, and key exchange steps.
title: TLS/SSL Handshake

definition: An authentication method where a server verifies user credentials and issues a signed token (e.g., JWT) to the client, which is then sent with subsequent requests instead of credentials. This stateless approach enhances scalability and security by avoiding server-side session storage.
examples: A user logging into a web application, receiving a JWT, and then including it in the `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header for all API calls.|OAuth 2.0 issuing access tokens for third-party applications to securely access protected resources on behalf of a user.|Firebase Authentication generating ID tokens for client-side use after a user signs in, allowing authenticated access to Firebase services.
title: Token-Based Authentication

definition: A stateless session management approach where session data, such as user identity or permissions, is encoded within a token issued to the client, rather than stored on the server. The client includes this token with each request, allowing the server to validate it and retrieve session information without server-side lookups.
examples: Using a JWT (JSON Web Token) to store a user's ID and roles directly within the token, allowing the server to validate it and use this information for authorization without querying a database.|Microservices environments where tokens are passed between services to maintain user context without needing a shared session store.|A mobile app persisting a refresh token locally to obtain new access tokens when the current one expires, without requiring the user to re-authenticate.
title: Token-Based Sessions

definition: Specific movements or interactions performed by a user on a touch-sensitive screen, enabling intuitive control and navigation within a mobile application or touch-enabled web interface. These gestures translate user input into software commands, enhancing user experience.
examples: Swiping left or right to navigate between tabs or screens in a social media app.|Pinching in or out on an image or map to zoom, indicating a change in scale.|Long-pressing an item in a list to reveal a context menu with additional options.
title: Touch Gestures

definition: A sequence of operations performed as a single, indivisible logical unit of work in a database, ensuring atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability (ACID properties). Either all operations within a transaction succeed and are committed, or none do and the transaction is rolled back.
examples: Transferring money between two bank accounts: deducting from one account and adding to another must both succeed or both fail to maintain data integrity.|Registering a new user where inserting user data into one table and creating a default profile in another must be an atomic operation.|Updating an order status and simultaneously decreasing inventory count in an e-commerce application, preventing overselling.
title: Transactions (Database)

definition: User Datagram Protocol, a connectionless transport layer protocol that prioritizes speed over reliability, sending independent packets (datagrams) without establishing a connection or guaranteeing delivery order. It's suitable for applications where occasional data loss is acceptable for lower latency.
examples: Online gaming for real-time player movement updates, where a dropped packet is less critical than the delay caused by retransmission.|DNS (Domain Name System) queries, where a lost query can simply be re-sent by the client with minimal impact.|Live video streaming or VoIP, where a slight drop in quality due to packet loss is preferable to pauses caused by retransmitting data.
title: UDP Protocol

definition: A type of software testing that verifies the functionality and appearance of a graphical user interface (GUI) by simulating user interactions and checking if the UI behaves as expected across different devices and conditions. It ensures the application's visual elements and user workflows are correct and consistent.
examples: Using Espresso (Android) or XCUITest (iOS) to automate clicking a button, entering text into a field, and verifying the displayed result.|Testing a web application with Selenium or Cypress to ensure form submissions, navigation, and display across various browsers and screen sizes.|Performing visual regression testing to detect unintended UI changes between software versions by comparing screenshots.
title: UI Testing

definition: A simple key-value store provided by Apple's Foundation framework for iOS applications, used to persistently store small amounts of user preferences, configuration settings, and application state data. Data is stored in a plist file and is accessible across app launches.
examples: Saving a user's dark mode preference (`UserDefaults.standard.set(true, forKey: 'isDarkModeEnabled')`) so it's remembered next time.|Storing a boolean flag indicating if a user has completed the onboarding tutorial, preventing it from showing again.|Persisting the last opened tab or view controller index to resume the app at the user's previous location.
title: User Defaults (iOS Persistence)

definition: The path a user takes to complete a specific task or achieve a goal within a website or application, encompassing every step from their entry point to their final interaction. Mapping user flows helps identify potential pain points, optimize navigation, and improve the overall user experience.
examples: The 'login' user flow: User navigates to login screen → enters credentials → clicks login button → lands on dashboard.|The 'purchase product' user flow: User searches for product → adds to cart → proceeds to checkout → enters shipping/payment info → confirms order.|A mobile app's onboarding flow guiding a new user through initial setup steps and permissions requests.
title: User Flow (UX)

definition: A system for tracking and managing changes to code and other files over time, allowing multiple developers to collaborate efficiently, revert to previous states, and manage different versions of a project. Git is a widely used distributed version control system.
examples: Using `git commit -m "Add login feature"` to save a snapshot of changes to the local repository.|Collaborating on a project by pushing local changes to a remote repository like GitHub and merging pull requests from teammates.|Reverting to an earlier stable version of a codebase using `git revert` or `git reset` after a critical bug is introduced.
title: Version Control (Git)

definition: The sequence of distinct states and events that an iOS `UIViewController` object goes through from its initialization to its deallocation, including loading its view, appearing on screen, disappearing, and being removed from memory. Developers can override specific lifecycle methods to perform actions at different stages of a view controller's existence.
examples: Performing initial UI setup or data loading in `viewDidLoad()`, which is called once the view controller's view is loaded into memory.|Refreshing data, starting animations, or subscribing to notifications in `viewWillAppear(_:)` before the view becomes visible to the user.|Saving transient state or stopping ongoing tasks like network requests in `viewWillDisappear(_:)` when the view is about to leave the screen.
title: View Controller Lifecycle (iOS)

definition: A feature in Android development that allows developers to more easily and safely interact with views by generating a binding class for each XML layout file. It eliminates the need for `findViewById()`, reducing boilerplate code and preventing null pointer exceptions by providing direct, type-safe references to views.
examples: Enabling ViewBinding in an Android project's `build.gradle` file (`buildFeatures { viewBinding true }`).|Accessing a `TextView` in an `Activity` directly via `binding.myTextView.text = "Hello"` instead of `findViewById<TextView>(R.id.myTextView).text = "Hello"`.|Inflating a layout in an `Activity` using `val binding = ActivityMainBinding.inflate(layoutInflater)` and setting it as the content view.
title: ViewBinding (Android)

definition: A class designed to store and manage UI-related data in a lifecycle-conscious way, surviving configuration changes like screen rotations. It separates UI logic from business logic, ensuring data persists across activity/fragment lifecycles and simplifying UI updates.
examples: A `UserViewModel` holding a `LiveData<User>` object that an Activity observes for updates to user data.|Fetching data from a repository in the `ViewModel` and exposing it to the UI, abstracting data source details from the view.|Using `ViewModelProvider` to get an instance of a `ViewModel` in an Activity or Fragment, ensuring the same instance survives configuration changes.
title: ViewModel (Android Architecture Components)

definition: An HTML `<meta>` tag used within the `<head>` of a web page to control the width and scaling of the viewport on different devices, especially mobile browsers. It is crucial for responsive web design, ensuring content is rendered correctly and legibly across various screen sizes.
examples: `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">` (the most common setting) tells the browser to set the viewport width to the device's width and not zoom initially.|Setting `user-scalable=no` within the content attribute to prevent users from zooming in or out of the page.|A developer might temporarily use `width=980px` for older, non-responsive sites to ensure they display as intended on mobile devices.
title: Viewport Meta Tag

definition: A lightweight, in-memory representation of a UI component's DOM structure, maintained by JavaScript frameworks like React and Vue. When the component's state changes, the framework first updates the Virtual DOM, then efficiently calculates the minimal differences (diffing) to update only the necessary parts of the actual browser DOM, optimizing performance.
examples: In React, when `setState()` is called, React creates a new Virtual DOM tree and compares it to the previous one to identify changes.|Vue.js uses a similar mechanism, where reactive data changes trigger a re-render of the component's virtual node tree.|Instead of directly manipulating the browser's slow DOM for every change, only the specific elements identified as different in the Virtual DOM comparison are updated, leading to faster UI rendering.
title: Virtual DOM

definition: Software-based emulations of physical computer systems, allowing multiple isolated operating systems to run concurrently on a single piece of hardware. They provide a sandboxed environment for testing, development, and deploying applications with specific OS requirements without needing multiple physical machines.
examples: Running Windows on a Mac using virtualization software like Parallels Desktop or VMware Fusion to access Windows-specific applications.|A web developer using a VM to test their application on various browser versions and operating systems (e.g., Ubuntu, Fedora) without needing to reconfigure their main machine.|Cloud providers like AWS EC2 or Google Compute Engine offering virtual machine instances for deploying and scaling web applications and services.
title: Virtual Machines

definition: The aesthetic arrangement and styling of all elements within a user interface, focusing on visual appeal, brand identity, and effectively guiding the user through the interface. It encompasses typography, color, imagery, spacing, and overall layout to create an intuitive and engaging experience.
examples: A mobile app consistently using a brand's specific color palette and typography for buttons, text, and headings to maintain a cohesive look and feel.|Using ample white space (negative space) effectively to create a clean, uncluttered layout that improves readability and reduces cognitive load.|Employing a consistent set of iconography and imagery that aligns with the target audience and enhances the user's comprehension of functionality.
title: Visual Design (UX)

definition: Reusable, self-contained building blocks in a Vue.js application, encapsulating their own template (HTML structure), script (JavaScript logic), and style (CSS). They allow for modular development, promoting maintainability, reusability, and easier management of complex UIs across different parts of an application.
examples: A `<Button>` component that handles its own click events, displays text from a prop, and applies specific styling.|A `<ProductCard>` component that receives product data as props and displays the product's image, name, and price.|A complex `<UserDashboard>` component composed of smaller, individual components like `<UserProfile>`, `<OrderList>`, and `<NavigationMenu>`.
title: Vue Components

definition: A special block of code executed by the processor in response to an interrupt event, temporarily pausing the main program execution to handle the event. definition: The mechanism by which an embedded system assigns different levels of importance to various interrupt sources, ensuring that higher-priority interrupts can preempt lower-priority ones, or that high-priority events are processed first. definition: A hardware mechanism that initializes a microcontroller or system to a known, stable state immediately after power is applied or restored, or when the reset button is pressed. definition: The set of components in an embedded system that generates, distributes, and manages the timing signals (clocks) required for synchronous operation of the processor, memory, and peripherals. definition: SRAM (Static Random-Access Memory) is a type of volatile memory that retains data as long as power is supplied, using latches (usually 6 transistors per bit) instead of capacitors. title: Electromagnetic Interference (EMI)

definition: The physical arrangement and routing of electronic components, traces, and planes on a laminated board to implement the electrical circuit design from the schematic. It is critical for performance, manufacturability, and signal integrity.
examples: Arranging components to minimize trace lengths for high-speed signals (e.g., USB, Ethernet).|Creating dedicated power and ground planes to reduce impedance and noise.|Routing differential pairs with controlled impedance for reliable data transmission.
title: Printed Circuit Board (PCB) Layout

definition: The process of creating a diagram that shows the electrical connections and components of an electronic circuit using standardized graphical symbols. It forms the blueprint for the PCB layout and overall circuit functionality.
examples: Drawing connections between a microcontroller, sensors, and power supply components.|Defining part values like resistors, capacitors, and ICs with their respective reference designators.|Using hierarchical blocks to manage complexity in large designs, such as power management or communication modules.
title: Schematic Design

definition: A comprehensive list of all raw materials, components, and sub-assemblies required to manufacture a product. It includes information such as part numbers, quantities, descriptions, and often manufacturer details.
examples: Listing all resistors, capacitors, integrated circuits, and connectors with their specific values and package types for a PCB assembly.|Specifying manufacturer names and part numbers to facilitate procurement and inventory management.|Calculating the total cost of components for a production run of an IoT device.
title: Bill of Materials (BOM)

definition: An electronic circuit that maintains a constant output voltage regardless of variations in the input voltage or changes in the load current. It is essential for providing stable power to sensitive electronic components.
examples: A 5V regulator providing stable power to a microcontroller from a fluctuating battery source.|A 3.3V regulator for digital sensors and communication modules, ensuring consistent operation.|Using a linear regulator for noise-sensitive analog circuits or a switching regulator for high efficiency.
title: Voltage Regulator

definition: A type of linear voltage regulator characterized by its ability to operate with a very small difference (dropout voltage) between its input and output voltages. LDOs are simple, low-noise, and widely used when input and output voltages are close.
examples: Powering a 3.3V microcontroller from a 3.7V LiPo battery in a battery-powered IoT device.|Providing a clean power rail for sensitive analog-to-digital converters (ADCs) due to their low output noise.|Used in designs where the input voltage is only slightly higher than the required output, and efficiency is less critical than noise performance.
title: Low-Dropout (LDO) Regulator

definition: A step-down switching regulator that efficiently converts a higher DC input voltage to a lower, regulated DC output voltage. It achieves high efficiency by rapidly switching a power transistor, minimizing energy loss.
examples: Converting 12V automotive power to 5V for a dashboard display or USB charger.|Stepping down a 24V industrial supply to 3.3V for a sensor network.|Efficiently powering a microcontroller from a higher voltage battery pack in an embedded system.
title: Buck Converter

definition: A step-up switching regulator that efficiently converts a lower DC input voltage to a higher, regulated DC output voltage. It stores energy in an inductor during one phase and releases it at a higher voltage during another.
examples: Powering a 12V device from a 3.7V single-cell LiPo battery in a portable IoT gadget.|Generating a higher voltage for an LCD backlight from a 5V system supply.|Boosting voltage for a motor driver in a robotics application from a low-voltage battery pack.
title: Boost Converter

definition: An electronic system that monitors and manages a rechargeable battery (cell or battery pack) to ensure its safe and optimal operation, longevity, and performance. It typically handles protection, cell balancing, and state estimation.
examples: Protecting a Li-ion battery from overcharge, over-discharge, over-current, and over-temperature conditions.|Balancing individual cell voltages in a multi-cell battery pack to maximize capacity and lifespan.|Estimating the battery's State of Charge (SoC) and State of Health (SoH) for accurate power management in a drone or electric vehicle.
title: Battery Management System (BMS)

definition: The application of techniques and strategies to reduce the energy consumed by an electronic device, particularly vital for battery-powered, energy-constrained, or environmentally critical embedded and IoT systems. This impacts battery life, heat generation, and operating costs.
examples: Implementing low-power modes (e.g., Sleep, Deep Sleep) in a microcontroller when idle.|Optimizing firmware algorithms for fewer clock cycles or less frequent data processing.|Selecting energy-efficient components and communication protocols (e.g., BLE instead of Wi-Fi for short-range).
title: Power Consumption Optimization

definition: Operating states in microcontrollers and other embedded components specifically designed to significantly reduce electrical power consumption by selectively deactivating or slowing down parts of the system. These modes extend battery life in portable and IoT devices.
examples: Putting a microcontroller into Sleep mode when waiting for an external sensor event.|Reducing the CPU clock frequency when processing light workloads.|Shutting down unused peripheral modules (e.g., ADC, SPI) when they are not actively required.
title: Low-Power Modes

definition: A common low-power mode in microcontrollers where the CPU typically stops executing instructions and its clock is halted, but peripherals and some memory (RAM) might remain powered and active. This allows for relatively quick wake-up times upon an event.
examples: An IoT sensor node going into Sleep mode after transmitting data and waking up on a timer interrupt to take a new reading.|A remote control unit entering Sleep mode until a button press triggers an external interrupt.|A display controller pausing its operation and entering Sleep until a frame update is requested.
semantic_tags: Low power|CPU idle|Quick wake-up|Peripherals active|Power saving|Microcontroller
title: Sleep Mode

definition: A more aggressive low-power mode than Sleep, where most system components, including the CPU and a significant number of peripherals, are powered down or put into a very low-power state. This significantly reduces power consumption but typically requires a longer wake-up time.
examples: A battery-powered environmental monitor waking up only once an hour from Deep Sleep to take readings and transmit data.|An asset tracker entering Deep Sleep mode between GPS pings to conserve battery over several days or weeks.|A wearable device entering Deep Sleep overnight, only waking for critical alarms or scheduled checks.
semantic_tags: Ultra low power|CPU shut down|Longer wake-up|Reduced functionality|Battery life|Microcontroller
title: Deep Sleep Mode

definition: The lowest power mode for an embedded system, often involving powering down almost all components and storing the system's volatile state (e.g., RAM content) to non-volatile memory before a complete shutdown. This enables very long battery life but incurs the slowest wake-up time.
examples: A smart utility meter entering Hibernate mode during periods of extreme inactivity or low demand to conserve power over years.|An embedded system periodically saving its operational state to flash memory and completely shutting down to achieve maximum battery conservation.|Devices in remote locations requiring infrequent operation to maximize their unattended lifetime.
semantic_tags: Extreme low power|State save|Non-volatile memory|Slowest wake-up|System shutdown|Battery conservation
title: Hibernate Mode

definition: A power management technique that adaptively adjusts the operating voltage and clock frequency of a processor or other digital circuits based on real-time workload demands. This optimizes energy consumption by reducing power during low-activity periods while maintaining performance during peak loads.
examples: A smartphone CPU scaling down its frequency and voltage when the user is simply browsing or the screen is off.|An embedded vision system increasing the clock speed and voltage of its image processor only during active frame capture and analysis.|IoT gateways reducing CPU power when only transmitting small amounts of data and scaling up for complex local analytics.
normalized_name: dynamic voltage and frequency scaling dvfs
title: Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS)

definition: The process of capturing and converting ambient energy from external sources (such as solar, thermal, kinetic/vibration, or radio frequency) into usable electrical power. This enables self-powered or extended-lifetime operation for low-power embedded and IoT devices.
examples: A small solar panel powering a remote weather sensor in an agricultural IoT application.|A piezoelectric transducer generating electricity from vibrations of machinery to power a condition monitoring sensor.|An RF energy harvester powering a passive RFID tag or a low-power wireless sensor node from ambient radio waves.
title: Energy Harvesting

definition: Strict timing requirements that an embedded system must meet to ensure correct and predictable operation, often involving deadlines for tasks or responses. Failure to meet these deadlines can lead to system malfunction or catastrophic consequences.
examples: An airbag deployment system activating within a few milliseconds of a collision detection.|A motor control loop updating its output every 1 millisecond to maintain stable speed and position.|An audio codec processing samples without dropouts to ensure continuous, high-quality sound output.
title: Real-time Constraints

definition: The characteristic of a system where, for a given initial state and sequence of inputs, it will always produce the exact same output in the exact same amount of time. This predictability is crucial for reliable operation in real-time embedded systems.
examples: A robotic arm executing a movement path with consistent timing and precision every time it receives the same command.|A control loop guaranteeing a sensor reading and actuator response within a specific, bounded timeframe.|Reproducible behavior in critical safety systems, where timing variations could lead to hazardous conditions.
title: Deterministic Behavior

definition: Jitter refers to the deviation from true periodicity of a signal or the variation in the latency of an event or task. In real-time systems, it quantifies the inconsistency in task execution times or signal delivery, which can impact system predictability.
examples: Inconsistent audio playback causing crackling sounds due to varying delays in data delivery.|A motor control system exhibiting imprecise speed due to fluctuating timing of PWM pulses.|Varying sensor sampling intervals leading to less accurate data acquisition in a monitoring system.
title: Jitter (Real-time)

definition: Latency is the time delay between the initiation of an event or the input of a signal and the system's corresponding response or output. In real-time systems, low and predictable latency is crucial for timely operations.
examples: The time taken for a sensor's input (e.g., button press) to trigger an actuator's output (e.g., LED turning on).|The delay experienced by a user's command sent to a smart home device before the action is performed.|The total time for a network packet to travel from a source IoT device to a cloud server.
title: Latency (Real-time)

definition: Throughput measures the rate at which a system or component can process data or complete tasks over a given period. It indicates the efficiency and capacity of a system to handle work.
examples: The number of sensor readings an embedded system can process per second.|The data transfer rate (e.g., Mbps) of an IoT gateway's network interface.|The maximum number of instructions a microcontroller can execute per second (MIPS).
title: Throughput (System performance)

definition: Reliability is the probability that a system or component will perform its required functions under stated conditions for a specified period of time without failure. It is a critical attribute for long-term operational integrity in embedded and IoT devices.
examples: An industrial control system operating continuously for years without unexpected shutdowns.|A medical implantable device consistently functioning correctly for its designed lifespan.|A smart meter accurately collecting and transmitting energy consumption data without data loss over months.
title: Reliability (System attribute)

definition: Safety-Critical Systems are systems whose failure or malfunction could lead to severe consequences, such as death, serious injury, significant environmental damage, or catastrophic financial loss. They demand rigorous design, verification, and validation processes.
examples: Automotive Anti-lock Braking Systems (ABS) or Advanced Driver-Assistance Systems (ADAS).|Control systems for nuclear power plants or chemical processing facilities.|Medical life-support equipment like pacemakers or ventilators.
title: Safety-Critical Systems

definition: Functional safety is the part of overall safety that depends on a system or equipment operating correctly in response to its inputs and preventing unacceptable risks. It involves identifying hazards, implementing safety functions to achieve or maintain a safe state, and managing these functions throughout the system's lifecycle.
examples: A control system for an industrial robot detecting a human presence in a hazardous zone and safely shutting down operations.|An autonomous vehicle's emergency braking system activating when a collision is imminent.|Software diagnostics in a medical device ensuring internal components are operating within safe parameters.
title: Functional Safety

definition: ISO 26262 is an international standard for functional safety of electrical and electronic (E/E) systems in road vehicles. It defines a lifecycle for the development of safety-critical automotive systems, including risk assessment, safety goal definition, and Safety Integrity Levels (ASILs).
examples: Designing an Electronic Control Unit (ECU) for an electric power steering system to meet ASIL D requirements.|Developing and testing autonomous driving software features according to the ISO 26262 safety lifecycle phases.|Performing hazard analysis and risk assessment for an automotive battery management system (BMS).
title: ISO 26262 Standard

definition: IEC 61508 is an international umbrella standard for functional safety of electrical, electronic, and programmable electronic (E/E/PE) safety-related systems, applicable across various industries. It provides a framework for designing and managing safety systems to achieve Safety Integrity Levels (SILs).
examples: Implementing a Safety Instrumented System (SIS) for a chemical processing plant to prevent overpressure.|Developing a control system for a nuclear power facility with high SIL requirements.|Designing safety logic for robotic manufacturing cells in an industrial automation setting.
title: IEC 61508 Standard

definition: Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) are integrations of computation, networking, and physical processes. They involve embedded computers and networks monitoring and controlling physical systems, typically with feedback loops where physical processes affect computations and vice-versa.
examples: Smart grids that integrate electricity generation, distribution, and consumption with information technology.|Autonomous vehicles combining sensors, computation, communication, and physical control for self-driving.|Industrial control systems (e.g., SCADA) managing factory automation and infrastructure.
title: Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS)

definition: An Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) is an electronic circuit that converts a continuous analog voltage or current signal into a discrete digital representation. This enables microcontrollers to read and process real-world physical quantities.
examples: Reading the temperature from a thermistor sensor connected to a microcontroller.|Measuring the remaining battery voltage in an IoT device.|Capturing audio signals from a microphone for digital processing.
title: Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC)

definition: A Digital-to-Analog Converter (DAC) is an electronic circuit that converts a discrete digital code into a continuous analog voltage or current signal. This allows microcontrollers to control analog devices or generate analog waveforms.
examples: Generating an audio waveform for playback through a speaker.|Controlling the speed of a variable-frequency motor with an analog voltage.|Setting a precise voltage reference for an external circuit or sensor.
title: Digital-to-Analog Converter (DAC)

definition: Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) is a technique used to control the average power delivered to an electrical device by rapidly switching the power supply on and off. The average power is proportional to the duty cycle, which is the fraction of time the signal is 'on'.
examples: Dimming an LED by varying the 'on' time of the power pulse.|Controlling the speed of a DC motor by changing the average voltage applied.|Generating an analog voltage output from a digital pin to control a servo motor position.
title: Pulse Width Modulation (PWM)

definition: A Timer/Counter is a versatile hardware peripheral in a microcontroller that can count up or down based on a clock source, generating interrupts or controlling outputs when specific values are reached. It is fundamental for timing events, generating delays, and measuring time intervals.
examples: Creating a precise 1-second delay for a blinking LED.|Scheduling tasks in a real-time operating system (RTOS) at regular intervals.|Measuring the duration of an external event, like a button press or sensor pulse.
title: Timer/Counter

definition: Input Capture is a microcontroller peripheral feature, often integrated with a Timer/Counter, that records the precise timestamp of an external event, typically a rising or falling edge of a digital signal. This allows for accurate measurement of pulse widths, periods, and frequencies.
examples: Measuring the period and frequency of an incoming square wave signal from a sensor.|Calculating the speed and direction of a motor using signals from a rotary encoder.|Determining the exact duration of an external pulse, such as an ultrasonic sensor echo.
title: Input Capture

definition: Output Compare is a microcontroller peripheral feature, often integrated with a Timer/Counter, that generates an output event when the timer's current value matches a pre-configured compare value. This event can be toggling a pin, setting an interrupt, or initiating a DMA transfer.
examples: Generating precise Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) signals for motor control or LED dimming.|Creating periodic interrupts for scheduling tasks in a multi-tasking embedded application.|Generating specific timing sequences or waveforms on an output pin.
title: Output Compare

definition: UART is a hardware communication protocol that allows two devices to communicate serially and asynchronously, meaning data is transmitted bit by bit without a shared clock signal. It is widely used for simple, point-to-point data exchange between microcontrollers and peripherals or debugging tools.
examples: Debugging a microcontroller by sending log messages to a connected computer's serial terminal.|Communicating with a GPS module to receive location data.|Interfacing with a Bluetooth or Wi-Fi module for wireless data transfer.
title: Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter (UART)

definition: SPI is a synchronous serial communication interface specification used for short-distance, high-speed communication, primarily in embedded systems between a master device and one or more slave devices. It uses separate lines for data (MOSI, MISO) and a shared clock (SCLK), along with a chip select (CS) for each slave.
examples: Communicating with an SD card to store or retrieve data.|Controlling an LCD or OLED display module.|Interfacing with flash memory chips, external ADCs/DACs, or various sensors requiring fast data rates.
title: Serial Peripheral Interface (SPI)

definition: I2C is a synchronous, multi-master, multi-slave serial communication bus used for connecting low-speed peripheral ICs to processors in embedded systems, requiring only two wires: Serial Data Line (SDA) and Serial Clock Line (SCL). It supports address-based communication.
examples: Reading data from an accelerometer/gyroscope sensor in a smartphone or drone.|Controlling an EEPROM or other memory devices.|Interfacing with Real-Time Clocks (RTCs) or small display modules.
title: Inter-Integrated Circuit (I2C)

definition: The CAN Bus is a robust vehicle bus standard designed to allow microcontrollers and devices to communicate with each other in applications without a host computer. It is message-based, supporting efficient and reliable communication in real-time embedded systems, especially in automotive and industrial automation.
examples: Communication between various Electronic Control Units (ECUs) in a car (e.g., engine, brakes, airbags, dashboard).|Industrial automation systems for connecting PLCs, sensors, and actuators on a factory floor.|Robotics platforms coordinating actions between different motor controllers and sensing modules.
title: Controller Area Network (CAN) Bus

definition: The Ethernet Media Access Control (MAC) layer is a sublayer of the data link layer (Layer 2) in the OSI model, responsible for managing hardware access to the physical transmission medium. It handles frame addressing, error detection, and contention resolution to enable reliable communication over an Ethernet network.
examples: An Ethernet controller chip in an IoT gateway forming and sending Ethernet frames to a router.|A network interface card (NIC) in an embedded Linux device using its unique MAC address to identify itself on a local network.|Communication between smart factory machines over a wired local area network (LAN).
title: Ethernet MAC

definition: A hardware component in an embedded system that manages communication with connected USB devices, acting as the master to initiate and control data transfers. It enumerates devices, allocates bandwidth, and handles data flow between the host system and peripherals.
examples: An embedded Linux board (e.g., Raspberry Pi) connecting to a USB keyboard or mouse.|An industrial HMI (Human-Machine Interface) panel reading data from a USB barcode scanner.|A custom medical device connecting to a USB flash drive for data logging.
title: USB Host Controller

definition: A hardware component in an embedded system that allows the system to function as a USB peripheral, responding to commands and requests from a USB host. It handles low-level USB signaling, packet assembly/disassembly, and endpoint management.
examples: A microcontroller (e.g., STM32) appearing as a USB serial port (CDC) to a PC.|An IoT sensor node sending data to a gateway via a USB mass storage class interface.|A custom medical device connecting to a PC for configuration and data download.
title: USB Device Controller

definition: A serial communication protocol commonly used in industrial automation for master-slave communication between devices over RS-232 or RS-485. It defines message structures for reading/writing data to registers or coils in a compact binary format.
examples: A PLC (Programmable Logic Controller) communicating with a temperature sensor over RS-485.|A SCADA system polling data from multiple motor controllers in a factory.|An embedded gateway translating Modbus RTU data to Modbus TCP.
title: Modbus RTU Protocol

definition: An adaptation of the Modbus protocol for use over TCP/IP networks, allowing Modbus messages to be exchanged over Ethernet. It encapsulates Modbus RTU messages within TCP frames, enabling communication between controllers, sensors, and HMIs across a network.
examples: A central control server communicating with PLCs and RTUs over an industrial Ethernet network.|An IoT gateway publishing sensor data to a cloud platform using Modbus TCP as an internal data exchange mechanism.|An HMI panel on a factory floor controlling multiple devices via Ethernet.
title: Modbus TCP Protocol

definition: A standard for serial communication that defines the electrical characteristics, signaling, and mechanical interface for point-to-point data exchange between DTE (Data Terminal Equipment) and DCE (Data Circuit-terminating Equipment). It uses single-ended signaling and is typically limited to short distances.
examples: Debugging output from an embedded system to a PC via a UART-to-RS232 converter.|Connecting an older industrial sensor or instrument to a microcontroller.|GPS modules communicating with embedded devices.
title: RS-232 Standard

definition: A standard for serial communication that defines the electrical characteristics for multipoint, differential data transmission, allowing multiple devices to communicate over long distances and in noisy environments. It uses a twisted-pair cable for robust communication.
examples: Connecting multiple Modbus RTU devices on a single bus in an industrial control system.|Building automation systems (e.g., HVAC control) communicating across large buildings.|DMX512 lighting control networks.
title: RS-485 Standard

definition: A low-cost, single-wire serial communication protocol primarily used in automotive applications for non-critical sub-systems. It operates as a master-slave network, where the master initiates all communication to up to 16 slave nodes.
examples: Controlling power windows, seat adjustments, or sunroofs in a car.|Communicating with small sensor modules within a vehicle door.|Managing dashboard indicators or simple lighting systems.
title: Local Interconnect Network (LIN) Bus

definition: A serial bus interface standard primarily used for connecting digital audio devices, such as ADCs, DACs, and digital signal processors, within an embedded system. It separates clock and data lines for robust, synchronous audio transfer.
examples: Connecting a digital microphone (MEMS) to a microcontroller for audio recording.|Sending audio data from an embedded processor to an audio DAC for playback.|Interfacing an audio codec chip with an application processor.
title: I2S (Inter-IC Sound) Bus

definition: A high-speed serial interface specification from MIPI Alliance designed for connecting displays to application processors in embedded systems, especially mobile and low-power devices. It uses differential signaling to transmit high-resolution video and display control data efficiently.
examples: Connecting an LCD panel to an embedded system's graphics processor in a smartphone or tablet.|Interfacing a small, high-resolution display in a wearable device.|Driving custom industrial displays from a single-board computer.
title: MIPI DSI (Display Serial Interface)

definition: A high-speed serial expansion bus standard used in embedded systems to connect peripheral devices that require high bandwidth, such as GPUs, NVMe storage, or high-performance network interfaces. It provides dedicated point-to-point connections, unlike the shared bus of traditional PCI.
examples: Integrating an AI accelerator card into an embedded vision system.|Adding NVMe SSD storage to an embedded industrial PC for high-speed data logging.|Connecting specialized data acquisition cards to an embedded controller.
title: PCI Express (PCIe) for Embedded

definition: A hardware module found in microcontrollers and embedded systems that can be configured for various timing-related tasks, such as generating delays, creating periodic interrupts, measuring pulse widths, or driving PWM outputs. They typically consist of a counter, a prescaler, and compare/capture registers.
examples: Generating a 1ms system tick interrupt for an RTOS scheduler.|Creating a precise PWM signal to control motor speed or LED brightness.|Measuring the duration of an input pulse from a sensor.
title: General Purpose Timer

definition: A simple, 24-bit down-counting timer present in ARM Cortex-M microcontrollers, typically used to provide a periodic interrupt for operating system tick functions or basic time-delay services. It is easily configured and integrated with the processor core.
examples: Implementing a system tick for FreeRTOS or other RTOS on a Cortex-M MCU.|Generating short, precise delays for peripheral initialization sequences.|Providing a basic time-base for a simple, non-OS-based application.
title: SysTick Timer

definition: Small, high-speed storage locations within the CPU that hold data, instructions, and memory addresses currently being processed. They are essential for the CPU's operation, facilitating quick access to operands and status information for computations and control flow.
examples: The Program Counter (PC) holding the address of the next instruction to execute.|General-purpose registers (e.g., R0-R12 in ARM) storing temporary data during calculations.|The Status Register (CPSR) indicating processor mode and flags.
title: CPU Registers

definition: A special-purpose CPU register that holds the memory address of the top of the current stack. It is crucial for managing function calls, local variables, and interrupt contexts by pushing and popping data onto and from the stack.
examples: During a function call, the return address and current register values are pushed onto the stack, and the SP is decremented.|When an interrupt occurs, the CPU's context is saved to the stack, with the SP indicating the top.|In C, local variables are often allocated on the stack, which implicitly uses the SP.
title: Stack Pointer

definition: A hardware component in many microcontrollers that arbitrates access to shared memory resources and peripherals from multiple masters (e.g., CPU, DMA controller). It intelligently routes data paths to prevent conflicts and ensure efficient resource utilization.
examples: A CPU fetching instructions from Flash memory while a DMA controller writes data to SRAM, both arbitrated by the bus matrix.|Multiple peripherals simultaneously accessing shared memory-mapped registers without collision.|Ensuring an efficient data flow between core, memories, and high-speed peripherals in an SoC.
title: Bus Matrix

definition: A hardware unit within an embedded system responsible for managing interrupt requests from various peripherals and external sources. It prioritizes, enables/disables, and dispatches interrupts to the CPU, ensuring timely responses to events without constant CPU polling.
examples: An external interrupt (EXTI) from a button press triggering an LED toggle.|A UART receive interrupt signaling new incoming data.|A timer interrupt periodically waking the CPU to perform a task.
title: Interrupt Controller (e.g., NVIC)

definition: A sophisticated interrupt controller, particularly prominent in ARM Cortex-M processors, that provides nested interrupt handling and vectoring. It allows interrupts to be assigned priorities, enabling higher-priority interrupts to preempt lower-priority ones, and automatically vectors to the correct Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) address.
examples: A critical motor overcurrent interrupt preempting a less urgent UART receive interrupt.|Configuring interrupt priorities using `NVIC_SetPriority()` in an ARM M-series microcontroller.|Automatically jumping to the specific ISR without software polling, as defined in the vector table.
title: Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller (NVIC)

definition: The process of setting up a General Purpose Input/Output (GPIO) pin on a microcontroller to operate as either an input (e.g., reading a sensor) or an output (e.g., driving an LED), and defining its specific electrical characteristics like pull-up/pull-down resistors, speed, and alternate functions.
examples: Setting `GPIOA->MODER |= (1 << (2*5));` to configure pin PA5 as output for an LED.|Configuring a pin as an input with an internal pull-up resistor for a push button.|Assigning an alternate function (AF) to a pin to enable UART or SPI communication.
title: GPIO Pin Configuration

definition: A resistor connected between an input pin and the positive supply voltage (VCC) to ensure the pin is at a defined high logic level when no other signal is actively driving it low. This prevents the input from floating and registering spurious values.
examples: Connecting a push button between a GPIO pin and ground, with an internal or external pull-up resistor on the pin.|I2C communication lines often use pull-up resistors to hold the lines high when inactive.|Ensuring a clear default high state for open-drain output devices.
title: Pull-up Resistor

definition: A resistor connected between an input pin and ground (GND) to ensure the pin is at a defined low logic level when no other signal is actively driving it high. This prevents the input from floating and registering spurious values.
examples: Connecting a switch between a GPIO pin and VCC, with an internal or external pull-down resistor on the pin.|Ensuring a default low state for inputs from open-collector devices.|Preventing noise from affecting an unconnected input.
title: Pull-down Resistor

definition: A type of digital output that can only pull the output line to ground (low) or leave it floating (high impedance), requiring an external pull-up resistor to define the high state. This configuration is often used for bus sharing (e.g., I2C) or driving devices that require current sinking.
examples: I2C bus communication where multiple devices share SDA/SCL lines using open-drain outputs.|Driving an LED by connecting its anode to VCC and its cathode to an open-drain pin (with current limiting resistor).|Connecting multiple open-drain outputs to a single interrupt line, forming a wired-OR configuration.
title: Open-drain Output

definition: A standard digital output configuration where the output stage consists of two transistors (one pulling high, one pulling low) that actively drive the output line to either VCC (high) or GND (low). This configuration provides stronger current sourcing and sinking capabilities compared to open-drain outputs.
examples: Driving a standard LED directly from a microcontroller pin (with current limiting resistor).|Controlling a motor driver enable pin.|Most general-purpose digital output pins on microcontrollers operate as push-pull.
title: Push-pull Output

definition: The process of temporarily disabling or ignoring specific hardware or software interrupts to prevent them from interrupting the CPU's current execution. This is typically achieved by setting bits in an interrupt mask register, either globally for the CPU or for individual peripheral interrupt sources.
examples: Disabling global interrupts using `__disable_irq()` (ARM Cortex-M) during a critical section of code to ensure atomicity.|Masking lower-priority interrupts while a higher-priority interrupt service routine (ISR) is executing.|Setting a bit in a peripheral's interrupt enable register to `0` to prevent its interrupts from propagating to the CPU.
title: Interrupt Masking

definition: A status bit in a peripheral or interrupt controller register that is automatically set by hardware when a corresponding interrupt event occurs, indicating that an interrupt is pending and waiting to be serviced. This bit signifies that the event has happened, regardless of whether the interrupt is enabled or masked.
examples: A UART peripheral's `RXNE` (Receive Not Empty) flag becoming set, indicating new data is available and an RX interrupt is pending.|A timer peripheral's `UIF` (Update Interrupt Flag) becoming set when the timer overflows.|Checking a `PIR` (Pending Interrupt Register) bit in an interrupt controller to identify which source requested an interrupt.
title: Interrupt Pending Bit

definition: A control bit in a peripheral or interrupt controller register that, when set, allows a specific interrupt source to trigger an interrupt to the CPU. If this bit is cleared, the corresponding interrupt is disabled, preventing it from reaching the CPU even if a pending event occurs.
examples: Setting the `RXNEIE` (Receive Not Empty Interrupt Enable) bit in a UART control register to enable receive interrupts.|Setting the `TIM_DIER_UIE` (Update Interrupt Enable) bit for a timer to allow its overflow interrupt to be generated.|Globally enabling all interrupts via a CPU status register like `PRIMASK` in ARM Cortex-M.
title: Interrupt Enable Bit

definition: Special interrupt service routines (ISRs) in an embedded system that are automatically invoked by the CPU in response to critical hardware or software errors (faults), such as illegal memory accesses, division by zero, or invalid instruction execution. They are crucial for debugging, diagnosing system failures, and implementing robust error recovery mechanisms.
examples: A `HardFault_Handler` catching a severe, unrecoverable processor error.|A `MemManage_Handler` dealing with an invalid memory access in an MPU-protected region.|Logging fault information (e.g., CPU registers, stack contents) to non-volatile memory or a debugger before attempting a system reset.
title: Fault Handlers

definition: The most severe and highest-priority type of fault on ARM Cortex-M processors, triggered when the CPU encounters an unrecoverable error that cannot be managed by other specific fault handlers (e.g., Memory Fault, Bus Fault, Usage Fault). It often indicates a critical system malfunction or a 'double fault' scenario where an exception occurs during the handling of another exception.
examples: A Bus Fault occurring when attempting to access a non-existent memory address, which then escalates to a Hard Fault if no dedicated Bus Fault handler is active.|Executing an instruction from an invalid memory region if the Memory Protection Unit (MPU) is not configured or a MemManage fault handler is not enabled.|Stack overflow causing an attempt to write to a protected memory area, leading to a memory fault that could escalate to a hard fault.
title: Hard Fault

definition: A type of fault on ARM Cortex-M processors that occurs when the CPU attempts to access memory or peripherals via the system bus incorrectly. This can happen due to issues like attempting to write to a read-only address, accessing an unaligned address, or encountering a hardware bus error during a memory transfer operation.
examples: Attempting to write to a peripheral register that is designed as read-only.|Accessing a 32-bit value at an odd memory address on systems requiring aligned access (if unaligned access is disabled).|A hardware-level bus error occurring during a DMA transfer to an invalid destination address.
title: Bus Fault

definition: On ARM Cortex-M processors, a fault triggered by violations of Memory Protection Unit (MPU) rules or other memory management constraints. definition: A mechanism by which an application task requests a service from the Real-Time Operating System (RTOS) kernel. definition: The different operational phases a task can be in during its lifetime, managed by the RTOS scheduler. definition: A scheduling approach where tasks voluntarily yield control of the CPU to the scheduler, rather than being preempted by an external event or timer. A task continues to run until it explicitly calls a yield function, enters a waiting state, or finishes its current unit of work.

definition: A static-priority, preemptive scheduling algorithm used in real-time systems where task priorities are assigned inversely proportional to their relative deadlines.
