definition: Constrained Devices are IoT endpoints with significant limitations in terms of processing power, memory, energy supply (e.g., battery-powered), and network bandwidth. These limitations necessitate the use of lightweight protocols, efficient operating systems, and optimized communication strategies.
examples: A wireless sensor node running on a coin cell battery, sending environmental data once an hour.|A smart meter with limited processing capability, designed for long-term deployment without maintenance.|A tiny microcontroller (e.g., ESP8266 or similar) with minimal RAM and flash memory for a simple embedded application.
title: Constrained Devices

definition: Resource-Constrained Networks are communication infrastructures characterized by limitations such as low bandwidth, high latency, potential unreliability, and limited message size, specifically designed to support constrained devices. These networks prioritize power efficiency and long-range communication over high data rates.
examples: A LoRaWAN network connecting thousands of battery-powered sensors over several kilometers.|A Zigbee mesh network in a smart home, offering low-power, short-range communication.|Cellular NB-IoT (Narrowband IoT) networks designed for massive machine-type communication with low power and extended coverage.
title: Resource-Constrained Networks

definition: 6LoWPAN (IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks) is an adaptation layer that allows IPv6 packets to be transmitted over low-power, typically IEEE 802.15.4-based, wireless networks. It provides header compression and fragmentation mechanisms to efficiently support IPv6 on resource-constrained devices and networks.
examples: An IPv6-enabled smart lightbulb communicating directly with a home router via a 6LoWPAN border router.|Connecting a mesh of environmental sensors to the internet using 6LoWPAN for IP-based communication.|Thread devices using 6LoWPAN to encapsulate IPv6 packets over their mesh network.
title: 6LoWPAN

definition: Thread is an IP-based wireless mesh networking protocol designed for reliable and secure communication between smart home and commercial building devices. It uses 6LoWPAN to carry IPv6 traffic, enabling direct IP connectivity to every device while ensuring low power consumption and high reliability.
examples: Smart thermostats, lighting, and door locks forming a robust mesh network that can self-heal.|Devices within a Thread network communicating directly with cloud services via an IP border router.|Matter-enabled devices using Thread as their underlying network layer for interoperation.
title: Thread Protocol

definition: Matter is an open-source, royalty-free connectivity standard built on IP that aims to ensure seamless interoperability between smart home devices from different manufacturers. It operates at the application layer and supports Wi-Fi, Thread, and Ethernet as underlying network technologies, simplifying device setup and control.
examples: A smart light bulb from one brand being controlled directly by a smart switch from another brand.|A single mobile app controlling various Matter-certified devices (e.g., smart plugs, sensors, thermostats) regardless of their manufacturer.|New Matter devices being easily onboarded into an existing smart home system using a QR code.
title: Matter Protocol

definition: Zigbee is a low-power, short-range wireless mesh networking standard based on the IEEE 802.15.4 specification, primarily used for home automation and industrial control. It enables devices to communicate in a self-organizing and self-healing network, ideal for applications requiring long battery life and modest data rates.
examples: Smart light bulbs, switches, and dimmers forming a mesh network in a home.|Wireless door/window sensors reporting status to a central Zigbee hub.|Industrial sensors collecting data in a factory environment over a Zigbee network.
title: Zigbee Protocol

definition: The Zigbee Cluster Library (ZCL) is a collection of standardized application profiles, commands, and attributes that define how devices interact and exchange information within a Zigbee network. It provides common building blocks for functionality, ensuring interoperability between devices from different manufacturers.
examples: The 'On/Off Cluster' defining how a smart light switch controls a smart bulb's power state.|The 'Temperature Measurement Cluster' standardizing how a sensor reports temperature values.|A 'Thermostat Cluster' defining commands for setting target temperatures and reporting current ones.
title: Zigbee Cluster Library

definition: Z-Wave is a proprietary, low-power wireless communication protocol specifically designed for smart home devices, allowing them to communicate and form a mesh network. It operates in the sub-1 GHz frequency band, which provides better range and less interference than 2.4 GHz bands, making it suitable for controlling various home automation components.
examples: Smart door locks, window sensors, and garage door openers integrated into a Z-Wave network.|A Z-Wave thermostat communicating with a central hub to manage home climate.|Lighting controls and dimmers using Z-Wave for reliable, low-latency operation.
title: Z-Wave Protocol

definition: Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) is a wireless personal area network technology designed for short-range communication, characterized by extremely low power consumption while maintaining communication range similar to classic Bluetooth. It is widely used in battery-powered IoT devices where energy efficiency is critical.
examples: A fitness tracker wirelessly syncing activity data with a smartphone.|Smartwatches connecting to mobile devices for notifications and data exchange.|Proximity beacons (Beacons) broadcasting advertisements to nearby phones for location-aware services.
title: Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE)

definition: BLE GATT Profiles are specifications built upon the Generic Attribute Profile (GATT) that define how data is organized, structured, and exchanged between BLE devices for specific use cases. They ensure interoperability by standardizing the services and characteristics required for a particular functionality.
examples: The Heart Rate Profile defines the services and characteristics for reporting heart rate measurements.|The Proximity Profile specifies how to measure and report the proximity between two BLE devices.|The Blood Pressure Profile outlines the data structure for blood pressure monitoring devices.
title: BLE GATT Profiles

definition: BLE Advertising is a connectionless communication method where a BLE device broadcasts small packets of data into the air to inform nearby devices of its presence or transmit small amounts of information. This process is crucial for device discovery and can be used for proximity applications without establishing a direct connection.
examples: A BLE beacon repeatedly broadcasting its unique ID to be detected by a smartphone application.|A smart thermometer advertising its current temperature reading periodically without requiring a connection.|A new BLE device announcing its availability for pairing to a central device.
title: BLE Advertising

definition: In BLE, a Service is a collection of related data (Characteristics) and their associated behaviors, exposed by a BLE peripheral device to a central device. Services are identified by UUIDs and represent a specific functional capability or data category of the device.
examples: A 'Heart Rate Service' containing characteristics like 'Heart Rate Measurement' and 'Body Sensor Location'.|A 'Battery Service' exposing a 'Battery Level' characteristic to indicate the device's remaining power.|A 'Device Information Service' providing static information such as 'Manufacturer Name' and 'Model Number'.
title: BLE Services

definition: BLE Characteristics are the fundamental data points exposed by a GATT (Generic Attribute Profile) service on a Bluetooth Low Energy device. Each characteristic consists of a value and properties (e.g., read, write, notify) that define how that value can be accessed or interacted with.
examples: A 'Temperature' characteristic with a 'read' property, allowing a client to retrieve the current temperature.|An 'LED Control' characteristic with a 'write' property, enabling a client to change an LED's state.|A 'Heart Rate Measurement' characteristic with a 'notify' property, pushing updates to a client when the heart rate changes.
title: BLE Characteristics

definition: Wi-Fi, based on the IEEE 802.11 standard, is a family of wireless networking protocols enabling devices to connect to a local area network (LAN) and the internet. It operates primarily in the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz ISM bands, offering high data rates over short to medium ranges.
examples: A smart thermostat connecting to a home Wi-Fi network to receive commands and send data to the cloud.|An IoT gateway using Wi-Fi to aggregate sensor data from multiple devices and transmit it to a central server.|A security camera streaming high-definition video over a local Wi-Fi connection.
semantic_tags: Wireless|Local Area Network|IEEE 802.11|High Bandwidth|Short Range|Internet Connectivity
title: Wi-Fi (802.11)

definition: LoRa (Long Range) is a proprietary physical layer (PHY) wireless modulation technology based on spread spectrum, optimized for long-range, low-power communication. It achieves excellent sensitivity and range, making it suitable for transmitting small amounts of data over vast distances with minimal energy consumption.
examples: A LoRa transceiver chip sending temperature and humidity readings from a remote agricultural field sensor.|A smart parking sensor using LoRa to communicate parking space availability to a central system.|A simple LoRa module exchanging data with a LoRa gateway located several kilometers away.
title: LoRa Protocol

definition: LoRaWAN (Long Range Wide Area Network) is a Media Access Control (MAC) layer protocol built on the LoRa physical layer, defining the network architecture for LoRa-based end-devices and gateways. It enables secure, bi-directional communication, mobility, and localization services for IoT applications across regional, national, or global networks.
examples: A smart city sensor sending data via a LoRaWAN network to a cloud application through a LoRaWAN gateway.|A cattle tracker using a LoRaWAN module to report its GPS coordinates over a wide area.|A LoRaWAN gateway forwarding messages from multiple end-devices to a network server.
title: LoRaWAN Protocol

definition: Narrowband IoT (NB-IoT) is a cellular Low-Power Wide-Area Network (LPWAN) technology standardized by 3GPP, designed for highly efficient and secure communication of small data volumes. It operates within existing LTE networks, offering deep indoor penetration, massive device connectivity, and exceptionally long battery life for IoT devices.
examples: Smart utility meters transmitting daily consumption readings to a central server.|Environmental sensors deployed in remote or hard-to-reach locations sending periodic data.|Asset trackers monitoring non-critical goods with infrequent updates over wide areas.
title: Narrowband IoT (NB-IoT)

definition: LTE-M (Long Term Evolution for Machines), also known as Cat-M1, is a cellular LPWAN technology standardized by 3GPP, offering a balance between power consumption, data rate, and mobility for IoT devices. It supports higher data rates and can handle voice-over-LTE (VoLTE) and full mobility, making it suitable for a broader range of IoT applications than NB-IoT.
examples: Wearable health monitors streaming real-time vital signs data.|Smart fleet management systems providing real-time vehicle tracking and diagnostics.|Connected point-of-sale (POS) terminals processing transactions in mobile environments.
title: LTE-M (Cat-M1)

definition: 5G NR (New Radio) for IoT refers to the application of the latest 5G cellular technology standard to support a wide range of IoT use cases. It promises three main categories: enhanced Mobile Broadband (eMBB), massive Machine-Type Communications (mMTC), and Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communications (URLLC), offering unprecedented speeds, ultra-low latency, and massive device connectivity.
examples: Real-time remote control of industrial robots in smart factories (URLLC).|High-bandwidth video surveillance and analytics for smart cities (eMBB).|Autonomous vehicle communication and data exchange for V2X (URLLC/eMBB).
title: 5G NR for IoT

definition: Near Field Communication (NFC) is a short-range wireless technology that enables two electronic devices to communicate when they are brought within a few centimeters (typically 4 cm) of each other. Built upon RFID principles, it allows for simple, secure, and intuitive data exchange without manual pairing.
examples: Making contactless payments by tapping a smartphone on a payment terminal.|Tapping an NFC tag to instantly configure a smart device or trigger an action.|Pairing Bluetooth headphones with a smartphone by simply touching them together.
title: Near Field Communication (NFC)

definition: Radio-Frequency Identification (RFID) is a technology that uses electromagnetic fields to automatically identify and track tags attached to objects. An RFID system typically consists of a reader (interrogator) and one or more transponders (tags) that store data and can be read wirelessly without direct line-of-sight.
examples: Inventory tracking in warehouses by scanning RFID tags on products.|Access control systems where users present RFID cards to readers for entry.|Electronic toll collection systems automatically identifying vehicles with RFID tags.
title: Radio-Frequency Identification (RFID)

definition: Ultra-Wideband (UWB) is a radio technology that uses a very wide spectrum of frequencies to transmit data over short distances at very high bandwidth, enabling extremely precise localization and secure short-range communication. Its low power spectral density allows it to coexist effectively with other wireless technologies.
examples: High-accuracy indoor positioning and navigation for asset tracking in complex environments.|Secure keyless entry systems for vehicles, precisely detecting the key fob's location.|Real-time location systems (RTLS) providing centimeter-level precision for tools or personnel in smart factories.
semantic_tags: Short Range|High Bandwidth|Localization|Precision Ranging|Secure Communication|Low Power
title: Ultra-Wideband (UWB)

definition: Cellular IoT is a category of IoT connectivity solutions that leverage existing and evolving cellular network infrastructure (e.g., 2G, 3G, 4G LTE, 5G) to connect devices to the internet. It offers wide area coverage, high reliability, and robust security, with various standards optimized for different IoT use cases, from low-power (NB-IoT, LTE-M) to high-bandwidth applications.
examples: Smart streetlights connected via LTE-M for remote monitoring and control.|Vending machines reporting inventory levels and sales data over 4G.|Remote patient monitoring devices transmitting vital signs using cellular data from a patient's home.
semantic_tags: Wide Area Network|Cellular Networks|Global Coverage|Reliability|LPWAN|Massive IoT
title: Cellular IoT

definition: Satellite IoT is an IoT connectivity solution that uses satellite constellations to provide global coverage, particularly vital in remote or inaccessible areas where terrestrial networks are unavailable. It is typically employed for low-data-rate applications, asset tracking, and monitoring in regions like oceans, deserts, or polar areas.
examples: Tracking cargo containers and ships across oceans and remote trade routes.|Environmental monitoring sensors collecting data from remote forests or wilderness areas.|Collecting data from oil and gas pipelines or remote agricultural equipment in areas without cellular coverage.
semantic_tags: Global Coverage|Remote Areas|Low Data Rate|Satellite Communication|Asset Tracking|Wide Area Network
title: Satellite IoT

definition: An MQTT Broker is a server that acts as an intermediary in the MQTT publish/subscribe messaging model. Its primary role is to receive messages from publishers, filter them by topic, and forward them to all subscribed clients, managing client connections, authentication, and message persistence.
examples: An Eclipse Mosquitto server hosting MQTT topics for smart home devices.|HiveMQ broker facilitating communication between industrial IoT sensors and a control application.|AWS IoT Core acting as an MQTT broker to ingest data from thousands of connected devices.
title: MQTT Broker

definition: An MQTT Client is a lightweight device or application that connects to an MQTT broker, capable of either publishing messages to specific topics or subscribing to topics to receive messages. It operates within the MQTT publish/subscribe messaging paradigm, enabling efficient communication in constrained environments.
examples: An ESP32 sensor node publishing temperature data to a 'home/livingroom/temperature' topic.|A mobile application subscribing to 'home/light/status' to display the current state of a smart light.|A server-side application subscribing to 'alerts/fire' to receive emergency notifications from smoke detectors.
semantic_tags: IoT Device|Publish/Subscribe|MQTT Protocol|Message Sender|Message Receiver|Constrained Devices
title: MQTT Client

definition: The MQTT Publish/Subscribe model is a messaging pattern where senders (publishers) do not send messages directly to receivers (subscribers), but instead publish messages to an intermediary (broker) categorized by 'topics'. Subscribers express interest in specific topics to the broker and receive all messages published to those topics, enabling decoupled and scalable communication.
examples: A smart thermostat publishes temperature data to the topic 'house/living_room/temperature', while a mobile app subscribes to that topic to display the temperature.|Multiple smart light switches publish 'on' or 'off' commands to 'house/kitchen/light/control', and the kitchen light bulb subscribes to this topic to react.|An anomaly detection system subscribes to 'machine/error' topics from various industrial sensors to receive alerts.
title: MQTT Publish/Subscribe Model

definition: The CoAP (Constrained Application Protocol) Request/Response model is a communication pattern similar to HTTP, where a client sends a request (e.g., GET, POST) to a CoAP server, and the server processes the request and sends back a response. It is specifically optimized for constrained devices and networks, offering efficiency improvements over HTTP for IoT.
examples: A smart light switch (CoAP client) sending a GET request to a smart bulb (CoAP server) to query its current status.|A client sending a PUT request with new configuration data to an IoT sensor to update its reporting interval.|A remote monitoring station sending a POST request to a CoAP server on a gateway to log an event.
title: CoAP Request/Response Model

definition: The CoAP Observe mechanism is an extension to the standard CoAP request/response model that allows a client to 'observe' a resource on a CoAP server. Instead of polling, the client receives automatic, asynchronous notifications from the server whenever the observed resource's state changes, optimizing bandwidth and energy for dynamic data.
examples: A client subscribing to a temperature sensor resource to automatically receive updates whenever the temperature reading changes.|A smart display observing a door sensor's state ('open'/'closed') to show real-time status without continuous polling.|A remote monitoring application observing a device's battery level to get alerts when it drops below a threshold.
title: CoAP Observe Mechanism

definition: RESTful APIs for IoT are Application Programming Interfaces designed following the principles of Representational State Transfer (REST), using standard HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) to interact with resources exposed by IoT devices or cloud platforms. They are stateless, scalable, and typically rely on simple data formats like JSON for data exchange.
examples: A smart home hub sending a GET request to a cloud API (e.g., `api.vendor.com/devices/light001`) to retrieve a device's current status.|A mobile application using a PUT request to `api.vendor.com/devices/bulb002/color` to change the color of a smart bulb.|An IoT device sending a POST request to `api.vendor.com/sensors/data` to upload sensor readings to a cloud backend.
title: RESTful APIs for IoT

definition: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a lightweight, human-readable, and language-independent data interchange format. It uses text to represent data objects consisting of attribute-value pairs and ordered lists of values (arrays), making it widely used for data transmission in web services and IoT applications.
examples: A sensor sending `{"sensorId": "temp01", "temperature": 23.5, "unit": "Celsius", "timestamp": 1678886400}` as its data payload.|A device configuration file stored as `{"device": "smart_bulb", "settings": {"color": "blue", "brightness": 80}}`.|An array of readings: `[{"value": 10}, {"value": 12}, {"value": 9}]`.
title: JSON Data Format

definition: CBOR (Concise Binary Object Representation) is a compact, binary data serialization format designed for small code footprint and message size, often used in constrained environments like IoT devices. It is semantically equivalent to JSON, meaning it can represent the same data structures, but it is optimized for efficiency over human readability.
examples: A sensor sending the CBOR binary `0xA16673656E736F7249646674656D7030316B74656D7065726174757265F941EA64756E69746743656C73697573` instead of the longer JSON string `{"sensorId": "temp01", "temperature": 23.5, "unit": "Celsius"}`.|An IoT device exchanging configuration data with a gateway using CBOR for reduced bandwidth usage.|Firmware updates or device commands encoded in CBOR for efficient over-the-air transmission.
semantic_tags: Binary Serialization|Constrained Devices|Compact|JSON Equivalent|Data Efficiency|IoT Protocol
title: CBOR Data Format

definition: Protocol Buffers (Protobuf) is an efficient, language-neutral, platform-neutral, extensible mechanism for serializing structured data. It optimizes for small message sizes and fast processing, making it ideal for resource-constrained IoT devices and network environments.
examples: Defining a schema for sensor readings like `message SensorData { float temperature = 1; int32 timestamp = 2; }`|Serializing sensor data into a compact binary format before transmitting it from an edge device to an IoT gateway.|Deserializing control commands received from a cloud platform on an embedded microcontroller to actuate a device.
title: Protocol Buffers (Protobuf) for IoT

definition: Data serialization is the process of converting an object or data structure into a format that can be easily stored or transmitted across a network. The inverse process, deserialization, reconstructs the original object from the serialized format.
examples: Converting a C++ struct of sensor readings into a byte array for network transmission.|Encoding a Python dictionary containing device status into a JSON string.|Using Protocol Buffers to serialize a complex telemetry message from an IoT device to a cloud server.
title: Data Serialization

definition: A sensor node is a fundamental component in an IoT system, typically comprising a sensor, a microcontroller, a power source, and a communication module. Its primary function is to collect environmental or physical data and transmit it, often wirelessly, to a gateway or directly to the cloud.
examples: A smart agriculture device measuring soil moisture and temperature, then sending data via LoRaWAN.|A wearable fitness tracker monitoring heart rate and activity levels, communicating via Bluetooth.|A smart home sensor detecting motion and light, reporting to a central hub via Zigbee.
semantic_tags: IoT device|Data collection|Embedded system|Wireless communication|Edge device|Microcontroller
title: Sensor Node

definition: An IoT gateway is a physical device or software program that acts as a bridge between IoT devices (sensor nodes, actuators) and the cloud. It performs crucial functions such as protocol translation, data preprocessing, security, and device management at the edge of the network.
examples: A Raspberry Pi collecting data from Zigbee-enabled smart home sensors and forwarding it to AWS IoT Core via MQTT.|An industrial gateway aggregating Modbus TCP data from PLCs and publishing it to a cloud platform over cellular networks.|A smart hub in a building translating Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) sensor data into Wi-Fi for uplink to a server.
semantic_tags: Edge computing|Connectivity|Protocol translation|Data aggregation|Device management|Network bridge
title: IoT Gateway

definition: Data aggregation in IoT is the process of collecting data from multiple sensors or devices and combining it into a single, summarized dataset. This is often performed at the edge (e.g., an IoT gateway) to reduce network traffic, minimize storage, and decrease processing load on cloud infrastructure.
examples: An IoT gateway collecting temperature readings from 10 sensors every minute and sending a single average temperature value every 10 minutes.|Combining individual smart meter readings into hourly total energy consumption before sending to the utility company's server.|Merging GPS location data from multiple vehicles into a single fleet tracking report to show overall movement patterns.
semantic_tags: Data processing|Edge computing|Data reduction|Data summary|Efficiency|Network optimization
title: Data Aggregation (IoT)

definition: Data filtering in IoT is the process of selectively removing unwanted, irrelevant, or erroneous data from a stream of IoT data. This operation, often executed at the edge, helps to reduce noise, save bandwidth, improve data quality, and focus on critical information for analysis.
examples: Discarding sensor readings that fall outside a predefined normal operating range (e.g., temperature below -20°C or above 100°C).|Only transmitting data when a significant change (e.g., >5% deviation) is detected in a sensor reading.|Ignoring duplicate messages received from an IoT device to prevent redundant data processing.
semantic_tags: Data quality|Noise reduction|Data preprocessing|Edge computing|Data selection|Bandwidth optimization
title: Data Filtering (IoT)

definition: Data preprocessing at the edge refers to the set of operations applied to raw IoT data at or near the source (e.g., on a sensor node or IoT gateway) before it is transmitted to the cloud. Its goal is to improve data quality, reduce data volume, and prepare it for more efficient analysis and storage.
examples: Performing data aggregation and filtering out erroneous readings on an IoT gateway.|Normalizing raw analog-to-digital converter (ADC) sensor values into meaningful engineering units (e.g., volts to Celsius).|De-duplicating messages or compressing data packets on an edge device before sending them over a constrained network.
semantic_tags: Edge computing|Data cleansing|Data transformation|Data reduction|Data preparation|Local processing
title: Data Preprocessing (Edge)

definition: Actuator control is the process of managing and operating physical devices (actuators) that affect the real world, typically in response to sensor data, system commands, or programmed logic within an embedded or IoT system. It translates digital signals into physical actions.
examples: Turning on an HVAC system when a smart thermostat's temperature sensor detects the room temperature rising above a set threshold.|Opening a smart lock via a mobile application command transmitted to an IoT gateway.|Adjusting the flow of water in an irrigation system based on soil moisture data and weather forecasts.

examples: A barometer integrated into a weather station to measure atmospheric pressure.|A sensor in a tire pressure monitoring system (TPMS) to alert drivers of low tire pressure.|A strain gauge-based pressure sensor used in a hydraulic system to monitor fluid pressure and prevent overloads.

definition: An accelerometer sensor is a device that measures proper acceleration (g-force) in its own rest frame. It detects both static acceleration due to gravity and dynamic acceleration resulting from motion or vibration, typically along one or more axes.
examples: Detecting sudden impacts or drops in a smart package tracking system.|Measuring steps and activity levels in a fitness tracker or smartwatch.|Determining device orientation (portrait/landscape) in a smartphone or tablet.
title: Accelerometer Sensor

definition: A gyroscope sensor is a device that measures angular velocity, which is the rate of rotation around an axis. It provides information about an object's rotational movement and changes in orientation, often complementing accelerometers for full 6-DoF motion tracking.
examples: Stabilizing a drone's flight by detecting and counteracting unwanted rotations.|Enabling precise head tracking for immersive experiences in virtual reality headsets.|Enhancing the accuracy of navigation systems by tracking rotational changes alongside linear motion.

examples: Providing a digital compass function in smartphones and navigation devices.|Detecting proximity to magnets in industrial automation for object sensing.|Used in geological surveys to map magnetic anomalies in the Earth's crust.
semantic_tags: Magnetic field|Compass|Orientation|Geomagnetic field|Ferrous detection|Inertial Measurement Unit
title: Magnetometer Sensor

definition: An Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) is an electronic device that measures and reports a body's specific force, angular rate, and sometimes magnetic field surrounding the body. It typically integrates accelerometers, gyroscopes, and magnetometers to provide comprehensive motion and orientation data.
examples: Providing attitude and heading reference for drones and autonomous vehicles.|Enabling precise motion tracking and gesture recognition in wearables and gaming controllers.|Stabilizing camera gimbals by detecting and correcting unwanted movements in real-time.
title: Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU)

definition: A GPS receiver is a device that receives signals from Global Positioning System (GPS) satellites to calculate its precise geographical position (latitude, longitude, and altitude) and accurate time. It is a cornerstone for location-based services and navigation.
examples: Tracking the real-time location of assets or vehicles in a logistics and fleet management system.|Providing navigation data for autonomous vehicles and delivery drones.|Geo-tagging environmental data collected by mobile IoT sensors for spatial analysis.
title: GPS Receiver

definition: A light sensor is a device that detects the intensity of ambient light and converts it into an electrical signal. It is commonly used for brightness control, presence detection, and monitoring environmental light conditions.
examples: Automatically adjusting smartphone screen brightness based on ambient light levels.|Controlling smart lighting systems in homes or offices to save energy and improve comfort.|Detecting occupancy in a room to activate or deactivate HVAC systems.

title: LIDAR Sensor

title: RADAR Sensor

definition: An acoustic-to-electric transducer that converts sound waves into electrical signals, used in IoT devices for sound detection, voice command input, or environmental noise monitoring.

title: Camera Module (IoT Application)

definition: A Passive Infrared (PIR) sensor detects infrared radiation emitted by objects, primarily used in IoT to sense the presence and motion of people or animals by detecting changes in infrared patterns, often for security and energy management.

definition: A device that detects the presence and concentration of specific gases in the ambient environment, crucial for safety, environmental monitoring, and air quality applications in IoT.

definition: A sensor designed to measure the concentration of tiny solid or liquid particles suspended in the air (particulate matter, PM), commonly used in IoT for real-time indoor and outdoor air quality monitoring.
