definition: Encourages the widespread dissemination of knowledge, best practices, and lessons learned across teams and organizations. It promotes transparency and collective learning, ensuring that insights gained in one area benefit the entire system.
examples: Documenting runbooks, architectural decisions, and post-mortem findings in a shared wiki.|Conducting 'lunch and learn' sessions to share new tools or techniques.|Creating internal communities of practice for specific technologies or roles.
title: Sharing Principle (DevOps)

definition: Involves creating rapid, frequent, and direct communication channels for information flow throughout the software delivery process, enabling quick detection of issues and continuous adaptation. Shortened feedback loops allow for early error detection and faster remediation.
examples: Unit tests providing immediate feedback on code correctness during development.|CI/CD pipelines failing quickly upon build errors or failed tests.|Real-time application monitoring alerting operations to production issues.
title: Feedback Loop Principle

definition: A mindset and set of practices where teams are constantly seeking ways to enhance processes, tools, and systems to achieve better outcomes. It involves regular retrospection, experimentation, and adaptation based on feedback and measurements.
examples: Holding regular retrospective meetings to identify process inefficiencies.|Experimenting with new deployment strategies to reduce downtime.|Automating previously manual steps after an incident reveals a weakness.
title: Continuous Improvement Culture

definition: A detailed analysis of an incident or failure conducted with the primary goal of understanding contributing factors and preventing recurrence, rather than assigning fault. It focuses on systemic improvements and learning from mistakes in a psychologically safe environment.
examples: After a production outage, conducting a meeting where team members analyze the sequence of events, technical failures, and communication breakdowns without fear of blame.|Documenting findings in a shared report that includes action items for system enhancements.|Identifying missing monitoring or insufficient testing as root causes, leading to improvements.
semantic_tags: Incident Management|Learning|Systemic Improvement|Psychological Safety|Root Cause Analysis|No Blame
title: Blameless Postmortem

definition: The practice of moving quality assurance, security, and testing activities earlier in the software development lifecycle. By integrating these concerns from the initial design and coding phases, potential issues can be identified and resolved sooner, reducing cost and effort.
examples: Developers running static code analysis tools on their local machines before committing code.|Security reviews being part of the design phase, not just before production deployment.|Writing unit tests and integration tests concurrently with feature development.
title: Shift Left Principle

definition: The practice of managing and provisioning IT infrastructure, applications, configurations, policies, and documentation using machine-readable definition files and version control systems, treating them like source code. This enables automation, consistency, and reproducibility.
examples: Defining cloud infrastructure using Terraform or AWS CloudFormation.|Managing application configurations with Helm charts or Ansible playbooks.|Storing network configurations and security policies in Git repositories.
semantic_tags: Infrastructure as Code (IaC)|Configuration as Code|Policy as Code|Version Control|Automation|Reproducibility
title: Everything as Code Principle

definition: A discipline that applies aspects of software engineering to operations problems, aiming to create ultra-scalable and highly reliable software systems. SRE focuses on balancing the need for system reliability with the need to ship new features quickly, using metrics like Service Level Objectives (SLOs).
examples: An SRE team defining and monitoring Service Level Objectives (SLOs) for an application's uptime and latency.|Automating operational tasks like deployments, rollbacks, and incident response.|Spending a percentage of their time (e.g., 50%) on engineering to improve system reliability and reduce toil.
title: Site Reliability Engineering Principle

definition: An approach where servers and other infrastructure components are never modified after being deployed; instead, if any changes are needed, a new, updated instance is built and deployed, replacing the old one. This ensures consistency, simplifies rollbacks, and prevents configuration drift.
examples: Deploying new Docker containers or Virtual Machine images for every application update.|Using tools like Packer to build machine images (AMIs, VMDKs) that are then deployed without modification.|Replacing an entire Kubernetes pod or deployment instead of patching a running container.
title: Immutable Infrastructure Principle

definition: An operational framework that uses Git as the single source of truth for declarative infrastructure and applications, enabling automated deployment, management, and monitoring of systems. All changes to infrastructure and applications are made through Git commits, which then drive automated updates.
examples: Committing a change to a Kubernetes manifest in a Git repository, which triggers a CI/CD pipeline to apply that change to the cluster.|Using Flux CD or Argo CD to continuously synchronize the desired state defined in Git with the actual state of the cluster.|Rolling back to a previous infrastructure state by reverting a Git commit.
title: GitOps Principle

definition: A discipline that brings financial accountability to the variable spend model of cloud, enabling organizations to make business trade-offs between speed, cost, and quality. It combines finance, technology, and business principles to drive financial accountability in the cloud.
examples: Teams analyzing cloud spend data to optimize resource usage and identify cost-saving opportunities (e.g., rightsizing instances).|Implementing budget alerts and cost allocation strategies for cloud resources.|Developers and operations teams collaborating with finance to understand the cost implications of architectural decisions.
semantic_tags: Cloud Cost Management|Financial Accountability|Cost Optimization|Cloud Economics|Business Value|Finance
title: FinOps Principle

definition: An extension of DevOps that integrates security practices throughout the entire software development lifecycle, from design to deployment and operations. It aims to embed security considerations into every stage, making security a shared responsibility rather than an afterthought.
examples: Integrating static application security testing (SAST) tools into the CI pipeline.|Conducting dynamic application security testing (DAST) in staging environments.|Automating security policy checks before infrastructure provisioning.
title: DevSecOps Principle

definition: A lean management technique used to visualize, analyze, and improve the flow of work required to deliver a product or service to a customer. It identifies all steps in a process, differentiating value-adding from non-value-adding activities, to reveal opportunities for optimization.
examples: Drawing a diagram that maps out all steps from a new feature idea to its deployment in production, including handoffs, wait times, and rework.|Identifying bottlenecks in the CI/CD pipeline, such as long manual testing phases or approval gates.|Using the map to prioritize improvements that reduce lead time and improve efficiency.
title: Value Stream Mapping

definition: A belief that one will not be punished or humiliated for speaking up with ideas, questions, concerns, or mistakes. In DevOps, it's crucial for effective collaboration, learning from failures, and fostering an environment where teams can openly experiment and improve without fear.
examples: Conducting blameless postmortems after an incident.|Encouraging team members to admit mistakes early without fear of reprisal.|Creating an environment where junior team members feel comfortable asking questions or challenging assumptions.
title: Psychological Safety (DevOps)

definition: The practice of creating independent lines of development within a Git repository, allowing multiple developers to work on different features or fixes concurrently without affecting the main codebase until their work is ready to be merged.
examples: Creating a `feature/new-login` branch to develop a new login page.|Using a `bugfix/issue-123` branch to fix a production bug.|Maintaining `main` (or `master`) and `develop` branches for stable releases and ongoing development respectively.
title: Git Branching

definition: The practice of marking specific points in a Git repository's history as important, typically used to denote release points (e.g., v1.0, v2.0). Tags are permanent pointers to a specific commit and are commonly used to create release versions of software.
examples: Creating a lightweight tag `git tag v1.0` after a successful production deployment.|Creating an annotated tag `git tag -a v2.0 -m "Release version 2.0"` for more descriptive release information.|Using tags to checkout specific historical versions of the codebase for auditing or bug reproduction.
title: Git Tagging

definition: A Git command used to display a history of commits in the current repository, showing details like commit hash, author, date, and commit message. It helps developers understand changes over time, track who made what, and pinpoint when specific modifications occurred.
examples: Running `git log` to view the full commit history.|Using `git log --oneline --graph` for a concise, graphical view of the commit history and branches.|Executing `git log -p filename.txt` to see the changes (diffs) made to a specific file across its history.
title: Git Log

definition: Git Diff is a command-line utility that shows the differences between two Git trees, such as commits, branches, files, or the working directory and the staging area. It highlights lines that have been added, removed, or modified, helping developers understand changes.
examples: `git diff` to show changes in the working directory not yet staged.|`git diff --staged` to show changes staged but not yet committed.|`git diff HEAD~1 HEAD` to compare the last two commits.
title: Git Diff

definition: Git Conflict Resolution is the process of manually resolving conflicting changes when Git cannot automatically merge divergent histories from different branches or commits. It typically involves editing the conflicting files, choosing which changes to keep, and then marking the conflict as resolved.
examples: Manually editing a file with `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>` markers to combine changes.|Using a merge tool like `git mergetool` to graphically resolve differences.|Deciding to accept changes from one branch over another when merging.
title: Git Conflict Resolution

definition: A Git Hook is a script that Git executes automatically before or after certain events, such as committing, pushing, or receiving commits. These hooks allow for custom automation and policy enforcement within a Git workflow.
examples: A `pre-commit` hook to run code linters and prevent commits with style violations.|A `post-receive` hook on a remote server to trigger a CI pipeline after a push.|A `prepare-commit-msg` hook to automatically add a Jira ticket ID to commit messages.
title: Git Hook

definition: Semantic Versioning (SemVer) is a versioning scheme that communicates the type of changes in a software release using a MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH format. MAJOR version increments for incompatible API changes, MINOR for new backward-compatible functionality, and PATCH for backward-compatible bug fixes.
examples: Changing from `1.0.0` to `2.0.0` indicates breaking changes in an API.|Changing from `1.0.0` to `1.1.0` indicates new features were added without breaking existing ones.|Changing from `1.0.0` to `1.0.1` indicates a bug fix that doesn't affect compatibility.
title: Semantic Versioning (SemVer)

definition: A Distributed Version Control System (DVCS) is a type of version control system where every user has a complete copy of the repository, including its full history, locally on their machine. This allows for offline work, faster operations, and greater resilience compared to centralized systems.
examples: Git, where each developer clones the entire repository and its history to their local machine.|Mercurial, which operates on a similar distributed model to Git.|Bazaar, another DVCS providing distributed revision control for software development.
title: Distributed Version Control System (DVCS)

definition: A Monorepo is a single repository that contains multiple distinct projects, often with unrelated or loosely related codebases. This approach can simplify dependency management, enable cross-project refactoring, and provide unified versioning for all included components.
examples: Google's single large repository containing code for many different services and applications.|A front-end application, its backend API, and shared UI component library all in one Git repo.|A company storing all its microservices within a single repository.
title: Monorepo

definition: A Polyrepo is a repository strategy where each project or component is managed in its own separate and independent version control repository. This approach allows for individual versioning, separate deployment cycles, and clear ownership boundaries for each codebase.
examples: A microservices architecture where each service has its own dedicated Git repository.|An organization managing a web application, a mobile app, and a backend API in three separate repos.|An open-source project where the core library, plugins, and documentation each reside in their own repository.
title: Polyrepo

definition: The Forking Workflow is a Git workflow commonly used in open-source projects, where developers create a personal copy (fork) of the main repository. Changes are made on the fork, then proposed back to the original repository via a pull request, allowing for review before merging.
examples: A contributor forks a public GitHub project, makes changes, and submits a pull request to the upstream repository.|An enterprise team uses forks to manage individual developer sandboxes before merging to a central repository.|A developer creating a personal fork to experiment with a new feature without affecting the main codebase.
title: Forking Workflow

definition: Revert Commit is a Git command that undoes changes introduced by a specific commit by creating a new commit that reverses the effects of the chosen commit. Unlike `reset`, `revert` creates new history, making it safe for shared branches as it doesn't rewrite history.
examples: `git revert HEAD` to undo the most recent commit by creating a new commit.|`git revert <commit-hash>` to undo a specific commit further back in history.|Reverting a merge commit to undo the entire merge operation while preserving subsequent history.
title: Revert Commit

definition: A CI Pipeline Definition is a configuration file, typically written in YAML or a domain-specific language (DSL), that outlines the automated steps and stages required to build, test, and package software. It defines the sequence of jobs executed by a CI/CD orchestrator upon specific triggers.
examples: A `.gitlab-ci.yml` file defining stages like `build`, `test`, `deploy` with associated jobs.|A `Jenkinsfile` written in Groovy DSL specifying pipeline steps for a multi-stage build.|A `azure-pipelines.yml` file configuring tasks for a .NET application's CI/CD process.
title: CI Pipeline Definition

definition: A Pipeline Trigger is an event or condition that initiates the execution of a CI/CD pipeline. These triggers automate the pipeline process, ensuring that builds and deployments run consistently in response to specific actions or schedules.
examples: A Git push to a specific branch (e.g., `main` or `develop`) automatically starting a build and test pipeline.|A scheduled cron job running a nightly build or deployment to a staging environment.|A manual trigger initiated by a developer for an on-demand deployment or specific test run.
title: Pipeline Trigger

definition: Unit Testing Execution involves running automated tests on the smallest testable parts of an application, known as units, in isolation from the rest of the code. The goal is to verify that each unit of code performs as expected.
examples: Running `pytest` or `unittest` commands in a Python project as a CI pipeline step.|Executing `npm test` for JavaScript applications with frameworks like Jest or Mocha.|Integrating JUnit tests in a Java build process using Maven or Gradle within a CI job.
title: Unit Testing Execution

definition: Integration Testing Execution involves running tests that verify the interactions and interfaces between different modules, components, or systems within an application. These tests ensure that separate units, when combined, function correctly as a group.
examples: A CI pipeline running tests that call multiple microservices to verify their communication and data flow.|Testing the interaction between a web application's frontend and its backend API.|Executing tests that interact with a database to ensure proper data storage and retrieval by application components.
title: Integration Testing Execution

definition: Code Linting is the process of statically analyzing source code to flag programmatic errors, bugs, stylistic errors, and suspicious constructs. It helps enforce coding standards, improve code quality, and identify potential issues early in the development cycle.
examples: Running ESLint on JavaScript code to enforce formatting rules and identify syntax errors.|Using Pylint or Flake8 in a Python project to check for style violations and potential bugs.|Integrating a linter like RuboCop into a Ruby CI pipeline to maintain code consistency.
title: Code Linting

definition: Dependency Scanning, also known as Software Composition Analysis (SCA), is the process of identifying known vulnerabilities and licensing issues in open-source components and third-party libraries used within a project. It helps manage supply chain security and compliance.
examples: Using tools like Snyk or OWASP Dependency-Check in a CI pipeline to scan `package.json` or `pom.xml` for vulnerable dependencies.|Identifying a high-severity CVE in a transitive dependency of a NodeJS application.|Checking if imported libraries have licenses compatible with the project's requirements.
title: Dependency Scanning

definition: Vulnerability Scanning in CI refers to integrating automated security scans directly into the Continuous Integration pipeline to detect security flaws in application code, container images, or infrastructure as code. This proactively identifies risks before deployment.
examples: Running SAST (Static Application Security Testing) tools like SonarQube on source code during the `build` stage.|Scanning Docker images for known vulnerabilities using tools like Trivy or Clair before pushing to a registry.|Executing DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing) against a deployed test environment to find runtime vulnerabilities.
title: Vulnerability Scanning (CI)

definition: Artifact Management is the process of storing, versioning, and distributing build outputs (artifacts) such as compiled binaries, executable files, container images, and deployment packages. An artifact repository centralizes these outputs, ensuring consistency and traceability across environments.
examples: Storing compiled Java JAR/WAR files in a Maven repository like Artifactory or Nexus.|Pushing Docker container images to a container registry like Docker Hub, GCR, or ECR.|Managing NuGet packages for .NET applications in a dedicated package feed.
title: Artifact Management

definition: Test Reporting is the process of collecting, aggregating, and presenting the results of automated tests executed during a CI/CD pipeline. These reports provide immediate feedback on code quality and functional correctness, indicating pass/fail statuses and detailed breakdowns.
examples: Generating an XML-based JUnit test report that CI/CD orchestrators can parse to display test outcomes.|Integrating with a test management system to centralize and visualize test execution trends and coverage.|Displaying a summary of unit, integration, and end-to-end test results directly in a GitLab CI/CD pipeline dashboard.
title: Test Reporting

definition: A Build Agent (also known as a CI runner or worker) is a software component or dedicated machine (virtual or physical) that executes jobs defined in a CI/CD pipeline. It communicates with the CI/CD orchestrator, pulls code, runs specified commands, and reports results.
examples: A Jenkins agent (slave) running on a virtual machine to build Java applications.|A GitLab Runner executing pipeline jobs in a Docker container on a Kubernetes cluster.|A self-hosted GitHub Actions runner installed on a developer's server for specific environment requirements.
title: Build Agent

definition: A CI/CD Orchestrator is a platform or tool that manages, schedules, and executes automated pipelines for Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery. It coordinates various stages like building, testing, scanning, and deploying software, providing a central control plane for the entire software delivery lifecycle.
examples: Jenkins, a popular open-source automation server for CI/CD.|GitLab CI/CD, integrated directly into the GitLab platform for seamless pipeline management.|GitHub Actions, providing workflow automation within GitHub repositories for CI/CD tasks.
title: CI/CD Orchestrator

definition: Running multiple independent steps or modules of a build process concurrently to reduce overall build time. This is achieved by distributing tasks across available resources, such as multiple CPU cores or build agents.
examples: Compiling different microservices in separate jobs simultaneously in a Jenkins pipeline.|Using `make -j` or Maven's `--threads` option to build different modules of a large project concurrently.|Running unit tests for frontend and backend code on different agents at the same time.
title: Parallel Build Execution

definition: The strategy and tools used within a CI/CD pipeline to store and reuse artifacts, dependencies, or intermediate build outputs from previous runs. This significantly reduces build times by avoiding redundant downloads or compilations.
examples: Caching `node_modules` directory in a GitLab CI pipeline to avoid re-downloading npm packages on subsequent builds.|Storing compiled `.o` files or Maven's `.m2` repository contents between Jenkins build jobs.|Using Docker layer caching to speed up subsequent image builds in a multi-stage Dockerfile.
title: Cache Management (CI/CD)

definition: Executing a build process inside an isolated container (e.g., Docker) rather than directly on the build agent's host system. This ensures a consistent and reproducible build environment, free from host-specific dependencies or conflicts.
examples: Running `mvn clean install` inside a `maven:3.8-openjdk-11` Docker container in a CI job.|Building a Node.js application inside a `node:16-alpine` container to guarantee specific Node.js and npm versions.|Using a custom Docker image containing all necessary compilers and tools for a complex C++ project.
title: Containerized Build

definition: The practice of defining and controlling configuration parameters and sensitive information within a CI/CD pipeline using environment variables. This allows dynamic configuration of build and deployment processes without hardcoding values directly into scripts.
examples: Setting `NODE_ENV=production` for a production build job in a GitHub Actions workflow.|Passing `DATABASE_URL` as an environment variable to a deployment script to connect to the correct database instance.|Using a `CI_COMMIT_SHA` environment variable provided by GitLab CI within a build script to tag Docker images.
title: Environment Variable Management

definition: The secure handling, storage, and access of sensitive information, such as API keys, database credentials, or private SSH keys, within a CI/CD pipeline. It aims to prevent secrets from being exposed in logs, version control, or insecure environments.
examples: Storing a `DATABASE_PASSWORD` in a secrets vault (e.g., HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) and injecting it into a CI/CD pipeline at runtime.|Using encrypted environment variables in GitHub Actions or GitLab CI to protect access tokens.|Limiting access to production credentials only to specific deployment agents or users via IAM roles.
title: Secret Management (CI/CD)

definition: A client-side Git hook that runs automatically before a commit is created, allowing validation or modification of the pending changes. It can be used to enforce code quality standards, run linters, or format code, preventing problematic commits from entering the repository.
examples: Running a Python linter (e.g., Black, Flake8) on staged files before allowing a commit.|Ensuring all code is formatted using Prettier before the commit is finalized.|Checking for common mistakes like debug statements or incomplete placeholder text in modified files.
title: Pre-commit Hook

definition: A server-side Git hook that executes after a successful merge operation to the repository. While less common in general CI/CD, it can be used for custom notifications, integration with external systems, or triggering specific actions after a merge event.
examples: Automatically updating a read-only mirror repository after a merge to the main branch.|Sending a custom notification to a chat channel (e.g., Slack) indicating a successful merge to a critical branch.|Triggering a specific external build system or reporting tool based on the merged changes.
title: Post-merge Hook

definition: A declarative or scripted description of the automated stages, steps, and conditions required to release software from version control through to production environments. It orchestrates testing, building, artifact management, and deployment processes.
examples: A `jenkinsfile` defining stages like `Build`, `Test`, `Deploy Staging`, `Approve`, `Deploy Production`.|A `.gitlab-ci.yml` file specifying jobs for `build`, `test`, `release`, and `deploy` to different environments.|An Azure DevOps YAML pipeline defining deployment stages to various environments with associated approvals.
title: CD Pipeline Definition

definition: A deployment strategy where new versions of an application are gradually rolled out by replacing instances of the old version one by one or in small batches. This minimizes downtime and risk by keeping a portion of the old version running while the new version is being deployed.
examples: Updating a Kubernetes Deployment by replacing old pods with new ones incrementally until all pods are updated.|Deploying a new version of a web application to one server at a time in a load-balanced cluster.|Cloud platforms like AWS ECS or Azure App Service performing rolling updates automatically for service tasks.
semantic_tags: Deployment strategies|Zero downtime|Incremental update|Risk reduction|High availability|Blue/Green
title: Rolling Deployment

definition: A deployment strategy that completely shuts down all instances of the old version of an application before starting up the new version. This method is simpler to implement but results in downtime for the duration of the deployment.
examples: Deleting all existing pods for a Kubernetes Deployment and then creating all new pods for the updated version.|Stopping all instances of a web application on a server, deploying the new code, and then starting all instances again.|Directly replacing an older Docker container with a new one, causing a brief service interruption.
title: Recreate Deployment

definition: A deployment strategy where different versions of an application or features are released simultaneously to distinct subsets of users to compare their performance and user engagement. This allows data-driven decisions on which version performs better before a full rollout.
examples: Releasing version A of a new checkout flow to 50% of users and version B to the other 50% to see which converts better.|Showing a new UI element to a segment of users while the rest see the old one, measuring click-through rates.|Using a feature flagging system to route different user groups to different backend API versions.
title: A/B Testing Deployment

definition: The practice of enabling or disabling specific features in an application dynamically at runtime, without requiring a new code deployment. This is achieved by using feature flags (also known as feature toggles), which are conditional switches within the codebase.
examples: Toggling a new payment gateway on or off for specific user groups via a remote configuration service.|Disabling a problematic feature immediately in production without rolling back the entire application.|Rolling out a new feature gradually to an internal team, then beta users, then the general public.
semantic_tags: Feature toggles|Dynamic configuration|Release management|Risk reduction|A/B testing|Dark launch
title: Feature Flag Management

definition: Deploying a new feature or service into a production environment, but keeping it hidden or inactive for end-users. This allows for real-world testing and performance monitoring without impacting the user experience, before officially activating the feature.
examples: Deploying a new recommendation engine that processes user requests in the background but doesn't influence what users see.|Releasing a new API endpoint to production but not exposing it through the frontend until thorough testing is complete.|Using feature flags to hide a complete UI overhaul from all users while collecting metrics on its performance.
semantic_tags: Progressive Delivery|Feature flags|Risk reduction|Production testing|Silent launch|Monitoring
title: Dark Launch

definition: An umbrella term for advanced deployment strategies that reduce risk by gradually exposing new software versions or features to an increasing subset of users or environments. This includes techniques like Canary deployments, A/B testing, and Dark Launches.
examples: First deploying a new service to an internal dogfooding environment, then to 5% of users, then 20%, and finally 100%.|Combining feature flags with a staged rollout to control both feature visibility and infrastructure scale.|Using tools like Argo Rollouts or Spinnaker to automate canary releases based on real-time metrics.
semantic_tags: Deployment strategies|Risk reduction|Canary release|A/B testing|Dark launch|Feature flags
title: Progressive Delivery

definition: The practice of embedding monitoring and observability tools and checks directly into the Continuous Delivery pipeline. This ensures that the health, performance, and behavior of deployed applications are continuously tracked and validated post-deployment.
examples: Automatically running synthetic tests and checking application metrics (e.g., latency, error rates) after a deployment to production.|Integrating a Datadog or Prometheus dashboard check into a CD pipeline, failing the deployment if critical metrics are breached.|Using log aggregation tools (e.g., ELK stack, Splunk) to monitor new deployments for unusual log patterns.
title: Continuous Monitoring Integration (CD)

definition: The automatic process of reverting an application or service to a previously stable version if a new deployment fails or introduces critical issues. This minimizes the impact of failed deployments by quickly restoring known good functionality without manual intervention.
examples: A Kubernetes deployment configured to automatically revert to the previous replica set if new pods fail health checks.|A CI/CD pipeline step that, upon detecting production errors (e.g., high error rates), triggers a redeployment of the last successful artifact.|Using an AWS CloudFormation change set to automatically revert if post-deployment tests fail.
title: Automated Rollback

definition: A mandatory manual or automated step within a Continuous Delivery pipeline that requires explicit approval before proceeding to the next stage, typically a sensitive environment like production. This ensures human oversight or compliance checks are met before critical deployments.
examples: Requiring a manual approval from a team lead before deploying to the production environment in Jenkins or Azure DevOps.|An automated security scan (e.g., SAST/DAST) whose successful completion is required before a deployment can proceed.|A ticket in an ITSM system (e.g., Jira, ServiceNow) needing to be marked "Approved" before the pipeline continues.
title: Approval Gate (CD)

definition: A strategy for gradually rolling out new software by deploying it to a series of progressively larger and more critical environments or user groups. Each ring serves as a test bed, validating stability and performance before moving to the next.
examples: Deploying to "internal development team" ring, then "alpha users" ring, then "beta users" ring, and finally "all users" ring.|Releasing to a "canary server" ring, then "staging servers" ring, then "production servers (regional)" ring.|Microsoft using "rings" to release Windows updates, starting with Insiders and gradually expanding to the general public.
semantic_tags: Progressive Delivery|Staged rollout|Risk reduction|Canary release|User groups|Environments
title: Deployment Ring

definition: A deployment strategy that ensures an application remains continuously available and accessible to users throughout the entire update process, with no service interruption. This typically involves running old and new versions concurrently for a period.
examples: Using a Blue/Green deployment where traffic is switched instantaneously from an old (blue) environment to a new (green) one.|Implementing a Canary deployment where a small subset of traffic is directed to the new version before a full rollout.|Kubernetes rolling updates that gracefully terminate old pods only after new ones are healthy and ready to serve traffic.
title: Zero Downtime Deployment

definition: A deployment process that can be run multiple times on the same target environment and produce the exact same desired state each time, without unintended side effects or failures on subsequent runs. This property makes deployments robust and recoverable.
examples: A configuration management script (e.g., Ansible, Chef) that ensures a file exists with specific content, creating it if absent or updating it if different, but doing nothing if it's already correct.|A database migration script that only applies schema changes if they haven't been applied yet, not attempting to create existing tables.|Deploying a Docker image to Kubernetes, where Kubernetes ensures the specified number of replicas are running the correct image, regardless of previous states.
title: Idempotent Deployment

definition: The process of packaging, configuring, and installing an application onto servers or infrastructure, making it available for use. It typically involves steps like artifact transfer, dependency installation, configuration setup, and service startup.
examples: Deploying a new version of a web application to a Kubernetes cluster using a CI/CD pipeline.|Copying WAR files to a Tomcat server's webapps directory and restarting Tomcat.|Using AWS CodeDeploy to push a new build to EC2 instances.
title: Application Deployment

definition: A rapid set of essential tests performed immediately after an application deployment to ensure that the core functionalities are working correctly and the application is stable enough for further testing or production traffic. It aims to catch critical issues early.
examples: Pinging a newly deployed web service endpoint to check for a 200 OK response.|Logging into the application's main page and verifying key UI elements load.|Executing a simple transaction to confirm database connectivity and basic business logic.
title: Post-deployment Smoke Testing

definition: A deliberate pause in an automated Continuous Delivery pipeline that requires human approval or action before the pipeline can proceed to subsequent stages. This is often used for critical deployments, regulatory compliance, or final go/no-go decisions.
examples: A pipeline stage that pauses and awaits a 'Release Manager Approval' click before deploying to production.|Requiring a security team's manual penetration test results to be uploaded before continuing.|A human-driven check of log files or monitoring dashboards after a canary deployment before promoting traffic.
title: Manual Intervention Step (CD)

definition: A strategy for coordinating software releases across multiple teams or components, where new features or updates are bundled together and released on a fixed, predictable schedule. This approach aims to synchronize development and deployment cycles, ensuring all components are tested and released concurrently.
examples: A large enterprise coordinating quarterly releases where multiple product teams contribute features to a single, synchronized deployment schedule.|SAFe (Scaled Agile Framework) often utilizes release trains to manage large-scale agile development and delivery.|A platform team pushing updates to microservices, all adhering to a monthly release cadence.
title: Release Train

definition: A language where you specify the *desired state* of a system without explicitly defining the step-by-step instructions on *how* to achieve that state. The underlying system interprets the declaration and figures out the necessary actions.
examples: A Kubernetes YAML manifest defining a `Deployment` with 3 replicas, leaving Kubernetes to figure out how to create/manage pods.|Terraform HCL defining an AWS S3 bucket and its properties, letting Terraform handle the API calls.|SQL DDL (Data Definition Language) like `CREATE TABLE users (...)`, where the database handles the physical creation.
title: Declarative Configuration Language

definition: A language where you specify the *exact steps or commands* that need to be executed in a specific order to achieve a desired system state. It focuses on *how* to change the system.
examples: A shell script with commands like `apt-get install nginx`, `cp nginx.conf /etc/nginx/`, `service nginx start`.|Python scripts using cloud provider SDKs to provision resources step-by-step.|Ansible playbooks can often be imperative when using tasks that explicitly define sequential actions.
title: Imperative Configuration Language

definition: The process of identifying unauthorized or unintended changes to infrastructure or application configurations from their defined baseline or desired state. It helps maintain consistency, security, and compliance.
examples: A monitoring tool alerting when an EC2 instance's security group rules deviate from the Terraform-defined state.|Using AWS Config to track changes to S3 bucket policies and compare them against a golden template.|Running a nightly script that compares the current state of a server's installed packages against an Ansible inventory.
title: Configuration Drift Detection

definition: In Infrastructure as Code, idempotence means that applying the same configuration or command multiple times will always result in the same system state, without causing unintended side effects after the initial application. This ensures consistent and predictable infrastructure provisioning.
examples: A Terraform `apply` command that creates an S3 bucket only if it doesn't exist, and does nothing if it already exists with the correct configuration.|An Ansible playbook task to `ensure state=present` for a package, which installs it once and does nothing on subsequent runs if already installed.|A `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` SQL command in a database migration script.
title: Idempotence (IaC)

definition: HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language) is a declarative configuration language used by Terraform to define infrastructure resources. It's designed to be human-readable and machine-friendly, allowing users to express infrastructure requirements in a clear, concise manner.
examples: Defining an AWS S3 bucket: `resource "aws_s3_bucket" "my_bucket" { bucket = "my-unique-bucket-name" }`.|Declaring an EC2 instance: `resource "aws_instance" "web_server" { ami = "ami-0abcdef1234567890" instance_type = "t2.micro" }`.|Using variables: `variable "region" { description = "AWS region" type = string default = "us-east-1" }`.
title: Terraform HCL

definition: Terraform State is a critical file (`terraform.tfstate`) that records the mapping between the resources defined in your HCL code and the real-world infrastructure provisioned by Terraform. It tracks metadata, dependencies, and resource IDs, enabling Terraform to understand the current state of your infrastructure and plan changes effectively.
examples: The `terraform.tfstate` file stored locally after a `terraform apply`.|Configuring an S3 bucket and DynamoDB table as a remote backend for shared and locked state.|Using `terraform state show aws_instance.web_server` to inspect a resource's state.
semantic_tags: Terraform|Infrastructure as Code|State File|Remote Backend|Resource Tracking|Consistency
title: Terraform State Management

definition: A configuration in Terraform that specifies a remote location (e.g., S3, Azure Blob Storage, Git, Terraform Cloud) to store the `terraform.tfstate` file, rather than locally. This enables team collaboration, state locking, and secure storage for managing shared infrastructure.
examples: Configuring an AWS S3 bucket as a backend: `backend "s3" { bucket = "my-tf-state-bucket" key = "path/to/my/app.tfstate" region = "us-east-1" }`.|Using Azure Blob Storage: `backend "azurerm" { resource_group_name = "tfstate-rg" storage_account_name = "mytfstateaccount" container_name = "tfstate" key = "path/to/my/app.tfstate" }`.|Utilizing Terraform Cloud as a remote backend.
title: Terraform Remote Backend

definition: HashiCorp's managed service offering for Terraform, providing features like remote state storage, state locking, team collaboration, policy enforcement (Sentinel), cost estimation, and a UI for running Terraform operations. Terraform Enterprise is the self-hosted version for private environments.
examples: Using Terraform Cloud to run `terraform plan` and `terraform apply` in a consistent, controlled environment.|Implementing OPA or Sentinel policies in Terraform Cloud to prevent the creation of unencrypted S3 buckets.|Collaborating on infrastructure changes with multiple developers using workspaces and run history.
title: Terraform Cloud/Enterprise

definition: A single, one-off command executed by Ansible directly from the command line, without needing to write a formal playbook. It's typically used for quick tasks like checking system status, restarting services, or applying simple changes across multiple servers.
examples: Ping all hosts in the inventory: `ansible all -m ping`.|Restart Nginx on web servers: `ansible webservers -a "systemctl restart nginx" --become`.|Check disk usage on a specific server: `ansible my_server -a "df -h"`.
title: Ansible Ad-hoc Command

definition: A public hub for finding, sharing, and reusing Ansible content, primarily roles. It allows users to download pre-built roles for common tasks (e.g., installing a web server, configuring a database) and contributes to the modularity and reusability of Ansible automation.
examples: Installing a role from Galaxy: `ansible-galaxy install geerlingguy.nginx`.|Listing downloaded roles: `ansible-galaxy list`.|Sharing a custom role developed by a team by publishing it to Ansible Galaxy.
title: Ansible Galaxy

definition: In SaltStack, a "state" (often defined in a `.sls` file) is a declarative specification of the desired configuration or condition of a system. Salt uses these states to ensure target systems (minions) conform to the defined configuration, applying changes only if necessary to achieve idempotence.
examples: A state file (`nginx.sls`) ensuring the Nginx package is installed: `nginx: pkg.installed`.|Defining a service to be running: `nginx: service.running`.|Managing a file's content and permissions: `my_config: file.managed path: /etc/my.conf contents: | ... mode: 644`.
title: SaltStack State

definition: A JSON or YAML formatted text file that declaratively defines the AWS resources you want to provision and manage as a single unit (a "stack"). It allows for automated, repeatable, and consistent infrastructure deployment in AWS.
examples: A YAML template defining an EC2 instance, an S3 bucket, and a security group.|Using parameters in a template to make it reusable across different environments.|Updating an existing stack by submitting a modified CloudFormation template.
title: CloudFormation Template

definition: An open-source software development framework that allows developers to define cloud infrastructure in familiar programming languages (e.g., Python, TypeScript, Java) and then synthesize it into CloudFormation templates. It combines the power of high-level programming constructs with Infrastructure as Code.
examples: Defining an S3 bucket in TypeScript: `new s3.Bucket(this, 'MyBucket', { versioned: true });`.|Creating a multi-tier application stack in Python using CDK constructs.|Deploying a CDK application using the `cdk deploy` command.
title: AWS Cloud Development Kit (CDK)

definition: A JSON file that declaratively defines the infrastructure and configuration for your Azure solutions. It allows you to deploy, update, and delete all resources for your solution in a single, coordinated operation, ensuring consistency and idempotence.
examples: A JSON template defining an Azure Virtual Machine, VNet, and Storage Account.|Using ARM templates for consistent deployment of environments (dev, staging, prod).|Deploying an ARM template via Azure CLI: `az deployment group create --resource-group myRG --template-file azuredeploy.json`.
title: Azure Resource Manager (ARM) Template

definition: A domain-specific language (DSL) that offers a more concise, readable, and type-safe authoring experience for defining Azure resources than traditional ARM JSON templates. Bicep transpiles into standard ARM JSON templates before deployment to Azure.
examples: Defining an Azure Storage Account in Bicep: `resource storage 'Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts@2021-09-01' = { name: 'mystorageaccount' location: resourceGroup().location sku: { name: 'Standard_LRS' } kind: 'StorageV2' }`.|Using modules in Bicep to reuse common infrastructure patterns.|Compiling a Bicep file to an ARM template: `az bicep build --file main.bicep`.
title: Azure Bicep Language

definition: An Infrastructure as Code service for Google Cloud Platform that allows you to define and manage Google Cloud resources using declarative configuration files (YAML or Python). It enables automated and repeatable deployments of complex resource stacks.
examples: A YAML configuration defining a Google Compute Engine instance, a network, and a firewall rule.|Using Jinja2 or Python templates within Deployment Manager to create dynamic configurations.|Deploying a manifest: `gcloud deployment-manager deployments create my-deployment --config my_config.yaml`.
semantic_tags: Google Cloud|Infrastructure as Code|Deployment Manager|Declarative|YAML|Python|Resource Management
title: Google Cloud Deployment Manager

definition: The Pulumi Programming Model allows developers to define, deploy, and manage cloud infrastructure using familiar programming languages like Python, TypeScript, Go, and C#. It treats infrastructure as code (IaC), enabling imperative and declarative resource definitions within a single program.
examples: Defining an AWS S3 bucket using Python: `s3_bucket = aws.s3.Bucket('my-bucket')`|Creating a Kubernetes Deployment using TypeScript: `new k8s.apps.v1.Deployment('my-app-dep', { /* ... */ });`
semantic_tags: Infrastructure as Code (IaC)|Pulumi|Cloud Infrastructure|Programming Languages|Deployment Automation
title: Pulumi Programming Model

definition: A Packer template is a JSON or HCL file that defines how to build custom machine images for various platforms, such as AWS AMIs, Azure VHDs, VMware VMs, or VirtualBox images. It specifies sources (builders), provisioning steps (provisioners), and post-processing actions.
examples: A JSON template defining an AWS AMI build, using a shell script provisioner to install software.|An HCL template for a VirtualBox VM, installing dependencies with Ansible and then compacting the disk image.
title: Packer Template

definition: A Vagrantfile is a Ruby-based configuration file used by Vagrant to define the settings and provisioning steps for a virtual machine or a multi-machine environment. It specifies the base box, network configuration, shared folders, and shell scripts or other provisioners.
examples: A Vagrantfile specifying `config.vm.box = 'ubuntu/focal64'` and forwarding port 8080.|A Vagrantfile defining two VMs, a web server and a database server, and provisioning them with Puppet modules.
title: Vagrantfile

definition: A Crossplane Custom Resource (XR) extends the Kubernetes API to enable the provisioning and management of external infrastructure resources (like databases, message queues, or object storage) directly from Kubernetes. XRs allow platform teams to define high-level abstractions for infrastructure that developers can consume without needing to understand the underlying cloud provider specifics.
examples: A `CompositeResourceDefinition` for a 'PostgreSQLInstance' that abstracts away whether it's an AWS RDS instance or an Azure Database for PostgreSQL.|A `Deployment` in Kubernetes referencing a Crossplane `XPostgreSQLInstance` custom resource, causing an external database to be provisioned and bound to the application.
semantic_tags: Crossplane|Kubernetes|Custom Resource Definition (CRD)|Infrastructure as Code (IaC)|Platform Engineering|Control Plane
title: Crossplane Custom Resource

definition: Dockerfile syntax is the set of instructions and arguments used within a Dockerfile to define the steps for building a Docker image. Each instruction creates a new layer in the image, facilitating caching and reproducibility.
examples: `FROM ubuntu:latest` - Specifies the base image.|`RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y nginx` - Executes commands during the image build.|`COPY . /app` - Copies files from the host to the image.|`CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]` - Defines the default command to execute when the container starts.
title: Dockerfile Syntax

definition: The `docker build` command is used to construct a Docker image from a Dockerfile and a 'build context' (a set of files at a specified path). It processes the instructions in the Dockerfile sequentially, creating image layers.
examples: `docker build -t myapp:1.0 .` - Builds an image named 'myapp' with tag '1.0' from the Dockerfile in the current directory.|`docker build -f custom/Dockerfile -t myapp:dev github.com/myuser/myrepo#main:app` - Builds from a specific Dockerfile path in a Git repository.
title: Docker Build Command

definition: A Docker Compose file (typically `docker-compose.yml`) is a YAML file that defines a multi-container Docker application. It specifies services, networks, and volumes, allowing a single command (`docker compose up`) to start, stop, and manage the entire application stack.
examples: A `docker-compose.yml` defining a `web` service (Nginx) and a `db` service (PostgreSQL), both running in separate containers and connected via a default network.|A Compose file for a microservices application, including `frontend`, `backend`, and `redis` services, with custom networks and named volumes.
title: Docker Compose File

definition: A Docker Registry is a centralized service for storing and distributing Docker images. It acts as a repository for container images, allowing users to pull (download) images and push (upload) their own built images. Docker Hub is the most well-known public registry, but private registries can also be deployed.
examples: Docker Hub (public registry where official images like `ubuntu`, `nginx` are stored).|Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR) or Google Container Registry (GCR) as private cloud-hosted registries.|A locally deployed self-hosted Docker Registry instance for internal use.
title: Docker Registry

definition: The Container Networking Model describes how containers communicate with each other and with external networks. It defines the network stack within a container, how IP addresses are assigned, and how different network drivers (e.g., bridge, host, overlay) facilitate connectivity for single hosts or across multiple hosts.
examples: Containers on a `bridge` network can communicate with each other but are isolated from the host's primary network unless ports are mapped.|Containers using `host` networking share the host's network namespace, bypassing network isolation.|An `overlay` network allows containers on different Docker daemon hosts to communicate as if they were on the same network.
title: Container Networking Model

definition: A Container Volume Mount is a mechanism to provide persistent storage to a container, allowing data to persist beyond the container's lifecycle or to be shared between multiple containers. It maps a directory or file from the host machine or a managed volume to a path inside the container.
examples: `docker run -v /host/path:/container/path myimage` - Mounts a directory from the host.|`docker run -v mynamedvolume:/data myimage` - Mounts a Docker-managed named volume.|A Kubernetes Pod definition using a `PersistentVolumeClaim` to attach persistent storage to a container.
title: Container Volume Mount

definition: A multi-stage build in Docker involves using multiple `FROM` instructions in a single Dockerfile, where each `FROM` starts a new build stage. This technique allows developers to copy only the necessary artifacts from an earlier stage into the final image, significantly reducing image size and attack surface.
examples: Building a Go application: first stage compiles the Go binary, second stage copies *only* the binary into a minimal `scratch` or `alpine` base image.|Building a React application: first stage runs `npm install` and `npm run build`, second stage copies the static `build` output into an Nginx image.
title: Multi-stage Build (Docker)

definition: Image Layer Caching is a feature in container build systems (like Docker) where individual layers of an image are cached. When building an image, if an instruction and its context haven't changed since the last build, the system reuses the existing cached layer instead of re-executing the instruction, speeding up subsequent builds.
examples: If a `RUN apt-get update` instruction is followed by many `COPY` instructions for application code, only the `COPY` layers will be rebuilt if the code changes, not the `apt-get` layer.|Placing less frequently changing instructions (like dependency installs) higher up in a Dockerfile maximizes cache hits for subsequent builds.
title: Image Layer Caching

definition: Container Port Mapping, also known as port forwarding or publishing, allows a service running inside a container to be accessible from the host machine or an external network. It maps a specific port on the host to a port exposed by the container.
examples: `docker run -p 8080:80 mywebapp` - Maps host port 8080 to container port 80.|`docker run -p 127.0.0.1:80:80 mynginx` - Maps host port 80 to container port 80, only accessible from the host's localhost interface.
title: Container Port Mapping

definition: Image Tagging is the process of assigning human-readable labels or versions to container images. Tags are crucial for identifying specific versions, builds, or configurations of an image stored in a registry, enabling easy retrieval and deployment of the correct image.
examples: `myrepository/myimage:latest` - The `latest` tag often points to the most recent stable build.|`myrepository/myimage:v1.2.3` - A specific version tag for a production release.|`myrepository/myimage:feature-branch-xyz` - A tag for a specific development branch build.
title: Image Tagging (Container)

definition: Podman CLI (Command Line Interface) is a command-line tool for managing OCI-compliant containers, pods, and container images. Unlike Docker, Podman is daemonless and rootless by default, directly interacting with `runc` and other components, making it popular for security-conscious environments.
examples: `podman run -it ubuntu bash` - Runs an interactive bash shell in an Ubuntu container.|`podman build -t myapp .` - Builds a container image from a Dockerfile in the current directory.|`podman ps -a` - Lists all containers, including exited ones.
title: Podman CLI

definition: The Open Container Initiative (OCI) Specification is a set of open standards for container technology, primarily comprising the Image Format Specification and the Runtime Specification. OCI aims to ensure interoperability, portability, and a common foundation for building, running, and managing container images across different container platforms and tools.
examples: Docker, Podman, and containerd all implement the OCI Runtime Specification to execute containers.|OCI-compliant images built by Docker can be run by Podman and vice-versa, demonstrating image portability.|The `config.json` file inside an OCI image's `rootfs` describes the container's runtime configuration according to the OCI specification.
title: Open Container Initiative (OCI) Specification

definition: Container Image Security Scanning involves analyzing container images for known vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and compliance issues before deployment. These scanners typically examine image layers, dependencies, and installed packages against vulnerability databases to identify potential risks.
examples: Using Trivy to scan a Docker image for CVEs: `trivy image myimage:latest`|Integrating a security scanner like Clair or Anchore into a CI/CD pipeline to automatically block deployments of images with critical vulnerabilities.|Scanning a base image `ubuntu:latest` to ensure it doesn't contain outdated or vulnerable packages.
title: Container Image Security Scanning

definition: Container Orchestration is the automated management of containers, encompassing tasks like deployment, scaling, networking, load balancing, and self-healing. It addresses the challenges of operating many containers across a cluster of machines, ensuring high availability and efficient resource utilization.
examples: Kubernetes automatically deploys a web application across multiple nodes, scales instances based on load, and restarts failed containers.|Docker Swarm manages a cluster of Docker hosts, enabling services to be deployed and scaled.|Amazon ECS schedules and runs Docker containers on a cluster of EC2 instances.
title: Container Orchestration Concept

definition: Kubernetes Cluster Architecture describes the structure and components of a Kubernetes cluster, which consists of a Control Plane (formerly Master) and one or more Worker Nodes. The Control Plane manages the cluster state, while Worker Nodes run the actual containerized applications.
examples: A Control Plane with `kube-apiserver`, `etcd`, `kube-scheduler`, `kube-controller-manager`, and `cloud-controller-manager` components.|Worker Nodes running `kubelet`, `kube-proxy`, and a container runtime (e.g., Containerd or CRI-O).|A multi-master cluster setup for high availability of the Control Plane.
title: Kubernetes Cluster Architecture

definition: Kubernetes Node Components are the essential services that run on each worker node in a Kubernetes cluster, enabling it to host pods and interact with the control plane. These components include the `kubelet`, `kube-proxy`, and a container runtime.
examples: `kubelet`: An agent that ensures containers are running in a Pod.|`kube-proxy`: Maintains network rules on nodes, facilitating network communication to your Pods.|Container Runtime (e.g., `containerd` or `CRI-O`): Software responsible for running containers.
title: Kubernetes Node Component

definition: The smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes, a Pod encapsulates one or more containers, storage resources, a unique network IP, and options that govern how the containers run. It represents a single instance of a running process in a cluster.
examples: A Pod running a single Nginx web server container.|A Pod running an application container alongside a sidecar container for logging or metrics collection.
title: Kubernetes Pod Object

definition: A Kubernetes controller that manages a set of identical Pods, ensuring a desired number are running and available. It provides declarative updates for applications, enabling rolling updates and rollbacks, primarily for stateless workloads.
examples: Deploying 3 replicas of a web application to ensure high availability.|Performing a rolling update to gradually upgrade an API service to a new version without downtime.
title: Kubernetes Deployment Object

definition: An abstract way to expose an application running on a set of Pods as a network service with a stable IP address and DNS name. It acts as a load balancer and service discovery mechanism, providing a consistent access point to ephemeral Pods.
examples: A `ClusterIP` Service exposing an internal microservice only within the cluster.|A `NodePort` Service making a web application accessible from outside the cluster via a specific port on each node.|A `LoadBalancer` Service integrating with a cloud provider's external load balancer for public access.
title: Kubernetes Service Object

definition: An API object that manages external access to services within a cluster, typically HTTP/S, by providing HTTP routing rules. It allows centralized management of external access points, often implemented by an Ingress Controller like Nginx or Traefik.
examples: Routing `api.example.com` to a backend service and `blog.example.com` to another.|Enforcing TLS termination for all incoming HTTPS traffic before forwarding to backend services.
semantic_tags: External Access|HTTP Routing|Load Balancing|TLS Termination|Edge|API Gateway
title: Kubernetes Ingress Resource

definition: Used to store non-confidential configuration data as key-value pairs, making it available to Pods as environment variables, command-line arguments, or volume-mounted configuration files. It decouples configuration from container images for better portability and management.
examples: Storing application environment variables like `API_URL` or `FEATURE_TOGGLE`.|Providing Nginx configuration files to a web server Pod via a mounted volume.
title: Kubernetes ConfigMap Object

definition: Used to store sensitive information like passwords, OAuth tokens, and SSH keys securely. It provides a mechanism to inject sensitive data into Pods as files in a volume or as environment variables, minimizing their exposure.
examples: Storing a database password for an application Pod.|Providing an API key for an external service integration.|Mounting TLS certificates for an HTTPS server within a Pod.
title: Kubernetes Secret Object

definition: Manages the deployment and scaling of a set of Pods with unique, stable network identities and persistent storage. It's designed for stateful applications requiring ordered deployment, unique hostnames, and stable, persistent volumes.
examples: Deploying a Kafka cluster where each broker needs a stable network identity and dedicated storage.|Running a MongoDB replica set or a PostgreSQL database, ensuring ordered startup and shutdown of replicas.
semantic_tags: Stateful Applications|Persistent Storage|Ordered Deployment|Stable Identity|Database|Replica Set
title: Kubernetes StatefulSet Object

definition: Ensures that a copy of a specified Pod runs on *all* (or a selection of) nodes in a cluster. It's typically used for cluster-level operations or agents that need to be present on every node.
examples: Running a log collector (e.g., Fluentd, Logstash) on every node to gather logs.|Deploying a node monitoring agent or a storage provisioner across all worker nodes.
title: Kubernetes DaemonSet Object

definition: Creates one or more Pods and ensures that a specified number of them successfully terminate. It's used for batch jobs or one-off tasks that run to completion, rather than long-running services.
examples: Running a data processing script that needs to complete once.|Performing a database migration task.
title: Kubernetes Job Object

definition: Creates Jobs on a repeating schedule, similar to the `cron` utility in Unix-like systems. It's used for time-based, recurring tasks within the cluster, such as backups or report generation.
examples: Performing daily database backups at 2 AM.|Running a nightly data cleanup script.|Generating hourly analytics reports.
title: Kubernetes CronJob Object

definition: Provides a mechanism for isolating groups of resources within a single cluster, enabling resource quotas, access control, and logical separation for different teams or environments. Resources within a Namespace must have unique names but can share names with resources in other Namespaces.
examples: Separating `development`, `staging`, and `production` environments within one cluster.|Isolating resources for `team-a` and `team-b` to prevent conflicts and enforce quotas.
title: Kubernetes Namespace Object

definition: A set of access parameters for a Kubernetes cluster, containing a cluster name, user authentication, and an optional namespace. It allows `kubectl` to quickly switch between different clusters, users, and namespaces without re-specifying credentials.
examples: Switching between `dev-cluster` and `prod-cluster` configurations using `kubectl config use-context`.|Configuring a context that uses a specific user's credentials to access a particular namespace.
title: Kubernetes Context (kubectl)

definition: The front-end component of the Kubernetes control plane, exposing the Kubernetes API. It processes REST requests, validates them, and updates the state of API objects in `etcd`, serving as the central management point for the cluster.
examples: `kubectl` sending a `create pod` command, which is processed by the API Server.|A controller watching for resource changes via the API Server to reconcile desired state.|Any interaction with the Kubernetes cluster, whether from a user or another component, goes through the API Server.
title: Kubernetes API Server

definition: A highly available and consistent key-value store used by Kubernetes as its backing store for all cluster data. It stores the cluster's desired state, actual state, and configuration data, making it a critical component for cluster reliability.
examples: Storing definitions of all Pods, Deployments, and Services in the cluster.|Persistently storing the current configuration and operational state of all Kubernetes objects.
title: Kubernetes etcd Datastore

definition: An agent that runs on each worker node in the cluster, ensuring that containers are running in a Pod. It communicates with the API Server, takes PodSpecs, and manages container lifecycle on its node, reporting status back to the control plane.
examples: Kubelet starting a Docker container for a Pod assigned to its node.|Reporting the health and status of Pods and their containers back to the Kubernetes API Server.
title: Kubernetes Kubelet Agent

definition: A network proxy that runs on each node in the cluster, maintaining network rules on nodes and performing connection forwarding. It enables network communication between Pods and Services, inside and outside the cluster, by implementing the Kubernetes Service concept.
examples: Kube-proxy creating `iptables` rules to load balance traffic across Pods belonging to a Service.|Ensuring that traffic destined for a Service's IP is correctly routed to an available Pod.
title: Kubernetes Kube-proxy Component

definition: A control plane component that runs controller processes. Each controller watches a specific resource type and works to move the current state of the cluster closer to the desired state specified in the API objects.
examples: The Deployment controller ensuring the correct number of Pod replicas are running.|The StatefulSet controller managing stable Pod identities and ordered operations.|The Node controller checking the health of nodes and updating their status.
title: Kubernetes Controller Manager

definition: A control plane component that watches for newly created Pods with no assigned node and selects an optimal node for them to run on. It considers resource requirements, hardware constraints, policy constraints, and affinity/anti-affinity specifications during its decision-making process.
examples: The Scheduler placing a Pod on a node with sufficient available CPU and memory resources.|Selecting a node based on a Pod's `nodeSelector` or `affinity` rules to ensure specific hardware or avoid other Pods.
title: Kubernetes Scheduler

definition: A package containing all the resource definitions necessary to run an application, tool, or service inside a Kubernetes cluster. It comprises templates, default values (`values.yaml`), and metadata (`Chart.yaml`), simplifying application deployment and management.
examples: A basic chart structure including `templates/deployment.yaml`, `templates/service.yaml`, `values.yaml`, and `Chart.yaml`.|A chart with subcharts for deploying a complex application with multiple dependencies.
title: Helm Chart Structure

definition: A single instance of a Helm chart deployed into a Kubernetes cluster. Each release has a name and version, allowing for independent management, upgrades, rollbacks, and tracking of deployed applications.
examples: Installing the `nginx` chart as a release named `my-nginx-web` in a cluster.|Upgrading the `my-app-api` release to a newer version of its corresponding Helm chart.
title: Helm Release

definition: A centralized location where Helm charts (packages of pre-configured Kubernetes resources) are stored, versioned, and shared. It acts as a catalog, allowing users to discover and install applications into their Kubernetes clusters.
examples: `helm repo add stable https://charts.helm.sh/stable`|Artifact Hub for public charts|A private ChartMuseum instance
title: Helm Repository

definition: A Kustomize overlay is a set of modifications applied to a base set of Kubernetes manifests to generate environment-specific configurations without templating. It allows for declarative customization, keeping the base manifests untouched.
examples: A `kustomization.yaml` defining a `dev` overlay that patches resource limits in a base deployment.|A `prod` overlay that sets a higher replica count and applies a different ingress hostname.|Customizing a third-party application's manifests for a specific cluster environment.
title: Kustomize Overlay

definition: The command-line tool for controlling Kubernetes clusters. Kubectl allows users to run commands against Kubernetes clusters to deploy applications, inspect and manage cluster resources, and view logs.
examples: `kubectl get pods` to list running pods|`kubectl apply -f my-app.yaml` to deploy an application|`kubectl logs <pod-name>` to view container logs
title: Kubectl CLI Tool

definition: An architectural pattern for handling communication between services in a microservices application. It uses a dedicated infrastructure layer, often implemented with sidecar proxies, to manage network traffic, security, and observability without requiring changes to application code.
examples: Istio|Linkerd|Consul Connect
title: Service Mesh Architecture

definition: The Istio control plane is the brain of the Istio service mesh, responsible for managing and configuring the data plane proxies (Envoy sidecars). It provides configuration APIs for traffic management, security, and policy enforcement across the mesh.
examples: Pilot, which handles traffic management configuration.|Citadel, which manages mTLS (mutual TLS) for security.|Galley, which validates and aggregates configuration from users.
title: Istio Control Plane

definition: The Linkerd control plane is responsible for aggregating telemetry, providing a user-facing API, and managing the Linkerd data plane proxies. It includes components for metrics collection, service discovery, and configuration.
examples: The `proxy-injector` automatically adding Linkerd's sidecar to pods.|The `controller` managing and serving configurations to data plane proxies.|The Linkerd dashboard displaying aggregated service metrics and traces.
title: Linkerd Control Plane

definition: An open-source platform that extends Kubernetes to provide serverless capabilities, allowing developers to deploy and manage modern serverless workloads. It focuses on building, deploying, and managing event-driven applications and functions.
examples: Deploying a Knative Service that scales to zero when idle and scales up rapidly on demand.|Using Knative Eventing to connect services to various event sources like Kafka or GitHub.|Knative Build for automating the container image creation process.
title: Knative Serverless

definition: An OpenShift Route exposes a service at a host name, making it reachable from outside the OpenShift cluster. It provides a way to define external access to applications, similar to an Ingress in native Kubernetes but with added features like custom hostnames and TLS termination.
examples: Creating a Route to expose a web application service at `myapp.example.com`.|Configuring a Route with edge TLS termination to handle HTTPS traffic.|Defining a wildcard Route for multiple subdomains.
title: OpenShift Route

definition: A Kubernetes Network Policy is a specification that defines how groups of pods are allowed to communicate with each other and with other network endpoints. It enables fine-grained control over network traffic within the cluster for security purposes.
examples: A policy allowing only frontend pods to communicate with backend pods on a specific port.|A policy restricting egress traffic from a sensitive application to only whitelisted external services.|Isolating a development namespace's pods from accessing production resources.
title: Kubernetes Network Policy

definition: A Kubernetes resource that automatically scales the number of pod replicas in a deployment or replica set based on observed CPU utilization or other select metrics. HPA ensures that applications have enough resources to handle varying loads.
examples: An HPA scaling a web server deployment between 2 and 10 replicas to maintain 50% average CPU utilization.|Scaling based on custom metrics like requests per second from a Prometheus query.|Reacting to an increase in message queue length by adding more worker pods.
title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA)

definition: A Kubernetes resource that automatically adjusts the CPU and memory requests and limits for containers in a pod. VPA learns resource usage patterns over time to recommend or apply optimal resource settings, improving cluster efficiency and reducing waste.
examples: A VPA recommending increased memory for a database pod that frequently OOMKilled.|Automatically setting lower CPU requests for a batch job that consistently uses minimal CPU.|Improving cluster utilization by right-sizing resources for all pods in a namespace.
title: Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA)

definition: A piece of code that intercepts requests to the Kubernetes API server *before* an object is persisted, but *after* the request is authenticated and authorized. Admission controllers can modify requests (mutating) or reject them (validating) to enforce policies and best practices.
examples: The `LimitRanger` admission controller automatically applying default resource limits to pods.|A custom admission controller enforcing that all images come from a trusted registry.|Preventing privileged containers from being deployed into a cluster.
title: Admission Controller (Kubernetes)

definition: A specific type of Admission Controller that can modify objects submitted to the Kubernetes API server before they are persisted. It allows dynamic changes to resource configurations based on predefined rules or external logic.
examples: Automatically injecting a sidecar container (e.g., an Istio Envoy proxy) into new pods.|Adding default labels or annotations to resources based on namespace or other criteria.|Patching environment variables into deployments for specific environments.
title: Mutating Webhook (Kubernetes)

definition: A specific type of Admission Controller that validates objects submitted to the Kubernetes API server and can reject them if they do not conform to defined policies. It ensures that only compliant resources are created or updated in the cluster.
examples: Preventing the creation of privileged containers or images from untrusted registries.|Ensuring all deployments define resource limits and liveness/readiness probes.|Rejecting any resource creation that violates a custom naming convention.
title: Validating Webhook (Kubernetes)

definition: A set of predefined Kubernetes security policies that specify different levels of isolation for pods, ranging from highly permissive to highly restrictive. PSS provides a standardized way to enforce security best practices for pods running in a cluster.
examples: The `Restricted` policy preventing hostPath mounts, privileged containers, and requiring non-root users.|The `Baseline` policy covering common security hardening, allowing some flexibility.|Applying the PSS to a namespace via an `AdmissionConfiguration` or `PodSecurityAdmission` controller.
title: Pod Security Standard (PSS)

definition: A virtual machine (VM) provided by a cloud provider, offering virtualized computing resources like CPU, memory, and networking. It allows users to run operating systems and applications in an isolated environment without managing underlying hardware.

title: Cloud Compute Instance (VM)

definition: A cloud storage architecture for handling large amounts of unstructured data, where data is stored as objects in buckets and accessed via HTTP(S) APIs. It's highly scalable, durable, and cost-effective for static content, backups, and data lakes.
examples: AWS S3 (Simple Storage Service) for storing website assets and backups.|Azure Blob Storage for archiving log files.|Google Cloud Storage used as a data lake for analytics.
title: Object Storage Service

definition: A cloud storage service that provides raw, unformatted storage volumes that can be attached to compute instances (VMs). It operates at the block level, allowing high-performance access suitable for databases, operating systems, and applications requiring persistent, low-latency I/O.
examples: An AWS EBS (Elastic Block Store) volume attached to an EC2 instance running a database.|Azure Disk Storage used as the primary drive for a virtual machine.|Google Persistent Disk providing storage for a stateful application on a GCE instance.
title: Block Storage Service

definition: A cloud storage service that provides shared file systems, accessible via standard network file protocols like NFS or SMB. It allows multiple compute instances to access and share the same files concurrently, suitable for enterprise applications and content management.
