This process is responsible for managing any child processes, handling signals gracefully, and preventing zombie processes, similar to `init` or `systemd` on a host system.
examples: If an application like Nginx is directly specified as the `CMD` or `ENTRYPOINT` and becomes PID 1, it must be capable of handling signals (e.g., `SIGTERM`) and reaping zombie processes.|Tools like `tini` or `dumb-init` are often used as PID 1 to correctly manage signals and prevent zombie processes for applications not designed to be an init system.|An application that fails to properly handle signals when running as PID 1 may not shut down gracefully.
title: Init process (container PID 1)

definition: The `ENTRYPOINT` instruction in a Dockerfile configures a container to run as an executable. It defines the command that will always be executed when the container starts, often used in conjunction with `CMD` to provide default arguments to the entrypoint command.
examples: `ENTRYPOINT ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]` makes `nginx` the primary process.|`ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/bin/supervisord"]` ensures `supervisord` is always the container's main process.|If you specify `docker run myimage ls -l`, `ls -l` would override `CMD`, but `ENTRYPOINT` would still be executed with `ls -l` as its arguments.
title: Entrypoint (Dockerfile)

definition: The `CMD` instruction in a Dockerfile provides default arguments for an `ENTRYPOINT` instruction, or defines the command to be executed if no `ENTRYPOINT` is specified. It can be easily overridden by providing arguments when running the container.
examples: `CMD ["python", "app.py"]` would run `python app.py` if no `ENTRYPOINT` is set.|If combined with `ENTRYPOINT ["nginx"]`, then `CMD ["-g", "daemon off;"]` passes arguments to nginx.|Running `docker run myimage echo "Hello world"` would override `CMD` with `echo "Hello world"`.
title: CMD (Dockerfile)

definition: The `ARG` instruction in a Dockerfile defines a variable that users can pass to the builder at build-time using the `docker build --build-arg` flag. These variables are only available during the image build process and are not persisted in the final container image.
examples: `ARG HTTP_PROXY` declares a build-time argument named `HTTP_PROXY`.|`ARG VERSION=1.0` sets a default value for the `VERSION` argument.|Building with `docker build --build-arg HTTP_PROXY=http://proxy.example.com .` passes a value to the argument.
title: ARG (Dockerfile)

definition: The `ENV` instruction in a Dockerfile sets environment variables within the container image, making them available to any process running inside the container. These variables persist in the final image and can be accessed by applications at runtime.
examples: `ENV NODE_ENV=production` sets an environment variable for a Node.js application.|`ENV PATH="/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:$PATH"` modifies the PATH variable for all subsequent commands and runtime.|You can inspect container environment variables using `docker exec -it mycontainer env`.
title: ENV (Dockerfile)

definition: The `LABEL` instruction in a Dockerfile adds metadata to an image as key-value pairs. This metadata can be used for organizing, filtering, documenting, or providing descriptive information about the image, without affecting its runtime behavior.
examples: `LABEL version="1.0.0"` adds a version label to the image.|`LABEL maintainer="John Doe <john@example.com>"` provides contact information.|`LABEL org.label-schema.build-date="2023-10-27T10:00:00Z"` is an example of a standardized label.
title: LABEL (Dockerfile)

definition: The `USER` instruction in a Dockerfile sets the username or UID (User ID) to be used for running subsequent instructions in the Dockerfile and for the container's runtime process. It is a security best practice to run containers as a non-root user whenever possible.
examples: `USER appuser` switches the user to 'appuser' for subsequent instructions.|`USER 1001` switches to the user with UID 1001.|You can temporarily run a container as a different user using `docker run -u root myimage`.
title: USER (Dockerfile instruction)

definition: The `WORKDIR` instruction in a Dockerfile sets the current working directory for any subsequent `RUN`, `CMD`, `ENTRYPOINT`, `COPY`, or `ADD` instructions. It also sets the default working directory for the container at runtime.
examples: `WORKDIR /app` sets `/app` as the working directory.|If `WORKDIR /app` is followed by `COPY . .`, files from the build context will be copied into `/app`.|When you execute `docker exec -it mycontainer /bin/bash`, you typically land in the directory specified by `WORKDIR` (unless overridden).
title: WORKDIR (Dockerfile)

definition: The EXPOSE instruction informs Docker that the container listens on the specified network ports at runtime. It serves as documentation, metadata, and an indication to users or linking services about which ports are intended to be published, but it does not actually publish them.
examples: EXPOSE 80|EXPOSE 80/tcp 443/tcp|EXPOSE 8080/udp
title: EXPOSE (Dockerfile)

definition: The VOLUME instruction creates a mount point with the specified name and marks it as holding externally mounted volumes from the native host or other containers. It is primarily used to persist data generated by the container, or to share data between containers, ensuring data integrity even if the container is removed.
examples: VOLUME /var/lib/mysql|VOLUME ["/data", "/app/logs"]
title: VOLUME (Dockerfile instruction)

definition: The ADD instruction copies new files, directories, or remote file URLs from a source path (`<src>`) and adds them to the filesystem of the image at the destination path (`<dest>`). It uniquely supports fetching remote URLs and automatically extracting compressed archives (tar, gzip, bzip2, xz) into the destination directory.
examples: ADD http://example.com/latest.zip /tmp/|ADD myapp.tar.gz /app/|ADD src/ /app/src/
title: ADD (Dockerfile)

definition: The COPY instruction copies new files or directories from a source path (`<src>`) within the build context and adds them to the filesystem of the image at the destination path (`<dest>`). It is generally preferred over `ADD` for local files due to its simpler and more transparent semantics, as it does not perform automatic extraction or URL fetching.
examples: COPY . /app/|COPY --chown=user:group config.txt /etc/|COPY ["src/main.go", "go.mod", "/app/"]
title: COPY (Dockerfile)

definition: The ONBUILD instruction adds a trigger instruction to the image that will be executed when the image is used as a base for another build. The trigger instruction is executed in the context of the child build, immediately after the `FROM` instruction in the downstream Dockerfile.
examples: ONBUILD COPY . /app/src|ONBUILD RUN go mod tidy
title: ONBUILD (Dockerfile)

definition: The HEALTHCHECK instruction tells Docker how to test if a container is still working correctly by periodically running a command inside the container. It helps ensure that a containerized application is not just running, but also responsive and functional, influencing orchestration decisions like restarting unhealthy containers.
examples: HEALTHCHECK --interval=5m --timeout=3s CMD curl -f http://localhost/ || exit 1|HEALTHCHECK CMD /usr/local/bin/check-db.sh
title: HEALTHCHECK (Dockerfile)

definition: The SHELL instruction allows the default shell used for `RUN`, `ENTRYPOINT`, and `CMD` instructions to be overridden. This impacts how commands are parsed and executed within the container build process and runtime, particularly useful for non-standard shells or Windows containers.
examples: SHELL ["powershell", "-command"]|SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-c"]
title: SHELL (Dockerfile)

definition: The STOP_SIGNAL instruction sets the system call signal that will be sent to the container to request it to exit. This allows for a graceful shutdown of the application by sending a specific signal, such as `SIGINT` or `SIGTERM`, instead of relying on the default `SIGTERM` which might not be handled optimally by all applications.
examples: STOP_SIGNAL SIGINT|STOP_SIGNAL 9
title: STOP_SIGNAL (Dockerfile)

definition: A Dockerfile technique that allows you to use multiple `FROM` statements to optimize image size and build efficiency. Intermediate build stages can contain build tools, source code, and dependencies needed only during the build process, which are then discarded, leaving a smaller, production-ready final image.
examples: FROM golang:1.16 as builder|FROM alpine:latest|COPY --from=builder /app/bin/myapp /usr/local/bin/
title: Multi-stage build

definition: In a multi-stage build, a target stage refers to a named `FROM` instruction that can be explicitly specified during the Docker build process. This allows stopping the build at an intermediate stage, which is particularly useful for debugging, testing, or creating different variants of an image without building the final production image.
examples: FROM golang:1.16 as build-env|docker build --target build-env -t myapp-debug .
title: Target stage (multi-stage build)

definition: Dockerd, also known as the Docker daemon, is the persistent background process that manages Docker objects such as images, containers, networks, and volumes. It listens for Docker API requests from clients (like the Docker CLI) and orchestrates all container operations on the host system.
examples: sudo systemctl start docker (starts dockerd)|journalctl -u docker.service (view dockerd logs)
title: Dockerd (Docker daemon)

definition: The Docker CLI (Command Line Interface) is the primary user tool for interacting with the Docker daemon (`dockerd`) to manage containers. It provides commands to build images, run, stop, and manage containers, networks, volumes, and other Docker objects.
examples: docker run -it ubuntu bash|docker build -t myimage .|docker ps
title: Docker CLI

definition: Containerd is a high-level container runtime that manages the complete container lifecycle on a host system, including image transfer and storage, container execution, and supervision. It provides a gRPC API and serves as a core component beneath Docker and Kubernetes (via CRI), abstracting away low-level runtime details.
examples: Used implicitly by `dockerd` for container management.|The `ctr` tool can interact with containerd directly.|Kubelet uses containerd as a CRI runtime.
title: Containerd

definition: The Container Runtime Interface (CRI) is a plugin interface that enables the `kubelet` (the agent running on each Kubernetes node) to use various container runtimes to manage containers on that node. It abstracts away the specifics of different container runtimes, ensuring interoperability and allowing Kubernetes to support multiple underlying runtime implementations like containerd or CRI-O.
examples: `containerd` implements the CRI.|`CRI-O` implements the CRI.|Kubelet communicates with container runtimes via CRI.
title: CRI (Container Runtime Interface)

definition: Runc is a low-level, lightweight, universal container runtime that implements the OCI (Open Container Initiative) specification for running containers. It creates and runs containers based on a generated `config.json` file, providing the fundamental process isolation and resource management for containers.
examples: Used by higher-level runtimes like `containerd` and `CRI-O`.|`runc spec` (generates OCI configuration)|`runc run mycontainer`
title: Runc

definition: CRI-O is a lightweight container runtime specifically designed to implement the Kubernetes Container Runtime Interface (CRI), providing a direct and lean execution layer for Kubernetes pods. It focuses solely on fulfilling the CRI specification, making it a highly optimized runtime for Kubernetes environments that avoids the overhead of a full Docker daemon.
examples: Used as a primary container runtime for Kubernetes clusters.|Can replace containerd or Docker as the runtime for Kubelet.|Configured via its `crio.conf` file.
title: CRI-O

definition: Podman is a daemonless container engine for developing, managing, and running OCI containers and pods on a Linux system. It provides a command-line interface highly compatible with Docker, making it a popular drop-in replacement that supports rootless containers and does not require a central daemon process.
examples: podman run -it fedora bash|podman build -t myimage .|podman ps
title: Podman

definition: Buildah is a command-line tool designed to build OCI-compatible container images from scratch or using Dockerfiles, without needing a container daemon. It provides granular control over image creation steps, allowing users to commit changes, mount container filesystems, and inject content, often used in conjunction with Podman.
examples: buildah bud -f Dockerfile -t myimage .|buildah from fedora|buildah commit container-id myimage
title: Buildah

definition: Skopeo is a command-line utility for working with container images and image repositories without needing to run a container daemon. It allows users to inspect image metadata, copy images between different registries or local storage, delete images, and sign/verify images.
examples: skopeo inspect docker://docker.io/library/alpine|skopeo copy docker://alpine:latest dir:./alpine-local|skopeo delete docker://myregistry.com/myimage:mytag
title: Skopeo

definition: Nerdctl is a Docker-compatible command-line interface for `containerd`, providing a similar user experience and command syntax to the Docker CLI but interacting directly with `containerd` instead of `dockerd`. It is particularly useful in environments like KinD (Kubernetes in Docker) or other `containerd`-centric setups.
examples: nerdctl run -it --rm alpine sh|nerdctl build -t myimage .|nerdctl ps
title: Nerdctl

definition: LXC is an operating-system-level virtualization method that allows running multiple isolated Linux systems (containers) on a single control host. It leverages Linux kernel features like cgroups and namespaces to provide resource isolation and security without the overhead of a traditional hypervisor.
examples: Running a lightweight Ubuntu distribution within a Debian host using LXC.|Isolating different development environments on a single server, each in its own LXC container.
title: LXC (Linux Containers)

definition: LXD is a next-generation system container manager that provides an experience similar to virtual machines but using Linux containers, building upon LXC. It offers an intuitive REST API and command-line tools for managing, snapshotting, and live-migrating system containers.
examples: Using `lxc launch ubuntu:20.04 mycontainer` to quickly create and start a new Ubuntu container.|Managing snapshots and storage volumes for a group of LXD containers hosting different services.
title: LXD (Linux Container Daemon)

definition: gVisor is an application kernel, written in Go, that intercepts system calls from containerized applications and services them in userspace. This provides an additional layer of isolation between the application and the host kernel, significantly enhancing security for untrusted workloads.
examples: Running a untrusted web server application inside a gVisor sandbox to mitigate potential kernel exploits.|Using gVisor with Kubernetes to provide increased security for specific pods that handle sensitive data.
title: gVisor

definition: Kata Containers is an open-source project that provides a secure container runtime, combining the isolation of virtual machines with the speed and manageability of containers. It achieves this by launching each container within its own lightweight virtual machine, ensuring strong workload isolation.
examples: Deploying confidential or multi-tenant workloads in Kubernetes using Kata Containers for enhanced isolation between pods.|Integrating Kata Containers with CRI-O or containerd as an alternative, secure runtime for specific container images.
title: Kata Containers

definition: Firecracker is an open-source virtual machine monitor (VMM) developed by AWS for creating lightweight virtual machines, known as microVMs. It is designed specifically for serverless workloads and container isolation, prioritizing minimal overhead, rapid startup times, and enhanced security.
examples: Powering AWS Lambda and AWS Fargate, isolating serverless functions and containers at the hardware level.|Running numerous isolated containerized applications on a single host with very low resource consumption per instance.
title: Firecracker (VMM)

definition: Rkt was an open-source container engine designed as an alternative to Docker, focusing on security, composability, and adherence to open standards, particularly the App Container Image (ACI) format. It aimed for closer integration with init systems like systemd and treated containers as a unit of execution rather than a standalone daemon.
examples: `rkt run coreos.com/etcd` to execute an etcd container using the Rkt runtime.|Managing the lifecycle of Rkt containers through systemd units.
title: Rkt (container runtime)

definition: A base image is a minimal, foundational container image that serves as the starting point for building other container images. It typically contains a basic operating system (like Alpine, Ubuntu, or Debian) and essential tools, upon which applications and their dependencies are added.
examples: Using `FROM ubuntu:22.04` in a Dockerfile to start with a full Ubuntu environment.|Selecting `FROM alpine:3.18` for a lightweight and secure base image due to its small footprint.
title: Base Image

definition: A scratch image is the smallest possible container image, essentially an empty filesystem, specified by `FROM scratch` in a Dockerfile. It contains no operating system or libraries and is primarily used for self-contained, statically compiled binaries, resulting in extremely small and secure images.
examples: Building a Go application into `FROM scratch` to produce a single, self-contained executable image.|Creating a tiny utility container for a single task using a static binary based on a scratch image.
title: Scratch Image

definition: Image pruning is the process of removing unused or 'dangling' container images and build cache from a local system to free up disk space. It specifically targets images that are no longer tagged or referenced by existing containers, or intermediate build layers.
examples: Running `docker image prune` to remove all dangling images.|Using `docker image prune -a` to clean up all unused images, including untagged ones that are not dangling.
title: Image pruning

definition: Image scanning is the automated process of analyzing container images for known vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and compliance issues. It inspects image layers, software packages, and dependencies against vulnerability databases and security policies.
examples: Integrating a tool like Trivy or Clair into a CI/CD pipeline to scan every new image build.|Scanning a deployed Docker image for newly discovered CVEs before it's promoted to production.
title: Image scanning

definition: Vulnerability scanning for container images is a specific type of image scanning focused on identifying known security vulnerabilities (CVEs) within the software components, libraries, and operating system packages included in an image. It compares the image's Bill of Materials (SBOM) against public and private vulnerability databases.
examples: Using Trivy to detect high-severity CVEs in the `glibc` package of a `ubuntu:latest` image.|Scanning a custom application image to ensure it does not contain known vulnerabilities like Log4j.
title: Vulnerability scanning (container image)

definition: Supply chain security for container images involves securing the entire lifecycle, from source code and base image selection through building, distributing, and deploying, to prevent tampering, unauthorized access, and the introduction of vulnerabilities. It establishes trust and integrity at every stage of the image's journey.
examples: Enforcing policies that only allow signed and scanned base images to be used in builds.|Implementing provenance tracking for all components within an image and verifying image integrity before deployment to production.|Using OPA Gatekeeper in Kubernetes to block deployment of images from untrusted registries or with known vulnerabilities.
title: Supply chain security (container images)

definition: Image signing is the process of digitally signing a container image to cryptographically verify its authenticity and integrity. This ensures that the image has not been tampered with since it was signed and originated from a trusted source, crucial for supply chain security.
examples: Using Docker Content Trust (powered by Notary) to sign a custom application image before pushing it to a registry.|Configuring a container runtime to only pull and run images that have valid digital signatures from approved keys.
title: Image signing

definition: Notary is an open-source project by Docker that provides a framework for secure content publishing and distribution, primarily used for signing and verifying container images. It implements The Update Framework (TUF) to establish and maintain trust over arbitrary data collections, crucial for preventing tampering.
examples: Setting up a Notary server to manage trusted publishers and sign specific Docker images for an organization.|Clients using Notary to cryptographically verify the integrity and authenticity of images pulled from a remote registry.
title: Notary (image signing)

definition: Content addressability is a system where a container image's identifier (its digest or manifest hash) is derived directly from the cryptographic hash of its content. This ensures that any change to the image's content, no matter how small, will result in a different identifier, providing inherent integrity verification and immutability.
examples: Referencing an image by its digest in a Kubernetes manifest: `myregistry/myimage@sha256:abcdef...`|Docker's image layers being identified by their content hash, guaranteeing that the layer content hasn't changed.
title: Content addressability (container images)

definition: The Docker Image Format defines the standardized structure for organizing and storing container images, typically based on a union file system with a layered architecture. It comprises image layers (tarballs of filesystem differences), a manifest describing the image, and a configuration JSON detailing runtime parameters and image history.
examples: An OCI Image Format compliant image containing configuration JSON, manifest, and multiple filesystem layer tarballs.|The output of a `docker save` command, which produces a tar archive conforming to this layered format.
title: Docker Image Format

definition: A Distribution Manifest List (also known as an 'image index' in OCI) is a mechanism that allows a single image reference (tag) to point to multiple image manifests, each tailored for a different architecture, operating system, or variant. This enables client-side detection and pulling of the correct image for its specific platform.
examples: A tag `myregistry/myimage:latest` pointing to separate manifests for `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64` architectures.|Using `docker buildx imagetools create` to build and push a multi-architecture manifest list for a single image tag.
title: Distribution Manifest List

definition: The build context refers to the set of files and directories located at a specified path (usually the current directory) that are sent to the Docker daemon when building an image from a Dockerfile. Only files within this context are accessible to instructions like `COPY` or `ADD` within the Dockerfile.
examples: When running `docker build .`, the current directory `.` becomes the build context.|A Dockerfile attempting to `COPY ../app.py` would fail if `../app.py` is outside the specified build context directory.
title: Build context (Dockerfile)

definition: A `.dockerignore` file is similar to a `.gitignore` file, specifying patterns for files and directories that should be excluded from the build context sent to the Docker daemon. This helps optimize build performance by reducing data transfer, minimize the final image size, and prevent sensitive or unnecessary files from being included in the image.
examples: Adding `node_modules/` to `.dockerignore` to prevent large dependency directories from being copied.|Including `*.log` and `.git/` in `.dockerignore` to keep build artifacts and version control data out of the image.
title: .dockerignore file

definition: The bridge network is the default networking mode for Docker containers, creating a private internal network on the host machine. Containers connected to the same bridge network can communicate with each other, and they can access the external network via NAT, but external hosts cannot directly access them unless ports are explicitly mapped.
examples: A web application container and a database container communicating over the default `bridge` network.|Using `docker run -p 80:80 mywebapp` to expose port 80 of a container on the host's bridge network to the external world.
title: Bridge Network (Docker)

definition: The Host Network mode in Docker allows a container to share the host machine's network namespace directly. This means the container uses the host's IP address and port space, effectively removing network isolation between the container and the host.
examples: Running `docker run --network host my_web_app` makes `my_web_app` accessible on the host's IP address and exposed ports directly.|A container configured with host networking will have `localhost` refer to the host machine itself, not the container's isolated loopback.
title: Host Network (Docker)

definition: The None Network mode creates a Docker container without any network interfaces or a loopback device. This completely isolates the container from all network communication, making it unable to send or receive data over any network.
examples: A container running `docker run --network none my_batch_job` for a CPU-intensive task that has no external communication needs.|Inspecting a container created with `--network none` will show no IP address assigned to it.
title: None Network (Docker)

definition: An Overlay Network in Docker Swarm is a distributed network that spans multiple Docker daemon hosts, enabling containers on different physical machines to communicate securely as if they were on the same local network. It typically uses VXLAN encapsulation to achieve this connectivity.
examples: `docker network create -d overlay my-swarm-net` creates an overlay network for services.|Services in a Docker Swarm cluster using an overlay network to communicate between containers running on `node1` and `node2`.
title: Overlay Network (Docker Swarm)

definition: A Macvlan network driver in Docker allows a container to be assigned its own unique MAC address and IP address directly from the host's physical network interface. This makes the container appear as a distinct physical device on the network, bypassing the need for port mapping.
examples: `docker network create -d macvlan --subnet=192.168.1.0/24 --gateway=192.168.1.1 -o parent=eth0 my-macvlan-net` to create a macvlan network.|Running a container with macvlan network, like `docker run --network my-macvlan-net my_app`, allows it to be accessed directly via its own IP address on the local network.
title: Macvlan Network (Docker)

definition: An IP address is a unique numerical label assigned to a container's virtual network interface, allowing it to be identified and communicate within its private container network and, potentially, with external networks via network address translation (NAT).
examples: A common Docker container IP address might be `172.17.0.2` within the default `bridge` network.|`docker inspect my_container` command output will show the assigned `IPAddress` under network settings.
title: IP address (container)

definition: Port mapping, often called port publishing, is the mechanism in container technologies like Docker that forwards traffic from a specific port on the host machine to a different, or the same, port inside a container. This makes services running inside the container accessible from outside the host.
examples: `docker run -p 8080:80 my_web_app` maps host port 8080 to container port 80.|Accessing a web application running inside a container by navigating to `http://localhost:8080` in a web browser.
title: Port Mapping (container)

definition: Port forwarding, in the context of containers, is the general networking technique of redirecting network traffic from one IP address and port number to another. For containers, it typically involves forwarding traffic from the host machine's interface and port to a container's internal port, enabling external access to containerized services.
examples: `kubectl port-forward my-pod 8080:80` forwards traffic from local port 8080 to port 80 of `my-pod`.|Using an SSH tunnel to forward a host port to a container port on a remote machine.
title: Port Forwarding (container)

definition: A veth (virtual Ethernet) pair is a unique Linux kernel network device that acts as a simple, full-duplex pipe connecting two network namespaces. Data sent into one end emerges from the other, making it fundamental for linking a container's network namespace to the host's network stack.
examples: Docker utilizes veth pairs to connect each container's `eth0` interface to a virtual bridge on the host.|Manually creating a veth pair with `ip link add veth0 type veth peer name veth1` and assigning each end to different network namespaces.
title: Virtual Ethernet Device (veth pair)

definition: IPtables is a user-space utility program that allows a system administrator to configure the IP packet filter rules of the Linux kernel firewall. It is extensively used by container runtimes to manage network address translation (NAT), port mapping, and packet filtering for containers.
examples: `iptables -A FORWARD -i docker0 -o eth0 -j ACCEPT` is a rule that might allow forwarding packets from the docker bridge to the host's physical interface.|Docker automatically creates complex iptables rules to implement published ports (`-p` flag) and internal container networking.
title: IPtables

definition: Netfilter is a framework provided by the Linux kernel that allows various network-related operations to be implemented in the form of customized handlers. It serves as the underlying infrastructure for packet filtering, network address translation (NAT), and connection tracking, which tools like IPtables configure.
examples: The `FORWARD` chain, `NAT` table, and `conntrack` (connection tracking) are all components and functionalities provided by the Netfilter framework.|IPtables and `nftables` are user-space tools that configure rules within the Netfilter framework.
title: Netfilter

definition: DNS resolution in a container context is the process by which a container translates human-readable hostnames (e.g., `my-database-service`) into their corresponding IP addresses. This enables containers to communicate with other services or external resources without needing to know their volatile IP addresses.
examples: A container trying to connect to `backend-service` by its service name, facilitated by the container runtime's internal DNS server.|Pinging `google.com` from inside a container, which requires the container to resolve the domain name to an IP address.
title: DNS resolution (container)

definition: Service discovery is the automatic process by which containers or microservices locate and communicate with each other on a network, typically using logical service names rather than static IP addresses. This is crucial in dynamic container environments where IP addresses are ephemeral.
examples: Kubernetes Services automatically registering endpoints and providing a stable DNS name for pods.|A front-end container finding and connecting to a back-end database container using a service name like `my-database`.
title: Service discovery (container)

definition: Ingress is a Kubernetes API object that manages external access to services within a cluster, typically HTTP and HTTPS. It provides features like HTTP routing, SSL termination, and name-based virtual hosting, acting as an entry point for external traffic.
examples: Configuring an Ingress to expose a web application to `www.example.com`.|Using `kubectl apply -f my-ingress.yaml` to define external routing rules for services.
title: Ingress (Kubernetes)

definition: Egress in Kubernetes refers to outbound network traffic originating from within the cluster to external destinations. This traffic can be managed and secured through Network Policies or specific routing configurations to control what a pod or service can access outside the cluster.
examples: A pod attempting to fetch data from an external API or database.|A Network Policy configured to restrict specific pods from connecting to any IP address outside a defined range.
title: Egress (Kubernetes)

definition: Load balancing for containers is the process of distributing incoming network traffic across multiple healthy instances of a containerized service. This ensures high availability, improves responsiveness, and optimizes resource utilization by preventing any single container from becoming a bottleneck.
examples: A Kubernetes Service automatically distributing incoming requests to multiple replica pods of a web application.|Docker Swarm's routing mesh handling requests and forwarding them to available service instances across different nodes.
title: Load balancing (container)

definition: A Kubernetes Network Policy is an API resource that specifies how groups of pods are allowed to communicate with each other and with other network endpoints, effectively acting as a firewall for pods. They provide granular control over ingress and egress traffic for enhanced security.
examples: A Network Policy allowing only frontend pods to initiate connections to backend pods within the same namespace.|Restricting all egress traffic from development pods except to specific internal services or an external registry.
title: Network Policy (Kubernetes)

definition: A CNI (Container Network Interface) Plugin is an implementation of the CNI specification, which defines a standardized interface for configuring network interfaces for Linux containers. These plugins are responsible for allocating IP addresses to containers, managing network connectivity, and configuring routes.
examples: Flannel, Calico, and Cilium are popular CNI plugins used in Kubernetes clusters.|The `bridge` CNI plugin creates a Linux bridge and connects containers to it via veth pairs.
title: CNI Plugin

definition: Flannel is a simple, easy-to-use Container Network Interface (CNI) plugin that provides a flat network layer for Kubernetes clusters. It typically uses VXLAN encapsulation to create an overlay network, enabling pods on different nodes to communicate seamlessly across the cluster.
examples: Deploying Flannel in a Kubernetes cluster using its manifest `kube-flannel.yml` to enable inter-node pod communication.|A pod on `node-1` communicating with a pod on `node-2` through Flannel's VXLAN tunnel.
title: Flannel (CNI)

definition: Calico is a robust and scalable Container Network Interface (CNI) plugin that provides network connectivity and security policy enforcement for containers and virtual machines. It leverages standard IP routing, often with BGP, for high-performance data plane and flexible Network Policy implementation.
examples: Implementing fine-grained Kubernetes Network Policies with Calico to define strict pod-to-pod communication rules.|Calico providing network connectivity in a multi-cloud Kubernetes deployment using BGP for route exchange.
title: Calico (CNI)

definition: Cilium is an advanced Container Network Interface (CNI) plugin that provides high-performance networking, security, and observability for Kubernetes clusters, powered by eBPF technology. It enables granular L7 policy enforcement and deep visibility into network traffic at the kernel level.
examples: Enforcing an HTTP-specific policy to allow only GET requests to a particular microservice endpoint.|Using Cilium's Hubble tool to visualize and troubleshoot network flows and security events in a Kubernetes cluster.
title: Cilium (CNI)

definition: A network proxy that runs on each node in a Kubernetes cluster, implementing the Kubernetes Service concept. It maintains network rules on the host to enable network communication to Pods from inside or outside the cluster.
examples: kube-proxy configuring iptables rules on a node to direct traffic for a `ClusterIP` Service to the correct backend Pods.|Proxying requests to different Pods belonging to a Service for load balancing.|Watching the Kubernetes API server for Service and Endpoint changes to update network rules.
title: Kube-proxy

definition: The default Kubernetes Service type that exposes a Service on a cluster-internal IP address, making it only reachable from within the cluster. It provides a stable IP address for internal communication between services.
examples:
A backend database Service only accessible by a frontend application within the same Kubernetes cluster.|An internal API service consumed by other microservices.|apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-backend
spec:
  selector:
    app: my-app
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
  type: ClusterIP
title: ClusterIP Service

definition: A Kubernetes Service type that exposes a Service on a static port on each Node's IP address. This allows external traffic to reach the Service via any Node's IP and the specified port, effectively opening a port on all cluster nodes.
examples:
Exposing a web application to the internet by accessing `http://<NodeIP>:<NodePort>`.|Providing external access to a development or testing environment.|apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-webapp
spec:
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
      nodePort: 30080
  type: NodePort
title: NodePort Service

definition: A Kubernetes Service type that exposes a Service externally using a cloud provider's load balancer. It automatically provisions and configures an external IP address, making the Service publicly accessible and distributing traffic across backend Pods.
examples:
Exposing a production web application publicly via an AWS Elastic Load Balancer (ELB) or Google Cloud Load Balancer.|Providing a stable, public IP for a public API endpoint.|apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-public-app
spec:
  selector:
    app: web-public
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
  type: LoadBalancer
title: LoadBalancer Service

definition: A Kubernetes Service type that maps a Service to an arbitrary external DNS name by returning a CNAME record. It acts as an alias to an external service outside the Kubernetes cluster, providing a consistent internal DNS name for external resources.
examples:
Connecting to an external SaaS database, e.g., `my-saas-db.example.com` mapped to an internal Kubernetes Service name `my-external-db`.|Redirecting traffic to a CDN endpoint.|apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-external-service
spec:
  type: ExternalName
  externalName: api.example.com
title: ExternalName Service

definition: A Kubernetes Service without a `ClusterIP`, used when direct access to individual Pods is required instead of relying on the Service's proxy for load balancing. It enables custom service discovery or allows clients to connect directly to specific Pods.
examples:
Used with StatefulSets for applications like Cassandra or Kafka, where each replica needs a unique, predictable network identity.|Custom service discovery mechanisms where clients directly query DNS for Pod IP addresses.|apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-stateful-app
spec:
  selector:
    app: stateful
  clusterIP: None
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
title: Headless Service

definition: An open-source service mesh that layers transparently onto existing distributed applications, providing capabilities for traffic management, policy enforcement, and telemetry collection. It enhances the reliability, security, and observability of microservices deployments.
examples: Implementing A/B testing or canary deployments for a new service version.|Enforcing mTLS (mutual TLS) encryption for all service-to-service communication.|Collecting detailed metrics and traces for request paths across multiple microservices.
title: Istio

definition: An ultralight, security-first service mesh for Kubernetes, designed to add reliability, observability, and security to microservices with minimal overhead. It uses a lightweight proxy (micro-proxy) injected alongside each service.
examples: Automatically retrying failed requests or adding timeouts to prevent cascading failures.|Enabling mutual TLS (mTLS) for all inter-service communication by default.|Gaining real-time visibility into service health and latency without modifying application code.
title: Linkerd

definition: Storage within a container's writable layer that is temporary and tied to the container's lifecycle. Any data written to ephemeral storage is lost when the container is stopped, deleted, or crashes.
examples: Log files generated by an application that are not critical for long-term retention.|Temporary cache data used during a container's runtime.|Any files written directly to the container's root filesystem (e.g., `/tmp`) without using a mounted volume.
title: Ephemeral storage (container)

definition: Storage that exists independently of a container's lifecycle, ensuring data survives container restarts, deletions, or moves to different hosts. It is crucial for stateful applications that require data retention.
examples: A database container storing its data in a mounted volume.|A file server container making user-uploaded files available across restarts.|Configuration files that need to persist even if the application container is replaced.
title: Persistent storage (container)

definition: The preferred mechanism for persisting data generated by and used by Docker containers, managed entirely by Docker and isolated from the host machine's filesystem. Docker Volumes provide better performance and security than bind mounts for many use cases.
examples: Creating a volume: `docker volume create my-data`.|Mounting a volume to a container: `docker run -v my-data:/app/data my-image`.|Listing all Docker volumes: `docker volume ls`.
title: Volume (Docker)

definition: A mechanism to mount a file or directory from the host machine's filesystem directly into a container, allowing the container direct access to host data. The host machine is responsible for managing the underlying file or directory.
examples: Mounting a host directory for development: `docker run -v /Users/john/app/src:/app/src my-dev-image`.|Injecting a host-based configuration file: `docker run -v /etc/host_config.json:/app/config.json my-app`.|Sharing logs between host and container.
title: Bind Mount (Docker)

definition: A temporary filesystem mount that stores data directly in the host's memory, providing very fast I/O but with data not persisting beyond the container's lifecycle or host reboot. It is ideal for storing sensitive or non-persistent data that requires high performance.
examples: Storing sensitive temporary files that should not be written to disk.|Providing a high-performance cache within a container.|`docker run --mount type=tmpfs,destination=/tmp/cache my-image`.
title: Tmpfs Mount (Docker)

definition: A specific type of Docker Volume identified by a user-defined name, making it easier to reference and manage persistent data across multiple containers. Docker manages its creation, location, and lifecycle, simplifying data persistence.
examples: Creating a named volume: `docker volume create my-db-data`.|Running a container with a named volume: `docker run -v my-db-data:/var/lib/mysql mysql:latest`.|Inspecting a named volume's details: `docker volume inspect my-db-data`.
title: Named Volume (Docker)

definition: A Docker plugin that allows volumes to be stored on remote hosts or cloud providers, extending Docker's storage capabilities beyond the local filesystem. This enables containers to access persistent storage from various external systems.
examples: Using a `rexray/s3fs` volume driver to store container data directly on Amazon S3.|Provisioning volumes from a cloud provider's block storage (e.g., EBS, Azure Disk) using a specialized driver.|`docker run --volume-driver=rexray/ebs -v my-ebs-volume:/data my-app`.
title: Volume Driver (Docker)

definition: The underlying technology Docker uses to store image layers and manage the writable layer of containers on the host's filesystem. It dictates how Docker images are built and stored, and how containers access and modify their filesystem.
examples: The `overlay2` storage driver, commonly used on Linux, efficiently stores image layers and container changes.|The `AUFS` storage driver, an older technology, used for managing layered filesystems.|Configuring Docker to use a specific storage driver in `/etc/docker/daemon.json`.
title: Storage Driver (Docker)

definition: An implementation of the Container Storage Interface (CSI) specification, enabling third-party storage providers to develop and integrate their storage solutions with Kubernetes. CSI drivers allow Kubernetes to orchestrate volumes on various storage systems without requiring core Kubernetes code changes.
examples: The AWS EBS CSI driver allowing Kubernetes Pods to use Amazon EBS volumes for persistent storage.|The Google Cloud Persistent Disk CSI driver enabling seamless integration with GCP's block storage.|Installing a Ceph CSI driver to use a Ceph storage cluster with Kubernetes.
title: CSI Driver (Kubernetes)

definition: A cluster-wide resource in Kubernetes that represents a piece of storage in the cluster, abstracting away the underlying storage implementation details like NFS, iSCSI, or cloud provider specific storage. PVs are provisioned by an administrator or dynamically by StorageClasses.
examples:
A 10GB `hostPath` PV manually created for development purposes.|A PV backed by a specific AWS EBS volume with `Retain` reclaim policy.|apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: my-pv
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 5Gi
  volumeMode: Filesystem
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  storageClassName: manual
  hostPath:
    path: "/mnt/data"
title: Persistent Volume (PV) (Kubernetes)

definition: A request for storage by a user or application within Kubernetes, consuming a portion of a Persistent Volume (PV) and making it available to a Pod. PVCs abstract the details of provisioning and management, allowing users to simply request storage based on their needs.
examples:
A Pod requesting 5GB of 'fast' storage using a PVC.|Claiming a specific PV by its name or matching criteria defined in the PVC.|apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: my-pvc
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 3Gi
  storageClassName: standard
title: Persistent Volume Claim (PVC) (Kubernetes)

definition: A Kubernetes resource that describes 'classes' of storage, used to dynamically provision Persistent Volumes (PVs) based on predefined attributes like performance, tier, or access mode. It enables administrators to offer different storage options to users without manually provisioning each PV.
examples:
A `standard` StorageClass for general-purpose SSDs and a `premium` StorageClass for high-performance SSDs.|Defining a `provisioner` (e.g., `kubernetes.io/aws-ebs`) and `parameters` (e.g., `type: gp2`) within a StorageClass.|apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: fast-storage
provisioner: csi.aws.amazon.com/ebs
parameters:
  type: gp3
reclaimPolicy: Delete
volumeBindingMode: Immediate
title: StorageClass (Kubernetes)

definition: A Kubernetes PersistentVolume access mode that allows the volume to be mounted as read-write by a single node. This means only one pod running on a specific node can have write access at any given time, although multiple pods on that same node can share it.
examples: A single pod running a database application requiring exclusive write access to its data directory.|A stateful application ensuring data integrity by allowing only one writer pod at a time, mounted on its host node.|Defining `accessModes: [ "ReadWriteOnce" ]` in a PersistentVolumeClaim YAML for a block storage volume.
title: ReadWriteOnce access mode

definition: A Kubernetes PersistentVolume access mode allowing the volume to be mounted as read-only by multiple nodes simultaneously. This enables many pods across different nodes to concurrently consume data from the volume, typically used for shared, immutable data.
examples: Serving static website content to numerous web server pods deployed across a cluster.|Distributing configuration files or machine learning model data to many worker pods for inference.|Specifying `accessModes: [ "ReadOnlyMany" ]` in a PersistentVolumeClaim for a network file system (NFS) shared volume.
title: ReadOnlyMany access mode

definition: A Kubernetes PersistentVolume access mode that allows the volume to be mounted as read-write by multiple nodes simultaneously. This mode is typically supported by network file systems (NFS) or distributed file systems, enabling collaborative applications or shared writable storage.
examples: A shared network drive where multiple applications on different nodes need to read and write to the same files concurrently.|A distributed logging system where agents on various nodes write logs to a central shared volume.|Using `accessModes: [ "ReadWriteMany" ]` in a PersistentVolumeClaim YAML for an NFS-backed volume.
title: ReadWriteMany access mode

definition: A Kubernetes volume type that mounts a file or directory from the host node's filesystem into a pod. It is often used for development, testing, or for accessing host-specific information, but comes with security and portability implications due to its direct reliance on the host.
examples: Mounting `/var/log` from the host into a log-collector pod for cluster-level logging.|Using a `HostPath` volume to make the Docker socket `/var/run/docker.sock` available to a Jenkins pod for Docker-in-Docker builds.|A pod YAML with `volumes: - name: host-data hostPath: { path: "/mnt/data", type: DirectoryOrCreate }`.
title: HostPath Volume (Kubernetes)

definition: A Kubernetes volume type that is created when a pod is assigned to a node, initially empty, and exists as long as the pod is running on that node. It's ideal for temporary data that needs to be shared between containers within the same pod or for scratch space, as its contents are lost when the pod is removed from the node.
examples: A multi-container pod where an init container downloads data into `EmptyDir` and a main container processes it.|Temporary caching or scratch space for complex computations within a pod.|Specifying `volumes: - name: shared-data emptyDir: {}` in a pod YAML for inter-container communication.
title: EmptyDir Volume (Kubernetes)

definition: A Kubernetes volume type that uses a ConfigMap resource to inject non-sensitive configuration data into a pod's filesystem as files. Each key in the ConfigMap can become a file with its corresponding value as the file's content, allowing applications to consume configuration easily.
examples: Storing environment-specific configuration files (e.g., `nginx.conf`, `app.properties`) for an application.|Providing database connection strings or API endpoints to multiple pods without embedding them in container images.|A pod YAML mounting a ConfigMap: `volumes: - name: app-config configMap: { name: my-app-config }`.
title: ConfigMap Volume (Kubernetes)

definition: A Kubernetes volume type that uses a Secret resource to make sensitive data, like passwords, OAuth tokens, or SSH keys, available inside a pod as files in a memory-backed filesystem. This mechanism helps manage and distribute sensitive information securely.
examples: Mounting an API key or database password into an application pod for secure access.|Providing TLS certificates and private keys to a web server pod for HTTPS communication.|A pod YAML mounting a Secret: `volumes: - name: db-secret secret: { secretName: my-database-credentials }`.
title: Secret Volume (Kubernetes)

definition: A Kubernetes volume type that maps several existing volume sources (Secret, ConfigMap, DownwardAPI, ServiceAccountToken) into a single directory within a pod. This allows different types of data from various sources to be presented as files in one unified volume, simplifying application configuration access.
examples: Combining a ConfigMap for application settings, a Secret for database credentials, and a ServiceAccountToken for API access into a single `/etc/config` directory.|Injecting pod metadata (via DownwardAPI) alongside other application configurations.|A pod YAML using a projected volume: `projected: { sources: [ { secret: { name: "my-secret" } }, { configMap: { name: "my-config" } } ] }`.
title: Projected Volume (Kubernetes)

definition: A point-in-time copy of the data in a persistent volume, enabling quick restoration to a previous state or the creation of new volumes from the snapshot. It's a key feature for data protection, disaster recovery, and creating consistent backups in cloud-native environments.
examples: Creating a snapshot of a database volume before applying a major schema migration as a rollback point.|Periodically taking snapshots of application data volumes for backup purposes.|Restoring a lost or corrupted PersistentVolumeClaim from a recent VolumeSnapshot.|Creating new PersistentVolumeClaims from an existing snapshot for testing or development environments.
title: Volume Snapshot

definition: The process of creating a new, independent PersistentVolume from an existing PersistentVolume, where the new volume initially contains all the data of the source volume. Unlike snapshots, cloning creates a fully functional, writable volume ready for immediate use, often used for quickly duplicating datasets.
examples: Spinning up development or testing environments with pre-populated data from a production volume clone.|Creating multiple copies of a large dataset for parallel processing by different pods.|Developing a new feature against a fresh, isolated copy of the production database.
title: Volume Cloning

definition: A core component within a container orchestrator (like Kubernetes or Docker Swarm) responsible for intelligently placing workloads (e.g., pods, services) onto available nodes in the cluster. It considers various factors such as resource requirements, policies, node constraints, and affinity/anti-affinity rules to make optimal placement decisions.
examples: The Kubernetes `kube-scheduler` component, which continuously watches for new pods without assigned nodes and assigns them to a healthy node.|A scheduler might place a high-CPU pod on a node with ample CPU resources and fewer existing high-CPU workloads.|In Docker Swarm, the manager node's internal scheduler distributes service tasks across worker nodes.
title: Scheduler (orchestrator)

definition: A group of interconnected physical or virtual machines (nodes) that work together to run containerized applications and services. An orchestration tool manages these nodes, distributing workloads and providing features like high availability, scalability, and efficient resource utilization.
examples: A Kubernetes cluster running microservices on a set of EC2 instances in AWS.|A Docker Swarm cluster managing Docker containers across several bare-metal servers.|An OpenShift cluster providing a robust platform for deploying and scaling enterprise containerized applications.
title: Container Cluster

definition: A single physical or virtual machine that forms part of a container cluster, where containerized applications are actually deployed and run. Nodes provide the compute, memory, and storage resources consumed by containers, executing instructions from the cluster's control plane.
examples: A virtual machine in a cloud provider (e.g., AWS EC2 instance, Google Compute Engine VM) running the `kubelet` agent.|A physical server dedicated to running Docker containers as part of a Docker Swarm.|The output of `kubectl get nodes` showing the individual machines participating in a Kubernetes cluster.
title: Node (orchestration)

definition: In a Kubernetes cluster, the Master Node (now commonly referred to as the Control Plane) hosts the core components that manage and control the cluster, such as the API server, scheduler, controller manager, and etcd. It is responsible for maintaining the desired state of the cluster and orchestrating workloads across worker nodes.
examples: The machine running `kube-apiserver`, which exposes the Kubernetes API.|In a highly available setup, multiple master nodes distribute control plane services for redundancy.|The server whose failure would prevent new pods from being scheduled or existing resources from being managed.
title: Master Node (Kubernetes)

definition: In a Kubernetes cluster, a Worker Node is a machine that runs application workloads in the form of pods. It hosts essential components like the `kubelet` (to communicate with the control plane), `kube-proxy` (for network proxying), and a container runtime (e.g., containerd) to execute containers.
examples: A VM hosting several application pods, managed and monitored by the Kubernetes control plane.|The machine where `kubectl logs <pod-name>` retrieves logs for a running container.|A node whose resources (CPU, memory) are consumed by user-defined Deployments and Services.
title: Worker Node (Kubernetes)

definition: In container orchestration, the desired state is a declarative specification of how a system *should* look, defining the desired number of replicas, resource limits, configurations, and other properties for applications and infrastructure. The orchestrator continuously works to reconcile the actual state with this declared desired state, aiming for eventual consistency.
examples: A Kubernetes Deployment YAML specifying `replicas: 3` for a web application, indicating three instances should always be running.|A Docker Swarm service definition declaring `mode: replicated`, `replicas: 5` for a specific service.|An orchestrator creating a new pod because the actual number of running pods is less than the desired state specified in a Deployment.
title: Desired State (orchestration)

definition: In container orchestration, the actual state refers to the current observed condition of the cluster and its deployed applications at any given moment. This includes real-time information about running pods, their resource consumption, network configurations, and node health. Orchestrators constantly monitor and compare the actual state against the desired state to initiate necessary changes.
examples: `kubectl get pods` showing 2 running pods when the desired state specified 3.|A container runtime reporting a specific container as crashed or restarting.|The current CPU and memory utilization of a node as reported by monitoring tools like Prometheus.
title: Actual State (orchestration)

definition: A distributed, consistent, and highly available key-value store used by Kubernetes as its primary backend for all cluster data, including cluster configuration, state, and metadata. It forms the single source of truth for the entire cluster, making its availability critical for Kubernetes operations.
examples: Storing the definitions of all Kubernetes objects like Pods, Deployments, Services, and ConfigMaps.|Used by the API server to persist changes and retrieve the current cluster state.|A critical component whose unavailability can halt Kubernetes cluster operations and prevent changes to the desired state.
semantic_tags: Kubernetes|Key-Value Store|Data Store|Distributed System|Consistency|High Availability|Control Plane
title: Etcd (Kubernetes)

definition: A native clustering and orchestration solution for Docker containers, integrated directly into the Docker Engine. It allows users to create and manage a swarm of Docker nodes, deploying and scaling services across them with a focus on simplicity and ease of use.
examples: Initializing a new swarm cluster on a host machine with the `docker swarm init` command.|Deploying a multi-service application using a `docker-compose.yml` file with `docker stack deploy` onto a swarm.|Scaling a web service within a swarm using `docker service scale webapp=5` to increase its running instances.
title: Docker Swarm

definition: In a Docker Swarm cluster, a Swarm Manager is a node responsible for managing the cluster, orchestrating tasks, and maintaining the desired state of services. It handles scheduling, cluster state management using Raft consensus, and exposes the Swarm API for interacting with the cluster.
examples: The node where `docker service create` commands are issued, as managers are the only nodes that can execute orchestration commands.|The node hosting the Raft consensus group that ensures the consistency and reliability of the swarm state.|In a multi-manager setup, if the primary manager fails, another manager automatically takes over its role, maintaining high availability.
title: Swarm Manager

definition: A Swarm worker node is a Docker engine instance that receives and executes tasks scheduled by a Swarm manager, running containers as part of a Docker Swarm cluster. It registers with a manager and reports its status and task execution results, contributing compute resources to the cluster.
examples: `docker swarm join --token <token> <manager-ip>:<port>` command to add a new worker.|A worker node running a web server container and a database container for a distributed application.|A physical or virtual machine provisioned and added to a Docker Swarm cluster to scale application capacity.
semantic_tags: Docker Swarm|Orchestration|Worker Node|Container Host|Distributed System|Task Execution
title: Swarm Worker

definition: Raft is a consensus algorithm designed for managing a replicated log in distributed systems, aiming for understandability and strong consistency. It ensures that all nodes in a cluster agree on the same sequence of operations, crucial for maintaining state consistency, leader election, and fault tolerance.
examples: Kubernetes's etcd database uses Raft to ensure consistent state across its control plane nodes.|Docker Swarm managers use Raft for electing a leader and replicating the cluster's desired state.|HashiCorp Consul utilizes Raft for its service discovery and configuration store to guarantee data consistency.
semantic_tags: Distributed Systems|Consensus Algorithm|Fault Tolerance|Consistency|Leader Election|Replicated Log
title: Raft Consensus

definition: Apache Mesos is an open-source cluster manager that abstracts CPU, memory, storage, and other compute resources away from machines, enabling fault-tolerant and elastic distributed systems. It acts as a distributed kernel, providing efficient resource isolation and sharing across multiple frameworks like Marathon or Spark.
examples: Running a Mesos cluster with the Marathon framework to deploy long-running containerized services.|Using Mesos to manage resources for a combination of big data workloads (Apache Spark) and web applications (Docker).|Twitter, Apple, and Airbnb have historically used Mesos to manage their large-scale infrastructure and diverse workloads.
semantic_tags: Cluster Management|Resource Orchestration|Distributed Systems|Container Orchestration|Data Center OS|Frameworks
title: Apache Mesos

definition: Marathon is a production-grade container orchestration platform for Apache Mesos, designed to manage long-running services and applications. It provides features like high availability, service discovery, load balancing, and health checks for applications deployed on a Mesos cluster, functioning as a 'datacenter-scale init system'.
examples: Deploying a stateless web application (e.g., Nginx) onto a Mesos cluster via Marathon's API or UI.|Using Marathon to automatically restart failing application instances and scale them based on defined policies.|Defining a JSON application definition to run multiple Docker containers as a resilient service on Mesos.
semantic_tags: Mesos Framework|Container Orchestration|Long-running Services|High Availability|Service Discovery|Application Management
title: Marathon (Mesos framework)

definition: HashiCorp Nomad is a flexible workload orchestrator that enables deploying and managing any type of application across a cluster of machines, including containerized, virtualized, and bare-metal applications. It offers a unified workflow for deploying, scheduling, and scaling services with high efficiency and simplicity.
examples: Deploying Docker containers using Nomad alongside Java JAR files and static web content on the same cluster.|Using Nomad to manage a game server fleet, scaling instances up and down based on player count or demand.|Defining a `.nomad` job specification file to run a batch processing task on a schedule or event-driven basis.
title: Nomad (HashiCorp)

definition: Amazon Elastic Container Service (ECS) is a fully managed container orchestration service that allows you to easily run, stop, and manage Docker containers on a cluster of Amazon EC2 instances or using AWS Fargate. ECS integrates deeply with other AWS services, providing a scalable and reliable way to deploy containerized applications.
examples: Running a microservices architecture where each service is an ECS task deployed on EC2 instances.|Deploying a high-traffic web application using an ECS service integrated with an Application Load Balancer.|Using ECS to run batch jobs by scheduling tasks that process data stored in S3 buckets.

definition: AWS Fargate is a serverless compute engine for Amazon ECS and EKS that allows you to run containers without having to provision, configure, or scale clusters of virtual machines. With Fargate, you only pay for the compute resources consumed by your containers, abstracting away the underlying infrastructure management completely.
examples: Running an ECS task for a web API without managing any EC2 instances, leveraging Fargate for compute.|Deploying Kubernetes Pods on EKS using Fargate profiles, simplifying node lifecycle management.|Scaling a containerized application automatically based on traffic without manually adding or removing servers.
title: AWS Fargate

definition: Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) is a fully managed Kubernetes service that simplifies deploying, managing, and scaling containerized applications on Azure. AKS handles the operational overhead of managing Kubernetes control plane nodes, allowing users to focus on application development and deployment without infrastructure concerns.
examples: Deploying a multi-container application to AKS using Azure DevOps CI/CD pipelines.|Scaling an AKS cluster horizontally by adding more worker nodes to handle increased traffic demands.|Integrating AKS with Azure Monitor for centralized logging and diagnostics, and Azure Active Directory for authentication.
title: Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)

definition: Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) is a managed environment for deploying, managing, and scaling containerized applications using Kubernetes on Google Cloud. GKE fully manages the Kubernetes control plane and provides features like auto-scaling, auto-upgrades, and deep integration with other Google Cloud services.
examples: Creating a GKE cluster to host microservices for a large-scale e-commerce platform.|Using GKE's Autopilot mode to automatically provision and manage cluster infrastructure, optimizing resource utilization.|Deploying an application to GKE and exposing it globally via a Google Cloud Load Balancer.
