title: Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)

definition: Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) is a managed Kubernetes service that makes it easy to deploy, manage, and scale containerized applications using Kubernetes on AWS. EKS provides a highly available and scalable control plane and allows you to run Kubernetes workloads on either EC2 instances or AWS Fargate.
examples: Migrating an existing on-premises Kubernetes workload to EKS to leverage AWS infrastructure and services.|Running machine learning inference services on EKS with GPU-enabled EC2 instances for high performance.|Integrating EKS with AWS services like IAM for authentication, CloudWatch for monitoring, and Route 53 for DNS.
title: Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS)

definition: Red Hat OpenShift is an enterprise-ready, container platform built on Kubernetes, enhanced with developer and operational tools to provide a complete application development and deployment experience. It integrates Kubernetes with a set of security, networking, storage, and CI/CD solutions, making it a comprehensive platform-as-a-service (PaaS).
examples: Developers using OpenShift's integrated image registry and CI/CD pipelines to build and deploy applications.|An enterprise running critical business applications on OpenShift, leveraging its enhanced security features and support.|Deploying a Java application on OpenShift that automatically builds from source code and scales using Kubernetes capabilities.
title: Red Hat OpenShift

definition: A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes, representing a single instance of a running process in your cluster. It encapsulates one or more containers, storage resources (volumes), a unique network IP, and options that control how the containers should run, acting as an abstraction over containers.
examples: A Pod running a single Nginx web server container.|A Pod containing a main application container and a 'sidecar' logging agent container, sharing resources.|A Pod specified in a YAML file: `apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: my-pod spec: containers: [...]`.
title: Pod (Kubernetes)

definition: A container in a Pod refers to the Docker (or other OCI-compatible) containers that execute the actual application logic or auxiliary processes within a Kubernetes Pod. While a Pod can contain multiple containers, they are designed to be tightly coupled and share resources like network namespace, IPC namespace, and storage volumes.
examples: A Pod running a `frontend` container (e.g., Nginx) and a `backend` container (e.g., Node.js API) that communicate via `localhost`.|A Pod with a `main-app` container and a `log-shipper` container that reads logs from a shared `emptyDir` volume.|A single-container Pod running a simple `hello-world` image, where the Pod just wraps this one container.
title: Container in Pod

definition: Init containers are specialized containers that run to completion before the application containers in a Pod start. They are used to perform setup tasks like initializing shared volumes, waiting for external services, or populating configuration files, ensuring the main application containers have a pre-configured and ready environment.
examples: An Init Container waiting for a database service to become available before the main application container attempts to connect.|Using an Init Container to clone a Git repository into a shared volume, which the main web server container then serves.|A Pod definition with `initContainers: - name: init-db-check image: busybox command: ['sh', '-c', 'until nc -z db-service 5432; do echo waiting for db; sleep 2; done;']`.
title: Init Container (Kubernetes)

definition: The Sidecar container pattern involves deploying an auxiliary container alongside a main application container within the same Kubernetes Pod, sharing its network namespace and storage volumes. The sidecar container extends or enhances the main application's functionality without modifying its core code, such as handling logging, monitoring, or configuration synchronization.
examples: A `main-app` container processing requests, with a `sidecar-logging` container tailing its logs and sending them to a centralized log aggregator.|An `envoy` sidecar proxy providing service mesh capabilities (traffic management, security, resilience) for an adjacent `application` container.|A `config-reloader` sidecar watching for configuration changes on a shared volume and signaling the `web-server` main container to reload.
title: Sidecar container pattern

definition: In Kubernetes, a 'Workload' refers to an application or service running on the cluster, defined by controller objects that manage a set of Pods. These controllers abstract the details of managing individual Pods, ensuring a desired state and facilitating operations like scaling, rolling updates, and self-healing.
examples: A `Deployment` managing a stateless web application across multiple Pods, ensuring desired replicas.|A `StatefulSet` running a database like PostgreSQL with persistent storage and ordered startup/shutdown.|A `DaemonSet` ensuring a logging agent or monitoring exporter runs on every eligible node in the cluster.
title: Workload (Kubernetes)

definition: A Kubernetes Deployment is a higher-level API object used to manage stateless applications, providing declarative updates for Pods and ReplicaSets. It describes the desired state for an application, such as the container image to use and the number of replicas, and automatically handles rolling updates, rollbacks, and self-healing.
examples: Creating a Deployment to run three replicas of an Nginx web server, ensuring high availability and load balancing.|Updating a Deployment to a new version of an application image, triggering a controlled rolling update of Pods.|A YAML manifest for a Deployment specifying `replicas: 3`, a `selector` to identify Pods, and a Pod `template`.
title: Deployment (Kubernetes)

definition: A Kubernetes ReplicaSet ensures a stable set of identical Pods is running at any given time, maintaining a specified number of replicas. It automatically replaces failing Pods and scales the number of Pods up or down to match the desired count, though it's typically managed indirectly by Deployments for most use cases.
examples: A ReplicaSet created automatically by a Deployment to manage 3 instances of a web application Pod.|If one of the Pods managed by a ReplicaSet crashes or is terminated, the ReplicaSet will automatically create a new one to maintain the target count.|A raw ReplicaSet YAML definition explicitly specifying `replicas: 5` and a Pod `template` to ensure five copies of a specific Pod are always running.
title: ReplicaSet (Kubernetes)

definition: A Kubernetes StatefulSet is a workload API object used to manage stateful applications, providing stable, unique network identifiers, stable persistent storage, and ordered graceful deployment and scaling. It is suitable for applications like databases, message queues, or distributed key-value stores that require stable hostnames and persistent data.
examples: Deploying a three-node Apache Cassandra cluster using a StatefulSet, where each node gets a unique network identity and dedicated persistent volume.|Running a PostgreSQL database where each replica needs its own dedicated persistent storage volume, managed by the StatefulSet.|A StatefulSet ensuring Pods are started and stopped in a specific, predictable order during updates or scaling operations, crucial for quorum-based systems.
title: StatefulSet (Kubernetes)

definition: A Kubernetes DaemonSet ensures that all (or some) nodes in a cluster run a copy of a specific Pod. It is typically used for cluster-level functionalities like monitoring agents, log collectors, or storage daemons that need to be present and run on every eligible node, providing consistent services across the cluster.
examples: Deploying a Fluentd logging agent DaemonSet to collect logs from every node in the cluster and send them to a centralized system.|A Prometheus Node Exporter DaemonSet to gather host-level metrics from each Kubernetes node for monitoring purposes.|An antivirus scanner DaemonSet ensuring every node has a security agent running to maintain compliance.
title: DaemonSet (Kubernetes)

definition: A Kubernetes Job creates one or more Pods and ensures that a specified number of them successfully terminate. It's used for short-lived, batch-oriented tasks that run to completion.
examples: Running a database migration script once.|Performing a data backup operation.|Processing a batch of images from a queue.
title: Job (Kubernetes)

definition: A CronJob creates Jobs on a repeating schedule, similar to the `cron` utility in Linux. It is used for scheduled tasks that need to run periodically.
examples: Scheduling a nightly report generation.|Running a daily data cleanup script.|Performing a weekly security scan.
title: CronJob (Kubernetes)

definition: Namespaces provide a mechanism for isolating groups of resources within a single Kubernetes cluster. They are used to divide cluster resources among multiple users or teams, or to separate environments (e.g., development, staging, production).
examples: Using `kubectl create namespace my-app-dev` to separate development resources.|Isolating the `kube-system` namespace for cluster components.|Running different microservices in their own dedicated namespaces.
title: Namespace (Kubernetes)

definition: A Kubernetes Service is an abstract way to expose an application running on a set of Pods as a network service. It provides a stable IP address and DNS name for accessing Pods, abstracting away their ephemeral nature.
examples: Exposing a web server Pods as a `ClusterIP` Service for internal communication.|Creating a `LoadBalancer` Service to expose an application to the internet.|Using a `NodePort` Service to make an application accessible from outside the cluster on a specific port on each node.
title: Service (Kubernetes)

definition: An Ingress is a Kubernetes API object that manages external access to services in a cluster, typically HTTP/S. It provides HTTP routing rules, SSL/TLS termination, and name-based virtual hosting.
examples: Routing `my-app.example.com` to a `frontend-service`.|Configuring TLS termination for `https://api.example.com`.|Defining path-based routing, like `/api` to `api-service` and `/web` to `web-service`.
title: Ingress Object (Kubernetes)

definition: An Ingress Controller is a specialized load balancer that watches the Kubernetes API for Ingress resources and fulfills the Ingress by routing traffic to services. It's not part of the `kube-controller-manager` and must be deployed separately.
examples: Deploying `nginx-ingress-controller` to manage Ingress resources.|Using `traefik-ingress-controller` for edge routing.|Leveraging cloud provider specific Ingress Controllers like GKE Ingress.
title: Ingress Controller (Kubernetes)

definition: An Endpoint resource in Kubernetes manually specifies the network endpoints (IP addresses and ports) that a Service should route traffic to. While often managed automatically by the Service controller for Pods, it can be created manually for external services.
examples: Manually defining an Endpoint for an external database accessible at `192.168.1.100:3306`.|Automatically generated Endpoint for Pods backing a `Service`.|Connecting a Kubernetes Service to a non-Kubernetes workload.
title: Endpoint (Kubernetes)

definition: EndpointSlices are an evolution of Endpoints designed for scalability, especially in large clusters. They group network endpoints (IP addresses, ports, and associated labels) into multiple smaller resources rather than a single large Endpoint resource, improving performance and API responsiveness.
examples: A Service with 1000 Pods might have 10 EndpointSlices, each containing 100 endpoints.|Used internally by `kube-proxy` for efficient service discovery.|Observing `EndpointSlice` objects in large-scale cluster debugging.
title: EndpointSlice (Kubernetes)

definition: Labels are key-value pairs attached to Kubernetes objects, used to identify and organize them. They are crucial for specifying selection criteria for controllers, services, and policies.
examples: Tagging Pods with `app: my-web-app` and `env: production`.|Selecting all Pods with `tier: frontend` for a Service.|Applying a network policy to Pods labeled `security: high`.
title: Label (Kubernetes)

definition: A Selector is a powerful mechanism that allows Kubernetes controllers and services to identify and operate on a subset of objects based on their Labels. It defines criteria for matching objects, often used to link Services to Pods or Deployments to their Pods.
examples: A Service's `selector: { app: my-app, tier: frontend }` to target specific Pods.|A Deployment's `selector: { matchLabels: { app: nginx } }` to manage its Pods.|Using `kubectl get pods -l app=my-app` to filter command output.

definition: Annotations are key-value pairs used to attach arbitrary non-identifying metadata to Kubernetes objects. Unlike labels, annotations are not used for identifying or selecting objects and typically store larger, unstructured data.
examples: Storing build information like a git commit hash (`build.jenkins.com/git-sha: abcdef123`) on a Deployment.|Adding contact information for the team responsible (`owner: ops@example.com`).|Providing a descriptive note or documentation (`description: 'My critical frontend service'`).

definition: A Resource Limit defines the maximum amount of a specific resource (CPU or memory) that a container is allowed to use. If a container tries to exceed its memory limit, it will be terminated; exceeding a CPU limit results in throttling.
examples: Setting `memory: "512Mi"` as a limit to prevent a container from consuming too much RAM.|Defining `cpu: "2"` (2 CPU cores) as a limit to cap CPU usage.|A Pod with a memory limit of `1Gi` being OOM-killed when it attempts to use 1.5Gi.

definition: A Resource Request specifies the minimum amount of a specific resource (CPU or memory) that a container requires. The Kubernetes scheduler uses requests to decide which node is suitable to host a Pod, ensuring that the requested resources are available.
examples: Setting `memory: "256Mi"` as a request to guarantee a container gets at least that much RAM.|Defining `cpu: "500m"` (0.5 CPU cores) as a request to reserve CPU time.|A Pod failing to schedule if no node has `1Gi` memory free to satisfy its request.
title: Resource Request (Kubernetes)

definition: Kubernetes assigns a Quality of Service (QoS) class to each Pod based on the `resource requests` and `limits` defined for its containers. This class determines the priority and eviction behavior of the Pod under resource contention.
examples: A Pod with identical requests and limits for memory and CPU gets a `Guaranteed` QoS class.|A Pod with requests but no limits, or different requests/limits, gets `Burstable`.|A Pod with no requests or limits for any container gets `BestEffort`.
normalized_name: quality of service qos class kubernetes
title: Quality of Service (QoS) Class (Kubernetes)

definition: A Pod receives the `Guaranteed` QoS class if every container within it has both CPU and memory `requests` and `limits` set, and these requests are equal to their respective limits. These Pods have the highest priority and are the last to be evicted.
examples: A critical database Pod with `requests: { cpu: 1, memory: 2Gi }` and `limits: { cpu: 1, memory: 2Gi }`.|A core networking component ensured stable resources.|Essential infrastructure services that must not be evicted first.
title: Guaranteed QoS Class

definition: A Pod receives the `Burstable` QoS class if it has at least one container with a CPU or memory `request` set, and its requests are not equal to its limits, or it has limits without requests. These Pods have medium priority and can be evicted after `BestEffort` Pods but before `Guaranteed` Pods.
examples: A web server Pod with `requests: { cpu: 500m, memory: 1Gi }` and `limits: { cpu: 1, memory: 2Gi }`.|A microservice that needs guaranteed minimums but can burst if resources are available.|Most common application workloads fall into this class.
title: Burstable QoS Class

definition: A Pod receives the `BestEffort` QoS class if none of its containers specify any CPU or memory `requests` or `limits`. These Pods have the lowest priority and are the first to be evicted when node resources are scarce.
examples: A development or test Pod where resource usage isn't critical, with no resource definitions.|Non-critical batch jobs that can tolerate eviction and restart.|A temporary utility Pod running a quick diagnostic command.
semantic_tags: Lowest Priority|No Guarantee|First Evicted|No Resource Constraints|Non-Critical|Opportunistic
title: BestEffort QoS Class

definition: A Liveness Probe periodically checks if a container is running and healthy, indicating whether the application inside is still alive. If the probe fails, Kubernetes restarts the container, aiming to recover from deadlocked states.

title: Liveness Probe (Kubernetes)

definition: A Readiness Probe periodically checks if a container is ready to serve traffic, indicating whether the application is fully initialized and functional. If the probe fails, Kubernetes removes the Pod's IP from the Service endpoints until it becomes ready again, preventing traffic from being sent to an unready instance.
examples: An HTTP `GET` probe to `/ready` endpoint; if it returns non-200, stop sending traffic.|A `tcpSocket` probe to a database port; if the connection fails, mark as unready.|An `exec` probe checking if a backend dependency is reachable before serving requests.

title: Readiness Probe (Kubernetes)

definition: A Startup Probe checks if an application inside a container has successfully started up. If configured, it disables Liveness and Readiness probes until it succeeds, ensuring slow-starting applications have enough time to initialize without being prematurely killed or marked unready.
examples: A `tcpSocket` probe to port `8080` with a long `failureThreshold` to give a slow database server ample startup time.|An `exec` probe that checks for a specific log entry indicating application initialization completion.|Allowing a large Java application to fully load its classpath and dependencies before Liveness/Readiness begin.

definition: A Kubernetes API object used to store non-confidential data in key-value pairs, making configuration data available to Pods. It decouples configuration from container images, enhancing portability and ease of management.

definition: A non-human account used by processes running in Pods to interact with the Kubernetes API server. It grants an identity to Pods, allowing them to perform actions within the cluster based on associated Roles and RoleBindings.

definition: A Kubernetes RBAC object that grants the permissions defined in a Role (or a ClusterRole, if bound to namespace-scoped resources) to a user, group, or Service Account within a specific namespace. definition: A Kubernetes RBAC object that grants the permissions defined in a ClusterRole to a user, group, or Service Account across the entire cluster. It links a ClusterRole's permissions to an identity, enabling them to perform cluster-wide actions or actions on non-namespaced resources.

definition: A callback mechanism in Kubernetes where an external HTTP endpoint is invoked by the API server to perform custom logic during the admission control phase of an API request. Webhooks allow for advanced validation or mutation of resources before they are persisted in `etcd`.

definition: A scheduling feature that constrains which nodes a Pod can be scheduled on, based on node labels. definition: A scheduling feature that constrains which nodes a Pod *cannot* be scheduled on, based on the labels of other Pods already running on those nodes. definition: A Taint is a property set on a Kubernetes node that repels a set of pods. Nodes can be tainted to indicate that they should not run certain pods unless those pods explicitly tolerate the taint, enabling workload isolation or special node usage.

definition: Preemption is a Kubernetes scheduling mechanism where the scheduler evicts lower-priority pods from nodes to make room for pending higher-priority pods that cannot be scheduled otherwise. This ensures critical applications get the resources they need even under resource contention.

definition: An API Object in Kubernetes is a 'record of intent' that represents the desired state of your cluster. definition: A minimal base image refers to using an extremely lightweight container image as the starting point for building application images, significantly reducing the final image size and attack surface. Examples include `scratch` (an empty image), Alpine Linux, or Google's Distroless images, which contain only the application and its runtime dependencies.
examples: Starting a Dockerfile with `FROM scratch` for a statically compiled Go application.|Using `FROM alpine:3.14` as the base for a Python application to create a smaller image.|Employing `FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs:16` to ensure only the Node.js runtime is present, without a shell or package manager.
title: Minimal base image (best practice)

definition: Using a non-root user is a container security best practice where the application inside the container runs with reduced privileges instead of as the `root` user. This minimizes the potential impact of a container compromise, as an attacker would gain access only to the limited permissions of the non-root user, significantly reducing the blast radius.
examples: Adding `USER appuser` in a Dockerfile after creating a dedicated user and group.|Configuring Kubernetes Pods with `securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true` and `runAsUser` to enforce non-root execution.|Running an Nginx container as the `nginx` user instead of `root` to prevent privilege escalation.
normalized_name: non root user container security best practice
title: Non-root user (container security best practice)

definition: An approach where infrastructure components, such as container images, are never modified after deployment. Instead, any changes or updates require building and deploying a completely new image, which then replaces the old component entirely. This practice ensures consistency, simplifies rollbacks, and reduces configuration drift.
examples: Updating a Docker application by building a new Docker image with the updated code and redeploying it, rather than patching the running container.|In Kubernetes, deploying a new version of an application by updating the image tag in the deployment manifest, causing Kubernetes to create new pods and terminate old ones.|Using GitOps principles where all infrastructure changes are driven by version-controlled image definitions, ensuring reproducibility.
title: Immutable infrastructure (container)

definition: An application design principle where the application does not store any client-specific data or session information locally on the server. Each request from a client contains all necessary information for the server to process it independently, allowing instances to be interchangeable and easily scaled horizontally.
examples: A REST API that processes requests based solely on the input parameters and headers, without maintaining user sessions on the API server itself.|A web server serving static content or acting as a reverse proxy, where session management (if any) is handled by an external database or caching service.|A microservice that consumes messages from a queue, processes them, and stores results in a persistent data store, discarding all internal state between message processing cycles.
title: Stateless application (container best practice)

definition: Automated probes configured for containers, typically managed by an orchestrator, to ascertain if an application is running, healthy, and ready to serve traffic. These checks are crucial for maintaining application reliability, ensuring only functional instances receive requests and problematic ones are recycled.
examples: A Kubernetes 'liveness probe' that performs an HTTP GET request to a `/healthz` endpoint; if the endpoint repeatedly fails, Kubernetes restarts the container.|A Kubernetes 'readiness probe' that executes a command like `cat /tmp/ready` inside the container; if the command fails, the container is not marked as ready to receive traffic.|A Docker Swarm health check that periodically runs `ps aux | grep myapp` to ensure the main application process is still active within the container.
title: Health checks (container best practice)

definition: Configuration settings that define the maximum amount of CPU and memory that a container is allowed to consume on its host. By setting limits, individual containers are prevented from monopolizing system resources, ensuring fair resource distribution, predictable performance, and overall system stability.
examples: Running a Docker container with `docker run --memory='512m' --cpus='0.5' myimage`, limiting it to 512MB RAM and 50% of one CPU core.|In a Kubernetes Pod definition, specifying `resources.limits.cpu: '500m'` and `resources.limits.memory: '256Mi'` to cap resource usage for a container.|A container orchestrator dynamically adjusting resource allocations based on defined limits and available host resources.
title: Resource limits (container best practice)

definition: The recommended practice for containerized applications to direct all log messages and error output to their standard output (stdout) and standard error (stderr) streams, respectively. This decouples log management from the application, allowing the container runtime or orchestrator to capture, aggregate, and process logs centrally without requiring internal log file management.
examples: A Node.js application using `console.log('User logged in')` and `console.error('Database connection failed')`, which outputs directly to stdout/stderr.|A Python script using `print('Processing data...')` or `sys.stderr.write('Warning: missing config')`.|Viewing captured logs for a Docker container using the `docker logs <container_id>` command, demonstrating the runtime's log aggregation capability.
normalized_name: logging to stdout stderr container best practice
title: Logging to stdout/stderr (container best practice)

definition: A temporary container that can be run inside an existing Kubernetes Pod, primarily for interactive debugging and troubleshooting. Unlike regular containers, ephemeral containers are started after a Pod is running and can share namespaces (like PID and network) with other containers in the Pod, allowing inspection of their environment and processes.
examples: Using `kubectl debug -it my-pod --image=busybox --target=my-app` to launch a `busybox` container inside `my-pod` and attach to the `my-app` container's process namespace to debug a running application.|Attaching an ephemeral container with `strace` to a misbehaving application container to trace system calls and diagnose runtime issues.|Running `tcpdump` in an ephemeral container within a Pod's network namespace to capture and analyze network traffic specific to that Pod.
title: Ephemeral Container

definition: The core component of the Linux operating system, responsible for managing hardware resources, executing processes, and providing system services. In containerization, the Linux kernel provides the fundamental mechanisms, such as namespaces and control groups (CGroups), that enable the isolation and resource management for containerized workloads.
examples: The `vmlinuz` file, which is the compressed Linux kernel image found on most Linux systems.|When a Docker container starts, it shares the host's Linux kernel but uses kernel features like namespaces to create an isolated view of system resources.|CGroups are a Linux kernel feature directly utilized by container runtimes to enforce resource limits on containers.
title: Linux Kernel (underlying)

definition: The programmatic interface through which a running computer program requests a service from the kernel of the operating system. In the context of containers, specific system calls like `clone()` and `unshare()` are critically used to create isolated execution environments by manipulating kernel namespaces and control groups.
examples: `open()`: A system call used by an application to request the kernel to open a file.|`fork()` and `execve()`: System calls for creating new processes and loading new programs.|`clone()`: A system call heavily used by container runtimes to create new processes with isolated namespaces, forming the basis of container isolation.
title: System Calls (Linux)

definition: A system call and command that changes the apparent root directory for the current running process and its children, confining them to a specific subtree of the file system. It's an early and rudimentary form of isolation, primarily used to isolate file system access but not other system resources like processes or network.
examples: `sudo chroot /mnt/new_root bash` command, which starts a new `bash` shell where `/mnt/new_root` acts as the root (`/`) directory.|Used in software build environments to test applications against different library versions or OS distributions without affecting the host system.|Historically employed for creating 'jails' for services or users with limited access, though less robust than modern container technologies for full isolation.
title: Chroot

definition: A type of file system mount (often implemented via OverlayFS on Linux) that layers one or more file systems on top of each other, presenting a unified view of their contents. This mechanism is crucial for container runtimes like Docker, allowing multiple containers to efficiently share read-only base image layers while providing each container with its own writable top layer.
examples: Docker's `overlay2` storage driver, where container image layers are read-only 'lower' directories, and a container's writable layer is an 'upper' directory, which are merged into a single view.|Using the `mount -t overlay overlay -o lowerdir=/base,upperdir=/changes,workdir=/work /merged` command to create a combined file system view.|Allowing changes made inside a running container to be stored separately without modifying the original, immutable base image layers.
title: Overlay mounts

definition: The initial version of Linux Control Groups, which allowed for the hierarchical organization of processes and the allocation of system resources among them. CGroups v1 utilized separate, independent hierarchies for each resource type (e.g., CPU, memory, I/O), making management and resource distribution somewhat complex.
examples: Limiting CPU usage by writing values to files in `/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/my_group/cpu.cfs_quota_us`.|Setting memory limits for a process group via `/sys/fs/cgroup/memory/my_group/memory.limit_in_bytes`.|Docker historically used CGroups v1 by default to enforce resource constraints on individual containers.
title: CGroups v1 subsystems

definition: The successor to CGroups v1, designed to simplify resource management by providing a single, unified hierarchy for all resource controllers. It offers improved consistency, better resource distribution logic, and enhanced delegation capabilities compared to v1, and is increasingly adopted by modern Linux distributions and container runtimes.
examples: Modern `systemd` installations on newer Linux distributions typically utilize CGroups v2 for process and resource management.|Booting a Linux kernel with `systemd.unified_cgroup_hierarchy=1` to enable the unified cgroup hierarchy.|Container runtimes like `crun` and `runc` are evolving to support or leverage CGroups v2 for more efficient and consistent resource control.
title: CGroups v2 unified hierarchy

definition: A Linux system call used to create a new process or thread with fine-grained control over resource sharing and isolation between the parent and child. It is a fundamental mechanism for containerization, as it allows a new process to be created within new, isolated namespaces (e.g., PID, network, mount), providing the basis for container isolation.
examples: A container runtime like `runc` using `clone()` with flags such as `CLONE_NEWPID`, `CLONE_NEWNET`, and `CLONE_NEWNS` to create a new process within isolated namespaces for a container.|Creating a new thread in a C program, which often involves the `clone()` system call under the hood.|Tools like `systemd-nspawn` leveraging `clone()` to create lightweight container environments with specific namespace isolation.
title: Clone system call

definition: A Linux system call that allows a running process to unshare (dissociate) specific execution contexts, such as namespaces, from its parent and other processes. This enables an existing process to dynamically move itself into a new, isolated namespace without creating a new process, facilitating runtime modification of process isolation properties.
examples: Running `unshare --pid --fork /bin/bash` to start a new `bash` shell with its own private PID namespace.|Using `unshare --net ip link set lo up && ip addr add 127.0.0.1/8 dev lo` to create a new network namespace for the current process and configure its loopback interface.|Custom containerization scripts or debugging tools might use `unshare()` to put a running process into a specific new namespace for inspection or modification.
title: Unshare system call

definition: Also known as a 'bare-metal' hypervisor, it runs directly on the host hardware, managing the hardware resources and allocating them to multiple guest operating systems. This type offers high performance, strong isolation between virtual machines, and is commonly used in enterprise data centers.
examples: VMware ESXi, which installs directly onto server hardware and allows creation of multiple VMs.|Microsoft Hyper-V, an enterprise virtualization platform built into Windows Server that runs directly on hardware.|Xen and KVM (when used with virtualization extensions), which function as bare-metal hypervisors.
title: Type 1 Hypervisor

definition: Also known as a 'hosted' hypervisor, it runs as a software application on top of a conventional host operating system. It relies on the host OS for device drivers and basic resource management, then provides virtualization services to guest operating systems, typically used for desktop virtualization.
examples: Oracle VirtualBox running on a Windows or macOS machine to host Linux or other Windows VMs.|VMware Workstation or Parallels Desktop, used by developers or users to run multiple guest OSes on their personal computers.|QEMU, often used as a Type 2 hypervisor for development and testing environments on a host OS.
title: Type 2 Hypervisor

definition: An operating system (e.g., Windows, Linux, macOS) that runs as a virtual machine on top of a hypervisor. Each guest OS instance is completely independent, having its own kernel, libraries, and applications, isolated from other guest OSes and the physical host system.
examples: A Windows Server 2019 instance running as a VM on a VMware ESXi hypervisor.|A developer's local machine running a Ubuntu Linux VM inside VirtualBox on a macOS host.|Multiple different Linux distributions (e.g., CentOS, Debian, Fedora) running concurrently as separate VMs on a single physical server.
title: Guest OS (VM)

definition: A virtualization technology where the kernel of a single host operating system is used to run multiple isolated user-space instances, commonly known as containers. These instances share the host kernel but have their own isolated file systems, process trees, and network interfaces, offering a lightweight and efficient alternative to traditional virtual machines.
examples: Docker containers leveraging Linux namespaces and CGroups to provide isolated application environments.|LXC (Linux Containers), which provides comprehensive OS-level virtualization features.|FreeBSD Jails and Solaris Zones, earlier implementations of OS-level virtualization on their respective operating systems.
title: OS-level virtualization

definition: Refers to the degree of separation and security between workloads and the host system. VMs provide strong, hardware-level isolation, each with its own dedicated kernel and resources. Containers offer OS-level isolation, sharing the host kernel, which is less isolated and potentially less secure than VMs but provides higher efficiency and faster startup.
examples: **VM Isolation**: A critical banking application in a Windows VM is deeply isolated from a development Linux VM on the same physical hardware, reducing cross-workload interference risks.|**Container Isolation**: Two Docker containers on the same host share the Linux kernel, with isolation primarily enforced by kernel namespaces and CGroups, which is robust for many use cases but has a smaller security boundary.|A kernel vulnerability could potentially affect all containers on a host, whereas a VM's guest OS kernel is distinct from other VMs and the host.
title: Isolation level (VM vs Container)

definition: The additional computational resources (CPU, memory, storage, network) consumed by the virtualization layer itself, beyond what the application directly uses. Virtual machines generally incur higher overhead due to requiring a full guest OS and hypervisor layer, while containers have significantly lower overhead because they share the host OS kernel and typically have smaller footprints.
examples: **VM Overhead**: A bare VM, before any applications are installed, might consume several hundred megabytes of RAM and a percentage of CPU simply for the guest OS to run and the hypervisor to operate.|**Container Overhead**: A simple Docker container running `nginx` adds only a few megabytes of memory and negligible CPU usage beyond the `nginx` process itself, as it reuses the host kernel.|Starting a VM typically takes minutes, while starting a container takes seconds or even milliseconds, reflecting their respective overheads.
title: Overhead (VM vs Container)

definition: Boot time compares the startup speed of virtual machines (VMs) and containers, highlighting that containers boot significantly faster. This difference arises because containers share the host OS kernel, whereas VMs must boot an entire guest operating system.
examples: A Linux VM might take 30-60 seconds to fully boot.|A Docker container typically starts in milliseconds.|Spinning up hundreds of web server instances is vastly quicker with containers than with VMs.
title: Boot time (VM vs Container)

definition: The CNCF Landscape is a comprehensive, interactive map that categorizes and showcases the vast array of open-source projects, products, and services within the Cloud Native Computing Foundation ecosystem. It serves as a guide for navigating the complex and rapidly evolving world of cloud-native technologies.
examples: Kubernetes, listed under Orchestration & Management.|Prometheus, found in the Monitoring & Observability category.|Envoy, categorized under Service Mesh.
title: CNCF Landscape

definition: Cloud Native principles are a set of architectural and operational guidelines for building and running applications that fully leverage the advantages of the cloud computing model. They emphasize agility, scalability, resilience, and maintainability, often involving containerization, microservices, declarative APIs, and continuous delivery.
examples: Using Docker and Kubernetes to package and orchestrate applications.|Designing applications as independent, loosely coupled microservices.|Implementing CI/CD pipelines for automated builds, tests, and deployments.
title: Cloud Native principles

definition: WebAssembly (WASM) is a binary instruction format for a stack-based virtual machine, designed as a portable compilation target for high-level languages like C/C++/Rust. It enables near-native performance for applications, originally in web browsers, but now expanding to server-side, edge, and other environments.
examples: Running a computationally intensive C++ game engine directly in a web browser.|Executing Rust-based serverless functions efficiently on the backend.|Using WASM for client-side image processing or video editing applications.
title: WebAssembly (WASM)

definition: WASI (WebAssembly System Interface) is a modular system interface for WebAssembly designed to allow WASM modules to run securely outside the web browser. It provides a standardized way for WASM code to interact with host environment resources, such as files, networking, and environment variables, similar to POSIX for native executables.
examples: A WASM module compiled from Rust using `std::fs::File::open()` to read a file from the host filesystem.|A WASM program making an HTTP request to an external API.|Accessing environment variables passed by the host to a WASM application.
title: WASI (WebAssembly System Interface)

definition: Wasmtime is a standalone runtime for WebAssembly and WASI, engineered for embedding into applications and executing WASM modules securely and efficiently outside of a web browser. It is a critical component for server-side WASM, allowing developers to leverage WASM's benefits in diverse backend and edge computing scenarios.
examples: Embedding Wasmtime into a Rust application to run untrusted plugins written in different languages.|Using Wasmtime as the execution engine for serverless functions.|A command-line tool executing a compiled WASM file via `wasmtime run my_program.wasm`.
title: Wasmtime

definition: Runwasi is an experimental project that integrates WebAssembly (WASM) runtimes with `containerd`, enabling WASM modules to be managed and orchestrated using existing container tools like Kubernetes. It provides a `containerd` shim that allows WASM workloads to be run and managed as if they were standard OCI (Open Container Initiative) containers.
examples: Deploying a WASM module to a Kubernetes cluster where `containerd` is configured with `runwasi`.|Using `ctr run` to execute a WASM application through the `runwasi` shim.|Orchestrating a mix of Docker containers and WASM modules on a single host using `containerd`.
title: Runwasi

definition: WasmEdge is a lightweight, high-performance WebAssembly (WASM) runtime optimized for serverless applications, edge computing, and microservices. It supports WASI and provides extensions for advanced functionalities like AI/ML inference and networking, aiming to be a universal runtime for next-generation cloud-native applications.
examples: Executing serverless functions written in Rust and compiled to WASM on FaaS platforms.|Running AI inference models directly at the edge with minimal overhead.|Building high-performance blockchain smart contracts using WasmEdge as the execution engine.
title: WasmEdge

definition: The Wasm Component Model is an extension to WebAssembly designed to enable true interoperability between modules written in different programming languages. It provides a standardized way to define interfaces, pass structured data, and call functions across module boundaries, fostering a robust, language-agnostic module ecosystem.
examples: A Rust WASM module directly invoking a function exported by a C++ WASM module.|Creating a plugin system where plugins, regardless of their source language, conform to a shared WASM component interface.|Sharing complex data structures like records or variants between components without serialization overhead.
title: Wasm Component Model

definition: A WASM sandbox refers to the secure, isolated execution environment provided for WebAssembly modules. This isolation ensures that WASM code cannot arbitrarily access host system resources or interfere with other modules without explicit, defined permissions, making it a cornerstone of WASM's security model.
examples: A web browser running an untrusted WASM module, preventing it from accessing local files or making system calls.|A serverless platform executing user-submitted WASM code, guaranteeing it operates within its allocated resources.|A plugin architecture where each plugin runs in its own isolated WASM sandbox to prevent security vulnerabilities from spreading.
title: WASM Sandbox

definition: A WASM module is a compiled binary unit of WebAssembly code, representing a self-contained program or library. It defines functions, imports, exports, and memory, and is designed to be loaded, instantiated, and executed by a WASM runtime, typically having been generated from higher-level languages like C, C++, or Rust.
examples: A `.wasm` file produced by compiling a Rust source code file.|A JavaScript application loading a `my_library.wasm` file and invoking its exported `calculate_sum` function.|A server-side WASM runtime instantiating a module to handle an incoming request.
title: WASM Module

examples: Building a sentiment analysis model to classify text as positive, negative, or neutral.|Developing a machine translation system (e.g., English to Spanish).|Creating a chatbot that understands user queries and responds appropriately.

title: Natural Language Processing (ML Task)

title: Computer Vision (ML Task)

definition: The process of analyzing data points collected over a period of time to identify patterns, trends, and seasonality, often for forecasting future values or understanding past behavior.
examples: Forecasting future sales based on historical sales data.|Predicting stock prices or cryptocurrency movements using past market data.|Analyzing sensor data from IoT devices to predict equipment failure before it occurs.

title: Time Series Analysis (ML Task)

definition: The subset of a dataset used to train a machine learning model, allowing it to learn the underlying patterns, relationships, and parameters necessary for making predictions.
examples: A CSV file containing historical customer data (features) and their churn status (labels) used to train a churn prediction model.|A collection of images with bounding box annotations for training an object detection model.|Using 80% of an entire dataset for model learning, typically after shuffling.
title: Training Data

definition: A separate subset of the dataset used during model training to tune hyperparameters, monitor performance, and prevent overfitting by evaluating the model on unseen data.
examples: Using a validation set to choose the optimal number of hidden layers in a neural network.|Monitoring the loss on the validation set to implement early stopping, preventing the model from overfitting.|Evaluating different learning rates on the validation set to find the best one for a model.
title: Validation Data

definition: A completely independent subset of the original dataset, held back until the very end, used to provide an unbiased evaluation of the final trained model's performance and generalization ability on truly unseen data.
examples: Reporting the F1-score of a classification model on the test set as its final, unbiased performance metric.|Using the test set to ensure the model performs well on new, never-before-seen data before deployment.|Evaluating the RMSE of a regression model on its final test set to confirm generalization.
semantic_tags: Model Evaluation|Generalization|Unbiased Performance|Final Assessment|Dataset Split|Performance Metric
title: Test Data

definition: Occurs when information from the test set or future data is inadvertently used during model training or validation, leading to an overly optimistic performance estimate and poor generalization on truly new data.
examples: Scaling data using statistics calculated from the entire dataset (including test data) before splitting.|Including features derived from the target variable that would not be available at inference time.|Using future time series data to engineer features for past time steps in a forecasting model.
title: Data Leakage

definition: A powerful ensemble machine learning technique that builds a strong predictive model by sequentially combining multiple weak prediction models, typically decision trees, where each new model corrects the errors of the previous ones.
examples: Using XGBoost or LightGBM for highly accurate tabular data classification or regression tasks.|Predicting customer churn with a gradient boosting model by combining many small decision trees.|Ranking search results using a gradient boosted decision tree (GBDT) model.
title: Gradient Boosting Machines

definition: The process of taking a pre-trained model (often a large neural network trained on a massive generic dataset) and further training it on a smaller, specific dataset to adapt it for a particular downstream task.
examples: Taking a pre-trained BERT model and fine-tuning it on a sentiment analysis dataset for movie reviews.|Adapting a pre-trained ResNet model (trained on ImageNet) to classify specific types of medical images.|Freezing initial layers of a pre-trained model and only training the final layers on new, task-specific data.
semantic_tags: Transfer Learning|Pre-trained Models|Neural Networks|Adaptation|Downstream Task|Model Customization
title: Fine-tuning

definition: An adaptive learning rate optimization algorithm that divides the learning rate by an exponentially decaying average of squared gradients, helping to converge faster in non-stationary objectives and resolve vanishing/exploding gradients in neural networks.
examples: Specifying `optimizer=tf.keras.optimizers.RMSprop(learning_rate=0.001)` when compiling a TensorFlow model.|Training a recurrent neural network (RNN) where gradients can be noisy or prone to explosion/vanishing.|When the learning objective landscape is highly irregular and standard SGD struggles.
semantic_tags: Optimizer|Adaptive Learning Rate|Gradient Descent|Neural Networks|Deep Learning|Optimization Algorithm
title: RMSprop

definition: An adaptive learning rate optimization algorithm that adapts the learning rate for each parameter, performing smaller updates for parameters associated with frequently occurring features and larger updates for rare ones, by dividing the learning rate by the square root of the sum of squared historical gradients.
examples: Using Adagrad for sparse data scenarios (e.g., NLP word embeddings) where some features appear much less frequently than others.|When training models where different parameters require different magnitudes of updates for optimal convergence.|Implementing `torch.optim.Adagrad(model.parameters(), lr=0.01)` in PyTorch for models with sparse gradients.
semantic_tags: Optimizer|Adaptive Learning Rate|Gradient Descent|Sparse Data|Neural Networks|Optimization Algorithm
title: Adagrad

definition: A regularization technique used in neural networks where a random subset of neurons is temporarily ignored (dropped out) during each training iteration, preventing complex co-adaptations between neurons and reducing overfitting.
examples: Adding `tf.keras.layers.Dropout(0.5)` after a dense layer in a neural network to randomly zero out 50% of the inputs.|Training a deep neural network on a relatively small dataset to prevent it from memorizing the training examples.|Using dropout to improve the generalization ability of a convolutional neural network (CNN).
title: Dropout

definition: The process of dynamically adjusting the learning rate during model training, typically by decreasing it over time, to allow for faster convergence early on and finer adjustments as the model approaches an optimum.
examples: Implementing a step decay schedule where the learning rate is multiplied by a factor every few epochs.|Using a cosine annealing scheduler to gradually decrease the learning rate and then reset it.|Applying a `ReduceLROnPlateau` callback that reduces the learning rate when a monitored metric stops improving.
title: Learning Rate Scheduling

definition: A harmonic mean of precision and recall, providing a single metric that balances both the ability of a model to make positive predictions correctly (precision) and its ability to find all positive samples (recall). It is particularly useful for imbalanced datasets.
examples: Evaluating a fraud detection model where identifying all fraudulent transactions (recall) is crucial, but false positives are also costly (precision).|Calculating F1-score for a medical diagnosis model where misclassifying either positive or negative cases has significant consequences.|In scikit-learn: `f1_score(y_true, y_pred)` for a binary or multi-class classification task.
title: F1-Score (Metric)

definition: Low-dimensional, dense vector representations of discrete variables (like words, entities, or categories) that capture semantic relationships and contextual information, allowing machine learning models to process them effectively.
examples: Word embeddings (e.g., Word2Vec, GloVe) where similar words have similar vector representations in a numerical space.|Category embeddings for tabular data, representing categorical features as dense vectors that models can learn from.|Node embeddings in graph neural networks, capturing structural roles and relationships of nodes within a graph.
semantic_tags: Vector Representation|Feature Engineering|Semantic Similarity|Neural Networks|NLP|Dimensionality Reduction
title: Embeddings (Concept)

definition: A hyper-surface or line in the feature space that separates different classes or regions predicted by a classification model, marking the points where the model's prediction switches from one class to another.
examples: A straight line separating two classes in a 2D scatter plot for a linear Support Vector Machine (SVM).|A complex, non-linear boundary for a neural network classifying images into different categories.|Visualizing the decision boundary to understand how a model distinguishes between 'spam' and 'not spam' emails based on their features.
title: Decision Boundary

definition: In an n-dimensional space, a hyperplane is a flat, n-1 dimensional subspace that divides the space into two half-spaces. In machine learning, it commonly serves as a decision boundary to separate different classes of data points.
examples: In a 2D scatter plot, a hyperplane is a straight line separating two classes (e.g., distinguishing between benign and malignant tumors based on two features).|In a 3D feature space, a hyperplane is a flat plane that separates data points.|The decision boundary learned by a Support Vector Machine (SVM) to classify data is a hyperplane (or multiple hyperplanes after transformation in non-linear cases).
title: Hyperplane

definition: Bagging is an ensemble meta-algorithm that improves the stability and accuracy of machine learning algorithms, primarily used for reducing variance. It involves training multiple models (e.g., decision trees) on different bootstrap samples (random samples with replacement) of the original dataset, and then averaging their predictions.
examples: Random Forest is a prominent example of bagging, where an ensemble of decision trees is trained on bootstrapped samples, and their predictions are averaged for regression or majority-voted for classification.|Training multiple SVMs on different subsets of a dataset and combining their outputs to get a more robust classification.|Using bagging with a neural network model to reduce overfitting and improve generalization on a complex dataset.
title: Bootstrap Aggregating (Bagging)

definition: Model bias refers to the error introduced by approximating a real-world problem, which may be complex, with a simplified model. It represents the difference between the average prediction of our model and the correct target value, leading to systematic errors and underfitting.
examples: Using a linear regression model to fit data that has an intrinsically quadratic relationship, resulting in high bias.|A neural network with too few layers or neurons (low model capacity) failing to capture complex patterns in image data, leading to underfitting.|A sentiment analysis model trained only on formal text failing to accurately classify sentiment in informal social media posts due to its inherent simplification of language nuances.
title: Bias (Model Bias)

definition: Model variance refers to the error from sensitivity to small fluctuations in the training dataset; a high-variance model performs well on training data but poorly on unseen data. definition: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is an iterative optimization algorithm used to minimize the objective function (loss function) of a model by updating its parameters. It allows the activation function to be shifted left or right, effectively allowing the model to fit a wider range of data patterns by providing an extra degree of freedom for the model to activate or deactivate neurons.

definition: Computational Linguistics is an interdisciplinary field that combines computer science and linguistics to model human language using computational methods. definition: Word Tokenization is the process of splitting a continuous sequence of text into discrete units called tokens, typically words. It's a fundamental step in Natural Language Processing, preparing text for further analysis by breaking it down into meaningful linguistic units.
examples: Input: 'Hello, world!' -> Output: ['Hello', ',', 'world', '!']|Input: 'The quick brown fox.' -> Output: ['The', 'quick', 'brown', 'fox', '.']|Using `nltk.word_tokenize()` in Python to segment a sentence into individual words and punctuation marks.
title: Word Tokenization

definition: Subword Tokenization is a method of breaking down text into units larger than characters but smaller than words, known as subword units or subword tokens. This approach effectively handles out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words by decomposing them into known subwords and manages vocabulary size more efficiently than pure word-level tokenization.
examples: The word 'unhappiness' might be tokenized into ['un', '##happi', '##ness'].|A rare word like 'supercalifragilisticexpialidocious' could be broken into common subwords, allowing the model to still understand its components.|Tokenizers like WordPiece, BPE, and SentencePiece are common subword tokenization algorithms used in LLMs.
title: Subword Tokenization

definition: WordPiece Tokenization is a subword tokenization algorithm that iteratively builds a vocabulary of subword units by merging frequently occurring characters or character sequences. It aims to optimize the likelihood of the training data when segmented into the smallest possible number of word pieces, effectively balancing vocabulary size and handling out-of-vocabulary words.
examples: The word 'tokenization' might be split into ['token', '##iza', '##tion'] based on the learned vocabulary.|Widely used in models like BERT and DistilBERT, where '##' prefixes indicate a subword that is part of a larger word.|Input 'running' could be tokenized as ['run', '##ning'] if '##ning' is a frequent suffix and 'run' is a root word.

definition: SentencePiece is a subword tokenization method that treats the input text as a raw stream of characters, including whitespace, rather than pre-tokenizing by space. It can implement both Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) and Unigram Language Model algorithms, allowing for consistent tokenization across various languages and simplifying reverse tokenization.

definition: In the context of tokenization (specifically SentencePiece), the Unigram Language Model algorithm treats subword units as tokens and assigns probabilities to them, then segments the input text into a sequence of subword units that maximizes the probability of the sequence. It allows for multiple possible segmentations for a given sentence and uses Viterbi algorithm for optimal segmentation.

definition: An N-gram Model is a type of probabilistic language model that predicts the next item in a sequence (e.g., a word or character) based on the preceding 'N-1' items. It estimates the probability of a word given the N-1 previous words by counting their frequencies in a large text corpus.

definition: GloVe (Global Vectors for Word Representation) is an unsupervised learning algorithm for obtaining vector representations (embeddings) for words. It captures global corpus statistics by co-occurrence counts and aims to represent words in a vector space such that the ratio of co-occurrence probabilities between words corresponds to their semantic and syntactic relationships.

title: GloVe Embeddings

definition: FastText Embeddings are word embeddings that represent each word as a sum of its character N-grams (subwords). definition: A Conditional Random Field (CRF) is a discriminative probabilistic model used for segmenting and labeling sequence data, often in NLP tasks like named entity recognition or part-of-speech tagging. definition: The Encoder-Decoder architecture is a neural network framework designed for sequence-to-sequence tasks, where an input sequence is mapped to an output sequence of potentially different length. title: Encoder-Decoder Architecture (General)

definition: A technique in neural networks that allows the model to dynamically weigh the importance of different parts of the input sequence when processing or generating a particular element of the output. It helps models focus on relevant information, akin to human selective attention.

title: Attention Mechanism (General)

definition: A numerical representation of a word whose vector changes based on its surrounding words in a sentence, capturing its meaning and syntactic role within that specific context. Unlike static embeddings, it can differentiate between polysemous words.
examples: The word 'bank' would have different contextual embeddings in 'river bank' versus 'financial bank'.|ELMo and BERT models generate contextual word embeddings for input tokens.
title: Contextual Word Embedding

definition: A fundamental component of the Transformer architecture responsible for processing an input sequence and generating a rich, contextualized representation for each token. It typically consists of a Multi-Head Self-Attention layer followed by a position-wise Feed-Forward Network, with residual connections and layer normalization.
examples: The core building block used repeatedly in models like BERT for understanding input text.|In an Encoder-Decoder Transformer, the encoder block transforms the source sentence into a sequence of continuous representations.
title: Encoder Block (Transformer)

definition: A key component of the Transformer architecture designed for generating an output sequence, typically token by token. It contains a masked Multi-Head Self-Attention layer, a Multi-Head Cross-Attention layer (if paired with an encoder), and a Feed-Forward Network, all with residual connections and layer normalization.
examples: The primary building block in autoregressive models like GPT for generating text.|In machine translation, the decoder block uses cross-attention to focus on relevant parts of the encoder's output while generating target language tokens.
title: Decoder Block (Transformer)

definition: The foundational attention mechanism where a Query vector interacts with Key vectors via dot products to compute similarity scores, which are then scaled by the square root of the key dimension to prevent vanishing gradients, and finally passed through a softmax function to obtain attention weights applied to Value vectors.
examples: The core calculation within every Multi-Head Attention layer in a Transformer model.|When a word's query vector finds similar key vectors among other words in a sentence, it assigns higher attention weights to their corresponding value vectors.
title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention

definition: Linear transformations applied to the input embeddings (or previous layer's output) to generate distinct Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V) matrices for each attention head. These projections allow the attention mechanism to learn different facets of relationships between tokens.
examples: For an input vector `x`, three separate weight matrices `W_Q`, `W_K`, `W_V` are multiplied with `x` to obtain the corresponding `q`, `k`, and `v` vectors.|In Multi-Head Attention, each head has its own set of `W_Q`, `W_K`, `W_V` matrices to project inputs into different representation subspaces.

definition: A mechanism to inject information about the absolute position of each token in a sequence into its embedding, as Transformers inherently lack sequence order awareness. This is typically achieved by adding fixed sinusoidal patterns or learned embeddings directly to the input token embeddings.
examples: The original Transformer paper used sine and cosine functions of varying frequencies to generate unique positional encodings for each position.|BERT and GPT models often use learned positional embeddings, which are simply embedding vectors assigned to each position and trained with the rest of the model.
title: Absolute Positional Encoding

definition: A method for incorporating positional information that allows the Transformer to attend to tokens based on their relative distance from each other, rather than their absolute position in the sequence. This can improve generalization to sequences longer than those seen during training.
examples: Transformer-XL's approach, which modifies the attention score calculation to include biases based on relative distances.|Shaw et al.'s method that adds content-dependent relative positional embeddings to the keys and values in the attention mechanism.
title: Relative Positional Encoding

definition: A type of relative positional encoding that applies a rotation matrix to queries and keys based on their absolute positions, effectively encoding relative position within the self-attention mechanism itself. This design enables longer context windows and improved perplexity for sequence tasks.
examples: Widely adopted in modern LLMs such as LLaMA, PaLM, and GPT-NeoX to enhance their ability to handle longer sequences.|It allows attention scores to implicitly capture the distance between tokens without explicitly computing relative position biases.

title: Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE)

definition: A positional encoding technique that directly biases attention scores based on the absolute distance between a query and key token, where tokens closer to each other receive a smaller penalty. Unlike other methods, it does not add positional information to embeddings but rather modifies the attention logits.
examples: Used in models like BLOOM, ALiBi enables the model to extrapolate to longer sequences than it was trained on without a significant drop in performance.|The bias is typically a fixed, non-trainable, negative slope applied to the attention logit, making attention to distant tokens less favorable.

definition: A sub-layer within a Transformer block that is applied independently and identically to each position in the sequence. It consists of two linear transformations with a non-linear activation function (like ReLU) in between, enhancing the model's capacity to learn complex patterns.
examples: In a Transformer layer, after the attention mechanism, the output of each token passes through this two-layer neural network.|The FFN can be represented as `max(0, xW1 + b1)W2 + b2`, where `x` is the input for a single position.
title: Feed-Forward Network (Transformer)

definition: A standard sub-layer in Transformer blocks comprising a residual connection (Add) that sums the input of a sub-layer with its output, followed by layer normalization (Norm). This combination helps mitigate vanishing/exploding gradients, stabilizes training, and speeds up convergence.
examples: After the Multi-Head Attention output, it's added to its input (`x + Attention(x)`) and then normalized using LayerNorm.|Similarly, after the Feed-Forward Network, its output is added to its input and then normalized.

title: Add & Norm Layer

definition: A variation of self-attention primarily used in Transformer decoders and autoregressive models, where a mask is applied to prevent tokens from attending to subsequent tokens in the sequence. This ensures that predictions for the current token are based only on preceding context.
examples: In GPT-style models generating text, each new word is predicted based only on the words that came before it due to masked self-attention.|Implementing this involves setting the attention scores for future positions to negative infinity before the softmax, effectively zeroing out their contribution.
title: Masked Self-Attention

definition: A specific type of masking strategy, primarily used in decoder blocks, where the attention mechanism is restricted such that a token can only attend to itself and tokens that appeared before it in the sequence. This strictly enforces an autoregressive property, preventing information leakage from future tokens.
examples: When training a large language model like GPT-3 for next-token prediction, causal masking ensures that the model only uses the left context.|Programmatically, this is often implemented by creating an upper triangular matrix of negative infinity (or large negative number) to hide future positions in the attention score matrix before softmax.
title: Causal Masking

definition: A masking strategy, often used in Transformer encoders, where specific tokens are prevented from attending to other tokens based on criteria other than strict temporal order. This is commonly employed for tasks like bidirectional context understanding or handling variable-length sequences.
examples: Padding mask: Preventing attention to padding tokens that are added to make sequences of equal length in a batch.|In BERT, the model can attend to all other tokens in the input sequence, except for special cases like masking out the [SEP] token in some tasks, which is a form of non-causal masking.
title: Non-Causal Masking

definition: An attention mechanism used in Transformer decoders that allows the decoder to attend to the output of the encoder. Queries are derived from the decoder's current state, while keys and values are derived from the encoder's final output, enabling the decoder to selectively focus on relevant parts of the input sequence.
examples: In machine translation, the decoder uses cross-attention to determine which words in the source sentence are most relevant for generating the current word in the target sentence.|The decoder's cross-attention layer receives its query (Q) from the previous decoder layer and its keys (K) and values (V) from the encoder's output.
title: Cross-Attention Mechanism

definition: A neural network-based language model that has been pre-trained on a vast amount of text data using self-supervised learning objectives, typically to learn general language understanding and generation capabilities. These models can then be fine-tuned for specific downstream NLP tasks.
examples: BERT, pre-trained on masked language modeling and next sentence prediction objectives.|GPT-3, pre-trained on a massive internet corpus to predict the next token.
title: Pre-trained Language Model (PLM)

definition: A Transformer architecture composed solely of stacked encoder blocks, designed primarily for tasks requiring deep, bidirectional understanding of an input text sequence. These models generate rich contextualized embeddings that are then typically fed to a task-specific head.
examples: BERT and RoBERTa are prime examples, used for tasks like sentiment analysis, natural language inference, and question answering.|It processes the entire input sequence simultaneously, allowing each token to attend to all other tokens.
title: Encoder-only Transformer

definition: A Transformer architecture consisting entirely of stacked decoder blocks, characterized by masked self-attention that ensures tokens can only attend to preceding tokens. This design makes them highly effective for autoregressive language generation tasks.
examples: GPT, GPT-2, GPT-3, LLaMA, and Falcon are prominent decoder-only models, specializing in text completion, summarization, and dialogue.|These models sequentially predict the next token given the context of previous tokens.
title: Decoder-only Transformer

definition: A Transformer architecture that combines both an encoder stack and a decoder stack, making it well-suited for sequence-to-sequence tasks where an input sequence is transformed into a distinct output sequence. The decoder uses cross-attention to attend to the encoder's output.
examples: T5 and BART are prominent examples used for tasks like machine translation, text summarization, and question answering (generative).|The encoder processes the entire input, and then the decoder generates the output token by token, leveraging the encoder's contextual representation.
title: Encoder-Decoder Transformer (LLM)

definition: A robustly optimized BERT approach that modifies key hyperparameters, removes the next sentence prediction objective, and trains with much larger mini-batches and learning rates over more data. It improves upon BERT's pretraining methodology for better downstream task performance.
examples: Fine-tuning RoBERTa for sentiment analysis on a movie review dataset.|Using a pre-trained `roberta-base` model from Hugging Face Transformers for text classification.|Applying RoBERTa for natural language inference tasks like SNLI.
title: RoBERTa Model

definition: An attention-based language model that uses a 'Replaced Token Detection' (RTD) pretraining task, where a small generator network replaces some tokens, and a discriminator network predicts which tokens were replaced. This method is more computationally efficient than masked language modeling as every token contributes to the loss.
examples: Training an ELECTRA model for text summarization.|Using `google/electra-base-discriminator` for identifying corrupted tokens in a sentence.|Applying ELECTRA for improved search relevance by detecting subtle word changes.
title: ELECTRA Model

definition: A generalized autoregressive pretraining method that combines the strengths of both autoregressive (like GPT) and autoencoding (like BERT) models. It uses a permutation-based approach to capture bidirectional context while avoiding the independence assumption of masked language modeling.
examples: Fine-tuning XLNet for question answering tasks that benefit from bidirectional context without [MASK] tokens.|Using XLNet for complex natural language understanding problems where long-range dependencies are crucial.|Applying `xlnet-base-cased` from Hugging Face for document classification.
title: XLNet Model

definition: A lite BERT (A Lite BERT) model that addresses the memory limitations and training speed of BERT by employing two parameter-reduction techniques: cross-layer parameter sharing and factorized embedding parameterization. These techniques significantly reduce the number of parameters while maintaining competitive performance.
examples: Deploying a smaller ALBERT model for on-device natural language understanding applications.|Fine-tuning `albert-base-v2` for text classification with reduced computational resources.|Using ALBERT as a more memory-efficient alternative to BERT for large-scale training.
title: ALBERT Model

definition: A "Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer" model that frames every NLP problem, from machine translation to question answering, as a text-to-text task. It uses a unified encoder-decoder architecture and is pretrained on a massive dataset called C4 (Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus).
examples: Using T5 for abstractive summarization, where the input is an article and the output is a summary.|Translating English to French using the T5 model by prefixing the input with 'translate English to French:'.|Generating answers for questions given a context, treating it as a text-to-text transformation.
title: T5 Model

definition: A denoising autoencoder for pretraining sequence-to-sequence models that uses a standard Transformer-based neural machine translation architecture. It trains by corrupting text with an arbitrary noising function and learning to reconstruct the original text.
examples: Applying BART for abstractive summarization by reconstructing a clean summary from a corrupted document.|Using BART for machine translation, where it denoises an input sentence into a target language sentence.|Fine-tuning `facebook/bart-large-cnn` for dialogue summarization tasks.
title: BART Model

definition: A large transformer-based language model developed by OpenAI, famous for its ability to generate coherent and diverse text. It is an autoregressive model, meaning it predicts the next token in a sequence based on all previous tokens, and was trained on a massive dataset called WebText.
examples: Generating creative stories or articles based on a given prompt.|Using GPT-2 for chatbots to produce human-like conversational responses.|Completing sentences or paragraphs in a document.
title: GPT-2 Model

definition: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is a reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) method that directly optimizes a policy for human preferences without needing to explicitly train a separate reward model. It reformulates the reward maximization problem as a classification-like objective, making it simpler and more stable to train.
examples: Training an LLM on a preference dataset where, for each prompt, a preferred response and a dispreferred response are provided, directly optimizing the model to generate the preferred one.|Aligning a chatbot's responses to be more helpful and harmless by applying DPO on human-annotated preferred and rejected dialogue turns.|Using DPO to fine-tune an LLM for creative writing, where human judges have indicated which story continuations are better for given prompts.
title: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)

definition: A preference dataset is a collection of human judgments indicating which of two or more model outputs is preferred for a given input prompt. It is crucial for methods like Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), enabling models to learn human values and align their behavior.
examples: For a prompt 'Write a short story about a cat', a dataset entry might be (Prompt, Response A, Response B, Human Chooses A).|A dataset containing (user query, LLM response 1, LLM response 2, human indicates response 1 is safer/more helpful).|Collecting pairs of summaries for the same document, where human annotators rank which summary is better, to train a summarization model.
title: Preference Dataset

definition: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) technique that injects trainable low-rank matrices into the transformer layers of a pre-trained LLM. By only training these small additional matrices while keeping the vast majority of the original model weights frozen, it significantly reduces the number of parameters to update and memory footprint.
examples: Fine-tuning a 7B LLM on a new task by only training LoRA adapters, which constitute less than 0.1% of the total parameters, then merging them for inference.|Using LoRA to adapt a single base LLM to multiple specialized tasks (e.g., medical, legal, creative writing) by training separate, small LoRA modules for each, rather than full fine-tuning.|Applying LoRA during fine-tuning on consumer-grade GPUs by only loading the base model once and attaching small LoRA weights.
title: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)

definition: Quantized LoRA (QLoRA) is an advancement of LoRA that further reduces memory requirements by quantizing the base pre-trained LLM to a lower precision (typically 4-bit) during fine-tuning, while keeping the LoRA adapters in full precision. This allows fine-tuning very large models on consumer-grade GPUs without significant performance degradation.
