examples: Fine-tuning a 65B LLM on a single GPU (e.g., 24GB VRAM) by quantizing the base model to 4-bit and applying LoRA adapters.|Using QLoRA to develop domain-specific variants of a massive foundational model, drastically lowering the hardware cost for adaptation.|Training a personalized chatbot by fine-tuning a large model with QLoRA on a user's private conversational data, ensuring privacy and efficiency.
title: Quantized LoRA (QLoRA)

definition: Adapter tuning is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) method where small, task-specific neural network modules, called 'adapters', are inserted between or within the layers of a pre-trained LLM. The majority of the base model's parameters remain frozen, and only these adapter modules are trained, significantly reducing computational cost and storage.
examples: Adding an adapter module after each transformer block in a pre-trained LLM and only training these modules for a specific downstream task like sentiment analysis.|Adapting a single large LLM to multiple languages by training a small, language-specific adapter for each language, rather than full fine-tuning for each.|Using adapter tuning to rapidly specialize a base model for different document types (e.g., legal, medical, financial) by creating and training distinct adapters.
title: Adapter Tuning

definition: Prefix tuning is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) technique that prepends a small, trainable sequence of continuous vectors, known as a 'prefix', to the input embeddings of each layer of a pre-trained LLM. The base model's weights remain frozen, and only these prefix vectors are optimized to steer the model's behavior for specific tasks.
examples: Training a prefix for a T5 model to perform summarization, where the prefix learns to guide the model towards generating summaries without modifying the core T5 weights.|Using prefix tuning to adapt a general-purpose LLM for specific question-answering formats, such as generating only short, concise answers.|Developing multiple task-specific prompts for an LLM by training distinct prefixes for tasks like translation, classification, and generation, all using the same frozen base model.
title: Prefix Tuning

definition: BitFit is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) method that selectively fine-tunes only a very small subset of a pre-trained LLM's parameters, specifically the bias terms in its layers. All other weights, including the much larger weight matrices, are kept frozen, drastically reducing the number of trainable parameters.
examples: Fine-tuning a large BERT model for text classification by only updating the bias vectors in its linear layers, leading to significant parameter reduction compared to full fine-tuning.|Adapting a pre-trained transformer for a new domain by only adjusting its bias terms, which can be sufficient for minor domain shifts.|Achieving competitive performance on downstream tasks with an LLM by fine-tuning just 0.1% of its parameters using the BitFit strategy.
title: BitFit

definition: A soft prompt is a sequence of learnable, continuous embedding vectors that are prepended or inserted into the input of a language model. Unlike discrete hard prompts, soft prompts are optimized through gradient descent to guide the model's behavior for a specific task without altering its core weights, offering greater flexibility and performance.
examples: In Prompt Tuning, a short sequence of learnable token embeddings is optimized to adapt a frozen LLM for text summarization.|A soft prompt might be learned for sentiment analysis, which when prepended to input text, makes the LLM more accurately classify positive or negative sentiment.|Using a soft prompt to condition a large generative model to produce outputs in a specific style or tone, by learning the optimal prompt embeddings.
semantic_tags: Prompt Engineering|Continuous Prompts|Learnable Prompts|PEFT|Token Embeddings|Input Conditioning
title: Soft Prompt

definition: A hard prompt is a discrete, natural language phrase or set of tokens manually engineered and explicitly appended to an input, instructing a language model on how to respond. These are human-readable text strings directly supplied to the model.
examples: "Translate the following to French: 'Hello, how are you?'"|"Summarize this article in 100 words: [article text]"|"Answer the question based on the text below: [text] Question: [question]?"
title: Hard Prompt

definition: Domain adaptation for LLMs involves adapting a model trained on a general source domain to perform effectively on a specific target domain where the data distribution may differ. This process aims to transfer knowledge and mitigate performance degradation when faced with out-of-distribution data, often without extensive task-specific labeling in the target domain.
examples: Adapting a general-purpose LLM trained on web text to effectively process specialized medical literature.|Fine-tuning an LLM trained on general English text to understand and generate responses in legal jargon for a legal AI assistant.|Using continual pre-training on a dataset of customer service logs to adapt a foundational model for call center automation.
title: Domain Adaptation (LLM)

definition: Continual pre-training is the process of further pre-training an already pre-trained Large Language Model on new data, typically to update its knowledge, adapt it to a specific domain, or incorporate more recent information. This differs from fine-tuning by maintaining the broad pre-training objective, rather than optimizing for a narrow downstream task.
examples: Taking a GPT-3 model and continuing its pre-training on a large corpus of scientific papers to enhance its understanding of scientific concepts and terminology.|Updating an LLM with newly published web data to ensure its knowledge base is current and reflects recent events.|Further training a general LLM on a proprietary dataset of financial reports to specialize it for financial analysis and reporting.
semantic_tags: Domain Adaptation|Knowledge Update|Lifelong Learning|Transfer Learning|Pre-training|Model Refresh
title: Continual Pre-training

definition: Model merging involves combining the weights of two or more distinct LLMs, or different fine-tuned versions of the same base model, to create a single new model. The goal is to aggregate capabilities, mitigate catastrophic forgetting, or achieve multi-task performance without retraining from scratch.
examples: Averaging the weights of an LLM fine-tuned for creative writing and another fine-tuned for factual accuracy to create a balanced model that excels at both.|Merging multiple LoRA adapters, each trained on a different task (e.g., summarization, translation, Q&A), into a single set of LoRA weights to serve diverse requests.|Using a task-arithmetic approach to sum the delta weights from several fine-tuned models to combine their specific skills into one unified model.
semantic_tags: Ensemble Learning|Weight Averaging|Model Combination|Multi-task Learning|Knowledge Integration
title: Model Merging (LLM)

definition: Knowledge distillation is a technique where a smaller, more efficient 'student' LLM is trained to mimic the behavior and outputs (e.g., logits, hidden states, or final predictions) of a larger, more powerful 'teacher' LLM. This process transfers the 'knowledge' from the teacher to the student, resulting in a compact model with comparable performance but reduced computational cost.
examples: Training a smaller Llama model to reproduce the responses and prediction probabilities of a larger GPT-4 model on a diverse dataset.|Distilling an ensemble of expert LLMs into a single, compact student model for faster inference and deployment.|Using a large, high-quality translation model as a teacher to train a much smaller, faster student model for real-time translation applications.
semantic_tags: Model Compression|Student-Teacher Learning|Efficiency|Transfer Learning|Model Shrinking|Performance Optimization
title: Knowledge Distillation (LLM)

definition: Self-correction in fine-tuning is a paradigm where an LLM is trained to identify and rectify its own errors, typically by generating an initial response, critically evaluating it against predefined criteria, and then producing a revised, improved answer. This process helps the model learn to introspect and refine its outputs.
examples: Fine-tuning an LLM on datasets where the model first generates a code snippet, then runs tests (or uses a 'critic' model to evaluate it), and finally produces a corrected version of the code.|Training an LLM to answer a question, then explicitly prompt it to 'Critique the above answer and provide a better one' based on self-generated or human-provided feedback.|A model fine-tuned to solve math problems by first generating an answer, then simulating a check (e.g., reverse calculation), and if incorrect, generating a new solution path.
title: Self-Correction (Fine-tuning)

definition: Prompt design, also known as prompt engineering, is the art and science of crafting effective inputs (prompts) for Large Language Models to elicit desired behaviors, responses, or outputs without altering the model's underlying weights. It involves selecting appropriate phrasing, structure, context, and examples to guide the model.
examples: Experimenting with different phrasings like "Translate this to Spanish:" versus "Spanish translation of:".|Adding few-shot examples (input-output pairs) to a prompt to teach the model a specific task or format.|Using techniques like Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, where intermediate reasoning steps are requested, to improve complex problem-solving abilities.
semantic_tags: Prompt Engineering|Input Crafting|Model Control|Instruction|Zero-shot Learning|Few-shot Learning
title: Prompt Design

definition: A prompting technique where a Large Language Model (LLM) performs a task without any prior examples in the prompt, relying solely on its pre-trained knowledge and the explicit task description.
examples: Prompt: 'Translate 'hello' to French.' Output: 'bonjour'|Prompt: 'Classify the sentiment of 'I love this product' as positive or negative.' Output: 'positive'
title: Zero-shot Prompting

definition: A prompting technique where a Large Language Model (LLM) performs a task after being provided with a small number of input-output examples directly within the prompt itself, helping the model understand the desired format or task style.
examples: Prompt: 'Translate: apple -> pomme, dog -> chien, cat -> ?' Output: 'chat'|Prompt: 'Sentiment: 'Great' -> positive, 'Terrible' -> negative, 'Okay' -> ?' Output: 'neutral'
title: Few-shot Prompting

definition: A prompting technique that encourages a Large Language Model (LLM) to generate intermediate reasoning steps or a 'chain of thought' before producing the final answer, significantly improving performance on complex reasoning tasks.
examples: Prompt: 'Q: The user bought 6 apples for $1 each and 3 oranges for $0.50 each. How much did they spend? A: First, calculate apple cost: 6 * $1 = $6. Then, calculate orange cost: 3 * $0.50 = $1.50. Finally, total cost: $6 + $1.50 = $7.50.'|Prompt: 'Explain why the sky is blue. First, describe Rayleigh scattering. Then, explain how it affects different wavelengths of light.'
title: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Prompting

definition: An advanced prompting framework that extends Chain-of-Thought by exploring multiple reasoning paths (a 'tree' of thoughts) and allowing for backtracking and pruning of unpromising paths, enabling more systematic problem-solving.
examples: Solving complex mathematical proofs by exploring different axiomatic starting points and logical deductions.|Strategic game playing where the model considers multiple sequences of moves and their potential outcomes.|Multi-step planning tasks, such as designing an itinerary, where initial choices lead to different subsequent options.
title: Tree-of-Thought (ToT) Prompting

definition: A sophisticated prompting technique that organizes generated thoughts into an arbitrary graph structure, enabling non-linear dependencies, cyclic reasoning, and complex interconnections between intermediate ideas beyond linear or tree-like approaches.
examples: Brainstorming interconnected ideas for a complex project where concepts influence each other in multiple directions.|Scientific discovery simulations where hypotheses, experiments, and observations form a dense network of relationships.|Debugging complex software systems where different components and potential issues are interlinked and can lead to cyclic dependencies.
title: Graph-of-Thought (GoT) Prompting

definition: A decoding strategy that samples multiple diverse reasoning paths from an LLM, then aggregates these paths (e.g., by majority vote or averaging probabilities) to select the most consistent or probable final answer, improving robustness and accuracy on complex tasks.
examples: Asking an LLM to solve a mathematical word problem 10 times with different random seeds, then taking the most frequently occurring answer.|Generating several logical arguments for a stance and identifying the common conclusion across them.
title: Self-Consistency Decoding

definition: A multi-step prompting technique where the Large Language Model (LLM) first generates relevant background knowledge or facts pertinent to a given query, and then uses this self-generated knowledge, alongside the original query, to produce a more informed and accurate final answer.
examples: Prompt: 'Generate facts about photosynthesis.' (LLM outputs facts) Then, 'Using these facts, explain how plants convert sunlight into energy.'|Prompt: 'Generate common misconceptions about black holes.' (LLM lists misconceptions) Then, 'Refute these misconceptions with accurate information.'
title: Generated Knowledge Prompting

definition: In a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) system, the Retriever Module is responsible for searching an external knowledge base to find and retrieve relevant documents or passages based on a user's query or an LLM's context.
examples: A user asks a question, and the retriever queries a vector database of Wikipedia articles to find the top-k most relevant article chunks.|Searching a company's internal documentation repository for answers to a specific technical support ticket.
semantic_tags: RAG|Information retrieval|Vector search|Knowledge base|Query processing|External data
title: Retriever Module (RAG)

definition: In a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) system, the Generator Module is typically a Large Language Model (LLM) that synthesizes a coherent and informative answer by integrating both the original user query and the context retrieved by the Retriever Module.
examples: An LLM takes the question 'What is photosynthesis?' and retrieved Wikipedia passages about photosynthesis, then crafts a concise answer.|Summarizing retrieved legal documents in response to a legal query, incorporating information from multiple sources.
title: Generator Module (RAG)

definition: In a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) system, the Embedding Model converts both the user's query and chunks of the external knowledge base into dense numerical vector representations (embeddings) to facilitate efficient semantic similarity search by the Retriever Module.
examples: A Sentence-BERT model transforming a user question into a vector for comparison.|An OpenAI embedding model converting paragraphs from a knowledge base into vectors for storage in a vector database.
title: Embedding Model (RAG)

definition: In a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) system, the Knowledge Base refers to the external repository of information (e.g., documents, articles, databases) that the Retriever Module queries to find relevant context to augment the LLM's generation.
examples: A collection of PDF manuals and technical specifications for a product.|A vector database containing vectorized chunks of scientific papers or news articles.|A traditional relational database holding structured facts about a company's products.
title: Knowledge Base (RAG)

definition: In the context of Large Language Models, an inference algorithm refers to the specific method used to generate a sequence of tokens (the output) from the model given an input prompt, encompassing various sampling and decoding strategies.
examples: Using greedy decoding to always pick the most probable next token.|Employing Beam Search to explore multiple promising sequences.|Applying temperature sampling for more creative and diverse outputs.
title: Inference Algorithm

definition: A decoding strategy that explores multiple probable sequences of tokens simultaneously (the 'beams') at each generation step, maintaining a fixed number of the most likely partial sequences and expanding them until a complete output is formed.
examples: Generating a translation where the model keeps track of the top-N most probable partial sentences in the target language.|Creating a summary where multiple plausible phrases are considered at each step before converging on the most likely coherent summary.
title: Beam Search Decoding

definition: A parameter used in LLM decoding that controls the randomness or 'creativity' of the generated text by scaling the logits before applying the softmax function, where a higher temperature makes the output more diverse and a lower temperature makes it more deterministic.
examples: Setting temperature=0.7 for creative writing tasks to encourage varied and imaginative outputs.|Setting temperature=0.1 for factual question-answering to ensure consistent and deterministic answers.
title: Temperature Sampling

definition: A decoding strategy where, at each token generation step, the Large Language Model considers only the 'k' most probable next tokens, and then samples one token (either uniformly or proportionally to their probabilities) from this restricted set.
examples: Generating text by considering only the 100 most probable next words instead of the entire vocabulary to improve coherence.|Using Top-k to avoid generating highly improbable or nonsensical tokens while still introducing some randomness.
title: Top-k Sampling

definition: A decoding strategy where, at each token generation step, the Large Language Model considers the smallest set of most probable next tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds a predefined threshold 'p', then samples a token from within this dynamically sized 'nucleus' set.
examples: Generating text by only considering tokens that collectively account for 90% of the probability mass (p=0.9).|Using Top-p to dynamically adjust the number of tokens considered based on the probability distribution, offering a balance between diversity and coherence.
title: Top-p (Nucleus) Sampling

definition: A decoding parameter that discourages the Large Language Model from repeating tokens or phrases in its generated output by reducing the probability of already generated tokens, thus promoting more diverse and coherent text.
examples: Setting a repetition penalty of 1.2 to prevent the model from getting stuck in a loop of repeating words or phrases.|Applying a penalty to avoid outputs like 'The the the cat cat cat sat sat sat' for improved readability.
title: Repetition Penalty

definition: A decoding method that balances two objectives: generating highly probable tokens (coherence) and generating tokens that are distinct from the input and previously generated context (diversity), aiming to produce outputs that are both fluent and non-redundant.
examples: Summarizing a document by selecting tokens that are relevant to the main topic but not direct copies or redundant phrases from the source.|Generating creative text that introduces novel ideas and vocabulary while maintaining grammatical correctness and contextual relevance.
title: Contrastive Search (Decoding)

definition: A decoding strategy that filters out 'atypical' tokens whose information content (surprisal) significantly deviates from the expected information content of a typical token at that position, then samples from the remaining 'typical' set.
examples: Generating dialogue that sounds natural and fluent by avoiding overly common or extremely rare words in specific contexts.|Creating text that maintains a consistent tone and style, reducing the chance of statistically unusual word choices disrupting the flow.
title: Typical Sampling

definition: The maximum number of tokens (words or subwords) that a Large Language Model can process and attend to as input at one time, including both the prompt and any previously generated output, which fundamentally limits the model's ability to understand and generate long sequences.
examples: An LLM with a 4096-token context window cannot directly process a 10,000-token document without chunking or external retrieval.|If a user's prompt consumes 3000 tokens of a 4096-token context window, only 1096 tokens remain for the model's subsequent output or internal reasoning.
title: Context Window Length

definition: The total number of tokens (including both input prompt and generated output) that a Large Language Model processes and can attend to at once. This effectively defines the model's 'context window' or memory capacity for a given interaction.
examples: A prompt 'Explain AI.' (2 tokens) plus a generated response 'AI is a field of computer science.' (7 tokens) results in a total sequence length of 9 tokens.|A model with a 4096-token sequence length can process an input prompt of 2000 tokens and generate an output of up to 2096 tokens.|Exceeding a model's maximum sequence length for the input prompt will result in truncation or an error.
semantic_tags: Context Window|Tokens|Input Length|Output Length|Transformer Architecture|Context Size
title: Sequence Length

definition: The maximum number of tokens an LLM is configured to generate in response to a single prompt, independent of the input prompt's length. This limit is set to control the verbosity of the model, prevent runaway generations, and manage computational resources.
examples: Setting `max_new_tokens=100` in a Hugging Face `generate` call limits the LLM's response to 100 tokens.|If an LLM is asked to write a short story but `max_output_length` is 50, the story will be truncated after 50 tokens.|Most LLM APIs have a default `max_output_length` parameter, often around 256 or 512 tokens.
semantic_tags: Generation Control|Token Limit|Output Tokens|Inference Parameters|Response Length|Safety
title: Maximum Output Length

definition: A mechanism used during autoregressive decoding to store previously computed Key (K) and Value (V) vectors for tokens, preventing redundant recomputation in subsequent generation steps. By caching these attention components, the model can efficiently attend to past tokens without recalculating their representations, significantly speeding up inference.
examples: When an LLM generates 'The quick brown fox...', after 'The quick' is generated, the KVs for 'The' and 'quick' are stored. When generating 'brown', the cached KVs for 'The quick' are reused, and only new KVs for 'brown' are computed.|Without a KV cache, generating an N-token sequence would involve N full attention passes, each recalculating KVs for all N tokens; with KV cache, only the new token's KVs are computed at each step.|Enabling KV caching is a default optimization in most modern LLM inference engines like vLLM or Hugging Face Transformers.
title: KV Cache (Key-Value Cache)

definition: An attention mechanism optimization that manages the KV Cache more efficiently by storing Key and Value tensors in non-contiguous 'pages' of memory, similar to operating system paging. This allows for flexible memory allocation, sharing pages across different requests in a batch, and significantly reduces memory fragmentation and waste, especially during continuous batching.
examples: In a high-throughput LLM serving system, PagedAttention allows multiple concurrent requests with varying sequence lengths to share GPU memory for their KV caches dynamically, maximizing GPU utilization.|PagedAttention mitigates the problem of KV cache fragmentation, where fixed-size memory blocks are allocated for requests even if not fully used, leading to wasted VRAM.|vLLM, a popular LLM serving engine, uses PagedAttention as a core component for its high performance.
title: PagedAttention

definition: An inference optimization technique where a smaller, faster 'draft' model proposes a sequence of candidate tokens, which are then verified in parallel by the larger, more powerful 'main' model. This allows for generating multiple tokens per main model step, significantly accelerating inference speed with minimal loss in output quality.
examples: A small 1B parameter model suggests 5 tokens. The main 70B parameter model then processes these 5 tokens in one forward pass, accepting valid ones and restarting if a token is rejected.|Instead of predicting one token at a time (autoregressive), speculative decoding can achieve 2-4x speedups by predicting and verifying multiple tokens simultaneously.|Google's Medusa and Lookahead Decoding are advanced forms of speculative decoding that use multiple prediction heads or tree-based search.
title: Speculative Decoding

definition: The process of reducing the precision of the numerical representations (e.g., weights and activations) within an LLM, typically from floating-point (FP32 or FP16) to lower-bit integers (e.g., INT8, INT4). This significantly reduces memory footprint and computational requirements during inference, enabling larger models to run on less powerful hardware or achieving higher throughput.
examples: Converting a 70B parameter LLM from FP16 to INT8 weights to reduce its memory footprint from 140GB to 70GB, making it runnable on a GPU with 80GB VRAM.|Deploying a quantized LLM (e.g., in INT4) on an edge device with limited memory and computational power.|Using `bitsandbytes` or `quanto` libraries to apply quantization to a PyTorch model.
title: Quantization (LLM Inference)

definition: A specific type of quantization that reduces the precision of an LLM's weights and/or activations to 4-bit integers. This offers substantial memory savings (typically 8x compared to FP32 or 4x compared to FP16) and faster computation, making it crucial for running very large models on consumer-grade hardware with limited GPU memory, often with a minor, acceptable trade-off in accuracy.
examples: Using the `load_in_4bit=True` option with the `bitsandbytes` library to load a 70-billion parameter LLM onto a single consumer GPU with 24GB of VRAM.|Deploying a highly memory-constrained LLM application where even 8-bit precision is too demanding for available hardware.|Techniques like QLoRA leverage 4-bit quantization for efficient fine-tuning of large models.
title: 4-bit Quantization

definition: A specific type of quantization that reduces the precision of an LLM's weights and/or activations to 8-bit integers. This provides significant memory and speed benefits (typically 4x compared to FP32 or 2x compared to FP16) while generally preserving more model accuracy than 4-bit quantization, and is widely supported by modern hardware accelerators.
examples: Running an LLM with INT8 weights on a GPU that has native INT8 tensor core support for faster inference and reduced memory usage.|Using the `load_in_8bit=True` option in Hugging Face Transformers to load models with 8-bit weights for a better balance between memory efficiency and accuracy.|Converting a model's weights to 8-bit using tools like NVIDIA's TensorRT for optimized deployment.
semantic_tags: Quantization|Memory Optimization|Inference Speed|Reduced Precision|Model Deployment|Accuracy Trade-off
title: 8-bit Quantization

definition: A collection of techniques and strategies aimed at reducing the computational resources (time, memory, power) required to run an LLM for prediction or generation. The primary goals are to maximize throughput, minimize latency, and enable deployment on constrained hardware while maintaining acceptable output quality.
examples: Applying KV caching, quantization, speculative decoding, and continuous batching to serve a large language model with high efficiency and lower operational costs.|Using specialized inference engines like TensorRT-LLM or ONNX Runtime to accelerate model execution on target hardware.|Implementing efficient data loading and preprocessing pipelines to minimize bottlenecks during inference.
title: Inference Optimization

definition: An inference optimization technique for LLMs that dynamically groups multiple independent requests into a single batch, adding new requests as they arrive and removing completed ones. This contrasts with static batching, which waits for a fixed number of requests, and significantly improves GPU utilization by minimizing idle time and maximizing throughput for variable-length sequences.
examples: An LLM serving server receives three user prompts; Continuous Batching starts processing them immediately. If a fourth prompt arrives before the first finishes, it's added to the active batch, ensuring the GPU is always busy.|In `vLLM`, continuous batching, combined with PagedAttention, allows for very high throughput by packing requests efficiently onto the GPU.|This technique is particularly effective for real-time applications where requests arrive asynchronously and have varying lengths.
title: Continuous Batching

definition: An NVIDIA library specifically designed to accelerate large language model inference on NVIDIA GPUs, providing highly optimized kernels, attention mechanisms, and efficient memory management. It often integrates with various quantization and speculative decoding techniques to deliver maximum performance, high throughput, and low latency for LLM deployments.
examples: Compiling a trained PyTorch or Hugging Face LLM model into a TensorRT-LLM engine for deployment in a high-throughput inference server on NVIDIA A100 GPUs.|Developers use TensorRT-LLM to achieve state-of-the-art inference speeds for models like Llama 2 or Mixtral.|Integrating TensorRT-LLM into an application to optimize the serving of a custom fine-tuned LLM.
title: TensorRT-LLM

definition: An open-source, cross-platform inference engine developed by Microsoft that optimizes and executes machine learning models. It supports models in the ONNX (Open Neural Network Exchange) format, enabling interoperability and efficient deployment of LLMs and other models across various hardware (CPUs, GPUs, edge devices) and operating systems.
examples: Exporting a PyTorch or TensorFlow LLM model to ONNX format and then using ONNX Runtime to run it efficiently on a CPU for serverless inference.|Deploying an LLM on an embedded device by converting it to ONNX and utilizing ONNX Runtime's highly optimized operators for that specific hardware.|Using ONNX Runtime with providers like DirectML or CUDA to leverage specialized hardware acceleration.
title: ONNX Runtime

definition: The capability of an LLM to identify when a user's prompt intends to invoke a specific external tool or API function and to generate a structured output (typically JSON) describing the function call and its arguments. This allows LLMs to interact with external systems, retrieve real-time information, and perform actions beyond their inherent knowledge base.
examples: A user asks: 'What's the weather like in Paris today?' The LLM generates `{"tool_name": "get_current_weather", "location": "Paris"}`, which an application then uses to call a weather API.|If a user says: 'Remind me to call John at 3 PM tomorrow', the LLM might generate `{"tool_name": "create_reminder", "contact": "John", "time": "tomorrow 3 PM"}`.|Google's Gemini and OpenAI's GPT models offer native function calling capabilities.
semantic_tags: Tool Use|API Interaction|External Tools|Structured Output|Agent|API Calls
title: Function Calling (LLM)

definition: The broader concept where an LLM agent strategically selects and utilizes external tools (e.g., APIs, databases, web search, code interpreters) to accomplish tasks that are beyond its inherent knowledge or capabilities. It involves the agent reasoning about when and how to use a tool, executing it, observing the results, and integrating that information to achieve a goal.
examples: An LLM agent, asked to plan a trip, might use a 'search' tool to find flight prices, a 'calendar' tool to check dates, and a 'booking' tool to finalize arrangements.|When asked to solve a complex math problem, an LLM agent might use a 'calculator' or 'Python interpreter' tool to perform calculations.|An agent using a 'web search' tool to find the latest news headlines before summarizing them for a user.
semantic_tags: Agentic Behavior|Function Calling|External Tools|API Integration|Problem Solving|Multi-modal
title: Tool Use (LLM Agents)

definition: The exhibition of autonomous, goal-oriented, and adaptive actions by an LLM, typically involving capabilities such as planning, self-correction, long-term memory, and the strategic use of external tools or functions. These LLMs act as 'agents,' iterating through steps to achieve complex objectives rather than simply generating a single response.
examples: An LLM given the goal 'Write an essay about quantum physics' might first search for relevant information, then outline the structure, then write paragraphs, then self-critique and revise, using a search tool and a text editor tool.|An agent attempting to book a flight might try several options, learn from failures (e.g., flight fully booked), and adjust its plan to find an alternative.|AutoGPT and BabyAGI are early examples of systems exhibiting agentic behavior by breaking down tasks and iterating towards a goal.
title: Agentic Behavior (LLM)

definition: A prompting strategy that combines 'Reasoning' (R) and 'Action' (Act) steps within an LLM's thought process, allowing it to explicitly verbalize its thoughts, choose tools, execute actions, and observe results. This enables the LLM to perform complex, multi-step tasks with better transparency, accuracy, and reduced hallucination by iteratively planning and executing.
examples: A prompt structured as `Thought: I need to find the current weather. Action: call_tool(get_weather, 'London') Observation: Temperature is 15C. Thought: Now I can answer. Action: print('The weather in London is 15C.')`|Using ReAct, an agent can explicitly state its plan, execute a web search, analyze the results, and then refine its answer based on the observed information.|Many advanced LLM agent frameworks utilize ReAct-like patterns for robust task execution.
title: ReAct Prompting

definition: An architectural pattern for LLM agents where the agent first generates a high-level plan for a task, then executes that plan step-by-step, often involving self-correction and replanning if execution deviates or fails. This separation of planning and execution helps with long-horizon tasks, reduces hallucination by grounding actions, and improves overall task success rates.
examples: An agent tasked with writing a blog post first generates a detailed outline (the 'plan'), then iteratively writes sections, reviews them, and makes corrections (the 'execute' phase).|When asked to create a travel itinerary, the agent first plans the sequence of destinations and activities, then executes each booking or information retrieval step.|If a planned action fails (e.g., a flight is full), the agent can revert to the planning phase to find an alternative before resuming execution.
title: Plan-and-Execute Agent

definition: The most common method for LLM text generation, where the model predicts one token at a time, conditioned on all previously generated tokens and the initial input prompt. Each newly generated token is appended to the sequence and becomes part of the context for predicting the next token, creating a sequential and coherent output.
examples: When generating 'The quick brown fox...', the model first predicts 'The', then predicts 'quick' based on 'The', then 'brown' based on 'The quick', and so on.|Most transformer-based LLMs like GPT-3, Llama, and Mistral use autoregressive generation.|This process can be visualized as a loop where the model constantly extends the output by one token.
title: Autoregressive Generation

definition: A generation paradigm where multiple tokens or an entire sequence are generated simultaneously or in a parallel fashion, rather than strictly one token at a time based on preceding tokens. While potentially offering significant speed advantages, it often presents challenges in maintaining coherence and high quality compared to autoregressive models.
examples: Masked language models like BERT can be adapted for non-autoregressive generation by filling multiple masked tokens in parallel.|Some neural machine translation models predict all target language tokens at once or iteratively refine a complete sequence in parallel.|Unlike autoregressive models that process a sequence from left-to-right, non-autoregressive models might fill in blanks or refine a rough draft concurrently.
semantic_tags: Parallel Generation|Decoding|Speed|Quality Trade-off|Masked Language Models|Sequence Generation
title: Non-Autoregressive Generation

definition: Mechanisms and policies implemented to ensure that Large Language Models operate within desired ethical, safety, and operational boundaries, preventing harmful, irrelevant, or off-topic outputs. These can involve input validation, output filtering, and adherence to specific content policies or rules.
examples: A guardrail that filters out hate speech or toxic language from an LLM's output before it reaches the user.|Implementing guardrails to prevent an LLM from discussing illegal activities or providing medical advice.|Ensuring an LLM used in a customer service context only answers questions related to a specific product catalog and avoids personal opinions.
title: Guardrails (LLM)

definition: Model steerability refers to the capability of guiding or controlling a Large Language Model's output to conform to desired characteristics, styles, or content, often to align with user intent or safety guidelines. This control can be achieved through various methods, including prompt engineering, fine-tuning, or adjusting decoding parameters.
examples: Prompting an LLM with 'Generate a cheerful, rhyming poem about nature' to control its style and topic.|Using a system prompt like 'Always respond as a polite, helpful customer service agent' to define its persona.|Adjusting the 'temperature' parameter during text generation to make the output more creative or deterministic.
title: Model Steerability

definition: LLM evaluation is the systematic process of assessing the performance, capabilities, and limitations of Large Language Models across various tasks and dimensions. It typically involves a combination of automated metrics, standardized benchmarks, and qualitative human judgment to measure aspects like accuracy, fluency, safety, and bias.
examples: Measuring an LLM's accuracy on a question-answering dataset using F1-score.|Conducting a human study to rate the coherence and relevance of summaries generated by an LLM.|Benchmarking an LLM's performance against the GLUE or SuperGLUE benchmarks.
title: LLM Evaluation

definition: Perplexity is a common intrinsic evaluation metric for language models that quantifies how well a probability model predicts a sample. It is the reciprocal of the probability of the dataset according to the model, normalized by the number of words, meaning lower perplexity indicates a better, more confident model.
examples: A language model trained on English text might achieve a perplexity of 50 on a held-out English corpus, indicating it predicts the text with a moderate level of uncertainty.|Comparing two LLMs, where one has a perplexity of 30 and another 60 on the same test set, suggests the first model is superior at predicting the natural language sequence.|An LLM with high perplexity might frequently generate grammatically incorrect or semantically nonsensical sentences.
title: Perplexity Metric

definition: ROUGE-N (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation) is an automated metric for evaluating the quality of text summaries or machine translations by comparing them against human-written reference texts. Specifically, ROUGE-N measures the overlap of N-grams (contiguous sequences of N words) between the candidate text and the reference(s).
examples: ROUGE-1 measures the overlap of unigrams (individual words). For 'the cat sat' (candidate) vs. 'the cat was big' (reference), 'the' and 'cat' are matches.|ROUGE-2 measures the overlap of bigrams (two-word sequences). For 'the cat sat' vs. 'the big cat sat', 'the cat' and 'cat sat' would be counted.|A high ROUGE-N score indicates that the generated text shares many common N-word sequences with the reference, implying good content coverage.
title: ROUGE-N

definition: ROUGE-L is a variant of the ROUGE metric family that evaluates text generation by measuring the longest common subsequence (LCS) between the candidate and reference texts. Unlike ROUGE-N, which focuses on consecutive N-grams, ROUGE-L captures sentence-level structure similarity without requiring consecutive matches, making it suitable for assessing fluency and overall content flow.
examples: Candidate: 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.' Reference: 'A quick brown fox jumps.' The LCS would be 'quick brown fox jumps', irrespective of their position in the full sentence.|If a generated summary rephrases sentences but retains the core information, ROUGE-L can still yield a good score due to shared subsequences.|A ROUGE-L score is often used in summarization tasks where exact word order is less critical than preserving main ideas.
semantic_tags: Summarization|Evaluation Metric|Longest Common Subsequence|Text Generation|Machine Translation|Reference-based
title: ROUGE-L

definition: METEOR (Metric for Evaluation of Translation with Explicit Ordering) is an evaluation metric for machine translation and text generation that aims to correlate better with human judgments than BLEU or ROUGE. It considers not only exact word matches but also stemming, synonymy (using WordNet), and paraphrasing, along with a penalty for word order differences.
examples: If a reference contains 'running' and the candidate has 'ran', METEOR will partially match them due to stemming.|If a reference uses 'car' and the candidate 'automobile', METEOR can match them as synonyms using external lexical resources.|A METEOR score of 0.3-0.5 is common for good quality machine translations, indicating a reasonable semantic and lexical overlap.
title: METEOR Score

definition: CIDEr (Consensus-based Image Description Evaluation) is a metric primarily used for evaluating the quality of image captioning models by measuring the consensus of a generated caption with a set of human-written reference captions. It calculates a TF-IDF weighted N-gram overlap between the candidate and references, giving higher importance to less frequent N-grams.
examples: Evaluating an AI system that generates 'A dog barks at a cat' for an image, against references like 'A dog barks' and 'A cat is seen', where CIDEr would assess the common elements.|A higher CIDEr score indicates that the generated caption is more descriptive and similar to human descriptions, capturing nuances of the image.|The TF-IDF weighting in CIDEr emphasizes descriptive words and phrases that distinguish a caption, reducing the impact of common words.
title: CIDEr Score

definition: BERTScore is a reference-based evaluation metric that leverages contextual embeddings from pre-trained BERT models to compute semantic similarity between candidate and reference sentences. Instead of relying on lexical overlap, it measures the cosine similarity between token embeddings, offering a more nuanced understanding of semantic equivalence in text generation tasks.
examples: BERTScore can give a high score for 'The vehicle traveled quickly' vs. 'The car went fast', as 'vehicle' and 'car' and 'traveled quickly' and 'went fast' are semantically similar in context.|Used for evaluating summarization, machine translation, and other generative NLP tasks where semantic meaning is crucial.|A BERTScore close to 1 indicates high semantic similarity between the generated text and the reference, even if word choices differ.
title: BERTScore

definition: The General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark is a collection of nine diverse natural language understanding (NLU) tasks designed to evaluate the performance of models, particularly for fine-tuning pre-trained language models. Its tasks span sentiment analysis, paraphrase detection, and natural language inference, providing a broad assessment of a model's general linguistic capabilities.
examples: **MRPC (Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus):** Determining if two given sentences are semantically equivalent.|**QNLI (Question-answering NLI):** Deciding if a statement (answer candidate) entails a question.|**SST-2 (Stanford Sentiment Treebank):** Classifying the sentiment (positive/negative) of movie review sentences.
title: GLUE Benchmark

definition: SuperGLUE is an expanded and more challenging benchmark compared to GLUE, designed to push the state-of-the-art in natural language understanding models by requiring more complex reasoning. It comprises eight tasks that often demand deeper linguistic understanding, common-sense knowledge, and multi-step inference, making it a robust test for advanced LLMs.
examples: **BoolQ:** Answering yes/no questions based on short passages, requiring textual inference.|**COPA (Choice of Plausible Alternatives):** Choosing the more plausible cause or effect from two options given a premise.|**ReCoRD (Reading Comprehension with Discontinuous Answers):** Answering questions requiring extraction from potentially multiple, non-contiguous text spans.
title: SuperGLUE Benchmark

definition: The Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) benchmark is a comprehensive evaluation suite designed to test the knowledge and reasoning abilities of LLMs across 57 diverse subjects, ranging from humanities and social sciences to STEM fields. It consists of multiple-choice questions and assesses a model's general world knowledge, problem-solving skills, and ability to handle various academic disciplines.
examples: Answering a multiple-choice question on US history, such as 'Who was the 16th president of the United States?'|Solving a chemistry problem involving balancing equations or identifying organic compounds.|Demonstrating understanding of advanced physics concepts through multi-choice questions that require reasoning.
title: MMLU Benchmark

definition: HELM (Holistic Evaluation of Language Models) is a broad and systematic framework for evaluating Large Language Models across a wide range of scenarios, metrics, and models to foster transparency. Beyond traditional accuracy, HELM assesses important aspects like fairness, robustness, efficiency, and environmental impact, providing a comprehensive view of a model's strengths and weaknesses.
examples: Comparing the carbon footprint (energy consumption) of different LLMs during inference on a specific task.|Evaluating an LLM's summarization performance while also measuring its fairness across various demographic subgroups.|Analyzing an LLM's robustness to slight input perturbations or typos by observing output consistency.
title: HELM Benchmark

definition: BIG-bench (Beyond the Imitation Game Benchmark) is a very large and diverse collaborative benchmark consisting of over 200 tasks designed to probe the current capabilities and extrapolate the future limitations of LLMs. Its tasks range from symbolic reasoning to multi-step arithmetic and often include intentionally difficult problems to challenge even the most advanced models.
examples: **Word Sorting:** Tasks requiring models to rearrange letters in a word to form another valid word.|**Casual Conversations:** Generating contextually appropriate and coherent responses in open-ended, multi-turn dialogues.|**Logical Deductions:** Solving riddles or inferring conclusions from complex premises, testing reasoning capabilities.
title: BIG-bench Benchmark

definition: Human evaluation in the context of LLMs is the process of having human annotators or experts assess the quality, correctness, safety, or other characteristics of an LLM's outputs. It is indispensable for evaluating subjective qualities like fluency, coherence, creativity, or helpfulness, which are difficult to capture with automated metrics alone.
examples: Rating the fluency, coherence, and relevance of an LLM-generated summary on a Likert scale from 1 to 5.|Asking human annotators to compare two LLM responses to a prompt and choose which one is more helpful or accurate.|Having human experts identify and flag instances of toxicity, bias, or factual errors in LLM-generated text.
title: Human Evaluation (LLM)

definition: Red teaming in LLM security is a proactive security testing methodology where a specialized team (the 'red team') intentionally attempts to find vulnerabilities, biases, and harmful capabilities in an LLM by crafting adversarial prompts and scenarios. The goal is to identify and mitigate potential risks, such as generating harmful content or misinformation, before the model is deployed.
examples: Prompting an LLM to generate instructions for illegal activities or to produce hate speech, testing its safety filters.|Attempting to 'jailbreak' an LLM to bypass its ethical guidelines and elicit private or sensitive information.|Using indirect or deceptive prompts to trigger an LLM to generate factually incorrect information or propagate stereotypes.
title: Red Teaming (LLM Security)

definition: An adversarial attack on an LLM involves making deliberate, often subtle, perturbations to the model's input (prompts) designed to cause it to produce incorrect, harmful, or unintended outputs. These attacks exploit vulnerabilities in the model's architecture or training data to bypass safety mechanisms or induce specific undesirable behaviors.
examples: Adding a few imperceptible tokens (e.g., 'Sure, here's how to...') to a benign prompt that then makes an LLM generate toxic content.|Crafting a 'jailbreak' prompt that subtly rephrases a forbidden request to circumvent an LLM's safety restrictions.|Modifying a factual question by one or two words to make the LLM provide a factually incorrect answer.
title: Adversarial Attack (LLM)

definition: Robustness in LLMs refers to the model's ability to maintain its performance and produce consistent, correct, and safe outputs despite variations, perturbations, or adversarial manipulations in its input. A robust LLM is resilient to minor changes in prompts, typos, rephrasing, or malicious attempts to provoke undesirable behavior.
examples: An LLM correctly answers a question even if the question is phrased slightly differently or contains minor grammatical errors.|The model resists generating harmful content even when faced with cleverly designed adversarial prompts attempting to bypass safety filters.|Maintaining consistent performance on a text classification task regardless of variations in sentence structure or word choice in the input.
title: Robustness (LLM)

definition: Bias detection in LLMs is the process of identifying and quantifying unwanted predispositions or prejudices in a model's behavior or outputs, often reflecting biases present in its training data. This typically involves assessing whether the LLM exhibits unfair treatment, stereotypical associations, or imbalanced representation towards certain demographic groups or concepts.
examples: Analyzing an LLM's generated text for stereotypical associations, such as consistently associating 'engineer' with 'male' pronouns.|Testing if an LLM provides different quality or types of responses based on the gender, race, or ethnicity mentioned in a prompt.|Using specific datasets designed to expose gender or racial bias in coreference resolution tasks, where the model must correctly link pronouns to their antecedents.
title: Bias Detection (LLM)

definition: Toxicity detection in LLMs is the task of identifying and classifying text that is rude, disrespectful, profane, hateful, or otherwise likely to create a negative or hostile environment. For LLMs, this often involves flagging or preventing the generation of such harmful content to ensure responsible and safe model deployment.
examples: A content moderation system using an LLM to identify user comments containing hate speech, cyberbullying, or sexual harassment.|An LLM's internal safety classifier preventing it from outputting sexually explicit, violent, or extremely offensive descriptions in response to a prompt.|Fine-tuning an LLM using filtered datasets to reduce its propensity to generate toxic or offensive language across various topics.
title: Toxicity Detection (LLM)

definition: Factuality evaluation of LLMs is the assessment of a model's ability to generate information that is factually correct, verifiable, and consistent with real-world knowledge, thereby avoiding hallucinations or misrepresentations. This evaluation is critical for applications where reliability and trustworthiness are paramount, such as knowledge retrieval, summarization, or news generation.
examples: Asking an LLM a series of factual questions about historical events or scientific principles and checking its answers against reliable sources.|Evaluating an LLM's generated summaries for accuracy, ensuring no false information or fabricated details are introduced.|Comparing claims made by an LLM about current events or specific entities to real-world data, encyclopedias, or vetted databases.
title: Factuality Evaluation (LLM)

definition: Hallucination Detection involves identifying instances where a Large Language Model (LLM) generates information that is factually incorrect, nonsensical, or contradicts the source input, despite presenting it confidently. This process is crucial for ensuring the reliability and trustworthiness of LLM outputs.
examples: Using a fact-checking API to verify claims made by an LLM in a generated news summary.|Employing a retrieve-then-generate framework where the LLM's output is cross-referenced against retrieved documents to ensure grounding.|Implementing human annotation tasks to flag portions of an LLM's text that are factually inaccurate or unsubstantiated.
title: Hallucination Detection

definition: A Truthfulness Metric is a quantitative measure used to assess the factual accuracy of an LLM's generated content, typically by comparing it against verifiable external knowledge sources, human judgments, or a predefined ground truth. It gauges the extent to which an LLM's output aligns with known facts.
examples: Calculating an F1-score on entity-level fact extraction tasks to compare extracted facts with a golden dataset.|A human evaluator rating an LLM's response on a Likert scale (e.g., 1-5) for factual correctness.|Using a specialized fact-checking model to assign a 'true' or 'false' label to claims within an LLM's output.
title: Truthfulness Metric

definition: A Consistency Metric for LLMs assesses how well a model maintains coherence and agreement within its own generated output, or with prior information, avoiding contradictions, logical fallacies, or shifts in stance. It ensures internal logical soundness and adherence to established context.
examples: Checking if an LLM's answers to follow-up questions within a dialogue do not contradict its initial responses.|Measuring the agreement between multiple generated summaries of the same document, or multiple generations from the same prompt.|Evaluating if an LLM maintains a consistent persona or tone across different segments of a long-form generation.
title: Consistency Metric (LLM)

definition: A Faithfulness Metric assesses how well an LLM's generated output, particularly in tasks like summarization or explanation, accurately reflects and is derivable from the original source text or input information. It ensures that the LLM's content is grounded in and attributable to its provided source.
examples: For a summary, checking that all factual claims made in the summary are explicitly supported by the source document.|Evaluating an LLM's explanation for a decision by verifying if the explanation exclusively uses features or information genuinely considered by the model.|Using Factual Consistency (FactCC) scores to determine if claims in a generated summary are entailed by the original article.
title: Faithfulness Metric (LLM)

definition: A Fairness Metric is a quantitative measure designed to assess and mitigate biases in an LLM's outputs, ensuring equitable treatment and representation across different demographic groups or sensitive attributes. These metrics help identify and quantify disparities in model performance or generated content.
examples: Measuring differences in sentiment analysis accuracy for reviews written by users from different gender groups.|Quantifying the prevalence of stereotypes (e.g., associating specific professions with certain genders) in text generated by an LLM.|Using metrics like Demographic Parity or Equalized Odds to compare predictive outcomes across different racial or ethnic demographics.
semantic_tags: Bias Detection|Equity|Ethical AI|Demographic Parity|Stereotype Mitigation|Algorithmic Fairness
title: Fairness Metric (LLM)

definition: An Interpretability Metric is a quantitative or qualitative measure used to assess how easily humans can understand the reasons behind an LLM's decisions, predictions, or generated outputs. It quantifies the degree of transparency and comprehensibility of a model's internal workings or explanations.
examples: Human rating of the clarity and informativeness of saliency maps or attention visualizations that highlight influential input tokens.|Measuring the complexity of decision rules or feature importance scores extracted from an LLM by a post-hoc explainability method.|Evaluating how well users can predict an LLM's output when provided with a simplified explanation of its internal logic.
title: Interpretability Metric (LLM)

definition: Explainable AI (XAI) for LLMs is a field focused on developing methods and techniques to make the decision-making processes and outputs of large language models understandable and transparent to humans. It aims to build trust, facilitate debugging, and ensure ethical deployment of LLMs.
examples: Applying LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) to explain why an LLM classified a specific text input into a particular category.|Using SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values to attribute the contribution of each input token to an LLM's generated output.|Visualizing attention weights in a transformer model to show which parts of the input an LLM focused on when generating a response.
title: Explainable AI (XAI for LLM)

definition: A Model Card is a standardized document providing crucial metadata and responsible AI considerations for a trained machine learning model, including its intended use, limitations, ethical implications, and evaluation results. It serves as a transparency and accountability tool for model developers and users.
examples: A PDF document accompanying a released LLM, detailing its training data sources, known biases, and performance metrics across various benchmarks.|A digital 'readme' file for an open-source model, explaining its proper usage, potential risks, and the methodology used for its evaluation.|Google's Model Card Toolkit assisting developers in generating comprehensive model cards for their LLMs.
title: Model Card

definition: A Dataset Card is a standardized document providing essential metadata and responsible AI considerations for a dataset, detailing its creation, composition, collection methodology, potential biases, and recommended uses. It enhances transparency and helps users understand the dataset's characteristics and limitations.
examples: A document accompanying a text corpus, describing its language, domain, demographic distribution of speakers, and the process of data collection and cleaning.|A 'readme' file for a benchmark dataset, outlining its licensing, potential biases found during analysis, and appropriate research applications.|The Hugging Face `datasets` library often integrates dataset cards to provide comprehensive information about each available dataset.
title: Dataset Card

definition: Calibration in LLMs refers to the process of ensuring that the model's predicted probabilities or confidence scores accurately reflect the true likelihood of an event occurring, rather than being overconfident or underconfident. A well-calibrated LLM assigns a probability of P to outcomes that truly occur P% of the time.
examples: If an LLM assigns a 90% probability to a generated fact being correct, that fact should actually be correct 90% of the time over many samples.|Adjusting an LLM's output probabilities using techniques like Platt scaling or isotonic regression to align them with empirical frequencies.|Evaluating calibration using reliability diagrams, which plot predicted probability against the observed frequency of correct predictions.
title: Calibration (LLM)

definition: Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) for LLMs is the systematic process of identifying, characterizing, and quantifying the various sources of uncertainty associated with a model's predictions or generated outputs. It provides measures of confidence or doubt in the LLM's responses.
examples: Using techniques like Monte Carlo dropout or ensembling multiple LLM outputs to estimate the predictive variance of a response.|Employing Bayesian neural networks to output probability distributions over predictions, rather than single point estimates, indicating model confidence.|Measuring the entropy of an LLM's output token distribution, where higher entropy suggests greater uncertainty in the next predicted token.
title: Uncertainty Quantification (LLM)

definition: Text Generation is the task where a Large Language Model (LLM) produces human-readable text based on a given prompt, context, or set of parameters. This core capability enables a wide range of applications from creative writing to factual reporting and conversational AI.
examples: Writing a short story or poem given a theme and starting sentence.|Completing a sentence or paragraph in an email draft.|Generating a product description from a list of features.
semantic_tags: Natural Language Generation (NLG)|Creative Writing|Content Creation|Conditional Generation|Language Modeling|Prompt Engineering
title: Text Generation (LLM)

definition: Code Generation is a specialized form of text generation where an LLM produces source code in various programming languages, often based on natural language descriptions, existing code snippets, or API specifications. It automates parts of the software development process.
examples: Generating a Python function to sort a list of numbers from a natural language prompt like 'write a function to sort a list'.|Autocompleting lines of code within an Integrated Development Environment (IDE) based on context.|Translating pseudocode or design specifications into functional program code in a language like Java or C++.
semantic_tags: Programming Assistance|Software Development|Code Completion|Semantic Parsing|Low-code/No-code|Developer Tools
title: Code Generation (LLM)

definition: Summarization is the task where a Large Language Model (LLM) condenses a longer input text into a shorter, coherent, and informative summary while preserving the most important information. It aims to provide an overview or extract key points efficiently.
examples: Creating a concise abstract for a lengthy research paper or scientific article.|Summarizing a long news article into a few sentences for a news brief.|Generating bullet-point summaries of meeting transcripts or audio recordings.
title: Summarization (LLM)

definition: Abstractive Summarization is a type of summarization where an LLM generates new phrases and sentences, often paraphrasing or reinterpreting the source text, to create a concise summary that may not contain exact sentences from the original document. This approach requires deeper semantic understanding and natural language generation capabilities.
examples: An LLM reading a news article and writing a completely new headline and lead paragraph that captures the main idea using novel phrasing.|Google's 'Squeeze' feature providing a summary of a webpage that uses new vocabulary and sentence structures not directly present in the original.|Generating a summary of a complex legal document using simpler, more accessible language for a lay audience.
semantic_tags: Paraphrasing|Natural Language Generation|Semantic Understanding|Rephrasing|Advanced Summarization|Creative Summarization
title: Abstractive Summarization

definition: Extractive Summarization is a type of summarization where an LLM identifies and extracts the most important sentences or phrases directly from the original source text to form a summary without generating new content. The summary is thus composed entirely of verbatim segments of the input.
examples: Highlighting key sentences in a long document to form a summary, such as in many 'smart' document readers.|Creating a summary by concatenating the top-ranked sentences from an article based on their importance scores, like in early text summarizers.|A simple algorithm selecting the first and last sentences of each paragraph as a summary.
semantic_tags: Sentence Selection|Information Retrieval|Keyphrase Extraction|Document Ranking|Direct Extraction|Simpler Summarization
title: Extractive Summarization

definition: Machine Translation (MT) with LLMs is the task where a model automatically converts text or speech from one natural language into another, aiming to preserve meaning, context, and fluency. LLMs have significantly advanced MT by learning complex linguistic patterns across languages.
examples: Translating a website from English to Spanish in real-time.|Real-time translation of a spoken conversation between two different language speakers.|Translating a research paper from German to English while maintaining scientific terminology and style.
semantic_tags: Cross-lingual|Language Conversion|Multilingual|Natural Language Processing (NLP)|Neural Machine Translation|Language Barrier
title: Machine Translation (LLM)

definition: Question Answering (QA) with LLMs is the task where a model receives a question in natural language and provides an accurate and relevant answer, often by retrieving information from a given text or its vast internal knowledge base. It demonstrates an LLM's comprehension and information retrieval abilities.
examples: Asking an LLM 'What is the capital of France?' and receiving 'Paris' as the answer.|Providing a paragraph about a historical event and asking 'Who was the main figure involved in this event?'|Using an LLM as a chatbot to answer user queries by searching through a company's product knowledge base.
semantic_tags: Information Retrieval|Text Comprehension|Knowledge Base|Dialogue Systems|Query Processing|Factoid QA
title: Question Answering (LLM)

definition: Open-Domain Question Answering (QA) is a type of Question Answering where an LLM can answer questions spanning a broad range of topics without being restricted to a specific document or knowledge source. It relies on the LLM's vast pre-trained knowledge or its ability to search and synthesize information from external, unstructured sources like the internet.
examples: Asking an LLM a general knowledge question like 'Who invented the light bulb?' without providing any context document.|A search engine's answer box that directly provides factual answers to broad questions by querying the entire web.|A conversational AI assistant answering varied questions about history, science, and current events interchangeably.
semantic_tags: General Knowledge|Broad Scope|Information Retrieval|Web Search|Unrestricted QA|Knowledge Synthesis
title: Open-Domain Question Answering

definition: Closed-Domain Question Answering (QA) is a type of Question Answering where an LLM is constrained to answer questions using information exclusively from a predefined, limited set of documents or a specific knowledge base. This focuses the model on a narrow topic and often leads to higher accuracy within that domain.
examples: An LLM answering questions solely from a single provided Wikipedia article about a specific historical figure.|A customer support chatbot answering questions strictly about a company's product manual or FAQ document.|A legal AI system answering queries exclusively based on a curated collection of legal statutes and case precedents.
semantic_tags: Specific Context|Limited Scope|Document Understanding|Factual Extraction|Focused QA|Domain-Specific Knowledge
title: Closed-Domain Question Answering

definition: The process of automatically identifying and extracting structured information from unstructured text data using LLMs, such as entities, relationships, and events. LLMs can achieve this by understanding context and patterns within the text, often performing tasks like summarization or data structuring.
examples: Extracting product names, prices, and quantities from customer reviews.|Identifying dates, locations, and participants from news articles about an event.|Parsing medical reports to pull out patient demographics, diagnoses, and treatments.
semantic_tags: Structured Data|Unstructured Text|Data Extraction|Entity Recognition|Relationship Extraction|NLP
title: Information Extraction (LLM)

definition: A specific subtask of information extraction where an LLM identifies and classifies named entities in text into predefined categories like persons, organizations, locations, dates, and more. LLMs leverage their vast knowledge and contextual understanding for high accuracy in pinpointing these key pieces of information.
examples: Identifying "Apple Inc." as an organization, "Tim Cook" as a person, and "Cupertino" as a location in a press release.|Detecting "July 4th, 1776" as a date and "Independence Hall" as a location in a historical document.|Extracting drug names and medical conditions from clinical notes.
title: Named Entity Recognition (LLM)

definition: The use of LLMs to determine the emotional tone or overall sentiment (e.g., positive, negative, neutral) expressed in a piece of text. LLMs excel at this by understanding nuances, sarcasm, and complex contextual cues within human language.
examples: Classifying customer reviews for a product as positive or negative to gauge satisfaction.|Analyzing social media posts about a brand to understand public perception.|Detecting the emotional tone in email communications to prioritize urgent customer service requests.
semantic_tags: Opinion Mining|Emotion Detection|Text Classification|NLP|Customer Feedback|Affective Computing
title: Sentiment Analysis (LLM)

definition: An AI program, often powered by an LLM, designed to simulate human conversation through text or voice. LLM-based chatbots can understand natural language queries, maintain context, and generate human-like, coherent responses across a wide range of topics or specific domains.
examples: A customer service bot answering FAQs and guiding users through troubleshooting steps.|A virtual assistant helping users schedule appointments or find information.|An interactive companion for casual conversation and entertainment.
semantic_tags: Conversational AI|Virtual Assistant|Dialogue System|Customer Service|Natural Language Understanding|Text Generation
title: Chatbot (LLM)

definition: A broader field encompassing technologies that enable machines to understand, process, and respond to human language in a natural, conversational manner, with LLMs being a core component. It involves more than just response generation, integrating dialogue management, context tracking, and intent recognition to facilitate complex human-computer interactions.
examples: Building a multi-turn dialogue system for booking travel, where the AI remembers previous preferences.|Developing an intelligent virtual assistant that can seamlessly switch between tasks and topics.|Creating an AI tutor that can engage in Socratic dialogue to help students learn.
semantic_tags: Natural Language Understanding|Dialogue Management|Human-Computer Interaction|Chatbot|Virtual Assistant|NLG
title: Conversational AI (LLM)

definition: The ability of an LLM to derive conclusions, make inferences, and logically connect information based on its training data and the given prompt. This often involves processing complex relationships, understanding implications, and generating coherent thought processes that go beyond simple fact retrieval.
examples: Answering "why" or "how" questions that require more than direct fact retrieval.|Summarizing a legal document by identifying the core arguments and their interconnections.|Explaining a scientific concept by breaking it down into its constituent parts and their logical flow.
title: Reasoning (LLM)

definition: A specific form of reasoning where an LLM applies formal rules of logic (e.g., deductive, inductive) to premises to reach valid conclusions. This involves identifying patterns, ensuring consistency, and following structured argument chains within the text or data, often requiring precise understanding of implications.
examples: Solving symbolic logic problems or syllogisms (e.g., "All A are B, C is A, therefore C is B").|Debugging code by logically tracing potential error points based on provided symptoms.|Analyzing contractual clauses to identify contradictions or implications.
title: Logical Reasoning (LLM)

definition: The capacity of an LLM to make inferences and understand situations based on a broad, intuitive understanding of the world, similar to human common sense. This involves drawing on implicit knowledge about everyday objects, actions, and social dynamics not explicitly stated in the text.
examples: Answering "If I put a book on a shelf, what happens?" (It stays there, it doesn't float away).|Resolving ambiguities in text where meaning depends on real-world knowledge (e.g., "The city council refused the demonstrators a permit because they feared violence." - Who feared violence?).|Explaining why a particular action in a story is unusual or expected based on typical human behavior.
title: Common Sense Reasoning (LLM)

definition: The application of LLMs to analyze a given problem, break it down into manageable steps, formulate strategies, and generate potential solutions. This often involves combining reasoning, knowledge retrieval, and creative generation capabilities to address complex challenges.
examples: Generating code to solve a programming challenge described in natural language.|Providing step-by-step instructions to fix a common household appliance issue.|Brainstorming multiple approaches to a business strategy problem or design challenge.
semantic_tags: Algorithmic Thinking|Heuristics|Strategy Generation|Solution Generation|Critical Thinking|Decision Making
title: Problem Solving (LLM)

definition: The use of LLMs to generate original and imaginative text, such as stories, poems, scripts, or marketing copy, demonstrating stylistic flair and coherence. LLMs leverage their vast training data to mimic human creativity, adapting to various genres, tones, and artistic constraints.
examples: Drafting a short story based on a few prompt words (e.g., "a lonely lighthouse, a stormy night, a forgotten secret").|Composing a sonnet in the style of Shakespeare or a modern free-verse poem.|Generating advertising slogans or jingles for a new product, tailored to a specific audience.
title: Creative Writing (LLM)

definition: A search paradigm powered by LLMs that understands the contextual meaning and intent behind a user's query, rather than just matching keywords. It retrieves results that are semantically relevant, even if they don't contain the exact terms from the query, leading to more accurate and comprehensive information retrieval.
examples: Searching for "ways to stay healthy" and getting results about exercise, diet, and mental well-being, not just pages with the word "healthy."|Querying a document database with "financial implications of Brexit" and finding reports that discuss the economic impact on the UK.|Finding images or videos related to a concept like "joy" rather than just the literal word.
semantic_tags: Vector Search|Contextual Search|Natural Language Understanding|Information Retrieval|Query Understanding|Meaning-based Search
title: Semantic Search (LLM)

definition: The ability of an LLM to understand natural language queries and translate them into structured database commands (e.g., SQL, NoSQL queries) to retrieve, update, or analyze data. It can also interpret complex database results back into human-readable language, effectively serving as a natural language interface for data management.
examples: A user asking "Show me all customers who spent more than $500 last month" and the LLM generating the corresponding SQL query.|An LLM parsing a CSV or JSON file to extract specific data points based on a natural language instruction.|Generating a summary report from a database by querying and aggregating data according to natural language criteria.
semantic_tags: NL2SQL|Data Query|Structured Data|Data Retrieval|Natural Language Interface|Database Management
title: Database Interaction (LLM)

definition: The use of LLMs to interpret high-level natural language instructions from humans and translate them into low-level executable commands for robots. This enables more intuitive human-robot interaction and facilitates complex task execution without explicit, pre-programmed robotic movements.
examples: Telling a robot arm "Pick up the red block and place it on the top shelf" and the LLM translates this into precise joint movements.|An LLM generating a sequence of actions for a mobile robot to navigate a room and find an object.|A human giving abstract goals like "Clean the kitchen" and the LLM decomposing it into sub-tasks for a robot vacuum and robotic arm.
semantic_tags: Human-Robot Interaction|Task Planning|Action Generation|Embodied AI|Natural Language to Action|Automation
title: Robotics Control (LLM)

definition: A Large Language Model trained to process and generate information across multiple modalities, such as text, images, audio, and video. It integrates diverse data types, allowing for a more holistic understanding and interaction with the world than text-only models, enabling cross-modal reasoning and generation.
examples: Answering questions about an image by analyzing both the visual content and textual context.|Generating a caption for a video clip that accurately describes the visual and auditory events.|Creating a short animation or 3D scene from a detailed text description.
title: Multimodal LLM

definition: A type of Multimodal LLM specifically designed to understand and relate information between visual (images, video) and textual modalities. VLMs can perform tasks like image captioning, visual question answering, and text-guided image generation by learning shared representations across these two domains.
examples: Given an image of a cat playing with yarn, generate the caption: "A cat playfully batting at a ball of yarn."|Answering the question "What color is the car?" after being shown a picture of a red car.|Searching for images by describing them in natural language (e.g., "a serene landscape with mountains and a lake").
